# Earth History

## Hadean Eon

Earth began as dust. A supernova seeded a dense corner of the Milky Way with heavy elements, a hydrogen cloud collapsed into the Sun, and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies until one of them was our planet. Then came violence: iron sank to the core, a Mars-sized body called Theia struck, and a magma ocean about 200 km deep covered the surface. Yet zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 billion years ago, astonishingly soon after Earth formed. This first eon is the story of how a molten ball became a world with seas.

- **A dying star seeds the Sun's birth cloud** — c. 4.57 billion years ago (4,570 Ma)

  Some of the atoms in Earth were forged in a star that exploded before the Sun existed. A supernova, the blast of a dying star, sent a shock wave through a dense part of the Milky Way and seeded it with heavy elements. That same shock wave may have triggered the collapse of the solar nebula, the gas cloud that became the Solar System, and set it spinning. Its signature survives in calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions, specks that formed 2 million years before chondrules.

  <!-- hade-001 -->

- **The Sun ignites and the Solar System begins** — 4.57 billion years ago (4,567.3 ± 0.16 Ma)

  Every date in Earth's history is counted from a handful of tiny white specks. About 25,000 light years from the center of the Milky Way, a hydrogen cloud collapsed rapidly and gave birth to the Sun. The spinning cloud flattened into a protoplanetary disk, a pancake of gas and dust circling the young T Tauri Sun, and it held the raw material of Earth. The first solids to condense from that hot disk were calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions. They date to 4,567.30 ± 0.16 million years ago, and that age defines the start of the Solar System and of the Hadean Eon. The young Sun did not wait long to tidy up. Its solar wind blew away most of the disk material not yet gathered into larger bodies, and by 10 million years the gas was gone. The star at the center was not yet the Sun we know. It has grown about 30% brighter since it formed, a slow change that shapes the puzzle of Why the early Earth did not freeze.

  <!-- hade-002 -->

  *Figure: The steps from a collapsing gas cloud to a cleared disc around the young Sun.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Hydrogen cloud collapses] --> B[Sun forms]
  A --> C[Cloud flattens into disc]
  C --> D[First solids condense]
  B --> E[Solar wind clears disc]
  C --> E
  ```

- **The iron catastrophe gives Earth its core** — during the Hadean, 4.57–4.03 billion years ago (4,567–4,031 Ma)

  Earth's magnetic shield was born when a planet's worth of metal fell inward. Radioactive heating and heat left from accretion melted the young Earth enough for metal to move. Dense iron and nickel then sank to the center, and the sinking itself released energy, driving a runaway process called the iron catastrophe. It was geologically brief, though still a postulated event. The result was Earth's layered structure: a metallic core, where siderophile, or iron-loving, metals gathered, beneath a primitive mantle and, later, a crust. The spinning molten metal set up the magnetic field that still shields the atmosphere and life from the solar wind. When it happened is uncertain. Hafnium–tungsten models give 30–100 million years after the first solids; other sources say 10 or about 500 million years in.

  <!-- hade-003 -->

  *Figure: How heat let iron sink and split Earth into layers.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Radioactive and accretion heat] --> B[Planet partly melts]
  B --> C[Iron and nickel sink]
  C --> D[Metallic core]
  C --> E[Primitive mantle]
  ```

- **Did plates already move in the Hadean?** — during the Hadean, 4.57–4.03 billion years ago (4,567–4,031 Ma)

  The young mantle churned hard. Radiogenic heat and trapped water lowered its viscosity, so Hadean convection was vigorous. Whether that motion drove plate tectonics or stayed trapped under a rigid lid is still debated. Some point to the removal of the CO2-rich early atmosphere, helped by carbonate sinking at subduction zones, as evidence for Hadean plates. Critics note the zircon evidence comes almost entirely from one Australian locality. One major paper argues global plate tectonics began only about 3.0 billion years ago, in the Archean.

  <!-- hade-004 -->

- **Earth assembles from colliding debris** — c. 4.54 billion years ago (4,540 ± 50 Ma)

  A day on the newborn Earth lasted only about six hours. The planet had just been built by collision. In runaway accretion, dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies, and the bigger a body grew, the faster it swept up more. The proto-Earth took shape at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone, the band around a star where liquid water can exist. It grew through a series of giant impacts. The work was fast. Accretion began soon after the first solids formed in The Sun ignites and the Solar System begins and was largely complete within 10–20 million years. One estimate allows 70–100 million years, while 2023 evidence suggests only about three million. Earth's official age, 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years, marks the final stages of accretion and differentiation, the sorting of the planet into layers. The fast spin was a leftover of all those collisions, and it would not last.

  <!-- hade-005 -->

  *Figure: Runaway accretion built Earth from dust through ever larger bodies.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Dust and debris] --> B[Larger bodies]
  B --> C[Giant impacts]
  C --> D[Earth]
  ```

- **A magma ocean covers the young Earth** — c. 4.53 billion years ago (4,533 Ma)

  For a time, Earth had no ground at all. Giant impacts and the heat of forming the core melted its outer layers into a magma ocean, a global sea of molten rock about 200 km deep. There were probably several such oceans. The last, raised by Theia strikes and the Moon is born, may have reached 2,000 km down, and siderophile elements in the mantle record depths of about 1,000 km during accretion. The first magma ocean solidified within about 5 million years. Hot volatiles it left behind formed a heavy carbon dioxide atmosphere. The evidence is weaker than on the Moon, because Earth recycles its crust and mixes its mantle. Sources also disagree: one cites chemical traces, another finds no evidence Earth ever had one.

  <!-- hade-006 -->

  *Figure: Estimates of magma-ocean depth grow with the size of the impact behind them.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Why the early Earth did not freeze** — c. 4.5 billion years ago (4,500 Ma)

  By rights, the young Earth should have been a snowball. The young Sun gave only about 70% of today's output, yet Earth seems to have had liquid water and life. How it stayed warm is an unsolved problem. The favored answer is a greenhouse. Models find that 4.5 billion years ago, under a 30% dimmer Sun, staying above freezing took at least 0.1 bar of carbon dioxide. A plausible upper limit is 10 bar. A natural thermostat may have helped: in the carbonate–silicate cycle, cold slows the weathering of rock, so carbon dioxide builds up. How much there really was is still debated, and other proposals include a darker, less reflective surface and mass loss from the young Sun. The Sun has brightened ever since and now shines 1.4 times as bright as 4.6 billion years ago.

  <!-- hade-007 -->

  *Figure: The carbonate–silicate cycle works as a thermostat: cold lets carbon dioxide build up and warm the planet.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cold climate] --> B[Slower rock weathering]
  B --> C[Less CO2 removed]
  C --> D[CO2 builds up in air]
  D --> E[Stronger greenhouse]
  E -.->|warms| A
  ```

- **Theia strikes and the Moon is born** — c. 4.5 billion years ago (4,500 Ma)

  The Moon is the wreckage of a planetary collision. In the explanation most astronomers favor, a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia struck the proto-Earth about 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed. The blow probably vaporized much of Earth's crust and upper mantle. The planet was wrapped in rock vapor, and any water already present was disrupted. Debris thrown into orbit lingered as rings for a few million years, then gathered into the Moon. Lunar rocks date it to 4.53 ± 0.01 billion years. The impact also reshaped Earth for good. It fed the last and deepest of the A magma ocean covers the young Earth episodes, and it stripped away the planet's first atmosphere. Over the long run, the Moon's pull steadied Earth's wobbling axis of rotation. That steadiness made the climate more regular, a quiet gift to everything that would later live here.

  <!-- hade-008 -->

  *Figure: The chain from Theia's impact to the Moon and a steadier Earth.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Theia strikes proto-Earth] --> B[Debris thrown into orbit]
  A --> R[Crust vaporized]
  B --> C[Rings for a few million years]
  C --> D[Moon gathers]
  D --> E[Earth's axis steadied]
  E --> F[More regular climate]
  ```

- **The Moon grows a pale crust** — c. 4.45 billion years ago (4,450 Ma)

  The bright patches on the Moon are its oldest skin. About 100 million years after the Moon formed, light plagioclase crystals floated up through its magma ocean, which was at first 200–300 km thick. They built the first crust, made of anorthosite, a pale rock dominated by that mineral. Ferroan anorthosites date to about 4.4 billion years ago, and anorthosite still forms the lunar highlands, about 80% of the Moon's surface.

  <!-- hade-009 -->

- **Earth's first oceans condense** — c. 4.4 billion years ago (4,404 ± 8 Ma)

  Earth had oceans almost as soon as it had a surface. Zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 ± 0.008 billion years ago, very soon after the planet formed. As the crust and surface cooled, water vapor condensed into a superocean that covered nearly the whole planet. Earth may have been mostly a water world between 4.4 and 4.3 billion years ago. The seas were hot, yet they stayed liquid, because the air pressed down at about 27 atmospheres and high pressure keeps water from boiling. Where did the water come from? Most likely from the mantle itself, released by outgassing. Isotopes, versions of an element that differ slightly in weight, make comets an unlikely main source. The water was not the clear sea of today. Dissolved carbon dioxide probably made it slightly acidic, about pH 5.5. Still, these were the oceans where life would later begin.

  <!-- hade-010 -->

  *Figure: Cooling turned water vapor into a global ocean.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Mantle outgassing] --> B[Water vapor]
  B --> C[Crust cools]
  C --> D[Vapor condenses]
  D --> E[Superocean]
  ```

- **A Jack Hills zircon, the oldest mineral on Earth** — 4.4 billion years ago (4,404 ± 8 Ma)

  The oldest piece of Earth anyone has dated is a grain of sand. It is a zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, 4.404 ± 0.008 billion years old. It sits in a conglomerate, a rock of cemented pebbles, in the Narryer Gneiss terrane, and most zircons there are only 3.6–3.8 billion years old. Even the record grain is a slight outlier; the oldest consistently dated zircons are closer to 4.35 billion years. Hadean zircons crystallized at fairly low temperatures from evolved melts and carry heavy oxygen, hinting at crust-forming processes like today's. They are rare worldwide because plate tectonics recycled the crust that held them.

  <!-- hade-011 -->

- **A second, carbon dioxide atmosphere** — c. 4.4 billion years ago (4,404 Ma)

  Earth lost its first sky in a single blow. Early Hadean Earth had a very thick atmosphere rich in hydrides, hydrogen compounds like those of the solar nebula, and the Moon-forming impact stripped it away. A second atmosphere rose from below. The cooling magma ocean released carbon dioxide and water, building a heavy CO2 atmosphere at about 230 °C and more than 27 atmospheres of pressure. Outgassing from the crust had built it by 4,404 million years ago at the latest. Comets and carbonaceous chondrites added water and possibly organic molecules. Over time, volcanic outgassing and impacts turned this air into the nitrogen- and CO2-rich, weakly reducing atmosphere of the Paleoarchean.

  <!-- hade-012 -->

  *Figure: Earth's air was replaced twice in the Hadean and early Archean.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Thick hydride-rich first atmosphere] -->|Moon-forming impact strips it| B[Magma ocean outgasses]
  B --> C[Heavy CO2 and water atmosphere]
  E[Comets add water] -.-> C
  C -->|volcanoes and impacts| D[Nitrogen- and CO2-rich Paleoarchean air]
  ```

- **Earth's first solid crust** — c. 4.4 billion years ago (4,400 Ma)

  Only crumbs survive of Earth's first crust. Zircons formed 4.4 billion years ago show that the crust solidified about 100 million years after the planet formed. One source puts a stable crust in place by 4,433 million years ago. It formed as the molten outer layer cooled, probably much like the Moon's first crust, from similar materials separating out of the magma. It was probably mafic, dark rock rich in iron and magnesium. Partial melting of it then made the first, more felsic continental crust, paler and richer in silica. Hafnium isotopes in zircons fit crust forming from 4.5 billion years ago onward. Yet only mineral grains remain; the oldest whole rock formations at the surface are Archean.

  <!-- hade-014 -->

- **A cool early Earth, and a paradox** — c. 4.4–4.0 billion years ago (4,400–4,000 Ma)

  Could the Hadean have been frozen? The cool early Earth hypothesis holds that temperatures were cold enough to freeze water between about 4.4 and 4.0 billion years ago. Its own source calls this somewhat of a paradox, since zircons show liquid water by 4.404 billion years ago. Another view allows a possible cool period within a Hadean otherwise dominated by bombardment. The question remains open.

  <!-- hade-013 -->

- **The last impact that boiled the oceans** — c. 4.3 billion years ago (4,300 Ma)

  Before about 4.3–4.2 billion years ago, Earth was very hostile to life. Impacts were the reason. They declined over time, and the last one big enough to vaporize the oceans struck about 4.3 billion years ago. Life probably emerged only after it. Later Hadean impacts came thousands to millions of years apart, but any young life stayed vulnerable to the largest of them.

  <!-- hade-015 -->

- **Possible microfossils in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt** — c. 4.28–3.77 billion years ago (4,280–3,770 Ma)

  Tiny structures in an ancient seabed in Quebec might be the oldest life on Earth, or nothing alive at all. They lie in hydrothermal-vent deposits of the Nuvvuagittuq Belt, dated anywhere from 3.77 to 4.28 billion years ago. At 4.28 billion years, they would suggest life emerged almost at once, in geological terms, after the oceans formed. But silica-rich waters, chemical gardens, hot fluids and volcanic debris can mimic such shapes, and the rocks' age is itself disputed.

  <!-- hade-016 -->

- **Light carbon in Jack Hills zircons** — c. 4.25 billion years ago (4,250 Ma)

  Living things prefer the lighter form of carbon, so light carbon can be a fingerprint of life. Jack Hills zircons in Western Australia, dated to 4.25 billion years, hold unusually light carbon isotopes in tiny pieces of diamond and graphite trapped inside them. The signal is far from settled. Studies in 2005, 2006 and 2009 found no light carbon of the kind behind earlier claims of Hadean life, and a biological origin is unproven.

  <!-- hade-017 -->

- **Hadean zircons in Guyana and Brazil** — c. 4.22 billion years ago (4,220 Ma)

  Old crust can hide inside younger rock. Zircon cores from the Iwokrama Formation of southern Guyana, in the Guiana Shield, have been dated to 4.22 billion years by uranium–lead laser analysis. Eastern Brazil has also yielded 4.22-billion-year-old material, rich in uranium and born from felsic magma. Hadean grains inside younger rocks show that those rocks formed on older crust and swallowed some of it.

  <!-- hade-018 -->

- **Hadean granite beneath the Acasta Gneiss** — c. 4.2 billion years ago (4,200 Ma)

  Some of Canada's oldest rocks are recycled. The Acasta gneisses of the Slave Craton are 3.94 billion years old. Yet they hold zircon xenocrysts, foreign crystals carried in from older rock, that date to 4.2 billion years. The gneisses partly derive from that older granite magma, so early crust was already being melted and reworked. Zircons from the granite resemble Western Australia's Yilgarn zircons and may record Hadean continental crust.

  <!-- hade-020 -->

- **LUCA, the ancestor of all life** — c. 4.2 billion years ago (4,200 Ma)

  Every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales, shares one ancestor: LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. A 2024 study put it at about 4.2 billion years ago, within a range of 4.33–4.09 billion. That date comes from a molecular clock, which counts genetic changes to time branches in the tree of life, not from any fossil. If it is right, only about 100–200 million years separated life's origin from LUCA, since the first habitable environments likely formed around 4.3–4.4 billion years ago. A 2018 study likewise placed LUCA before the Late Heavy Bombardment, over 3.9 billion years ago. Other estimates run from 4.52–4.48 billion down to 3.8–3.5 billion years ago. Most agree LUCA existed by 3.5 billion years ago.

  <!-- hade-021 -->

  *Figure: Different molecular-clock studies place LUCA anywhere across a billion-year window.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **How much continent did the Hadean have?** — c. 4.2–4.0 billion years ago (4,200–4,000 Ma)

  Nobody agrees how much land the Hadean held. In some models a global ocean covered Earth. Models by Korenaga and colleagues go to the other extreme, with continental crust reaching today's volume between 4.2 and 4.0 billion years ago. Dhuime and colleagues estimate only 25% of today's continental area by the end of the eon. The estimates rest on disputed models of early tectonics. Small proto-continents are generally thought to have existed before 4,280 million years ago. Continents may even have appeared in the mid-Hadean, then vanished beneath a thick ocean by the eon's end.

  <!-- hade-019 -->

- **Nuvvuagittuq, perhaps Earth's oldest rock** — 4.16 billion years ago (4,157 Ma)

  A single dated dike sets the floor for one of Earth's oldest rock bodies. The dike, a sheet of gabbro that once cut through Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt as magma, dates to 4,157 million years, so the dark rocks it crosses are older. A 2012 samarium–neodymium study gave the belt 4,321 million years, which would make it Earth's oldest known rock. Other studies accept only a minimum of 3.75 billion years and argue the older signal was inherited from melted Hadean crust.

  <!-- hade-022 -->

- **How and where life may have begun** — c. 4.1 billion years ago (4,100 Ma)

  No one knows when life began, and the sources call the evidence for Hadean life controversial. The geologic record puts its emergence most likely between 4.32 and 3.48 billion years ago. Geochemical evidence suggests possibly as early as 4.1 billion, and some models propose nearly 4.5 billion. Two settings lead the list. Hot springs on volcanic land, common in the Hadean, may have let RNA, a molecule that can carry genetic information, form and copy itself. Evidence suggests the first RNA molecules formed before 4.17 billion years ago. Alternatively, life began in hydrothermal vents, shielded from impacts and ultraviolet light, perhaps as early as 4.4 billion years ago. A deep-vent origin would allow 4.0–4.2 billion.

  <!-- hade-024 -->

- **Possible life-made carbon in a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon** — c. 4.1 billion years ago (4,100 Ma)

  A speck of carbon in a single crystal may be the oldest trace of life on Earth. It sits in 4.1-billion-year-old zircon from Western Australia, and it may be the remains of living things. Such carbon-isotope anomalies are chemical fossils: no shapes, only a chemical signature. The evidence is preliminary and still needs confirmation, and the carbon may not be biological at all.

  <!-- hade-025 -->

- **The Late Heavy Bombardment, real or imagined** — c. 4.1–3.8 billion years ago (4,100–3,800 Ma)

  The Moon's battered face may record a storm that also hit Earth. Crater counts suggest intense impacts from about 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, cratering the Moon and, by inference, Earth, Mercury, Venus and Mars. The main evidence is a cluster of ages, about 3.8 to 4.1 billion years, in impact-melted rock brought back by Apollo. Most samples came from near the Imbrium Basin. Once widely accepted, the idea is now debated. Critics see the cluster as debris from one large impact, and some evidence favors bombardment spread from 4.2 to 3.5 billion years ago. If there was a spike, Neptune migrating outward may have caused it. Either way, life most likely survived the barrage, and the heat of hydrothermal systems may even have helped it begin.

  <!-- hade-023 -->

## Archean Eon

The Archean is the eon of the oldest rocks that still stand intact. Zircons in Canada's Acasta Gneiss crystallized about 4.03 billion years ago, and Greenland's Isua belt holds the oldest known banded iron formations. Around 3,800 million years ago the first cratons, whole continental masses built of granite blocks, appeared. Over this stretch the carbon cycle took its basic form, the last great impacts faded, and life left its first faint chemical traces.

### Eoarchean Era

The Eoarchean opens with Earth's oldest known felsic crust, the Acasta Gneiss, about 4.03 billion years old. Impacts stayed frequent, with the final phase of the Late Heavy Bombardment placed at about 3,920–3,850 million years ago. Meanwhile the first cratons began to form: the Pilbara of Western Australia, the Yangtze Block of South China, the first rocks of the East European Craton. In Greenland, graphite low in carbon-13 and the oldest banded iron formations hint that life may already have been at work.

- **The Acasta Gneiss, Earth's oldest intact rock** — 4.03 billion years ago (4,031 ± 3 Ma)

  On a remote river in Canada's Northwest Territories sits the oldest intact rock on Earth. Zircons in the Acasta Gneiss Complex crystallized about 4.03 billion years ago. As of 2026 these beds are Earth's oldest known felsic crust, the pale, silica-rich rock of continents. The rock is so important that it sets the calendar. The International Commission on Stratigraphy starts the Archean Eon at 4,031 ± 3 million years ago, the age of the oldest known intact rock formations. The gneiss belongs to the Slave Craton and records more than a billion years of melting and remaking, from over 4.0 to 2.9 billion years ago. Its tonalites, from about 4.0 billion years ago, are among the first larger pieces of continental crust. They formed from light rock that rose during partial melting. Even older crust is hidden inside: 3.94-billion-year-old gneisses partly derive from the 4.2-billion-year-old granite of Hadean granite beneath the Acasta Gneiss. Crust was already being reworked at the very start of the Archean.

  <!-- arch-001 -->

  *Figure: Dates recorded in the Acasta Gneiss, from its parent magma to its youngest rocks.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The carbon cycle takes its basic form** — c. 4 billion years ago (4,000 Ma)

  Carbon was moving around Earth in familiar ways four billion years ago. Early carbon isotope ratios closely match today's, suggesting the carbon cycle's fundamental features were established as early as about 4 billion years ago. Much of the carbon dioxide in the young atmosphere dissolved in water. There it reacted with calcium and magnesium from weathered rock, locking the carbon away in carbonate sediments, limy deposits on the seafloor.

  <!-- arch-002 -->

- **DNA takes over from RNA** — c. 4 billion years ago (4,000 Ma)

  Life's first genes were probably written in RNA. DNA evolved later, a more chemically stable store of genetic information, and LUCA most likely already had it. Virologist Luis Villarreal proposes that viruses carried RNA genes into DNA genomes during this switch, around 4 billion years ago, before LUCA, the ancestor of all life. That date rests on his proposal alone. The exact timeline and mechanism remain open questions.

  <!-- arch-003 -->

- **The Napier mountains rise in Antarctica** — c. 4 billion years ago (4,000 ± 200 Ma)

  Some of Earth's first metamorphic rocks may come from Antarctica. Mountain building raised the Napier range of East Antarctica, dated to 4000 ± 200 million years ago. Its faulting and folding may have produced some of the planet's first metamorphic rocks, rocks remade by heat and pressure without melting. The range is one of the earliest orogenies, or mountain-building episodes, on record.

  <!-- arch-004 -->

- **The bombardment winds down** — c. 3.92–3.85 billion years ago (3,920–3,850 Ma)

  Earth's gold may owe a debt to falling rocks. Tungsten isotopes suggest most gold in the crust came from the mantle after a meteorite bombardment about 3.9 billion years ago. The final phase of the Late Heavy Bombardment is placed at about 3,920–3,850 million years ago, though impacts stayed frequent in the early Archean. Lunar melt ages cluster near 3.9 billion years, but critics and impact models favor several smaller episodes over one cataclysm. Whether a distinct spike happened at all is still debated.

  <!-- arch-005 -->

- **Akilia graphite and the hunt for early life** — c. 3.85 billion years ago (3,850 Ma)

  A smudge of graphite on a small Greenland island set off a long argument about the first life. The graphite, in metamorphosed rock on Akilia Island, is low in carbon-13, which may mark organic matter from living things. An igneous band cutting the rock shows it is no younger than 3.85 billion years. Yet the rock's sedimentary origin, its age and its carbon have all been questioned, and the find sparked debate over photosynthetic life before 3.8 billion years ago.

  <!-- arch-006 -->

- **The East European Craton begins** — c. 3.8 billion years ago (3,800 Ma)

  The ground beneath Ukraine and western Russia holds some of Europe's oldest crust. The first rocks of the Ukrainian Shield and Voronezh Massif were laid down around 3.8 billion years ago, starting the East European Craton. This Archean crust, 3.2–3.8 billion years old, lies in the craton's southwest and east. Its Sarmatian part holds Archean terranes, blocks of crust joined to the craton, of about 3.7–2.7 billion years.

  <!-- arch-007 -->

- **The first cratons, cores of the continents** — c. 3.8 billion years ago (3,800 Ma)

  Every continent today is built around an ancient, stubborn core. These cores are cratons: old, stable parts of the continental lithosphere, the rigid outer shell, with deep roots. The first complete continental masses of this kind, built of granite blocks, appeared around 3,800 million years ago, and most cratons formed in the Archean. One of the first great continental masses began to gather on the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton, where felsic magmas rose. Antarctic zircons of 3.9–3.0 billion years suggest that recycling within the crust, melting old rock into lighter new rock, was key to building them. The work was substantial: about 39% of modern continental crust formed in the Archean.

  <!-- arch-008 -->

- **The oldest banded iron formations** — c. 3.8 billion years ago (3,800 Ma)

  Rocks striped in rust and silica record a world almost without oxygen. Banded iron formations are made of thin alternating layers rich in iron and in silica. The oldest known lie at Isua, in Greenland's greenstone belt, and date from about 3,800–3,700 million years ago. Their iron isotopes point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by Photosynthesis without oxygen. Iron formations of this Algoma type formed mainly in the Archean, and deposition later peaked near the eon's end.

  <!-- arch-010 -->

- **Greenland's Isua Greenstone Belt** — c. 3.8–3.7 billion years ago (3,800–3,700 Ma)

  Pillows of lava in Greenland prove there was water to erupt into. The Isua belt was built from volcanic and sedimentary layers about 3,800 and 3,700 million years old. It is the largest exposure on Earth of Eoarchean supracrustal rock, rock formed at the surface. Its pillow basalt formed in an underwater eruption, so liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago. How the belt formed, by plate tectonics or by heat-pipe or plume volcanism, is still contentious.

  <!-- arch-009 -->

- **South China's Yangtze Block takes shape** — c. 3.8–3.2 billion years ago (3,800–3,200 Ma)

  China's oldest rocks lie in the Yangtze Block. This northwestern part of the South China Craton is thought to have formed around 3.8–3.2 billion years ago. Detrital zircons, grains worn from older rock, 3.8 billion years old preserve remnants of that ancient crust. Its Kongling Complex holds the country's oldest rocks, with zircon ages of 3.3–2.9 billion years.

  <!-- arch-012 -->

- **The Pilbara Craton, a pristine Archean survivor** — c. 3.8–2.7 billion years ago (3,800–2,700 Ma)

  Only two places on Earth keep Archean crust in near-original condition, and Western Australia's Pilbara Craton is one of them. The other is South Africa's The Kaapvaal Craton of South Africa. The Pilbara holds crust up to 3.8 billion years old, intruded by granite domes and greenstone belts of about 3.5–3.2 billion years. Its story starts before its oldest rocks. Detrital zircons of 3.8–3.6 billion years show that crust was already eroding 300 million years before the oldest rocks that survive. The craton stabilized around 3,600 million years ago, as continents possibly gathered into Vaalbara. By 2.97 billion years ago the West Pilbara Terrane had collided with the East Pilbara Terrane and joined it.

  <!-- arch-011 -->

- **Photosynthesis without oxygen** — c. 3.7 billion years ago (3,700 Ma)

  The first sun-powered life gave off no oxygen at all. Anaerobic microbes, which live without oxygen, appear from about 3.7 billion years ago, among them chemotrophs that fed on chemicals and early photosynthesizers. Their simpler, anoxygenic photosynthesis used hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron in place of water, so it released no oxygen. These bacteria made ATP, the cell's energy currency, from a proton gradient across a membrane, a mechanism nearly all later organisms still use. The first of them may have lived at acidic hydrothermal vents, using faint geothermal light. Geochemical evidence suggests this photosynthesis emerged 3.3–3.5 billion years ago, and fossils thought to be filamentous photosynthesizers date to 3.4 billion.

  <!-- arch-013 -->

- **Earth's magnetic field switches on** — c. 3.7 billion years ago (3,700 Ma)

  An invisible shield was already around Earth 3.7 billion years ago. Evidence from Greenland, published in 2024, shows the planet had a magnetic field by 3,700 million years ago. Earlier work on magnetism frozen into Australian lava and South African conglomerate had traced it back to at least about 3,450 million years ago. Earth, like most planets, makes its field through the motion of electrically conducting fluids. Here that fluid is the molten outer core left by The iron catastrophe gives Earth its core. By 3.5 billion years ago its currents drove a field that helped stop the solar wind from stripping away the atmosphere.

  <!-- arch-014 -->

- **Disputed traces of life at Isua** — c. 3.7 billion years ago (3,700 Ma)

  Whether life left marks at Isua depends on whom you ask. Metasedimentary rocks about 3.7 billion years old in Greenland hold graphite whose carbon isotopes suggest sorting by living things. It is the earliest such evidence from a rock unit rather than a single mineral grain. In 2016 a team reported dome-shaped stromatolites 1–4 cm high, 220 million years older than those of Dresser stromatolites, the earliest undisputed life. The layers sit on volcanic rock dated 3.709 billion years and beneath beds dated 3.695 billion. Then a 2018 study, joined by one original proponent, blamed the shapes on rock deformation. Both the carbon and the stromatolites remain disputed; the earliest undisputed life is about 3.5–3.48 billion years old.

  <!-- arch-015 -->

- **The Kaapvaal Craton of South Africa** — c. 3.7–2.6 billion years ago (3,700–2,600 Ma)

  South Africa's gold and diamonds sit on one of the oldest stable slabs of crust anywhere. The Kaapvaal Craton formed and stabilized between 3.7 and 2.6 billion years ago, as batholiths, huge bodies of granite that cooled underground, thickened its crust. With the Pilbara it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts known. Its oldest parts are tonalitic gneisses of about 3.6–3.7 billion years, joined by granite-greenstone terranes of 3.0–3.5 billion. From 3.0 to 2.7 billion years ago, collisions between the continent and volcanic arcs built basins filled with thick volcanic and sedimentary piles. Its granite is exposed today in the core of the Vredefort impact structure.

  <!-- arch-016 -->

### Paleoarchean Era

The Paleoarchean is where life stops being a maybe. Stromatolites in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation, laid down about 3,483–3,479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life, and microbes may already have lived around hot springs on land. Meanwhile the continents were taking shape: the Wyoming and Dharwar cratons began, and the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents. Above it all hung a stable atmosphere of nitrogen, methane and carbon dioxide, and below it, spherule layers at Barberton record giant impacts still striking.

- **The Wyoming Craton begins** — c. 3.6–3.0 billion years ago (3,600–3,000 Ma)

  Beneath the Rocky Mountains lies a block of crust older than almost anything on the continent. The Wyoming Craton began as a 100,000 km² Archean craton with gneisses of 3.6–3.0 billion years. Its rocks reach 3.5 billion years, and detrital zircons in them go back 4.0 billion. Late Archean magmatism and plate movements reworked it, and by the end of the eon its three subprovinces had joined.

  <!-- arch-019 -->

- **Vaalbara, a first supercontinent?** — c. 3.6–2.8 billion years ago (3,600–2,800 Ma)

  South Africa and Western Australia have rock records that match too well to be chance, or so one hypothesis argues. The Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents, as far back as about 3.6 billion years ago. They show strikingly similar rock sequences from 3.5 to 2.7 billion years ago and share impact spherule layers of 3.5–3.2 billion years. The case is far from closed. Paleomagnetic data hint at a link even at 3.87 billion years, but an early Vaalbara cannot be proven. By 2.78–2.77 billion years ago the cratons lay 30° of latitude apart, so it had broken up by about 2.8 billion. Some scientists explain the shared features as global processes, and Vaalbara competes with the largely incompatible Ur, a contested early supercontinent hypothesis.

  <!-- arch-018 -->

- **India's Dharwar Craton forms** — c. 3.6–2.5 billion years ago (3,600–2,500 Ma)

  The oldest part of the Indian peninsula was built by ocean floor sinking and melting. India's Dharwar Craton formed between 3.6 and 2.5 billion years ago. Around 3350 million years ago, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle. The melting slab produced its TTG crust of tonalite, trondhjemite and granodiorite, light granite-like rocks. Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 million years ago, closing all of its subduction zones, where one plate dives beneath another.

  <!-- arch-017 -->

- **The Barberton Greenstone Belt** — c. 3.5–3.2 billion years ago (3,500–3,200 Ma)

  Some of Africa's oldest mountains rise on the border of South Africa and Eswatini. Lavas and sediments of the Barberton belt were laid down there between 3.5 and 3.2 billion years ago. The area grew in two episodes of terrane accretion, about 3.5 and 3.2 billion years ago, each matching a pulse of TTG magma. Its Makhonjwa Mountains are among the oldest in Africa, and its rocks hold some of the oldest traces of life.

  <!-- arch-020 -->

- **Spherule layers record giant impacts** — c. 3.5–3.2 billion years ago (3,500–3,200 Ma)

  Thin beds of glassy beads are all that remain of asteroids that hit the early Earth. These spherules are droplets of rock melted and thrown out by an impact, then rained back down. Spherules 3.5 billion years old in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth. In the Barberton belt, eight spherule layers, named S1 to S8 and about 3.5–3.2 billion years old, record at least four and perhaps eight or more impacts. A 2024 review counts 36 layers, from 3.47–3.22 billion and 2.63–2.49 billion years ago, and reads them as a tail of the Late Heavy Bombardment. The objects were not small: the record from 3.2 billion years includes impacts by bodies up to 100 km wide.

  <!-- arch-021 -->

  *Figure: Impact spherule layers cluster in two windows of time, read as a tail of the bombardment.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Dresser stromatolites, the earliest undisputed life** — c. 3.48 billion years ago (3,483–3,479 Ma)

  In the red hills of Western Australia's Pilbara lies the oldest life no one seriously disputes. Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation, deposited about 3483–3479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life. Stromatolites are layered mounds built as microbial mats trap sediment, layer upon layer. The evidence runs deeper than the mounds. Microbially induced sedimentary structures of the same age record microbial mats, the earliest life with good fossil evidence. The formation's North Pole chert, a glassy silica rock, holds microfossils, mat fabrics, and carbon and sulfur signatures that suggest heat-loving microbes. The setting was hot and wet. The stromatolites grew mostly in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera, a collapsed volcanic crater, where seawater mixed with hydrothermal fluids. Some formed near hot springs on land, a clue explored in Life may reach the land. Older claims, such as those at Disputed traces of life at Isua, remain disputed. The stromatolite record gives the earliest undisputed evidence of life from at least 3.5 billion years ago.

  <!-- arch-022 -->

- **Life may reach the land** — c. 3.48 billion years ago (3,480 Ma)

  Life on land may be almost as old as life itself. Microbes may have lived on land by 3.48 billion years ago: geyserite, a mineral crust laid down by hot springs, in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation holds possible traces. The veins of one 3.5-billion-year-old hot-spring setting held elements life needs, such as phosphorus, boron, nitrogen and sulfur. Some evidence of prokaryotes, simple cells without a nucleus, colonizing land predates 3 billion years and may reach back to 3.5 billion. Fossil microbes from land-based mats show life was established on land by 3.22 billion years ago. By at least 2.7 billion years ago microbes had built land ecosystems, with organic-rich soils and ponds recorded by 2,800 million years ago.

  <!-- arch-023 -->

- **The Apex chert microfossils** — c. 3.46 billion years ago (3,465 Ma)

  A few dark threads in Australian chert may be the oldest fossils of life, or not fossils at all. The 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert of the Pilbara may hold permineralized microorganisms, cells turned to stone by minerals. Fossils from the Warrawoona Group were once likened to cyanobacteria, but cyanobacterial fossils this old are considered possible yet questionable. Nearby 3.47-billion-year-old baryte and Mount Ada Basalt hold further possible traces. Whether the Apex structures are biological is contested.

  <!-- arch-024 -->

- **Strelley Pool stromatolites react to change** — c. 3.43 billion years ago (3,430 Ma)

  These stromatolites seem to respond to their surroundings, as living communities do. In Western Australia's 3.43-billion-year-old Strelley Pool Formation, they change in ways that suggest microbial communities reacting to shifting conditions. They imply photosynthesis, with or without oxygen, since at least 3.43 billion years ago, and the formation holds diverse microfossil shapes too. A 2009 find gave strong evidence of microbial stromatolites by 3.45 billion years, the oldest life visible to the naked eye.

  <!-- arch-025 -->

- **Methane microbes beneath Barberton's seafloor** — c. 3.42 billion years ago (3,420 Ma)

  Life may already have been living underground, below the seafloor. About 3.42 billion years ago, threadlike filaments, possibly of microbes that made or ate methane, lived in a vein system beneath the seabed at Barberton. Nearby, the Buck Reef and Josefsdal cherts hold microbial mats with fossil bacteria, and Kromberg microbes show reproduction by fission, splitting in two. Flat-layered stromatolites occur in the 3.46 Hooggenoeg, 3.42 Kromberg and 3.33-billion-year-old Mendon formations.

  <!-- arch-026 -->

- **A nitrogen sky with almost no oxygen** — c. 3.4 billion years ago (3,400 Ma)

  A visitor to the Archean would have suffocated. By about 3.4 billion years ago, nitrogen was the main gas of a stable second atmosphere that also held methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases. Volcanic outgassing made it, with extra gases from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment. It was anoxic and weakly reducing. Oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 billion years ago. Any oxygen made by early photosynthesis was quickly used up oxidizing iron, sulfur and methane. Sulfur-isotope signals rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 billion years ago. River and delta grains of pyrite, siderite and uraninite older than 2.4 billion years tell the same story, since these minerals break down in oxygen.

  <!-- arch-027 -->

- **Granite intrudes at the Johannesburg Dome** — 3.34 billion years ago (3,340 ± 3 Ma)

  Johannesburg sits on a dome of very old granite. Tonalitic and trondhjemitic magma, both granite-like, intruded dark mafic–ultramafic greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome. Uranium–lead dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 million years, the oldest granitoid phase recognized there so far. Later mafic dikes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 million years, support the view that the craton grew in episodes, piece by piece.

  <!-- arch-028 -->

- **The Zimbabwe Craton welds together** — c. 3.3 billion years ago (3,300 Ma)

  Diamonds come from deep roots, and the Zimbabwe Craton has one. Its Tokwe and Rhodesdale segments, with rocks as old as 3.46 billion years, stabilized about 3.3 billion years ago. The craton formed where these two smaller blocks were sutured, or welded, together. With the Kaapvaal Craton and Limpopo Belt, it rests on a buoyant mantle root about 250 km thick that yields diamonds.

  <!-- arch-029 -->

- **Fig Tree microfossils** — c. 3.26 billion years ago (3,260 Ma)

  Some of the first creatures ever named are microscopic and 3.26 billion years old. South Africa's Fig Tree Formation, about 3.28–3.22 billion years old, holds stromatolites and fossils of microscopic life from about 3.26 billion years ago. Among its fossils are Archaeosphaeroides barbertonensis and Eobacterium, simple cells preserved in stone from the Archean seafloor.

  <!-- arch-030 -->

- **The S2 impact, a planet-shaking blow** — c. 3.26 billion years ago (3,260 Ma)

  About 3.26 billion years ago, an asteroid about 37–58 km wide hit Earth. The only direct trace is the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt, but the scale of the blow is staggering. Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of Chicxulub's, the crater linked to the dinosaurs' end. The impact probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes. It raised megatsunamis thousands of meters high. Its heat boiled the surface of the sea, evaporating tens of meters of the global ocean. Any microbial mats in the shallows would have felt it.

  <!-- arch-031 -->

- **Microbial mats on Moodies tidal flats** — c. 3.22 billion years ago (3,220 Ma)

  Tides were already washing over sand and mud 3.22 billion years ago, and microbes were living on them. The Moodies Group of South Africa and Eswatini, laid down then, holds Earth's oldest well-preserved siliciclastic tidal deposits, made of sand and mud grains. Microbial mats flourished on its tidal flats, and its microfossils are among the few accepted Archean examples. It overlies the Fig Tree microfossils rocks in the Barberton belt.

  <!-- arch-032 -->

### Mesoarchean Era

In the Mesoarchean, Earth learned to make oxygen. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, and a brief rise in oxygen followed around 2,980–2,960 million years ago. The planet was warm, perhaps very warm, yet it also saw the Pongola glaciation, the oldest known on Earth. Continental crust grew fast, the hypothetical supercontinent Ur may have formed, and plate tectonics may have begun, though its timing is still debated.

- **Cyanobacteria learn to make oxygen** — c. 3.2 billion years ago (3,200 Ma)

  Every breath you take traces back to a microbe that learned to split water. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, with local free oxygen around stromatolites on carbonate platforms. The pioneers were cyanobacteria. They arose in fresh water or on land in the middle Archean. Some claims reach back to 3.5 billion years, and 2026 genetic work considers an origin 2.9–3 billion years ago established. Unlike Photosynthesis without oxygen, they split water and released oxygen as waste. That oxygen did not fill the air at once. It first oxidized iron dissolved in the oceans, forming iron ore. It built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria, and eventually triggered the Great Oxygenation Event after the Archean. Some evidence once seemed to settle the question early. Pilbara biomarkers of 2.7 billion years were read as signs of cyanobacteria and eukaryotes, but were later shown to be contamination. The timing remains debated.

  <!-- arch-034 -->

  *Figure: How oxygen from cyanobacteria first rusted the oceans, then built up.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cyanobacteria split water] --> B[Oxygen released]
  B --> C[Dissolved iron oxidized]
  C --> D[Iron ore forms]
  B --> E[Oxygen builds slowly]
  E --> F[Great Oxygenation Event]
  ```

- **A hot world under a methane greenhouse** — during the Mesoarchean, 3.2–2.8 billion years ago (3,200–2,800 Ma)

  Archean seas may have been hot enough to scald. Oxygen isotopes in Mesoarchean cherts suggest ocean temperatures of about 55–85 °C, though weathering studies suggest averages below 50 °C. Either way, the climate was at least temperate. High levels of methane and carbon dioxide may explain the warmth. Volcanoes supplied the carbon dioxide and early microbes the methane, which lasted longer in an atmosphere without oxygen. Nitrogen levels were probably similar to today's, so nitrogen did little warming. There was a brake, too: sunlight breaking apart methane may have made an organic haze with a cooling, anti-greenhouse effect.

  <!-- arch-033 -->

- **Ur, a contested early supercontinent** — c. 3.1 billion years ago (3,100 Ma)

  Pieces of India, western Australia and southern Africa may once have been a single landmass. Ur is a hypothetical supercontinent of those rocks, formed around 3.1 billion years ago. Its assembly is put at 3,200–2,600 million years ago, and it would have covered only 12–16% of today's continental crust. The main argument is that cratons stable by about 3 billion years ago all sat in one region of Pangaea. Rogers proposed that Ur later grew into East Gondwana by joining East Antarctica. But a conflicting hypothesis joins western Australia and southern Africa as Vaalbara, a first supercontinent?, and most proposed Archean supercontinents remain controversial.

  <!-- arch-036 -->

  *Figure: The two rival Archean supercontinent hypotheses join different cratons.*

  | Hypothesis | Pieces now in | Timing |
  |---|---|---|
  | Ur | India, western Australia, southern Africa | Formed around 3.1 Ga |
  | Vaalbara | Western Australia and southern Africa (Pilbara and Kaapvaal) | Proposed rival |

- **The Saamian orogeny builds Fennoscandia's core** — c. 3.1–2.9 billion years ago (3,100–2,900 Ma)

  The heart of a future supercontinent was forged in what is now northern Europe. Between 3.1 and 2.9 billion years ago, the Saamian orogeny built a wide area of tonalitic-trondhjemitic crust, light granite-like rock, in Fennoscandia. Gneiss and greenstone belts of the Baltic Shield were laid down in the Kola Peninsula, Karelia and northeastern Finland around 3,100 million years ago. This crust later formed the core of Kenorland, a possible supercontinent.

  <!-- arch-035 -->

- **Miralga, an impact crater of disputed age** — c. 3.02 billion years ago (3,024 Ma)

  One crater has been given three very different ages in two years. Shatter cones, cone-shaped fractures made by an impact's shock wave, near Marble Bar in the Pilbara reveal the Miralga, or North Pole Dome, impact structure. Its crater may have exceeded 100 km. A March 2025 study dated it to 3,470 ± 2 million years, which would make it the oldest known impact structure by over a billion years. A July 2025 study found shatter cones in rocks younger than 2.71 billion years, so the impact came after then and before 400 million years ago. A 2026 study dated impact-recrystallized zircon to 3.024 billion years and hydrothermal apatite to 3.019 billion. The age remains disputed.

  <!-- arch-037 -->

- **Maniitsoq, a doubtful impact in Greenland** — 3 billion years ago (3,000.9 ± 1.9 Ma)

  Not every round structure is a crater. One at Maniitsoq, West Greenland, was proposed as an ancient impact site, with an age refined to 3000.9 ± 1.9 million years. The impact evidence is highly contentious. Ultramafic intrusions there formed at 3013 million years ago, too old to have been made by the supposed impact, which argues against the idea.

  <!-- arch-038 -->

- **When did plate tectonics begin?** — c. 3 billion years ago (3,000 Ma)

  The ground beneath your feet moves a few centimeters a year, but when did it start moving? A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 billion years ago, yet its timing is still debated. The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, where one plate dives beneath another. It includes an oceanic arc, a chain of volcanoes over a sinking plate, at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 billion years ago. Diamonds add more clues. Minerals trapped in them suggest the supercontinent cycle, the repeated gathering and breakup of continents, began roughly 3 billion years ago. Diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 billion. Earlier, the picture differs. A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics, and some suggest a stagnant lid, a single unbroken shell, instead. Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 billion years ago, to 2.2 billion years, or just 800 million years for fully modern-style tectonics. The debate links back to Did plates already move in the Hadean?.

  <!-- arch-039 -->

  *Figure: Proposed starts of plate tectonics spread across billions of years.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Continental crust grows fast** — c. 3.0–2.5 billion years ago (3,000–2,500 Ma)

  Before 3.7 billion years ago, continents held under 10% of today's continental crust. Then they grew quickly. There is little evidence of continental crust before 3.5 billion years ago, but roughly 20–25% of today's crust existed by 3.0 billion. After rapid crustal evolution, it reached about 60% by 2.6 billion years ago, with widespread mantle melting on the shields between 3.0 and 2.5 billion. Much of the new crust was TTG rock, formed when water-rich mafic rock partly melted at high pressure. Whether subduction drove that melting is debated. The remaining fifth of the continental crust formed only during the last 2.5 billion years.

  <!-- arch-040 -->

  *Figure: Most of today's continental crust had formed by the end of the Archean.*

  | When | Share of today's continental crust |
  |---|---|
  | Before 3.7 Ga | Under 10% |
  | By 3.0 Ga | Roughly 20–25% |
  | By 2.6 Ga | About 60% |
  | Last 2.5 billion years | The remaining fifth |

- **The Pongola glaciation, Earth's first known ice age** — c. 2.98–2.84 billion years ago (2,985–2,837 Ma)

  In a warm Archean world, ice suddenly appears in the rocks of southern Africa. The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 billion years ago, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth. Its traces are diamictites, jumbled mixtures of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, in the Mozaan Formation of the Pongola Supergroup. They crop out in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini. The cold was an interruption. The Mesoarchean climate was otherwise warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide, as in A hot world under a methane greenhouse. Ice reached a palaeolatitude, an ancient latitude, of 48 degrees. Whether it pushed further toward the tropics is uncertain. What cooled the planet? No one knows for sure. Sulfur-isotope changes suggest a link to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere, described in Oxygen's first brief rise. If so, the first ice age on record was tied to the first stirrings of oxygen.

  <!-- arch-041 -->

  *Figure: The Pongola ice broke into a warm climate, possibly linked to a brief oxygen rise.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Warm climate from methane and CO2] --> B{Early oxygenation?}
  B -.->|sulfur isotopes hint| C[Pongola glaciation]
  C --> D[Diamictites in Mozaan Formation]
  ```

- **Oxygen's first brief rise** — c. 2.98–2.96 billion years ago (2,980–2,960 Ma)

  Oxygen made a short, early appearance long before it came to stay. A transient episode of higher oxygen occurred around 2,980–2,960 million years ago, in an atmosphere that otherwise had almost no free oxygen. By the Mesoarchean, oases of relatively high oxygen already existed in some nearshore shallow seas, around the cyanobacteria making it. Sulfur isotopes link this episode to the Pongola glaciation of the same age.

  <!-- arch-042 -->

- **The Witwatersrand Basin gathers its gold** — c. 2.97–2.71 billion years ago (2,970–2,710 Ma)

  More gold has come out of one South African basin than anywhere else on Earth: over 40,000 tonnes mined, about 22% of all gold above ground. From about 2.97 to 2.71 billion years ago, rivers and a sea laid 5–7 km of mostly sedimentary rock in the Witwatersrand Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. As uplift pushed the sea back, braided river deltas on a wide coastal plain concentrated heavy minerals there: gold, pyrite and uraninite.

  <!-- arch-043 -->

- **The North Atlantic Craton assembles** — c. 2.95–2.58 billion years ago (2,950–2,580 Ma)

  Rocks in Greenland, Labrador and Scotland were once one block. That block is the North Atlantic Craton, which grew as terranes collided in a series of orogenies. The Akia, Isukasia and Kapisilik terranes collided about 2950 million years ago. More terranes merged between 2850 and 2700 million years ago, and around Nuuk between 2650 and 2580 million. Regional magmatism, deformation and metamorphism then reworked and stabilized the craton.

  <!-- arch-044 -->

- **The Yilgarn Craton and its gold** — c. 2.94–2.63 billion years ago (2,940–2,630 Ma)

  Western Australia's goldfields sit on a craton built from many pieces. The Yilgarn Craton was assembled between about 2.94 and 2.63 billion years ago from many terranes of older crust, mostly formed 3.2–2.8 billion years ago. Its bedrock includes the Narryer Gneiss, home of the A Jack Hills zircon, the oldest mineral on Earth, beneath greenstone belts of about 2.70–2.55 billion years. Most of its gold was deposited 2650–2630 million years ago, after an earlier gold event at 2660–2655 million as the crust stretched.

  <!-- arch-045 -->

### Neoarchean Era

The Neoarchean is the age of supervolcanoes and stitched-together continents. In Ontario and Quebec the Abitibi greenstone belt formed, home to the Blake River Megacaldera Complex, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, and around 2,705 million years ago a possibly global eruption of komatiite lava may mark an overturn of the mantle. Cratons welded together: the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe along the Limpopo Belt, and many more into the hypothetical supercontinent Kenorland. Meanwhile, about 2,700 million years ago, another pulse of oxygen hinted at the great change to come.

- **The Abitibi greenstone belt** — c. 2.8–2.6 billion years ago (2,800–2,600 Ma)

  One of the world's largest Archean greenstone belts stretches across Ontario and Quebec. The Abitibi belt formed between 2,800 and 2,600 million years ago. It is mostly volcanic, a stack of thrusted slices like those of paired volcanic arcs and back-arc basins, with intrusions of 2,675–2,700 million years throughout. It contains the huge 2,707–2,696-million-year-old The Blake River supervolcano.

  <!-- arch-046 -->

- **The Limpopo Belt welds two cratons** — c. 2.8–2.5 billion years ago (2,800–2,500 Ma)

  A 250 km wide seam of crumpled rock joins two of Africa's oldest cratons. Late Archean metamorphism welded the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe cratons along the Limpopo Belt about 2.8–2.5 billion years ago. High-pressure granulites, rocks cooked deep in the crust, formed in the belt about 2.69 billion years ago. Once the two cratons were stabilized together, the high-grade metamorphism in the belt ceased.

  <!-- arch-047 -->

- **North China's ancient basement forms** — c. 2.8–2.5 billion years ago (2,800–2,500 Ma)

  Most of the deep rock under northern China dates from a single era. Neoarchean crust makes up 85% of the North China Craton's basement and formed in two pulses, 2.8–2.7 and 2.6–2.5 billion years ago. Banded iron formations and schists were laid down after the Fupingian orogeny of 2550 million years ago. Whether the craton's blocks joined about 2.5 billion years ago, in Kusky's model, or only at 1.85 billion, in Zhao's, is debated.

  <!-- arch-048 -->

- **The Fortescue and Hamersley basins fill** — 2.77 billion years ago (2,768 ± 16 Ma)

  Some of Australia's famous iron country began as a long-lived basin. From about 2.78 to 2.42 billion years ago, a thick pile of sedimentary and volcanic rock filled the Fortescue, Hamersley and Turee Creek basins on the Pilbara. Uranium–lead dating puts the base of this pile, the Mount Bruce Supergroup, at 2768 ± 16 million years. The Hamersley Basin was the last stable marine and river setting between the Yilgarn and Pilbara before rifting split them.

  <!-- arch-049 -->

- **The Slave Craton gains its deep root** — c. 2.75 billion years ago (2,750 Ma)

  Canada's diamond mines tap the deep keel of the Slave Craton. Its main stabilization came about 2.75 billion years ago, marked by abundant peridotite, a dense mantle rock, in its root. Kaapvaal shows a similar growth peak, suggesting much of Earth's continental lithospheric mantle formed in the Neoarchean. Diamonds from craton roots are often over 3 billion years old, and the Slave's oldest, 3.5–3.3 billion years, imply a thick root far earlier.

  <!-- arch-050 -->

- **Tumbiana lakes and their puzzling microfossils** — c. 2.73–2.71 billion years ago (2,727–2,715 Ma)

  The oldest known lakes rich in carbonate held life that is hard to classify. Western Australia's Tumbiana Formation, about 2727–2715 million years old, was laid down in such a lake system. Its limestones hold stromatolites such as Alcheringa narrina and organic-walled microfossils. Their size and protrusions resemble eukaryotic microbes, cells with a nucleus, but such features are not unique to eukaryotes, so what they were remains obscure.

  <!-- arch-051 -->

- **Kenorland, a possible supercontinent** — c. 2.72 billion years ago (2,720 Ma)

  Around 2.72 billion years ago, the scattered cratons may have gathered into a single landmass. Kenorland is a hypothetical supercontinent formed by the accretion of Neoarchean cratons and new continental crust. Its core was the Baltic, or Fennoscandian, Shield, traced back over 3.1 billion years, and Arctica, a northern continent formed part of it. Its final assembly was finished by 2,600–2,550 million years ago, with the Superior and Wyoming provinces side by side. It broke up sometime after 2.45–2.1 billion years ago, into proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn and Kalahari. Not everyone accepts it. Alternatively, the cratons formed separate supercratons, Superia and Sclavia; the Slave collided with Sclavia by 2.6 billion years ago, and Superia's final assembly came at 2520 million.

  <!-- arch-052 -->

- **Ventersdorp lavas bury the gold fields** — c. 2.71 billion years ago (2,715 Ma)

  A flood of lava sealed the Witwatersrand's gold beneath it. Massive outpourings, the Ventersdorp lavas, erupted about 2.715 billion years ago and abruptly ended deposition of the gold-rich Central Rand Group. Their cause is speculative: one source links them to the Kaapvaal craton's collision with the Zimbabwe Craton, another places them in a phase of rifting. The lavas and the Transvaal Supergroup above them were later warped into rings by the Vredefort impact.

  <!-- arch-053 -->

- **The Blake River supervolcano** — c. 2.71–2.70 billion years ago (2,707–2,696 Ma)

  The first known Precambrian supervolcano rose in what is now Ontario and Quebec. The Blake River Megacaldera Complex began forming about 2,707 million years ago. Its first caldera, Misema, is 80 km long and 40 km wide, built from at least two merging mafic shield volcanoes. Later phases built the New Senator Caldera, 2704–2701 million years ago, and the Noranda Caldera, 2696 million years ago, piling up 7–9 km of erupted rock.

  <!-- arch-054 -->

- **Komatiite floods and a mantle overturn** — c. 2.71 billion years ago (2,705 Ma)

  The hottest lavas in Earth's history erupted almost only in the Archean. Komatiite magma forms when 30–40% of mantle rock melts at very high pressure, and its lavas erupted at up to about 1600 °C. The mantle then may have been 100–250 °C hotter than now. Around 2,705 million years ago, a major and possibly global komatiite eruption occurred, and it may mark an overturn of the mantle.

  <!-- arch-055 -->

- **Another pulse of oxygen** — c. 2.7 billion years ago (2,700 Ma)

  Oxygen crept upward again about 2,700 million years ago. Skewed sulfur isotopes in pyrites, crystals of iron sulfide, show a small rise in atmospheric oxygen around this time. Cyanobacteria had appeared by at least 2.7 billion years ago, and an atmosphere containing oxygen began to develop in the late Archean. Some consider this pulse a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event, the first lasting rise of oxygen in the air. Most scholars still place that start later, in the Paleoproterozoic, about 2,400 million years ago.

  <!-- arch-058 -->

- **The Stillwater complex, a layered treasure chest** — c. 2.7 billion years ago (2,700 Ma)

  Montana's Beartooth Mountains expose a slice through a frozen magma chamber. The Stillwater complex, a large layered mafic intrusion, was injected into older gneisses about 2.7 billion years ago, and its minerals settled out in layers as it cooled. About 5,500 m of those layers are exposed along 48 km of the range. It holds large reserves of chromium and platinum-group metals such as palladium, and it resembles South Africa's Bushveld complex.

  <!-- arch-059 -->

- **Stromatolite reefs spread** — c. 2.7 billion years ago (2,700 Ma)

  Microbes built the world's first reefs. Stromatolites occur throughout the Archean. From about 2,700 million years ago they became a major part of the fossil record, common late in the eon. The earliest of confirmed microbial origin is 2.724 billion years old. In Zimbabwe, stromatolites of the Bulawayo series formed the first verified reef community on Earth.

  <!-- arch-060 -->

- **Sturgeon Lake Caldera** — c. 2.7 billion years ago (2,700 Ma)

  A collapsed volcano in northwestern Ontario is one of the best-preserved ore-bearing calderas in the world. Sturgeon Lake Caldera formed about 2.7 billion years ago. Explosive felsic eruptions and submarine lava domes left nearly 3,000 m of fill inside it. Its Mattabi pyroclastic flow, a racing avalanche of hot ash and gas, is considered the third most voluminous eruptive event.

  <!-- arch-061 -->

- **Fossil raindrops weigh the ancient air** — c. 2.7 billion years ago (2,700 Ma)

  Raindrops that fell 2.7 billion years ago left a measurement behind. Their fossil imprints in volcanic ash of South Africa's Ventersdorp Supergroup show air less than twice as dense as today's, likely similar or thinner. Gas bubbles in lava that set at sea level at the same time point to an air pressure of only 0.23 ± 0.23 bar. Both results contradict the idea that very high carbon dioxide or nitrogen kept the Archean warm under the faint young Sun.

  <!-- arch-062 -->

- **The Algoman orogeny builds the Superior Craton** — c. 2.7–2.5 billion years ago (2,700–2,500 Ma)

  The largest Archean craton on Earth was stitched together from many pieces. In the Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny, repeated continental collisions, compression and subduction built mountains in the late Archean. Terranes now in the Canadian Shield collided about 2,700–2,500 million years ago, adding land along a belt from South Dakota to Sudbury, Ontario. Between 2720 and 2680 million years ago, a run of these collisions assembled the Superior Craton. Subduction drove the docking, and dates of about 2,700 million years near Rainy Lake, Ontario, favor a model of moving plates. The orogeny closed the Archean about 2,500 million years ago. By then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick.

  <!-- arch-056 -->

- **The oceans run short of nickel** — c. 2.7–2.4 billion years ago (2,700–2,400 Ma)

  A shortage of one metal may have tipped the balance toward oxygen. From 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, nickel deposition fell steadily from 400 times today's level. Methane-making microbes need nickel. As volcanic nickel dwindled, oxygen producers began to outcompete them. The balance between the two kinds of microbe shifted toward oxygen.

  <!-- arch-057 -->

- **Carbonate platforms grow in the Transvaal** — c. 2.64–2.52 billion years ago (2,640–2,516 Ma)

  Microbes built limestone shelves the size of seas. Between about 2.640 and 2.516 billion years ago, stromatolites built two successive carbonate platforms in the Transvaal Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. These are thick shelves of limy rock in shallow water. The oldest known giant carbonate platform dates from about 2,600 million years ago, and a rising Transvaal sea flooded tidal flats about 2.550 billion years ago.

  <!-- arch-063 -->

- **The Great Dyke slices across Zimbabwe** — c. 2.58 billion years ago (2,575 Ma)

  A ribbon of rock 550 km long runs straight across Zimbabwe. This Great Dyke is a band of layered ultramafic intrusions, 3–12 km wide, emplaced about 2.575 billion years ago. It has stayed undeformed since, showing that the craton had already stabilized. It holds major chromium and platinum resources, and it is one of the world's three most significant platinum sources.

  <!-- arch-064 -->

- **Arctica, a northern continent** — c. 2.56 billion years ago (2,565 Ma)

  Siberia and Canada may once have shared one landmass. Arctica, a hypothetical continent, formed about 2.565 billion years ago from the Siberian, Slave, Wyoming, Superior and North Atlantic cratons. The The Algoman orogeny builds the Superior Craton assembled it from the Canadian Shield and the Siberian craton. Rogers argued that it later rifted apart and reassembled along the 1.8-billion-year-old Trans-Hudson and Taltson-Thelon orogenies.

  <!-- arch-065 -->

- **Microbes begin to burn sulfur** — c. 2.52 billion years ago (2,520 Ma)

  Some microbes learned to live by oxidizing sulfur, and they did it early. The earliest evidence, about 2.52 billion years old, comes from South Africa's Gamohaan Formation. It shows that sulfur-oxidizing bacteria evolved before the Great Oxygenation Event, while oxygen in the air was still scarce, drawing energy from sulfur compounds in their surroundings.

  <!-- arch-066 -->

- **An oxygen pulse closes the Archean** — c. 2.5 billion years ago (2,501 Ma)

  The Archean ended with oxygen knocking at the door. Appreciable free oxygen was probably absent from the atmosphere until about 2,500 million years ago. Then, around 2,501 million years ago, a pulse of higher oxygen appeared, and some see it as a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event. The research is far from settled: studies from 2016–2022 put the onset anywhere from 2.7 to 2.3 billion years ago, including 2.501–2.434 billion.

  <!-- arch-067 -->

- **The continents rise from the sea** — c. 2.5 billion years ago (2,500 Ma)

  For most of the Archean, there was almost nowhere to stand. Much continental crust lay under a superocean deeper than today's, and Paleoarchean crust was still submerged. Only at the end of the eon did the continents likely rise above the water. By then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick. As land emerged, more continental weathering brought the oxygen isotopes of the oceans down toward modern levels.

  <!-- arch-068 -->

## Proterozoic Eon

The Proterozoic is the eon in which Earth's air changed for good. Free oxygen built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change never reversed. It reshaped everything it touched: banded iron formations precipitated across most continents, new minerals multiplied, and the gas proved toxic to many of the anaerobic microbes that had ruled until then. Ice spread in the Huronian glaciations, and a supercontinent began to rift apart above plumes of magma.

### Paleoproterozoic Era

The Paleoproterozoic opens with the planet rusting. Massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents as oxygen met the iron dissolved in seawater, and the Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity. Life paid a price, since free oxygen was toxic to a biosphere built of anaerobes. On land, rifting began to split a low-latitude supercontinent, giant swarms of dikes cut the cratons, and a series of glaciations left their boulder beds near Lake Huron.

#### Siderian Period

The Siderian takes its name from the Greek word for iron, and iron is its signature. Banded iron formations piled up across most continents, their red layers made of oxidized iron. At the same time oxygen began to build up in the air for the first time, an irreversible change that may have wiped out many early organisms. Plume-driven rifting cracked a supercontinent, the Mistassini dikes cut the Superior Craton, and the first of the Huronian ice ages began.

- **Banded iron formations reach their peak** — c. 2.50–2.42 billion years ago (2,500–2,420 Ma)

  Most of the iron ore that built the modern world was laid down around 2.5 billion years ago. At that time, massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents, and deposition peaked. Their red layers are oxidized iron; the Siderian period takes its name from the Greek for iron. Deposition began on the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons. Australia's Brockman Supersequence, 2500–2449 million years old, holds iron-formation sediments laid down as seas rose. The Hamersley Range iron formations, laid down 2470–2450 million years ago, are the world's thickest and most extensive, over 900 m thick.

  <!-- prot-003 -->

- **Oxygen multiplies the world's minerals** — c. 2.5–1.9 billion years ago (2,500–1,900 Ma)

  More than two-thirds of all mineral species owe their existence to life. The Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity, as many elements near the surface took oxidized forms. About 2,500 new minerals formed in the oxygenation stage from 2.5 to 1.9 billion years ago, lifting the total above 4,000. Oxidized uraninite, a uranium ore, alone gave rise to over 200 new uranyl minerals.

  <!-- prot-002 -->

- **Kenorland breaks apart** — c. 2.48–2.10 billion years ago (2,480–2,100 Ma)

  A supercontinent took hundreds of millions of years to tear itself apart. Between 2.48 and 2.45 billion years ago, rifting driven by plumes of magma began in a supercontinent that had sat at low latitudes, usually identified as Kenorland, a possible supercontinent. The drawn-out breakup left mafic dikes, rift basins and rifted margins on many continents through the Siderian and Rhyacian. Final breakup produced large swarms of mafic dikes and sills across the North American provinces 2.2–2.1 billion years ago. Its fragments became proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn craton and Kalahari, and the breakup is associated with the era's glaciations. Kenorland itself is hypothetical. In the alternative view, the Sclavia supercraton broke up during a global pulse of mantle-plume magma around 2.33–2.1 billion years ago.

  <!-- prot-004 -->

  *Figure: Kenorland's breakup left fragments that became later proto-continents.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Matachewan dike swarm** — c. 2.47–2.45 billion years ago (2,470–2,450 Ma)

  Thousands of magma-filled cracks mark where a continent began to split. About 2470 million years ago the Mistassini dike swarm, itself a large igneous province over 100,000 km², cut the Superior Craton. A large igneous province is a vast outpouring of magma. The related Matachewan swarm followed, covering at least 300,000 km² between Lake Superior and James Bay. Both are read as rifting above a hotspot near Sudbury, Ontario, at the onset of Kenorland breaks apart.

  <!-- prot-005 -->

- **The Great Oxidation Event** — c. 2.46–2.06 billion years ago (2,460–2,060 Ma)

  Once, there was no oxygen in the air to breathe. Then, early in the Proterozoic, free oxygen built up in the atmosphere and shallow seas for the first time. It turned a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change was irreversible. Every breathing animal since depends on it. Cyanobacteria, the first known oxygen producers, are generally credited. They had been releasing oxygen for a long time, as in Cyanobacteria learn to make oxygen. But oxygen won out only once surface reductants, chemicals that grab oxygen such as ferrous iron, sulfur and methane, were used up. The rise was steep. Between 2410 and 2320 million years ago, the oxygen partial pressure climbed from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths. By the end of the event, oxygen had risen from almost none to as much as 10% of the modern level. The rocks record the switch. Sulfur isotope anomalies typical of an oxygen-free sky vanish after 2.4–2.3 billion years ago, and rust-red beds appear in soils by 2.3 billion.

  <!-- prot-006 -->

  *Figure: Oxygen won out only after surface reductants were used up.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cyanobacteria make oxygen] --> B[Iron, sulfur, methane use it up]
  B --> C[Reductants exhausted]
  C --> D[Free oxygen builds up]
  D --> E[Oxidizing atmosphere]
  ```

- **The Oxygen Catastrophe, the first mass extinction** — c. 2.45 billion years ago (2,450 Ma)

  The gas that sustains animals today was, at first, a poison. Free oxygen was toxic to the mostly anaerobic biosphere, and it may have wiped out many early organisms, mostly colonies of archaea, an ancient group of single-celled microbes. It is described as the first known mass extinction, killing most of the planet's obligate anaerobes, organisms that cannot survive oxygen. It may have been the worst ever, but early life is too poorly known to compare it with the Big Five extinctions of later times. It is also the only well-documented extinction before the Phanerozoic, since earlier life was microbial or soft-bodied and left few fossils.

  <!-- prot-007 -->

- **Turee Creek microfossils and reefs** — c. 2.45 billion years ago (2,450 Ma)

  Black chert, a hard glassy silica rock, in Australia's Turee Creek Group preserves some of the oldest known microfossils, dated to 2450 million years. Some of these carbon-rich fossils have been interpreted as iron-oxidizing bacteria, microbes that lived by rusting iron. The group also holds the Kazput Reef Complex, dated 2400–2300 million years old, the oldest known reef complex of the Proterozoic.

  <!-- prot-008 -->

- **The Sleaford orogeny shapes the Gawler Craton** — c. 2.44–2.42 billion years ago (2,440–2,420 Ma)

  South Australia's oldest crust was born crumpled. The Gawler craton formed about 2,440 million years ago, and the Sleaford orogeny deformed it from 2440 to 2420 million years ago. It did not settle down quickly. Before 1550 million years ago, the craton was a set of active mountain belts reaching back to at least 2450 million years.

  <!-- prot-010 -->

- **The Dhala impact in India** — c. 2.44–2.24 billion years ago (2,440–2,240 Ma)

  India's largest impact scar is a puzzle in both size and age. An impact struck the Bundelkhand craton and left the largest impact structure in the country. Its diameter is estimated at 3 km by some sources and 11 km by others. Its age is poorly constrained, somewhere between about 2.44 and 2.24 billion years ago, so how it fits into Earth's story remains uncertain.

  <!-- prot-009 -->

- **Dike swarms cut Scotland and Australia** — c. 2.42–2.38 billion years ago (2,418–2,375 Ma)

  Scotland and Western Australia share a moment of cracking. The Scourie dike swarm, a set of magma-filled cracks, cut Scotland's Lewisian gneisses, overlapping a phase of crustal deformation called the Inverian at the start of the Proterozoic. Around 2410 million years ago, the Widgiemooltha swarm intruded the Yilgarn Craton, close in time to the Sebanga Poort dike in Zimbabwe.

  <!-- prot-011 -->

- **The Ongeluk filaments, perhaps the first fungi** — c. 2.4 billion years ago (2,400 Ma)

  Fungi-like life may have lived inside volcanic rock 2.4 billion years ago. Filaments that grew inside cracks and gas bubbles of basalt in South Africa's Ongeluk Formation have been suggested to be fossils of fungus-like organisms. They are the earliest fossils with features typical of fungi: bottom-dwelling, multicellular, with threads able to fuse together. Ukraine's much younger Volyn biota is cited as further support for their fungal nature.

  <!-- prot-012 -->

- **The Huronian glaciation** — c. 2.4–2.1 billion years ago (2,400–2,100 Ma)

  Oxygen, the gas of life, may have plunged the planet into its first great ice age. Rising oxygen cut atmospheric methane from 300 to 4 ppmv, parts per million by volume, weakening the greenhouse that had kept Earth warm. Average global temperatures fell below 0 °C. The result was a series of glacial periods, also called the Makganyene glaciation. It is named for diamictite-bearing rocks of the Huronian Supergroup near Lake Huron; diamictite is a jumble of boulders and mud dropped by ice. The Siderian record dates three pulses: about 2440–2420 million years ago (Duitschland), 2380–2360 million (Makganyene) and 2340–2310 million (Gowganda or Rietfontein). The ice was widespread. Glacial deposits occur on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, and correlate with beds in Western Australia. This is the earliest well-established ice age, with ice on land.
