Only The Pongola glaciation, Earth's first known ice age is older.

  <!-- prot-013 -->

  *Figure: How rising oxygen led to a frozen Earth.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Oxygen rises] --> B[Methane falls 300 to 4 ppmv]
  B --> C[Greenhouse weakens]
  C --> D[Global average below 0 °C]
  ```

  *Figure: The three glacial pulses of the Huronian glaciation.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

#### Rhyacian Period

The Rhyacian is the period of the first complex cells. Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen when an Asgard archaeon took in an alphaproteobacterium, and sexual reproduction probably appeared too. Oxygen surged, leaving the largest carbon isotope excursion known and the first continental red beds, while the Makganyene ice may have frozen the planet as far as the tropics. By the period's end, collisions in West Africa and South America had begun gathering Earth's continents into the supercontinent Columbia.

- **Makganyene, a possible snowball Earth** — c. 2.3–2.2 billion years ago (2,300–2,200 Ma)

  Ice may have reached the equator 2.2 billion years ago. South Africa's Makganyene glaciation has been proposed as a snowball Earth, a near-total freeze of the planet, set off by the evolution of cyanobacteria. Its glacial sediments, slightly younger than the Huronian deposits, were possibly laid down at tropical latitudes. Paleomagnetic evidence, the magnetism frozen into rocks, places South African glacial deposits of 2.2 billion years near the equator. Cap carbonates, limestone layers typical of the end of a deep freeze, sit above its glacial beds.

  <!-- prot-015 -->

- **The Lomagundi-Jatuli carbon swing** — c. 2.3–2.1 billion years ago (2,300–2,100 Ma)

  Seafloor limestones from this time hold the strangest carbon signal in Earth's history. Marine carbonates record the largest and longest-lasting positive carbon isotope excursion known, with δ13C values of +5 to +30‰. Put simply, the carbon in the sea became unusually heavy, because life buries the light carbon it takes up. Matching it would have needed the burial of organic carbon to double or triple for millions of years. It accompanied a massive rise in atmospheric oxygen, an expansion of life and more burial of organic matter. Oxygen climbed around 2.3 billion years ago, then fell around 2.1 billion in the Shunga-Francevillian event, letting organic-rich black shales accumulate. If the excursion was globally synchronous, it lasted between about 128 and 249 million years.

  <!-- prot-014 -->

- **The Yarrabubba impact** — 2.23 billion years ago (2,229 ± 5 Ma)

  An asteroid may have punched through a sheet of ice to hit Western Australia. The impactor, about 7 km wide, struck the Yilgarn craton and left a crater 30–70 km across. Its date, 2.229 billion years ago, falls near the end of the Huronian glaciation, and simulations fit an impact into a 2-km-thick ice sheet. It was the oldest impact structure of confident age until 2025, when Miralga displaced it, and a later study challenged its date, suggesting a much younger impact.

  <!-- prot-016 -->

- **The Eburnean orogeny shapes West Africa** — c. 2.2–2.0 billion years ago (2,200–2,000 Ma)

  West Africa's ancient heart was assembled in one long episode of mountain building. The Eburnean orogeny was a series of tectonic, metamorphic and plutonic events, the last meaning magma intruded and cooled underground. It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and structured its Birimian domain. Together with the Transamazonian orogeny, it welded South American and West African cratons, an early step toward Columbia. Around 2070 million years ago, an upwelling of the asthenosphere, the soft layer beneath the plates, released a large volume of magma after the mountains had formed.

  <!-- prot-017 -->

- **The first red beds rust on land** — c. 2.2–1.8 billion years ago (2,200–1,800 Ma)

  Red rock is a sign of oxygen in the air. Continental red beds formed as iron in weathered sandstone was exposed to oxygen and rusted to hematite, a red iron oxide. The first were laid down in the Rhyacian, signaling rising atmospheric oxygen. Iron in ancient soils shows oxygen reaching 5–18% of present levels around 2,200 million years ago, a big step from the near-zero of the Archean.

  <!-- prot-018 -->

- **The first eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus** — c. 2.15–1.95 billion years ago (2,150–1,950 Ma)

  Every plant, animal and fungus descends from a single act of swallowing. Eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, are thought to have arisen in the Rhyacian when an Asgard archaeon, a single-celled microbe, took in an alphaproteobacterium. The swallowed bacterium stayed on inside its host. Sexual reproduction probably appeared then too. The earliest known eukaryotic acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, date from between 2150 and 1950 million years ago. Yet when eukaryotes first appeared is debated. Claimed eukaryote records from 2.1 billion years ago are considered questionable. Another view puts the earliest evidence at 1.85 billion years, from symbiogenesis, the merging of archaea and proteobacteria under the new stress of oxygen. The oldest unambiguous eukaryote remains, from China, are 1.8–1.6 billion years old. Whatever the exact date, the rise of oxygen in The Great Oxidation Event probably set the scene.

  <!-- prot-019 -->

  *Figure: Competing dates for the earliest eukaryotes.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Transamazonian orogeny** — c. 2.14–1.94 billion years ago (2,140–1,940 Ma)

  Parts of Brazil and the Guianas were made when two small continents collided. The Gavião and Jequié blocks, Archean proto-continents, ran into each other in the Transamazonian orogeny. The collision shaped what are now the São Francisco Craton and the Guiana Shield. Together with West Africa's The Eburnean orogeny shapes West Africa, it marks the start of Columbia's assembly, the gathering of a new supercontinent.

  <!-- prot-020 -->

- **The Francevillian disks of Gabon** — c. 2.1 billion years ago (2,100 Ma)

  Strange disks up to 17 cm across lie flattened in Gabon's black shales. They come from the Francevillian B Formation, about 2.1 billion years old. Some authors read them as the earliest multicellular life and the earliest eukaryotes. A 2023 isotope study found an enrichment in light zinc that could reflect eukaryotic metabolism. Whether they are fossils at all is disputed. A 2017 review called their biological origin questionable. A 2023 review suggested they may be artifacts of diagenesis, the chemical changes that turn sediment into rock. Recent reviews lean toward a non-biological origin.

  <!-- prot-022 -->

- **Columbia, a supercontinent assembles** — c. 2.1–1.8 billion years ago (2,100–1,800 Ma)

  Almost every piece of continent on Earth was once gathered into one. Global-scale collisions gathered almost all continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna. Its proto-cratons became the cores of Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, possibly with Siberia, North China and Kalaharia. The collisions that joined them have their own names: the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies. Each was a long-running crash of crust that left a mountain belt behind. The mountains were huge. Zircons record an extensive high range, the Nuna Supermountains, between 2.0 and 1.8 billion years ago. Eroding peaks of that scale would have fed sediment and nutrients to the seas. Columbia may also mark a change in how the planet works. Modern plate tectonics may have emerged by at least 2.2 billion years ago, with Columbia's formation, linking back to the debate in When did plate tectonics begin?.

  <!-- prot-021 -->

  *Figure: Columbia's proto-cratons became the cores of later continents.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Shungite, Earth's oldest petroleum** — c. 2.09–1.98 billion years ago (2,090–1,980 Ma)

  Some of the oldest oil on Earth formed in a lagoon in Russian Karelia. Organic-rich muds settled there in brackish water during active rifting, and volcanic nutrients may have raised biological productivity. The sequence is dated by a 1980 ± 27 million-year-old gabbro intrusion and underlying dolomites of 2090 ± 70 million years. The deposit holds over 250 gigatonnes of carbon. Metamorphism turned these oil source rocks into shungite, and its veins are migrated petroleum, now bitumen, of confirmed biological origin.

  <!-- prot-023 -->

#### Orosirian Period

The Orosirian is a period of giant blows and great collisions. An asteroid perhaps 20–25 km wide struck South Africa's Kaapvaal craton, and nearby, magma rose to form the largest layered intrusion in Earth's crust. Around the world, mountain belts stitched cratons together: Baltica from three blocks, Laurentia through the Trans-Hudson orogeny, Atlantica from West African and South American cratons. Meanwhile, black chert on the shore of Lake Superior preserved microbes like cyanobacteria.

- **The Bushveld Igneous Complex** — c. 2.05 billion years ago (2,050 Ma)

  Most of the world's platinum comes from one frozen magma body in South Africa. Mantle magma rose through long cracks in the Kaapvaal crust and formed the largest layered igneous intrusion in Earth's crust. Layered like a cake, it includes three platinum-bearing layers called reefs. It holds the world's largest reserves of platinum-group metals, plus vast amounts of iron, tin, chromium, titanium and vanadium. The intrusion predates the nearby The Vredefort impact, Earth's largest crater by about 30 million years.

  <!-- prot-025 -->

- **The Vredefort impact, Earth's largest crater** — c. 2.02 billion years ago (2,023 ± 4 Ma)

  The largest verified impact structure on Earth lies just south of Johannesburg. About 2.02 billion years ago, an asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa. It was first put at 10–15 km wide; in 2022 it was estimated at 20–25 km. The original crater was 170–300 km across, possibly larger than Chicxulub. Little of it survives as a hole. Erosion of 7–11 km has removed the crater itself. What remains is the Vredefort Dome, a 70 km ring of hills that is the crater's rebounded central uplift, where deep rock sprang back up after the blow. It was one of two of the largest known impacts of the Orosirian. It also left a gift. By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the strike preserved rich gold deposits, laid down in The Witwatersrand Basin gathers its gold, that would otherwise have been eroded away.

  <!-- prot-026 -->

- **The Glenburgh orogeny joins Pilbara and Yilgarn** — c. 2.00–1.92 billion years ago (2,005–1,920 Ma)

  Western Australia's two great cratons were joined in a single collision. The Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane, a block of crust with its own history, collided with the Yilgarn craton in the Glenburgh orogeny. The crash brought substantial granite magmatism to the Glenburgh Terrane. It also brought intense deformation and metamorphism, the remaking of rock by heat and pressure. Two cratons that had evolved apart now formed one block.

  <!-- prot-028 -->

- **Atlantica, a continent spanning the future Atlantic** — c. 2 billion years ago (2,000 Ma)

  Africa and South America were neighbors long before Pangaea. Around 2 billion years ago, cratons now in West Africa and eastern South America joined to form the continent Atlantica. It included Amazonia and the Congo, West Africa and North Africa cratons. It is not generally regarded as a supercontinent, since it gathered only part of the world's land.

  <!-- prot-029 -->

- **The Svecofennian orogeny builds Scandinavia** — c. 2.0–1.8 billion years ago (2,000–1,800 Ma)

  The bedrock of Sweden and Finland is the root of a mountain range that has long since vanished. The Svecofennian orogeny affected what are now Sweden, Finland and Russia, joining cratons of Baltica within Columbia. Subduction closed an ocean basin and, about 1950 million years ago, emplaced the Jormua and Outokumpu ophiolites, slices of ocean floor pushed onto land. Continent–continent collision lasted from 1870 to 1790 million years ago, overlapping with extension in the south. Then the mountains collapsed under their own weight, from 1790 to 1770 million years ago.

  <!-- prot-032 -->

- **The Trans-Hudson orogeny forges North America** — c. 2.0–1.8 billion years ago (2,000–1,800 Ma)

  The core of North America was welded together along a single great seam. The Trans-Hudson orogeny is the largest Paleoproterozoic mountain belt in the world, and it formed the Canadian Shield and the North American craton, Laurentia. It sutured the Hearne-Rae, Superior and Wyoming cratons into the continent's core. Old cratonic blocks, island arcs and ocean deposits were folded, thrust, metamorphosed and intruded by hundreds of huge granite bodies. Final closure of the Manikewan Ocean around 1.83 billion years ago merged the Hearne, Superior and Sask cratons, and metamorphism peaked about 1.82–1.8 billion years ago. Following the Wopmay orogeny, it was the culminating event of Laurentia's assembly from six or seven Archean fragments.

  <!-- prot-034 -->

- **Baltica assembles from three blocks** — c. 2.0–1.7 billion years ago (2,000–1,700 Ma)

  The ancient core of Europe was built from three pieces. Baltica formed from the collision of Fennoscandia, Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia. Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia joined first, as Proto-Baltica, around 2.0 billion years ago. Proto-Baltica then collided with Fennoscandia about 1.8–1.7 billion years ago. One account puts the meeting of Sarmatia and Fennoscandia at 1.84–1.82 billion years ago, after a calm period following subduction.

  <!-- prot-030 -->

  *Figure: Baltica was assembled in two steps from three blocks.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sarmatia] --> C[Proto-Baltica, c. 2.0 Ga]
  B[Volgo-Uralia] --> C
  C -->|c. 1.8–1.7 Ga| E[Baltica]
  D[Fennoscandia] --> E
  ```

- **The early Ruker orogeny shapes Antarctica** — c. 2.0–1.7 billion years ago (2,000–1,700 Ma)

  Part of Antarctica was once joined to a continent no one has identified. The early Ruker orogeny was mountain building that marked a key event in Antarctica's assembly. It joined East Antarctica to an unknown continental block as Columbia formed, between about 2.0 and 1.7 billion years ago. The other block is still unidentified, but the collision left its mark on the rocks beneath the ice.

  <!-- prot-031 -->

- **The Nagssugtoqidian orogeny in Greenland** — c. 1.91–1.77 billion years ago (1,910–1,770 Ma)

  Greenland's ice hides the scar of a long-lost ocean. In the Nagssugtoqidian orogeny, mountain building formed the northern boundary of the mainly Archean North Atlantic craton. Island-arc terranes and two possible sutures, the seams where colliding plates joined, record subduction zones that have since vanished. It was one of the orogens that sutured Laurentia's cratonic blocks within Columbia.

  <!-- prot-035 -->

- **The Circum-Superior large igneous province** — c. 1.88–1.87 billion years ago (1,884–1,870 Ma)

  A ring of ancient magma more than 3,400 km long wraps around Canada's oldest craton. Between 1,884 and 1,870 million years ago, widespread mafic and ultramafic magma built the Circum-Superior Belt, a large igneous province, along the Superior craton's margin. Its dikes, sills and lavas stretch from Manitoba to Labrador and were emplaced in an extremely short geological time. It erupted while the Trans-Hudson, New Quebec and Penokean orogenies surrounded the craton. In the Labrador Trough, its 1,880-million-year-old event covered about 30,000 km². Its origin is unclear, and proposals include rifting, mantle plumes and microcontinent breakup. It hosts major copper, nickel and platinum-group deposits, including Manitoba's Thompson nickel belt, and a rare Proterozoic komatiite belt.

  <!-- prot-036 -->

- **The Wopmay orogeny, plate tectonics in action** — c. 1.88 billion years ago (1,882 ± 4 Ma)

  Northern Canada preserves a textbook case of plates colliding. The Hottah terrane, a continental arc of volcanoes, collided with the Archean Slave Craton, closing the Coronation Ocean between them. The belt it left is about 500 km long and 200 km wide, and Great Bear arc magma kept erupting until about 1.84 billion years ago. Its oceanic crust, island arcs and colliding continents show that modern plate-tectonic forces were at work in the early Proterozoic.

  <!-- prot-037 -->

- **The Gunflint chert microfossils** — c. 1.88 billion years ago (1,878 ± 1.3 Ma)

  On the north shore of Lake Superior, black chert holds a snapshot of microbial life. Layers of it, set in banded iron formation, preserve microfossils of microbes like cyanobacteria. The rock is built of stromatolites, and in Ontario some cyanobacterial colonies have turned to jasper, a red form of silica. The fossils carry a message about the air. This microbiota shows that photosynthesis was under way and that the atmosphere held enough oxygen to sustain microbial life. Uranium–lead dating gives a consensus age of about 1.878 billion years, and interbedded ash layers date to 1.86–1.99 billion.

  <!-- prot-038 -->

- **Grypania, a coil of uncertain nature** — c. 1.87 billion years ago (1,870 Ma)

  A coiled ribbon over a centimeter long is one of the most common large fossils of the Proterozoic. Grypania's oldest probable specimens date to about 1870 million years ago, redated from 2100 million, and the genus lasted into the Ediacaran. What it was is uncertain: a giant bacterium, a bacterial colony or a eukaryotic alga. If it was an alga, eukaryotes with organelles, specialized parts inside the cell, had already evolved.

  <!-- prot-039 -->

- **The Penokean orogeny around Lake Superior** — c. 1.86–1.83 billion years ago (1,860–1,830 Ma)

  The Great Lakes region carries the crumpled record of a collision. Mountain building struck the Lake Superior area, in an embayment on the southern margin of the Superior Craton. A collision between two crustal domains drove rock northward in thrusts and folds, and reactivated the Great Lakes tectonic zone. It was one of the orogens of 1.9–1.8 billion years ago that sutured Laurentia's blocks during Columbia's assembly.

  <!-- prot-040 -->

- **Viruses that prey on bacteria** — c. 1.85 billion years ago (1,850 Ma)

  Viruses are among life's oldest companions. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, emerged before, or soon after, the lineages of prokaryotes and eukaryotes diverged. Prokaryotes are cells without a nucleus; eukaryotes have one. Their emergence is dated to about 1.85 billion years ago. That makes bacterial viruses nearly as old as the great division of cellular life itself.

  <!-- prot-041 -->

- **Banded iron formations disappear** — c. 1.85 billion years ago (1,850 Ma)

  After more than a billion years, the striped iron rocks suddenly stop. Banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide after 1.85 billion years ago. Their end is read as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized and dropped out. Before then, the ocean was persistently iron-rich, with possible intervals of euxinia, oxygen-free water laced with sulfide. The only extensive iron formations laid down later are tied to Cryogenian glacial deposits. An odd coincidence marks the turning point. A 10 km asteroid struck water about 1,000 m deep 1.849 billion years ago, just as iron-formation deposition paused.

  <!-- prot-042 -->

  *Figure: Banded iron formations stopped once the iron in seawater had been used up and the deep ocean took up oxygen.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Iron-rich ocean] -->|oxygen oxidizes iron| B[Banded iron formations laid down]
  B --> C[Dissolved iron used up]
  C --> D[Deep ocean oxygenated]
  D --> E[Banded iron formations vanish after 1.85 Ga]
  ```

- **The Trans-North China Orogen** — c. 1.85 billion years ago (1,850 Ma)

  When did North China become one block? Its Eastern and Western Blocks collided over a subduction zone, forming the Trans-North China Orogen, and Zhao ties this to Columbia's assembly about 1.85 billion years ago. Kusky instead dates the joining to 2.5–2.3 billion years ago and reads the later event as a collision with Columbia. Earlier, about 1.95 billion years ago, the Yinshan and Ordos blocks collided to form the Western Block and the Khondalite Belt. The dispute is unresolved.

  <!-- prot-043 -->

- **The Sudbury impact** — c. 1.85 billion years ago (1,849 Ma)

  One of Canada's richest mining districts sits inside a 1.85-billion-year-old crater. A chondritic bolide, a stony asteroid 10–15 km wide, struck the Nuna supercontinent in what is now Ontario. It left one of the oldest and largest known impact structures, and its debris would have been scattered across the globe. The Sudbury Igneous Complex formed at the same time, and its ores hold nickel, copper, platinum-group metals, gold and silver. The blow may have reached the seas as well. Some propose that it mixed the layered ocean through tsunamis, vaporized seawater and runoff from wrecked continental margins. It was one of the two largest known impacts of the Orosirian, near the period's end, alongside The Vredefort impact, Earth's largest crater.

  <!-- prot-044 -->

- **The Capricorn orogeny reworks Western Australia** — c. 1.83–1.78 billion years ago (1,830–1,780 Ma)

  Even after two cratons joined, the crust between them kept churning. The Capricorn orogeny followed the collision of the Pilbara Craton and Glenburgh Terrane with the Yilgarn craton. It was the most important and widespread of the four orogenies that shaped the Gascoyne Complex, marked by reworking inside the continent. Voluminous Moorarie granites intruded the complex, and flood basalts erupted in the Yerrida Basin around 1830 million years ago.

  <!-- prot-045 -->

- **Columbia keeps growing at its edges** — c. 1.82–1.50 billion years ago (1,820–1,500 Ma)

  A supercontinent does not stop growing once it forms. After its final assembly about 1.82 billion years ago, Columbia kept growing until 1.5 billion years ago, as subduction fed magma and added crust at its margins. A great magmatic belt formed along what are now the southern margins of North America, Greenland and Baltica. Similar belts grew around Amazonia, the North Australia and Gawler cratons, and North China. Extensive magmatism about 1,750 million years ago in Baltica, Sarmatia, Siberia, Laurentia and West Africa shows these cratons were linked, part of one slowly enlarging landmass.

  <!-- prot-046 -->

#### Statherian Period

The Statherian marks the start of a long, quiet stretch sometimes called Earth's Middle Ages, a span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago of tectonic stability, steady climate and slow evolution. Quiet did not mean idle. The oldest sand seas spread across several cratons, island arcs crashed into proto-North America, and in what is now Gabon, uranium deposits ran as natural nuclear reactors. In North China, the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes appear in the rocks.

- **The oldest sand seas** — c. 1.8 billion years ago (1,800 Ma)

  Deserts of shifting dunes are far older than any plant. Around 1.8 billion years ago, the oldest ergs, or sand seas, developed on several cratons. An erg is a vast field of wind-blown sand dunes, like those of the Sahara today. Their appearance shows that broad, dry continental interiors already existed, with winds strong enough to pile sand into dunes.

  <!-- prot-049 -->

- **The Boring Billion** — c. 1.8–0.8 billion years ago (1,800–800 Ma)

  For about a billion years, Earth seemed to hold its breath. The Boring Billion, or Earth's Middle Ages, is an informal span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago. It was marked by tectonic stability, climatic stasis and slow biological evolution. Oxygen stayed very low and no glaciations occurred, though a Scottish lake froze over in winter 1 billion years ago. The oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and starved of nutrients, ruled by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water, a so-called Canfield ocean. The carbon isotope record shows no major excursions. Mesoproterozoic temperatures may have averaged about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today. The span ended with the breakup of Rodinia, a second oxygenation event and the Cryogenian Snowball Earth.

  <!-- prot-050 -->

- **The Yavapai orogeny** — c. 1.71–1.68 billion years ago (1,710–1,680 Ma)

  The rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon were born as island chains crashed into a continent. The Yavapai island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona. It was one of several arc terranes added to Laurentia's 1800-million-year-old core; related events include the Colorado and Central Plains orogenies. The Grand Canyon's Vishnu basement schists formed 1.75–1.73 billion years ago as island arcs collided with the mainland.

  <!-- prot-051 -->

- **The Oklo natural nuclear reactors** — c. 1.7 billion years ago (1,700 Ma)

  Nuclear fission ran in Africa long before anyone built a reactor. About 1.7 billion years ago, natural nuclear fission reactors were generating power in what is now Oklo, Gabon. Concentrated uranium deposits started reacting after groundwater flooded them, since water slows neutrons enough to keep a chain reaction going. The reactions ran on and off, probably never above 100 kilowatts.

  <!-- prot-052 -->

- **The Mazatzal orogeny** — c. 1.65–1.60 billion years ago (1,650–1,600 Ma)

  Southern North America grew by accretion, one island arc at a time. After the Yavapai collision, the Mazatzal island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona. It was the next pulse in the growth of southern Laurentia. Between the two orogenies, short-lived basins opened as the crust stretched, and they filled with quartzite, once quartz sand, and rhyolite, a pale volcanic rock.

  <!-- prot-054 -->

- **The first multicellular eukaryotes** — c. 1.63 billion years ago (1,630 Ma)

  Life was learning to build bodies from many cells. North China's Chuanlinggou Formation, in the Yan Mountains, preserves the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes: Qingshania, Tawuia and Changchengia. Qingshania, dated elsewhere to 1.7 billion years, appears to consist of nearly identical cells. Multicellular organisms with differentiated cells, performing specialized jobs, began to appear around 1.7 billion years ago. Multicellular eukaryotes probably evolved about 2–1.4 billion years ago, likely from colonies of single cells. Such finds show that Mesoproterozoic life was not purely microbial, as was once thought, even in the low-oxygen world of The Boring Billion.

  <!-- prot-055 -->

- **The Shoemaker impact structure** — c. 1.63 billion years ago (1,630 ± 5 Ma)

  Shatter cones and shocked quartz are the calling cards of an impact. Both turn up in Western Australia's Mid West, where a structure at least 30 km across marks an ancient strike. Its most cited age, about 1,630 million years, records a reheating of the granite. That reheating may date the impact, or only a regional tectonic event, so the impact's true age is uncertain.

  <!-- prot-056 -->

### Mesoproterozoic Era

The Mesoproterozoic is when the first algae turned sunlight into food. Around 1.6 billion years ago some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria and gained photosynthesis, and India's Chitrakoot Formation preserves the earliest known red algae. Oxygen may have risen briefly to about 4% of present levels. Columbia began to break apart, great igneous provinces flooded the continents, and in Africa a series of orogenies ran on until Rodinia was assembled about 1,000 million years ago.

#### Calymmian Period

The Calymmian is a period of new life and a fraying supercontinent. Eukaryotes took cyanobacteria inside their cells and became the first algae, and odd forms like Horodyskia, a string of beads on a thread, appeared. Oxygen may have pulsed briefly upward. Meanwhile Columbia began to fragment, rifts opened along the margins of Laurentia and other continents, and a deep rift basin on Laurentia's edge filled with the mud of the Belt Supergroup.

- **The earliest red algae** — c. 1.6 billion years ago (1,600 Ma)

  Red seaweed has a family tree reaching back 1.6 billion years. India's Chitrakoot Formation, in the Vindhya Range, preserves the earliest known red algae, Rafatazmia and Ramathallus. Algae are eukaryotes that make their own food by photosynthesis. The oldest known red algal mats date to about 1.6 billion years ago. They show that complex, sun-powered eukaryotes were already part of The Boring Billion.

  <!-- prot-057 -->

- **The Isan orogeny and Mount Isa's ores** — c. 1.6 billion years ago (1,600 Ma)

  One of the world's great metal mines owes its riches to mountain building. The Isan orogeny affected Queensland's Mount Isa Block about 1,600 million years ago, as large lead, silver, copper and zinc deposits were laid down. Mount Isa's lower lead–zinc–silver ore and upper copper ore lie in the 1,000 m thick Urquhart Shale, on one limb of a faulted fold. The belt is one of the 1.8–1.5-billion-year-old magmatic belts that grew along the North Australia Craton's margins.

  <!-- prot-059 -->

- **Eukaryotes capture cyanobacteria and become algae** — c. 1.6–1.5 billion years ago (1,600–1,500 Ma)

  Every green leaf on Earth contains the descendant of a captured microbe. Around 1.6 billion years ago, some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, partners living inside their cells. They gained oxygen-making photosynthesis through plastids, the organelles descended from those captured cells. This was the second great act of swallowing, after the one in The first eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus. The new partnership produced the algae. Over time, they overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers, the organisms that make food at the base of the food web. The fossil record follows. North China's Gaoyuzhuang Formation, about 1,589 million years old, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata. A diverse collection of fossil algae occurs in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 billion years. Red algae appear too, as in The earliest red algae.

  <!-- prot-058 -->

  *Figure: Algae arose when eukaryotes kept captured cyanobacteria as plastids.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Eukaryote cell] --> C[Endosymbiosis]
  B[Cyanobacterium] --> C
  C --> D[Plastid gives photosynthesis]
  D --> E[Algae]
  E --> F[Dominant primary producers]
  ```

- **A brief Mesoproterozoic rise in oxygen** — c. 1.59–1.36 billion years ago (1,590–1,360 Ma)

  In the middle of the long, oxygen-starved Boring Billion, oxygen may have briefly spiked. It is proposed to have risen at times to about 4% of present levels between 1.59 and 1.36 billion years ago. Gaoyuzhuang rocks in North China suggest a rise near 1.57 billion years ago. Formations in Australia, Russia and North China show oxygenation near 1.4 billion, though how global it was is unclear. Early in the Ectasian, about 50–80% of the seafloor was oxidized, a share that later declined. Otherwise, oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels, stalling complex life.

  <!-- prot-061 -->

- **The Volyn biota of Ukraine** — c. 1.5 billion years ago (1,500 Ma)

  Life may have lived inside solid rock 1.5 billion years ago. In what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rocks. They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms. They may be among the first fossils of the deep biosphere, the life that dwells within rock and sediment far below the surface.

  <!-- prot-064 -->

- **Columbia breaks apart** — c. 1.5–1.2 billion years ago (1,500–1,200 Ma)

  The supercontinent built over hundreds of millions of years came apart just as slowly. Columbia began to fragment about 1.5–1.35 billion years ago, with rifting along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China. Widespread magma rose far from any mountain belt, forming suites of anorthosite, mangerite, charnockite and granite in North America, Baltica, Amazonia and North China. Atlantica split from Nena, and North China broke away along the Zhaertai–Bayan Obo rift, where mafic sills record the event. Final breakup came about 1.3–1.2 billion years ago, marked by the 1.27-billion-year-old Mackenzie and 1.24-billion-year-old Sudbury dike swarms in North America. The fragments later reassembled into Rodinia assembles.

  <!-- prot-063 -->

  *Figure: Columbia came apart in stages, ending with great dike swarms in North America.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Horodyskia, a string of beads** — c. 1.48 billion years ago (1,480 Ma)

  One of the oldest complex organisms looks like a necklace. Horodyskia is a string of beads joined by a fine thread, and its fossils span 1,480 to 550 million years ago. It is one of the oldest known eukaryotes and ranks among the first structurally complex ones. Its identity is unsettled: it may have been an early animal, or a colonial foraminiferan, a single-celled organism that builds a shell.

  <!-- prot-065 -->

- **The Belt Basin fills** — c. 1.45–1.40 billion years ago (1,450–1,400 Ma)

  The peaks of Glacier National Park were once mud at the bottom of a basin. Much of the Belt Supergroup was laid down about 1450–1400 million years ago in a rift basin bounded by faults, on the edge of Laurentia within Columbia. Mostly fine mud, silt and sand piled up more than 15 km thick over some 200,000 km². The basin was probably closed or lake-like. Its rocks hold stromatolites and rich lead, zinc and silver ores.

  <!-- prot-066 -->

- **The Picuris orogeny and its granites** — c. 1.43–1.30 billion years ago (1,430–1,300 Ma)

  A fifth of the Precambrian rock exposed in New Mexico and the Rockies comes from one age of granite. From 1.43 to 1.3 billion years ago, mountain building struck what is now the southwestern United States. Its batholiths, huge bodies of once-molten rock about 1,400 million years old, make up over 20% of exposed Precambrian rock there. Much of the mid-continent is underlain by the 1,450–1,350-million-year-old Granite-Rhyolite crustal province.

  <!-- prot-067 -->

#### Ectasian Period

In the Ectasian, one supercontinent finished falling apart and the next began to form. A large igneous province about 1,380 million years ago marks Nuna's breakup, and from about 1,270 million years ago a massive igneous event spread across 2.7 million km² of the Canadian Shield. Fragments of the old supercontinent then began colliding to build Rodinia. Through it all, stromatolites reached their greatest abundance and diversity.

- **The Kibaran orogeny in Africa** — c. 1.4–1.0 billion years ago (1,400–1,000 Ma)

  Central Africa's mountain belts record a very long collision. A series of Kibaran orogenic events ran from about 1,400 million years ago until about 1,000 million, when Rodinia was assembled. From 1.4 to 1.2 billion years ago, it fused the Tanzanian and Congo cratons. In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 million years ago that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

  <!-- prot-068 -->

- **A superplume splits Columbia** — c. 1.38 billion years ago (1,380 Ma)

  The same flood of magma now lies scattered across five continents. A major large igneous province about 1,380 million years ago links Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, Congo and West Africa, and it formed as Nuna, or Columbia, broke up. Magma of the same age in Congo and Siberia shows those two stayed close for at least 120 million years. Metamafic rocks of 1.37–1.35 billion years suggest a superplume, a giant upwelling of hot mantle, drove Columbia's breakup.

  <!-- prot-069 -->

- **The Mackenzie Large Igneous Province** — 1.27 billion years ago (1,267 ± 2 Ma)

  About 3 million km³ of magma flooded the Canadian Shield in one event. Starting about 1,270 million years ago, it built a province of 2.7 million km², from Arctic Nunavut to the Great Lakes, linked to the Mackenzie hotspot. It includes three famous parts: the Muskox layered intrusion, the Coppermine River flood basalts and the huge Mackenzie dike swarm, whose cracks fan out across the shield. Those dikes mark the final breakup of Columbia, the last stage of Columbia breaks apart.

  <!-- prot-070 -->

- **Rodinia assembles** — c. 1.26–0.90 billion years ago (1,260–900 Ma)

  The broken pieces of one supercontinent came back together as another. Fragments of Columbia, scattered by Columbia breaks apart, accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago. Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, sat at its center. Around it, Rodinia grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks. Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies, between 1.1 and 0.9 billion years ago. A single global ocean, Mirovia, surrounded it. Later, the proto-Pacific Panthalassa grew at Mirovia's expense. For all its size, Rodinia remains shadowy. Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents. Its later breakup, in Rodinia breaks apart, would matter just as much as its assembly.

  <!-- prot-071 -->

  *Figure: The blocks gathered around Laurentia into Rodinia.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Stromatolites peak, then fall** — c. 1.25 billion years ago (1,250 Ma)

  For most of Earth's history, the most visible life was a mound of slime and sediment. Stromatolites, mounds built by microbial colonies, reached their greatest abundance and diversity about 1.25 billion years ago. Widespread colonies and reefs of cyanobacteria then dominated the tidal zones of oceans and seas. After that, they declined steeply, perhaps as predators began grazing on stromatolites and acritarchs. The decline sped up around 1 billion years ago, at the end of the Stenian, and grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation. By the start of the Cambrian they had fallen to 20% of their peak.

  <!-- prot-073 -->

- **The Grenville orogeny** — c. 1.25–0.98 billion years ago (1,250–980 Ma)

  The roots of the Appalachian Mountains go back more than a billion years. A long-lived mountain-building event, tied to the assembly of Rodinia, raised a belt from Labrador to Mexico and on to Scotland. Laurentia collided with other blocks, notably Amazonia, beginning the construction of what are now the Appalachians. Its main pulses were the Elzevirian (1240–1220 million years ago), Ottawan (1090–1020 million) and Rigolet (1010–980 million). From about 1190 to 980 million years ago, two continental blocks collided with Laurentia, folding mountains from Newfoundland to North Carolina. Crust of this age turns up worldwide, where the same events are called Kibaran in Africa, Dalslandian in western Europe and Sunsás in Brazil.

  <!-- prot-072 -->

  *Figure: The Grenville orogeny came in three main pulses.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Musgrave orogeny in central Australia** — c. 1.22–1.12 billion years ago (1,220–1,120 Ma)

  In the red center of Australia, a magma plume built a region of 220,000 km². This Musgrave Province was shaped by three orogenic events between 1.22 and 1.12 billion years ago. The Musgravian orogeny, about 1,200 million years ago, melted the lower crust and generated the voluminous Kulgera granites. The province is one of the many belts of crust formed or reworked as Rodinia came together.

  <!-- prot-074 -->

#### Stenian Period

The Stenian is the period of sex, failed rifts and growing supercontinents. Bangiomorpha, a red alga from Arctic Canada, carries the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction, and the earliest known fungus appears in shale nearby. In the middle of North America, the crust began to split along a rift 2,000 km long, then stopped. Mountain building in Scandinavia and the Grand Canyon's first layers record a world assembling Rodinia, while an impact in Scotland left its debris but no crater anyone has found.

- **The Stac Fada impact and its missing crater** — c. 1.2 billion years ago (1,200 Ma)

  An asteroid left its debris behind but hid its crater. The Stac Fada Member, a layer of rock, records an impact about 1.2 billion years ago. From that layer, geologists infer a crater about 40 km wide. Yet the crater itself has never been found, so the impact is known only from the debris it scattered.

  <!-- prot-077 -->

- **The Grand Canyon Supergroup** — c. 1.20–0.74 billion years ago (1,200–740 Ma)

  Deep in the Grand Canyon, tilted layers record an ancient seafloor. Nine formations of the Grand Canyon Supergroup were laid down in a sea between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago. The Chuar Group formed in coastal and shallow seas. Its oldest layer, averaging 1250 million years, is the oldest in the canyon with fossils, stromatolites. The Cardenas Basalt, 1070 ± 70 million years old, tops the Unkar Group. About 800 million years ago the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the supergroup 15° and broke it into fault blocks.

  <!-- prot-075 -->

- **The Sveconorwegian orogeny** — c. 1.14–0.96 billion years ago (1,140–960 Ma)

  Southern Norway and southwestern Sweden were remade during Rodinia's assembly. A mountain-building system was active there from 1140 to 960 million years ago. Its most active phase, 1050–980 million years ago, metamorphosed and thickened the crust. A collision between Amazonia and Baltica may have caused it. It is grouped with the Grenvillian orogens, such as The Grenville orogeny, that assembled Rodinia.

  <!-- prot-078 -->

- **The Midcontinent Rift, a split that failed** — c. 1.1 billion years ago (1,100 Ma)

  Lake Superior fills the valley of a rift that almost tore North America in two. About 1.1 billion years ago, the continent's core began to split apart, opening a rift 2,000 km long through its middle. Lava poured from cracks along the rift valley. Its arms meet at Lake Superior. The western arm runs through Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Nebraska, and the eastern arm reaches central Michigan. Then the rift failed. It left thick layers of igneous rock and became the deepest failed rift on Earth. Magmatism of about the same age struck Africa, India and South America.

  <!-- prot-080 -->

  *Figure: The failed Midcontinent Rift's two arms meet at Lake Superior.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Nonesuch lake fossils** — c. 1.08–1.07 billion years ago (1,083–1,070 Ma)

  A billion-year-old lake in Michigan held enough oxygen to keep its microbes in fine detail. The lake lay in the Midcontinent Rift, and its exceptionally preserved freshwater microbes make it a Lagerstätte, a site of unusually good fossils. Its shale, siltstone and sandstone, 150–210 m thick, extend from Michigan and Wisconsin to Iowa. It offers a rare look at life in fresh water, far from the sea.

  <!-- prot-082 -->

- **The Warakurna large igneous province** — 1.08 billion years ago (1,076 ± 6 Ma)

  Central Australia was flooded with magma about 1.08 billion years ago. The Warakurna large igneous province intruded the Giles Complex and Winburn granites and erupted the volcanic rocks of the Bentley Supergroup. Some have looked for a link to a 1110-million-year-old event in Africa, India and Amazonia. A link is possible but unlikely, so Warakurna appears to stand as its own event.

  <!-- prot-083 -->

- **Bangiomorpha, the first known sexual organism** — c. 1.05 billion years ago (1,047 Ma)

  The oldest evidence of sex comes from a tiny red seaweed in the Canadian Arctic. Bangiomorpha pubescens, a multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia. Its differentiated reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and of meiosis, the cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual set of genes. It is also the earliest known organism that certainly had differentiated, specialized cells. And it is the oldest belonging to a living phylum, one of the major branches of life. Why does it matter? Sex mixes the genes of two parents, so it increased genetic variation. That variation sped up evolution and the diversification of eukaryotes. The boom described in Eukaryotes diversify as acritarchs boom may owe something to this small alga.

  <!-- prot-084 -->

- **The Lakhanda Group fossils** — c. 1.03–1.00 billion years ago (1,030–1,000 Ma)

  Even a billion years ago, microbes were eating each other. The Lakhanda Group of Russia's Uchur-Maya Depression preserves a community dominated by anaerobic bacteria, microbes that live without oxygen. The fossils also show evidence of food-web interactions, organisms feeding on other organisms. That makes the site a Lagerstätte, an unusually rich fossil bed, and an early glimpse of an ecosystem with links between its members.

  <!-- prot-085 -->

- **Ourasphaira, the earliest known fungus** — c. 1.01–0.89 billion years ago (1,010–890 Ma)

  Mushrooms have a very long pedigree. Shale of the Grassy Bay Formation, in the Canadian Arctic, preserves Ourasphaira giraldae, multicellular organic-walled microfossils with fungal affinity. Dated to 1.01–0.89 billion years, it is the earliest known fungus. Older fossils, from 1.43 billion years ago, have also been interpreted as multicellular fungi with differentiated cells, so the group may be older still.

  <!-- prot-086 -->

### Neoproterozoic Era

The Neoproterozoic is the era in which life began to get big. Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, green algae became multicellular, and sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals. A second great rise in oxygen swept the air and oceans. Meanwhile Rodinia began to rift apart, island arcs built the Arabian-Nubian Shield, and the pieces of a new southern continent, Gondwana, started to come together.

#### Tonian Period

The Tonian is when eukaryotes finally stepped forward. They diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, dominated fresh water in Scotland's Torridon lakes, and by about 800 million years ago left fossils notably more complex and numerous. Oxygen began its second great rise, and the first possible animals appear as sponge-like fossils. Under it all, the supercontinent Rodinia started to break apart, opening new oceans as old ones closed.

- **Eukaryotes diversify as acritarchs boom** — c. 1 billion years ago (1,000 Ma)

  After a long, quiet career, eukaryotes suddenly bloomed. Around 1 billion years ago they diversified rapidly. Acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, boomed in abundance, diversity, size and shape in their first large radiation, growing more and longer spines. The spines may have been armor. The first dinoflagellates, some of which ate prey, may have been the first predators, pushing acritarchs into an arms race of defenses. Life got faster too. After 1 billion years ago, species lasted only about 100 million years, perhaps because early protists, single-celled eukaryotes, grazed more heavily.

  <!-- prot-087 -->

  *Figure: Early predators may have driven acritarchs into an arms race of defenses.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[First dinoflagellates eat prey] --> B[Acritarchs under attack]
  B --> C[More and longer spines]
  A --> D[Heavier grazing by protists]
  D --> E[Species last about 100 million years]
  ```

- **Eukaryotes take over fresh water** — c. 1 billion years ago (1,000 Ma)

  Lakes and rivers belonged to complex cells by a billion years ago. Abundant eukaryotic microfossils from Scotland's freshwater Torridon Group suggest eukaryotes dominated non-marine habitats by then, including multicellular forms. Nutrients from continental runoff probably favored them near the continents. Phosphatic microfossils from Scotland's Diabaig Formation, 994 ± 48 million years old, are among the oldest known non-marine eukaryotes. Molecular-clock evidence goes further. It suggests that photosynthetic, multicellular eukaryotes and fungi had moved onto land by 1000 million years ago.

  <!-- prot-088 -->

- **Proterocladus, the first multicellular green alga** — c. 1 billion years ago (1,000 Ma)

  Every land plant descends from green algae, and the oldest many-celled one is about 1 billion years old. Proterocladus antiquus is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae. Around this time, the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae. Where a colony of cells ends and a true multicellular organism begins is blurred. Still, Proterocladus shows green algae building bodies of many cells. They joined the red algae of Bangiomorpha, the first known sexual organism among the first seaweeds.

  <!-- prot-089 -->

- **The late Ruker orogeny under Antarctic ice** — c. 1 billion years ago (1,000 ± 150 Ma)

  Antarctica hides a mountain range beneath its ice, and it may be a billion years old. Around 1 billion years ago, a mountain-building event, also called the Nimrod orogeny, struck the continent. It may have begun the Gamburtsev mountain range and the Vostok Subglacial Highlands, hidden today beneath the ice. Its date is uncertain by about 150 million years either way.

  <!-- prot-090 -->

- **The Rayner orogeny joins India and Antarctica** — c. 1.0–0.9 billion years ago (1,000–900 Ma)

  Part of Antarctica is a continuation of India. Proto-India and Antarctica collided in the Rayner orogeny, from about 1,000 million years ago until about 900 million. Rocks of East Antarctica's Rayner Complex and northern Prince Charles Mountains are an extension of India's Eastern Ghats. They belong to a Grenville-age belt along East Antarctica's coast, read as a suture with southern Africa, India and western Australia.

  <!-- prot-091 -->

- **Bitter Springs microfossils** — c. 896–767 million years ago (896–767 Ma)

  Some fossils are so well preserved that their insides still show. Cherts of Australia's Bitter Springs Group preserve stromatolites and exceptionally well-preserved cyanobacteria in silica. Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae, among the earliest plants, though that claim is debated. This style of preservation ended in the late Neoproterozoic, when organisms that secrete silica appeared.

  <!-- prot-093 -->

- **The first possible animals** — c. 890 million years ago (890 Ma)

  The animal kingdom may have begun as something like a sponge on a reef. Sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals, but their identity is highly debated. The first putative animal fossils date to the middle to late Tonian, about 890–800 million years ago. Otavia, about 800 million years old, has been described as a primitive sponge. Molecular studies place the base of the animal family tree in the Tonian, though physical evidence for such early animals is lacking. Sponges, a basal animal group, emerged in the Tonian and survived the glaciations that followed.

  <!-- prot-094 -->

- **The Arabian-Nubian Shield begins** — c. 870–550 million years ago (870–550 Ma)

  The gold of the pharaohs came from rocks made by colliding island chains. From 870 million years ago, island arcs began building the Arabian-Nubian Shield as the Mozambique Ocean closed. Arc collisions and terrane suturing followed at 780 million years ago, with final assembly by 550 million. Gold mined in antiquity in Egypt and Sudan comes almost entirely from these Neoproterozoic rocks.

  <!-- prot-095 -->

- **The Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event** — c. 850–540 million years ago (850–540 Ma)

  Oxygen's second great rise prepared the world for animals. Called the Second Great Oxidation Event, it raised oxygen in the air and oceans about 850–540 million years ago. Marine rocks of 850–720 million years record a large positive carbon-isotope excursion, a sign that more organic carbon was being buried. The numbers are dramatic. During 900–815 million years ago, oxygen rose from under 0.1% of present levels to over 13%, and possibly to about 50% in the Cryogenian interglacial. Oxygen rose above 1% of the atmosphere for the first time. Air bubbles trapped in 813-million-year-old rock salt hold 10.9% oxygen. The change was uneven. It may have been one global event or a series of regional episodes. The deep ocean stayed anoxic and iron-rich as late as 580 million years ago. Still, the surge drove rapid evolution of multicellular life late in the era. Some authors credit it with letting the oxygen-hungry Ediacaran biota spread. It echoes, on a grander scale, The Great Oxidation Event.

  <!-- prot-096 -->

  *Figure: Oxygen climbed steeply during the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Huainan worms** — c. 840–740 million years ago (840–740 Ma)

  Some of the first creatures you could see without a microscope lived in what is now China. Near Huainan City, in Anhui, small worm-shaped organisms large enough to see with the naked eye record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 million years ago. A similar biota, about 1 billion years old, was found on Russia's Timan Ridge. Both hint that life was moving from microbes toward larger, more complex forms.

  <!-- prot-099 -->

- **The Adelaide Rift Complex opens** — c. 830 million years ago (830 Ma)

  One Australian basin holds a diary of the late Precambrian. Deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin began just before 830 million years ago, as Laurentia started to rift away from Australia. Its rift troughs and passive-margin basins kept developing until about 550 million years ago. Its rocks record Rodinia's breakup, two Snowball Earth glaciations, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation and the Ediacaran fauna.

  <!-- prot-100 -->

- **Eukaryotes grow more complex** — c. 800 million years ago (800 Ma)

  Around 800 million years ago, eukaryote fossils became notably more complex and numerous, as sulfide in the oceans fell. By about 750 million years ago, some small algae were mineralized, probably as armor against single-celled eukaryotic predators. The arms race of Eukaryotes diversify as acritarchs boom had moved on to hard shells. Yet persistent anoxia and euxinia, oxygen-free and sulfide-rich water, kept overall eukaryotic diversity low through the late Tonian.

  <!-- prot-102 -->

- **Cyanobacteria take to the open sea** — c. 800 million years ago (800 Ma)

  Tiny floating cells may have helped freeze the planet. Marine planktonic cyanobacteria, drifting in open water, first appeared about 800 million years ago, descended from seafloor and freshwater ancestors, and helped oxygenate the oceans. Their spread is thought to have sped oxygenation and the removal of carbon dioxide, helping explain the severe Cryogenian glaciations. Later, planktonic nitrogen fixers ended a long shortage of ammonium that had held back multicellular life.

  <!-- prot-104 -->

- **The Pharusian Ocean opens and closes** — c. 800 million years ago (800 Ma)

  As Rodinia tore apart, a new ocean opened along the edge of West Africa. Rifting along the eastern margin of the West African craton opened the Pharusian Ocean about 800 million years ago. It did not last. It began to close about 730 million years ago, as the Tilemsi arc, a chain of volcanoes, was subducted eastward against the Hoggar region.

  <!-- prot-105 -->

- **The East African Orogeny begins Gondwana** — c. 800–650 million years ago (800–650 Ma)

  Africa, India and Arabia were welded together along a single mountain belt. Gondwana, the great southern continent, began to form about 800–650 million years ago, as India and Madagascar collided with East Africa in the East African Orogeny. It was the main stage in joining East and West Gondwana along the Mozambique Belt, uniting Africa, India and Arabia. The Arabian-Nubian Shield collided with eastern Africa in the Kenya–Tanzania region. The Mozambique Ocean, between Madagascar–India and the Congo–Tanzania craton, began closing between 700 and 580 million years ago. In one model, arc accretion became a full continental collision when Azania struck the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block around 640 million years ago.

  <!-- prot-101 -->

- **The Kaigas glaciation that never was** — c. 750 million years ago (750 Ma)

  Sometimes a glaciation disappears from the textbooks. Conglomerates of the Kaigas Formation on the Kalahari Craton were once read as the mark of a Snowball Earth glaciation about 750 million years ago, before the Sturtian. Then the formation proved to be non-glacial. That leaves no evidence for any Neoproterozoic glaciation before the Sturtian, and the Kaigas glaciation is now rejected.

  <!-- prot-109 -->

- **Rodinia breaks apart** — c. 750–633 million years ago (750–633 Ma)

  The breakup of a supercontinent may have set off the coldest era in Earth's history. Rifting in Rodinia began as early as 850–800 million years ago, perhaps driven by a superplume. Most agree the breakup proper began about 750 million years ago, with eruptions on most continents. Rodinia split into Proto-Laurasia, the Congo craton and Proto-Gondwana. New oceans, such as the Adamastor and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa, opened as Mirovia closed. By 750 million years ago Gondwana had rotated away, leaving Laurentia isolated near the equator. When the breakup ended, about 600 million years ago, Baltica was left isolated for some 200 million years. Between 650 and 550 million years ago the Iapetus Ocean opened, and the Adamastor and Mozambique oceans closed, forming Gondwana, begun in The East African Orogeny begins Gondwana. The consequences reached far beyond geography. The breakup may have triggered the Cryogenian Snowball Earth and the rapid evolution of life that followed.

  <!-- prot-108 -->

  *Figure: Rodinia's breakup, from first rifting to the forming of Gondwana.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rifting begins 850 to 800 Ma] --> B[Breakup proper about 750 Ma]
  B --> C[Proto-Laurasia]
  B --> D[Congo craton]
  B --> E[Proto-Gondwana]
  E --> F[Iapetus opens, oceans close]
  F --> G[Gondwana forms]
  ```

#### Cryogenian Period

The Cryogenian is the age when the planet nearly froze solid. It opened with magma flooding more than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland, and soon after came a worldwide glaciation that lasted some 57 million years. The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that the surface froze nearly completely, twice, in the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations. Yet life did not stop. Shelled amoebae, sponges and seaweeds appear in these rocks, and red and green algae took over the ocean plankton.

- **Franklin magma floods the Arctic and cools the world** — 720–719 million years ago (719.9–718.6 Ma)

  More than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland vanished under magma in about two million years. The Franklin Large Igneous Province, a vast outpouring of basalt lava, ranks among the largest magmatic episodes in Earth's history. Uranium-lead dating puts its rapid emplacement at about 719.9 and 718.6 Ma. Together with the Irkutsk province in Siberia, it marks where Siberia rifted away from Laurentia. Its effect on climate was swift. As fresh basalt weathered, it drew carbon dioxide out of the air, and glaciation began just 0.9–1.6 million years after the lava cooled.

  <!-- prot-110 -->

  *Figure: Follow the chain from flood basalt to ice.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Franklin magma floods the Arctic] --> B[Fresh basalt weathers]
  B --> C[Carbon dioxide drawn down]
  C --> D[Glaciation begins]
  ```

- **The Sturtian: fifty-seven million years of ice** — c. 717–660 million years ago (717–660 Ma)

  Ice at or below sea level, on a continent near the equator: that is the evidence that the Sturtian glaciation was global. It lasted from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years. It was the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages and the longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian. The supercontinent Rodinia then straddled the equator, yet its glaciers reached the shore. The cold arrived only 0.9–1.6 million years after Franklin magma floods the Arctic and cools the world erupted. One explanation joins the two: weathering of fresh basalt pulled carbon dioxide from the air, while Rodinia's breakup left mid-ocean ridges releasing little of it. In the snowball episodes, ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures near −50 °C. How far the ice reached is still debated. It may have been a Snowball Earth, with ice at very low latitudes. It may instead have been several regional glaciations, or a slushball with open water at the equator. That the glaciation happened is not in dispute.

  <!-- prot-112 -->

  *Figure: Possible causes of the Sturtian cold after Rodinia's breakup.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rodinia breaks up] --> B[Basalt weathering]
  A --> C[Low ridge CO2 output]
  B -.-> D[Sturtian glaciation]
  C -.-> D
  ```

- **Snowball Earth: did the whole planet freeze** — c. 717–635 million years ago (717–635 Ma)

  Glacial deposits laid down in the tropics turn up on every continent. Glaciers once reached sea level near the equator. From this comes the Snowball Earth hypothesis: that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most often linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian. Not everyone accepts the full freeze. The glaciation itself is accepted, but scientists still dispute whether ice covered the whole planet or left a slushball, with an open band of water around the equator. Either way, life struggled. Thick ice blocking sunlight would have severely hindered primary production, the growth of algae and other organisms that make food from light, in shallow seas. The trigger is thought to lie in Rodinia's breakup. The same breakup is linked to the rapid evolution of the Ediacaran and Cambrian. The frozen world sits right before the great burst of complex life.

  <!-- prot-111 -->

  *Figure: The two disputed versions of a Cryogenian frozen Earth.*

  | Version | Ocean surface |
  |---|---|
  | Full snowball | Froze nearly completely |
  | Slushball | Open equatorial band of water |

- **Shelled amoebae appear in the ice age** — c. 700 million years ago (700 Ma)

  Single cells began building houses around 700 Ma. Fossils of testate amoebae, or Arcellinida, single-celled organisms with shells, first appear then, in the middle of the Cryogenian. They were not alone. Porter (2000) suggests red and green algae, stramenopiles, ciliates and dinoflagellates also evolved during this period, so the ice age was a time of new microbial branches.

  <!-- prot-113 -->

- **A warm pause between two snowballs** — c. 660–650 million years ago (660–650 Ma)

  Between the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations came a relatively warm interval. Seas rose and the oceans were anoxic, short of dissolved oxygen. Global biodiversity stayed very low. Oxygen may have reached about 50% of present levels, though chromium isotopes suggest oxygenation was slow and subdued, a lull in the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.

  <!-- prot-115 -->

- **Island arcs crash into Gondwana's northern edge** — c. 660–540 million years ago (660–540 Ma)

  As the Sturtian glaciers retreated, chains of volcanic islands began colliding with the margin of future Gondwana. The collisions laid down the terranes, crustal blocks, of Avalonia, Armorica and Iberia. An Andean-type volcanic arc formed about 650–600 Ma. Behind it a basin opened 590–560 Ma and closed again 545–540 Ma, while the Avalonian belt struck Gondwana around 650 Ma.

  <!-- prot-114 -->

- **Algae seize the ocean's plankton** — c. 659–645 million years ago (659–645 Ma)

  Algae multiplied a hundred to a thousandfold. About 659–645 Ma, red and green algae replaced planktonic cyanobacteria as the main marine phytoplankton, the drifting organisms at the base of the ocean food web. Unicellular algae diversified rapidly, and they kept that role until the Permian extinction. The change rippled upward. Late in the Cryogenian, heterotrophic plankton appeared, drifting organisms that fed on algae and prokaryotes rather than making their own food. Bacteria had ruled the oceans for ages; now their dominance was over.

  <!-- prot-116 -->

  *Figure: Each change in the plankton opened the way for the next.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Planktonic cyanobacteria dominate] --> B[Red and green algae take over]
  B --> C[Heterotrophic plankton feed on algae]
  C --> D[Bacterial dominance ends]
  ```

- **Sponges survive the snowball** — c. 650 million years ago (650 Ma)

  Sponges came through the Cryogenian glaciations alive. They had emerged in the Tonian, and demosponges appear around 650 Ma, building skeletons of spicules, tiny struts made of spongin protein and silica. The oldest fossils are another matter. Some researchers argue that the oldest sponge fossils, and so the oldest animal fossils, are Cryogenian. Others think they may be proto-sponges or microbial structures, and the question is unsettled. Even the oldest sponge spicules, about 580 Ma from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are challenged. Sponges that are unmistakably sponges, such as the non-mineralized Helicolocellus, appear only in the latest Ediacaran.

  <!-- prot-117 -->

- **Songluo seaweeds in a break from the ice** — c. 650 million years ago (650 Ma)

  In a short break in the Marinoan glaciation, around 650 Ma, large seaweeds grew in what is now South China. These macroalgae fossils form the Songluo Biota. It is the only known macrofossil biota from the Cryogenian, the first large carbonaceous fossils found in rocks of that age.

  <!-- prot-118 -->

- **The Marinoan, the last great snowball** — c. 639–635 million years ago (639–635 Ma)

  The Marinoan glaciation is described as the most significant snowball Earth event, global in scope. Also called the Varanger or Elatina glaciation, it came late in the Cryogenian. Diamictites, jumbled glacial rubble, record it in South Australia's Adelaide Geosyncline. Its timing is poorly constrained; a 2025 study dates it to 639–635 Ma. The thaw came from the planet's own chemistry. Volcanic carbon dioxide and dissolving clathrates, gas trapped in ice, ended it, perhaps hastened by methane from permafrost near the equator. It was the last major snowball. Later ice ages covered less of the planet.

  <!-- prot-119 -->

#### Ediacaran Period

The Ediacaran begins at a layer of limestone laid directly on top of the last great glacial deposits. What follows is a world in motion: mountains rose in Antarctica, Australia and the Baltic Shield, and the Pan-African orogeny welded continents into Gondwana. A mantle plume pushed Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean. By about 600 Ma enough oxygen had built up to form an ozone layer. In the rocks of South China appear embryo-like animals and some of the oldest large, complex fossils known.

- **Cap carbonates seal the last snowball** — c. 635 million years ago (635 Ma)

  Glacial rubble, then suddenly limestone. Across the world, Neoproterozoic glacial deposits are commonly capped by a sharply overlying layer of precipitated limestone or dolomite, metres to tens of metres thick. The Ediacaran Period itself begins at one: the Nuccaleena Formation, directly above Elatina glacial deposits in South Australia's Flinders Ranges. A favored explanation runs like this. After a snowball, carbon-dioxide-rich acid rain weathered rock and washed calcium into the sea, where it settled as carbonate layers. The glacial link is questioned, though: some caps are too thick for a rapid thaw, and many glacial sequences lack them. The boundary also marks the start of a distinctive pattern of carbon-isotope changes.

  <!-- prot-120 -->

  *Figure: The favored explanation links the thaw to the limestone cap.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Snowball ends] --> B[CO2-rich acid rain]
  B --> C[Rock weathers]
  C --> D[Calcium washes into sea]
  D --> E[Cap carbonate forms]
  ```

- **Big, spiny microfossils replace the old plankton** — c. 635–575 million years ago (635–575 Ma)

  Plankton that had changed little for ages largely died out as the Ediacaran began. Larger, shorter-lived acritarchs, microfossils of uncertain origin, replaced them. From 635 to about 575 Ma, ornamented forms usually over 100 μm across dominated. They largely vanish before 560 Ma, about when the Ediacara biota arose. If they were animal resting stages, they fit the frequent anoxia of the Ediacaran.

  <!-- prot-121 -->

- **Beardmore mountains rise in Antarctica** — c. 633–620 million years ago (633–620 Ma)

  A supercontinent's pieces began drifting home. From about 633 to 620 Ma, the Beardmore orogeny, a mountain-building episode, raised ranges in Antarctica. It reflects the final breakup of Rodinia. As that supercontinent came apart, its fragments started moving back together, toward a new assembly called Pannotia.

  <!-- prot-122 -->

- **The Petermann orogeny raises the rocks of Uluru** — c. 630–520 million years ago (630–520 Ma)

  Uluru owes its rise to a collision far away. Between 630 and 520 Ma, the Petermann orogeny deformed central Australia's Musgrave basement and Amadeus Basin sediments, mountain building in the middle of a continent. Its belt runs unusually east to west, suggesting India struck Western Australia from the northwest as Gondwana assembled. It thrust up the rocks that now form Uluru, laid down around 550–530 Ma.

  <!-- prot-123 -->

- **Tidal layers record a 21.9-hour day** — c. 620 million years ago (620 Ma)

  About 620 Ma a day lasted 21.9 ± 0.4 hours, and a year held about 400 days and 13.1 lunar months. The record comes from tidal rhythmites, layers of sand and silt laid down off estuaries with strong tides, which preserve daily, monthly and seasonal cycles. Tides slow Earth's spin as the Moon recedes. Since then the Moon has moved away an average of 2.17 cm a year, about half today's rate.

  <!-- prot-124 -->

- **The Timanide orogeny, Precambrian's last mountain belt** — c. 620–550 million years ago (620–550 Ma)

  From about 620 to 550 Ma, the Timanide orogeny reshaped the northern Baltic Shield. It is called the last major orogenic event of the Precambrian. Around 555 Ma, Baltica's northern margin turned active and gathered in new crust: the Timan-Pechora Basin, the northern Urals and Novaya Zemlya.

  <!-- prot-125 -->

- **Weng'an: embryos turned to stone** — c. 609–570 million years ago (609–570 Ma)

  Embryo-like animals, preserved in three dimensions, lie in calcium phosphate in China's Weng'an biota, 609–570 Ma. Its richest layer postdates the Gaskiers glaciation. The rocks belong to the Doushantuo Formation, which spans about 635–551 Ma and bridges the poorly known time between the Cryogenian and the Avalon explosion. Among its finds is Caveasphaera, a 609-million-year-old multicellular organism that may record one of the earliest steps in animal evolution.

  <!-- prot-126 -->

- **Lantian: seaweeds and possible cnidarians** — c. 602 million years ago (602 ± 7 Ma)

  Some of the oldest large, complex fossils known come from the Lantian Biota of South China, dated by the rhenium-osmium method to 602 ± 7 Ma. It includes macroalgae and fossils that may be cnidarian-grade animals. Even older macrofossils, the Ancanping assemblage of about 620–610 Ma, occur in the Doushantuo Formation.

  <!-- prot-127 -->

- **A mantle plume splits Laurentia from Baltica** — c. 600 million years ago (600 Ma)

  A plume of hot mantle rock, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean between them. Rifting began with the Egersund dike swarm in Norway around 650 Ma. From 600 Ma the two continents rotated by up to 180°. The ocean opened in stages. Its eastern part opened around 590 Ma, and its southern arm, between Laurentia and South America, about 550 Ma. The Tornquist Sea, between Avalonia and Baltica, probably formed at the same time. Bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents, the Iapetus lasted from about 600 to 425 Ma in the Southern Hemisphere.

  <!-- prot-128 -->

  *Figure: The Iapetus opened in stages, oldest first.*

  | Ma | Event |
  |---|---|
  | 650 | Egersund dikes: rifting begins |
  | 600 | Laurentia and Baltica start rotating |
  | 590 | Eastern Iapetus opens |
  | 550 | Southern arm opens |
  | 425 | Ocean ends |

- **The ozone shield goes up** — c. 600 million years ago (600 Ma)

  Sunlight was dangerous before about 600 Ma. Until then, any life on land probably needed other chemicals to screen out ultraviolet radiation. Atmospheric oxygen stood between 1% and 18% of present levels at 800 Ma. Around 600 Ma it began rising more significantly, and enough had accumulated to form an ozone layer, the high gas that filters ultraviolet light.

  <!-- prot-129 -->

- **The Pan-African orogeny welds Gondwana together** — c. 600 million years ago (600 Ma)

  Africa was built in collisions. The Pan-African orogeny, a series of major mountain-building events, assembled the supercontinents Gondwana and Pannotia about 600 Ma. It began around 635 Ma, when the West African and Saharan cratons, the old stable cores of continents, collided and closed the Pharusian Ocean. By about 600 Ma most of western Gondwana had joined, though Australia and East Antarctica were still separate. All the African cratons were in place by about 550 Ma. The result lasted. Gondwana remained one landmass from about 600 Ma until Pangaea broke up in the Early Jurassic.

  <!-- prot-130 -->

  *Figure: Gondwana came together in stages, oldest first.*

  | Ma | Step |
  |---|---|
  | 635 | West African and Saharan cratons collide |
  | 600 | Most of western Gondwana joined |
  | 550 | All African cratons assembled |

- **Pannotia, a supercontinent that may never have been** — c. 600–560 million years ago (600–560 Ma)

  Pannotia may have been a supercontinent for only about 50 million years. Also called Greater Gondwana, it is proposed to have formed around 600 Ma during the Pan-African orogeny. It broke up about 560 Ma as the Iapetus Ocean opened, with Laurentia rifting from South America around 565 Ma. Whether it ever fully existed is debated. A 2022 paper argues it began breaking apart before it was fully assembled. Its breakup, real or partial, came with rising seas, dramatic changes in climate and ocean chemistry, and rapid animal diversification.

  <!-- prot-131 -->

- **The Acraman impact strikes South Australia** — c. 590 million years ago (590 Ma)

  About 590 Ma, a chondritic impactor, a stony meteorite, struck what is now the Gawler Ranges of South Australia. The age comes from its ejecta in nearby basins. The crater has eroded, and estimates of its original size range from 35–40 km to 85–90 km. The larger figure implies an explosion of 5.2 million megatons of TNT. Its debris travelled far. An ejecta layer with shocked minerals and an iridium anomaly lies in Flinders Ranges rocks at least 300 km east. Just above that layer begins a radiation of acritarch microorganisms, and some authors suspect a link.

  <!-- prot-132 -->

- **Cnidarians: the first animals everyone accepts** — c. 580 million years ago (580 Ma)

  The earliest widely accepted animal fossils look surprisingly modern. They are cnidarians, possibly about 580 Ma, though the Doushantuo fossils are only roughly dated. Their presence means the cnidarian and bilaterian lineages had already split well over 580 Ma. Animals may be older still. Microfossils from 632.5 Ma, just after the Cryogenian ice, may be embryonic resting stages of the earliest known animals.

  <!-- prot-134 -->

- **The Damara orogeny closes the Adamastor Ocean** — c. 580–550 million years ago (580–550 Ma)

  Between 580 and 550 Ma the Damara orogeny stitched the Congo–São Francisco and Río de la Plata cratons together, forming northern Gondwana with India. The Adamastor Ocean closed from north to south, from the Araçuaí Belt to the Kaoko Belt. In Brazil, the Ribeira Belt collision did most of its deformation 590–563 Ma.

  <!-- prot-133 -->

- **Gaskiers, a short and sharp ice age** — 580 million years ago (579.9–579.6 Ma)

  In about 250,000 years, 579.88–579.63 Ma, glacial deposits formed across eight paleocontinents, some at only 10–30° latitude. This was the Gaskiers glaciation, the last major glacial event of the Proterozoic. It was the shortest of at least three Neoproterozoic ice ages, and unlike the Sturtian and Marinoan, probably not a Snowball Earth. Its deposits lie just below some of the oldest Ediacaran fossils, though a 9-million-year gap separates them. A proposed scheme would place the base of an Upper Ediacaran series at this glaciation.

  <!-- prot-135 -->

- **The Avalon explosion: big life arrives** — c. 575 million years ago (575 Ma)

  Some 36 million years before the Cambrian explosion, life got big. A proposed burst of evolution about 575 Ma, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota. These were large, mostly soft-bodied organisms, often fixed in place, shaped like tubes and fronds. They are the earliest known complex multicellular life. The diversity of metazoans, many-celled animals, rose quickly, and the first cnidarians and bilaterians joined them. Yet the newcomers are hard to classify. Their place in the tree of life is unclear, and it is not even established that most of them were animals. The explosion's definition is itself contested. A 2008 analysis of shape diversity gave the event its name, and that analysis has been disputed; the Ediacaran biota itself is not. Most of these organisms died out in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 Ma.

  <!-- prot-136 -->

- **The Shuram excursion, carbon's biggest swing** — c. 573–562 million years ago (573–562 Ma)

  The largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth's history took 50 million years to recover. The Shuram excursion is a shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in Ediacaran rocks, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation. Its timing is debated: it began around 573 Ma and ended around 562 or 551 Ma. Diagenesis, chemical change after burial, may exaggerate it. No one knows what caused it. The oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, apparently exploiting a surplus of oxidants. It may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

  <!-- prot-137 -->

- **Charnia, the fossil that opened the Precambrian** — c. 570–550 million years ago (570–550 Ma)

  Charnia was the first Precambrian fossil recognized as such, found in England's Charnwood Forest. It was a frond, with leaf-like ridges branching alternately from a zig-zag midline, living on deep sea floors 570–550 Ma. It is among the most iconic Ediacaran forms, and among the hardest to place in the tree of life.

  <!-- prot-138 -->

- **The first burrows: animals start to move** — c. 567 million years ago (567.3 Ma)

  Something began crawling about 575–560 Ma. Mobile organisms left the earliest trails, moving on and just beneath the microbial mats that carpeted the sea floor. These Ediacaran traces are simple, near-horizontal feeding trails. The first widely accepted burrows come from the lower Blueflower Formation, about 567.3 Ma. The movers grew more complex. Bilaterians, animals with a left and right side, were present by 555 Ma. By 551 Ma an animal with leg-like appendages was leaving tracks in mud.

  <!-- prot-139 -->

- **Mistaken Point: a deep-sea community under ash** — c. 565 million years ago (565 ± 3 Ma)
