  Volcanic ash buried the sea floor at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, and preserved its life in fine detail. The ash dates the fossils to 565 ± 3 Ma. The site holds one of the most diverse and best-preserved collections of Precambrian fossils. It defines the deep-water Avalon assemblage, the oldest locality rich in Ediacaran fossils, some of which survive to the base of the Cambrian.

  <!-- prot-140 -->

- **A failing magnetic field and a young inner core** — c. 565 million years ago (565 Ma)

  Rocks formed about 565 Ma record a geomagnetic field that was unusually weak and pointed in two distinct directions. Reversals were frequent then. One reading is that Earth's solid inner core was only beginning to form, an idea that new Cambrian data appear to support. A 2016 dynamo model predicted a weak field from 1.0 to 0.6 Ga and a strong one after the core began to freeze. The inner core's age remains unresolved, with estimates from 0.5 to 2 billion years.

  <!-- prot-141 -->

- **The earliest possible arthropods** — c. 560 million years ago (560 Ma)

  Arthropods, the jointed-legged animals, may date to about 560 Ma. Ediacaran forms such as Spriggina, Parvancorina and Yilingia have been interpreted as arthropods, though the link is debated, especially for Parvancorina. Embryos 543 million years old suggest that aspects of arthropod development arose in the late Proterozoic.

  <!-- prot-142 -->

- **White Sea and Ediacara Hills: crowded sea floors** — c. 560–550 million years ago (560–550 Ma)

  One bed on Russia's White Sea coast holds the highest diversity of Ediacaran fossils found, with real ecological complexity. The White Sea biota flourished from 560 to 550 Ma. In South Australia lie the Ediacara Hills, the type locality that names the period. They preserve abundant fossils of about 555 Ma, like a community of the same age in Sonora, Mexico.

  <!-- prot-143 -->

- **Dickinsonia, a quilted disc that left trails** — c. 558 million years ago (558 Ma)

  Dickinsonia was a large, slow-moving disc with a quilted surface, first appearing about 558 Ma. In 2018, cholesterol found in its fossils was taken as evidence that it was an early animal, though the molecule may instead point to fungi or red algae. Its fossils often lie at the end of trails matching its shape, perhaps left while it fed.

  <!-- prot-144 -->

- **Kimberella grazes the sea floor** — c. 555 million years ago (555 Ma)

  Kimberella left scratch marks, perhaps from a radula, a rasping tongue, beside a grazing trail called Kimberichnus. It crawled and fed on the sea floor from about 555 Ma. Some call it mollusc-like; others say only that it was probably a bilaterian with three tissue layers. If it was mollusc-like, the two great branches of bilaterian animals split well before 550 Ma.

  <!-- prot-145 -->

- **Dengying: the last snapshot before the Phanerozoic** — c. 551–543 million years ago (551–543 Ma)

  Several sites in China's Dengying Formation, dated 551–543 Ma, preserve life just before the Phanerozoic. The Jiangchuan biota is dominated by giant thallophytes, simple plant-like organisms, but contains animals similar to later Cambrian sites. At Gaojiashan, fossils turned to pyrite record how the tubes of Cloudina grew.

  <!-- prot-146 -->

- **Cloudina builds the first animal skeletons** — c. 550 million years ago (550 Ma)

  Holes drilled through tiny tubes prove that something was hunting by the late Ediacaran. The tubes belonged to Cloudina, one of the cloudinids, an early animal family that lived about 550 Ma. Cloudina, Namacalathus and a dozen other organisms built mineralized tubes in carbonate rocks 549–542 Ma. They are among the earliest and most abundant small shelly fossils with mineral skeletons. Why build a skeleton then? Rising oxygen lowered ocean acidity and raised seawater calcium around the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, which may have prompted it. Predatory borings are common in Cloudina tubes, so predation was at least present. The cloudinids died out at the base of the Cambrian.

  <!-- prot-147 -->

  *Figure: Changing sea chemistry may have prompted the first skeletons.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rising oxygen] --> B[Lower ocean acidity]
  A --> C[More seawater calcium]
  B --> D[Skeleton-building]
  C --> D
  ```

- **The Proto-Tethys Ocean opens** — c. 550 million years ago (550 Ma)

  The Proto-Tethys Ocean lasted from the latest Ediacaran to the Carboniferous, about 550–330 Ma. It lay between Baltica and Laurentia to the north and Gondwana to the south. After the Cadomian events, it formed the eastern part of an ocean system that was sinking, or subducting, beneath Gondwana's northern margin.

  <!-- prot-150 -->

- **A supermountain feeds the Cambrian explosion** — c. 550 million years ago (550 Ma)

  A mountain range more than 8,000 km long and 1,000 km wide rose as the East African Orogeny raised the Transgondwanan Supermountain. Erosion tore it down. Its debris built the Gondwana Super-fan, over 100 million km³ of sediment laid down over 260 million years. That flood of sediment coincided with the Cambrian explosion and probably helped early animals diversify. By the Ordovician, the great range had been worn down to a plain in what is now Ethiopia.

  <!-- prot-151 -->

- **Nama: the thin last chapter of the Ediacaran** — c. 550–539 million years ago (550–539 Ma)

  By the end of the Ediacaran, no more than a dozen of 92 possible modes of life were occupied. The Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran biotic interval, about 550–539 Ma, was depauperate, short of species. It never regained the diversity lost as the White Sea biota gave way. Namibia's Nama Group sites preserve Rangea, erniettomorphs and true animals from shallow seas shaped by tides, storms and deltas.

  <!-- prot-149 -->

- **The Malagasy orogeny: India joins Africa** — c. 550–515 million years ago (550–515 Ma)

  India rammed into Africa in the Malagasy orogeny, a collision that ran from the Ediacaran into the Cambrian. It struck a block already joined from Azania and the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block. The collision deformed Madagascar, eastern East Africa and southern India about 550–515 Ma, adding another seam to assembling Gondwana.

  <!-- prot-148 -->

- **The Baykonurian, a late Ediacaran ice age** — c. 547–540 million years ago (547–540 Ma)

  Ice returned late in the Ediacaran. The Baykonurian glaciation lasted from around 547 to 540 Ma. Its deposits occur in Asia and Africa, and it apparently affected both hemispheres. It has been proposed as one contributor to the Cambrian explosion that followed.

  <!-- prot-153 -->

- **Trail-makers grow longer and sense farther** — c. 540 million years ago (540 Ma)

  By the terminal Ediacaran, the animals that left trails had bodies over eight times longer than wide. They grew steadily more elongate. Their trails formed tighter, more accurate loops, and around 540 Ma their sensory range grew from millimetres or centimetres to decimetres. Some of the behavioral and sensory novelties credited to the Cambrian may therefore have begun in the last stretch of the Ediacaran.

  <!-- prot-154 -->

- **The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen floods with magma** — c. 540 million years ago (540 Ma)

  Roughly 250,000 km³ of magma spread over about 40,000 km² of what is now Oklahoma. The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen, a failed arm of a continental rift, formed between 525 and 550 Ma as Laurentia split. Its other two arms became spreading zones of the young Iapetus Ocean. Its flood basalts began or peaked around 540 Ma and are linked to an end-Ediacaran event. The magma came in two phases, first gabbro and then rhyolite.

  <!-- prot-155 -->

- **The end-Ediacaran extinction clears the stage** — 539 million years ago (538.8 ± 0.2 Ma)

  Very few organisms crossed the line. The end-Ediacaran extinction, also called the Kotlin Crisis, is a mass extinction near the close of the Ediacaran, the last period of the Proterozoic. It swept away the old world. Acritarch diversity fell sharply. The soft-bodied Ediacaran biota disappeared, and so did the shelled Cloudina and Namacalathus. Both groups vanish abruptly, at 538.8 ± 0.2 Ma. Because the soft and the shelled went together, their loss cannot simply reflect a closing window of preservation. The chemistry of the sea shifted too. A major negative carbon-isotope excursion marks the boundary, and in Oman it coincides with the last Namacalathus and Cloudina. The survivors' descendants inherited an emptied world. Cambrian animals radiated into the vacant niches.

  <!-- prot-156 -->

  *Figure: The Ediacaran biota vanished and Cambrian animals filled the gap.*

  ```mermaid

  A[Ediacaran biota disappears] --> B[Few cross the boundary]
  B --> C[Niches left vacant]
  C --> D[Cambrian animals radiate]
  ```

## Phanerozoic Eon

The Phanerozoic is the eon of visible animal life, and it begins with a burrow. A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, marks its base, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows. From about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly and produced the first members of most modern animal phyla. Seas rose, continents collided, and the chemistry of the ocean swung between oxygen-rich and oxygen-starved. Everything that follows, from trilobites to the present, belongs to this one eon.

### Paleozoic Era

The Paleozoic, the era of ancient life, opens at the same burrowed layer as the Phanerozoic itself. In its first period, sea level began a long, gradual rise, and shallow seas crept over the continents. Tiny mineral tubes, spicules and plates, often only millimetres long, record the first animals to build hard parts. Mountains rose on Gondwana's western margin while the Kalahari and Mawson cratons joined to complete its south. This era carries life from the first shelly seafloor to the eve of the dinosaurs.

#### Cambrian Period

Few stretches of time changed life as much as the Cambrian. Beginning about 538.8 Ma, animals diversified suddenly, and the first members of most modern phyla appeared. An asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now Estonia, and the first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma. Under the seafloor, carbon and pyrite were buried in waters short of oxygen, and the chemistry of the sea rose and fell with each pulse. The period is the stage on which the animal kingdom took its modern shape.

##### Terreneuvian Epoch

The Terreneuvian is the Cambrian's first epoch, named for Newfoundland, where Fortune Head marks its base. Its rocks hold small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes and plates, in a nearly continuous record. Gondwana completed its southern half as the Kalahari and Mawson cratons met. Carbon and sulphur isotopes trace pulses of oxygen that spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas. Around 529 Ma a carbon spike and two new molluscs mark the epoch's first internal boundary.

- **Fortune Head: where the Cambrian begins** — 539 million years ago (538.8 ± 0.6 Ma)

  A burrow marks the start of the Cambrian. At Fortune Head, Newfoundland, a rock section serves as the formal base of the period, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows. That trace fossil is linked to early priapulid worms. When finds turned up a few metres below the boundary, geologists began using its whole trace assemblage instead. Modern radiometric dating puts the boundary at 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; in 2022 the age was revised from 541 Ma. It opens the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon, and now lies below the first trilobites and small shelly fossils. Several chemical markers show a drastic change in the environment around this time.

  <!-- camb-001 -->

- **The Cambrian explosion** — c. 539–521 million years ago (538.8–521 Ma)

  In about 20–25 million years, life went from a handful of body plans to nearly all of today's. Beginning about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly and produced the first representatives of most modern animal phyla. This is the Cambrian explosion. Its rate of diversification is unmatched among marine animals, though how explosive it really was is still debated. Animals changed in every way at once. They gained mineralized skeletons, more complex bodies and more complex behavior. They began to burrow, churning the sea floor and opening new ecosystems below it. Oxygen may have lit the fuse. Molybdenum isotopes tie rising early Cambrian biodiversity to the spread of oxygenated bottom waters, which supports oxygen as a driver. The burst did not last forever. Its high evolutionary rates had ended by 521 Ma, when Trilobites arrive with calcite eyes.

  <!-- camb-002 -->

  *Figure: Two drivers of the Cambrian explosion and what they changed.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Oxygenated bottom waters spread] --> B[Biodiversity rises]
  C[Animals begin burrowing] --> D[Sea floor changes]
  D --> E[New ecosystems open]
  ```

- **Orthid brachiopods open their shells** — during the Early Cambrian, 539–506 million years ago (538.8–506.5 Ma)

  Orthida, an order of brachiopods, shelled animals that look like clams but are not, appeared in the Early Cambrian, in the Botomian. They began to differentiate late in the Early Cambrian. By the late Cambrian they had diversified into many forms, 2–5 cm wide. In the shelf seas of the Ordovician they became very diverse.

  <!-- camb-007 -->

- **Small shelly fossils: the first hard parts** — c. 539–506 million years ago (538.8–506.5 Ma)

  Most are only millimetres long: mineralized tubes, spicules and plates. These small shelly fossils form a nearly continuous record from the latest Ediacaran to the end of the Early Cambrian. Graham Budd's scheme divides them into worlds. A Tube world ran from 550 to 536 Ma; a Sclerite world of halkieriids, tommotiids and hyoliths ended about 525 Ma. The record matters because it is fairly continuous. It shows phyla appearing in a rapid but orderly sequence, not a sudden jumble. Marks of selective predator attacks suggest predation helped drive new species. Most were thought wiped out in the end-Botomian extinction, but their apparent disappearance may partly reflect the loss of phosphate preservation.

  <!-- camb-010 -->

- **The Cambrian sea rises over the continents** — c. 539–487 million years ago (538.8–486.9 Ma)

  As the Cambrian began, the sea started to rise, and it kept rising gradually through the whole period. This marine transgression was the second-greatest sustained sea-level rise of the Phanerozoic, driven as the climate grew warmer. Shallow seas spread across flat, eroded surfaces such as the sub-Cambrian peneplain and the Great Unconformity, burying them under marine sediments. Water covered Baltica and much of Antarctica, and marine invertebrates flourished in the shallows. In North America this Sauk transgression began in earnest only in the middle Cambrian.

  <!-- camb-004 -->

- **The Neugrund impact strikes Estonia** — c. 535 million years ago (535 Ma)

  Around 535 Ma, an asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now the Gulf of Finland, off Estonia. Accounts of the crater differ: the Cambrian page describes a complex crater about 20 km wide with inner ridges, while the Neugrund page gives 8 km. It was once dated to the Ordovician, around 470 Ma, before newer research gave it a Cambrian age.

  <!-- camb-013 -->

- **The Pampean orogeny builds Gondwana's western edge** — c. 535–520 million years ago (535–520 Ma)

  Long before the Andes, mountains rose on Gondwana's western margin. The Pampean orogeny built them between about 535 and 520 Ma. It partly involved an exotic terrane, a crustal block from elsewhere, that docked against Gondwana's proto-Pacific edge. A belt of its igneous rocks formed from 525 to 515 Ma.

  <!-- camb-014 -->

- **Cuyania breaks away from Laurentia** — c. 530 million years ago (530 Ma)

  Part of Argentina began life in North America. Around 530 Ma, a block called Cuyania rifted away from Laurentia's Ouachita embayment. The split opened a new ocean that kept widening into the Early Ordovician. Paleomagnetic evidence, the record of ancient magnetism in rocks, supports Cuyania's Laurentian origin. It later docked against Gondwana.

  <!-- camb-016 -->

- **First footprints on land** — c. 530 million years ago (530 Ma)

  Could Cambrian animals walk out of the sea? The first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma, though the evidence that arthropods were ashore so early is unconfirmed. Early Cambrian trace fossils suggest mollusc-like animals could spend at least 15 minutes out of water. Later tracks are clearer. At the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, about 490 Ma, large amphibious arthropods, perhaps euthycarcinoids, left trails across coastal dunes.

  <!-- camb-017 -->

- **Kuunga–Damara collisions complete Gondwana** — c. 530 million years ago (530 Ma)

  Around 530 Ma the Kalahari and Mawson cratons met in the Kuunga–Damara orogeny, completing southern Gondwana. Collisions in East Antarctica's Lützow-Holm and Prydz belts climaxed at the same time. In the Damara orogeny, deformation and metamorphism peaked between 530 and 500 Ma. The west took longer. A narrow ocean separated Amazonia from Gondwana until about 530 Ma. In the mid-Cambrian, Amazonia collided with the São Francisco–Congo and Río de la Plata blocks, stitching West Gondwana together along the Transbrasiliano lineament. The last stages of this assembly overlapped with the Cambrian explosion.

  <!-- camb-018 -->

- **A carbon spike and two molluscs mark Stage 2** — c. 529 million years ago (529 Ma)

  Geologists need markers they can find anywhere. Around 529 Ma, a positive carbon isotope excursion called the ZHUCE coincides with the first appearances of two molluscs, Watsonella crosbyi and Aldanella attleborensis. Together these markers reliably indicate the boundary between the Fortunian and Cambrian Stage 2.

  <!-- camb-020 -->

- **Oxygen pulses breathe life into Cambrian seas** — during the Cambrian Stages 2–3, 529–514 million years ago (529–514.5 Ma)

  The early Cambrian ocean breathed in and out. In Stages 2 and 3, linked carbon and sulphur isotope excursions record heavy burial of organic carbon and pyrite in productive seafloor waters short of oxygen. Burial locked away material that would otherwise use up oxygen. Oxygen-rich waters then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor. Each pulse undid itself. Oxygenation cut burial rates, and anoxia returned; the cycle repeated several times. The pulses match the radiation of small shelly fossils and the Cambrian arthropod radiation isotope excursion, or CARE. Meanwhile, rising strontium ratios in seawater show stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

  <!-- camb-019 -->

  *Figure: The cycle of burial, oxygen and anoxia repeated several times.* (cycle; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Baltica collides with Arctida** — c. 528–510 million years ago (528–510 Ma)

  Between 528 and 510 Ma, Baltica and Arctida collided, and the Timanide Orogen rose where they met. The mountains did not last. Erosion of the belt began in the Cambrian and grew stronger in the Ordovician, shedding sediment as the range wore down.

  <!-- camb-022 -->

- **Ramgarh, an impact crater of uncertain age** — c. 528–395 million years ago (528–395 Ma)

  Somewhere between 528 and 395 Ma, an impact struck what is now Ramgarh in India. Uranium–lead dating gives that wide window. Other studies propose a younger age still. The crater is a reminder that not every event can be pinned to a date, and that some impacts of this era remain loosely placed in time.

  <!-- camb-021 -->

- **Archaeocyaths build the first animal reefs** — c. 525 million years ago (525 Ma)

  The oldest large structures built by animals were reefs of sponges. Archaeocyaths, cup-shaped sponges fixed to the seafloor with porous skeletons of lime, are first known from East Siberia at the start of the Tommotian, 525 Ma. With cyanobacteria, they built the reefs of the early Cambrian in warm tropical seas. They diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.

  <!-- camb-023 -->

- **Sirius Passet: a Cambrian window in Greenland** — c. 523–518 million years ago (523–518 Ma)

  In northern Greenland, Sirius Passet preserves a whole early Cambrian community. Part of the Buen Formation, dated about 523–518 Ma, it holds a fauna like that of China's Maotianshan Shales. Its animals were most likely preserved under a death mask of microbial mat that sealed them after death. With the Burgess Shale and the Maotianshan Shales, it ranks among the major Lagerstätten, sites of exceptional preservation, of the Cambrian.

  <!-- camb-025 -->

##### Cambrian Series 2 Epoch

Trilobites define this epoch: their body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, with exoskeletons of calcite. Radiodonts, the giant predators of the Cambrian, and eocrinoid echinoderms join them. China's Maotianshan Shales preserve an extremely diverse fauna, soft tissues and all, and among them the earliest known vertebrates. Mountains rose in Antarctica and South Australia. The epoch ends in crisis: the Sinsk Event, the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, removed over 60% of animal species.

- **Trilobites arrive with calcite eyes** — c. 521 million years ago (521 Ma)

  Even the earliest trilobites had complex compound eyes with lenses of calcite, the same mineral as their armor. Their body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, as trilobites evolved mineralized calcite exoskeletons. That first appearance is the proposed base of Cambrian Series 2 and Stage 3, and the top of the Terreneuvian. The animals may be older than their shells. Trace fossils such as Rusophycus and Cruziana, claimed as trilobite tracks, appear from about 537 Ma. Once armored, trilobites spread fast. They quickly diversified into the typical Cambrian orders: Redlichiida, Ptychopariida, Agnostida and Corynexochida. Within a short time they were the most diverse animals of the early Cambrian, and their hard parts made them some of the best-recorded animals of the period.

  <!-- camb-028 -->

  *Figure: The typical Cambrian trilobite orders.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

  *Figure: Trilobite tracks appear before their body fossils.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Eocrinoids, the first stalked echinoderms** — during the Stage 3, 521–514 million years ago (521–514.5 Ma)

  Eocrinoids, an extinct class of echinoderms, the group that includes starfish and sea urchins, first appear in Cambrian Stage 3. They were the earliest known stalked echinoderms with brachioles, slender food-gathering arms. They became the most common echinoderms of the Cambrian and lasted into the Silurian.

  <!-- camb-026 -->

- **Radiodonts, the giant predators** — during the Series 2, 521–506 million years ago (521–506.5 Ma)

  The largest animal in Cambrian seas was Anomalocaris, up to 2 m long. It was a radiodont, one of an order of stem-group arthropods, early relatives of the arthropods that branched off before the living groups. Radiodonts appear in Cambrian Series 2 and thrived worldwide through the period. Most dwarfed the animals around them. Large species were typically 30–50 cm long.

  <!-- camb-027 -->

- **The Ritland crater, Norway** — c. 520 million years ago (520 ± 20 Ma)

  About 520 ± 20 Ma, an impact blasted a crater about 2 km across at Ritland, in Norway. It is a confirmed impact crater, one of several from the Cambrian. Its small size points to a modest impactor, but the age carries a wide margin of uncertainty, as many ancient impact dates do.

  <!-- camb-030 -->

- **The Ross orogeny lifts the Transantarctic Mountains** — c. 520–450 million years ago (520–450 Ma)

  Antarctica's great mountain spine began in the Cambrian. After rifting early in the period, Antarctica deformed, and the Transantarctic Mountains rose in the mid-Cambrian. From about 520 to 450 Ma, Cambrian sediments there were uplifted, folded and metamorphosed, changed by heat and pressure. Huge bodies of granite, called batholiths, intruded them.

  <!-- camb-031 -->

- **Chengjiang: the Cambrian explosion in full color** — c. 518 million years ago (518 Ma)

  About ten million years before the Burgess Shale, a sea floor in what is now Yunnan, China, preserved animals soft tissues and all. The Maotianshan Shales of Chengjiang were laid down no earlier than 518 Ma. They hold the oldest diverse animal assemblage of the Phanerozoic, the best record of the Cambrian explosion. Chengjiang has all the animal groups of the Burgess Shale despite being so much older. That implies animals diversified earlier, or faster, than the younger site alone would suggest. Its chordates include Haikouella, Yunnanozoon and early fish such as Haikouichthys. Its arthropods also occur at other sites, which suggests they ranged worldwide. Some of its residents defy classification. About one in eight of its animals are problematic forms whose relationships remain uncertain.

  <!-- camb-033 -->

- **The first fish swim in Chengjiang** — c. 518 million years ago (518 Ma)

  Our own lineage appears in rocks about 518 Ma. The earliest known vertebrates, animals with a backbone, belong to China's Chengjiang biota, though fish are thought to have begun evolving around 530 Ma. Two species stand out. Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia had fins, vertebrate muscles and gills, and Haikouichthys had distinct vertebrae. They belonged to the chordates, a group that also includes tunicates. In the Cambrian, chordates diversified as mid-sized suspension feeders in open water or near the bottom. A later example comes from the Burgess Shale, about 505 Ma. Metaspriggina had an elongate body, prominent eyes and gills. For all their later success, early vertebrates remain rare in the Cambrian record.

  <!-- camb-034 -->

  *Figure: Milestones in the earliest history of fish.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The first crustaceans** — c. 517 million years ago (517 Ma)

  Crustaceans, the group of crabs, shrimps and their kin, had appeared by 517 Ma, in the Stage 3 Chengjiang biota. Sunella, a possible early relative of ostracods, suggests modern pancrustaceans existed by then. Their Cambrian record is sparse, despite an apparently early, hidden diversification. Even so, most major crustacean groups, the branchiopods, maxillopods and malacostracans, appear before the end of the Cambrian.

  <!-- camb-037 -->

- **The last of the Ediacaran fronds** — c. 516 million years ago (516 Ma)

  Frond-shaped animals typical of the Ediacaran biota, the petalonamids, are dated from about 635 to 516 Ma. The group is taken to include Stromatoveris from the lower Cambrian and, in a 2022 study, the middle Cambrian Thaumaptilon. Rare possible Ediacaran survivors occur as late as 510–500 Ma. Whether any truly survived is disputed: no Cambrian report is widely accepted.

  <!-- camb-039 -->

- **Emu Bay Shale: muscle turned to mineral** — c. 514–512 million years ago (514–512 Ma)

  The oldest phosphatized muscle tissue comes from South Australia's Emu Bay Shale. Dated to Stage 4, about 514–512 Ma, it preserves soft tissue mineralized as apatite, a calcium phosphate, or as calcium carbonate. It is younger than the Chengjiang and Sirius Passet sites, adding a later snapshot of the Cambrian explosion.

  <!-- camb-042 -->

- **The Delamerian orogeny folds South Australia** — c. 514–490 million years ago (514–490 Ma)

  From about 514 to 490 Ma, the Delamerian orogeny ended deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin and folded and deformed its rocks. Australia's eastern margin was turned inside out. It became a subduction zone, where the ocean floor of the Palaeo-Pacific sank beneath the continent.

  <!-- camb-041 -->

- **The Sinsk Event: the first Phanerozoic mass extinction** — c. 513–509 million years ago (513–509 Ma)

  Over 60% of animal species disappeared. The Sinsk Event, about 513.5 Ma, began the end-Botomian crisis of Stages 4 and 5, the first mass extinction of the Phanerozoic. The killer was the sea itself. A major transgression brought deep water without oxygen onto the shelves, spreading black shales. The nearly simultaneous Kalkarindji eruptions probably drove warming and deoxygenation. Reefs suffered most. The archaeocyath sponges that dominated them were devastated, along with halkieriids and much of the small shelly fauna. Many early branches of sponges, cnidarians, brachiopods and molluscs died out. Mobile animals such as trilobites recovered fast, but diversity stayed low into the early Ordovician. Deep-water communities, such as the later Huayuan biota, may have come through largely intact in refuges.

  <!-- camb-046 -->

  *Figure: How eruptions and anoxic water drove the first Phanerozoic mass extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Kalkarindji eruptions] --> B[Warming and deoxygenation]
  C[Sea transgression] --> D[Anoxic water on shelves]
  D --> E[Black shales spread]
  B --> F[Over 60% of species lost]
  D --> F
  ```

- **Kalkarindji floods Australia with basalt** — c. 511 million years ago (511 Ma)

  Lava eventually covered over 2,100,000 km² of what is now Australia. Around 511 Ma, flood basalts of the Kalkarindji large igneous province began to erupt. It was one of the largest such provinces and the earliest of the Phanerozoic. The eruptions, in Stage 4 and the early Miaolingian, released carbon dioxide, methane and sulphur dioxide. Climate changed rapidly and the seas warmed. Three large, rapid carbon isotope excursions record the upheaval. The timing suggests the eruptions helped cause the early to middle Cambrian mass extinction.

  <!-- camb-048 -->

  *Figure: The eruptions' gases led through climate change to extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Kalkarindji flood basalts] --> B[CO2, methane, SO2 released]
  B --> C[Rapid climate change, warmer seas]
  C --> D[Carbon isotope excursions]
  C --> E[Early to middle Cambrian extinction]
  ```

- **Blackberry Hill: animals walk onto tidal flats** — c. 510–500 million years ago (510–500 Ma)

  On sandy tidal flats around 510 Ma, something heavy dragged itself along and left Climactichnites, the largest Cambrian trace fossil. Blackberry Hill in Wisconsin preserves some of the oldest evidence of animals leaving the sea for land: large molluscs and euthycarcinoid arthropods. The Protichnites trackways come from Blackberry Hill and from the Potsdam Sandstone of Quebec.

  <!-- camb-050 -->

- **The Glikson crater, Western Australia** — c. 508 million years ago (508 ± 5 Ma)

  The Glikson crater in Western Australia is about 19 km across. Its age is hard to fix. Nearby dolerite, a dark volcanic rock, is dated 508 ± 5 Ma, and that suggests the impact is younger, probably Paleozoic. Like other old craters, it is better known for its size than for its timing.

  <!-- camb-053 -->

- **The Burgess Shale** — c. 508–505 million years ago (508–505 Ma)

  Thin dark films of carbon on British Columbia slate turned out to be animals no one had imagined. The Burgess Shale, about 508–505 Ma, preserves soft-bodied creatures that elsewhere would have rotted away. It is one of the best-known Lagerstätten, or sites of exceptional preservation, of the Cambrian, and a key record of the Cambrian explosion. Its cast is strange. Opabinia is one of several odd arthropods there. Anomalocaris was the first great apex predator. Metaspriggina, an early vertebrate with prominent eyes and gills, swam among them, and medusa-stage jellyfish such as Burgessomedusa drifted overhead. The site is younger than Chengjiang: the Cambrian explosion in full color, yet it was the Burgess Shale that first revealed how varied Cambrian life had been.

  <!-- camb-052 -->

##### Miaolingian Epoch

The Miaolingian opens with a die-off: the first major trilobite extinction removed the olenellids, eodiscids and most redlichiids. In their place, Paradoxides, the largest trilobites of the Cambrian, spread around the world. Conodonts, eel-like jawless animals known mainly from their teeth, make their first appearance, and the Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open along Gondwana's northern margin. Meteorites left craters from Norway to North Dakota. By its end, around 497.05 Ma, the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event had already begun.

- **Trilobites suffer their first great extinction** — c. 506 million years ago (506.5 Ma)

  At the boundary between Series 2 and the Miaolingian, the first major trilobite extinction removed the olenellids, the eodiscids and most redlichiids. A carbon isotope event called ROECE marks the boundary. It coincides with the main phase of Kalkarindji volcanism. Spain's Murero site records this end-Lower Cambrian extinction, the Valdemiedes event, in detail. The survivors changed. Trilobite orders that came through evolved larger tails and thicker cuticles, better at resisting predators.

  <!-- camb-062 -->

- **Conodonts: teeth that lasted 300 million years** — during the Middle Cambrian, 506–497 million years ago (506.5–497 Ma)

  For more than 300 million years, from the Cambrian to the start of the Jurassic, the seas held conodonts. These eel-like jawless animals are known mostly from their tooth elements, which survive where their soft bodies do not. They first appear in the Middle Cambrian. Their teeth are so durable and so widespread that they turn up across a vast stretch of the fossil record.

  <!-- camb-058 -->

- **The Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open** — during the Middle Cambrian, 506–497 million years ago (506.5–497 Ma)

  An ocean that would last about 400 million years began as a crack along Gondwana's northern margin in the Middle Cambrian. The Paleo-Tethys Ocean grew through the Paleozoic as land split away from the supercontinent. It finally closed in the Late Triassic. Its long life spans most of the story of the Paleozoic seas told in the coming chapters.

  <!-- camb-060 -->

- **Paradoxides, the giant trilobites** — during the Miaolingian, 506–497 million years ago (506.5–497 Ma)

  Paradoxides was a genus of large to very large trilobites, the biggest of the Cambrian. In the Middle Cambrian, the Miaolingian, they lived throughout the world. They spread after Trilobites suffer their first great extinction had cleared away older trilobite groups, and their wide range makes them familiar fossils of the epoch.

  <!-- camb-061 -->

- **DICE: deep anoxic water rises again** — c. 504 million years ago (504.5 Ma)

  Around 504.5 Ma, deep water short of oxygen rose into shallower seas as the sea advanced over the land. That rise caused the Drumian carbon isotope excursion, or DICE, which marks the start of the Drumian age. It came at a bad time. Reef ecosystems were still recovering from the early to middle Cambrian mass extinctions, and DICE held that recovery back.

  <!-- camb-064 -->

- **The Dresbachian extinction** — c. 502 million years ago (502 Ma)

  About 502 Ma, the Dresbachian extinction struck, one of the Cambrian crises before the Cambrian–Ordovician extinction. Its own page calls it the second of two severe Cambrian extinctions, after the end-Botomian. North America's Dresbachian stage spans 501 to 497 Ma. Carbonate sequences such as those of the North China Craton record Cambrian extinction events like the biomeres, bands of rock bounded by trilobite die-offs.

  <!-- camb-068 -->

- **The Gardnos impact hits a shallow sea** — c. 500 million years ago (500 ± 10 Ma)

  A meteorite 200–300 m across struck Buskerud, Norway, about 500 ± 10 Ma, leaving the 5 km Gardnos crater. The sediments laid down afterward show it hit a shallow sea. When the crater rim was breached, rock avalanches and debris flows poured in.

  <!-- camb-070 -->

- **The Mizarai crater, Lithuania** — c. 500 million years ago (500 ± 20 Ma)

  In Lithuania lies the Mizarai crater, 5 km across, formed by an impact about 500 Ma. It is one of a cluster of craters dated to around the end of the Cambrian, from Norway to North America. Like many old impact sites, it is known mainly from its size and approximate age.

  <!-- camb-071 -->

- **The Newporte structure, North Dakota** — c. 500 million years ago (500 Ma)

  Under North Dakota lies the Newporte structure, 3.2 km across, an impact formed about 500 Ma or slightly later. It joins other craters of roughly the same age in Norway, Lithuania and Quebec. Its age, like theirs, is known only approximately.

  <!-- camb-072 -->

- **Orsten: microscopic animals of the seafloor** — c. 500 million years ago (500 Ma)

  Some of the most revealing Cambrian fossils are too small to see without a microscope. Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale reveal the oldest well-documented meiofauna, the tiny animals that live among seafloor grains. Among them are microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids. These sites show that the Cambrian sea floor teemed with life at a scale larger fossils miss.

  <!-- camb-073 -->

- **The Presqu'île crater, Quebec** — c. 500 million years ago (500 Ma)

  The Presqu'île crater in Quebec is 24 km across, the scar of a sizeable impact. It is estimated to be less than 500 million years old. That loose upper limit is all the dating allows, so the crater sits among the late Cambrian impacts only provisionally, waiting for a firmer date.

  <!-- camb-074 -->

- **The Great Ordovician Biodiversification begins** — c. 497 million years ago (497.1 Ma)

  The great Ordovician radiation began before the Ordovician. A biodiversity study across the Paleozoic dates its start to 497.05 Ma, in the late Cambrian. Its first phase was tied to plankton, as invertebrate lineages moved into open water and started new food chains. Oxic waters spread into deep and shelf seas, while burrows deepened and body plans grew more complex.

  <!-- camb-077 -->

##### Furongian Epoch

The Furongian is the Cambrian's last epoch, and it was a hard one. One extinction cut species diversity by 45%, and after a brief recovery another cut it by 55.2%. A global carbon event, SPICE, ran between about 497 and 494 Ma. Yet new things arrived: Plectronoceras, the earliest undisputed cephalopod, and the first brittle stars. Mountain building began that would raise the Caledonides and reshape South America, and the epoch closed with another extinction at the boundary with the Ordovician.

- **The end-Marjuman extinction strips the shallows** — c. 497 million years ago (497 Ma)

  Species diversity fell by 45% in an extinction that began in the mid-Guzhangian. It ended early in the Furongian, perhaps mid-Paibian, about 3 million years later. In South China it came in two phases: a slight decline over about 1.8 million years, then a sharper one over 1.2 million years. The ocean was slowly suffocating. Gradual deoxygenation from the Guzhangian into the Jiangshanian, along with the linked SPICE: a carbon spike in a suffocating sea, likely caused it. Spreading anoxia killed off marjumiid and damesellid trilobites. Deep-water olenimorph trilobites replaced the shallow-water polymerids. The second wave matches the start of that carbon event, and diversity recovered at the very start of the Jiangshanian.

  <!-- camb-079 -->

- **SPICE: a carbon spike in a suffocating sea** — c. 497–494 million years ago (497–494 Ma)

  Mountains wearing away on Gondwana drove seawater strontium ratios to a peak. At the same time, anoxia spreading across the seafloor boosted the burial of organic matter and pyrite. The result was the Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion, or SPICE, a global event between about 497 and 494 Ma that began near the Guzhangian–Paibian boundary. It came with sea-level changes, cooling of surface water, anoxia, and extinctions of trilobites and brachiopods. Its end matches the End-Steptoean biomere extinction. Then came a turn. The rise in oxygen that followed opened niches for photosynthetic plankton and helped drive their radiation.

  <!-- camb-084 -->

  *Figure: Two sources fed the SPICE excursion, and its aftermath fed the plankton.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Gondwana mountains erode] --> B[Strontium ratio peaks]
  C[Seafloor anoxia spreads] --> D[Organic matter and pyrite buried]
  D --> E[SPICE carbon excursion]
  E --> F[Oxygen rises]
  F --> G[Photosynthetic plankton radiate]
  B --> E
  ```

- **The first cephalopods take to the water** — during the Late Cambrian, 497–487 million years ago (497–486.9 Ma)

  Plectronoceras, from the Late Cambrian, is the earliest undisputed cephalopod, the group that includes nautiluses and squid. Its shell was divided by septa, internal walls, and threaded by a siphuncle, a tube that ran through the chambers. Nautiloids originated in the same epoch. They were already diverse in the Fengshan Formation of northeastern China, then a warm shallow sea. The earliest nautiloids typically had siphuncles along the underside, like the later ammonites.

  <!-- camb-080 -->

- **The Ollo de Sapo magmatic event** — c. 495–470 million years ago (495–470 Ma)

  A mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep in the Earth, fed magma into northwestern Gondwana. It struck from the Furongian to the end of the Early Ordovician, about 495–470 Ma. That region is now the Iberian Peninsula. The Ollo de Sapo event ran long enough to span the boundary between two periods.

  <!-- camb-085 -->

- **The Jiangshanian extinction** — during the Jiangshanian, 494–491 million years ago (494.2–491 Ma)

  Recovery did not last. After diversity rebounded at the start of the Jiangshanian, a new extinction cut species diversity by 55.2%, a deeper cut than the end-Marjuman crisis that came just before. Small fluctuations in species richness followed and lasted until shortly after the Ordovician began. The late Cambrian thus ended with repeated blows rather than a single clean break.

  <!-- camb-087 -->

- **The Famatinian orogeny raises western South America** — c. 490–460 million years ago (490–460 Ma)

  A chain of volcanoes, the Famatinian magmatic arc, rose along what is now western South America. The Famatinian orogeny that built it ran from the Late Cambrian to at least the Late Devonian, with mountain building peaking about 490–460 Ma. Plutonic rocks south of Chile's Salar de Atacama formed with it in the Cambrian and Ordovician. Its climax came from a collision. The orogeny peaked when the Cuyania terrane struck Pampia in the Ordovician. From 480 to 435 Ma, rocks of the Cordillera Oriental were deformed as the arc developed.

  <!-- camb-091 -->

- **The Caledonian orogeny begins to close the Iapetus** — c. 490–390 million years ago (490–390 Ma)

  Mountains in northern Britain and Ireland, Scandinavia, Svalbard, East Greenland and north-central Europe share one origin. They rose in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collided. Its mountain-building events span the Ordovician to the Early Devonian, roughly 490–390 Ma, though its onset has also been dated to about 500 Ma. The ocean between them had to disappear first. The Iapetus, widest in the Late Cambrian and Early Ordovician, began closing by subduction between 500 and 488 Ma. In the Late Cambrian its mid-ocean ridge sank beneath Gondwana, opening large basins behind the volcanic arcs.

  <!-- camb-090 -->

- **The earliest brittle stars** — c. 488 million years ago (488 Ma)

  The earliest brittle stars, or ophiuroids, appear about 488 Ma. These echinoderms, with slender arms around a small central disc, arrived at the very end of the Cambrian. They are a small sign of the new kinds of animals that would fill the Ordovician seas.

  <!-- camb-092 -->

- **The Cambrian–Ordovician extinction** — 487 million years ago (486.9 ± 1.5 Ma)

  An extinction closed the Cambrian. It eliminated many brachiopods and conodonts and severely reduced the number of trilobite species. Almost all Redlichiida and most Late Cambrian trilobite stocks died out, and agnostid diversity fell sharply. The cause is uncertain. Volcanism, especially from large igneous provinces, has been suggested. Some researchers go further and argue the extinction is only apparent, an artifact of a gap in the rock record. Whatever happened, another radiation followed, and it established the animals that would dominate the rest of the Paleozoic.

  <!-- camb-093 -->

#### Ordovician Period

In the Ordovician, the sea filled up. Marine animal life radiated through the period, and the Cambrian fauna gave way to one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. Nautiloids reached their peak variety, starfish and brittle stars appeared, and new reef builders brought reefs back after a long lull. The Iapetus Ocean, over 4,000 km wide at the start, began to narrow. The period opens with a single conodont species, Iapetognathus fluctivagus, appearing in the rock record.

- **The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event** — during the Ordovician, 487–443 million years ago (486.9–443.1 Ma)

  Global marine diversity rose severalfold in the Ordovician. Through the period, marine animal life radiated and replaced the Cambrian fauna with one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. The animal phyla filled out with many new classes and smaller groups. This was the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, or GOBE. It was not one sudden burst. Different groups diversified at different times, from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician, and not everywhere at once. What drove it is still argued. Proposed causes include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower. Whatever the mix, the outcome was lasting. The GOBE set the ecological template of the seas for the rest of the Paleozoic.

  <!-- ordo-009 -->

  *Figure: Proposed drivers of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rising ocean oxygen] -.-> E[Marine diversity rises]
  B[Taconic nutrients] -.-> E
  C[Global cooling] -.-> E
  D[Meteorite shower] -.-> E
  ```

- **The Iapetus Ocean narrows** — during the Ordovician, 487–443 million years ago (486.9–443.1 Ma)

  At the start of the Ordovician, the Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide. It did not stay that way. Baltica drifted toward Laurentia, while island arcs and microcontinents such as Ganderia were added to Laurentia and Avalonia. As the gap closed, animals responded. Seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents, while ostracods and fishes stayed isolated. Sources differ on the ending. Several say Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia had joined by the end of the Ordovician, forming Euramerica, also called Laurussia. Others place the final Laurentia–Baltica collision in the Silurian, during the Caledonian orogeny.

  <!-- ordo-010 -->

- **Nautiloids at their height** — during the Ordovician, 487–443 million years ago (486.9–443.1 Ma)

  Straight, curved and coiled shells lived side by side in Ordovician seas, as nautiloids reached their peak variety. They spread from shallow waters into the open ocean at all latitudes. New orders such as Bisonocerida and Dissidocerida appear in the Early Ordovician, and Ascocerida early in the Middle Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-012 -->

##### Early Ordovician Epoch

The Early Ordovician was a time of rising water and new arrivals. Sea level climbed almost without pause, and shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana. Into them came phacopid trilobites, starfish, reef-building stromatoporoid sponges and strophomenid brachiopods. Several invertebrate lineages took to open water and started new food chains. Morocco's Fezouata Shale preserves the soft-bodied animals of this world, while trackways in Western Australia may record animals walking on land.

- **Green Point: where the Ordovician begins** — 487 million years ago (486.9 ± 1.5 Ma)

  One tiny tooth-bearing animal marks the start of a period. The Ordovician begins with the first appearance of the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus in the rock record. Its reference section, the GSSP, lies in the cliffs at Green Point in western Newfoundland, dated at 486.85 Ma. The period lasts about 43.75 million years, until the Silurian begins at 443.1 Ma. It is named after the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe of north Wales, where its rocks were first identified.

  <!-- ordo-013 -->

- **Rising seas drown the continents** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Through the Early Ordovician, sea level rose more or less continuously, levelling off only around mid-period. Shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana. The flooding of Laurentia created warm shallows where shelled sea life thrived. North America's Transcontinental Arch, a ridge of high ground, went under water and would not reappear until the Devonian.

  <!-- ordo-001 -->

- **Phacopid trilobites and their crystal eyes** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Trilobites with schizochroal eyes, built of separate, larger lenses, appear suddenly in the early Ordovician. The order Phacopida probably first appears then too; nine other trilobite orders had arisen in the Cambrian. During the Ordovician radiation, a new trilobite fauna replaced the old Cambrian one.

  <!-- ordo-004 -->

- **The first starfish and brittle stars** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Starfish fall apart after death, which is why their fossil record is so sparse. The first true starfish lived in the Early Ordovician, alongside brittle stars, as echinoderm diversity rose and new classes appeared, among them the diploporitans. Paracrinoids appear in the Early Ordovician and cystoids in the Middle Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-005 -->

- **Stromatoporoid sponges start building reefs** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Stromatoporoids, extinct sea sponges that built reefs, first appear unambiguously in the Tremadocian, at the start of the Early Ordovician. Their reefs grew in South China from the start of the period and spread to North America and North China by mid-period. The first order, Labechiida, quickly spread worldwide in the Middle Ordovician and diversified abruptly in the mid-to-late Darriwilian.

  <!-- ordo-006 -->

- **The seas turn to calcite** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  The chemistry of seawater decides which minerals shells and cements form from. In the Cambrian, seas were mixed, precipitating both aragonite and calcite, two forms of calcium carbonate. By the early Ordovician they had given way to fully calcite seas, where calcite was the mineral that formed.

  <!-- ordo-007 -->

- **The Ordovician plankton revolution** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  More plankton meant more of everything else. From the end of the Cambrian into the early Ordovician, several invertebrate lineages colonized open waters and started new food chains. This first phase of the GOBE, tied to plankton, ended in the late Early Ordovician. Microscopic life boomed. Chitinozoans, flask-shaped microfossils, radiated explosively across the Tremadocian and later became key markers for dating rocks. Acritarchs, mostly marine algae, peaked in diversity and variety of form in the Middle Ordovician. With more food drifting overhead, suspension feeders on the seafloor and swimmers in the water column multiplied.

  <!-- ordo-014 -->

- **Reefs return after a Cambrian lull** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Since the archaeocyath sponges died out, reefs had been rare. New reef-building corals changed that as they diversified in the Ordovician. Coral reefs emerged in the early Ordovician, including the earliest known octocorals, soft corals with eight-fold symmetry. By the middle Tremadocian, reefs of microbes and sponges occupied deeper water, as in South Korea's Dumugol Formation.

  <!-- ordo-016 -->

- **The Sauk Sea retreats from North America** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  At its peak, the shallow Sauk Sea had covered most of North America. Early in the Ordovician, a marine regression, a retreat of the sea, ended the Sauk sequence of rocks it had laid down. The Tippecanoe sequence followed later in the period, when the sea returned.

  <!-- ordo-017 -->

- **Strophomenid brachiopods spread across the shelves** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Strophomenida, an order of articulate brachiopods, lived from the Early Ordovician to the mid Carboniferous. They were among the most diverse and abundant brachiopods of the Ordovician. Orthid brachiopods reached their peak diversity at the same time, in shallow-shelf seas. The Late Ordovician mass extinction hit the strophomenids hard.

  <!-- ordo-018 -->

- **Tumblagooda: footprints of uncertain age** — during the Early Ordovician, 487–471 million years ago (486.9–471.3 Ma)

  Trackways in Western Australia's Tumblagooda Sandstone are read by some as the earliest evidence of animals living fully on land. Both that reading and the age are uncertain. Conodonts in overlying beds now point to an early Ordovician age, though a Silurian age was once favored. Because the unit is so poorly dated, it cannot show whether plants, which colonized land in the mid-Ordovician, got there first.

  <!-- ordo-019 -->

- **Fezouata: a Burgess Shale for the Ordovician** — c. 485 million years ago (485 Ma)

  Aegirocassis, a filter-feeding arthropod over 2 m long, was the largest animal of its time, and it comes from Morocco's Fezouata Shale. This Early Ordovician site preserves exceptional soft-bodied fossils: over 1,500 specimens of 50 taxa. They resemble the Burgess Shale biotas of the Cambrian. That makes Fezouata a bridge between the Cambrian explosion and the GOBE, showing that soft-bodied communities carried on into the Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-021 -->

- **Armored jawless fish with true bone** — c. 485 million years ago (485 Ma)

  The first vertebrates with true bone, jawless fishes, appear around 485 million years ago. Armored jawless fish called ostracoderms rose to prominence and remained the main vertebrates until the Devonian. Some accounts place the first small armored forms, such as a plated Laurentian group, already in the late Cambrian. They stayed close to shore. Early fishes lived mainly in near-shore settings such as intertidal zones and shallow lagoons. The oldest named thelodonts, small fish covered in scales, Larolepis and Stroinolepis, come from the Late Ordovician Sandbian stage.

  <!-- ordo-022 -->

- **The Early Ordovician super-greenhouse** — c. 485–470 million years ago (485–470 Ma)

  Sea surface temperatures may have reached 43.9 °C at 485 Ma. The Early Ordovician was very hot, comparable to the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, with very high carbon dioxide at the start of the period. One set of estimates shows the seas cooling to 37.1 °C by 470 Ma. The long-lasting heat shaped the biodiversification that followed in the Middle Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-020 -->

  *Figure: One set of estimates shows the sea surface cooling from 485 to 470 Ma.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Avalonia breaks free and opens the Rheic Ocean** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  Pieces of future Newfoundland, southern Britain and New England once sat on the edge of Gondwana. Around 480 Ma they broke free as the microcontinent Avalonia. A rift between them grew into a mid-ocean ridge, opening the Rheic Ocean in the Early Ordovician. As Avalonia drifted north, it closed the Iapetus Ocean ahead of it and opened the Rheic behind it. It was not alone. Ganderia probably separated from Gondwana near the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, and Carolina, Armorica and other terranes on Gondwana's northern margin also broke away during the Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-024 -->

- **Damara thrusting comes to an end** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  Gondwana's last seam closed slowly. In the Damara orogeny, thrusting onto the Kalahari Craton continued until 480 Ma, long after the main collisions. The Damara–Kuunga orogeny was the final joining of northern and southern Gondwana, and with its end the supercontinent was complete.

  <!-- ordo-025 -->

- **The first crinoids, the sea lilies** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  The earliest unequivocal crinoids, or sea lilies, date to about 480 million years ago, in the middle Tremadocian. These stalked echinoderms, with feathery arms that catch food, went through the first of their two major adaptive radiations during the Ordovician. They became a lasting part of Paleozoic seafloors.

  <!-- ordo-026 -->

- **The first eurypterids, the sea scorpions** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  The earliest known eurypterids, or sea scorpions, date to the Tremadocian, about 480 million years ago. Several branches already existed by the Middle Ordovician, which suggests the group arose in the Cambrian. The first truly successful ones were the Laurentian megalograptids, which radiated in the Late Ordovician. Most groups appear in the Silurian.

  <!-- ordo-027 -->

- **The first horseshoe crabs** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  Horseshoe crabs, or xiphosurans, first appear in the Early Ordovician, around 480 million years ago. The oldest known specimens come from Morocco's Fezouata Formation and are still undescribed. The oldest named early relative, Lunataspis, lived in what is now Canada about 445 Ma.

  <!-- ordo-028 -->

- **Insects begin, by a molecular estimate** — c. 480 million years ago (480 Ma)

  Insects are estimated to have originated about 480 million years ago, around when land plants appeared. The estimate comes from a 2014 study that compared genes, not from fossils. It allows an origin as early as the Early Ordovician or even the Cambrian. In this version, insects' early radiation happened no later than 479 Ma, in marine or coastal settings.

  <!-- ordo-029 -->

- **The Taconic orogeny raises the first Appalachians** — c. 480–430 million years ago (480–430 Ma)

  A great mountain chain once ran from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States. It rose when volcanic island arcs collided with Laurentia in the Taconic orogeny, the first Paleozoic mountain building in North America. A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician prepared the collision, and the orogeny affected most of New England. The mountains reached far beyond themselves. Their erosion fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE. Later, the weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew down CO2 in the Late Ordovician.

  <!-- ordo-030 -->

  *Figure: The Taconic mountains fed the oceans and later cooled the air.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Island arcs collide with Laurentia] --> B[Taconic mountains rise]
  B --> C[Erosion]
  C --> D[Iron and phosphorus to oceans]
  D -.-> E[Proposed driver of the GOBE]
  B --> F[Weathering]
  F --> G[CO2 drawn down]
  ```

##### Middle Ordovician Epoch

The Middle Ordovician is when the climate turned. Oxygen isotopes in conodonts show the shift from greenhouse to icehouse beginning, and a long ice age followed. On land, the spores of the first plants appear about 470 million years ago, and atmospheric oxygen began a long rise. In space, the break-up of an asteroid sent fragments toward Earth, and craters from Iowa to Quebec date to this time. The first sea urchins appear in the seas below.

- **From greenhouse to icehouse** — c. 471 million years ago (471.3 Ma)

  By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude sea surfaces had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures. Oxygen isotopes in conodont teeth show the shift from greenhouse to icehouse beginning at the end of the Early Ordovician. A sharp rise in carbon isotope ratios in the Floian may mark cooling through the burial of organic carbon, and it is proposed to have kick-started the GOBE. Life and cold rose together. Biodiversity climbed in step with cooling during the GOBE. Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse state by about 460 million years ago.

  <!-- ordo-031 -->

- **The Decorah impact in Iowa** — c. 470 million years ago (470 Ma)

  A meteor about 200 m wide struck what is now Decorah, Iowa, around 470 million years ago. It released energy equal to 1,000 megatons of TNT. The possible crater, about 5.6 km across, now lies buried under the Winneshiek Shale. It may be part of the Ordovician meteor event, a shower of impacts from a shattered asteroid.

  <!-- ordo-033 -->

- **The first land plants leave their spores** — c. 470 million years ago (470 Ma)

  The first land plants are known by their spores. Cryptospores appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossil assemblages for some 60 million years. The plants that made them evolved from green algae. The earliest were bryophytes, similar to mosses and liverworts. Baltica was an early cradle. By the Darriwilian it already held a diverse flora. Small as they were, these plants changed the planet. By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down CO2 and transforming both land environments and the global climate. There were limits to what they could do. Without deep roots, they did little to break rock into soil, a job left to the larger plants that came later.

  <!-- ordo-034 -->

  *Figure: How the first land plants arose and began changing climate.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Green algae] --> B[Bryophyte-like plants]
  B --> C[Organic carbon buried]
  C --> D[CO2 drawn down]
  D --> E[Climate transformed]
  ```

- **Clearwater East: one crater, not a twin** — c. 470–460 million years ago (470–460 Ma)

  Two craters sit side by side in Quebec, but they are not twins. The 26 km Clearwater East crater formed about 460–470 Ma, by argon-argon dating of its impact melt. Its neighbor, Clearwater West, formed much later, in the Early Permian, and the two carry different meteorite signatures. Clearwater East's central peak lies hidden under lake water and sediment; depth surveys and core drilling confirmed it.

  <!-- ordo-032 -->

- **The Paleozoic Oxidation Event begins** — c. 470–400 million years ago (470–400 Ma)

  Between 470 and 400 Ma, oxygen in the air rose in what is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. The first land plants, spreading from about 470 to 445 Ma, helped drive it. They trapped organic carbon in sediments, where it could no longer react with oxygen, so less oxygen was used up. The rise kept going. Oxygen later reached and exceeded today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

  <!-- ordo-035 -->

- **The Ordovician meteor shower** — c. 468 million years ago (467.5 ± 0.28 Ma)

  About 100 times as many meteorites struck Earth each year as today, and the raised rate lasted for millions of years. The cause lay in space: the break-up of the parent body of the L-chondrite meteorites sent fragments into orbits crossing Earth's. The evidence still falls from the sky. Many L-chondrites that land today carry shock ages from the break-up, and helium-3 in seafloor sediments supports the event. Craters such as Ames, 16 km across in Oklahoma, Rock Elm, 6 km in Wisconsin, and Slate Islands, and possibly Decorah and Granby, may belong to this shower. It was once suggested to have sparked the GOBE, but other evidence puts it about 600,000 years after the Darriwilian diversity burst.

  <!-- ordo-037 -->

- **The first sea urchins** — c. 465 million years ago (465 Ma)

  The earliest echinoid fossils, the first sea urchins, date to the Middle Ordovician, around 465 million years ago. They joined the growing list of echinoderm classes that appeared in the Ordovician. The shallow-water limestones of Estonia, from the Ordovician and Silurian, are famous for their echinoids.

  <!-- ordo-038 -->

- **The Winneshiek Shale fills an impact crater** — c. 460 million years ago (460 Ma)

  An impact crater became a fossil trap. Sediments that filled the Decorah crater in Iowa preserve conodonts, bivalved arthropods and the earliest eurypterids in exceptional detail. The quiet, enclosed basin left by the impact kept these animals intact, giving a rare view of Ordovician life in about 460 million-year-old rock.

  <!-- ordo-041 -->

- **The Early Paleozoic Ice Age** — c. 460–420 million years ago (460–420 Ma)

  Ice spread over Gondwana while carbon dioxide was still high. A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago. Glaciers were probably present by the Sandbian, with several short glaciations then and in the Katian. In the Ordovician the ice centered on the Sahara; in the Silurian it shifted to South America. It is known from Arabia, West Africa and the Andes. Geography may explain it. Gondwana sat over the South Pole, which may have let ice form despite the high CO2. As ice caps grew and melted, sea level rose and fell.

  <!-- ordo-040 -->

##### Late Ordovician Epoch

The Late Ordovician begins with continents on the move and ends in catastrophe. Terranes split from Gondwana, Avalonia struck Baltica, and huge eruptions blanketed Laurentia in ash. Impacts scarred Sweden and Estonia, and a brief warming built reef mounds across Europe. Arthropods left the oldest clear evidence of animals on land. Then extinction rates began to climb, several million years before a great glaciation.

- **The Hunic terranes split from Gondwana** — during the Late Ordovician, 458–443 million years ago (458.2–443.1 Ma)

  Behind a line of volcanoes, the crust stretched and tore. This back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes, a group of crustal blocks, away from Gondwana in the late Ordovician. The split opened the Paleo-Tethys Ocean behind them. The terranes then began moving north toward Euramerica, a journey that would carry them to the future Europe.

  <!-- ordo-043 -->

- **The Kazakh terranes gather into Kazakhstania** — during the Late Ordovician, 458–443 million years ago (458.2–443.1 Ma)

  Near the equator lay an archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, the Kazakh terranes. They merged as part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt. Crust was added to paleo-Kazakhstan until the accretion was complete, by the end of the Ordovician and Silurian. Another account places their final assembly into Kazakhstania in the late Silurian.

  <!-- ordo-044 -->

- **The last agnostid trilobites** — during the Late Ordovician, 458–443 million years ago (458.2–443.1 Ma)

  Agnostids, a group of small trilobites, had already declined sharply across the Cambrian–Ordovician transition. The last of them died out in the Late Ordovician. The Ordovician mass extinction ended them, along with the once-successful Telephinidae, closing two long-lived trilobite lineages.

  <!-- ordo-045 -->

- **The Ural Ocean forms** — during the Late Ordovician, 458–443 million years ago (458.2–443.1 Ma)

  Large islands from Siberia collided with Baltica in the Late Ordovician, and the Ural Ocean formed between them. It was one more new basin in a world of shifting plates, where terranes were splitting from Gondwana and older oceans were closing. This ocean was only beginning its life.

  <!-- ordo-046 -->

- **Lockne and Målingen: twin craters in Sweden** — c. 458 million years ago (458 Ma)

  An asteroid about 600 m across blasted the 7.5 km Lockne crater in what is now northern Sweden. Just 16 km away lies the smaller Målingen crater, which may be its twin, made by a body about 250 m across. Chitinozoan microfossils date the impact to about 458 million years ago.

  <!-- ordo-047 -->

- **The Kärdla crater, Estonia** — c. 455 million years ago (455 Ma)

  About 455 million years ago, a meteorite struck what is now Estonia and left the 4 km Kärdla crater. It came during a time of frequent impacts in the Ordovician. Estonia, Sweden and North America all hold craters from this stretch of the period.

  <!-- ordo-048 -->

- **Deicke and Millbrig: ash falls bigger than Toba** — c. 454 million years ago (454 Ma)

  The largest ash fall of the last 590 million years came down about 454 Ma. Huge eruptions during the Taconic orogeny, probably from a volcanic arc, buried Laurentia in ash. Today it survives as the Deicke and Millbrig bentonites, clays formed from altered volcanic ash. Millbrig was the larger. Each eruption's ash layer was larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.

  <!-- ordo-049 -->

- **The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion** — c. 453 million years ago (452.8 Ma)

  The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion began just above the base of the Katian Stage, dated to 452.8 million years ago. Its base helps fix that boundary at Black Knob Ridge, Oklahoma. It works together with the first appearance of the graptolite Diplacanthograptus caudatus, giving geologists two markers to find the same moment.

  <!-- ordo-052 -->

- **The Boda warming event** — during the Katian, 453–445 million years ago (452.8–445.2 Ma)

  In the early Katian, global temperatures rose briefly in what is called the Boda Event. The warmth built reef mounds and spread animals across Europe. It was a short warm spell in a cooling world, and it came before the great Hirnantian ice that ended the period.

  <!-- ordo-050 -->

- **Extinction rates rise in the Katian** — during the Katian, 453–445 million years ago (452.8–445.2 Ma)

  The Late Ordovician extinction did not come out of nowhere. Extinction rates rose significantly in the early or middle Katian, several million years before the Hirnantian glaciation. This early phase is linked to large igneous province activity, possibly the Alborz province of northern Iran, and to the Boda event. Bryozoan losses were drawn out: extinction rates were higher in the early and late Katian, and new species appeared far less often late in the stage.

  <!-- ordo-051 -->

- **Arthropods walk onto land** — c. 450 million years ago (450 Ma)

  The oldest clear evidence of animals on land belongs to arthropods, around 450 Ma. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods began colonizing land at least from the Ordovician. They may have thrived on food provided by early land plants. Late Ordovician trace fossils, a little over 445 Ma, probably record invertebrates living on land.

  <!-- ordo-054 -->

- **Avalonia collides with Baltica** — c. 450 million years ago (450 Ma)

  At about 30°S, eastern Avalonia rammed into Baltica and closed the Tornquist Sea between them. The collision formed the northwestern part of the Trans-European Suture Zone and coincided with the Shelveian orogeny of western England and Wales. It also ended the Rheic Ocean's widening south of Avalonia. Huge magmatism followed in Avalonia, and a gigantic ash fall in Baltica. Avalonian magmatism peaked between 457 and 449 Ma.

  <!-- ordo-055 -->

- **The Charlevoix impact, Quebec** — c. 450 million years ago (450 ± 20 Ma)

  A stony meteorite struck what is now Charlevoix, Quebec, leaving a structure about 54 km across. Its age, 450 ± 20 million years, spans the Ordovician to the Silurian. The margin of error is wide enough that the impact cannot yet be placed in one period or the other.

  <!-- ordo-056 -->

- **The Alice Springs Orogeny tilts Uluru** — c. 450–300 million years ago (450–300 Ma)

  Mountain building in central Australia lasted from about 450 Ma to about 300 Ma, far from any plate edge. The Alice Springs Orogeny shortened the crust north to south by under 100 km. Beginning in the Late Ordovician, it folded central Australian basins and had raised the MacDonnell Ranges by the Carboniferous. It may also have tilted the sandstone layers of Uluru to near vertical.

  <!-- ordo-053 -->

- **Deniliquin: an impact that might have triggered the ice** — c. 445 million years ago (445.2 Ma)

  Deep under south-east Australia lies a buried structure of multiple rings at Deniliquin. It has been dated to around the start of the first extinction pulse. A 2023 paper proposed that an impact there caused an impact winter that triggered the Hirnantian glaciation and extinction. The idea remains untested, and the structure is not listed as a confirmed impact crater.

  <!-- ordo-061 -->

- **HICE: a carbon marker for the Hirnantian** — c. 445–444 million years ago (445.2–443.8 Ma)

  Through the Hirnantian, a positive carbon isotope excursion, the HICE, ran alongside a short but large glaciation. Its cause is still debated. Its value is practical: it is a key marker for defining the Ordovician–Silurian boundary worldwide. Its exact age is uncertain, because the Hirnantian is short and dating errors are comparatively large.

  <!-- ordo-058 -->

- **The Hirnantian glaciation at its peak** — during the Hirnantian, 445–443 million years ago (445.2–443.1 Ma)

  Sea level fell from about 220 m above today's to about 141 m. A sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary rapidly expanded glaciers in one of the most severe glaciations of the Phanerozoic. Ice caps covered Gondwana over the South Pole, in what is now Africa and South America. The cold was probably harsher than the Last Glacial Maximum. The chemistry of the sea records the shock. Oxygen isotope ratios jumped by an extraordinary 2–4‰ at the start of the Hirnantian, and CO2 dropped sharply. Then it ended as abruptly as it began. The ice retreated at the end of the Hirnantian, and Earth returned to a much warmer climate in the Rhuddanian. The cold and the thaw each brought their own wave of death, in The Late Ordovician mass extinction.

  <!-- ordo-059 -->

  *Figure: Sea level fell sharply during the Hirnantian glaciation.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Hirnantian ocean loses its oxygen** — during the Hirnantian, 445–443 million years ago (445.2–443.1 Ma)

  As the glaciers retreated, black shales spread from isolated basins to all latitudes and depths, the mark of a global anoxic event. Repeated spells of anoxia mark the Ordovician–Silurian boundary. Anoxia is the most common suspect for the extinction's second pulse. Sudden volcanism may have supplied sulphur dioxide that favored euxinia, water both oxygen-free and rich in hydrogen sulfide. The Hirnantian–Rhuddanian anoxia may be one of the longest-lasting anoxic events in geologic time, and its cause is uncertain.

  <!-- ordo-060 -->

  *Figure: The retreat of the ice brought the second killer.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Glaciers retreat] --> B[Black shales spread worldwide]
  B --> C[Global anoxic event]
  C --> D[Second extinction pulse]
  E[Sudden volcanism] -.-> F[Sulphur dioxide]
  F -.-> G[Euxinia]
  ```

- **Beecher's Trilobite Bed: soft parts in gold** — c. 445 million years ago (445 Ma)

  The soft parts of trilobites rarely survive, but in a thin shale bed in Oneida County, New York, they do. Trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni have their soft tissues replaced by pyrite, fool's gold. The bed ranks among the world's best examples of near-perfect fossil preservation.

  <!-- ordo-062 -->

- **The first jawed fish** — c. 445 million years ago (445 Ma)

  The jaw may have appeared in the Late Ordovician, about 445 Ma. The first jawed vertebrates, or gnathostomes, arose from among the armored jawless ostracoderms. The earliest evidence is microscopic. Late Ordovician scale microfossils, possibly from acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', are the oldest signs of jawed fish. They took time to flourish. Jawed fish became common only in the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes'.

  <!-- ordo-063 -->

- **The Late Ordovician mass extinction** — c. 445 million years ago (445 Ma)

  Only one extinction in Earth's history was larger. The Late Ordovician mass extinction, the first of the 'Big Five', removed by various estimates from about 60% of marine genera to 85% of marine species. Only the end-Permian extinction surpassed it. It came in two pulses. The first, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary, is tied to the sudden Hirnantian glaciation. The second, later in the Hirnantian, came with warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated. Trilobites lost about 70% of their genera and 50% of their families. Many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished. Yet for all its severity, it changed the structure of ecosystems little, and diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.

  <!-- ordo-064 -->

  *Figure: The two pulses of the Late Ordovician extinction and their triggers.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Hirnantian glaciation] --> B[First pulse]
  A --> C[Ice retreats]
  C --> D[Warming and anoxia]
  D --> E[Second pulse]
  ```

  *Figure: Trilobite losses in the Late Ordovician extinction.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

#### Silurian Period

The Silurian is the period of fish and the first green coasts. Jawed fish diversified into placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish, while armored jawless fish reached their height. Nematophytes, strange land organisms, towered over the small plants beside them. Old groups bowed out, from asaphid trilobites to eocrinoid echinoderms. Far to the south, the Rheic Ocean opened to its greatest width, about 4,000 km.

- **Armorica drifts away from Gondwana** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  The Armorican Terrane Assemblage, a set of crustal blocks that now lie in western Europe, split away from Gondwana in the Silurian. Its complete separation, across the young Paleo-Tethys, is thought to have come toward the end of the period. Through the Devonian it drifted toward Laurussia. Late in the Carboniferous it collided with Laurussia in the Variscan orogeny.

  <!-- silu-001 -->

- **Armored jawless fish reach their peak** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  By the Late Silurian, armored jawless fish, the ostracoderms, had reached the high point of their evolution. Anaspids appear in the early Silurian. Osteostracans, probably arising in Euramerica, appear in the Llandovery or Wenlock. Thelodont scales turn up worldwide, and the tadpole-like archipelepidiforms lived from the late Telychian to the Sheinwoodian. Heterostracans of the order Traquairaspidiformes appear in the Late Silurian. Their success was short. The Silurian rise of jawed fish coincided with a sharp decline of jawless forms such as conodonts and ostracoderms.

  <!-- silu-002 -->

- **The asaphid trilobites die out** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Asaphida, a large and varied trilobite order known since the Middle Cambrian, died out during the Silurian. Its last members, the Trinucleioidea, disappeared before the end of the period. Their loss closed a lineage that had lasted through the whole of the Ordovician and its great extinction.

  <!-- silu-003 -->

- **The Clinton ironstones of the Appalachians** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  From New York to Alabama, layers of shale, mudstone, sandstone and iron-rich rock built up in the Appalachian Foreland Basin in the early Silurian. These are the Clinton Group and its 'Clinton Ironstones'. They are richly fossiliferous, an important record of early Silurian marine life. They are best known, though, as a significant source of iron ore.

  <!-- silu-004 -->

- **Jawed fish diversify** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  The fish families of today's oceans began in the Silurian. A major milestone of the period was the diversification of jawed fish: placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish. Cartilaginous and bony fish, the jawed groups still alive, appeared by the late Silurian. The branching was fast. By about 419 Ma, jawed fish had split into placoderms, bony fish, and a group joining the spiny sharks with the cartilaginous fish. The placoderm Entelognathus already had a bony jaw skeleton. Lobe-finned fish, or Sarcopterygii, emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian, all still living in water. Fish diversified greatly through the Silurian and Devonian.
