Even so, they produced fewer new body plans than animals did in the Cambrian explosion.

  <!-- silu-009 -->

  *Figure: Jawed fish had split into three main groups by about 419 Ma.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The last dissidocerid cephalopods** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Dissidocerida, an order of cephalopods with straight shells, had lived since the Early Ordovician. Its last appearance is in the Early Silurian. The order was one of several that arose in the Ordovician heyday of the nautiloids and faded after the period's great extinction.

  <!-- silu-011 -->

- **The last eocrinoids** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Eocrinoids, the early stalked echinoderms, had been around since Cambrian Stage 3. They make their last appearance in the Silurian. Once the most common echinoderms of the Cambrian, they outlasted the end-Ordovician extinction before finally disappearing.

  <!-- silu-012 -->

- **The last nektaspid arthropods** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Nektaspida, trilobite-like arthropods without mineral shells, had lived since the early Cambrian. They last appear in the upper Silurian. Because their bodies were not mineralized, they are known only from sites of exceptional preservation, which makes their long survival easy to overlook.

  <!-- silu-013 -->

- **The last paracrinoids** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Paracrinoids, echinoderms of shallow seas, lived from the Early Ordovician to the Early Silurian. They were among the new classes of the Ordovician echinoderm radiation, and among the first of those classes to vanish. Their span covers barely more than one period.

  <!-- silu-014 -->

- **Stromatoporoid sponges branch out** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  Most stromatoporoid sponge orders, including Amphiporida and Stromatoporida, originated in the Silurian. Clathrodictyids and actinostromatids diversified strongly while the older labechiids declined. Amphiporida is first recorded in the Ludlow. These sponges helped build the expanding reefs of the period.

  <!-- silu-016 -->

- **Nematophytes tower over early plants** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  The tallest things on Silurian land were not true plants. Nematophytes, a loose group of land organisms including some plants and algae, towered over even the largest land plants. They formed networks of large, mycorrhizal forms, living in partnership with fungi. Nematothallus is first recorded in the Ludfordian, alongside Cooksonia in Ludlow rocks. They lasted into the Early Devonian, and truly larger plants came only in the Early Carboniferous.

  <!-- silu-017 -->

- **The Rheic Ocean at its widest** — during the Silurian, 443–420 million years ago (443.1–419.6 Ma)

  As Avalonia and Carolina drifted north from Gondwana, the ocean behind them kept widening. In the Silurian, the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width, about 4,000 km. It separated Laurussia to the north from Gondwana to the south. From then on it could only narrow.

  <!-- silu-019 -->

##### Llandovery Epoch

The Llandovery opens on a recovering world. Its base lies at Dob's Linn in southern Scotland, just after the end-Ordovician extinctions, and as melting ice re-flooded the shelves, life rebounded. Reefs spread, land plants covered much of the land surface, and the oldest unambiguous jawed vertebrates appear in China. Milder glaciations came and went. Meanwhile Baltica and Laurentia began their slow collision in the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny.

- **Dob's Linn: where the Silurian begins** — 443 million years ago (443.1 Ma)

  In a small valley in southern Scotland, Dob's Linn, lies the reference section for the Ordovician–Silurian boundary and the base of the Llandovery. The boundary is set where two graptolites, Parakidograptus acuminatus and Akidograptus ascensus, first appear in the Birkhill Shale. It follows the end-Ordovician extinctions, which wiped out up to 60% of marine genera.

  <!-- silu-020 -->

- **Life rebounds after the end-Ordovician extinction** — c. 443–439 million years ago (443.1–438.6 Ma)

  Animals that seemed extinct came back. Many 'Lazarus taxa' missing from the latest Ordovician reappeared in the Silurian, so small populations must have survived in refuges. As melting ice raised sea level and re-flooded the continental shelves, biodiversity rebounded within the surviving orders. Early Silurian communities were simpler and broader in their habits, but faunas became among the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic. Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors in the earliest Rhuddanian. Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian, while pentamerid brachiopods waited until the Aeronian. Bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

  <!-- silu-015 -->

- **The first placoderms, armored jawed fish** — during the Llandovery, 443–433 million years ago (443.1–432.9 Ma)

  The vertebrate jaw probably evolved in the Silurian, and it appeared in placoderms, armored jawed fish. The first identifiable placoderms appear in the late Llandovery. Their Silurian record is fragmentary, probably because they lived where fossils rarely formed. A rare near-complete find is the antiarch Silurolepis, from Ludlow rocks of Yunnan. Placoderms diversified further in the Devonian.

  <!-- silu-006 -->

- **Land plants spread across the continents** — during the Llandovery, 443–433 million years ago (443.1–432.9 Ma)

  Mercury isotopes in the rocks show that by the Early Silurian, land plants had spread across much of Earth's land surface. Plants were already moving onto land in the Llandovery. Eohostimella, probably a land plant, is known from rocks about 440–430 Ma, and spores and plant microfossils of this age come from China and Pennsylvania. Silurian floras were broadly similar across the globe, with little regional difference.

  <!-- silu-010 -->

- **Silurian reefs spread to high latitudes** — during the Llandovery, 443–433 million years ago (443.1–432.9 Ma)

  Silurian barrier reefs covered much more seafloor than reefs do today, and they grew even at high latitudes. Widespread reef building began in the Llandovery and continued into the Devonian. Tabulate corals formed prominent mounds. Coral photosymbiosis, a partnership with light-using algae, may have begun in the Llandovery, and corals with it appear by the Middle Silurian. Hederelloids flourished, some living in symbiosis with the rugose coral Entelophyllum.

  <!-- silu-018 -->

- **The Taconic orogeny comes to an end** — c. 440 million years ago (440 Ma)

  The Taconic orogeny, which built mountains across New England, ended about 440 Ma. Subduction stopped, and the Iapetus Terrane was welded onto eastern North America. Then erosion took over. Through the Silurian and Devonian, sediment from the wearing mountains spread over the Appalachians and the North American midcontinent.

  <!-- silu-024 -->

- **Silurian glaciers shift to South America** — c. 440–420 million years ago (440–420 Ma)

  After the Hirnantian ice age, milder glaciations continued through the Silurian, the last in the Late Silurian. The center of glaciation moved from the Sahara to South America, with ice recorded in Arabia, West Africa, the Amazon and the Andes. Glacial phases struck in the early and latest Aeronian, the late Telychian to mid-Sheinwoodian, the Homerian and the Ludfordian. The ice caps were smaller than the Late Ordovician ones, and glaciers almost vanished by mid-Silurian. A lack of tillites, glacial deposits turned to rock, in the middle to late Silurian makes ice a problematic explanation for its climate swings.

  <!-- silu-023 -->

- **The oldest unambiguous jawed fish** — c. 439 million years ago (439 Ma)

  Teeth and scales from Guizhou, China, about 439 Ma, are the oldest unambiguous remains of jawed vertebrates. They belong to Qianodus and Fanjingshania, from Aeronian rocks. Both are acanthodian-grade stem chondrichthyans, early relatives of the cartilaginous fish; possibly older Ordovician records exist. Acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', arose about 50 million years before the first true sharks. By the early Silurian, jawed-vertebrate fossils, mostly primitive acanthodians, are unmistakable, and by the Devonian they are abundant.

  <!-- silu-025 -->

- **Chongqing: complete early jawed fish** — c. 436 million years ago (436 Ma)

  Near Chongqing, China, the Huixingshao Formation, about 436 Ma, preserves complete fossils of the earliest jawed vertebrates. It also holds galeaspids, a group of jawless fish, and eurypterids. One fish of this age, Shenacanthus, had armor plates on its chest like those of placoderms, a hint of how early jawed fish mixed features.

  <!-- silu-026 -->

- **The first bony fish** — c. 436 million years ago (436 Ma)

  Every land vertebrate descends from a fish with bones. The oldest known bony-fish fossils, about 436 million years old, have teeth arranged midway between those of sharks and those of true bony fish. Their skeletons were still mostly cartilage. Their novelty was foregut pouches that later became swim bladders and lungs. Bony fish appeared in the Silurian and became common and diverse in the Devonian. One branch, the lobe-finned fish, later gave rise to all land vertebrates. Guiyu oneiros, about 425 Ma from Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest articulated bony fish. It mixes placoderm-like traits with those of ray- and lobe-finned fish.

  <!-- silu-027 -->

- **The Scandian collision of Baltica and Laurentia** — c. 435–410 million years ago (435–410 Ma)

  The edge of Baltica was dragged about 120 km down into the Earth around 429 Ma, deep enough to form micro-diamonds. This was the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny, when Baltica and Laurentia collided from about 435 to 410 Ma. Avalonia, Baltica and Laurentia drifted together near the equator and began to form Euramerica. The collision folded coastal sediments that had built up for ages, raising mountains from New York State through Greenland and Britain to Norway. Thrusting built Scotland's Moine Thrust Belt, 435–420 Ma, and in Scandinavia great sheets of rock called nappes stacked on top of one another. Life noticed the closing ocean. Trilobite faunas from both sides mixed as the water between them narrowed.

  <!-- silu-029 -->

  *Figure: Drifting continents collided to raise the Caledonian mountains.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Avalonia, Baltica, Laurentia drift together] --> B[Baltica meets Laurentia]
  B --> C[Coastal sediments folded]
  C --> D[Caledonian mountains rise]
  B --> E[Euramerica begins]
  ```

- **Cooksonia, the first vascular plant** — c. 433 million years ago (433 Ma)

  A small Silurian plant carries one of evolution's great inventions. Cooksonia, the oldest known vascular plant, appears in the Wenlock, in the middle of the Silurian. Vascular plants, or tracheophytes, have internal tubes that carry water through their bodies. Cooksonia lasted. It remained an important part of the flora until the end of the Early Devonian, spanning 433 to 393 Ma. One species from about 432 Ma, C. barrandei, is known from its spore-bearing stage, the sporophyte. Most rocks that hold it are marine, so the plants probably grew along rivers and streams. They may not have been the first. Slightly later, more complex plants from Gondwana such as Baragwanathia suggest vascular plants have a longer history, perhaps reaching into the early Silurian.

  <!-- silu-031 -->

##### Wenlock Epoch

The Wenlock is short and turbulent. It opens with the Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, which lasted about 200,000 years. Carbon and oxygen isotopes swung after it, and two more crises followed, the Lundgreni and Mulde events. Yet the epoch also saw the first scorpions and the start of a long rise in oxygen, as vascular plants and fungi began to colonize dry land.

- **The Ireviken extinction event** — c. 433 million years ago (432.9 ± 1.2 Ma)

  In about 200,000 years, 80% of conodont species vanished worldwide. The Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, struck at the Llandovery–Wenlock boundary. At Ireviken on Gotland, over half the trilobite species died out. It began in the deep ocean and spread to the shelf seas. Graptolites, conodonts and trilobites suffered most, while shallow reefs were barely touched. It is linked to global cooling, and Carbon spikes after the Ireviken event followed. Its eight extinction steps appear to track Milankovitch cycles, regular wobbles in Earth's orbit. Its sediments show enrichment in metals.

  <!-- silu-032 -->

- **The last bisonocerid nautiloids** — during the Wenlock, 433–427 million years ago (432.9–426.7 Ma)

  Bisonocerida, a nautiloid order dating from the Tremadocian, last appears in the Wenlock. It had arisen in the Early Ordovician, when nautiloids were at their height, and lasted through the end-Ordovician extinction before disappearing. Its end is one more sign of the slow fading of the old Ordovician nautiloid groups.

  <!-- silu-033 -->

- **Carbon spikes after the Ireviken event** — c. 431 million years ago (431 Ma)

  After the first Ireviken extinctions, the carbon isotope value δ13C rose from +1.4‰ to +4.5‰. Oxygen isotopes rose too, from −5.6‰ to −5.0‰. This early Silurian excursion, about 431 Ma, resembles the Cambrian SPICE event, peaking near +4.5‰. The Silurian had more such isotope excursions, a sign of climate swings, than any other period.

  <!-- silu-035 -->

- **The Lundgreni event** — during the Homerian, 431–427 million years ago (430.6–426.7 Ma)

  Graptolite diversity hit a global low in the middle Homerian, and the cyrtograptids died out. This was the Lundgreni event, or Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis, recorded in Iberia, Bohemia and Poland. It hit graptolites, seafloor animals and microscopic plankton hardest. Eutrophication, an overload of nutrients, and anoxia are blamed. A double-peaked positive carbon isotope excursion began with it.

  <!-- silu-036 -->

- **The first scorpions** — c. 430 million years ago (430 Ma)

  Scorpions date back to the Silurian, about 430 Ma. The oldest known, Dolichophonus loudonensis, lived in what is now Scotland. Whether early scorpions lived in water or on land is debated, though early forms like Eramoscorpius had book lungs, stacked plates for breathing air. Land scorpions appear in timelines at about 420 Ma.

  <!-- silu-038 -->

- **The Great Glen Fault cuts across Scotland** — c. 430–390 million years ago (430–390 Ma)

  The Scottish Highlands take their shape from a fault. The Great Glen Fault formed late in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia and Baltica collided, probably between 430 and 390 Ma. It is a product of the same collision that raised mountains from Norway to New York.

  <!-- silu-039 -->

- **Oxygen climbs to modern levels** — c. 428–359 million years ago (428–359 Ma)

  In the early Silurian, oxygen stood near 13% of today's level; by the Devonian it approached modern levels. This stepwise rise to and above modern levels, the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event, ran from about 428 to 359 Ma, alongside the spread of vascular plants. Plants likely drove it. Their higher photosynthetic yield released more oxygen, and burying organic carbon in rocks cut the oxygen sink. Carbon trapped in rock also meant less CO2 in the air, and the climate cooled.

  <!-- silu-041 -->

  *Figure: Plants raised oxygen and lowered CO2 by the same route.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Vascular plants spread] --> B[Higher photosynthetic yield]
  A --> C[Organic carbon buried in rock]
  B --> D[Oxygen rises]
  C --> D
  C --> E[Less CO2]
  E --> F[Climate cools]
  ```

- **The Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution** — c. 428–359 million years ago (428–359 Ma)

  The continents turned green. From 428 to 359 Ma, land plants, especially vascular plants, and fungi rapidly colonized and diversified on dry land. The critical phase came in the Late Silurian and Early Devonian. Vascular plants arose from simpler land plants. Fungi spread, and myriapods, arachnids and hexapods became fully terrestrial. Plant diversity rose on a scale compared with the Cambrian explosion of animals, notably in tall, woody vascular plants that later formed canopies. Volcanic islands of the Rheic Ocean were hotspots of plant evolution. The new vegetation reshaped the water cycle and the global climate. It changed ocean nutrients and sediment cycling worldwide, likely feeding plankton blooms tied to the Late Devonian extinction.

  <!-- silu-042 -->

  *Figure: How plants and fungi on land reshaped climate and the oceans.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Plants and fungi colonize land] --> B[Water cycle and climate reshaped]
  A --> C[Ocean nutrients changed]
  C -.-> D[Plankton blooms]
  D -.-> E[Late Devonian extinction]
  ```

- **The Mulde extinction event** — c. 427 million years ago (427.4 ± 0.5 Ma)

  The Mulde event, an anoxic event, was the second of three relatively minor Silurian mass extinctions. It coincided with a global drop in sea level and was closely followed by an isotope excursion. Carbon isotopes suggest a sustained drop in CO2 at the time. Its onset matches the Fröjel Formation of Gotland. Some apparent conodont losses may reflect changed sediments rather than real extinction.

  <!-- silu-043 -->

##### Ludlow Epoch

In the Ludlow, the land was still nearly empty, but the first settlers had arrived. Clubmoss-like lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving plant lineages, date to about 425 million years ago, and so do the oldest definite millipedes, from Kerrera in Scotland. At sea, the story turned harsher. A final glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian and is tied to the Lau event, the last of three Silurian extinctions, which may have ended the ancient palaeoscolecid worms. Sea scorpions and the earliest sac fungi were close behind.

- **Baragwanathia, a clubmoss ahead of its time** — c. 425 million years ago (425 Ma)

  Most plants of the Middle Silurian stood less than 10 cm tall. Baragwanathia had leaves that alone could match that height. This clubmoss, known from Australia, Canada and China, carried branching stems and needle-like leaves 10–20 cm long, and it looks advanced for its age. It belongs to the lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving lineages of vascular plants, which are plants with internal tubes for moving water. The lineage goes back to about 425 million years ago. One early lycophyte order, the Drepanophycales, lasted from the Late Silurian to the Late Devonian, roughly 430 to 360 million years ago.

  <!-- silu-048 -->

- **Kerrera's millipedes, among the first animals ashore** — c. 425 million years ago (425 Ma)

  On the small Scottish island of Kerrera, rocks about 425 million years old hold the oldest definite millipedes. Two species, Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus, settle the question that older, vaguer fossils leave open. Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals, and among the first animals of any kind to colonize land. Kerrera is not alone. Air-breathing arthropods from Ludlow, in England, date to about 420 million years ago. Both sites are older than the zircon age of Pneumodesmus, another early land walker met in Pneumodesmus, the oldest known air breather, whose own date is disputed. These small creatures were pioneers, but quiet ones. Land animals made little impact on Earth as a whole until they diversified in the Devonian, when soils, forests and food webs on land became far richer.

  <!-- silu-052 -->

- **Palaeoscolecid worms make their final appearance** — during the Ludfordian, 425–423 million years ago (425–422.7 Ma)

  A lineage of worms that had crawled through the seafloor since the late Early Cambrian vanished in the Ludfordian. These were the palaeoscolecids, armored with tiny plates along their bodies. Their last fossils appear in this age, and The Lau event, the Silurian's last extinction may have been what finished them off.

  <!-- silu-049 -->

- **Ice returns and the sea drains off the shelves** — during the Ludfordian, 425–423 million years ago (425–422.7 Ma)

  The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian. In the middle of the age, growing ice locked away seawater. The oceans pulled back in a major regression, a retreat of the sea from the coasts. Vast new land lay exposed. Life moved in fast: plants and mats of cyanobacteria, the photosynthesizing microbes, quickly colonized the bare ground, pushing plant diversification further. The same cold snap is tied to The Lau event, the Silurian's last extinction, the extinction that followed.

  <!-- silu-051 -->

- **The Lau event, the Silurian's last extinction** — c. 424 million years ago (424 Ma)

  Conodonts, tiny eel-like animals with teeth, took the hardest blow in the last of three Silurian extinctions. It began at the start of the late Ludfordian and is named after Lau parish on the island of Gotland. Graptolites, colonial floating animals, suffered in the Kozlowskii event just after, which may have been the same crisis. The timing points to a cause. The event coincided with a glacially driven global sea-level low, part of Ice returns and the sea drains off the shelves, and most major groups saw higher extinction rates. Rated 6.2 in severity, it permanently altered marine communities. In the gap, stromatolites and microbial mats spread, the same pattern seen after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions. It may also have ended the palaeoscolecid worms.

  <!-- silu-054 -->

  *Figure: Glacial cold, a sea-level low and the Lau extinction arrived together.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Ludfordian glaciation] --> B[Global sea-level low]
  B -.-> C[Lau event]
  C --> D[Conodonts hit hardest]
  C --> E[Microbial mats spread]
  ```

- **Sea scorpions at the height of their reign** — c. 423–419 million years ago (423–419.2 Ma)

  Acutiramus, a Late Silurian sea scorpion, reached about 2 m long. Sea scorpions, or eurypterids, were major parts of Silurian marine faunas, and most of their groups are first recorded in Silurian rocks. Their diversity peaked in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 million years ago. One group, the eurypterines, make up 90% of the eurypterids in most beds. Large pterygotids, with rudder-like tails and big pincers, also appeared in the Late Silurian. The most abundant of all was Eurypterus, which lived from about 432 million years ago to the end of the Pridoli. Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage of them.

  <!-- silu-055 -->

- **The oldest sac fungi** — c. 423–419 million years ago (423–419 Ma)

  Most familiar molds and yeasts belong to the ascomycetes, or sac fungi. The earliest known members date from 423 to 419 million years ago, in the Silurian. They belong to a larger group, the dikaryan fungi, which began expanding and diversifying during this period.

  <!-- silu-056 -->

##### Pridoli Epoch

The Pridoli, the last and shortest epoch of the Silurian, saw the land come alive. Oxygen rose high enough for the first wildfires, and Scotland's Pneumodesmus is among the oldest creatures known to have breathed air on land. By about 420 million years ago, millipedes shared the ground with centipedes and spider relatives, and the first ray-finned fish may have swum in the seas. Meanwhile the Iapetus Ocean closed entirely, and falling seas left salt basins from Michigan to West Virginia.

- **Charcoal marks the first wildfires** — during the Pridoli, 423–420 million years ago (422.7–419.6 Ma)

  Fire needs fuel and it needs oxygen. By the Pridoli, both were finally present. The first charcoal in the fossil record appears in this epoch, showing that atmospheric oxygen had risen high enough to sustain wildfires. Silurian charcoal suggests oxygen had crossed about 15% of the air, the threshold for burning. From here on, fire becomes a recurring force in the history of land plants.

  <!-- silu-059 -->

- **The Šilalė event strikes the conodonts** — during the Pridoli, 423–420 million years ago (422.7–419.6 Ma)

  Early in the Pridoli, conodonts suffered another extinction, the Šilalė event. It is marked by a negative carbon isotope excursion, a sudden shift in the chemistry of carbon. That shift is traced from cores in Lithuania to the Appalachian Basin of North America. While conodonts declined, brachiopods grew in diversity and abundance. The crisis coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year cycle in the shape of Earth's orbit.

  <!-- silu-062 -->

- **Pneumodesmus, the oldest known air breather** — c. 423–413 million years ago (422.7–413 Ma)

  Small holes in a fossil's skin made it famous. Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, has openings in its cuticle read as spiracles, the breathing pores of a tracheal system. That makes it the earliest known arthropod built to breathe air, and among the oldest creatures known to have lived on land. Its age, though, is disputed. It was once put at about 428 million years old, in the Wenlock. A 2023 study defended the Wenlock age, about 430 million years ago. Zircon dates and a 2025 study instead favor the Pridoli to Lochkovian, about 414 million years ago. Either way, it belongs with the millipedes, which first appear in the Silurian as among the oldest known land animals.

  <!-- silu-061 -->

  *Figure: The proposed ages of Pneumodesmus span the Wenlock to the Lochkovian.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Arachnids and centipedes join the millipedes** — c. 420 million years ago (420 Ma)

  Millipedes did not have the land to themselves for long. By the Pridoli, about 420 million years ago, centipedes and trigonotarbid arachnids, extinct spider relatives, had joined them. Timelines list the earliest trigonotarbids and land scorpions at about the same date. Some of the newcomers were predators, so there must have been prey, which ate plants or detritus, the dead remains of living things. Simple food webs had formed on land. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods all became fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

  <!-- silu-063 -->

- **Andreolepis, perhaps the first ray-finned fish** — c. 420 million years ago (420 Ma)

  Almost every fish alive today, from tuna to goldfish, is a ray-finned fish, with fins held up by thin bony rods. The earliest known member of the group may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 million years old, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia. Timelines put the first ray-finned fish at about the same date. The group took a long time to hit its stride. Its crown group, the lineage that includes all living members, arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.

  <!-- silu-064 -->

- **The Iapetus closes and Laurussia is born** — c. 420 million years ago (420 Ma)

  An entire ocean disappeared by the end of the Silurian. The Iapetus Ocean had closed completely by about 420 million years ago, leaving a seam called the Iapetus Suture. Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, a mountain-building collision, and formed Laurussia. That continent would later become the northern part of Pangaea. Convergence between Laurentia and Avalonia, and subduction of the Iapetus seafloor, had ceased by about 420 million years ago. The collision shaped Laurussia's southern margin, and rocks in Scandinavia's thrust sheets reached peak metamorphism, their deepest heating and squeezing, at about the same time.

  <!-- silu-065 -->

  *Figure: Three continents fused in the Caledonian orogeny to make Laurussia.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Avalonia] --> D[Laurussia]
  B[Baltica] --> D
  C[Laurentia] --> D
  D --> E[Northern Pangaea, later]
  ```

- **Ascocerid nautiloids vanish** — c. 420 million years ago (419.6 Ma)

  The ascocerids, an odd group of shelled cephalopods, came back from near-ruin once. Cut back by the end-Ordovician extinction, they recovered in the Silurian. Then, at the end of the Silurian, they died out abruptly.

  <!-- silu-066 -->

- **Seas fall and salt fills the Salina basin** — c. 420 million years ago (419.6 Ma)

  Sea level had risen through the first half of the Silurian and fell through the rest. At the period's end it dropped again, leaving evaporite basins, where seawater dried into salt, from Michigan to West Virginia. A warm, arid climate over a shallow inland basin laid down the Salina Group evaporites, 120–800 m thick. Meanwhile the new mountains eroded rapidly.

  <!-- silu-067 -->

#### Devonian Period

The Devonian is popularly called the Age of Fishes, and with reason: jawed vertebrates, rare before, became common, and armored placoderms appeared in sudden diversity at its start. On land, the period's story is about plants. As they spread, carbon dioxide dropped steeply, and oxygen, only a fraction of today's level in the early Silurian, rose to near-modern levels. Beneath it all, the crust kept moving, from an island arc docking with Patagonia to huge alkaline magmas on Russia's Kola Peninsula.

- **Jawed fishes take over in the Age of Fishes** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  The Devonian earned its popular name, the Age of Fishes, honestly. Jawed vertebrates had appeared in the late Ordovician, but only now did they become common. Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks. The family tree had already branched. By about 419 million years ago jawed fishes had split into three lines. They were the armored placoderms, the bony fishes, and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish. Both cartilaginous and bony fishes diversified through the period and played a large role in Devonian seas. Among the bony fishes, the lobe-finned forms, such as coelacanths and lungfish, were the most diverse. That detail matters, because the lobe-fins are the group from which four-limbed animals would later come.

  <!-- devo-001 -->

  *Figure: The main Devonian fish groups.*

  | Group | Note |
  |---|---|
  | Ostracoderms | Variety rose greatly |
  | Placoderms | Split by about 419 Ma |
  | Lobe-finned fishes | Most diverse bony fishes |
  | Early sharks | Variety rose greatly |

- **The Chaitenia arc docks with Patagonia** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  A chain of volcanic islands called Chaitenia crashed into Patagonia during the Devonian. Its remains sit in what is now south-central Chile. The event was part of a larger change: Patagonia's margin turned convergent, with crust moving together, which led to a collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous.

  <!-- devo-003 -->

- **Kola's alkaline volcanoes** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  Russia's Kola Peninsula holds an estimated 15,000 ± 2,700 cubic km of Devonian igneous rock. Magmas there built carbonatites, kimberlite pipes and the large nepheline syenite massifs of Khibiny and Lovozero. They came from small melt fractions of garnet peridotite beneath lithosphere about 200 km thick. This Kola large igneous province erupted about when the Viluy and Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets provinces did, and is a suggested trigger of the The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian.

  <!-- devo-006 -->

- **Roots pull carbon dioxide from the sky** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  Plants changed the air simply by putting down roots. As land plants spread through the Devonian, carbon dioxide levels dropped steeply. Roots broke up rock and increased silicate weathering, a chemical reaction that locks carbon dioxide away; carbonates formed in ancient soils record it. The growing plant cover probably also buffered carbon dioxide while anoxic events in the oceans grew longer. The long-term fall in carbon dioxide, together with rising oxygen, led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse.

  <!-- devo-007 -->

  *Figure: Follow the chain from spreading roots to the late Paleozoic icehouse.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Land plants spread] --> B[Roots boost silicate weathering]
  B --> C[CO2 drops steeply]
  C --> D[Late Paleozoic icehouse]
  ```

- **Oxygen climbs toward modern levels** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  Early in the Silurian, the air held only about 13% of today's oxygen level. By the end of the Devonian it was near modern. Early in the Devonian oxygen was still fairly low, possibly about half of modern values. The climb from 470 to 400 million years ago is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. It is explained by early plants trapping organic carbon in sediments, so that it could not use up oxygen by decaying. As plants spread over the continents, they buried more carbon still. The richer air may have favored vertebrates able to breathe it, helping push tetrapods onto land.

  <!-- devo-009 -->

  *Figure: Buried plant carbon let oxygen climb, which may have helped tetrapods ashore.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Plants spread over land] --> B[Organic carbon buried]
  B --> C[Oxygen near modern levels]
  C -.-> D[Air-breathing vertebrates favored]
  ```

- **Placoderms, the armored rulers of Devonian waters** — during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

  Placoderms burst onto the scene at the very start of the Devonian, already in seemingly sudden diversity. These armored jawed fishes went on to dominate almost every known aquatic ecosystem, fresh water and salt water alike. One group, the petalichthyids, peaked early in the period and lived worldwide. A 419-million-year-old placoderm, Entelognathus, had a bony mouth skeleton like a bony fish's, a hint of how the groups are related. At the top end, giants such as Dunkleosteus grew up to seven meters long.

  <!-- devo-011 -->

##### Early Devonian Epoch

The Early Devonian rearranged both the map and the tree of life. The Caledonian mountains began to collapse, the Rheic Ocean began to close, and Asian blocks pulled away from Gondwana to open the Paleo-Tethys. Red sediments spread over a continent that would be called the Old Red Sandstone Continent. In the water, lobe-finned fishes and the first ammonoids appeared while jawless armored fishes peaked and began to fade. On land, Scotland's Rhynie chert froze an early ecosystem of plants, fungi and arthropods in stone.

- **The Caledonian mountains begin to collapse** — during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)

  Mountains can fall under their own weight. After Baltica's margin was subducted and overridden by nappes, huge sheets of rock, the Caledonian mountain belt began to collapse in the Early Devonian. Burial peaked about 410 million years ago, recorded in Norway's Western Gneiss Region, and those rocks were brought back up about 400–385 million years ago. The collapse stretched and lowered the crust, and in Scandinavia it lasted a long time.

  <!-- devo-002 -->

- **Jawless armored fishes peak, then fade** — during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)

  Cephalaspis, the most advanced jawless fish, appeared about 415 million years ago. Its kind, the armored jawless ostracoderms, peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian, and so did the scale-covered thelodonts. Both then declined. By the Middle Devonian jawed fishes were thriving while the ostracoderms dwindled, never to recover.

  <!-- devo-005 -->

- **The last of the radiodonts** — during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)

  The radiodonts, the group of Cambrian predators that includes Anomalocaris, outlasted the Cambrian by a very long way. Their last appearance comes in the Early Devonian. One late survivor was Schinderhannes bartelsi, from Germany.

  <!-- devo-008 -->

- **Asian blocks drift away and open the Paleo-Tethys** — during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)

  Pieces of future Asia were once part of Gondwana. North and South China, along with Tarim, rifted from Gondwana's northern margin, and a new ocean, the Paleo-Tethys, opened behind them. South China and Indochina had split away in the Silurian and moved north, shrinking the older Proto-Tethys ahead of them. South China and Annamia, today's Southeast Asia, later collided in the Carboniferous. The blocks did not go far at first. Their Devonian fossils resemble Australian species more than north Asian ones.

  <!-- devo-010 -->

- **The Rheic Ocean begins to close** — during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)

  At the start of the Devonian, a wide ocean, the Rheic, separated Laurussia from Gondwana. In the Early Devonian it began to shrink. Gondwana moved toward Euramerica as the Rheic seafloor was subducted, pulled down beneath the plates. Near the end of the Early Devonian, two small blocks, Franconia and Saxothuringia, struck Laurussia and pinched out the eastern part of the ocean. The closure would not finish until the Mississippian, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

  <!-- devo-012 -->

  *Figure: The Rheic Ocean closed in stages, from Devonian subduction to Pangaea.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rheic seafloor subducted] --> B[Gondwana nears Euramerica]
  B --> C[Franconia and Saxothuringia hit Laurussia]
  C --> D[Mississippian collision forms Pangaea]
  ```

- **The Old Red Sandstone builds a red continent** — c. 419–358 million years ago (419–358 Ma)

  So many red rocks formed in this age that a whole continent took their name. Old Red Sandstone sediments began accumulating around 419 million years ago across Britain, Ireland, Norway, northeastern North America, Greenland and Svalbard. These mostly Devonian rocks were laid down in varied settings from the late Silurian into the earliest Carboniferous. Their red beds gave Laurussia the nickname Old Red Sandstone Continent. In Scotland, uplifted Silurian rocks eroded into fresh water, probably large river deltas, between 408 and 370 million years ago. Around 370 million years ago, at Siccar Point, rainy-season rivers near the equator laid iron-rich sands that winds then reworked into dunes.

  <!-- devo-013 -->

- **Lobe-finned fishes appear and divide** — c. 418 million years ago (418 Ma)

  The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 million years ago, looked a lot like spiny sharks. Little hinted at what they would become. In the Early Devonian, between 416 and 397 million years ago, they split into two main lineages: the coelacanths and the rhipidistians. While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-fins moved into fresh water, between 416 and 385 million years ago. The coelacanths had their heyday later, in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous, from 385 to 299 million years ago.

  <!-- devo-014 -->

  *Figure: Lobe-finned fishes appeared, split and spread over a long span.*

  | Million years ago | Lobe-finned fishes |
  |---|---|
  | 418 | First lobe-fins, like spiny sharks |
  | 416–397 | Split into coelacanths and rhipidistians |
  | 416–385 | Some move into fresh water |
  | 385–299 | Coelacanth heyday |

- **Arthropods settle coasts and floodplains** — c. 415 million years ago (415 Ma)

  By about 415 million years ago, numerous arthropods lived along coasts and on alluvial plains, the flat land beside rivers, and some were eating plants. Early rooted plants had built the first stable soils. Mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods made homes in them. Land animals began to have a major impact on Earth only once they diversified in the Devonian.

  <!-- devo-015 -->

- **The first true nautilids** — c. 410 million years ago (410 Ma)

  The order of the living chambered nautilus has roots around 410 million years ago. Rutocerina, the earliest true nautilid, had a shell like those of the oncocerid nautiloids, its likely ancestors. Nautilids then flourished as their cousins declined: by the Middle Devonian there were about 22 genera, while other nautiloids dwindled.

  <!-- devo-020 -->

- **Rhynie chert, an ecosystem frozen in stone** — c. 410 million years ago (410 Ma)

  Hot springs in Scotland turned a whole community to stone. Silica-rich water from volcanic springs petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals in place, almost instantly. The result is the Rhynie chert, formed about 410 million years ago in the Pragian. It is one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, caught at an early stage of land colonization. Its animals include euthycarcinoids, branchiopods, arachnids and hexapods, and Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its jaws. The plants were rootless and leafless, and fungi living among them suggest fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land. The chert also holds the last nematophytes, enigmatic land organisms known since the Silurian.

  <!-- devo-022 -->

- **Trimerophytes and the start of the leafy plants** — c. 410 million years ago (410 Ma)

  Ferns, seed plants and most of the green world belong to one great clade, the euphyllophytes. Its early members are known from Early Devonian fossils. Among them were the trimerophytes, a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian. Timeline of life puts the earliest trimerophytes and lycophytes at 410 million years ago.

  <!-- devo-023 -->

- **Ammonoids coil into existence** — c. 410–408 million years ago (410–408 Ma)

  Ammonoids, with their tightly coiled shells, began as straight shells. The earliest appeared in the Emsian, around 410–408 million years ago, descended from straight-shelled bactritid nautiloids. Transitional fossils show the shell coiling step by step. Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian, and their radiation alongside the ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water. One early group, the agoniatitids, radiated in the Emsian, and a new order, the Goniatitida, arose before 391.9 million years ago and gave rise to later ammonoid orders. The line would become abundant in the Mesozoic and vanish around the end-Cretaceous extinction.

  <!-- devo-019 -->

- **Tungsenia and the fish ancestors of tetrapods** — c. 409 million years ago (409 Ma)

  Every four-limbed animal traces its roots to a group of Devonian fishes, the tetrapodomorphs. The oldest known member, Tungsenia from China, dates to about 409 million years ago. A little later, about 395 million years ago, a small Chinese lobe-fin called Kenichthys shows the internal nostril, or choana, caught midway through its evolution. This group did well for itself. Its relatives became the most numerous bony fishes of Devonian and Carboniferous rivers and streams.

  <!-- devo-024 -->

- **Jaekelopterus, the largest arthropod ever** — c. 409–392 million years ago (409–392 Ma)

  A single claw from Germany's Klerf Formation reveals the largest arthropod ever known. It belonged to the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae. Complete, this pincer would have been about 45.5 cm long. Size did not save the group. Eurypterines lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.

  <!-- devo-025 -->

- **Pyrite-coated fossils of the Hunsrück Slate** — c. 408–400 million years ago (408–400 Ma)

  Many fossils in Germany's Hunsrück Slate wear a coat of pyrite, the shiny iron mineral. Dating from the latest Pragian to early Emsian, it is one of few marine Devonian Lagerstätten, sites that preserve soft tissue. Its fauna includes the trilobite Chotecops and the puzzling placoderm Stensioella.

  <!-- devo-026 -->

- **Rhyniognatha and the first insects** — c. 400 million years ago (400 Ma)

  The oldest proposed insect is known only from a pair of jaws. Rhyniognatha hirsti is about 400 million years old, but whether it really is an insect is contested. The first possible insect fossils appear around 416 million years ago. Early Devonian rocks of about 400 million years ago preserve only a few kinds of insects, and none could fly. The group that would later outnumber all other animals began small and grounded.

  <!-- devo-028 -->

- **Laurussia completed** — c. 400 million years ago (400 Ma)

  By about 400 million years ago, Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and smaller terranes had collided in the Caledonian orogeny to form Laurussia, also called Euramerica. In Scotland's northwest Highlands, part of the Iapetus Ocean closed as Laurentia met Baltica. The collision raised a string of mountain ranges along the new continent's southeastern coast. Laurussia lay in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north and turned counterclockwise. Low seas in the Early Devonian split its seafloor animals into separate provinces, which were united again by the Middle Devonian.

  <!-- devo-031 -->

- **Lungfish and the dipnoan renaissance** — c. 400 million years ago (400 Ma)

  Lungfish appeared about 400 million years ago and evolved so quickly that the burst is called the dipnoan renaissance. By the Middle Devonian, 397–385 million years ago, they had evolved proto-lungs and proto-limbs. These let them spend spells outside the water.

  <!-- devo-032 -->

- **Sharks and their kin arrive** — c. 395 million years ago (395 Ma)

  Shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician, but the oldest unambiguous fossils of cartilaginous fishes are Middle Devonian. By about 395 million years ago these fishes, the sharks, rays and chimaeras, had appeared, evolving from acanthodians, the spiny sharks. Their skeletons are made of cartilage rather than bone. They quickly became diverse and important in Devonian seas.

  <!-- devo-033 -->

##### Middle Devonian Epoch

In the Middle Devonian, Earth grew its first forests. Cladoxylopsid trees stood in the Eifelian, progymnosperms appeared, and the new woods drew carbon from the air and buried it. Reefs of stromatoporoid sponges reached their peak, and in a Polish lagoon something with toes left the oldest tetrapod tracks. But the seas were turning dangerous. The Kačák event raised sea level and spread anoxia, and the Taghanic event followed with another oxygen crisis.

- **Cladoxylopsid trees grow the first forests** — during the Eifelian, 393–388 million years ago (393.5–387.9 Ma)

  At the start of the Devonian, plants stood about 30 cm tall. By its end, the tallest reached 30 m. Somewhere in between, Earth grew its first forests. The pioneers were cladoxylopsid trees, which formed the first forests in Earth history during the Eifelian. Trees over eight meters tall had appeared by the Middle Devonian, and the earliest known fossil forest dates from the Eifelian. Cladoxylopsids were not alone. Lower, shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms spread too. The leap to height happened more than once. By the late Givetian, three separate groups had evolved tree-like forms: the cladoxylalean ferns, the lycopsids and the progymnosperms. Height is a race for light, and several lineages joined it at once. The consequences went far beyond the forest floor, because so much new plant matter changed the air, the soils and the rivers, as Forests cool the Middle Devonian and Tree roots teach rivers to meander show.

  <!-- devo-036 -->

- **Sponge and coral reefs flourish** — during the Eifelian, 393–388 million years ago (393.5–387.9 Ma)

  A Devonian barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region once stretched 350 km along a continent's edge. Reefs like it were built either by microbes or by stromatoporoids, layered sponges, together with tabulate and rugose corals. Stromatoporoids recovered strongly in the Early and Middle Devonian and peaked in diversity in the Eifelian. Reefs also lined Laurussia's southeast coast, now southern England and Belgium. Climate decided who built them: microbes in warm periods, corals and stromatoporoids in cooler times.

  <!-- devo-041 -->

- **Forests cool the Middle Devonian** — during the Middle Devonian, 393–382 million years ago (393.5–382.3 Ma)

  The new forests did more than shade the ground. They drew carbon out of the air and buried it in sediments, where it could no longer trap heat. That drawdown may be reflected in a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C.

  <!-- devo-038 -->

- **The progymnosperms appear** — during the Middle Devonian, 393–382 million years ago (393.5–382.3 Ma)

  Progymnosperms, plants that came before the seed plants, first appear in the Middle Devonian. The group lasted a long time, into the Lopingian of the late Permian. Their best-known order, the Archaeopteridales, spans the Middle and Late Devonian.

  <!-- devo-039 -->

- **The Variscan mountains begin to rise** — during the Middle Devonian, 393–382 million years ago (393.5–382.3 Ma)

  A mountain belt that would deform crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic started to grow in the Middle Devonian. This was the Variscan orogeny, and it continued into the early Permian. Its engine was a set of Armorican terranes, small blocks of crust drifting north. They closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia. From about 390 million years ago, Rheic seafloor subducted beneath the Mid-German highs south of Laurussia. By the end of the Devonian, all the Armorican terranes were joined to Laurussia.

  <!-- devo-040 -->

- **The Catskill Delta spreads west** — c. 393–359 million years ago (393.5–358.9 Ma)

  A wedge of red sandstone up to 3,000 m thick lies under Pennsylvania and New York. Rivers and marshes built it as the Catskill Delta, carrying sediment eroded from the Acadian Mountains west into the inland Kaskaskia Sea. It records large-scale deposition on land during the Acadian orogeny. It also preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, key evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

  <!-- devo-035 -->

- **Zachełmie, the oldest tetrapod tracks** — c. 390 million years ago (390 Ma)

  Some prints in a Polish quarry show toes. The tracks at Zachełmie, from the Eifelian, are the oldest evidence of tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates. They predate the oldest tetrapod body fossils by about 18 million years. They were made in shallow lagoons on a marine carbonate platform, which supports a tidal-shore origin for land vertebrates. If genuine, they turn Tiktaalik-like elpistostegids into late-surviving relics; the next oldest tracks, about 385 million years old, come from Valentia Island, Ireland. Not everyone agrees they are tracks at all. Some researchers read them as fish feeding traces instead.

  <!-- devo-042 -->

- **The Kačák event darkens the seas** — c. 388 million years ago (387.9 Ma)

  Near the end of the Eifelian, the oceans warmed, rose and lost their oxygen. The Kačák event lasted perhaps 200,000 to 700,000 years. High sunlight probably heated the seas, raising sea level as water expanded, and strengthened monsoons that filled Scotland's Achanarras lake, the deepest in the Orcadian Basin. Anoxia, a lack of oxygen, laid down black shales. Open-ocean animals were hit hardest: agoniatitid ammonoids suffered heavy losses while tornoceratids diversified. Warming wrecked the cool-water Malvinoxhosan Realm off Gondwana. Estimates put the loss at about 24% to 32% of marine genera, milder than the Late Devonian extinctions to come.

  <!-- devo-043 -->

- **The Taghanic event suffocates the shallows** — c. 386 million years ago (386 Ma)

  Trilobites lost an entire order, the Lichida, in the Givetian. The cause was the Taghanic event, an extinction driven by hypoxia, low oxygen, after an anoxic event drained the oceans of oxygen. It sharply cut trilobite diversity, especially in shallow water. One study ranks it as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction. Another account places it at the Givetian/Frasnian boundary and credits it with wiping out about half of coral genera.

  <!-- devo-044 -->

- **Wetlands and the first modern land ecosystems** — c. 385–359 million years ago (385–359 Ma)

  Land ecosystems that would look familiar today appeared only in the Late Devonian, about 385 to 359 million years ago. Plants stabilized the edges of fresh water, and the first wetlands developed, with increasingly complex food webs. These wetlands later gave way to the coal forests of the Early Carboniferous.

  <!-- devo-046 -->

##### Late Devonian Epoch

The Late Devonian was a time of giants, impacts and loss. In Western Australia, the Gogo Formation preserved soft tissues down to nerves and embryos, while deep-sea oxygen finally stabilized near modern levels. Meteorites struck from Russia's Kaluga to Sweden's Siljan Ring, the largest impact structure in Europe. Flood basalts erupted in Siberia, and mountains rose from the Canadian Arctic to the ancestral Sierra Nevada. Underneath it all, oxygen-starved seas buried organic matter, setting up some of the deadliest extinctions in Earth's history.

- **The Chilenia terrane docks** — during the Late Devonian, 382–359 million years ago (382.3–358.9 Ma)

  Subduction off western South America kept dragging crust toward the continent. In the Late Devonian it brought a block called the Chilenia terrane into collision with the western border of the Precordillera, where it accreted, welded on for good.

  <!-- devo-048 -->

- **The Innuitian mountains rise in the Arctic** — during the Late Devonian, 382–359 million years ago (382.3–358.9 Ma)

  Mountains rose across the Canadian Arctic and northernmost Greenland in the Innuitian, or Ellesmere, orogeny. It ran from the Late Devonian into the early Carboniferous. When the range later collapsed, it opened the Sverdrup Basin on Laurussia's northern margin.

  <!-- devo-051 -->

- **The Late Devonian warms again** — during the Late Devonian, 382–359 million years ago (382.3–358.9 Ma)

  After a cooler middle, the Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels. More continental weathering and the spread of plants show it. Oddly, carbon dioxide did not rise to match. Arid climates shrank while temperate climates became more common.

  <!-- devo-052 -->

- **Dead seas make Devonian oil** — during the Late Devonian–Early Mississippian, 382–347 million years ago (382.3–346.7 Ma)

  The Williston Basin's Bakken shales cover about 520,000 km2 and are a prolific source of oil. They began with suffocated seas. During the Late Devonian extinctions, widespread anoxia halted decay, so organic matter piled up in seafloor mud. Some Bakken layers formed in euxinic waters, without oxygen and full of hydrogen sulfide. Paired with porous reef rocks that hold oil, this made Devonian rocks an important oil source, especially in Canada and the United States.

  <!-- devo-047 -->

- **The Viluy Traps flood Siberia with basalt** — c. 381–366 million years ago (381–366 Ma)

  At the edge of the Siberian Platform, a three-armed rift opened, and deep mantle plumes fed it with lava. These were the Viluy, or Vilyuy, Traps, Siberian flood basalts first erupted in the Late Devonian. The main eruptions ran from about 381 to 366 million years ago, give or take 5 million years, with a later pulse near the end of the Devonian. Dating finds two volcanic phases, the first matching the age of the Kellwasser event. Their role in the extinction is debated. Long thought a major cause of the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, the main eruptions now seem to predate it.

  <!-- devo-053 -->

- **The Antler orogeny starts the western mountains** — c. 380 million years ago (380 Ma)

  Western North America's long run of mountain building had a beginning. Subduction of Panthalassic ocean floor along Laurussia's western margin drove the Antler orogeny, in the region of the ancestral Sierra Nevada. It began a series of orogenies that culminated in the Laramide. Sources disagree on its start: most say the Late Devonian, but its own article says it began after the Devonian.

  <!-- devo-054 -->

- **Oxygen settles in the deep sea** — c. 380 million years ago (380 Ma)

  Before about 380 million years ago, oxygen in the deep ocean came and went, sporadic and variable. Only after that date did it stabilize near modern levels.

  <!-- devo-055 -->

- **Gogo's fossils and the oldest live birth** — c. 380 million years ago (380 Ma)

  In Western Australia, fossils about 380 million years old still show nerves. The Gogo Formation, from the Frasnian, preserves soft tissues in three dimensions, down to embryos with umbilical cords. Those embryos belong to the placoderms Materpiscis, Incisoscutum and Austroptyctodus, the oldest known examples of live birth. Over fifty fish species have been described from Gogo, along with arthropods. Among them is Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs.

  <!-- devo-056 -->

- **The buried Kaluga crater** — c. 380 million years ago (380 ± 5 Ma)

  Under about 800 m of sediment in Russia's Kaluga Oblast lies a crater 15 km across. An impact made it 380 ± 5 million years ago, in the Late Devonian. It is not exposed at the surface.

  <!-- devo-057 -->

- **The Ilyinets crater** — c. 378 million years ago (378 ± 5 Ma)

  Ukraine's Ilyinets crater, 8.5 km across, formed about 378 ± 5 million years ago. It is one of several Late Devonian impact scars found in Europe.

  <!-- devo-059 -->

- **The Alamo impact hits a Nevada sea** — c. 378–377 million years ago (378–377 Ma)

  One or more objects traveling at hypervelocity slammed into shallow seas in what is now southeastern Nevada, 377–378 million years ago. It is among the best-exposed and most accurately dated impacts. It came about 5.9 million years before the Frasnian-Famennian extinctions and probably did not affect them. Its age roughly matches the earliest Antler orogeny deposits, and it may have knocked loose huge slide blocks.

  <!-- devo-058 -->

- **Siljan, Europe's largest impact scar** — c. 377 million years ago (376.8 ± 1.7 Ma)

  A ring of lakes in central Sweden marks the largest impact structure in Europe. A meteorite struck what is now Dalarna and left the Siljan Ring, about 52 km across. The impact is dated to 376.8 ± 1.7 or 377 ± 2 million years ago, in the Frasnian. It was once proposed as a cause of the Kellwasser extinction. That link has weakened, because the extinction has since been dated later, to 371.93–371.78 million years ago.

  <!-- devo-060 -->

- **The Acadian orogeny raises the Atlantic seaboard** — c. 375 million years ago (375 Ma)

  For about 50 million years from roughly 375 million years ago, mountains grew along North America's Atlantic seaboard. This was the Acadian orogeny, which lasted into the early Mississippian. Its cause was the accretion of Avalonian terranes to Laurentia's eastern margin, most likely starting late in the Early Devonian. Collisions with this crust, broken from Gondwana, closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 million years ago. In New England, volcanoes and uplift shed sediment into an inland sea, and The Catskill Delta spreads west filled the basin at the mountains' foot. Across the ocean, Acadian squeezing of 404–394 million years ago joined the British Isles into their present shape.

  <!-- devo-061 -->

- **Tiktaalik, a fish halfway to land** — c. 375 million years ago (375 Ma)

  In Frasnian rocks of Nunavut, Canada, lay a fish with a neck and the makings of limbs. Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish about 375 million years old, had many tetrapod-like features. It bridges fishes such as Panderichthys, about 380 million years old, and early tetrapods such as Acanthostega. Its group, the elpistostegalians, disappeared at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. There is a twist. If the older Zachełmie, the oldest tetrapod tracks were made by tetrapods, Tiktaalik's group was an evolutionary dead end, not a direct ancestor.

  <!-- devo-062 -->

- **The Cerberean Caldera supereruption** — c. 374 million years ago (374 Ma)

  In what is now Victoria, Australia, the Cerberean Caldera is thought to have produced a supereruption about 374 million years ago. It has been suggested as an overlooked contributor to the Kellwasser extinction.

  <!-- devo-063 -->

- **The Kellwasser event, a Big Five extinction** — c. 372 million years ago (372.1 Ma)

  About 70% of species died in the Late Devonian crisis. Its sharpest blow, the Kellwasser event, is named for Germany's Kellwassertal valley and struck at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. It ranks among the Big Five mass extinctions. The crisis came in pulses, from the mid-Givetian to the end of the Famennian. Marine life suffered most, and the warm shallow reefs worst of all. Their builders, stromatoporoid sponges and rugose and tabulate corals, were devastated, ending the great reefs of Sponge and coral reefs flourish. Most remaining jawless fishes died. Placoderms lost much of their diversity. All Frasnian tetrapods vanished, and only two trilobite orders survived. Why it happened is still uncertain. Suggested causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling, and nutrient runoff from the roots of new forests, which fed blooms in the sea. Volcanism is debated. The likeliest story may be several causes working together, but researchers have not settled it.

  <!-- devo-067 -->

  *Figure: Suggested causes of the Kellwasser extinction, none yet certain.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rising seas] --> B[Anoxia spreads]
  B -.-> E[About 70% of species lost]
  C[Global cooling] -.-> E
  D[Tree-root nutrient runoff] -.-> E
  ```

- **Magma floods the Dnieper-Donets rift** — during the Famennian, 372–359 million years ago (372.1–358.9 Ma)

  A mantle plume drove magmatism in the Dnieper-Donets rift of the East European Platform. It started in the late Frasnian and peaked in the Famennian, when rifting was also most active. This Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets igneous province has been linked to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

  <!-- devo-064 -->

- **The first seeds** — during the Famennian, 372–359 million years ago (372.1–358.9 Ma)

  Seeds let plants leave the riverbanks behind. Seed plants first appear in the Famennian, the last Devonian stage, as a sister group to the archaeopteridaleans or to the progymnosperms. A 385-million-year-old seed-plant precursor from Belgium predates them by about 20 million years. By the Famennian, seed plants had already diversified substantially; the earliest seed ferns are Late Devonian lyginopterids. Pollen first appears in the Late Devonian too, still indistinguishable from spores. Seeds sped plants' spread on land and let them exploit uplands away from the water's edge.

  <!-- devo-065 -->

- **Hyneria, a giant hunter in murky rivers** — during the Famennian, 372–359 million years ago (372.1–358.9 Ma)

  Hyneria lindae reached about 2.5–3 meters long, possibly 3.5. This tristichopterid lobe-finned fish hunted Famennian rivers, using large sensory canals to find prey in murky water. It was the largest and most common lobe-fin of Pennsylvania's Red Hill Shale. A second species, up to 2.7 m long, comes from Waterloo Farm in South Africa.

  <!-- devo-066 -->

- **Large wildfires take hold** — during the Famennian, 372–359 million years ago (372.1–358.9 Ma)

  Fire had been possible since the Silurian, but only in the late Famennian did oxygen rise high enough for regular, large-scale wildfires. For the first time, burning became a routine part of life on land.

  <!-- devo-068 -->

- **Archaeopteris forests change the world** — c. 370 million years ago (370 Ma)

  Archaeopterid trees grew up to 30 m tall, and in the Late Devonian their forests spread rapidly, even onto Gondwana's coasts. Giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity Famennian flora. Its order, the Archaeopteridales, ranges through the Middle and Late Devonian. These forests had global effects, part of what is called the Late Devonian wood crisis. Trees drew down carbon dioxide, cooling the climate toward the coming ice age. Their deepening roots raised weathering and washed nutrients into the sea, feeding algal blooms that stripped oxygen from deeper waters.

  E --> F[Algal blooms]
  F --> G[Deep-water anoxia]

- **Cladoselache, an early shark** — c. 370 million years ago (370 Ma)

  Cladoselache appears about 370 million years ago. It was an early shark and the first abundant genus of cartilaginous fish.

  <!-- devo-070 -->

- **Tree roots teach rivers to meander** — c. 370 million years ago (370 Ma)

  Roots changed the shape of rivers. By 370 million years ago, abundant trees such as Archaeopteris bound soils firmly. Rivers switched from mostly braided, splitting into many channels, to mostly meandering, swinging in single looping channels.

  <!-- devo-072 -->

- **Acanthostega and Ichthyostega grow legs** — c. 365 million years ago (365 Ma)

  Acanthostega had legs, lungs and gills, yet its limbs were too weak to carry it on land. That paradox sums up the first tetrapods. Limbed vertebrates such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from fossils about 365 million years old, were among the earliest able to walk. Their legs came from fins. In the Famennian, fins with bones and joints became the two pairs of walking legs of the first tetrapods. The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland, but by the end of the period tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana. The road was not smooth. The Late Devonian extinctions bottlenecked the stem-tetrapods twice, and each time they selected against the most aquatic forms. The survivors were the ones least tied to water, a filter that helped shape the land animals to come.

  <!-- devo-075 -->

- **Tadpole shrimps, living fossils** — c. 365 million years ago (365 Ma)

  Tadpole shrimps living today, Triops and Lepidurus, look much as their kind has since the end of the Devonian. The oldest known notostracan, Strudops goldenbergi, comes from the Famennian of Belgium, about 365 million years ago.

  <!-- devo-076 -->

- **The Woodleigh impact structure** — c. 364 million years ago (364 ± 8 Ma)

  Western Australia's Woodleigh impact structure measures somewhere from 60 to 160 km across. It is dated to 364 ± 8 million years ago, between the Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous. That age roughly matches the Late Devonian extinction.

  <!-- devo-077 -->

- **Flynn Creek, a well-kept crater** — c. 360 million years ago (360 ± 20 Ma)

  About 360 million years ago, an object perhaps 90–190 m wide hit a shallow sea in what is now Tennessee. It blasted a crater 3.8 km across and 150 m deep, raised a central hill and shattered rock 200 m down. At least half the broken rock was thrown out. Within a few million years, shales of the Chattanooga Sea buried it, so it is one of the best-preserved ancient impact structures.

  <!-- devo-078 -->

- **The Late Paleozoic Ice Age begins** — c. 360 million years ago (360 Ma)

  Large ice sheets returned to the land in the Late Devonian and stayed into the Late Permian. The Late Paleozoic Ice Age lasted from about 360 to 255 million years ago. Its first glacial episodes came in the late Famennian and Tournaisian, and the shift from greenhouse to icehouse came in steps. Late Devonian glacial deposits lie in Brazil's Solimoes, Amazonas and Paranaiba basins and in Bolivia, then near the South Pole. Plants burying carbon, along with the uplift of Gondwana, tipped Earth into an icehouse that lasted through the Carboniferous and Permian.

  <!-- devo-081 -->

- **Waterloo Farm, a fossil coast near the pole** — c. 360 million years ago (360 Ma)

  Near Makhanda, South Africa, a fossil site about 360 million years old opens a window on a near-polar coast. Waterloo Farm, in the Witpoort Formation, is the only record of such an ecosystem, and it overturned assumptions about high latitudes in the latest Devonian. It is the most important Late Devonian fossil site of southern Gondwana.

  <!-- devo-082 -->

- **The proposed Warburton twin impacts** — c. 360–300 million years ago (360–300 Ma)

  Two asteroids 10 km wide may have struck Australia's West and East Warburton Basins, leaving an impact zone 400 km across. The basins have been linked to the Late Devonian extinction, about 360 million years ago. These craters remain hypothetical, proposed but not confirmed.

  <!-- devo-080 -->

- **The placoderms disappear** — c. 359 million years ago (358.9 Ma)

  The armored fishes that had ruled Devonian waters did not see the Carboniferous. All placoderms died out in the end-Devonian The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian, and no species is confirmed afterward. They had already been reduced in the Kellwasser event. Now the last arthrodires, antiarchs, phyllolepids and ptychodontids vanished abruptly. Their loss opened space for bony and cartilaginous fishes, which radiated in the Carboniferous.

  <!-- devo-083 -->

- **The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian** — c. 359 million years ago (358.9 Ma)

  Two ash beds in Poland pin down a catastrophe. They bracket a black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 million years ago. That shale records the Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, which closed the Famennian. The toll was heavy. It killed the last placoderms and the stromatoporoid reef sponges. It left Proetida as the only trilobite order and nearly wiped out the ammonoids. Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages. One estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though land plants were spared. The likely trigger was cold. Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian marked the start of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age and may have driven the losses. Other proposed causes pile up: anoxia from high plankton productivity, volcanism in Kola and Timan-Pechora, ozone loss hinted at by malformed spores, and even a nearby supernova. None is settled, and several may have acted together.

  <!-- devo-084 -->

  *Figure: What the Hangenberg event did to major groups.*

  | Group | Fate |
  |---|---|
  | Placoderms | Last ones died |
  | Stromatoporoid sponges | Last ones died |
  | Trilobites | Only Proetida left |
  | Ammonoids | Nearly exterminated |
  | Plants | Spared |

- **The last armored jawless fishes** — c. 359 million years ago (358.9 Ma)

  The jawless armored fishes went out in stages. Osteostracans, galeaspids and heterostracans had died out by the end of the Frasnian. Thelodonts barely made it into the Famennian; the last named, Arianalepis, lived in Iran and Australia. The last ostracoderms became extinct at the end of the Devonian.

  <!-- devo-086 -->

- **The chitinozoans vanish** — c. 359 million years ago (358.9 Ma)

  Chitinozoans, microfossils of filter-feeding organisms that drifted in open water, appear to have died out at the end of the Devonian. Rare later finds may be older specimens reworked into younger rocks.

  <!-- devo-087 -->

#### Carboniferous Period

The Carboniferous is the period of coal swamps, and some of its plants, such as the Cordaitales, grew right in them. In fresh water, giant lobe-finned fishes were the top predators. In the rocks of Scotland, a rare bed preserved a conodont with its body intact. And far to the east, Siberia, independent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania and raised the Altai Mountains.

- **Cordaitales grow in the coal swamps** — during the Carboniferous, 359–299 million years ago (358.9–298.9 Ma)

  Cordaitales, an order of gymnosperms, seed plants with naked seeds, range from the Carboniferous into the Permian. They took many forms in the coal swamps: tall trees, shrubs, and mangrove-like plants rooted in the wet ground.

  <!-- carb-006 -->

- **Giant lobe-finned fish rule fresh water** — during the Carboniferous, 359–299 million years ago (358.9–298.9 Ma)

  Rhizodus hibberti, from Great Britain, reached up to 6 m long. It was the largest of the non-tetrapod lobe-finned fish, which were the dominant predators of Carboniferous and Permian fresh waters.

  <!-- carb-007 -->

- **The Granton Shrimp Bed** — during the Carboniferous, 359–299 million years ago (358.9–298.9 Ma)

  Soft bodies rarely fossilize. Scotland's Granton Shrimp Bed preserves Clydagnathus windsorensis, one of only three conodont species known with its trunk.

  <!-- carb-008 -->

- **Siberia joins the growing supercontinent** — during the Carboniferous, 359–299 million years ago (358.9–298.9 Ma)

  Siberia had been an independent continent since the early Paleozoic. Then it collided with Kazakhstania, raising the Altai Mountains. The Turkestan Ocean closed, bringing northern Tarim against Kazakhstania from the mid-Carboniferous to the start of the Permian. With Kazakhstania joined to Laurussia, Siberia was effectively part of Pangaea by 310 million years ago, though the blocks kept sliding past each other into the Permian.

  <!-- carb-009 -->

##### Mississippian Subperiod

The Mississippian opens just after the Hangenberg extinction, with survivors moving in. Sharks and ray-finned fish took over the seas, and crinoids grew so thick that whole limestones are made of them. Stem tetrapods had already split into the lines leading to amphibians and amniotes, though their fossils are strangely scarce in a span called Romer's gap. Warm shallow seas laid down limestone across Britain and Ireland, but glaciers were building in South America. Seawater itself was changing, as aragonite seas replaced calcite seas.

- **La Serre marks the start of the Carboniferous** — 359 million years ago (358.9 ± 0.19 Ma)

  A rock face at La Serre, in the Montagne Noire of southern France, marks where the Carboniferous begins. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Siphonodella sulcata, descended from S. praesulcata. The marker has a flaw. Later study found S. sulcata below the boundary, weakening it.

  <!-- carb-002 -->

- **Crown tetrapods split and walk ashore** — c. 359 million years ago (358.9 Ma)

  Every living four-limbed animal descends from one of two lines that had already parted by the very start of the Carboniferous. Stem tetrapods had split into two crown lines: one leading to modern amphibians, the other to amniotes. The earliest confirmed land-dwelling tetrapods come from early Carboniferous deposits, some 20 million years after the first Devonian forms. Along the way, lineages with extra digits died out, which is why hands and feet carry no more than five. The survivors radiated on dry land and became the dominant land animals of the Carboniferous and Permian.

  <!-- carb-004 -->

- **Romer's gap, a hole in the tetrapod record** — during the Tournaisian, 359–347 million years ago (358.9–346.7 Ma)

  For a stretch from the Tournaisian into the early Visean, tetrapod fossils are strikingly scarce. Paleontologists call it Romer's gap. Land vertebrates were recovering from the Hangenberg extinction, and the ichthyostegalian forms gave way to temnospondyls and reptiliomorphs. New finds at Blue Beach, Nova Scotia, and in Scotland are filling the gap, showing stem tetrapods and amphibians diversifying rapidly.

  <!-- carb-012 -->

- **Tropical seas build the Carboniferous Limestone** — during the Tournaisian–Visean, 359–330 million years ago (358.9–330.3 Ma)

  The Yorkshire Dales and the Mendips were once warm tropical seabed. Shallow seas teeming with life laid down limestone widely across Britain and Ireland, in basins separated by landmasses such as the Wales-London-Brabant Massif. The rock is built from the shells and hard parts of corals, brachiopods and crinoids, set in carbonate mud. Later uplifted, it forms karst country, landscapes shaped by dissolving rock.

  <!-- carb-014 -->

- **Crinoids at their peak** — during the Mississippian, 359–323 million years ago (358.9–323.4 Ma)

  Near Clitheroe, England, some limestones consist almost entirely of crinoids, the stalked relatives of starfish. Camerate crinoids peaked in diversity in the Mississippian, and Agaricocrinus, about 345 million years old, was part of the radiation. From the Middle Mississippian their diversity fell, as shell-crushing fish and sharks multiplied.

  <!-- carb-003 -->

- **The last cladoxylopsid trees** — during the Early Carboniferous, 359–323 million years ago (358.9–323.4 Ma)

  The cladoxylopsids built Earth's first forests in the Devonian. These large trees, ancestors of the ferns, and their order Pseudosporochnales lasted into the Early Carboniferous, and then they were gone.

  <!-- carb-010 -->

- **Sharks and ray-finned fish inherit the seas** — during the Early Carboniferous, 359–323 million years ago (358.9–323.4 Ma)

  When the placoderms vanished, two groups moved into their place. After the end-Devonian Hangenberg extinction, sharks and their kin and ray-finned fish took over in diversity and abundance. Both had suffered too, since few Devonian species of either survived. Cartilaginous fish went through a major radiation, especially holocephalans such as the stethacanthids. The helicoprionids appeared, with a single circular whorl of teeth in the lower jaw. Around 350 million years ago, the first large sharks, ratfishes and hagfish appear.

  <!-- carb-013 -->

- **The Early Tournaisian Warm Interval** — c. 358–353 million years ago (358–353 Ma)

  A brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary did not last. The climate warmed again in the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval, 358–353 million years ago. The global average temperature was about 22 °C, with the tropics near 30 °C and the polar regions about 1.5 °C.

  <!-- carb-015 -->

  *Figure: The warm interval still had a wide spread from tropics to poles.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Early Mississippian glaciations** — c. 350 million years ago (350 Ma)

  By about 350 million years ago, glacial layers were building up in the sub-Andean basins of Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay. A mid-Tournaisian glaciation left species-poor, frigid tundra in western Argentina. These short, minor glaciations came before the main ice age, steps in a gradual shift from greenhouse to icehouse.

  <!-- carb-016 -->

- **Temnospondyls begin the Age of Amphibians** — c. 350 million years ago (350 Ma)

  The first temnospondyls left their footprints before their bones. Their earliest traces are Tournaisian tracks, about 350 million years old; the first body fossils, such as Balanerpeton, are Visean, around 330 million years old. Often seen as primitive amphibians, temnospondyls flourished worldwide through the Carboniferous, Permian and Triassic. All their clades except one, the stereospondylomorphs, appeared during the Carboniferous. Their rise as the dominant land vertebrates earned the period the name Age of Amphibians.

  <!-- carb-017 -->

- **Lepidodendron, the scale tree** — c. 347 million years ago (346.7 Ma)

  Lepidodendron was a lycophyte, a relative of today's small clubmosses, but it grew into a massive tree. It first appeared near the Tournaisian–Visean boundary. With Sigillaria, it went on to dominate the coal swamps, with horsetails and seed ferns growing between them. Their order, the Lepidodendrales, lasted from the Carboniferous to the Late Permian.

  <!-- carb-021 -->

- **Aragonite seas replace calcite seas** — during the Middle Mississippian, 347–330 million years ago (346.7–330.3 Ma)

  Seawater's chemistry decides what shells can be made of. From the early Carboniferous, the ratio of magnesium to calcium in seawater rose. By the Middle Mississippian, aragonite seas, which favor shells of the mineral aragonite, had replaced calcite seas. Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, followed in the Pennsylvanian.

  <!-- carb-018 -->

- **Insects take to the air** — during the Middle Mississippian, 347–330 million years ago (346.7–330.3 Ma)
