  When did animals first take wing? The oldest known winged insects appear in the mid-Mississippian, though flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian. Once airborne, they spread fast. Winged insects, the pterygotes, went through a major radiation across the Carboniferous, 358 to 299 million years ago. Sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids dominated at first, and cockroach relatives, the Blattoptera, became the most successful insects by the Pennsylvanian. Two more innovations came in the Pennsylvanian. The Neoptera appeared. And the Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis, a life cycle with a separate larva, pupa and adult. Flight and metamorphosis together set up the insects for the success that followed.

  <!-- carb-020 -->

- **The Visean Warm Interval** — during the Visean, 347–330 million years ago (346.7–330.3 Ma)

  In the Visean Warm Interval, glaciers nearly vanished. They survived only in the proto-Andes of Bolivia and Argentina and in highlands of Brazil and southwest Africa, a pause before the ice returned in force.

  <!-- carb-022 -->

- **A long boom in marine life** — c. 347–299 million years ago (346.7–298.9 Ma)

  Some single-celled fusulinids grew so large that they hosted photosynthetic algae inside them. These foraminifera, with the brachiopods, led a long radiation of marine life, the Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event. It began in the Visean, with the main phase of the ice age. Fusulinids diversified extremely fast and peaked in the Visean, and so did bryozoans, renewed after the Hangenberg extinction. Cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined. The likely driver was geography. Closure of the Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, where species could evolve apart.

  <!-- carb-019 -->

  *Figure: A divided ocean may have driven the long marine radiation.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rheic Ocean closes] --> D[Oceans split into isolated regions]
  B[Sea level falls] --> D
  C[Pangaea assembles] --> D
  D -.-> E[Marine biodiversification]
  ```

- **East Kirkton's early land animals** — c. 341 million years ago (341 ± 3 Ma)

  A Scottish quarry holds a crowd of early land animals. East Kirkton preserves land and freshwater life, and its richest layer dates to about 341 million years ago, in the Visean. It has yielded dozens of early tetrapods, including the temnospondyl Balanerpeton and the proto-amniote Westlothiana, nicknamed Lizzie, plus scorpions and eurypterids. Its mostly land-dwelling fauna reflects a wider Carboniferous move away from amphibious life.

  <!-- carb-023 -->

- **The Variscan collision at full strength** — c. 340–295 million years ago (340–295 Ma)

  Europe's Variscan mountains and North America's Alleghanian mountains were two parts of one continental collision. Gondwana and the terranes around it struck Laurussia obliquely, with metamorphism, igneous activity and large-scale deformation, and full collision came around 340 million years ago. Northwest Africa met southeastern Euramerica, raising the southern Appalachians and the Meseta and Mauritanide mountains. The main squeezing, the Sudetic phase, ran from about 330 to 320 million years ago, when Hercynian granites intruded central Europe. Together the two belts raised the Central Pangean Mountains, which reached their greatest height by about 295 million years ago.

  <!-- carb-024 -->

- **Pangaea comes together** — c. 335 million years ago (335 Ma)

  Around 335 million years ago, the world's continents became one. Gondwana, Euramerica (Laurussia) and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea. The assembly was not gentle. Plate motions sped up as the pieces converged, and the Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia closed. Pangaea was never truly finished, either: blocks kept joining and rifting away into the early Mesozoic. All told, it lasted about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 million years ago. The supercontinent left its own proof. Glacial deposits of this age lie scattered from South America to Australia, on lands now oceans apart. Ice could not have spread across such distant places unless they were once joined, and those deposits later helped prove continental drift and the existence of Pangaea. The same collisions raised mountain belts such as The Variscan collision at full strength and set up the climates and ice ages of the following periods.

  <!-- carb-025 -->

  *Figure: Pangaea's assembly and the start of its breakup.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Gondwana] --> D[Pangaea about 335 Ma]
  B[Euramerica] --> D
  C[Siberia] --> D
  D --> E[Rheic Ocean closes]
  D --> F[Breakup begins about 175 Ma]
  ```

- **The first reptiliomorphs** — c. 335–325 million years ago (335–325 Ma)

  The first reptiliomorphs, tetrapods on the line toward reptiles, appear between 335 and 325 million years ago. By the Visean, early tetrapods had radiated into at least three or four main branches. The reptile-like Westlothiana lived then.

  <!-- carb-026 -->

- **The ice age tightens its grip** — c. 335–290 million years ago (335–290 Ma)

  Around 330 million years ago, an ice sheet kilometers thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole. It belonged to the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. That phase began between 335 and 330 million years ago, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and carbon dioxide fell. The onset reshaped coastlines everywhere. Sea level fell worldwide, leaving unconformities, gaps in the rock record lasting millions of years. Ice spread from up to 30 centers across Gondwana. Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells, and the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian. The ice left thick evidence. Its deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group. Those piles of scraped and dumped rock record ice that came and went for tens of millions of years.

  <!-- carb-027 -->

  *Figure: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age left very thick glacial deposits.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Ouachita orogeny** — during the Late Mississippian, 330–323 million years ago (330.3–323.4 Ma)

  South America, then part of Gondwana, struck Laurussia's southern margin at an angle in the Ouachita orogeny. The collision began in the Late Mississippian. The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins, low areas in front of the range, such as the Delaware Basin. They fed rivers with sediment through the Pennsylvanian and Permian.

  <!-- carb-031 -->

- **The Serpukhovian extinction** — during the Serpukhovian, 330–323 million years ago (330.3–323.4 Ma)

  The worst extinction of the Carboniferous removed about 31% of marine genera in the early Serpukhovian. A major glaciation at the Visean–Serpukhovian boundary cooled the seas, picking off species adapted to narrow, tropical temperature ranges. Diverse crinoid and rugose-coral communities gave way to species-poor, cosmopolitan ones. Trilobites declined sharply while ammonoids peaked. It was driven more by a lack of new species than by high extinction, and its long-term ecological impact may have exceeded the end-Ordovician extinction's. It ties with the Hangenberg event as the seventh-worst post-Cambrian mass extinction. Its severity is debated: a 2026 study finds it weaker in North America, and sources dispute whether diversity afterward stagnated or surged.

  <!-- carb-032 -->

- **The Millstone Grit spreads over northern England** — during the Serpukhovian–Bashkirian, 330–315 million years ago (330.3–315.2 Ma)

  The moors and rocky edges of the Pennines are made of old delta sand. With Britain near the equator, rivers from northern uplands and the Wales-Brabant High carried sand and mud into the Pennine Basin. When sea level fell as southern ice caps grew, deltas advanced across the region and left thick sandstones, the Millstone Grit. These gritstones lie beneath the Coal Measures.

  <!-- carb-030 -->

- **Avion's early insects** — during the Serpukhovian–Moscovian, 330–307 million years ago (330.3–307 Ma)

  Insects from the Avion locality in Pas-de-Calais, France, include the earliest known thrips and titanopterans.

  <!-- carb-029 -->

- **Amniotes and the egg that left the water** — c. 330–320 million years ago (330–320 Ma)

  An egg that dries out is a dead egg. One tetrapod lineage solved that problem. It evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land, and these animals are the amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals. When they arose is disputed. Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 million years ago, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 million years ago. Another account puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous. Clawed footprints from the Tournaisian of Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks. If so, amniotes go back to the start of the period or earlier. Researchers have not settled the question. What is clearer is how they took over. Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes rose in their place.

  <!-- carb-033 -->

- **Patagonia meets Gondwana** — c. 330–320 million years ago (330–320 Ma)

  Igneous rocks 330–320 million years old under the North Patagonian Massif record subduction. It began in the early Carboniferous and lasted about 20 million years. The Patagonian landmass first touched Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous, and the broader collision came in the early Permian.

  <!-- carb-034 -->

- **Fossil Grove, a forest still standing** — c. 325 million years ago (325 Ma)

  In a Glasgow park, the stumps of an ancient forest still stand where they grew. About 325 million years ago, sediments buried tree-like lycopsids at Fossil Grove while they were upright. These Lepidodendron trees grew when Scotland lay in the tropics, near the equator.

  <!-- carb-036 -->

- **The Alleghanian orogeny builds the Appalachians** — c. 325–260 million years ago (325–260 Ma)

  Africa and North America collided in at least five separate deformation events. Africa was then part of Gondwana and North America part of Euramerica. The Alleghanian orogeny began about 325 million years ago and lasted some 65 million years, into the Permian. It built the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains, a wide, high chain along today's eastern seaboard, and helped form Pangaea. Sediment from the rising mountains filled basins such as the Black Warrior Basin. When West Africa struck in the Late Pennsylvanian, the compression turned northwest, and the same grinding raised the Little Atlas range around 300 million years ago.

  <!-- carb-035 -->

- **The Bear Gulch Limestone** — c. 324 million years ago (324 Ma)

  Central Montana's Bear Gulch Limestone preserves an unusually diverse fauna of cartilaginous fish, relatives of sharks, rays and chimaeras. Brachiopods, ray-finned fish and arthropods occur there too, along with Typhloesus, a puzzling animal that may be a mollusc.

  <!-- carb-037 -->

##### Pennsylvanian Subperiod

The Pennsylvanian was the age of coal. Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land, and oxygen climbed to 25–30%, above today's 21%, while carbon dioxide crashed to one of its lowest levels ever. Ice sheets spread from southern Africa and South America, and repeating rock cycles called cyclothems record the seas rising and falling with them. Arachnids, myriapods and flying insects radiated, cycads and conifers appeared, and by the end the equatorial belt was drying out.

- **Arrow Canyon marks the Pennsylvanian** — 323 million years ago (323.4 ± 0.4 Ma)

  In Arrow Canyon, Nevada, a single layer of rock marks the start of the Pennsylvanian and its first stage, the Bashkirian. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Declinognathodus noduliferus.

  <!-- carb-040 -->

- **The first great glacial maximum** — during the Bashkirian, 323–315 million years ago (323.4–315.2 Ma)

  In North America, a gap in the rocks separates the Mississippian from the Pennsylvanian. That unconformity is the scar of a falling sea. The ice age's first major glacial period, from the Serpukhovian to the Moscovian, spread ice sheets from cores in southern Africa and South America. In the Bashkirian, a global sea-level fall marked its first major glacial maximum. At the boundary, a positive oxygen-isotope excursion, a chemical sign of growing ice, matches sea-level falls and glacial deposits across southern Gondwana. Early in the Bashkirian, the ocean gateway between the Rheic and the Tethys closed. That changed ocean circulation and added to the cooling.

  <!-- carb-050 -->

- **All modern classes of fungi appear** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  By the late Carboniferous, every modern class of fungi had appeared. Rocks of Pennsylvanian age preserve them, showing that the fungal world of today was already fully sketched out among the coal swamps.

  <!-- carb-038 -->

- **Oxygen reaches its all-time high** — during the Pennsylvanian, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  Today the air is 21% oxygen. In the Pennsylvanian it reached 25 to 30%. All models agree on the rise, from 15–20% at the start of the Carboniferous to those highs. Pyrite, an iron sulfide mineral, gives a more detailed record. It suggests about 15% early in the period, over 25% in the Pennsylvanian, then a drop below 20% toward its end. Charcoal tells the same story. Remains of wildfires grow more common from the Late Devonian into the Carboniferous, because fire burns more readily in richer air. The source of the extra oxygen was the coal forests. Their photosynthesis released oxygen into the air, and their buried peat kept the carbon from taking it back by decay, as Coal forests cover the tropics describes. Whether the oxygen-rich air let arthropods and other animals grow large is still debated.

  <!-- carb-039 -->

  *Figure: Carboniferous oxygen rose well above today's level.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Carbon dioxide falls to an all-time low** — during the Pennsylvanian, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  Carbon dioxide in the air fell below 300 ppm in the Pennsylvanian and early Permian, one of its lowest levels ever. Several processes pulled it down: burial of organic matter, widespread ocean anoxia, and weathering of the rising Central Pangean Mountains. Fast-growing coal forests locked away more carbon, and a very late Carboniferous forest resurgence brought polar ice back to Gondwana. Near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, erosion of dark, iron-rich mountain rocks pushed carbon dioxide as low as 175 ppm, and it stayed under 400 ppm for 10 million years. Then the trend reversed. From a record low about 298 million years ago, carbon dioxide rose fourfold by 294 million years ago.

  <!-- carb-041 -->

  *Figure: Carbon dioxide sank to some of its lowest levels ever.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Mountains bring monsoon rains** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  The Central Pangean Mountains made their own weather. They set up a perennial monsoon over today's Europe and eastern North America, keeping those lands swampy while the Colorado Plateau stayed dry. Climate models suggest the range helped lay down vast coal deposits. The first signs of moisture moving toward the poles appeared in the late Carboniferous.

  <!-- carb-042 -->

- **The Cimmerian blocks break away** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  A string of blocks that now lies in Asia began its journey from Gondwana. Rifting between India and the Cimmerian superterranes started in the Early Carboniferous, and the blocks pulled away in the Late Carboniferous. Stretching along Gondwana's northern margin set up their break-away and the opening of the Neo-Tethys in the early Permian. They would dock with Asia in the Triassic and Jurassic.

  <!-- carb-043 -->

- **Coal forests cover the tropics** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  About 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history. The source was a world of swamps. Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the Pennsylvanian and lasted into the Permian. Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated equatorial Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants, and peat mires also ringed the North and South China cratons. When the trees died, they piled up as peat, and the buried peat became coal. The ice age helped. Glacial falls in sea level exposed wide shelves where peat mires grew, and rising seas in warmer spells then buried them. Why coal formation peaked so sharply is debated. One idea is a lag before fungi evolved that could digest lignin, the tough material in wood. The other is a unique mix of equatorial lands, high plant productivity and sinking wet basins.

  <!-- carb-044 -->

  *Figure: How sea-level swings grew peat mires, then buried them to make coal.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Glacial sea level falls] --> B[Wide shelves exposed]
  B --> C[Peat mires grow]
  C --> D[Interglacial seas rise]
  D --> E[Peat buried]
  E --> F[Peat becomes coal]
  ```

- **Cyclothems, stripes of a swinging sea** — during the Pennsylvanian, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  The rocks of the Pennsylvanian repeat like a song. Cyclothems, repeating cycles of sediment, formed in shallow seas across tropical Laurussia and the China cratons. Each records a sea-level fall and rise over about 100,000 years, as Gondwana's ice sheets advanced and retreated on a Milankovitch cycle, a rhythm in Earth's orbit. The swings reached up to 120 m. Falls were slow and rises rapid, because ice sheets grow slowly but melt quickly.

  <!-- carb-045 -->

  *Figure: Each cyclothem records one turn of this ice-driven loop.* (cycle; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Equatorial Pangaea dries out** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  The swamps did not last forever. Toward the end of the Carboniferous, Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier, beginning a dry trend that lasted into the Triassic. After about 318 million years ago, seasons swung often between humid and arid. A cycle of drying began in the late Moscovian, with abrupt changes in animal life. Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained, more stable landscapes. Weaker weathering in the drier climate even lowered the seawater strontium-isotope ratio. Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling carbon dioxide and low-latitude aridity brought a permanent shift to seasonally dry woodland.

  <!-- carb-046 -->

- **Conifers and cycads appear** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  Conifers began on dry ground. Early walchian conifers such as Walchia favored the higher, drier land where gymnosperms grew in the Pennsylvanian. The Voltziales conifers, cycads and Callistophytales seed ferns appeared in the late Carboniferous, and ginkgophytes also arose in the period. The oldest probable cycad leaves, such as Crossozamia from South Korea and China, date to around 300 million years ago.

  <!-- carb-047 -->

- **Arthropods grow to giant sizes** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  Meganeura, a griffinfly, had wings spanning about 75 cm, the largest of any flying insect ever. It dominated the skies around 305 million years ago. On the ground crawled Arthropleura, a millipede-like animal up to 2.6 m long and the largest land invertebrate of all time. Arachnids, myriapods and especially flying insects underwent a major radiation in the late Carboniferous. Giant insects, millipedes and scorpions thrived while tetrapods stayed small, until The Carboniferous rainforest collapse. The gigantism may reflect high oxygen levels, though how oxygen shaped body size is debated.

  <!-- carb-049 -->

- **The Oslo Rift tears open** — during the Late Carboniferous, 323–299 million years ago (323.4–298.9 Ma)

  Around today's Oslo, the crust began to pull apart in the late Carboniferous, opening a graben, a block dropped between faults. The tearing came in the last phase of the Variscan orogeny and coincided with the Moscovian–Kasimovian boundary and the rainforest collapse. It ended in heavy volcanism: in Vestfold, rhomb porphyry lavas piled up about 3,000 m thick.

  <!-- carb-051 -->

- **The Ural Mountains begin to rise** — c. 323 million years ago (323 Ma)

  The Ural Mountains began rising about 323 million years ago. The Uralian orogeny started in the Late Carboniferous and went on through the Permian. Earlier, the Magnitogorsk island arc had collided with Baltica's margin from the Late Devonian to early Carboniferous. Then, as the Ural Ocean closed in the Bashkirian, Kazakhstania began colliding with Laurussia. Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica joined to form Laurasia, the basis of most of present-day Eurasia. Granites intruded the region as deformation continued, and around 300 million years ago the Urals were uplifted as Pangaea was finally sutured.

  <!-- carb-052 -->

  *Figure: Three blocks collided in the Uralian orogeny to form Laurasia.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Siberia] --> D[Laurasia]
  B[Kazakhstania] --> D
  C[Baltica] --> D
  D --> E[Most of Eurasia]
  ```

- **Synapsids and sauropsids part ways** — c. 320 million years ago (320 Ma)

  Every mammal and every bird traces back to a single fork in the amniote family tree. Amniotes split into two lines: synapsids, the mammal lineage, and sauropsids, the line of reptiles and birds. Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 million years ago and the first synapsids around 318 million years ago. The earliest fossils of both date to about 313 million years ago. Synapsid pelycosaurs appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate land for some 40 million years. By the period's end, amniotes had diversified into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

  <!-- carb-053 -->

  *Figure: Amniotes split into the mammal line and the reptile and bird line.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Ice fills the young Karoo Basin** — c. 317–288 million years ago (317–288 Ma)

  Southern Africa lay inside the Antarctic Circle. Subduction under Gondwana and the rising Gondwanide mountains made room for a foreland basin, the Karoo Basin. Ice sheets buried the highlands around it, while floating glaciers filled its lowlands. Their deposits, tillites, diamictites and scratched rock pavements of the Dwyka Group, begin the Karoo Supergroup and reach about 800 m thick in the south.

  <!-- carb-057 -->

- **Hylonomus at Joggins, the oldest reptile** — c. 315 million years ago (315 Ma)

  The sea cliffs at Joggins, Nova Scotia, preserve a whole land ecosystem: lycopsid trees, giant arthropods and fish. They also yield Hylonomus, the oldest known sauropsid and one of the oldest reptiles in the fossil record. Here, in the coal-age forest, the reptile line makes its first clear appearance.

  <!-- carb-060 -->

- **The magnetic field stops flipping** — c. 312–262 million years ago (312–262 Ma)

  Earth's magnetic field normally reverses every so often. From about 312 to 262 million years ago, it did not. For more than 50 million years it held reversed polarity, with north and south swapped from today's arrangement. This stretch, the Kiaman superchron, spans the late Carboniferous to the late Permian. Comparable spells are the Cretaceous Normal Superchron and a possible one in the Ordovician.

  <!-- carb-062 -->

- **Mazon Creek's ironstone treasures** — c. 310 million years ago (310 Ma)

  The Tully monster, Tullimonstrum, is known from only one place: Mazon Creek, near Morris, Illinois. There a large delta preserved fossils in ironstone concretions in exceptional detail. Its roughly 200 insect species, some gigantic, show that insects already filled their main modern roles as plant eaters, scavengers of dead matter and insect eaters.

  <!-- carb-065 -->

- **A brief, intense Kasimovian glaciation** — during the Kasimovian, 307–304 million years ago (307–303.7 Ma)

  Early in the Kasimovian, a glaciation lasting less than a million years drove carbon dioxide as low as 180 ppm. It was short but intense. It ended abruptly as carbon dioxide rose quickly, but by then the wetland forests had been restructured and the tree lycopsids lost.

  <!-- carb-067 -->

- **The Alykaevo Climatic Optimum** — during the Kasimovian–Gzhelian, 307–299 million years ago (307–298.9 Ma)

  Between the ice age's first and second major glacial periods came a warmer break. The Alykaevo Climatic Optimum, a relatively warm interglacial, spanned the Kasimovian and Gzhelian before the ice returned.

  <!-- carb-066 -->

- **The Carboniferous rainforest collapse** — c. 305 million years ago (305 Ma)

  The great coal forests did not die out all at once; they broke into pieces. A cooler, drier climate first fragmented the rainforests and then collapsed them. Tree lycopsids and other wetland groups were lost in the Kasimovian glacial interval, as A brief, intense Kasimovian glaciation describes. It was a replacement more than an ending. Lycopsid forests gave way to tree-fern forests, a complex change, not the loss of all rainforest. Scale trees largely vanished from North America and Europe but persisted in Cathaysia, where coal forests even revived at the very end of the period. Animals felt it too. Amphibians and amniotes were both hit, and the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes. It was a minor extinction on land and at sea. But it left vast deserts across the continental interior, the landscape of the Permian to come.

  <!-- carb-071 -->

  *Figure: How a drier climate turned coal forests into fern forests and deserts.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cooler, drier climate] --> B[Rainforest fragments]
  B --> C[Lycopsid forests collapse]
  C --> D[Tree-fern forests]
  C --> E[Interior deserts]
  ```

- **The first diapsid reptiles** — c. 305 million years ago (305 Ma)

  Petrolacosaurus, around 305 million years old, is among the first diapsid reptiles, the group with two openings behind each eye. By the end of the Carboniferous, amniotes included saurians and araeoscelids among several new groups. The reptile family tree was branching fast.

  <!-- carb-072 -->

- **The Ancestral Rocky Mountains** — c. 300 million years ago (300 Ma)

  Long before today's Rockies, another range stood in the same region. Around 300 million years ago, mountain building raised the Ancestral Rocky Mountains in what are now Colorado and New Mexico, with a prong into Wyoming. The Colorado orogeny that built them also began the Denver Basin. The range later eroded away.

  <!-- carb-074 -->

- **Hamilton Quarry's mixed fossils** — c. 300 million years ago (300 Ma)

  In Kansas, a probable estuary, where a river met the sea, mixed fossils from many settings. Hamilton Quarry preserves well-kept marine, brackish, freshwater, flying and land animals and plants side by side.

  <!-- carb-075 -->

- **The ice age peaks** — c. 300 million years ago (300 Ma)

  Around 300 million years ago, a very large part of Gondwana lay under glacial conditions. This exceptionally intense cooling marked the peak of the ice age across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary. A second major glacial period began in the late Gzhelian, with ice sheets spreading from cores in Australia and India into the early Permian. In the glacial maximum, 299–293 million years ago, the global average temperature was about 13 °C. Not everywhere froze at once. Brazil's Paraná Basin had its last glaciation in the early Gzhelian.

  <!-- carb-076 -->

- **Montceau-les-Mines fossil site** — c. 300 million years ago (300 Ma)

  Montceau-les-Mines, in France, preserves late Carboniferous life in exceptional detail, much like Mazon Creek. Its finds include vertebrates, arthropods and plants, among them temnospondyls, velvet worms and arachnids.

  <!-- carb-077 -->

#### Permian Period

In the Permian, almost every major landmass was gathered into one supercontinent, Pangaea. Its climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons that brought harsh dry seasons to the interior. In the south, mountain building folded Gondwana from South America to New Guinea, and Glossopteris seed plants spread across the land. Among the reptiles, the lineage leading to lizards split from its sister group.

- **Glossopteris forests rule the south** — during the Permian, 299–252 million years ago (298.9–251.9 Ma)

  Across the southern continents, one kind of tree came to dominate. Glossopteridales, an extinct order of seed plants, are known from the Permian of Gondwana. Once Gondwana had fused with Pangaea, glossopterid trees, chiefly Glossopteris, dominated large parts of the south. As glaciation waned in the Middle Permian, the Glossopteris flora flourished, and huge coal deposits formed from it, as in southern Brazil and Uruguay. These forests lasted until the end-Permian mass extinction, when they collapsed.

  <!-- perm-005 -->

- **The Gondwanide orogeny folds the south** — during the Permian, 299–252 million years ago (298.9–251.9 Ma)

  South Africa's Cape Fold Belt and Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana are the folded remains of one Permian mountain belt. Mountain building deformed southern Gondwana, in what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea. Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two. In South Africa, folding entered a new phase from about 260 million years ago. By then the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, had spread.

  <!-- perm-006 -->

- **Lizards' ancestors part from the archelosaurs** — during the Permian, 299–252 million years ago (298.9–251.9 Ma)

  Lizards, snakes and their kin descend from a lineage called the Lepidosauromorpha. It is thought to have split from its sister group, the Archelosauria, during the Permian, a quiet fork in the reptile family tree with large consequences.

  <!-- perm-008 -->

- **Pangaea complete** — during the Permian, 299–252 million years ago (298.9–251.9 Ma)

  In the Permian, almost every major landmass on Earth was part of a single continent. The supercontinent Pangaea stretched from the equator to both polar regions. Only parts of East Asia, such as Cathaysia, lay apart. Gondwana's collision with the northern continents had completed most of it, leaving the Appalachian and Ouachita mountains near its center. The last pieces arrived during the Permian itself. Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian. Siberia joined in the late Permian, and North China, South China and Indochina fused with Pangaea by the period's end. The supercontinent did not have long to enjoy its completion. Pangaea was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction. Its shape set the climate of the age: a single vast landmass spanning the globe, with an interior far from the sea, as The Pangean megamonsoon describes.

  <!-- perm-013 -->

  *Figure: The order in which the last blocks joined Pangaea.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Kazakhstania strikes Baltica] --> B[Siberia joins]
  B --> C[North and South China, Indochina fuse]
  ```

- **The Pangean megamonsoon** — during the Permian, 299–252 million years ago (298.9–251.9 Ma)

  Pangaea's interior swung between parched months and violent rain. Permian climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons, giant seasonal wind systems that brought high aridity and harsh seasons inland. The monsoon shows in Permian rocks: Early Permian wind directions record a summer wet season. As the continents drifted north and spread more evenly across the equator, the megamonsoon grew stronger. Dryness alternating with seasonal rain became the normal climate across much of the continent.

  <!-- perm-014 -->

  *Figure: Northward drift strengthened the monsoon that ruled Pangaea.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Continents drift north] --> B[Spread evenly across equator]
  B --> C[Megamonsoon intensifies]
  C --> D[Dryness and seasonal rain]
  ```

##### Cisuralian Epoch

The Cisuralian, the first Permian epoch, opened in the grip of an ice age and ended in a warming world. Carbon dioxide hit a record low and then rose fourfold within a few million years. Pelycosaurs such as Dimetrodon were the dominant land animals, insects diversified dramatically, and the first beetles appeared. Meanwhile the map kept shifting: Kazakhstania struck Baltica, Patagonia completed its collision, and the Cimmerian blocks broke away from Gondwana.

- **Aidaralash marks the start of the Permian** — 299 million years ago (298.9 ± 0.15 Ma)

  In the Aidaralash River valley near Aqtöbe, Kazakhstan, a layer of rock marks the start of the Permian. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Streptognathodus isolatus.

  <!-- perm-001 -->

- **Insects diversify into modern orders** — during the Early Permian, 299–274 million years ago (298.9–274.4 Ma)

  Most living insect orders arose during the Permian. Insects diversified dramatically in its early part, and those with complete metamorphosis radiated. Scorpionflies, true dragonflies and barklice first appeared. Older dominant groups faded: the palaeodictyopterans and giant griffinflies declined, and the palaeodictyopteran decline from the mid-Permian is linked to a change in plants. Insects and plants were already locked in an arms race, with insects chewing and plants evolving defenses.

  <!-- perm-007 -->

- **Cimmeria rifts away and the Neo-Tethys opens** — during the Early Permian, 299–274 million years ago (298.9–274.4 Ma)

  A strip of continent tore off Gondwana's northern edge in the Early Permian. Rifting broke away the Cimmerian blocks, including Sibumasu (Shan–Thai), Qiantang and Lhasa. As they drifted toward Laurasia, they closed the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them. Behind them opened a new ocean, the Neo-Tethys. It grew from a rift in what is now the Himalayan region and would dominate much of the Mesozoic.

  <!-- perm-012 -->

- **Patagonia completes its collision** — during the Early Permian, 299–274 million years ago (298.9–274.4 Ma)

  The Patagonian landmass had first touched south-western Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous. In the early Permian came the broader collision. Deformation and metamorphism from it carried on into the Permian, welding Patagonia firmly to the supercontinent.

  <!-- perm-015 -->

- **Synapsids rule the land** — during the Cisuralian, 299–274 million years ago (298.9–274.4 Ma)

  For some 40 million years, the dominant land animals were relatives of mammals. Pelycosaurs, early synapsids, peaked in the Cisuralian. Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, thrived and diversified greatly, quickly growing large. In North America and Europe, Early Permian faunas were led by plant-eating edaphosaurids and meat-eating sphenacodontids, alongside diadectids and amphibians. Pelycosaurs and their descendants, the therapsids, are the commonest land vertebrates in the best-known Permian fossil beds. A few pelycosaurs lingered late; the youngest known, from South Africa, is about 260 million years old.

  <!-- perm-017 -->

- **Kazakhstania meets Baltica and the Urals rise** — during the Cisuralian, 299–274 million years ago (298.9–274.4 Ma)

  During the Cisuralian, the Kazakhstania block collided with Baltica. The collision belonged to the Uralian orogeny, which built the Ural Mountains during the Permian. Deformation carried on from the Carboniferous, and granites intruded the region extensively. The mountains mark the seam where these old continents were stitched into Pangaea.

  <!-- perm-018 -->

- **Carbon dioxide quadruples after a record low** — c. 298–294 million years ago (298–294 Ma)

  About 298 million years ago, carbon dioxide hit a record low. By 294 million years ago it had risen fourfold. Cooling had limited plant growth, and rising oxygen fed more fires; both returned carbon to the air, which reached about 300 ppm in the Permian. Rising seas drowned the coal swamps that had been burying carbon, so more stayed in the atmosphere and warmed the planet. By the Cisuralian, oxygen and carbon dioxide had returned to more normal levels.

  <!-- perm-019 -->

- **The Skagerrak large igneous province** — c. 297 million years ago (297 ± 4 Ma)

  Magma spread over at least 0.5 million km² around today's Skagerrak strait, 297 ± 4 million years ago. This large igneous province reached the Oslo and Skagerrak grabens, south-western Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea. It is the oldest of a series tied to the African superplume, a vast upwelling deep in the mantle. Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic followed. With Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province, it is tied to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 million years ago.

  <!-- perm-021 -->

  *Figure: Skagerrak opened a series of provinces tied to the African superplume.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Skagerrak] --> B[Bachu]
  B --> C[Emeishan]
  C --> D[Siberian Traps]
  D --> E[Central Atlantic]
  ```

- **The Central Pangean Mountains at their height** — c. 295 million years ago (295 Ma)

  In the early Permian, a mountain range along the equator rivaled today's Himalayas. The Central Pangean Mountains rose where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies. Those collisions began about 340 million years ago and ended about 295 million years ago. Their western part, the Appalachians, was uplifted then. The range cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later helped lay down Europe's Zechstein salt. Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian, spreading sandstone and conglomerate across Europe. The Appalachians, Ouachitas, Atlas and Bohemian Massif are its remnants.

  <!-- perm-022 -->

  *Figure: One equatorial range reshaped the climate on either side of it.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Central Pangean Mountains] --> B[Rain shadow]
  B --> C[Coal swamps turn seasonally dry]
  B --> D[Zechstein salt later]
  A --> E[Weathering halves the peaks]
  ```

- **Dimetrodon appears** — c. 295 million years ago (295 Ma)

  The pelycosaur Dimetrodon evolved about 295 million years ago. Pelycosaurs like it diversified widely, and its remains turn up at Bromacker in Germany and in the Red Beds of Texas.

  <!-- perm-023 -->

- **The first beetles** — c. 295 million years ago (295 Ma)

  Beetles became one of the four great insect radiations, and they began near the start of the Permian, about 295 million years ago. By the Late Permian there were members of the Archostemata, the Adephaga and probably the Polyphaga, today the most diverse group of beetles.

  <!-- perm-024 -->

- **The Dobele crater** — c. 290 million years ago (290 ± 35 Ma)

  An impact formed a crater 4.5 km across at Dobele, Latvia. Its age is about 290 ± 35 million years, in the Cisuralian. The wide margin of error leaves its place in the Permian story loose.

  <!-- perm-028 -->

- **The Panjal Traps erupt** — 289 million years ago (289 ± 2 Ma)

  Lavas up to 2,500 m thick lie in Ladakh and Kashmir. They are the Panjal Traps, a large igneous province in what is now northwestern India, and zircons date them to 289 ± 2 million years ago. They may once have covered over 200,000 square km, comparable to the Emeishan Traps. The eruptions took place at about 33 degrees south and are tied to the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which carried the Cimmerian blocks away. Their lava chemistry shifts from continental types to ocean-floor types. Once linked to later extinctions, they are far too old; the Siberian Traps are the better candidate.

  <!-- perm-029 -->

- **The Artinskian warming melts the ice** — c. 287 million years ago (287 Ma)

  When the Permian began, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age was at its peak. It did not stay that way. Ice sheets shrank from the late Sakmarian on. By 287 million years ago temperatures had risen and the south polar ice cap had retreated, in the Artinskian Warming Event. Glaciers clung on only in eastern Australia's uplands. Around 285.1 million years ago, orbital cycles stopped driving ice growth and began driving marine anoxia and aridity instead, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse. As the glaciers receded, seas rose and the continental interiors dried out.

  <!-- perm-030 -->

  *Figure: The Artinskian warming turned an icehouse into a greenhouse.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Temperatures rise] --> B[South polar ice retreats]
  B --> C[Sea levels rise]
  B --> D[Continental interiors dry out]
  E[Orbital cycles] --> F[Marine anoxia and aridity]
  ```

- **The Clearwater West crater** — 286 million years ago (286.2 ± 2.6 Ma)

  Two craters sit side by side in Quebec, but they are not twins. Clearwater West, 36 km across, formed 286.2 ± 2.6 million years ago. Its neighbor, Clearwater East, is about 460–470 million years old, and different magnetic and meteorite signatures confirm separate impacts. Clearwater West is a complex crater: its central peak formed when the walls collapsed and the floor rebounded.

  <!-- perm-031 -->

- **The Choiyoi volcanic province** — c. 286–247 million years ago (286–247 Ma)

  Volcanic rock covers at least 200,000, and probably 500,000, square km of today's Argentina and Chile, 2–4 km thick. Subduction along Gondwana's western margin built this Choiyoi province from about 286 to 247 million years ago. Its rocks include lavas, breccias and rhyolitic ignimbrites, deposits of hot volcanic ash flows. During the Permian the volcanic arc migrated 350 km inland, reaching San Rafael about 280 million years ago. In Patagonia, late in the Permian, a sinking slab broke off and melted the crust above it. Choiyoi has been suggested as an additional cause of the end-Permian extinction.

  <!-- perm-032 -->

- **Mesosaurs and the oldest amniote embryos** — c. 285–275 million years ago (285–275 Ma)

  The earliest known amniote embryos come from the Mangrullo Formation of Brazil and Uruguay, of Artinskian age. The rocks are rich in mesosaurs. Mesosaurus fossils also occur in Permian black shales of Brazil's Paraná Basin, alongside Glossopteris coals.

  <!-- perm-034 -->

- **A late Kungurian cool spell** — during the late Kungurian–early Capitanian, 283–260 million years ago (283.3–259.9 Ma)

  Cooling resumed in the late Kungurian, bringing a cool glacial interval that lasted into the early Capitanian. Weathering of large igneous provinces from the Kungurian drew down carbon dioxide and brought on this P3 glaciation. Even so, temperatures stayed much higher than at the start of the Cisuralian, and in Australia the ice was largely alpine.

  <!-- perm-035 -->

- **The first Bennettitales** — c. 281 million years ago (281 Ma)

  Leaves from the Upper Shihhotse Formation of Shanxi, China, about 281 million years old, are the oldest confirmed bennettitalean fossils. The group stayed minor for a long time. It became a prominent part of floras only in the Late Triassic and held that place for much of the Mesozoic. Its oldest reproductive structures, the Williamsonia flowers, come from the Early Triassic of Australia.

  <!-- perm-038 -->

- **The Ternovka crater** — c. 280 million years ago (280 ± 10 Ma)

  At Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, a buried crater 11 km across records an impact about 280 ± 10 million years ago, in the Early or Middle Permian.

  <!-- perm-039 -->

- **Coconino dunes cover the Grand Canyon region** — c. 275 million years ago (275 Ma)

  The pale cliffs of the Coconino Sandstone in the Grand Canyon are fossil sand dunes. About 275 million years ago the region dried out, and quartz sand spread across a growing desert. Wind piled it into large cross-bedded dunes, now famous for trackways of scorpion-like arthropods and early tetrapods. Deserts seem to have been widespread on Pangaea, whose interior was dominated by dunes and evaporites.

  <!-- perm-040 -->

- **The first therapsids** — c. 275 million years ago (275 Ma)

  Therapsids, the synapsid line leading to mammals, split from pelycosaur-grade synapsids around 275 million years ago. Their earliest history is missing. No confirmed therapsid fossils come from the Early Permian, leaving a long ghost lineage, a stretch of time a group must have existed without leaving fossils. Raranimus, from the early Middle Permian of China, is probably the earliest-diverging therapsid known. Accounts differ on when all the major therapsid groups had appeared: by 275 million years ago, or by 265 million years ago in the Wordian.

  <!-- perm-041 -->

##### Guadalupian Epoch

The Guadalupian, the Middle Permian, was a time of reefs and new predators. Reef building peaked, with reefs from the Delaware Basin to the Tethys. On land, therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large animals, and saber-toothed gorgonopsians evolved. The epoch ended in crisis, as the Emeishan flood basalts erupted in China and the Capitanian extinction struck.

- **Ceratitid ammonoids appear** — during the Middle Permian, 274–260 million years ago (274.4–259.9 Ma)

  Ceratitid ammonoids arose in the Middle Permian from the daraelitid family of prolecanitids. Barely touched by the Capitanian extinction, they radiated to dominate Late Permian ammonoids as the goniatitids declined. They went on to include almost all Triassic ammonoid genera.

  <!-- perm-043 -->

- **Reefs peak and the Capitan Reef rises** — during the Guadalupian, 274–260 million years ago (274.4–259.9 Ma)

  Texas's Capitan Formation, curving around the Delaware Basin, is called the world's best-preserved Paleozoic reef complex. It may have risen 61–91 m above the seafloor. Reef building peaked in the Guadalupian, with reefs abundant from the Delaware and Zechstein basins to the Tethys and cool Panthalassa shelves. The Capitan Reef was built mainly by calcareous sponges and encrusting algae, not corals, and brachiopods were key ecosystem engineers. Its end came from geography. Tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel, rising heat and salinity killed the reef, and brines laid down the Castile Formation evaporites.

  <!-- perm-045 -->

- **Therapsids take over from the pelycosaurs** — during the Guadalupian, 274–260 million years ago (274.4–259.9 Ma)

  As the Permian world grew drier, the land changed hands. Therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals in the Guadalupian, and they kept that role into the Early Triassic. How the takeover unfolded is hidden. A poor fossil record across Olson's Gap leaves the transition mostly unseen. What follows it is clear. Giant dinocephalians, both plant-eaters and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian faunas of South Africa and Russia. Therocephalians arose and took over the role of saber-toothed predator. Those two regions share animals for a reason. Coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea let animals migrate between what are now South Africa and Russia. The therapsids would go on to produce The first cynodonts, the line that eventually led to mammals.

  <!-- perm-047 -->

- **Sea level falls to a Paleozoic low** — during the Roadian–Wuchiapingian, 274–254 million years ago (274.4–254.1 Ma)

  Through the Early Permian, the sea stood several tens of meters higher than today. A sharp fall began in the Roadian and reached the lowest level of the whole Paleozoic, near today's, in the Wuchiapingian. This Permian regression may be tied to the formation of Pangaea. Falling seas, rising carbon dioxide and a worsening climate marked the Lopingian, ending in the end-Permian extinction.

  <!-- perm-046 -->

- **Olson's Extinction** — c. 273 million years ago (273 Ma)

  Most pelycosaur lineages vanished around 273 million years ago, long before the end-Permian crisis. Edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out near the Kungurian–Roadian boundary, while caseids and therapsids diversified. Temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply afterward, and extinction rates in fish rose. Extreme environments in Kansas, combining heat and acidic waters, coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause. This proposed extinction is contested. A review of Kungurian and Roadian beds found the turnover real. Some authors argue it reflects poor sampling or gradual change, and the timing of Olson's Gap is disputed.

  <!-- perm-048 -->

- **Saber-toothed gorgonopsians appear** — c. 270 million years ago (270 Ma)

  Inostrancevia reached 3.5 m long and about 300 kg, with saber teeth. It belonged to the gorgonopsians, which first evolved about 270 million years ago and lasted until about 252 million years ago. They started small, with skulls 10–15 cm long. The oldest identifiable one, Phorcys, dates to about the Wordian–Capitanian boundary, though finds show the group was already diversifying earlier in the Wordian. Once the Capitanian extinction removed the dinocephalians, gorgonopsians became the apex predators.

  <!-- perm-050 -->

- **The Hunter–Bowen orogeny** — c. 270–230 million years ago (270–230 Ma)

  About 2,500 km of eastern Australia's margin was crumpled by island arcs colliding with it in the Permian and Triassic. Pangaea's counterclockwise rotation drove sideways squeezing along the subduction zone there. A megafold had formed earlier, around 290 million years ago. Major contraction came about 270–260 and around 253 million years ago, with a later phase about 235–230 million years ago. In front of the mountains, the Sydney–Bowen basins filled with sediment that built vast coal deposits.

  <!-- perm-051 -->

- **A cooling recorded in carbon** — during the Capitanian, 264–260 million years ago (264.3–259.9 Ma)

  Marine limestones of Capitanian age record a rise in carbon-13, the heavier form of carbon, a sign of global cooling. That cooling may have caused the end-Capitanian extinction of warm-water species: large fusulinids, alatoconchid bivalves and waagenophyllid rugose corals.

  <!-- perm-055 -->

- **The Capitanian mass extinction** — c. 262–259 million years ago (262–259 Ma)

  About 60–63% of marine species died out at the close of the Middle Permian. The Capitanian extinction began around 262 million years ago and peaked around 259 million years ago. It took about 33–35% of marine genera. Ammonoids, corals, reef algae, foraminifera, bryozoans and brachiopods suffered most. On land, the dinocephalians and the last varanopids vanished, and anomodont diversity halved. It is linked to The Emeishan Traps erupt, which drove two ocean anoxic events and acidification, and to a sea-level fall that killed reefs. How severe and how global it was is still debated. Some rank it fifth worst ecologically; others see only a regional crisis in South China, or losses limited to low-latitude northern species.

  <!-- perm-056 -->

- **The Emeishan Traps erupt** — c. 262–259 million years ago (262–259 Ma)

  In south-western China, basalt covers more than 250,000 km², up to 5.5 km thick, an estimated 300,000 km³ in all. These Emeishan Traps began erupting 265 million years ago or earlier, peaked between 262 and 261 million years ago, and ended about 259 million years ago. They had global ecological impact and are tied to the Capitanian extinction, though the later Siberian Traps dwarfed them. Around 260 million years ago they caused the Emeishan Thermal Excursion, a warm interruption of a cool period. Afterward, weathering of the basalts drew down carbon dioxide and cooled the early Wuchiapingian. Coronene at the boundary, with no iridium anomaly, points to volcanism rather than an impact.

  <!-- perm-057 -->

  *Figure: The Emeishan eruptions began, peaked and ended within a few million years.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The first cynodonts** — c. 260 million years ago (260 Ma)

  Cynodonts, the therapsid group ancestral to mammals, first appeared in the Late Permian, about 260 million years ago, and spread worldwide. The earliest known, Charassognathus, comes from the Wuchiapingian. They are the only major therapsid group with no Middle Permian record. Their big moment came later: they diversified rapidly after the end-Permian extinction.

  <!-- perm-060 -->

##### Lopingian Epoch

The Lopingian, the last epoch of the Permian and of the Paleozoic, opened with one of the largest retreats of the sea in the Phanerozoic. Advanced therapsids ruled the land, from saber-toothed gorgonopsians to beaked dicynodonts, and the first archosauromorphs and gliding reptiles appeared. In Europe the Zechstein Sea spread and laid down black shale and thick salt, while the long Late Paleozoic icehouse finally ended. Then, in Siberia, basalt lava flooded a vast area, about 7 million km² of which remains today.

- **The sea retreats and the reefs fail** — c. 260 million years ago (259.9 ± 0.084 Ma)

  Ash beds date the end of the Middle Permian to 259.857 ± 0.084 million years ago, and at that moment the sea drained off the continents. The boundary coincided with one of the most prominent marine regressions of the Phanerozoic. Evaporites and land deposits lie over marine limestones, and a vast unconformity marks it in rocks worldwide. Falling seas and regional swings in salinity ended the golden age of reef building, in what is called the end-Guadalupian reef crisis. Closure of the Sino-Mongolian Seaway has been proposed as a driver of losses in the Paleo-Tethys. Global diversity, rebuilt by disaster species late in the Guadalupian, dropped again in the Wuchiapingian.

  <!-- perm-064 -->

  *Figure: A sea-level fall at the boundary left its marks worldwide.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Major marine regression] --> B[Evaporites over limestones]
  A --> C[Worldwide unconformity]
  A --> D[End-Guadalupian reef crisis]
  ```

- **The last callistophytalean seed ferns** — during the Wuchiapingian, 260–254 million years ago (259.9–254.1 Ma)

  The Callistophytales were seed ferns whose coal forests had once covered South China. They make their last appearance in the Wuchiapingian, one more Carboniferous lineage gone before the great extinction.

  <!-- perm-067 -->

- **Dicynodonts and pareiasaurs flourish** — during the Late Permian, 260–252 million years ago (259.9–251.9 Ma)

  Beaked plant-eaters called dicynodonts became some of the most successful therapsids of all, surviving almost to the end of the Triassic. They flourished after the Capitanian extinction. Late Permian lands were dominated by advanced therapsids, saber-toothed gorgonopsians and dicynodonts, alongside large plant-eating pareiasaurs. South Africa's Beaufort Group shows the setting: a semi-arid cold steppe, crossed by seasonal rivers draining into the Karoo Sea.

  <!-- perm-063 -->

- **The first archosauromorphs** — during the Late Permian, 260–252 million years ago (259.9–251.9 Ma)

  Dinosaurs, pterosaurs and crocodile relatives all trace back to a group of reptiles that first appeared in the Late Permian. These were the archosauromorphs, which diversified before the period ended. The first archosauriforms appeared in the latest Permian. A molecular estimate puts the split of turtles from the line of birds and crocodilians at about 255 million years ago. A marine group of ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians and thalattosaurs may also have come from archosauromorphs in the Late Permian. Their real burst came later. Archosauromorphs exploded in diversity after the end-Permian extinction.

  <!-- perm-065 -->

- **The first gliding vertebrates** — during the Late Permian, 260–252 million years ago (259.9–251.9 Ma)

  Weigeltisaurids were lizard-like reptiles with extendable wings, like modern gliding lizards. They are the oldest known gliding vertebrates. Their worldwide spread shows that tall, thin forests, the kind a glider needs, had become widespread by the Late Permian.

  <!-- perm-066 -->

- **Rifting begins along the future Atlantic** — during the Late Permian, 260–252 million years ago (259.9–251.9 Ma)

  Pangaea's breakup can loosely be traced back to about 252 million years ago. From the latest Permian, a broad zone of stretching formed across the supercontinent along the line of the future Central Atlantic. Extension spread across Laurussia from central Europe to eastern Canada, opening north–south rift valleys.

  <!-- perm-069 -->

- **The Kupferschiefer, a copper-bearing black shale** — 257 million years ago (257.3 ± 1.6 Ma)

  A layer usually only 30–60 cm thick spreads over 600,000 square km across six countries. The Kupferschiefer formed about 257 million years ago in the enclosed Zechstein basin. Oxygen-free water there laid down a black shale and marl holding up to 30% organic matter. Mineral-rich groundwater later formed sulfide ores in it. It became one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199 AD.

  <!-- perm-071 -->

- **The Zechstein Sea lays down thick salt** — c. 257–251 million years ago (257.3–251 Ma)

  Beneath the North Sea, lowland Britain, Germany and Poland lies salt about 1,000 m thick. A rise in sea level, probably tied to melting ice, created the Zechstein Sea, a hypersaline inland sea. It sat near the equator in the rain shadow of the Central Pangean Mountains, and at least five cycles of evaporation piled up salt, anhydrite and dolomite. The sea's eventual disappearance was part of the regression around the end-Permian extinction.

  <!-- perm-072 -->

- **The longest icehouse ends** — c. 255 million years ago (255 Ma)

  The final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia around 255 million years ago. With them ended the Late Paleozoic icehouse, under way since the Late Devonian. It was the most extensive and longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic. The ending was slow. The great southern ice sheets had shrunk long before, in the Artinskian warming, but cold returned in spells. A last regional glaciation, P4, lasted in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian. Only then did the ice go for good. By one account, the most recent greenhouse period began in the late Permian as this ice age ended. The timing matters. The world entered the end-Permian crisis already warm and ice-free, and The end-Permian hothouse would push it much further.

  <!-- perm-074 -->

- **The Araguainha impact** — c. 255 million years ago (254.7 ± 2.5 Ma)

  An impact left a crater 40 km wide on the border of Mato Grosso and Goiás, Brazil, probably in a shallow sea. Its age, 254.7 ± 2.5 million years, overlaps the Permian–Triassic boundary. Some suggest the warming it caused helped trigger the extinction.

  <!-- perm-076 -->

- **Salt fills the Delaware Basin** — during the Changhsingian, 254–252 million years ago (254.1–251.9 Ma)

  Tectonics pinched the Hovey Channel shut. The deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico was cut off from the sea, and its brines grew ever saltier. Up to 91 m of finely layered gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep. Thick halite of the Salado followed. By the end of the Ochoan, the basin had filled to the top of the Capitan Reef and was mostly dry land.

  <!-- perm-077 -->

- **The Siberian Traps flood a continent** — c. 252 million years ago (252 Ma)

  About 7 million km² of basalt still covers Siberia today, some 4 million km³ of rock. It is what remains of the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years. The eruptions went on for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary. The lava alone was not the main danger. Magma heated the coal- and evaporite-rich rocks of the Tungus basin, which can release large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, halogens and metals poured out. They drove warming, ocean anoxia and acidification, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning. Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the end-Permian extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause. Each of the killing mechanisms that follow, from The end-Permian hothouse to Seas without oxygen, leads back here.

  <!-- perm-078 -->

  *Figure: How the Siberian Traps led to the end-Permian extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Magma heats Tungus basin rocks] --> B[Toxic and greenhouse gases]
  B --> C[Warming]
  B --> D[Ocean anoxia, acidification]
  B --> E[Ozone loss, acid rain]
  C --> F[Mass extinction]
  D --> F
  E --> F
  ```

- **The Glossopteris flora collapses** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  In Australia, the Glossopteris forests collapsed around 370,000 years before the Permian–Triassic boundary. In western Gondwana they went probably a few hundred thousand years before it. These trees had dominated much of southern Gondwana since their order arose at the start of the Permian. Most or all of its members died out in the extinction, 251.9 million years ago. Just above the boundary, an Australia-wide conifer flora largely replaced them.

  <!-- perm-079 -->

- **A carbon signature of catastrophe** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Carbon atoms record the extinction even where rocks cannot be dated by radioactivity. A large, abrupt global fall in δ13C, the share of heavy carbon, coincides with the extinction and helps locate the boundary. Carbonate rocks worldwide record a swift drop of about 1% in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12. The excursion measured 4–7% and lasted about 500,000 years, though altered rocks blur its exact size. Methane from frozen seabed clathrates was once the favored source of the light carbon. Isotopes now point mainly to volcanic carbon dioxide and methane cooked out of rocks by the Siberian Traps. Methane-producing microbes may explain some of the swings.

  <!-- perm-081 -->

- **The end-Permian hothouse** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Tropical seas off Iran topped 35 °C. The Siberian Traps released more than 5 teratonnes of carbon dioxide, more than doubling the atmosphere's share. Carbon dioxide rose from around 400 to 2,500 ppm as some 3,900–12,000 gigatonnes of carbon entered the oceans and air. Average surface temperature jumped from about 18 °C to as much as 35 °C. This rapid greenhouse release caused the extinction and began an extreme hothouse that lasted several million years into the Triassic.

  <!-- perm-082 -->

  *Figure: Carbon dioxide before and after the Siberian Traps eruptions.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

  *Figure: Average surface temperature nearly doubled.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Great Dying** — 252 million years ago (251.9 ± 0.024 Ma)

  About 81% of marine species vanished. On land, 70% of vertebrate species went with them. The end-Permian extinction is Earth's most severe known extinction, removing about 57% of families and 62% of genera. It was fast. The main marine pulse took 60,000–100,000 years, and dating of ash beds at Meishan, China, places it between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. The consensus cause is The Siberian Traps flood a continent. Their carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide brought global warming, sulfurous oxygen-starved seas and acidified oceans. No group was safe. Shell-building marine animals suffered most. On land, it was the largest insect mass extinction, and it was equally catastrophic for plants. The Great Dying ended the Paleozoic Era. Recovery was slow: land ecosystems needed some 30 million years to rebuild.

  <!-- perm-084 -->

  *Figure: Losses in the end-Permian mass extinction.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Acid seas and acid rain** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  The oceans grew more acidic by up to 0.7 pH units as carbon dioxide rose. That matches the pattern of loss, which fell hardest on heavily calcified animals. Acidification was worst at mid-latitudes, and together with anoxia a rising sea devastated shallow shelf communities. On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped erosion, washing organic matter from the land into the sea.

  <!-- perm-085 -->

- **Seas without oxygen** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Even the sunlit shallows filled with poison. Oxygen-starved, hydrogen-sulfide-rich waters, called euxinic, spread through the oceans from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic. Across most of the Tethys and Panthalassa, anoxia appears at the extinction itself, though at some sites it began earlier. Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrived and filled the sea with hydrogen sulfide. That gas, escaping from the sea, may have poisoned life on land and in the water. The extinction, triggered by runaway carbon dioxide from the Siberian Traps, was marked throughout by this loss of oxygen. Ocean overturn has also been proposed.

  <!-- perm-086 -->

  *Figure: From volcanic carbon to poisoned seas.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Siberian Traps CO2] --> B[Ocean deoxygenation]
  B --> C[Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrive]
  C --> D[Hydrogen sulfide fills the sea]
  D -.-> E[Life poisoned at sea and on land]
  ```

- **Sea level swings at the boundary** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Global sea level is reported to have fallen 250 m during the Permian–Triassic extinction. The drastic regression shrank shallow shelf habitats and hastened the final decline of trilobites. Other work tells a different story, tying the main warming to a rise in sea level, which with anoxia ravaged shallow shelf life.

  <!-- perm-088 -->

- **The last spiny sharks** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  The acanthodians, or spiny sharks, were an early class of jawed fishes. Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian. The Permian–Triassic extinction finished them.

  <!-- perm-089 -->

- **The last fusulinids** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Fusulinid foraminifera, large single-celled shell-builders, were already nearly gone. The Capitanian crisis had cut them down to dwarf forms. The Permian–Triassic extinction ended them. Lagenid forams survived, probably thanks to a wider tolerance of conditions and a wider range.

  <!-- perm-090 -->

- **The last gorgonopsians** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  The top land predators of the Late Permian, the saber-toothed gorgonopsians, died out in the extinction's final phase. They began disappearing from Africa and Eastern Europe just before it. Biarmosuchians vanished too, while dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts shrank to a handful of species each.

  <!-- perm-091 -->

- **The last griffinflies** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Several Paleozoic insect groups were extinct by the end of the Permian, including the giant griffinflies and the palaeodictyopteroids. Only three Paleozoic insect groups are known after it. This was the largest known mass extinction of insects.

  <!-- perm-092 -->

- **The last progymnosperms** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants. Their last surviving group, the Noeggerathiales, persisted until the end of the Permian.

  <!-- perm-093 -->

- **The Paleozoic corals vanish** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost in the Permian–Triassic extinction. Among the casualties were the rugose and tabulate corals, the reef-building corals of the Paleozoic, which died out entirely. Their loss left the seas without the reef builders that had served them through the Paleozoic.

  <!-- perm-094 -->

- **The last lycopsid swamps** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Carboniferous-style swamps of lycopods and horsetails survived to the end of the Permian in only one place: Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China. Even there, tree lycopsids had become rare, marginal plants, no longer the main makers of coal.

  <!-- perm-095 -->

- **The last trilobites** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Trilobites had thrived since the Cambrian. At the end of the Permian, after nearly 300 million years, they were gone. Only one order, the Proetida, had survived the Devonian, and it lasted to the end. By the Changhsingian a handful of genera remained, by one count just two. Their final decline came shortly before the main extinction, as falling sea level shrank the shallow shelves where they lived.

  <!-- perm-096 -->

- **Pangaea dries out** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Near the end of the Permian, Pangaea grew drier as the supercontinent came together. Volcanism and global warming at the very end of the period sharply worsened the aridity. In Siberia's Kuznetsk Basin, drying killed the humid-adapted Cordaites forests a few hundred thousand years before the boundary.

  <!-- perm-097 -->

- **The impact idea, largely rejected** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Could an asteroid have caused the Great Dying? The idea is now largely rejected. Candidate craters include the 250 km Bedout structure off northwest Australia and a hypothesized 480 km Wilkes Land crater in Antarctica. Reported clues include shocked quartz, fullerenes with extraterrestrial gases and meteorite fragments. But iridium is not anomalous, and many boundary sites lack impact evidence. The proposed craters remain contentious, with their ages and origins still debated.

  <!-- perm-098 -->

- **The last sea scorpions** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  Eurypterids, the sea scorpions, dwindled in numbers and diversity through the Permian. When they finally died out is contentious: either early in the Middle Permian or in the Permian–Triassic extinction, 251.9 million years ago. A cuticle fragment from the very end of the Permian in Australia, once called the youngest eurypterid, may instead be a scorpion.

  <!-- perm-100 -->

### Mesozoic Era

The Mesozoic opens on a wrecked world and a single giant landmass. Pangaea's land area had just peaked, and a megamonsoon of record strength swept across it, while even the poles lay free of ice. In the seas, shell-crushing and boring predators began an arms race that would reshape seafloor life for the whole era. On land, the plant-eater Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, and beaked rhynchosaurs joined a burst of new reptiles. Yet the Siberian Traps kept erupting, and the hottest stretch of the Phanerozoic held recovery back for millions of years.

#### Triassic Period

One supercontinent, one monsoon and no ice: that is the Triassic world. Pangaea reached its greatest land area after Siberia and the China cratons joined it, and its megamonsoon blew at full strength. Oxygen-poor seas and a searing Early Triassic climate, fed by repeated Siberian Traps eruptions, slowed life's return from the Great Dying. Still, new players appeared almost at once: rhynchosaurs, early neopterygian fishes, and coelacanths in their greatest burst of diversity. Microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow seas while the survivors regrouped.

- **Pangaea's megamonsoon blows at full strength** — during the Triassic, 252–201 million years ago (251.9–201.4 Ma)

  When nearly all the land on Earth sits in one block, the weather follows. The Pangean megamonsoon, a vast seasonal swing of wind and rain, reached its greatest strength in the Triassic. It peaked when Pangaea's land area was largest, after Siberia and the China cratons, ancient continental cores, had joined it. Its circulation may have reversed part of the global easterly winds, sending westerlies onto the west coast. Those shifting winds carried moisture to the previously dry Colorado Plateau. Meanwhile a greenhouse climate kept every continent free of ice, even at the poles.

  <!-- tria-018 -->

- **A buried crater scars North Dakota** — during the Triassic, 252–201 million years ago (251.9–201.4 Ma)

  Some 2,000 m beneath McKenzie County, North Dakota, lies the scar of an ancient impact: the Red Wing Creek structure, about 9 km across. Thick Jurassic rocks fill the disturbed ground, which suggests a Triassic strike, and its age is estimated at 200 ± 25 million years. It was once grouped with Manicouagan, Saint Martin and Rochechouart as a single multiple impact. Those craters later proved to be millions of years apart.

  <!-- tria-019 -->

##### Early Triassic Epoch

The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, and life paid for it. Oxygen-poor waters lingered, the Siberian Traps erupted again and again, and recovery from the largest mass extinction took millions of years. On land, Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, while temnospondyl amphibians bounced back first. In the sea, microbial reefs spread, coelacanths diversified, and shell-crushing predators began the Mesozoic marine revolution. Across Europe, desert playas laid down the red Buntsandstein.

- **Shell-crushers launch the Mesozoic marine revolution** — c. 252 million years ago (251.9 Ma)

  On the Mesozoic seafloor, sitting still became dangerous. With the new era began the Mesozoic marine revolution, an arms race marked by more shell-crushing and boring predators and more animals bulldozing the seafloor. As predators grew steadily more capable, they stressed animals fixed in place. The balance shifted, because some prey adapted faster than others. Stalked crinoids, sea lilies anchored to the bottom, made easy targets for the shell-crushers from the Triassic on.

  <!-- tria-014 -->

- **Beaked rhynchosaurs appear in the aftermath** — during the Induan, 252–251 million years ago (251.9–250.8 Ma)

  Barely after the extinction, a new kind of plant-eater appeared: the rhynchosaurs, reptiles with beaks. They arose in the Induan, the first age of the Triassic, within a major diversification of reptiles. Early forms such as Noteosuchus come from the earliest Triassic of South Africa's Eastern Cape. Their peak came much later, in the Carnian, when they were abundant worldwide, and they died out early in the Norian.

  <!-- tria-009 -->

- **Stifling, acidic seas stall the ocean's recovery** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  Poison gas drifted into sunlit shallows. Chemical fossils of green sulfur bacteria, microbes that need both light and hydrogen sulfide, show the gas reaching shallow water from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic. Oxygen-poor water lingered through the whole epoch, which may explain why sea life, especially on the seafloor, recovered so slowly. Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea also hampered shell builders. Seafloors flipping between oxygen-rich and oxygen-free states may explain the carbon-isotope swings of the time, shifts in the balance of heavy and light carbon.

  <!-- tria-002 -->

- **Desert playas lay down the red Buntsandstein** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  From England to Poland, the ground of the Germanic Basin turned red. Arid playas, dry desert lake beds, laid down the Buntsandstein: red sandstones and conglomerates with little clay, holding small reptiles, plants and Chirotherium footprints. It is the first part of the three-part Germanic Trias, followed by the Muschelkalk and the Keuper. A major late Anisian rise in sea level ended it, flooding the basin with a tropical sea where the Muschelkalk began.

  <!-- tria-004 -->

  *Figure: The Buntsandstein forms the bottom of the three-part Germanic Trias, below the Muschelkalk and Keuper.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Coelacanths and lungfishes enjoy their heyday** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  Two famous 'living fossil' groups had their best days right after the worst disaster. Coelacanths, lobe-finned fishes, had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after the Great Dying. Lungfishes reached their peak variety during the Triassic. Today only three lungfish genera survive.

  <!-- tria-005 -->

- **Pangaea bakes in the Phanerozoic's fiercest heat** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  At the equator, average temperatures may have reached 32–35 °C. The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, the age of abundant animal life. It came during and just after the Siberian Traps' huge release of greenhouse gases. Equatorial temperatures may have jumped 8–10 °C at the start of the Triassic. Pangaea's interior was mostly hot and arid, with widespread deserts, while even the poles were merely temperate. The heat came in waves. A thermal maximum struck at the Permian–Triassic boundary. A brief Dienerian cooling followed, from 251 to 249 million years ago. Then came the Latest Smithian Thermal Maximum, about 249–248 million years ago. The toll on land may have been stark. Between about 30°N and 40°S, extreme heat may have left the land without tetrapods, four-limbed animals, from the Induan until the early Spathian.

  <!-- tria-007 -->

  *Figure: The Early Triassic heat came in waves rather than one long peak.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **New-finned fishes arrive as ray-fins boom** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  A predatory fish more than 1.2 m long, a saurichthyid, hunted Triassic waters as ray-finned fishes diversified remarkably, peaking in the Middle Triassic. Among them were the neopterygians, the 'new-finned' fishes. Their earliest unmistakable members, including early holosteans, appear near the start of the Triassic, though a Permian origin is suspected. Later in the period they became leading fishes of fresh and salt water, spreading through Norian seas as ceratitid ammonites declined.

  <!-- tria-008 -->

- **Lystrosaurus spreads to every corner of Pangaea** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  In some of the earliest Triassic land faunas, nine animals in ten were the same beast. The pig-sized Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating dicynodont from the mammal-relative line, made up as much as 90% of some land vertebrate faunas. It was the most common land vertebrate and spread to every corner of Pangaea after the extinction. Trackways in South Africa's Karoo Basin show dicynodonts were abundant right after the crisis. Herding, tolerance of extreme and changeable climates, very fast growth and early sexual maturity probably explain its success. Some recent evidence questions its usual label as a disaster taxon, a species that booms in the wreckage of an extinction.

  <!-- tria-013 -->

- **Microbes build reefs in the extinction's wake** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  With most reef animals gone, microbes took over the job. In the earliest Triassic, microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow, mostly low-latitude seas, in both oxygen-poor and oxygenated water. Mixed microbe–animal reefs, built partly by keratinous sponges, steadied many damaged communities. Microbial mats, thin carpets of microbes, left wrinkled surfaces at sea and on land. Their later disappearance signals burrowing animals returning as ecosystems recovered.

  <!-- tria-015 -->

- **The Siberian Traps erupt again and again** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  The great eruptions that ended the Permian did not stop when the Triassic began. Swings in carbon isotopes and spikes of mercury suggest that massive Siberian Traps activity recurred several times in the Early Triassic.
