These pulses caused further extinctions and may have kept the climate hot. Later bursts are linked to the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian and Anisian crises. A release of methane, often blamed for such swings, cannot explain carbon-isotope shifts this large and this repeated.

  <!-- tria-022 -->

- **Life crawls back from the worst extinction ever** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  On land, full recovery took about 30 million years. That is how deep the wound of the largest mass extinction ran, and how harsh the Early Triassic climate was. Successive extinction waves and prolonged environmental stress held recovery back again and again. Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide, the same few survivors turning up everywhere. The sea healed faster, but not quickly. Seafloor communities stayed low in diversity until the end of the Early Triassic, about 4 million years after the extinction. On land, episodes of acidity stunted ecosystems well into the Triassic. Then, in the Anisian, marine recovery accelerated explosively. Crowded niches sharpened competition, and life began to diversify on every front.

  <!-- tria-023 -->

  *Figure: The sea floor recovered far sooner than ecosystems on land.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Temnospondyl amphibians bounce back first** — during the Early Triassic, 252–247 million years ago (251.9–247 Ma)

  Big amphibians were the quickest to recover. Temnospondyls, a large group of extinct amphibians, peaked in diversity in the early Triassic, when most major stereospondyl subgroups, such as capitosaurs and trematosaurs, appeared. In the Induan they shrank, while tupilakosaurids thrived as disaster taxa. By the Olenekian they had regained their pre-extinction sizes. Then they declined through the Middle and Late Triassic, and only brachyopoids and trematosauroids survived beyond it.

  <!-- tria-024 -->

- **Moenkopi tidal flats redden the American Southwest** — during the Early Triassic–Middle Triassic, 252–237 million years ago (251.9–237 Ma)

  Up to about 550 m of red rock records a coastline that came and went. Rivers, tidal flats and brief marine floods laid down the Moenkopi Formation's red sandstones and siltstones across the American Southwest. Its fossils point to a warm tropical climate, perhaps with monsoonal wet and dry seasons. Its Early Triassic bivalves, 27 species in 18 genera, cast doubt on the idea that bivalves recovered only in the Middle Triassic.

  <!-- tria-017 -->

- **Seas creep up from a Permian–Triassic low** — c. 252–227 million years ago (251.9–227.3 Ma)

  The Triassic began with the sea at its lowest. Sea level bottomed out at the Permian–Triassic boundary and stayed low through the period compared with other periods. Starting near today's level, it rose to about 10–20 m above present during the Early and Middle Triassic. The rise sped up in the Ladinian and peaked in the Carnian, at up to 50 m above today's level.

  <!-- tria-021 -->

  *Figure: Triassic sea level climbed from today's level to a Carnian peak.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Guiyang fossils capture an entire marine food web** — c. 251 million years ago (250.8–250.7 Ma)

  From grazers to top predators, a whole ocean community survives in one set of rocks. The Guiyang biota, from China's Daye Formation, is an exceptionally preserved late Induan assemblage dating to about 250.8 million years ago. It holds every trophic level, every rung of the food chain, from primary consumers to apex predators. So soon after the extinction, the sea already had a complete food web.

  <!-- tria-025 -->

- **Cynodonts and dicynodonts rise among the survivors** — during the Olenekian, 251–247 million years ago (250.8–247 Ma)

  Of all the therapsids, the mammal-relative group, only three lines made it through: dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts. Cynodonts and dicynodonts soon dominated, and among dicynodonts only the stocky kannemeyeriiforms thrived. Cynognathians led the Early and Middle Triassic cynodonts, and Cynognathus was a top predator of Olenekian and Anisian Gondwana. Around 240 million years ago cynodonts diversified again, and plant-eating traversodontids peaked in the Late Triassic, mainly in Gondwana.

  <!-- tria-027 -->

- **Dinosaur cousins leave their first footprints** — during the Olenekian, 251–247 million years ago (250.8–247 Ma)

  The first hint of the dinosaur line is a set of footprints. Fossil footprints from the Olenekian are the first signs of dinosauromorphs, the group that holds dinosaurs and their closest relatives. Argentina's Chañares Formation preserves early dinosaur-like animals such as Lagosuchus and Lagerpeton. Their wider group, the avemetatarsalians, played only a minor part in Triassic ecosystems. Yet it eventually produced the first pterosaurs and dinosaurs.

  <!-- tria-029 -->

- **Dicroidium seed ferns take over Gondwana** — c. 251–201 million years ago (250.8–201.4 Ma)

  Across much of the southern supercontinent, the forests had fern-like leaves but bore seeds. Dicroidium, a seed fern, took hold around the Induan–Olenekian boundary and its trees came to dominate large parts of Gondwana through the Triassic. Its flora peaked in diversity in the Anisian. The end-Triassic extinction brought these ecosystems down, leaving only a relict in Antarctica.

  <!-- tria-028 -->

- **Triadobatrachus, the oldest known frog, appears** — c. 250 million years ago (250 Ma)

  About 250 million years ago lived Triadobatrachus massinoti, the earliest known frog. It belongs with the lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, which first appeared in the Triassic; frog forerunners were present by the Early Triassic. Stem relatives of salamanders and of caecilians, legless burrowing amphibians, also arose. Yet modern amphibians stayed uncommon until the Jurassic. They spread only as the older temnospondyls waned.

  <!-- tria-031 -->

- **Ichthyosaurs carry reptiles back to the sea** — c. 250 million years ago (250 Ma)

  Just two million years after the end-Permian extinction, reptiles were already heading back to sea. Ichthyosaurs, the 'fish lizards', evolved from land reptiles that returned to the water, much as the ancestors of whales and dolphins later did. They appeared around 250 million years ago, among the first marine reptiles. The oldest remains of their wider group, the ichthyopterygians, come from Olenekian rocks on Spitsbergen, and early forms lined northern Pangaea's coasts from Japan and China to Canada. Ichthyosaurs in the narrow sense arose about 245 million years ago, and by the Middle Triassic some were very large. The line endured until about 94 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.

  <!-- tria-032 -->

- **South China docks as Pangaea reaches its peak** — c. 250 million years ago (250 Ma)

  A single ocean, Panthalassa, covered almost 70% of Earth's surface. The rest was mostly one landmass. Pangaea reached its height about 250 million years ago, at the start of the Triassic. Around then South China collided with the Qinling complex and North China, joining the supercontinent and forming the Sichuan Basin.

  <!-- tria-033 -->

- **Mountain building strikes western North America** — c. 250 million years ago (250 Ma)

  Western North America crumpled twice in a row. Long after the Late Devonian Antler orogeny, the Sonoma orogeny, a new mountain-building episode, struck around the Permian–Triassic transition. It is linked to Sonomia, an island arc or small continental fragment, joining the continent's western edge. Not everyone agrees on the mechanism: some geologists dispute whether converging plates produced it.

  <!-- tria-034 -->

- **Colliding blocks piece together East Asia** — c. 250–230 million years ago (250–230 Ma)

  East Asia was built like a pileup. Between about 250 and 230 million years ago, the crustal blocks of Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang and Lhasa collided with South China and each other, raising the Indosinian orogeny. This southern Asian landmass then hit North China, Tarim and other blocks about 240–220 million years ago, along the Central China orogen. That collision closed the Qinling ocean, and deep subduction destroyed part of the North China craton's root. Final closure of the Paleoasian Ocean, about 240–230 million years ago, joined Tarim and North China to Kazakhstan and Siberia. These additions gave Pangaea its greatest land area as climate changed sharply and the megamonsoon developed, though any link is still being studied.

  <!-- tria-030 -->

  *Figure: East Asia was assembled in stages as blocks collided and oceans closed.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang, Lhasa] -->|collide with South China| B[Indosinian orogeny]
  B --> C[Southern Asian continent]
  C -->|hits North China and Tarim| D[Qinling ocean closes]
  E[Paleoasian Ocean closes] --> F[Central Asian orogenic belt]
  D --> G[Pangaea's greatest land area]
  F --> G
  ```

- **A second blow: the Smithian–Spathian extinction** — c. 249 million years ago (249.4 Ma)

  Life had barely started to recover when it was knocked down again. The Smithian–Spathian boundary event, the second extinction after the end-Permian one, struck during the Olenekian. The late Smithian crisis was a widespread ocean anoxic event, a spell when much of the sea lost its oxygen. Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism has been linked to it, and the Smithian closed with a thermal maximum around 249–248 million years ago. Grim episodes like this kept returning through the Early Triassic and delayed life's recovery. Idaho's Paris biota is the first diverse fossil assemblage known after it.

  <!-- tria-035 -->

- **Idaho's Paris biota marks a fresh start** — c. 249 million years ago (249 Ma)

  About 3 million years after the end-Permian extinction, a shallow sea off Pangaea's west coast teemed with life again. Idaho's Paris biota is an exceptionally diverse marine assemblage from the earliest Spathian, about 249 million years ago. Its animals lived in a near-equatorial sea, and beds with its ammonoids are dated to 248.853 ± 0.086 million years. It is the first diverse assemblage after the Smithian–Spathian extinction.

  <!-- tria-036 -->

- **Flipper-limbed sauropterygians take to the water** — c. 248–247 million years ago (248–247 Ma)

  Soon after the end-Permian extinction, another line of land reptiles traded legs for flippers. Sauropterygians, flipper-limbed marine reptiles, first appeared about 248–247 million years ago, in the Spathian, and were already notably diverse. With hupehsuchians and ichthyopterygians they were among the first marine reptiles, entering the scene in the Olenekian. They flourished through the Triassic. At the period's end, all but the plesiosaurs died out.

  <!-- tria-037 -->

- **A sharp cooling ends the Early Triassic heat** — c. 248–247 million years ago (248–247 Ma)

  The Early Triassic heat finally broke. During the Latest Olenekian Cooling, from 248 to 247 million years ago, temperatures fell by about 6 °C. The Middle Triassic stayed cooler, with temperatures falling through most of the Anisian. In those cooler Anisian oceans, reefs built by animals became common again.

  <!-- tria-039 -->

##### Middle Triassic Epoch

A third extinction since the Permian closed the Early Triassic, yet what followed was a rebound. Within 4–6 million years of the Great Dying, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals began to re-form, as fossils such as China's Luoping biota record. Archosaurs pushed the therapsids aside to rule the land, while placodonts, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs at sea. Stony corals, the first stem turtles and the oldest sure lepidosaur all appear. Underneath it all, Pangaea began to crack: rift valleys opened soon after the Siberian Traps fell silent, and the Tethys pushed west.

- **A third extinction closes the Early Triassic** — c. 247 million years ago (247 Ma)

  Life had been knocked back twice since the Permian, and now it happened a third time. A new extinction event struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic. Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it. The same volcanic source has also been tied to later crises in the Middle–Late Anisian and at the Anisian–Ladinian boundary.

  <!-- tria-048 -->

- **Pangaea starts to tear along the future Atlantic** — c. 247 million years ago (247 Ma)

  The Atlantic Ocean began as a string of rift valleys. Shortly after the Siberian Traps eruptions ended, around 247 million years ago, the crust started pulling apart; rift sediments in the Fundy and Argana basins date to then. Extension began in the northern Central Atlantic in the Anisian and in the southern part in the Carnian. By 230 million years ago, new rift valleys had formed and filled. From about 227 to 202 million years ago, deep half-graben basins between New Jersey and Morocco held large rift lakes, red beds and shales: the Newark Supergroup. Rifting spread to Newfoundland and Iberia, the eastern Mediterranean, and southwestern Gondwana and Patagonia, opening basins such as the Lusitanian and Cuyo. Three-armed grabens joined into the future Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Yet Pangaea had not separated. Laurasia parted from Gondwana only between 215 and 175 million years ago.

  <!-- tria-049 -->

  *Figure: Stages of Pangaea's Triassic and Jurassic rifting.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Luoping fossils track the seas' revival** — c. 247–245 million years ago (247–245 Ma)

  The sea was coming back to life, and Yunnan, China, kept the evidence. The Luoping biota, about 247–245 million years old, preserves varied marine animals that record the recovery of sea life after the extinction. It is one of a series of Triassic Chinese marine biotas, alongside the older Guiyang biota.

  <!-- tria-045 -->

- **The first stony corals, tomorrow's reef builders** — during the Anisian, 247–241 million years ago (247–241.5 Ma)

  Every Mesozoic and modern reef rests on one group of animals: the scleractinians, or stony corals. They first appeared in the late Anisian. Their big break came later, during The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green, when they diversified rapidly. That burst is linked to symbiotic dinoflagellates, called zooxanthellae, settling in their tissues as partners. Reefs built by modern-type stony corals first became relatively common in the Carnian. Even so, these corals did not become the dominant reef builders until the end of the Triassic.

  <!-- tria-043 -->

- **Archosaurs push the mammal relatives aside** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  At first archosaurs were the underdogs, rarer than the therapsids. They began displacing them in the mid-Triassic and were the dominant land vertebrates by the Middle Triassic. From the early Triassic they took most medium to large meat-eating roles on land. Over 35 million years they came to include crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs. Crocodile-line pseudosuchians dominated, from plant-eating aetosaurs to big 'rauisuchian' predators, while dinosauromorphs shared the land. Large cynodonts such as traversodontids still held some big plant-eater and predator roles.

  <!-- tria-040 -->

- **Dinoflagellates leave their first fossil cysts** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  Chemical traces say dinoflagellates may have drifted in the sea since the Early Cambrian. Their first true fossils, though, appear only in the mid-Triassic, mostly as tough resting cysts. These single-celled plankton then radiated in shape from the Late Triassic through the Middle Jurassic. By then they had become prominent phytoplankton, the drifting algae of the open sea.

  <!-- tria-042 -->

- **Turtles start out without a shell** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  The first turtles had no shell at all. Pappochelys, a stem turtle from the Middle Triassic, an early member of the turtle line, had only a short torso, broad ribs and long back vertebrae. By the Late Triassic, Odontochelys carried a complete bony plastron, the belly shell, but only part of a carapace, the upper shell. The traits that built the shell may first have helped these animals dig.

  <!-- tria-044 -->

- **Placodonts, nothosaurs and kin crowd Triassic seas** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  Nothosaurs 5–7 m long hunted Middle Triassic waters, and they had plenty of company. Placodonts, thalattosaurs, the long-necked Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians. Pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurs were common, especially around the Tethys. Atopodentatus is the earliest known plant-eating marine reptile, and some ichthyopterygians reached very large body masses. South China has yielded almost every known clade, or branch, of Triassic marine reptile.

  <!-- tria-046 -->

- **Seas and lakes rebuild complex food webs** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  Fossil dung from Chinese lakes tells the story. By the early Ladinian, these coprolites record freshwater food webs with six or more trophic levels, rungs from grazers up to top predators. Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals had begun to re-form. Carbon-isotope swings abruptly calmed, and the recovery of shelled sea life soon followed. Marine reptiles, ray-finned fishes, ammonoids, bivalves and gastropods all grew more diverse, crinoids regained ecological dominance, and phytoplankton, corals and crustaceans recovered. Even so, full recovery took about 30 million years. Global marine diversity regained its old level only in the Middle Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-047 -->

- **The Tethys pushes west and floods central Europe** — during the Middle Triassic, 247–237 million years ago (247–237 Ma)

  Central Europe went under the sea. In the Middle Triassic the Tethys, a vast gulf on Pangaea's eastern side, opened farther west as the older Paleo-Tethys shrank. Rising seas spread the shallow Muschelkalk Sea across central Europe, as far as the North Pyrenean Zone. Rifting also began in the Anisian to form a new ocean basin, the Meliata.

  <!-- tria-050 -->

- **France's Grès à Voltzia keeps the first aphids** — c. 245 million years ago (245 Ma)

  The oldest known aphids come from a sandstone in France. The Grès à Voltzia, about 245 million years old, is a Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional fossil preservation. Its varied arthropods also include finely detailed myriapods, the many-legged group of centipedes and millipedes.

  <!-- tria-051 -->

- **Agriodontosaurus, the oldest sure lepidosaur** — c. 244–242 million years ago (244–241.5 Ma)

  The family tree of every lizard and snake runs back to a small reptile from England. Agriodontosaurus, a rhynchocephalian about 244–241.5 million years old, is the oldest definite lepidosaur. Lepidosaurs are the ancestors of lizards, snakes and the tuatara. The next oldest rhynchocephalian, Wirtembergia, is Ladinian, and the Early Triassic Sophineta may be a lepidosaur relative. The group later diversified during The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green.

  <!-- tria-052 -->

- **Monte San Giorgio's lagoon preserves sea reptiles** — c. 242 million years ago (242 Ma)

  A stagnant lagoon made a perfect tomb. At Monte San Giorgio on Lake Lugano, a Middle Triassic lagoon sat behind reefs, and its oxygen-free bottom was ideal for fossilization. Its Besano Formation, about 242 million years old and now a World Heritage Site, preserves fish and marine reptiles such as Neusticosaurus and Tanystropheus.

  <!-- tria-054 -->

- **A long cooling settles over the Ladinian and Carnian** — c. 242–233 million years ago (242–233 Ma)

  After the Anisian chill, the world kept drifting cooler. The Ladinian–Carnian Cooling ran from 242 to 233 million years ago, and global temperatures were still relatively cool as the Carnian began. Then abrupt warming from the Wrangellia eruptions around 234 million years ago ended the trend.

  <!-- tria-053 -->

- **True flies take wing** — c. 240 million years ago (240 Ma)

  One wing, 10 mm long, from Mt. Crosby in Australia is unusually large for a Triassic fly. The first true flies, the Diptera, appeared in the Middle Triassic around 240 million years ago and spread widely through the Middle and Late Triassic. They form one of the four great insect radiations, evolutionary bursts. Many new species of lower flies arose around 220 million years ago.

  <!-- tria-057 -->

- **Cimmerian blocks drift north and close the Paleo-Tethys** — c. 240–200 million years ago (240–200 Ma)

  An ocean that had lasted about 400 million years was squeezed shut. A string of continental fragments, the Cimmerian blocks, drifted north, closing the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them and opening the Neo-Tethys behind. By the Late Triassic the old ocean had shrunk to a narrow seaway. Its closure raised the Cimmerian orogeny, which began about 240–200 million years ago as the blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China. The Qiangtang terrane of northern Tibet joined Asia in the Late Triassic. The western arm stayed open until about 205 million years ago, when Iranian blocks hit Eurasia's Turan platform. The finished belt ran from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.

  <!-- tria-055 -->

  *Figure: As the Cimmerian blocks drifted north, one ocean closed while another opened.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cimmerian blocks drift north] --> B[Paleo-Tethys closes ahead]
  A --> C[Neo-Tethys opens behind]
  B --> D[Narrow seaway by Late Triassic]
  D --> E[Cimmerian orogeny]
  ```

##### Late Triassic Epoch

The Late Triassic opens with a crisis at sea and a shock to the climate. Marine reptiles had just suffered their highest extinction rates, and then the Wrangellia flood basalts poured out over about 5 million years, jolting global climate for perhaps 1–2 million years. In the rains and rivers of that world, the first true dinosaurs appeared and quickly split into sauropodomorphs and meat-eating theropods. Rift basins in Argentina and Virginia buried them with fish, insects and reptiles, while a vast delta plain spread across the Boreal Ocean. Even the oldest probable moth scales turn up, swallowed by a plant-eater.

- **Marine reptiles suffer their steepest extinction rates** — c. 237 million years ago (237 Ma)

  For the sea reptiles of the Mesozoic, no moment was deadlier. At the end of the Ladinian, which closed the Middle Triassic, they suffered their highest extinction rates. Like fishes, marine reptiles lost much of their diversity between the Middle Triassic and the Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-058 -->

- **Specialist rhynchosaurs spread across the globe** — during the Carnian, 237–227 million years ago (237–227.3 Ma)

  A crisis gave one narrow branch the whole world. Rhynchosaurs had diversified around 240 million years ago, but the lines common in the Middle Triassic died out during The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green. The specialized hyperodapedontines were left. They became widespread and abundant in the late Carnian, giving rhynchosaurs their broadest, truly global range.

  <!-- tria-062 -->

- **A giant delta plain fills the Boreal Ocean** — c. 237–227 million years ago (237–227 Ma)

  Rivers built new land across a whole sea floor. From 237 to 227 million years ago, a vast delta plain spread across northern Pangaea's Triassic Boreal Ocean, today's Barents Sea. Rapid sedimentation after the extinction had already built a shallow basin, with Induan silts spanning 1,000 km. Deposition slowed in the Olenekian and Anisian, then revived in the Ladinian, as deltas advanced more than 500 km. By 237 million years ago, the plain had formed.

  <!-- tria-064 -->

- **Chalk-plated coccolithophores join the plankton** — during the Late Triassic, 237–201 million years ago (237–201.4 Ma)

  Since about 220 million years ago, the seafloor has never stopped collecting microscopic chalk plates. Calcareous nannofossils, those tiny chalky remains, have a continuous record from the Late Triassic to the present. The oldest known coccolithophores, algae armored with plates called coccoliths, date from around the Norian–Rhaetian boundary. One source puts the first coccoliths, with dinoflagellates, in the plankton earlier, during The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green. Coccolithophores radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic, becoming prominent members of the phytoplankton.

  <!-- tria-060 -->

- **Moth scales turn up in fossil dung** — c. 236 million years ago (236 Ma)

  The oldest probable trace of moths was eaten by accident. Scales about 236 million years old, found in a plant-eater's dung in Argentina, are the earliest probable fossils of Lepidoptera, the moths and butterflies. Wing scales of several moth groups occur as rare microfossils at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary in a core near Braunschweig, Germany. Possible stem relatives of caddisflies and moths are known from the Triassic.

  <!-- tria-065 -->

- **Wrangellia floods the land with basalt** — c. 234 million years ago (234 Ma)

  A belt of lava 2,500 km long now marks one of the Triassic's great eruptions. For about 5 million years, the Wrangellia flood basalts poured onto land and built a large igneous province, a huge pile of volcanic rock. The eruption around 234 million years ago caused abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling. Carbon and osmium isotopes tie it to the Carnian climate upheaval, and seawater osmium shifted at the Ladinian–Carnian boundary. Its rocks belong to the Wrangellia terrane, a crustal fragment later added to western North America.

  <!-- tria-067 -->

- **The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green** — c. 234–232 million years ago (234–232 Ma)

  For perhaps 1–2 million years, it rained on Pangaea as never before. Around 234–232 million years ago, in the Carnian pluvial episode, global climate shifted sharply, changing life on land and in the sea. The trigger was volcanic. Eruptions off North America, the Wrangellia large igneous province, set off abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling. Pangaea's arid climate turned hotter and more humid. Rainfall and runoff surged, and the dry interior became lush forests along rivers. At sea, carbonate platforms, shallow limestone shelves, shrank, and many invertebrates died out, especially ammonoids, bryozoans and crinoids. Yet the same upheaval was a beginning. Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms, mammals and their closest kin, diversified during the event, and coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

  <!-- tria-066 -->

  *Figure: How Wrangellia volcanism turned Pangaea's interior wet.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Wrangellia volcanism] --> B[Abrupt global warming]
  B --> C[Hotter, more humid climate]
  C --> D[Rainfall and runoff surge]
  D --> E[Lush alluvial forests]
  ```

- **The first true dinosaurs appear** — c. 233 million years ago (233.2 Ma)

  Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor were not giants, but they were dinosaurs. The earliest true dinosaurs likely appeared in the Carnian, around the time of the Carnian pluvial episode, and diversified rapidly. Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, radiometrically dated to 233.23 million years ago, and Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, 231–230 million years old, hold some of the oldest. Nyasasaurus, from Tanzania's Manda Formation, hints that the line may reach back to the Anisian, about 243 million years ago. Dinosaurs arose from avemetatarsalians, a minor part of Triassic ecosystems. They became dominant only in the Jurassic. Did the rains drive their rise? That is doubtful, because avemetatarsalian diversity grew faster in the Ladinian and Norian than during the wet spell.

  <!-- tria-068 -->

  *Figure: Dated early dinosaur finds.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Brazil yields the first sauropodomorphs** — c. 233 million years ago (233.2 Ma)

  The line that would produce the largest land animals began with small creatures in Brazil. Buriolestes and Saturnalia, from the Santa Maria Formation dated to 233.23 million years ago, are early sauropodomorphs, the dinosaur branch that includes the sauropods. Eoraptor, once grouped with herrerasaurids, now counts as an early sauropodomorph too. Timeline of Earth lists the earliest sauropods at about 233 million years ago, and four-legged sauropodomorphs appeared later in the Late Triassic.

  <!-- tria-069 -->

- **Ischigualasto's ash and mud bury early dinosaurs** — c. 232–225 million years ago (231.7–225 Ma)

  Volcanic ash helped bury some of the first dinosaurs. The site is a reactivated half-graben, a rift basin tilted along one fault, in northwestern Argentina. There, rivers from volcanic highlands laid down sandstones, mudstones and ash beds up to about 1 km thick. Rain came in strong seasons; one study traces a shift from warm, humid conditions to drier ones around 229.5 million years ago, with partial recovery by 227.8 million. The Ischigualasto Formation is dense with fossils, including Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor among abundant rhynchosaurs and cynodonts.

  <!-- tria-070 -->

- **Theropods, the meat-eating dinosaurs, arrive** — c. 231 million years ago (231 Ma)

  The lineage that would one day include the great predators began about 231 million years ago. The first theropods, the meat-eating dinosaur line, shared the Carnian with early sauropodomorphs. Their more advanced members, the neotheropods, first appeared later in the Late Triassic.

  <!-- tria-071 -->

- **Virginia's Cow Branch Formation keeps fish and insects** — c. 230 million years ago (230 Ma)

  Spiders' kin, insects, fish and reptiles share the same rocks in Virginia. The Cow Branch Formation, about 230 million years old, is a Lagerstätte that preserves a wide range of these animals. It gives a rare look at a whole Late Triassic community, small and soft creatures included.

  <!-- tria-072 -->

- **Madygen yields over 20,000 fossil insects** — c. 230 million years ago (230 Ma)

  More than 20,000 fossil insects have come out of a single formation in Kyrgyzstan. The Madygen Formation, about 230 million years old, is one of the richest Triassic Lagerstätten. Fish, amphibians, reptiles and synapsids, the mammal line, turn up too. Among them is Kyrgyzsaurus, the earliest known drepanosaurid.

  <!-- tria-073 -->

- **Pterosaurs take to the Triassic skies** — c. 228 million years ago (228 Ma)

  A little after the first true dinosaurs, about 228 million years ago, reptiles took to the air. Pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, sprang from the avemetatarsalians, like dinosaurs a minor part of Triassic ecosystems. Feathers may already have been present in the two groups' common ancestor in the Early Triassic. Early long-tailed pterosaurs appeared in the Norian and quickly spread worldwide. Norian lagoon deposits in northern Italy, such as the Calcare di Zorzino, about 216.6–212 million years old, preserve them beside other reptiles.

  <!-- tria-074 -->

- **An impact carves Manitoba's Saint Martin crater** — 228 million years ago (227.8 ± 1.1 Ma)

  A crater about 40 km across lies in Manitoba, Canada: the Saint Martin structure. Geologists once linked it with Manicouagan and Rochechouart as a single multiple impact. Its age of 227.8 ± 1.1 million years broke that idea, showing the craters formed millions of years apart.

  <!-- tria-075 -->

- **A disputed end-Carnian crisis drowns a delta** — c. 227 million years ago (227.3 Ma)

  Repeated floods drowned the vast Boreal Ocean delta plain, shifting shorelines more than 1,000 km and wiping out many of its organisms. Several plant-eating archosauromorph groups died out, and big plant-eating therapsids such as kannemeyeriid dicynodonts dwindled across Laurasia. Coastal habitat loss hit semi-aquatic crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals, and a reef crisis struck South China. Still, sources hedge on whether this was a distinct extinction, partly because the age of the Carnian–Norian boundary is itself disputed.

  <!-- tria-078 -->

- **Tuatara relatives spread around the world** — c. 227 million years ago (227.3 Ma)

  Today the tuatara is a lonely survivor, but its relatives once ranged worldwide. By the end of the Carnian, rhynchocephalians had spread across the globe. They went on to be the dominant small reptiles of the Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-081 -->

- **Rivers and ash build the colorful Chinle Formation** — during the Norian, 227–206 million years ago (227.3–205.7 Ma)

  The bands of the Painted Desert are a Triassic landscape turned to stone. Rivers, lakes and floodplains, with much volcanic ash, laid down the colorful Chinle Formation across the American Southwest. Exposed there and in Petrified Forest National Park, it holds a unique record of life on land from the late Carnian to the early Norian. U-Pb dating and magnetostratigraphy confirm a Norian age for the lower Chinle.

  <!-- tria-076 -->

- **Plant-eating dinosaurs spread through the Norian** — during the Norian, 227–206 million years ago (227.3–205.7 Ma)

  Plateosaurus, an early sauropodomorph, evolved around 214 million years ago and roamed Europe, Greenland and North America. It belonged to the plant-eating sauropodomorphs, which diversified in the Norian and began to displace large plant-eating therapsids, perhaps because they coped better with growing aridity. Most Triassic dinosaurs, though, were small predators. Coelophysis, 1–2 m long, was one of the few common ones. Even now, crurotarsan archosaurs, the crocodile line, still filled more ecological niches than dinosaurs did.

  <!-- tria-077 -->

- **The last rhynchosaurs vanish** — during the Norian, 227–206 million years ago (227.3–205.7 Ma)

  Once among the most abundant plant-eaters on Earth, the beaked hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs died out in the early Norian. Brazil's Teyumbaita is the only rhynchosaur known with confidence to have survived into that age. The exact date of their end is uncertain. They lasted at least into the early to middle Norian, though one suggestion places their extinction in an end-Carnian crisis instead.

  <!-- tria-079 -->

- **A mid-Norian die-off strikes the seas** — during the Norian, 227–206 million years ago (227.3–205.7 Ma)

  Single-celled radiolarians, sponges, eel-like conodonts and Triassic ammonoids all took losses in the middle of the Norian. This marine extinction has been blamed on An asteroid 5 km wide blasts out Manicouagan. That impact may also have hastened the slide of conodonts and ammonoids toward their final end-Triassic extinction.

  <!-- tria-080 -->

- **Sea level sinks to a Rhaetian low** — during the Norian–Rhaetian, 227–201 million years ago (227.3–201.4 Ma)

  From a Carnian high of up to 50 m above today's level, the sea began to retreat in the Norian. It bottomed out about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian, and low levels lasted into the earliest Jurassic. Ice cannot explain the swing, because there is no evidence of Triassic ice sheets. At the very end of the Triassic, the sea flooded most of central and western Europe, turning it into an archipelago. A drop in sea level seen in Europe and the Middle East at the extinction now looks regional rather than global.

  <!-- tria-082 -->

  *Figure: Sea level swung from well above today's to well below it.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Mammaliaforms, the closest kin of mammals, appear** — c. 227 million years ago (227 Ma)

  Tiny, nocturnal and warm-blooded, the first mammaliaforms lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs. Mammaliaforms are mammals plus their closest extinct kin, and they arose from advanced probainognathian cynodonts in the Late Triassic. Exactly when is still argued. Some studies place their origin in the Carnian pluvial episode, others in the Norian or at the very end of the Triassic. Unambiguous forms such as morganucodonts and haramiyids appeared in the Norian across Europe and Greenland, as probainognathians became prominent. Older claims look shaky. Tikitherium may be a misidentified Cenozoic shrew, and Adelobasileus is no older than 225 million years. These early animals were small, mostly insect-eating, and their bodies were already changing: bones of the old jaw were moving into the middle ear. Cynodonts were the only therapsids to outlast the Triassic, and mammaliaforms went on to diversify widely in the Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-084 -->

- **A cooler spell follows the Carnian heat** — c. 227–217 million years ago (227–217 Ma)

  After the Carnian's rains and warmth, the climate turned cooler. The Early Norian Cool Interval lasted from about 227 to 217 million years ago, following the Mid-Carnian Warm Interval that the Carnian pluvial episode had brought. At the Carnian–Norian boundary, a positive carbon-isotope excursion, a shift toward heavier carbon, suggests more organic carbon was being buried.

  <!-- tria-083 -->

- **Teleosts, today's dominant fishes, first appear** — c. 225 million years ago (225 Ma)

  More than 99% of living ray-finned fishes are teleosts, and the group first appears around 225 million years ago. Early stem teleosts such as Prohalecites swam in the western Tethys. From those modest beginnings came the fishes that now dominate rivers, lakes and oceans worldwide.

  <!-- tria-085 -->

- **Warmth returns, and Pangaea turns swampy** — c. 217–209 million years ago (217–209 Ma)

  Earth's orbit helped turn deserts into swamps. Warmer conditions, the Mid-Norian Warm Interval, lasted from about 217 to 209 million years ago. Around 214 million years ago a brief cooling interrupted it, possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact. Around 212 million years ago, a peak in orbital eccentricity, the stretching of Earth's path around the Sun, made much of Pangaea swampy and shrank its arid zones.

  <!-- tria-089 -->

- **An asteroid 5 km wide blasts out Manicouagan** — 215 million years ago (215.4 ± 0.16 Ma)

  Shocked quartz from a single strike in Quebec turns up as far away as England and Japan. An asteroid about 5 km wide hit there, excavating a multiple-ring crater about 100 km across, among the largest on Earth. Of all Mesozoic impacts, only Chicxulub was bigger. It may have caused a brief cooling, a mid-Norian marine extinction and the Adamanian–Revueltian turnover on land, but direct evidence is lacking. Some 13 million years older than the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it is no longer thought to have caused the end-Triassic extinction.

  <!-- tria-090 -->

- **A turnover reshapes Southwest faunas** — c. 215 million years ago (215 Ma)

  In the rocks of the Chinle Formation, several land animals vanish quickly around 215 million years ago. Trilophosaurus, Desmatosuchus, dicynodonts and many phytosaurs disappeared from the American Southwest, and new aetosaurs and phytosaurs replaced them. Pollen shifted to dry-adapted plants, suggesting rising aridity, and the Manicouagan impact is one proposed cause. Both the cause and the importance of this turnover are debated. It may have been only a small, local extinction.

  <!-- tria-091 -->

- **Argoland begins to splinter off Australia** — c. 215 million years ago (215 Ma)

  Gondwana started shedding pieces. Around 215 million years ago, Argoland, on Australia's northern margin, began breaking into microcontinental fragments. It happened during Late Triassic rifting that pulled the Lhasa terrane away from Gondwana. A major Norian rifting episode, about 210 million years ago, split Gondwana in two parts.

  <!-- tria-092 -->

- **Proganochelys completes the turtle shell** — c. 215 million years ago (215 Ma)

  The turtle shell took millions of years to finish. In the Norian, the earliest true turtles appeared, among them Proganochelys and Proterochersis. Proganochelys completed what Turtles start out without a shell had begun, with a fully developed carapace and plastron. Side-necked and hidden-necked turtles, the two lines that include all living turtles, are estimated to have split about 210 million years ago.

  <!-- tria-093 -->

- **Early dinosaur rivals vanish in the mid-Norian** — c. 215 million years ago (215 Ma)

  The dinosaurs' rise owed something to their rivals' bad luck. About 215 million years ago, a range of basal archosauromorphs, early-branching archosaur relatives including the protorosaurs, died out. It was the first of two Triassic extinctions that removed most of the early dinosaurs' competitors. Early dinosaur lineages diversified through the Carnian and Norian, possibly filling the emptied niches.

  <!-- tria-094 -->

- **A cool Rhaetian ends in extreme heat** — c. 209–201 million years ago (209–201 Ma)

  The Triassic's last cool spell ended in a furnace. A cooler phase, the Rhaetian Cool Interval, lasted from about 209 to 201 million years ago. Then an extreme warming, the Volcanic carbon drives an extreme end-Triassic warming, closed the period, and it is blamed for the mass extinction.

  <!-- tria-095 -->

- **An asteroid strikes an island in western France** — 207 million years ago (206.9 ± 0.2 Ma)

  Near Limoges, an asteroid hit an island on the edge of the Massif Central, close to the sea. It left the Rochechouart structure, about 23 km across, and probably raised a large tsunami. Its age has long been debated, with estimates from under 150 to over 240 million years, but recent dates converge on 203–207 million years ago. That puts it a few million years before the Triassic–Jurassic boundary. Even so, it seems too small to have caused the mass extinction.

  <!-- tria-096 -->

- **The giant shastasaurs vanish from the seas** — c. 206 million years ago (205.7 Ma)

  Shonisaurus grew to 15 m long, one of the shastasaurian ichthyosaurs that reached huge sizes in the Carnian and Norian. These giants seem to have vanished at the end of the Norian, as ichthyosaur variety declined. Growing competition from sharks, teleost fishes and the first plesiosaurs may explain the decline.

  <!-- tria-097 -->

- **A disputed die-off at the Norian–Rhaetian boundary** — c. 206–205 million years ago (205.7–205.3 Ma)

  Monotis, a large bivalve once found worldwide, lost almost all its species. Its last shells lie between ash beds dated 205.70 and 205.30 million years old. The same extinction near the Norian–Rhaetian boundary hit ammonoids, other bivalves, conodonts and radiolarians, and a sharp negative carbon-isotope spike is tied to it. Alaska's Angayucham large igneous province or the Rochechouart impact may have caused it. Yet one source calls it an alleged, much smaller event, and its dating and effects remain uncertain.

  <!-- tria-099 -->

- **Marine life falters before the final crisis** — during the Rhaetian, 206–201 million years ago (205.7–201.4 Ma)

  Mean annual temperatures rose 7–9 °C from the late Norian into the Rhaetian. The seas were already in trouble. Gastropods, or snails, suffered steady losses through the late Norian and Rhaetian, and offshore bryozoans had been declining since the Norian. Anoxia struck northeastern Panthalassa during the Rhaetian, and the carbon cycle was disturbed before the main crisis began.

  <!-- tria-098 -->

- **The Karoo igneous province stirs** — c. 204 million years ago (204 Ma)

  A volcanic giant began to wake on the northern edge of what is now southern Africa's Karoo. Igneous activity of the Karoo large igneous province started about 204 million years ago on its northern margin. Its later Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts are tied to the Toarcian extinction of the Early Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-100 -->

- **Plesiosaurs appear at the end of the Triassic** — c. 203 million years ago (203 Ma)

  Of all the flipper-limbed sauropterygians, only one branch survived the end of the Triassic, and it had only just arrived. Plesiosaurs first appeared in the latest Triassic, possibly in the Rhaetian, about 203 million years ago. At least six plesiosaur lineages crossed into the Jurassic, while every other sauropterygian died out. They became especially common in the Jurassic and lasted until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

  <!-- tria-101 -->

- **The Central Atlantic magmatic province erupts** — 202–201 million years ago (201.6–201.4 Ma)

  Lava covered about 11 million km² across four continents. As central Pangaea rifted, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, or CAMP, built Earth's largest continental igneous province, with 2–6 million km³ of lava. The first lavas date to 201.566 ± 0.031 million years ago and the last to 201.36 ± 0.02 million years ago. The eruptions came in four main pulses. Each lasted no more than about 100 years, and together they were spread over some 600,000 years. Large bodies of magma had built up about 100,000 years before the eruptions began. CAMP ended the long rifting of the Central Atlantic. It is widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, a link that became firmer in 2013.

  <!-- tria-102 -->

  *Figure: From buried magma to CAMP eruptions and the end-Triassic extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Large magma bodies build up] --> B[Four lava pulses]
  B --> C[Central Atlantic rifting ends]
  B -.-> D[Triassic-Jurassic extinction]
  ```

- **Volcanic carbon drives an extreme end-Triassic warming** — c. 201 million years ago (201.4 Ma)

  Tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide, trapped in CAMP basalts, hold the smoking gun. They show the volcanism helped trigger the End-Triassic Thermal Event, an extreme warming at the very end of the Triassic that drove the mass extinction. The pulses released their carbon over mere centuries, a pace that invites comparison with today's human-caused warming. Longer-term warming and ocean acidification followed the eruptions. A thermal spike marks the start of the Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-103 -->

  *Figure: Carbon from the CAMP eruptions drove the warming behind the end-Triassic extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[CAMP volcanic pulses] -->|carbon over centuries| B[End-Triassic Thermal Event]
  B --> C[Mass extinction]
  A --> D[Longer-term warming]
  A --> E[Ocean acidification]
  ```

- **The end-Triassic extinction hands the land to dinosaurs** — 201 million years ago (201.4 ± 0.2 Ma)

  About 46–72% of marine genera disappeared. One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions ended the Triassic 201.4 million years ago, driven by CAMP volcanism and the warming it caused. In the sea, ammonites were nearly wiped out, conodonts vanished and reefs collapsed, completing the oceans' shift to the modern evolutionary fauna. On land, most archosaurs died out except crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs, along with most therapsids and large amphibians. One estimate puts tetrapod losses at 42%. Plants turned over too, with 17–73% of Rhaetian plants lost by various estimates, though some researchers see a restructuring rather than a plant mass extinction. The crisis removed the crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals. That opening let dinosaurs dominate the Jurassic.

  <!-- tria-104 -->

  *Figure: How major groups fared in the end-Triassic extinction.*

  | Group | Fate |
  |---|---|
  | Dinosaurs | Survived, then dominated |
  | Pterosaurs | Survived |
  | Crocodylomorphs | Survived |
  | Crurotarsans | Removed |
  | Ammonites | Nearly wiped out |
  | Conodonts | Vanished |

- **Oceans lose their oxygen and turn acidic** — c. 201 million years ago (201.4 Ma)

  Misshapen nannoplankton tell of seas turned corrosive. Black shales and a sharp negative uranium-isotope shift show that ocean oxygen fell steeply during the extinction. Anoxia reached the western and eastern Tethys and Panthalassa and lasted into the Hettangian, as nutrients from the land fed the seas. Green sulfur bacteria, which photosynthesize with hydrogen sulfide, grew markedly across the boundary. A worldwide pause in carbonate deposition adds to the evidence of severe acidification. This is the best-established case of acidification causing a marine mass extinction, selectively killing organisms with thick skeletons of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.

  <!-- tria-105 -->

- **The last dicynodonts disappear** — c. 201 million years ago (201.4 Ma)

  The group of Lystrosaurus had a long run. Dicynodonts were among the most successful therapsids of the Permian and stayed large plant-eaters until they died out at the end of the Triassic. Their last appearance is uncertain. They survived at least into the late Norian or earliest Rhaetian.

  <!-- tria-108 -->

- **Phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians die out** — c. 201 million years ago (201.4 Ma)

  The crocodile line ruled much of the Late Triassic, and almost all of it was lost at once. Phytosaurs and aetosaurs, common in Late Triassic faunas, were completely wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction. Among the pseudosuchians, only small crocodylomorphs survived. Plant-eaters like aetosaurs and the meat-eating rauisuchids died out. The timing is hard to pin down, because the Rhaetian and Hettangian hold few large land animals and some groups may have vanished earlier.

  <!-- tria-110 -->

#### Jurassic Period

The Jurassic begins with the land drying out and the dinosaurs moving in. As Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried, the great Pangean megamonsoon began to fall apart, and the Farallon plate started sinking beneath western North America as Pangaea broke up. With their reptile rivals gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and abundance, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. In the sea, ammonoids that had nearly vanished radiated into the ammonites proper, and plesiosaurs were already richly varied. Even the amphibians changed, as the first modern frogs and salamanders began to diversify.

- **Modern amphibians branch out: the first frogs and salamanders** — during the Jurassic, 201–143 million years ago (201.4–143.1 Ma)

  Every frog and salamander alive today belongs to a lineage that began spreading out in the Jurassic. Lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, diversified then, producing the first modern frogs and salamanders. Eocaecilia, a stem relative of today's limbless caecilians, already lived in Early Jurassic Arizona. Stem-frogs and the extinct albanerpetontids followed in the Middle Jurassic. Meanwhile the old guard faded. Of the once-diverse temnospondyls, only the brachyopoids survived into the Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-019 -->

- **Pangaea's great monsoon starts to fail** — during the Jurassic, 201–143 million years ago (201.4–143.1 Ma)

  The rains that had swept Pangaea for an entire period began to fail. At the start of the Jurassic, the Pangean megamonsoon started falling apart. Gondwana, the southern half of Pangaea, dried out, and so did southern Laurasia. As the continents drifted apart, the monsoon kept weakening through the rest of the Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-026 -->

##### Early Jurassic Epoch

In the wreckage of the end-Triassic extinction, the Early Jurassic rebuilt fast. British seafloor communities began recovering almost at once, despite repeated relapses into anoxia, and ammonites and neoselachian sharks radiated through the seas. On land, dinosaurs surged into the space left by vanished rivals, crocodylomorphs found new niches, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. Plant life turned over too: conifers replaced the hot fernlands of China's Sichuan Basin, while Dicroidium lingered only in Antarctica. Even ocean chemistry shifted, from aragonite seas to calcite seas.

- **Plesiosaurs crowd the earliest Jurassic seas** — during the Hettangian, 201–200 million years ago (201.4–199.5 Ma)

  Even ichthyosaurs, fast fish-shaped marine reptiles, had something to fear. Large plesiosaurs joined sharks and other ichthyosaurs as their predators. A rich radiation of plesiosaurs is known from the Hettangian, which implies the group had already diversified in the Late Triassic. Most in the Hettangian Blue Lias were short-necked rhomaleosaurids. Plesiosaurs also invaded fresh water, and small forms are known from Jurassic China and Australia. By the Toarcian, about 180 million years ago, longer-necked plesiosaurids reached up to 10 meters.

  <!-- jura-028 -->

- **Conifers reclaim the fernlands of Sichuan** — c. 201–193 million years ago (201.4–192.9 Ma)

  Ferns were the survivors. Plants with dissected leaves coped better with the end-Triassic crisis and spread across the boundary into the Jurassic. In China's Sichuan Basin, hot, arid fernlands covered the land at the Triassic–Jurassic transition. In the Hettangian and Sinemurian they gave way to cheirolepid conifers, an extinct family known by its Classopollis pollen. These conifers stayed abundant through the whole Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-006 -->

- **Seafloor life recovers in fits and starts** — c. 201–193 million years ago (201.4–192.9 Ma)

  In Britain, seafloor life started recovering almost as soon as the extinction ended. The comeback was not smooth. Repeated relapses into anoxia interrupted it, and oxygen loss and nutrient runoff lasted into the Hettangian, perhaps delaying recovery. In Argentina's Neuquén Basin, communities rebuilt from the late early Hettangian and reached a new balance of diversity by the late Hettangian. The carbon cycle settled only in the Sinemurian, when brachiopods and dasycladacean algae rediversified. Tropical reefs, which had collapsed, did not fully recover until much later in the Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-018 -->

- **Ammonites rebound from near-extinction** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  Ammonoids came within a whisker of extinction at the end of the Triassic. Then they exploded into many new forms with complex sutures, the wavy seams between shell chambers: the ammonites proper. Six orders, from Psiloceratina to Ancyloceratina, all appeared during the Jurassic. Their faunas formed about 20 provinces, grouped into a northern Pan-Boreal and a southern Pan-Tethyan realm. Serpenticone ammonites, coiled like snakes, are abundant in Europe's Jurassic rocks.

  <!-- jura-001 -->

- **The last coelophysoids and massospondylids disappear** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  Not every dinosaur line that survived the end-Triassic extinction lasted long. Basal neotheropods such as coelophysoids and dilophosaurs made it into the Early Jurassic but were gone by the Middle Jurassic. Two-legged basal sauropodomorphs such as the massospondylids also died out by the start of the Middle Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-003 -->

- **Crocodile relatives multiply, and some go to sea** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  Among the crocodile line's few survivors, one branch went to sea. Crocodylomorphs radiated rapidly in the Early Jurassic, filling niches different from those of their Triassic relatives. The mostly marine thalattosuchians first appeared then and became a prominent part of marine ecosystems. One of the oldest, a basal teleosauroid from Morocco, dates from the Hettangian–Sinemurian. On land, a protosuchid from Arizona is the earliest known plant-eating crocodylomorph.

  <!-- jura-008 -->

- **Dinosaurs take over the land** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  When the end-Triassic extinction cleared away their reptile rivals, dinosaurs did not just survive. They surged. In the Early Jurassic they grew rapidly in both diversity and abundance, and land faunas changed hands. Through the Triassic, dinosauromorphs and pseudosuchians, the crocodile line, had shared the land. Now dinosaurs ruled it alone. From the Early Jurassic on, dinosaurs and pterosaurs were the commonest land reptiles, while lizards and tuatara relatives filled the roles of small reptiles. By the Early Jurassic at the latest, dinosaurs had spread to every continent. Their reign was long. They stayed the dominant land vertebrates through the rest of the Jurassic and the whole Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-009 -->

- **The first certain ornithischians appear** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  One of the great dinosaur branches finally shows itself plainly in the Early Jurassic. The earliest definitive ornithischians, the 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, appeared and diversified then. They were small basal forms such as Lesothosaurus, the heterodontosaurids and early thyreophorans, the armored line. From these modest plant-eaters the group would grow into one of the dinosaurs' main branches.

  <!-- jura-010 -->

- **The Farallon plate dives beneath North America** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  As Pangaea broke apart, an ocean plate began sliding under the American West. In the Early Jurassic, the Farallon plate started sinking beneath western North America. Mountains in Nevada and California kept rising as plate motions pushed North America northward.

  <!-- jura-011 -->

- **Dicroidium makes a last stand in Antarctica** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  The seed fern that once ruled Gondwana's forests ended its days in Antarctica. Dicroidium survived there only as a relict into the Early Jurassic. Its relative Lepidopteris, a peltasperm, likewise lingered in Patagonia.

  <!-- jura-017 -->

- **Modern sharks and the first rays appear** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  Every shark and ray alive today traces back to a radiation that began in the Early Jurassic. Neoselachians, the group of all living sharks and rays, spread out from then on. Rays first appear in the Early Jurassic; the oldest confirmed ray, Antiquaobatis, is from the Pliensbachian of Germany. The oldest six-gilled and carpet sharks come from the Pliensbachian and Toarcian of Europe. By the Late Jurassic, neoselachians had largely replaced hybodonts, the Triassic's dominant sharks. Timelines of Earth and of life date the first rays later, to about 165 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-021 -->

- **Seawater flips from aragonite to calcite** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  Seawater itself changed character in the Early Jurassic. The world's oceans shifted from aragonite-sea to calcite-sea chemistry, two states named for the two forms of calcium carbonate. The new chemistry favored dissolving aragonite and precipitating calcite.

  <!-- jura-024 -->

- **Cimmeria closes the Paleo-Tethys Ocean** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  An old ocean disappeared from west to east, like a zip being closed. In the Early Jurassic, Paleo-Tethys ocean floor subducted beneath the Cimmerian plate, sinking under it until the ocean was gone. The closure was part of the Cimmerian orogeny. Around 200 million years ago, the Tethyan Trench formed as the Cimmerian plate itself subducted beneath eastern Laurasia.

  <!-- jura-025 -->

- **The Viking Corridor links two oceans** — during the Early Jurassic, 201–175 million years ago (201.4–174.7 Ma)

  A seaway several hundred kilometers wide opened between the Baltic Shield and Greenland. From the Early Jurassic, this Viking Corridor linked the Boreal Ocean in the north to the proto-Atlantic. Waters and sea life that had been separated could now mix.

  <!-- jura-029 -->

- **Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates fill the plankton** — c. 201–162 million years ago (201.4–161.5 Ma)

  The ocean's chemistry was changed by organisms too small to see. Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates, both first seen in the Triassic, radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic and became prominent phytoplankton. Coccolithophores have been an integral part of marine plankton ever since. The rise of calcareous plankton in the Middle Jurassic altered ocean chemistry. Their chalky remains, piling up on the seafloor, buffered the oceans against large CO2 emissions. Calcareous nannoplankton kept growing more diverse through the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

  <!-- jura-005 -->

  *Figure: Calcareous plankton changed ocean chemistry by burying their chalky remains.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Coccolithophores radiate] --> B[Calcareous plankton rise]
  B --> C[Chalky seafloor deposits]
  C --> D[Buffer against large CO2 emissions]
  ```

- **Blue Lias layers keep time with Earth's orbit** — c. 201–198 million years ago (201–198 Ma)

  Stripe by stripe, the Blue Lias records the wobble of Earth's orbit. Alternating beds of limestone and shale were laid down from the latest Triassic into the early Sinemurian. Their rhythm records short climate swings driven by Milankovitch cycles, regular changes in Earth's orbit. The rocks are rich in fossils, and most of their Hettangian plesiosaurs are rhomaleosaurids.

  <!-- jura-030 -->

- **The Andes begin to rise** — c. 200 million years ago (200 Ma)

  The mountain building that raised the Andes has been going on for about 200 million years, and it has not stopped. The Andean orogeny began in the Early Jurassic. Subduction-related volcanism has continued along western South America ever since. The first phases actually stretched the crust, bringing rifting, back-arc basins and the emplacement of large batholiths, huge bodies of cooled magma. Early subduction built the La Negra volcanic arc in northern Chile. The Atacama Fault is thought to have formed as the orogeny began.

  <!-- jura-031 -->

- **Conodonts vanish after more than 300 million years** — c. 200 million years ago (200 Ma)

  Few animal groups last 300 million years. Conodonts, jawless fish whose tooth-like elements are key index fossils, had survived since the Cambrian. By the end of the Triassic only a handful of species remained, their decline perhaps hastened by the mid-Norian marine crisis linked to the Manicouagan impact. They vanished first in the Tethys and eastern Panthalassa. The last survivors lasted into the earliest Hettangian of Hungary and central Panthalassa, and around 200 million years ago they were gone.

  <!-- jura-033 -->

- **The Navajo sand sea buries western North America** — c. 200–195 million years ago (200–195 Ma)

  The cliffs of Zion Canyon are fossil dunes, up to 670 m thick. In the Jurassic the Colorado Plateau grew ever drier until some 388,000 km² of western North America became a vast desert like the Sahara. The Navajo Sandstone formed in this erg, a sand sea, on western Pangaea, swept by winter monsoon winds. A 2019 radioisotopic study puts its start around 200–195 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-034 -->

- **Pangaea tears into Laurasia and Gondwana** — c. 200–160 million years ago (200–160 Ma)

  The supercontinent that held every major landmass began to come apart around 200 million years ago. By then the Central Pangean Mountains had worn down to a few uplands, and widespread magmatism, including the Karoo and Ferrar provinces, preceded the rupture. The breakup ran to about 160 million years ago. Through the Early Jurassic, Pangaea split into Laurasia, Eurasia and North America, in the north and Gondwana in the south. By the Middle Jurassic it had fully broken up. The parting opened the Tethys between the landmasses and greatly strengthened the water cycle. Another source has the Tethys Seaway splitting Pangaea in two only in the Late Jurassic, though. North and South America separated in the Late Jurassic. By about 150 million years ago, their divergence was making oceanic crust off Colombia's Pacific coast.

  <!-- jura-035 -->

  *Figure: Pangaea split into a northern and a southern landmass.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **A seaway opens between the Americas** — c. 200–154 million years ago (200–154 Ma)

  When the Jurassic began, North and South America were still joined. By the start of the Late Jurassic they had rifted apart, and a seaway ran between them. The Central American Seaway, also called the Hispanic Corridor, formed between about 200 and 154 million years ago, during the first breakup of Pangaea. It linked the North Atlantic and Tethys with eastern Panthalassa. Fossils suggest it was already open in the Early Jurassic. It closed only when the Isthmus of Panama formed.

  <!-- jura-032 -->

- **Vulcanodon and the first true sauropods** — during the Sinemurian, 200–193 million years ago (199.5–192.9 Ma)

  Ledumahadi of South Africa already weighed about 12 tonnes, far more than other early sauropodomorphs, and it walked on four legs. Soon after, the true giants' line appeared. Gravisaurian sauropods first appeared in the Early Jurassic, and the oldest definite one, Vulcanodon of Zimbabwe, is likely Sinemurian. By the end of the Early Jurassic, possibly after a global warming event, sauropods had become the dominant large plant-eaters on land.

  <!-- jura-038 -->

- **Sea level climbs, then falls back** — c. 200–184 million years ago (199.5–184.2 Ma)

  The early Jurassic sea rose and fell like a slow tide. Through the Hettangian and Sinemurian it stayed near today's level. In the late Sinemurian and Pliensbachian it rose several tens of meters. By the late Pliensbachian it had fallen back to near present levels.

  <!-- jura-039 -->

- **Saltriovenator, the oldest known ceratosaur** — c. 199–198 million years ago (199.3–197.5 Ma)

  Italy holds the oldest known ceratosaur. Saltriovenator comes from the early Sinemurian, 199.3–197.5 million years ago. It belongs to the averostrans, an advanced group of theropods whose earliest members appeared in the Early Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-040 -->

- **A long cool spell chills the Early Jurassic** — c. 199–183 million years ago (199–183 Ma)

  Dropstones, rocks carried by ice and dropped into seafloor mud, turn up in northeastern Siberia. With glendonites, crystals that form in cold water, they point to cold winters in the Early to Middle Jurassic. The first part of the Jurassic was a cool interval lasting from about 199 to 183 million years ago. Evidence suggests the late Pliensbachian was an icehouse, perhaps with Northern Hemisphere glaciation early and late in the stage. The cool interval ended with a 4–8 °C warming spike in the early Toarcian.

  <!-- jura-041 -->

- **Lyme Regis mudstones yield the armored Scelidosaurus** — c. 196–188 million years ago (196–188 Ma)

  Complete skeletons of an armored dinosaur come out of the cliffs of Lyme Regis and Charmouth, England. The Charmouth Mudstone yields Scelidosaurus along with plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs. It also holds large numbers of exceptional fish and a diverse insect fauna.

  <!-- jura-044 -->

- **The Puchezh-Katunki impact scars western Russia** — 196 million years ago (195.9 ± 1 Ma)

  Buried beneath western Russia lies one of the major impact scars of the Jurassic. Argon–argon dating places the strike, in today's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, at 195.9 ± 1.0 million years ago, in the Sinemurian. The crater is 40 km across from rim to rim. Including its ring terrace, it spans about 80 km.

  <!-- jura-046 -->

- **Eocarcinus, the first true crab** — during the Pliensbachian, 193–184 million years ago (192.9–184.2 Ma)

  The first true crab did not yet look like a crab. Eocarcinus praecursor, from the early Pliensbachian of England, is the earliest true crab, but it still lacked the body shape of modern crabs. Crabs and shrimp both appear in the Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-049 -->

- **Volcanoes erupt across southern Sweden** — c. 191–178 million years ago (191–178 Ma)

  A volcanic mudflow made a time capsule in Sweden. In central Skåne, volcanism had its first and main phase from the late Sinemurian to the Toarcian, about 191 to 178 million years ago. At Korsaröd a lahar, a flow of volcanic mud, buried Early Jurassic wood, pollen and spores and preserved them exceptionally well.

  <!-- jura-051 -->

- **The first pliosaurs enter the seas** — c. 190 million years ago (190 Ma)

  About 190 million years ago, pliosaurs, short-necked plesiosaurs, entered the fossil record. They arrived in busy seas. Many groups of primitive sea invertebrates appeared about the same time, and sponge reefs developed extensively.

  <!-- jura-053 -->

- **The Pacific plate is born as a microplate** — c. 190 million years ago (190 Ma)

  Today's largest tectonic plate began as a small one. Around 190 million years ago, the Pacific plate originated as a microplate where three plates met: the Farallon, Phoenix and Izanagi. A kink in one plate boundary turned this stable triple junction into an unstable one ringed by transform faults. The new plate formed at its center. It was born far from the margins of the Paleo-Pacific Ocean, in central Panthalassa.

  <!-- jura-054 -->

- **A small impact leaves the Viewfield crater** — c. 190 million years ago (190 ± 20 Ma)

  Not every impact is a giant. A small one made the Viewfield crater in Saskatchewan, Canada, just 2.5 km across. It struck about 190 ± 20 million years ago, in the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-055 -->

- **Dilophosaurus, the double-crested hunter of Arizona** — c. 186 million years ago (186 Ma)

  At about 7 m long and 400 kg, Dilophosaurus was the largest known land animal in North America in its day. This theropod, with a pair of thin arched crests on its skull, lived about 186 million years ago. Known from Arizona's Kayenta Formation, it was one of the earliest large predatory dinosaurs and is cast as a top predator of its time. Eubrontes footprints are widely credited to a theropod like it.

  <!-- jura-056 -->

- **Eutriconodont mammals make their debut** — during the Toarcian, 184–175 million years ago (184.2–174.7 Ma)

  When eutriconodonts first show up, in the Toarcian, they already come in several groups, such as Argentoconodon. These early mammals went on to live across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas during the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

  <!-- jura-059 -->

- **The Toarcian extinction wipes out most Tethyan corals** — c. 183 million years ago (183 Ma)

  For the corals of the Tethys, it was a catastrophe: 90.9% of species and 49% of genera were wiped out. The Toarcian extinction, about 183 million years ago, struck in two pulses, the Pliensbachian–Toarcian boundary event and the larger pulse of Oxygen drains from the Toarcian oceans. Ammonoids, already squeezed by the Gibbosus Event a million years earlier, suffered further losses. On land, seed ferns and spore plants declined, possibly from mercury poisoning. Later in the Toarcian, megalosaurid dinosaurs diversified, perhaps filling niches the die-off had emptied.

  <!-- jura-065 -->

  *Figure: Tethyan corals lost almost all their species and about half their genera.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Karoo-Ferrar lavas flood southern Gondwana** — c. 183 million years ago (183 Ma)

  About 2.5 million cubic kilometers of magma poured out across southern Africa and Antarctica. The Karoo and Ferrar provinces erupted about 183 million years ago, just before Gondwana's breakup, making one of Earth's most extensive large igneous provinces. As southern Africa passed over the Bouvet hotspot, basalt flooded the Clarens desert and covered nearly all of southern Africa. Magmatism spread to Namibia, Lesotho, Lebombo and Antarctica by 184–175 million years ago. Patagonia's Chon Aike province peaked 183–173 million years ago. The timing matters. It matches the Toarcian anoxic event and the Pliensbachian–Toarcian extinction, tying these eruptions to one of the Jurassic's great crises.

  <!-- jura-067 -->

- **Holzmaden's Posidonia Shale preserves skin and blood cells** — c. 183 million years ago (183 Ma)

  An ichthyosaur 182.7 million years old still held collagen and blood cells. It comes from the Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, Germany, laid down about 183 million years ago during the Toarcian anoxic event. The stagnant, oxygen-free basin preserved superb complete skeletons of fish and marine reptiles, and one plesiosaur kept traces of its skin. Its quality of preservation became a benchmark for other fossil sites.

  <!-- jura-069 -->

- **Oxygen drains from the Toarcian oceans** — c. 183 million years ago (183 Ma)

  About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide areas of the ocean. This Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event is the only one documented from the Jurassic. It was possibly the most extreme case of widespread ocean deoxygenation in the whole Phanerozoic. The chain began with volcanoes. Carbon dioxide from the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and sped up weathering on land. The flood of nutrients washed into the sea and eutrophied it, overfeeding plankton until the water lost its oxygen. The carbon release was large enough to disrupt the otherwise steady 9-million-year carbon cycle of the Jurassic. The stagnant seas laid down organic-rich black shales, including oil shales now mined commercially in China.

  <!-- jura-071 -->

  *Figure: How Karoo-Ferrar CO2 led to the Toarcian ocean anoxia.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Karoo-Ferrar CO2] --> B[Warming and acidification]
  A --> C[More weathering]
  C --> D[Nutrient flood]
  D --> E[Seas eutrophied]
  E --> F[Ocean anoxia]
  F --> G[Black shales]
  ```

- **A Toarcian heat spike pushes seas past 30 °C** — c. 183–174 million years ago (183–174 Ma)

  Pangaea's interior probably passed 40 °C, and sea surface temperatures likely topped 30 °C. Early in the Toarcian, global temperatures spiked by about 4–8 °C, and the warm interval lasted until about 174 million years ago. A brief cold snap interrupted the warming just before the anoxic event. The rapid heating intensified tropical storms worldwide, and a stronger water cycle made lakes expand. Sea level rose gradually through the Toarcian to a peak about 75 meters above today's.

  <!-- jura-072 -->

  *Figure: The Toarcian spike pushed both sea and land to extreme temperatures.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Central Atlantic begins to open** — c. 180 million years ago (180 Ma)

  Some of the oldest ocean floor still on Earth, about 180–200 million years old, lies in the northwest Atlantic and west Pacific. Its story starts in the Early Jurassic. Rifting between North America and Africa came first, opening rift basins such as the Newark Basin from Mexico to Nova Scotia. About 180 million years ago, the central Atlantic began opening as a narrow ocean between Pangaea's northern and southern parts. Seafloor spreading between North America and Africa–South America began the breakup of Pangaea. The North Atlantic stayed narrow through the Jurassic, and the South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.

  <!-- jura-075 -->

- **Gondwana starts to come apart** — c. 180 million years ago (180 Ma)

  The southern supercontinent began to break after a burst of lava. Gondwana started fragmenting around 180 million years ago, following the fast emplacement of the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts. Madagascar and Antarctica began rifting away from Africa, opening the western Indian Ocean. The oldest magnetic anomalies show the first break in today's southern Weddell Sea, about 180 to 160 million years ago. Farther west, rifting at Falkland latitudes began about 190 million years ago, pushing Patagonia westward. The breakup sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely complete by its end.

  <!-- jura-076 -->

##### Middle Jurassic Epoch

The Middle Jurassic opens with the Toarcian heat fading into a long cool interval, from about 174 to 164 million years ago. Sea level climbed steadily from the Aalenian, and the shallow Sundance Sea spread across northwest North America, while long-isolated terranes docked on the continent's western edge. At sea, most old ichthyosaur lines vanished and new long-necked plesiosaurs appeared. On land, tetanuran theropods reached every continent and split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs, carnosaurs and the first unequivocal stegosaurs appeared, and dinosaurs left their tracks on Skye. Even familiar living things show up: the first true Ginkgo trees and the first octopuses.

- **Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs reshuffle their ranks** — c. 175–171 million years ago (174.7–170.9 Ma)

  The sea reptiles of the Middle Jurassic were not the same cast as before. Between the end of the Toarcian and the start of the Bajocian, most ichthyosaur lineages appear to have died out. Ophthalmosaurids appeared in the early Bajocian and from then on made up almost all ichthyosaurs. Plesiosaurs changed too. Microcleidids died out and rhomaleosaurids nearly so, while cryptoclidids, the dominant group of the later Jurassic, appeared in the Bajocian.

  <!-- jura-083 -->

- **The first true Ginkgo trees appear** — during the Middle Jurassic, 175–162 million years ago (174.7–161.5 Ma)

  The ginkgo trees that line city streets today have relatives that look strikingly familiar in Middle Jurassic rocks. The earliest members of the genus Ginkgo, with ovule and pollen organs like the living species, appear then in the Northern Hemisphere. Their wider order, the Ginkgoales, was among the most important parts of Eurasian Jurassic floras.

  <!-- jura-079 -->

- **The first octopuses appear** — during the Middle Jurassic, 175–162 million years ago (174.7–161.5 Ma)

  Soft-bodied and boneless, octopuses rarely fossilize, yet their story reaches back to the Middle Jurassic. The earliest octopuses appeared then, after splitting from the vampyromorphs sometime in the Triassic to Early Jurassic. Molecular evidence suggests the squid and octopus lineage split from the belemnoids much earlier, in the Permian. One timeline even lists the oldest known octopus fossil at about 296 million years old.

  <!-- jura-081 -->

- **The Sundance Sea floods northwestern North America** — during the Middle Jurassic, 175–162 million years ago (174.7–161.5 Ma)

  Five times the sea rolled in over northwest North America. From the Middle Jurassic, the shallow Sundance Sea covered much of the region in five successive marine transgressions. Dinosaurs left tracks along its shores, as at Red Gulch in Wyoming. Late in the Jurassic it retreated for the last time, buried by the river sediments of the Morrison Formation.

  <!-- jura-085 -->

- **Long-isolated terranes dock with North America** — during the Middle Jurassic, 175–162 million years ago (174.7–161.5 Ma)

  Pieces of crust that had drifted alone in Panthalassa finally reached land. In the Middle Jurassic, the Alexander and Wrangellia terranes were accreted, or welded, onto western North America. The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-086 -->

- **Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs** — during the Middle Jurassic, 175–162 million years ago (174.7–161.5 Ma)

  The first theropods to top 2 tonnes were the allosauroids. By the Middle Jurassic, tetanuran theropods had reached every continent and split into two great branches. One was the allosauroids, the first giant theropods; Asfaltovenator of South America may be the oldest. The other was the coelurosaurs, which first appeared at the same time. Among them were early tyrannosauroids such as Proceratosaurus, from the Bathonian of Britain.

  <!-- jura-087 -->

  *Figure: By the Middle Jurassic, tetanuran theropods had split into two great branches.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Seas rise toward a Late Jurassic high** — c. 175–149 million years ago (174.7–149.2 Ma)

  By the end of the Jurassic, the sea may have stood 140 meters above today's level. Sea level had fallen sharply in the Early Jurassic and stayed low through the Middle Jurassic. Yet it rose steadily from the Aalenian, apart from dips in the Bajocian and near the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary.
