It peaked, possibly at that 140-meter mark, at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary, probably because seafloor spreading sped up. The rising water deepened the seaways between continents.

  <!-- jura-084 -->

- **Carnosaurs join the ranks of predators** — c. 174 million years ago (174 Ma)

  Some predator lines come and go quickly; the carnosaurs stayed. They first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago, and hunted on through most of the Cretaceous. Their last definite family, the carcharodontosaurids, died out only about 90 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-089 -->

- **Dinosaur tracks and bones on the Isle of Skye** — c. 174–166 million years ago (174–166 Ma)

  Scotland's Isle of Skye is one of the best places to see Middle Jurassic dinosaurs. Rocks of its Trotternish peninsula, about 174–166 million years old, preserve both footprints and bones. Bones of large theropods, sauropods and thyreophorans, the armored dinosaurs, have been found there. Footprints of all three turn up at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point.

  <!-- jura-091 -->

- **Toarcian warmth gives way to a cool spell** — c. 174–164 million years ago (174–164 Ma)

  After the Toarcian heat, the climate swung cool, perhaps cold. The Toarcian Warm Interval ended around 174 million years ago, and the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval followed, lasting until about 164 million years ago. Brief icehouse episodes may have broken it, including a possible short-lived ice age in the late Bajocian. Europe turned noticeably more humid at the Aalenian–Bajocian boundary, then drier during the middle Bajocian. The Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, as the cool interval closed, saw especially marked global cooling, possibly even an ice age.

  <!-- jura-090 -->

- **The first unmistakable stegosaurs appear** — c. 171–165 million years ago (170.9–165.3 Ma)

  Footprints came before bones. Aalenian tracks from England called Deltapodus are the oldest probable record of stegosaurs, the plated dinosaurs. The earliest unequivocal stegosaur skeletons, such as Adratiklit, Bashanosaurus and Thyreosaurus, come from the Bajocian–Bathonian.

  <!-- jura-093 -->

- **Long-necked cryptoclidids and elasmosaurids appear** — c. 170 million years ago (170 Ma)

  Some elasmosaurids had as many as 76 neck vertebrae, more than any other known vertebrate. These plesiosaurs, which grew up to 15 m long, first appeared around 170 million years ago along with the cryptoclidids. By about 160 million years ago cryptoclidids were present: fairly short plesiosaurs with long necks and small heads.

  <!-- jura-097 -->

- **Megalosaurids appear in Europe** — c. 170 million years ago (170 Ma)

  The oldest radiation of tetanuran theropods began in Europe. Megalosaurids first appeared there during the Bajocian, around 170 million years ago. By the late Middle Jurassic, megalosaurines were already among the largest land predators.

  <!-- jura-098 -->

- **Salamanders and newts emerge** — c. 170 million years ago (170 Ma)

  Around 170 million years ago, the first salamanders and newts appeared. Early crown-group salamanders, members of the living group, such as Chunerpeton and Pangerpeton are known from China's Middle–Late Jurassic Yanliao Biota. By the end of the Jurassic, salamanders had reached North America, as Iridotriton from the Morrison Formation shows.

  <!-- jura-099 -->

- **The young Atlantic becomes a seaway** — c. 170–150 million years ago (170–150 Ma)

  A narrow strip of water now separated Europe from North America. As Pangaea broke up between about 170 and 150 million years ago, the young Atlantic Ocean began to form a seaway, the 'Atlantic Gateway'. By the Late Jurassic the still-narrow Atlantic had just separated the two continents. A rift spread from the Central Atlantic along the margin of northwestern France toward Aquitaine. In the Oxfordian, deep basins formed as an extension of the Central Atlantic rift; they would later hold the Paratethys.

  <!-- jura-096 -->

- **A weak magnetic field leaves faint seafloor stripes** — c. 170–130 million years ago (170–130 Ma)

  The ocean floor records Earth's magnetic field in stripes, but Jurassic stripes are faint. From about 170 to 130 million years ago, the field was weak, so the deep seafloor of that age carries weak magnetic anomalies. Found off eastern North America, northwest Africa and in the western Pacific, they were once read as a 'Jurassic Quiet Zone' without reversals. Rocks on land, however, record reversals. The oldest seafloor surviving today dates to about 170 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-102 -->

- **Iberia slides away from Europe** — c. 170–120 million years ago (170–120 Ma)

  Spain and Portugal took a long sideways journey. From 170 to 120 million years ago, Iberia slid more than 200 km past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks. In the Late Jurassic, the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them.

  <!-- jura-100 -->

- **The Obolon' impact strikes Ukraine** — c. 169 million years ago (169 ± 7 Ma)

  Beneath Poltava Oblast in Ukraine lies a buried scar about 20 km across. The Obolon' crater is a confirmed impact structure. One estimate puts its age at 169 ± 7 million years, in the Middle Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-103 -->

- **Lizards and snakes enter the fossil record** — during the Bathonian, 168–165 million years ago (168.2–165.3 Ma)

  Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards, and their earliest fossils date to between 167 and 143 million years ago. They belong to the squamates, the lizards and snakes. The oldest unambiguous squamate fossils are Bathonian, from the Northern Hemisphere, when many modern groups first appear. A timeline dates the first lizards to about 168 million years ago. The group itself is older. Crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic. Their last common ancestor is estimated at about 190 million years ago, and one timeline puts the first squamates at about 199. A claimed Late Triassic crown squamate, Cryptovaranoides, would push the origin back, but its identity has been disputed since 2023. Squamates diversified through the Jurassic and Cretaceous. By the Late Jurassic, early gecko relatives such as Eichstaettisaurus and the oldest accepted anguimorph, Dorsetisaurus, had appeared.

  <!-- jura-106 -->

- **Choristoderes, puzzling freshwater reptiles, appear** — c. 168–166 million years ago (168–166 Ma)

  Nobody is sure where choristoderes belong on the reptile family tree. These freshwater aquatic reptiles first appear in Britain's Bathonian rocks, about 168–166 million years ago, with the small, lizard-like Cteniogenys. Coeruleodraco, from China's Late Jurassic, was more advanced but still small and lizard-like. The order lasted until the Miocene.

  <!-- jura-108 -->

- **Multituberculates begin a 100-million-year run** — c. 168–166 million years ago (168–166 Ma)

  No mammaliaform order has lasted longer. Multituberculates survived and dominated for more than 100 million years, until the Oligocene, making them one of the most successful mammal orders. The earliest known, such as Hahnotherium and Kermackodon, come from Bathonian rocks of England and Russia, about 168–166 million years old. In the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous they were abundant and widespread across Laurasia.

  <!-- jura-109 -->

- **The mammal family tree forks into modern branches** — c. 167 million years ago (167 Ma)

  Teeth from Madagascar help date the birth of modern mammals. Those fossils, with Ambondro, Amphilestes and Amphitherium, about 167 million years old, show the monotreme and therian lines had already split. That split marks the crown group, the living mammals and their common ancestor. Other sources place its origin earlier, probably late in the Early Jurassic. Mammaliaforms diversified widely in the Jurassic, and the docodont Castorocauda shows they already had fur. Most stayed under 10 kilograms but spread widely. About 150 million years ago, the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor seems to have dug into social-insect nests, probably termites'. Cladotherians appeared around 170 million years ago, and their dryolestidans became among the most diverse mammals of Late Jurassic North America and Europe.

  <!-- jura-110 -->

- **The Turgai Sea parts Europe from Asia** — during the Callovian, 165–162 million years ago (165.3–161.5 Ma)

  For land animals, Europe and Asia became separate worlds. During the Callovian, the Turgai Epicontinental Sea formed, a shallow sea spread over the continent. It stood as a marine barrier between Europe and Asia, cutting the two apart.

  <!-- jura-114 -->

- **Liopleurodon's sea: the Oxford Clay** — during the Callovian–Oxfordian, 165–155 million years ago (165.3–154.8 Ma)

  Liopleurodon hunted the sea that laid down the Oxford Clay. This marine mudstone, of Callovian–Oxfordian age, settled over much of southeast England, from Dorset to Yorkshire. Its waters also held the plesiosaur Cryptoclidus, marine crocodiles, the ichthyosaur Ophthalmosaurus, belemnites and bivalves such as Gryphaea. Its lower Peterborough Member is a fossil-rich organic mudstone. At Christian Malford, Wiltshire, it preserves exceptionally detailed coleoids, the squid-like cephalopods.

  <!-- jura-113 -->

- **The Gulf of Mexico opens** — c. 165 million years ago (165 Ma)

  The Florida Platform was once part of Africa. When the Gulf of Mexico opened, it stayed with North America and gathered carbonate, evaporite and siliciclastic sediments. The opening began in the Early Jurassic, as North America started separating from South America in a new rift beside what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Seafloor spreading in the gulf began about 165 million years ago. As the gulf widened and North America drifted northwest, away from Pangaea, the Maya Block was carried away from the Laurentian craton. How Middle America's crustal blocks moved after 170 million years ago is still not widely agreed upon.

  <!-- jura-115 -->

- **A small crater forms at Zapadnaya, Ukraine** — c. 165 million years ago (165 ± 5 Ma)

  In Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, a small impact left the Zapadnaya crater. It is about 3.2 km across, a fraction the size of the great Triassic craters. It formed about 165 ± 5 million years ago, in the Middle Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-119 -->

- **Rocky Mountain building begins in western North America** — c. 165–155 million years ago (165–155 Ma)

  The Rocky Mountains have Jurassic roots. Between 165 and 155 million years ago, an exotic terrane, the Mezcalera promontory, began to be subducted, and Rocky Mountain orogenesis began. A volcanic flare-up ran in the Sierra Nevada arc from 170 to 150 million years ago. Deformation in the southern Sevier fold-and-thrust belt began around 160 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-117 -->

- **Layers of ash save China's Yanliao Biota** — c. 165–150 million years ago (165–150 Ma)

  Volcanic ash, falling again and again, preserved some of the world's best Jurassic fossils in northeastern China. The Yanliao Biota spans about 165 to 150 million years ago and includes the Tiaojishan and Haifanggou formations. Alternating tuff, compacted ash, and sediment entombed dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects, lizards and plants. The Daohugou beds formed between 164 and 158 million years ago. The Tiaojishan Formation spans from 165 million years ago to between 156 and 153. The Haifanggou Formation adds fossil arthropods, amphibians, pterosaurs and mammaliaforms.

  <!-- jura-118 -->

  *Figure: The Yanliao Biota spans several overlapping rock units.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval brings heat and rain** — c. 164–150 million years ago (164–150 Ma)

  Fossil wood says this was one of the wettest stretches of the Jurassic. The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval followed the Middle Jurassic cool spell and lasted from about 164 to 150 million years ago. Very high carbon dioxide drove high temperatures around the globe through the greenhouse effect. A widening Central Atlantic and western Indian Ocean supplied new moisture, softening seasonal swings in the Pangaean interior. Europe, though, grew steadily more arid over the Late Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-122 -->

- **The first pterodactyloid pterosaurs appear** — c. 163 million years ago (163 Ma)

  A new kind of pterosaur took to the air around 163 million years ago: the pterodactyloids. Their arrival came as the flying reptiles headed for their high point. Pterosaur diversity peaked in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.

  <!-- jura-123 -->

- **Lhasa begins docking with Qiangtang** — c. 163–145 million years ago (163–145 Ma)

  Southern Tibet is a piece of Gondwana. The Lhasa terrane, with West Burma, rifted from northern Gondwana in the Triassic and Jurassic. About 163–145 million years ago it began colliding with the Qiangtang terrane, joining it along the Bangong suture, and the collision lasted into the early Late Cretaceous. The sutured Lhasa terrane now forms southern Tibet.

  <!-- jura-124 -->

##### Late Jurassic Epoch

By the Late Jurassic, the map and the menu had both changed. Africa separated from Antarctica around 160 million years ago, and in Asia the Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean shut in a scissor-like collision. Reefs of sponges and stony corals expanded across warm seas, teleost fishes began their great diversification, and the two living turtle lines had already parted. On land, the Morrison Formation and Tanzania's Tendaguru Beds buried some of the richest dinosaur faunas known, while the first ceratopsian, Yinlong, and the oldest known eutherian, the shrew-like Juramaia, appeared. Offshore, the Kimmeridge Clay gathered the reptiles and plankton that would one day become North Sea oil.

- **The two living turtle lineages part ways** — c. 162 million years ago (161.5 Ma)

  Every living turtle either tucks its neck sideways or pulls it straight back. Those two groups, the side-necked Pleurodira and hidden-necked Cryptodira, had diverged by the start of the Late Jurassic. The oldest pleurodires, the Platychelyidae, and the oldest unambiguous cryptodire, Sinaspideretes from China, are Late Jurassic. The Thalassochelydia, a diverse marine turtle lineage unrelated to modern sea turtles, lived in Late Jurassic Europe and South America.

  <!-- jura-135 -->

- **Kimmeridge Clay: the mud that became North Sea oil** — c. 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  North Sea oil began as algae and bacteria buried in Jurassic seafloor mud. The Kimmeridge Clay and its equivalents are the province's major source rock. They built up from the Late Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous, from Dorset to Lincolnshire and the North Sea. The fossil-rich clay also holds ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs. Elsewhere, Jurassic rocks fuel other oil fields: the Sargelu and Naokelekan formations source Iraq's oil, and the Middle–Late Jurassic Arabian Intrashelf Basin holds the world's largest oil reserves.

  <!-- jura-134 -->

- **The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean snaps shut** — during the Late Jurassic, 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  Like the blades of a pair of scissors, two landmasses swung together. The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean had been closing gradually from west to east since the Late Triassic. It finally shut in a rapid scissor-like collision of Siberia with the North China–Amuria and Erguna blocks, raising Siberia's Verkhoyansk–Kolyma mountain belt. Paleomagnetic data suggest its oceanic crust subducted beneath Mongolia's terranes in the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.

  <!-- jura-137 -->

- **Reefs return, and crabs move in** — during the Late Jurassic, 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  Crabs, rare until now, suddenly became abundant, and reefs explain why. Reefs had declined at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, but in the Late Jurassic they expanded greatly, both sponge reefs and reefs of scleractinian, stony, corals. They resembled modern reefs but had more microbial carbonate and hypercalcified sponges, and weaker biological binding. Their crevices sheltered crabs from predators, and the crabs moved in.

  <!-- jura-138 -->

- **Teleost fishes begin their great radiation** — during the Late Jurassic, 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  Today, teleosts make up over 99% of living ray-finned fish. Their major diversification began in the Late Jurassic. Early members of modern groups such as Elopomorpha, the eel line, and Osteoglossoidei appeared then. The earliest known ellimmichthyiforms, and clupeomorphs, the herring group, as a whole, come from the Late Jurassic of Peru. The oldest anatomically modern gars also appeared in the Late Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-139 -->

- **Tanzania's Tendaguru beds and the towering Giraffatitan** — during the Late Jurassic, 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  More than a thousand bones of one stegosaur, Kentrosaurus, have come out of Tanzania's Tendaguru Beds. This Lagerstätte, known for large dinosaur bonebeds, is the richest Late Jurassic rock in Africa. It also yielded Giraffatitan, the tallest and heaviest dinosaur known from good skeletons. Its animals lived on semi-arid subtropical coastal plains that alternated with shallow seas. The fauna resembles the Morrison Formation's and stayed stable through the Late Jurassic.

  <!-- jura-140 -->

- **The Zuñi transgression begins** — during the Late Jurassic, 162–143 million years ago (161.5–143.1 Ma)

  North America's interior began to flood again, in a cycle that would outlast the dinosaurs. The Zuñi sequence, the continent's major cratonic sequence after the Absaroka, is a great package of rock laid down as seas spread over the stable core. It began in the latest Jurassic, peaked in the Late Cretaceous and ended by the Paleocene.

  <!-- jura-141 -->

- **Yinlong, the earliest ceratopsian** — c. 161 million years ago (161 Ma)

  Long before Triceratops, its family began with a small Chinese dinosaur. Ceratopsians, the horned-dinosaur line, appear in the fossil record around 161 million years ago, represented by Yinlong. These first ceratopsians belonged to the Chaoyangsauridae and lived in Late Jurassic China.

  <!-- jura-142 -->

- **Juramaia, a shrew-like start to the placental line** — c. 160 million years ago (160 Ma)

  The ancestors of whales, bats and people may have looked like a shrew. Juramaia sinensis, a small, shrew-like mammal from China dated to about 160 million years ago, is the oldest known eutherian. Eutherians are the branch of mammals that includes the placentals. Juramaia sits closer to the ancestry of placental mammals than to marsupials, so the split between the two lines had already happened by its time.

  <!-- jura-144 -->

- **New ocean floor splits East and West Gondwana** — c. 160 million years ago (160 Ma)

  Around 160 million years ago, Africa separated from Antarctica, and India would follow in the Early Cretaceous. Gondwana was splitting into two halves. East Gondwana held Antarctica, Australia, India and Madagascar; West Gondwana held Africa, Arabia and South America. New oceanic crust formed between them about 160–155 million years ago, and narrow ocean basins opened between both halves and Laurasia. East Antarctica moved south faster than Africa and South America, opening the Weddell, Riiser-Larsen, Mozambique and Somali basins. Spreading in the Weddell Sea began about 147 million years ago. Australia and Antarctica began pulling apart in the Late Jurassic. Magmatism of the Australia–India breakup, 158–136 million years ago, built the Wallaby Plateau.

  <!-- jura-145 -->

  *Figure: Gondwana split into an eastern and a western half.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Vepriai, Lithuania's largest impact crater** — c. 160 million years ago (160 ± 10 Ma)

  Lithuania's largest crater is 8 km across. An impact made the Vepriai crater sometime in the Middle or Late Jurassic. Its age is estimated at more than 160 ± 10 million years.

  <!-- jura-147 -->

- **The Morrison floodplains teem with giant sauropods** — 156–147 million years ago (156.3–146.8 Ma)

  At the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry, dinosaurs died around a pond as a drought tightened its grip, leaving the densest known concentration of Jurassic dinosaurs. It is one window into the Morrison Formation of western North America, mostly river and floodplain deposits laid down between about 156.3 and 146.8 million years ago. The formation built up as the Sundance Sea retreated before highlands rising to the west. The Morrison holds one of the best-known sauropod faunas anywhere, with 24 recognized species. Among them are Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Barosaurus, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus. Predators hunted them. Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus and Torvosaurus left bite marks on bones at the Mygatt-Moore Quarry. Morrison quarries about 150 million years old are dense with dinosaurs, making this one of the richest records of Jurassic life on land.

  <!-- jura-148 -->

  *Figure: Sauropods and predators of the Morrison Formation.*

  | Role | Examples |
  |---|---|
  | Sauropods | Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus |
  | Predators | Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus, Torvosaurus |

- **Argoland: a disputed landmass off Australia** — c. 155 million years ago (155 Ma)

  Argoland may not have been a continent at all. This hypothetical landmass has been suggested to have rifted off northwestern Australia about 155 million years ago. A 2023 reconstruction treats it instead as an archipelago of microcontinental fragments, now in southwest Borneo and nearby. Its form, and where its remains lie, are still debated.

  <!-- jura-150 -->

- **Stegosaurs reach their peak** — c. 155 million years ago (155 Ma)

  Stegosaurus itself walked the Kimmeridgian floodplains of Wyoming, in the upper Morrison Formation. Its group had come a long way. Huayangosaurus, an early stegosaur, lived in China in the Bathonian, about 166 million years ago. By the Callovian–Oxfordian, much larger stegosaurs such as Tuojiangosaurus followed. Stegosaurids had their greatest radiation in the Late Jurassic, and stegosaurs and theropods diversified around 155 million years ago.

  <!-- jura-152 -->

- **The Nevadan orogeny raises the ancestral Sierra Nevada** — c. 155–145 million years ago (155–145 Ma)

  The Sierra Nevada has ancestors. From about 155 to 145 million years ago, the Nevadan orogeny built mountains along western North America's margin. It began as an Andean-type magmatic arc, a chain of volcanoes over the subducting Farallon plate. From the mid-Jurassic, the first of several massive batholiths, huge bodies of cooled magma, were emplaced in the northern Cordillera. Arc magmatism and the accretion of oceanic arcs built the ancestral Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains. Terranes such as the Tuolumne River and Slate Creek were added, and the Josephine Ophiolite, a slice of ocean crust, formed about 155–150 million years ago. Mountain building continued in the Cretaceous Sevier and Laramide orogenies.

  <!-- jura-151 -->

- **Eathiestrobus and the first pines** — c. 153 million years ago (153 Ma)

  A single cone from Scotland is the pine family's only certain fossil from before the Cretaceous. Eathiestrobus, from the Kimmeridgian, is the oldest unambiguous member of the family. The earliest pine trees are dated to about 153 million years ago. By the end of the Jurassic, most modern conifer groups had appeared, descended from voltzialean ancestors.

  <!-- jura-156 -->

- **Archaeopteryx and the first birds** — c. 150 million years ago (150 Ma)

  Its feathers were already built for flight. Archaeopteryx lived around 150 million years ago in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago, and has long been considered the earliest bird. The line between birds and other dinosaurs is blurry, though, and drawing it is not simple. Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves. The first stem-group birds appeared in the Jurassic, several sources say the Late Jurassic. The earliest avialans, the bird branch, appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic, and Archaeopteryx represents them definitively. Its fossils carry advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic. Birds share a Jurassic debut with lizards, both among the living reptile groups that first appeared then.

  <!-- jura-158 -->

  *Figure: Birds descend from small predatory theropods.*

- **Cimmeria finally docks against Laurasia** — c. 150 million years ago (150 Ma)

  After crossing an ocean, Cimmeria finally ran aground. About 150 million years ago, it collided with Laurasia and stalled. The ocean floor behind it buckled under, forming the Tethys Trench. In Greece, the Hellenic orogeny records Late Jurassic collisions of Cimmerian crustal fragments with Eurasia.

  <!-- jura-160 -->

- **A cool interval closes the Jurassic** — c. 150 million years ago (150 Ma)

  The Jurassic ended in a chill rather than a heat wave. About 150 million years ago, the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval began, and it lasted well into the Early Cretaceous. Within it came a marked temperature drop during the Tithonian, known as the Early Tithonian Cooling Event. The warmth of the Kimmeridgian was over.

  <!-- jura-163 -->

- **Solnhofen's lagoons preserve feathers and jellyfish** — c. 149–148 million years ago (149–148 Ma)

  A jellyfish has almost nothing to fossilize, yet Bavaria's Solnhofen limestones hold their imprints. These Tithonian rocks, about 149–148 million years old, form a Konservat-Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional soft-tissue preservation. The area was an archipelago at the edge of the Tethys, with salty lagoons whose oxygen-free bottom waters kept scavengers away. Animals and plants washed in were buried in soft carbonate mud, preserving dragonfly wings and stray feathers. Over 600 species are known, including 29 kinds of pterosaur and the famous early bird Archaeopteryx. Nearby sites of the same archipelago, such as Ettling, add fish, horseshoe crabs, beetles, crustaceans and turtles.

  <!-- jura-167 -->

- **The Arctic Ocean begins to open** — c. 148–70 million years ago (148–70 Ma)

  The Arctic Ocean is younger than the dinosaurs. As Pangaea's breakup continued across the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, it opened the Amerasian Basin and the Arctic Ocean. The opening ran from around 148 to 70 million years ago. Volcanism of the High Arctic Large Igneous Province accompanied it.

  <!-- jura-168 -->

- **The Morokweng asteroid strikes South Africa** — 146 million years ago (146.1 ± 0.16 Ma)

  An asteroid 5–10 km wide hit what is now South Africa's North West province about 146 million years ago, in the Tithonian. It was an L-chondrite, a common type of stony meteorite. The size of the buried crater is debated, with estimates from 75–80 km to 240 km; the latest is about 190 km. It struck several million years before the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary. An iridium layer in Tithonian rocks of Brazil's Araripe basin may be linked to it.

  <!-- jura-170 -->

  *Figure: Estimates of the Morokweng structure's size vary more than threefold.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The last Karoo eruptions flicker out** — c. 145 million years ago (145 Ma)

  The Karoo large igneous province did not end with one great blast. It faded with scattered eruptions around its edges, about 145 million years ago. They broke out in Patagonia, the Antarctic Peninsula, northern South Africa, Kerala and southeast Australia, places now spread across several continents.

  <!-- jura-172 -->

- **Tamu Massif, perhaps Earth's largest volcano, erupts** — 145 million years ago (144.6 ± 0.8 Ma)

  A single volcano about as big as New Mexico lies on the floor of the northwest Pacific. Tamu Massif's basalt dome spans about 450 by 650 km, with slopes of at most one degree. It is the oldest and largest part of the Shatsky Rise, Earth's third-largest oceanic plateau, built by lava at the Pacific–Farallon–Izanagi triple junction. Tamu formed in one brief eruptive period of a few million years and then went extinct. It is likely the largest volcano yet found on Earth, though gaps in seismic profiles leave open whether it is one volcano or several. Its origin is debated: a mantle plume, melting at a mid-ocean ridge, or a recycled mantle slab.

  <!-- jura-173 -->

- **Extinction or turnover? The Jurassic draws to a close** — 143 million years ago (143.1 ± 0.6 Ma)

  The end of the Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions. Now it looks more like a complex turnover, with some groups rising and others declining, and sources disagree on whether it was a minor mass extinction at all. The evidence is mainly European. Sea level probably drove it, falling in the late Tithonian and rising again at the boundary. Reefs declined sharply at the close of the Jurassic, cutting the diversity of decapod crustaceans. Most life was not strongly affected, and several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed the boundary. The boundary itself, 143.1 ± 0.6 million years ago, is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP, an agreed reference point in the rocks.

  <!-- jura-174 -->

#### Cretaceous Period

The Cretaceous is named for chalk, and more of it formed now than in any other Phanerozoic period. The seas rose in earnest, standing roughly 250 meters above today's by the Cenomanian, and an inland sea, the Eromanga, covered much of Australia. Gondwana's breakup, begun in the Jurassic, sped up and was largely finished by the period's end. Strange box-shaped bivalves called rudists built the reefs of the Tethys, while new life appeared on every front: the first raptors, sea turtles, social ants and termites, and birds with short, fused tails. The period began 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years.

- **Tiny algae build the chalk of Dover's cliffs** — during the Cretaceous, 143–66 million years ago (143.1–66 Ma)

  The white cliffs of Dover are made of algae. Chalk is built of coccoliths, the tiny calcite plates of coccolithophores, which thrived in Cretaceous seas. More chalk formed in the Cretaceous than in any other Phanerozoic period, and the period is named for it. Upper Cretaceous chalk forms the cliffs of Dover and similar cliffs on the Normandy coast of France. Coccolithophores and other calcareous nannoplankton kept diversifying through the Mesozoic, peaking at about 150 species in the Late Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-003 -->

- **Rising seas drown a third of the land** — during the Cretaceous, 143–66 million years ago (143.1–66 Ma)

  At its peak, the Cretaceous sea covered one-third of today's land area. Sea level rose in earnest from the early Cretaceous, and by the Cenomanian it stood roughly 250 meters above today's. Other estimates put it about 300 meters higher, in a hot, humid world without permanent ice. Part of the cause lay on the ocean floor. Many small, fast-recycled ocean plates made ocean basins shallower, pushing the water up. In North America this flooding, the Zuñi sequence, may have been driven by the Mid-Cretaceous Superplume, and it receded late in the period.

  <!-- cret-006 -->

  *Figure: Different estimates put Cretaceous sea level far above today's.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Gondwana shatters into the southern continents** — during the Cretaceous, 143–66 million years ago (143.1–66 Ma)

  The breakup began near Tasmania. Gondwana had started to fragment in the Jurassic, but in the Cretaceous the pace quickened, and by the period's end the job was largely done. Pangaea completed its breakup into the present continents, though they sat in quite different positions. South America, Antarctica and Australia rifted away from Africa, while India and Madagascar stayed joined. In the gaps, two oceans were born, the South Atlantic and the Indian. The breakup had consequences for life. As the landmasses parted, dinosaurs became strongly differentiated by landmass by the Early Cretaceous, each continent developing its own fauna.

  <!-- cret-013 -->

- **Strange bivalves called rudists build the Tethys reefs** — during the Cretaceous, 143–66 million years ago (143.1–66 Ma)

  The main reef builders of the Cretaceous were not corals but clams. Rudists, box-, tube- or ring-shaped bivalves that arose in the Late Jurassic, became major reef builders of the Tethys. Their reefs may have driven scleractinian corals off many tropical shelves, including today's Caribbean and Mediterranean. Rudists had collapsed by the K–Pg extinction and vanished completely at the close of the Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-016 -->

##### Early Cretaceous Epoch

The Early Cretaceous begins 143.1 million years ago, with impacts on either side of the boundary: one in central Australia, another on the floor of the Barents Sea. Europe began rifting away from North America, and Australia filled with the inland Eromanga Sea. In the lagoons of southern England's Purbeck Group, insects, early mammals and dinosaur footprints were buried in great variety. Large carcharodontosaurid predators spread across the world, the first raptors appeared, and birds diversified into many forms. Smaller newcomers mattered too: orb-weaver spiders, social ants and termites, and the oldest known sea turtles.

- **The Cretaceous begins without an agreed starting line** — 143 million years ago (143.1 ± 0.6 Ma)

  Every other period boundary has an agreed reference point in the rocks. The base of the Cretaceous does not. The period and its first stage, the Berriasian, begin 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years. With no agreed reference section, or GSSP, the base is formally undefined. One proposed marker is the first appearance of Calpionella alpina. It was a calpionellid, one of the enigmatic planktonic protists with urn-shaped calcite shells that were briefly abundant from the latest Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-001 -->

- **Raptors appear: the first dromaeosaurs** — c. 143 million years ago (143.1 ± 0.6 Ma)

  Teeth that may belong to dromaeosaurs, the 'raptors', turn up in Jurassic rocks. Their bodies do not. No dromaeosaur body fossils are known until the Cretaceous, and the first dromaeosaurs are placed at the start of that period.

  <!-- cret-011 -->

- **Purbeck's lagoons hold insects, mammals and footprints** — during the Berriasian, 143–137 million years ago (143.1–137.1 Ma)

  Hundreds of fossil insect species come from the Purbeck Group of southern England. These beds span the latest Jurassic and earliest Cretaceous, and they hold one of the world's most diverse earliest Cretaceous faunas. They formed in a semi-arid setting of freshwater lakes, brackish water, tidal flats and lagoons. Besides insects, they preserve reptiles, early mammals from the famous 'Mammal Bed', and dinosaur footprints.

  <!-- cret-015 -->

- **Shark-toothed giants spread across the globe** — during the Early Cretaceous, 143–100 million years ago (143.1–100.5 Ma)

  Big predators can cross continents when land bridges allow. In the Early Cretaceous, large carcharodontosaurids spread worldwide, reaching Africa, North America and South America. Dinosaur footprints suggest part of the route passed through Apulia in Italy, then joined to Africa by a land bridge.

  <!-- cret-002 -->

- **Early birds branch out, and enantiornithines take over** — during the Early Cretaceous, 143–100 million years ago (143.1–100.5 Ma)

  Most Cretaceous birds belonged to a group with no living members: the enantiornithines. They dominated birdlife until they died out with other dinosaur groups at the end of the Mesozoic. Archaic birds had appeared in the Jurassic, and now avialans diversified into a wide variety of forms; some had short, fused pygostyle tails by the Early Cretaceous. True toothless birds arose from toothed ancestors in the Cretaceous. China's Jehol Biota holds a great diversity of birds, including the earliest advanced ones, and Las Hoyas in Spain preserves many enantiornithines.

  <!-- cret-007 -->

- **The Eromanga Sea floods inland Australia** — during the Early Cretaceous, 143–100 million years ago (143.1–100.5 Ma)

  In the Early Cretaceous, Australia's dry heart lay under water. An inland sea, the Eromanga Sea, covered a large part of the continent. It was home to the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus, a short-necked marine reptile.

  <!-- cret-008 -->

- **Social ants and termites make their debut** — during the Early Cretaceous, 143–100 million years ago (143.1–100.5 Ma)

  Ants and termites, the great social insects, first appeared in the Early Cretaceous. They arrived as insects diversified through the period. Stem-group ants such as Gerontoformica are preserved in Albian–Cenomanian amber from France. Many ant groups were present in the Cretaceous, but ants became dominant, with larger colonies, only much later, in the Eocene.

  <!-- cret-010 -->

- **The first sea turtles take to the oceans** — during the Early Cretaceous, 143–100 million years ago (143.1–100.5 Ma)

  Sea turtles and soft-shelled turtles both make their first appearance in the Early Cretaceous. The first freshwater pelomedusid turtles followed around 135 million years ago. Turtles became highly diverse in the Cretaceous, as the warm climate favored their spread around the globe.

  <!-- cret-012 -->

- **A comet or asteroid strikes central Australia** — c. 142 million years ago (142.5 ± 0.8 Ma)

  The ring of hills at Gosses Bluff, 5 km across, is only the eroded core of a much larger crater. An asteroid or comet struck central Australia about 142.5 million years ago, very close to the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary. The original rim, now worn away, was about 22 km across. Abundant shatter cones, cone-shaped fractures formed by shock, are the strongest evidence of an impact.

  <!-- cret-019 -->

- **Mjølnir: a bolide hammers the Barents Sea floor** — c. 142 million years ago (142 ± 2.6 Ma)

  A bolide about 2 km wide hit the seafloor of what is now the Barents Sea, off Norway. It left a crater 40 km across, named Mjølnir, dated to 142.0 ± 2.6 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-020 -->

- **Orb-weaver spiders appear, spinning wheel-shaped webs** — c. 140 million years ago (140 Ma)

  The classic spider web, a wheel of spokes and spirals, goes back to the Early Cretaceous. Orb-weaver spiders, the builders of these wheel-shaped webs, appeared around 140 million years ago, as insects, their prey, were diversifying.

  <!-- cret-022 -->

- **Europe pulls away from North America** — c. 140–120 million years ago (140–120 Ma)

  Laurentian rocks ended up in north-west Europe, and Avalonian rocks were stranded in Newfoundland, because the new Atlantic did not follow the old Iapetus suture. Between 140 and 120 million years ago, Europe rifted away from North America in a second major phase of North Atlantic breakup. The opening seaway let cool water flow from the Boreal Ocean into the Tethys. About 140 million years ago, the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift began forming, a first stage of Greenland's separation. The Bay of Biscay began opening around 126 million years ago and was complete by 85, uplifting the Armorican Massif.

  <!-- cret-024 -->

- **Volcanic plateaus rise where Gondwana split three ways** — c. 140–95 million years ago (140–95 Ma)

  Where Gondwana split into Antarctica, South America and Africa, the seafloor swelled with lava. The Southeast African large igneous province formed there from 140 to 95 million years ago. The Mozambique Ridge grew first, 140–122 million years ago, peaking about 120 million years ago above the Africa–Antarctica spreading zone. In a later pulse, 100–94 million years ago, the Agulhas Plateau formed over the Bouvet hotspot, along with the Northeast Georgia Rise and Maud Rise.

  <!-- cret-023 -->

- **The Eastern Alps begin to stack up** — c. 140–84 million years ago (140–84 Ma)

  The Alps began to rise long before Africa and Europe actually collided. In the first, Eo-Alpine, mountain-building phase, from 140 to 84 million years ago, the Austroalpine nappes of the Eastern Alps were stacked like folded sheets of rock. Africa was moving toward Europe again, and ocean crust of the Piemont-Liguria Ocean was subducted beneath the Apulian plate. The first continental collision, of the Adriatic subplate with Europe, came in the Late Cretaceous. The main Alpine mountain building followed in the Paleocene–Eocene.

  <!-- cret-021 -->

- **The Sevier orogeny raises the western mountains** — c. 140–50 million years ago (140–50 Ma)

  Western North America's mountains rose over an extraordinarily long stretch. The Sevier orogeny ran from 140 to 50 million years ago. It has been tied to the continent's collision with a chain of island arcs about 125 million years ago. In Utah, the Willard thrust sheet moved around 120 million years ago. As the mountains rose in the west, the Western Interior Basin to the east widened.

  <!-- cret-025 -->

- **Cold spells bring ice to the Early Cretaceous** — during the Valanginian–Aptian, 137–113 million years ago (137.1–113.2 Ma)

  The Mesozoic was long thought to be free of ice. The rocks disagree. As the cooling of the latest Jurassic continued into the Berriasian, snow fell often at high latitudes. Records suggest glacial periods in the Valanginian, Hauterivian and Aptian. Ice-rafted dropstones hint that Northern Hemisphere ice sheets may have reached as far south as Iberia in the Hauterivian and Aptian. Deposits laid down directly by glaciers, though, are known only from the Early Cretaceous of the Eromanga Basin in southern Australia. The early Barremian Hauptblatterton Thermal Event finally ended the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.

  <!-- cret-026 -->

- **Titanosaurs, the last great sauropods, appear** — c. 136 million years ago (136 Ma)

  Titanosaur bones have been found on every continent, Antarctica included. This last great sauropod group lived from about 136 to 66 million years ago and was the dominant plant-eating group of its time. An early subadult from Paraíba, Brazil, is about 136 million years old. The group spread almost worldwide. Not all were giants: on the islands of Cretaceous Europe, some, such as Magyarosaurus, were likely island dwarfs.

  <!-- cret-027 -->

- **Paraná–Etendeka flood basalts pour out as Gondwana splits** — c. 136–132 million years ago (136–132 Ma)

  Its lavas covered about 1,000,000 km², from South America to Namibia and Angola. The Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province spans the Paraná Basin of South America and the split-off Etendeka traps of Africa. Its original volume is projected at over 2.3 million km³. These flood basalts erupted over the Tristan hotspot and were tied to Gondwana's rifting and the opening of the South Atlantic. Their activity caused a warming event, the middle Valanginian Weissert Thermal Excursion.

  <!-- cret-028 -->

- **Jehol: volcanic ash buries feathered dinosaurs** — c. 135–121 million years ago (135–121 Ma)

  The first known feathered dinosaurs that were not birds came out of lake beds in north-eastern China. The Jehol Biota is the ecosystem preserved there between 135 and 121 million years ago, in lake sediments and volcanic ash of the Yixian and Jiufotang formations. It holds many birds, the largest known Mesozoic mammals, the earliest known flowering plants, and insects, fish, pterosaurs and amphibians in huge numbers. It also has the earliest members of groups that later spread worldwide: neoceratopsians, therizinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and oviraptorids. Radiometric dating in 2021 placed the Yixian between 125.755 and 124.122 million years ago, a span of about 1.6 million years.

  <!-- cret-030 -->

- **The Weissert Event: a sudden heat spike** — c. 134–132 million years ago (134.5–132.4 Ma)

  In the middle of a mild, cool interval, the planet suddenly overheated. The Weissert Event was a hyperthermal, a rapid global warming. Carbon dioxide from the Paraná–Etendeka province is the leading suspected trigger, though its drawn-out eruption leads some to doubt it. Its carbon-isotope excursion began about 134.5 million years ago and its plateau lasted to about 132.4; estimates of its length run from 1.4 to 2.08 million years. The warming brought oceanic anoxia but, unusually, no widespread black shales, while nannoconid plankton bloomed as productivity soared. Its end brought sharp cooling, about 1–2 °C in southern France and up to 4 °C around the Boreal Ocean, perhaps even a brief ice age.

  <!-- cret-031 -->

  *Figure: The Weissert Event ran from a volcanic trigger to warming and then a sharp cooling.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Paraná–Etendeka CO2] -.->|suspected trigger| B[Rapid global warming]
  B --> C[Oceanic anoxia]
  B --> D[Nannoconid plankton bloom]
  B --> E[Sharp cooling at the end]
  ```

- **The first flowering plants leave their pollen** — c. 134 million years ago (134 Ma)

  The first flowers announced themselves with dust. The earliest widely accepted evidence of flowering plants is single-grooved pollen from the late Valanginian, about 134 million years ago, found in Israel and Italy. Flowering plants appeared in the Early Cretaceous and began to diversify rapidly, one of the major changes of the epoch. Their oldest larger fossils come soon after. Montsechia grew in Barremian Spain, and Archaefructus, 124.6 million years old, comes from China's Yixian Formation. Pollen typical of eudicots, the largest modern branch, first appears in the late Barremian, and the earliest monocots, the grass and lily branch, are known from the Aptian. Flowering plants radiated first in the tropics. Then, helped by the gentle difference in temperature between equator and poles, they spread toward the poles.

  <!-- cret-032 -->

- **The Faraoni Event brings another warm pulse** — during the Hauterivian, 133–126 million years ago (132.6–125.8 Ma)

  The Weissert Event was not the last of the Early Cretaceous warmings. In the middle Hauterivian came the next in the series, the Faraoni Thermal Excursion. A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded mostly around the Atlantic, has also been proposed for the Hauterivian.

  <!-- cret-033 -->

- **Australia begins its slow parting from Antarctica** — c. 132–96 million years ago (132–96 Ma)

  Australia took tens of millions of years to leave Antarctica. Separation began about 132 million years ago, and by 96 million years ago the two had begun rifting, with seafloor spreading following. The Australian plate was born as it parted from Antarctica and Zealandia, a split finished in the Cenomanian. By 96 million years ago a shallow seaway had begun forming, leaving only a narrow link along the South Tasman Rise and Wilkes Land. A narrow land connection between South America, Antarctica and Australia lasted until about 50 million years ago. The general consensus places full separation by 60 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-034 -->

  *Figure: Australia's parting from Antarctica stretched over tens of millions of years.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The first anglerfish appear** — c. 130 million years ago (130 Ma)

  Today's anglerfish dangle a lure in front of their mouths to catch prey. Their line is ancient. The earliest anglerfish appeared about 130 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous, while dinosaurs still walked the land.

  <!-- cret-035 -->

- **The South Atlantic begins to open** — c. 130 million years ago (130 Ma)

  Africa became an island continent, and stayed one through most of the Cenozoic. The South Atlantic started to open about 130 million years ago. The Falkland Plateau, broken from southern Africa at 132 million years ago, moved west. South America drifted west away from Africa, while Laurasia rotated clockwise and moved north. Paraná–Etendeka magmatism drove further seafloor spreading about 135–130 million years ago, south of the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise. The split also opened the West and Central African Rift System, including the Benue Trough. By the Aptian–Albian, Africa was cut off from the rest of Gondwana and Laurasia.

  <!-- cret-041 -->

- **India breaks loose from Australia and Antarctica** — c. 130–125 million years ago (130–125 Ma)

  India's long voyage north began with a break from its southern neighbors. Between 130 and 125 million years ago, the Indian plate broke off from Australia and Antarctica, opening the 'South Indian Ocean'. The Indian Ocean began opening about 130 million years ago, its spreading ridge near the Kerguelen hotspot. Rifts along East Africa, Antarctica and Madagascar formed the southwestern Indian Ocean, and later India and Madagascar began to part. Madagascar stopped moving independently around 120 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-038 -->

- **North China's craton loses its deep root** — c. 130–120 million years ago (130–120 Ma)

  Cratons are usually the most stable parts of a continent, but North China's lost its foundation. Around 130–120 million years ago, tectonics there switched to extension, its mountain belts and plateau collapsed, and the deep mantle root was replaced. Retreating Paleo-Pacific subduction may have thinned the craton's lithosphere. A large igneous province on the Liaodong Peninsula was active about 131–117 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-039 -->

- **Colombia's Paja shales preserve sea reptiles** — c. 130–113 million years ago (130–113 Ma)

  The world's most complete record of Early Cretaceous marine reptiles lies in Colombia. Its shales and mudstones settled in a warm, shallow, anoxic sea that covered much of the present-day country. The IUGS, the international geology body, lists the Paja Formation as a geological heritage site for that record.

  <!-- cret-040 -->

- **High Arctic magma helps open the Arctic Ocean** — c. 130–80 million years ago (130–80 Ma)

  Even after much has eroded, its lavas still cover more than 1,000,000 km². The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, or HALIP, is one of Earth's largest magmatic complexes, active from 130 million years ago to about 60 million. Its first phase ran to 80 million years ago with dikes, sills and basalt flows. It broke up part of the Arctica continent, opened the Arctic Ocean and left radiating dike swarms. Crustal stretching began in the Canadian Arctic Rift System 130 million years ago, with widespread sills and dikes intruded 129–127 million years ago. The Iceland hotspot may have started as a plume under the Alpha Ridge about 130–120 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-037 -->

- **Tookoonooka: a crater buried deep in Australia** — c. 128 million years ago (128 ± 5 Ma)

  Deep beneath Australia's Eromanga Basin lies a crater 55–66 km across. Shocked quartz in drill core proved that an impact made it, about 128 ± 5 million years ago. The nearby Talundilly structure may be its twin.

  <!-- cret-042 -->

- **A Belgian coal mine full of Iguanodon** — c. 126–122 million years ago (126–122 Ma)

  At least 38 Iguanodon skeletons turned up deep in a coal mine at Bernissart, Belgium, in the Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation. Iguanodon bernissartensis, the one well-supported species, lived in Europe about 126–122 million years ago and grew to about 9 m long. The bones were once read as a herd that died together. They now seem to record at least three separate die-offs, probably from flash floods.

  <!-- cret-043 -->

- **Earliest marsupial and placental relatives appear in China** — c. 125 million years ago (125 Ma)

  Two small mammals from the same Chinese shale stand at the base of two great branches. Sinodelphys, from 125-million-year-old rocks in Liaoning, is the earliest known metatherian, the marsupial line, and it had climbing feet. Eomaia, a eutherian of the same age, shared features with marsupials that the placental line later lost. Both already stood with upright, non-sprawling limbs. Other therian mammals are unknown before the Early Cretaceous, and even the Jurassic Juramaia may itself be Early Cretaceous. The finds suggest early mammals began to diversify from Asia.

  <!-- cret-045 -->

- **Las Hoyas preserves a Spanish wetland in stone** — c. 125 million years ago (125 Ma)

  About 125 million years ago, a freshwater wetland in Spain turned into fine limestone. At Las Hoyas, it preserves dinosaurs and many enantiornithine birds in exquisite detail. It also yields Montsechia, one of the oldest flowering-plant fossils larger than pollen.

  <!-- cret-047 -->

- **Flowers and pollinators remake life on land** — c. 125–80 million years ago (125–80 Ma)

  For nearly all of Earth's history, the sea held more species than the land. In the mid-Cretaceous, that reversed. The change came with the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, from around 125 to 80 million years ago. In it, flowering plants diversified intensely alongside the pollinating insects that coevolved with them. Animal-pollinated flowers set off a burst of coevolution. Beetles were pollinating by the earliest Late Cretaceous, and moths and butterflies have coevolved with flowers ever since. By 110–90 million years ago, flowering plants dominated forest trees. By the period's end they had displaced conifers, cycads and bennettitaleans, though full ecological dominance came only in the early Cenozoic. Their spread may have sped up weathering and nutrient flow into the oceans, a possible driver of the Shell-crushers launch the Mesozoic marine revolution.

  <!-- cret-046 -->

  *Figure: Flowering plants, their pollinators and a possible link to the sea.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Flowering plants diversify] --- B[Pollinating insects coevolve]
  A -.-> C[Faster weathering]
  C -.-> D[Nutrients to oceans]
  D -.-> E[Mesozoic marine revolution]
  ```

- **Stressed forests pour out resin, and amber piles up** — c. 125–75 million years ago (125–75 Ma)

  Trees bleed resin when they are hurt, and Cretaceous trees were hurt often. From 125 to 75 million years ago, heat-driven storms, hurricanes, wildfires and insect damage made them produce huge amounts of it. By the Early Cretaceous, amber, fossilized resin, formed in concentrations matching or exceeding those of the Carnian.

  <!-- cret-044 -->

- **Koolasuchus, the last temnospondyl amphibian** — during the Aptian, 121–113 million years ago (121.4–113.2 Ma)

  The temnospondyls had outlived the end-Permian and end-Triassic crises, and their last stand came in Australia. Koolasuchus, a chigutisaurid from the Aptian, is the latest known temnospondyl. Stereospondyls, including brachyopoids, had survived from the Triassic into the Cretaceous. All were gone by the Late Cretaceous, leaving lissamphibians, the frogs, salamanders and their kin, as the only amphibians.

  <!-- cret-049 -->

- **Thalattosuchian sea crocodiles fade away** — during the Aptian, 121–113 million years ago (121.4–113.2 Ma)

  In the Jurassic, sea-going crocodile relatives called thalattosuchians were abundant. By the Early Cretaceous they had become scarce and mostly tropical. Their last records come from the Aptian, and after that this long marine experiment of the crocodile line was over.

  <!-- cret-050 -->

- **The plated stegosaurs make their last stand** — during the Aptian–Albian, 121–100 million years ago (121.4–100.5 Ma)

  As seaways spread in the Early Cretaceous, the high-browsers lost ground. Sauropods, stegosaurs and other groups that fed high above the ground declined. The youngest definitive stegosaurs, including Mongolostegus from Mongolia and Yanbeilong from China, date to the Aptian–Albian. Stegosaurs appear to have died out in the late Early or early Late Cretaceous. Reported later finds have mostly proved misidentified.

  <!-- cret-051 -->

- **Earth's magnetic field stops flipping for 37 million years** — 121 million years ago (121 Ma)

  For about 37 million years, compasses would have pointed the same way. From the Aptian through the Santonian, Earth's magnetic field kept normal polarity with no reversals. On the calibrated time scale, this superchron, chron C34n, began at 120.964 million years ago and ended at 83.650. Reversals had grown steadily rarer in the run-up to it. It is one of two well-established superchrons, alongside the Permian Kiaman. All Ontong Java Plateau lavas are normally magnetized, so they presumably erupted after it began.

  <!-- cret-052 -->

- **The Selli Event chokes the oceans of oxygen** — c. 120 million years ago (120.5 Ma)

  Perhaps 9,000 Gt of carbon, released by magma intruding beneath the Barents Sea, may have set it off. At the start of the Aptian, the Selli Event, or OAE1a, stripped oxygen from oceans worldwide. Tied to large-igneous-province volcanism, it killed marine life through warming, acidification and oxygen loss. Its carbon-isotope shift began within 22,000–47,000 years. The event lasted about 1.1–1.3 million years, and recovery took over a million more. With OAE2, it was one of the two Cretaceous anoxic events that most changed ocean chemistry, leaving black shales worldwide.

  <!-- cret-053 -->

  *Figure: Carbon from volcanism set off the Selli Event's chain of harm to sea life.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Barents Sea intrusions] -->|carbon release| B[Warming]
  B --> C[Ocean acidification]
  B --> D[Oxygen loss]
  C --> E[Marine life dies]
  D --> E
  D --> F[Black shales worldwide]
  ```

- **Egg-laying monotremes appear in Australia** — c. 120 million years ago (120 Ma)

  The platypus has very old roots in Australia. Teinolophos, which lived there about 120 million years ago, is one of the earliest known monotremes, the egg-laying mammals. Steropodon, from Australia about 105 million years ago, has also been called the oldest monotreme.

  <!-- cret-055 -->

- **The last mammal-like tritylodontids vanish** — c. 120 million years ago (120 Ma)

  Some cynodonts came so close to being mammals that they are called extremely mammal-like. Tritylodontids, plant-eaters, were the last surviving cynodonts outside the mammaliaforms. In Asia they persisted into the Barremian–Aptian, at least until around 120 million years ago, as Fossiomanus from China shows. They died out in the Early Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-057 -->

- **A small impact scars Ukraine** — c. 120 million years ago (120 ± 10 Ma)

  A crater just 2.7 km wide lies at Rotmistrivka in Ukraine. It is dated to 120 ± 10 million years ago. Under Early Cretaceous sediments, it holds a lens of granite breccia, broken rock cemented together, and impact glass.

  <!-- cret-059 -->

- **The Kerguelen hotspot piles up a giant plateau** — c. 120–95 million years ago (120–95 Ma)

  About 25 million km³ of lava built a plateau in the southern Indian Ocean. The Kerguelen hotspot's output peaked 120–95 million years ago, building the Southern and Central Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge, which together cover 2,300,000 km². Its earliest products include Australia's Bunbury Basalt, 137–130.5 million years old. India's Rajmahal and Sylhet Traps, 118–115 million years old, came next, linked to the opening of the eastern Indian Ocean. Growth of the Southern Kerguelen Plateau 118–119 million years ago contributed to oceanic anoxic event 1. The Kerguelen microcontinent may even have carried dense conifer forest in the mid-Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-056 -->

- **The Aptian–Albian Cold Snap chills the planet** — c. 118–111 million years ago (118–111 Ma)

  Global mean surface temperature fell to about 20.7 °C. After the Barremian–Aptian Warm Interval, the Aptian–Albian Cold Snap began about 118 million years ago. Glacial dropstones in western Tethys sediments hint at an ice age. The cold ended around 111 million years ago with the Paquier/Urbino Thermal Maximum.

  <!-- cret-060 -->

- **A minor extinction strikes the Aptian seas** — c. 117 million years ago (117 Ma)

  Around 116 or 117 million years ago, a minor extinction struck, seen mostly in marine rocks. It may be linked to the Rajmahal Traps eruptions in India, fed by the Kerguelen hotspot. Minor as it was, for the history of plants it is an important episode, deserving more weight than other small events.

  <!-- cret-061 -->

- **Ontong Java: the greatest eruption in 200 million years** — c. 116 million years ago (116 Ma)

  Up to 22 km³ of magma a year, for 3 million years. The 'Ontong Java event' was the largest volcanic event of the past 200 million years. The Ontong Java, Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus in the south-west Pacific probably formed as one contiguous large igneous province, by far Earth's largest. When the eruptions ended, it covered 1% of Earth's surface with 80 million km³ of basalt, several times the Deccan Traps. The Ontong Java Plateau formed around 116 million years ago, with a much smaller event around 90 million years ago. Renewed rifting about 116 million years ago split Manihiki from Hikurangi. The eruptions were long thought to coincide with OAE1a, the Selli Event. But basalt ages of 117–108 million years and the lavas' normal magnetization make that unlikely.

  <!-- cret-062 -->

- **Subduction zones begin to ring the Pacific** — c. 115 million years ago (115 Ma)

  The Pacific Ring of Fire, today's loop of volcanoes and earthquakes, began to take shape in the Early Cretaceous. About 120–115 million years ago, the Farallon plate was subducting beneath the Americas and north-east Asia, and the Izanagi plate beneath east Asia. By about 115 million years ago, today's subduction zones had begun to form the ring around South America, North America and Asia.

  <!-- cret-064 -->

- **Vista Alegre crater scars Brazil's basalts** — c. 115 million years ago (115 Ma)

  An impact punched into the basalt plains of southern Brazil, near the Vargeão Dome. The Vista Alegre crater lies in those dark volcanic rocks. Geologists have only recently dated it, to about 115 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-065 -->

- **Deinonychus: the sickle claw that remade dinosaur science** — c. 115–98 million years ago (115–98 Ma)

  One dinosaur changed how scientists imagine all the others. Deinonychus, a dromaeosaurid up to 3.4 m long with a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot, lived in North America about 115–98 million years ago. Its 1969 description revealed an active, agile predator, launching the 'dinosaur renaissance' and a debate over warm-blooded dinosaurs. Its bird-like forelimbs led Ostrom to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs, now almost universally accepted.

  <!-- cret-063 -->

- **The first grasses take root** — during the Albian, 113–100 million years ago (113.2–100.5 Ma)

  Grasses, the plants of lawns and prairies, first appear in the fossil record in the Albian. Those are the oldest known grass fossils. By the end of the Cretaceous, grasses had already diversified into modern groups.

  <!-- cret-067 -->

- **Brazil's Crato lake preserves soft parts in stone** — c. 113–92 million years ago (113–92 Ma)

  Fish from Brazil's Crato Formation still hold their last meals. The formation was laid down about 113 million years ago in a semi-arid lake wetland, where limestone nodules formed around carcasses and preserved soft parts and stomach contents. With the Romualdo Formation, it makes up the Santana beds of north-east Brazil, which preserve pterosaurs, fish, invertebrates and plants exceptionally well. Lying near the ancient equator, they are key sites for Early Cretaceous insects.

  <!-- cret-068 -->

- **Borealopelta, an armored dinosaur 'mummy' from Alberta** — c. 112–110 million years ago (112–110 Ma)

  Pigments in its skin suggest Borealopelta was reddish-brown and countershaded, darker above and lighter below. That camouflage implies even this 5.5 m armored nodosaurid faced predators. After death, it washed out to sea and was buried in marine sands and shales of Alberta's Clearwater Formation about 110–112 million years ago. It is among the best-preserved dinosaurs of its size, keeping armor, keratin sheaths, skin and stomach contents.

  <!-- cret-070 -->

- **More anoxic events strike the Albian seas** — c. 112–100 million years ago (112–100 Ma)

  The Albian oceans lost their oxygen again and again. Further oceanic anoxic events, OAE1b, 1c and 1d, struck around 112–100 million years ago. Their black shales lie mostly in the Atlantic region, and some researchers blame local conditions rather than global change. They fall within one of the longest anoxic intervals in geologic history, about 125–80 million years ago, perhaps paced by orbital cycles.

  <!-- cret-069 -->

- **Snakes emerge from their lizard ancestors** — c. 112–94 million years ago (112–94 Ma)

  The oldest true snakes swam in the sea. They are marine simoliophiids such as the Cenomanian Haasiophis from the West Bank, dated 112–94 million years ago, though timelines of life put snake origins near 90. Najash, about 95 million years old, kept a lizard-like skull with some of the mobile joints of modern snakes. Tetrapodophis, 113 million years old and hailed as a snake in 2015, was later placed among lizards. Snakes evolved from lizards, perhaps burrowers or mosasaur relatives, and in the Late Cretaceous they recolonized land and kept diversifying.

  <!-- cret-071 -->

- **The Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse switches on** — c. 111 million years ago (111 Ma)

  Late Albian tropical seas averaged about 30 °C. Temperatures rose sharply after the cold snap ended around 111 million years ago, opening the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse, which lasted until the early Campanian. A string of Albian hyperthermals followed: Leenhardt at about 110 million years ago, l'Arboudeyesse, Amadeus at about 106, Event 6 at about 102.5 and Breistroffer at about 101. Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show gradual warming from the Albian to peak warmth in the Turonian. On land, arid belts repeatedly pushed north. In the Cloverly Formation, cool conditions lingered until a late-Albian warming pulse brought on the hothouse.

  <!-- cret-073 -->

  *Figure: A string of short heat spikes followed the end of the cold snap.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Giganotosaurus prowls Patagonia** — c. 111–106 million years ago (111–106 Ma)

  Giganotosaurus rivaled Tyrannosaurus among the largest predators ever. This huge carcharodontosaurid lived in Argentina about 111–106 million years ago. A 2026 study re-dated its rock formations from the Cenomanian to the early Albian. Its South American lineage may have been split from African relatives as Gondwana broke up in the Aptian–Albian.

  <!-- cret-072 -->

- **South America and Africa finally let go** — c. 110 million years ago (110 Ma)

  Identical dinosaur footprints in Brazil and Cameroon, about 120 million years old, suggest the two continents were still linked by land in the early Aptian. North of the equator, rifting began after 120.4 million years ago and lasted until about 100–96 million years ago; the Benue Trough rifted about 118 million years ago. By 110 million years ago, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean and South Atlantic, separating South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length. The breakup may have split South America's carcharodontosaurids from their African relatives. Around 100 million years ago, South Atlantic spreading sped up sharply. The ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km, and Africa began moving north-east.

  <!-- cret-075 -->

- **Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan, the titanosaur giants** — c. 106 million years ago (106 Ma)

  Argentinosaurus was about 30–35 m long and weighed 65–80 tonnes, among the largest land animals ever. It comes from Argentina's Huincul Formation, which a 2026 study placed in the Albian, about 106 million years ago; earlier work suggested a younger Cenomanian–Turonian age. Its close relative Patagotitan, from Patagonia's Cerro Barcino Formation, comes from rocks about 101.62 million years old. Patagotitan was first billed as the largest land animal, at 37 m and 69 tonnes. Later estimates cut it to about 31 m and 50–60 tonnes. Both belong to the titanosaurs, the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-076 -->

  *Figure: Revised estimates shrank Patagotitan below Argentinosaurus.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Dinosaurs endure the polar night at Dinosaur Cove** — c. 106 million years ago (106 Ma)

  Inside the Antarctic Circle, small dinosaurs lived through the polar winter. Dinosaur Cove's fossil beds, about 106 million years old, formed on a rift-valley floodplain as Australia began to separate from Antarctica. Its 'polar dinosaurs' include small plant-eaters such as Leaellynasaura and Atlascopcosaurus, and one fossil hints at adaptations to low light. The poles were seasonally cold but much milder than today's, and some dinosaurs lived in the polar forests year-round.

  <!-- cret-077 -->

- **The granite of Half Dome and El Capitan forms** — c. 105–85 million years ago (105–85 Ma)

  Half Dome and El Capitan are cooled magma from the Cretaceous. As the Farallon plate subducted beneath North America, rising magma built the plutons of the Sierra Nevada Batholith, and most of its granite formed 105–85 million years ago. Subduction flattened about 80–76 million years ago, shutting down arc magmatism, and pluton formation ended around 70 million years ago. Uplift and erosion later exposed the batholith as the granite peaks of the High Sierra, Mount Whitney among them.

  <!-- cret-078 -->

- **Burmese amber traps a lost island world** — c. 101–99 million years ago (101–99 Ma)

  Chimerarachne, a 100-million-year-old arachnid, had silk spinnerets and a tail. It is one of over 1,000 species, mostly insects, found in Burmese amber from Myanmar's Hukawng Valley, 101–99 million years old. The amber formed on the Burma terrane, then an island in the Tethys Ocean near the equator, and preserves its small life in exquisite detail. Its trade is ethically controversial.

  <!-- cret-079 -->

##### Late Cretaceous Epoch

The Late Cretaceous began in a hothouse and ended in catastrophe. For 34 million years a shallow sea split North America in two, while giant spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids ruled the tidal flats of North Africa. In the oceans, marine reptiles perfected the art of crushing shells. On land and in the air, the ancestors of modern birds and the first true crocodilians appeared, both lineages that would outlast the dinosaurs. Meanwhile Zealandia began to tear away from Antarctica, part of a long breakup that would reshape the southern continents.

- **Antarctica, the land bridge between two continents** — during the Late Cretaceous, 100–66 million years ago (100.5–66 Ma)

  Kangaroos have South American roots, and the route they took ran across Antarctica. In the Late Cretaceous and early Paleogene, Antarctica joined Australia and South America by land. Marsupials appear to have crossed from South America through Antarctica to reach Australia. Traffic ran both ways: platypus-like monotremes made the opposite trip, arriving in southern South America in the latest Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-080 -->

- **The thylacocephalans, a crustacean riddle, disappear** — during the Late Cretaceous, 100–66 million years ago (100.5–66 Ma)

  Some animals leave behind more questions than answers. Thylacocephala, an enigmatic class of crustaceans, is one of them. These shelled sea creatures, relatives of crabs and shrimp, puzzle researchers to this day. Their long story closed in the Late Cretaceous, when the last of the class went extinct, one quiet loss among the many changes reshaping the seas.

  <!-- cret-082 -->

- **Meridiolestidans, South America's forgotten mammal rulers** — during the Late Cretaceous, 100–66 million years ago (100.5–66 Ma)

  Long before llamas or armadillos, South America's mammals belonged to a group few people have heard of. Meridiolestidans were the dominant mammals of the continent in the Late Cretaceous. They came in surprising variety, from the sabre-toothed Cronopio to plant-eating mesungulatids. The group also proved remarkably durable: it outlasted the age of dinosaurs and lingered in Patagonia until the Miocene.

  <!-- cret-083 -->

- **Shell-crushers perfect the Mesozoic marine revolution** — during the Late Cretaceous, 100–66 million years ago (100.5–66 Ma)

  In Late Cretaceous seas, a shell was no longer a safe place to hide. Shell-crushing predation, the force behind the Mesozoic marine revolution, was perfected by marine reptiles and other hunters. Sea urchins joined in, radiating into predatory niches and probably perfecting the grazing of corals. Even the land may have fed the arms race: faster weathering and nutrients washing off from the boom in flowering plants may have helped drive it.

  <!-- cret-084 -->

- **The Mississippi embayment, cradle of a great delta** — c. 100 million years ago (100 Ma)

  The Mississippi River Delta has a surprisingly deep history. It traces back about 100 million years, to the Late Cretaceous, when a broad low trough called the Mississippi embayment formed. That embayment, an arm of lowland open to the sea, gave the future river a path to the Gulf. Everything the delta became later was built on this ancient foundation.

  <!-- cret-087 -->

- **Modern birds take flight in the Cretaceous** — c. 100 million years ago (100 Ma)

  Every duck, sparrow and ostrich alive today descends from birds that shared the world with dinosaurs. Modern birds, the Neornithes, probably arose around the boundary between the Early and Late Cretaceous, about 100 million years ago. Around then, their ancestors evolved a more open pelvis for laying larger eggs, and by about 95 million years ago they had a sharper sense of smell. A 2015 study placed their last common ancestor near 95 million years ago and the fowl–Neoaves split at 85. A 2024 genomic study pushed that split back to about 100.5 million years ago. The dating is contested, though: molecular clocks favor a Cretaceous radiation, while fossils point to a Paleogene one, a dispute called 'rocks versus clocks'. Only waterfowl and shorebirds have an established Late Cretaceous fossil record. The birds diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction.

  <!-- cret-088 -->

- **Spinosaurus and the giant hunters of North Africa** — c. 100–94 million years ago (100–94 Ma)

  Few places have ever held so many giant meat-eaters at once. In the mid-Cretaceous, North Africa was ruled by abelisauroids, spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids, found side by side in the Kem Kem, Bahariya and other beds. Carcharodontosaurus lived there about 100–94 million years ago, and Spinosaurus shows up in the record 100–95 million years ago. Their world bordered the Tethys Sea: a mangrove coast of vast tidal flats and winding waterways.

  <!-- cret-086 -->

- **Zealandia tears away from West Antarctica** — c. 100–84 million years ago (100–84 Ma)

  A continent most people have never heard of began breaking loose about 100 million years ago. Zealandia includes New Zealand, the Campbell Plateau, Chatham Rise, Lord Howe Rise, Norfolk Ridge and New Caledonia. Around 100 million years ago, volcanism along its margin shifted from arc magmatism, fed by a sinking plate, to rift magmatism, fed by crust pulling apart. At about the same time the Hikurangi Plateau first slid beneath New Zealand, during its collision with Gondwana. The West Antarctic Rift System began stretching in the Late Cretaceous, before the Campbell Plateau broke away. The split from West Antarctica was complete by about 84 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-090 -->

- **The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two** — c. 100–66 million years ago (100–66 Ma)

  For 34 million years, a person could have sailed from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean straight across North America. The Western Interior Seaway lasted from about 100 to 66 million years ago. It began as an Arctic arm pushing south, the Mowry Sea, which later merged with a southern embayment. The result split the continent into western and eastern landmasses, isolating their plants and animals. The seaway's bottom waters repeatedly lost their oxygen, leaving organic-rich shales that are now a major source of oil. Late in the Cretaceous the sea narrowed into an inland arm of the Gulf, and it vanished in the early Cenozoic.

  <!-- cret-089 -->

  *Figure: How the Western Interior Seaway formed, divided the continent and disappeared.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Mowry Sea pushes south from Arctic] --> C[Seaway joins Gulf to Arctic]
  B[Southern embayment] --> C
  C --> D[North America split in two]
  C --> E[Anoxic bottom waters]
  E --> F[Oil-rich shales]
  C --> G[Narrows to Gulf arm]
  G --> H[Vanishes in early Cenozoic]
  ```

- **The long-necked giants vanish from North America** — c. 98 million years ago (98 Ma)

  Around 98 million years ago, the sauropods simply disappear from western North America. The gap that follows, lasting through most of the Late Cretaceous, is called the 'sauropod hiatus'. Proposed causes include competition with ornithischian dinosaurs, habitat lost to The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two, or gaps in sampling. Even revised dates leave a hole from the mid-Cenomanian to the mid-Campanian. The hiatus ended shortly before the Cretaceous closed, when Alamosaurus, probably an immigrant from South America, arrived. In Europe, trackways and a tooth suggest sauropods never left.

  <!-- cret-091 -->

- **The first true crocodilians** — c. 95 million years ago (95 Ma)

  Today's crocodiles, alligators and gharials belong to a lineage older than Tyrannosaurus. The first true crocodilians, the group called Crocodylia, evolved around 95 million years ago. Their ancestors had been around much longer, but this is when the line leading to every living crocodile and alligator began. That line would go on to outlast the dinosaurs around it.

  <!-- cret-093 -->

- **Lebanon's Sannine fossil beds** — c. 95–94 million years ago (95–94 Ma)

  In the hills of Lebanon, the stone splits open to reveal fish so perfect they look freshly caught. The Sannine Formation sites at Haqel, Hjoula and al-Nammoura are famous Cenomanian Lagerstätten, deposits of exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Shrimp, octopus, stingrays and bony fish are common finds. The octopuses are the true treasures, since fossil octopuses are among the rarest of all.

  <!-- cret-094 -->

- **A shallow sea splits Africa in half** — c. 95–90 million years ago (95–90 Ma)

  For a while in the Cretaceous, Africa was not one continent but two. Around 95–90 million years ago, a seaway linking the Mediterranean and the proto-Atlantic partly flooded the Tuareg Shield. A rising sea also drowned the Kem Kem world of Spinosaurus and the giant hunters of North Africa. Bivalve fossils show that a shallow sea later split Africa in half, joining the Tethys to the South Atlantic. The Benue Trough probably formed the main link to the Gulf of Guinea, through the Chad and Iullemmeden basins.

  <!-- cret-095 -->

- **The Caribbean large igneous province floods the sea floor** — c. 95–83 million years ago (95–83 Ma)

  Most of the Caribbean plate is made of lava from a single colossal outpouring. The Caribbean large igneous province holds roughly 4.4 million cubic kilometers of volcanic rock. This mass, the Caribbean–Colombian oceanic plateau, now makes up most of the plate's crust. The Galápagos hotspot began building it in the eastern Pacific about 95–90 million years ago. Volcanism spanned 139–69 million years ago but peaked between 95 and 88 million years ago. Argon–argon dating puts the main magmatism at 95–83 million years ago, with a second pulse at 81–69. A plume arriving about 86 million years ago spread eruptions into north-west South America. The main phase coincides with the oceanic anoxic event of OAE2: the last time the whole ocean suffocated, suggesting one helped cause the other.

  <!-- cret-092 -->

  *Figure: The phases of Caribbean volcanism, with its main burst in the middle.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)
