- **The first mosasaurs slip into the sea** — c. 94 million years ago (94 Ma)

  The most fearsome hunters of the late Cretaceous oceans started out modestly. The first mosasaurs, marine reptiles, appear around 94 million years ago. From that start they went on to rule the Late Cretaceous seas. They filled the role left empty by the ichthyosaurs, whose decline is told in Ichthyosaurs, the fish-lizards, die out.

  <!-- cret-096 -->

- **The Cenomanian–Turonian extinction** — c. 94 million years ago (93.9 Ma)

  For years some researchers wondered whether this extinction was real or just a trick of poor preservation. Recent work settles it: vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes truly died out at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, about 93.9 million years ago. Planktic foraminifera, tiny shelled drifters of the open sea, vanished in five phases. The variety of burrows and tracks plummeted as the event began. It was one of the lesser extinctions tied to oceanic anoxia, when seawater runs out of oxygen, and it mostly struck marine life. Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven it.

  <!-- cret-097 -->

- **OAE2: the last time the whole ocean suffocated** — c. 94 million years ago (93.9 Ma)

  About 93.9 million years ago, the world's oceans began to choke. The Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, OAE2, is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event. Sulfidic, oxygen-free water rose into the sunlit surface ocean. On the seafloor, black shale piled up, including the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio in Italy. Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to undersea volcanism from large igneous provinces as a likely trigger. The event left a positive carbon isotope excursion, a shift in the ratio of carbon types that ranks among the Mesozoic's main carbon events. The interval had the highest carbon dioxide levels of the Cretaceous and was one of the hottest times of the Phanerozoic.

  <!-- cret-098 -->

  *Figure: The proposed chain from undersea volcanism to black shale in OAE2.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Large igneous province volcanism] -.-> B[Oxygen-free sulfidic water]
  B --> C[Reaches sunlit surface ocean]
  B --> D[Black shale laid down]
  D --> E[Carbon isotope excursion]
  ```

- **The Cretaceous Thermal Maximum: a hothouse planet** — c. 94–90 million years ago (93.9–89.8 Ma)

  Crocodile-like reptiles once basked in the Canadian Arctic. Warming that began at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition peaked about 90 million years ago, in one of the hottest intervals of the Phanerozoic. Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose above 1,000 ppm, against a pre-industrial 280 ppm, and sea level stood high. Tropical seas reached at least 30 °C, perhaps 33–42 °C. The difference between equator and pole was unusually gentle. Champsosaurs lived in the Arctic, where mean yearly temperatures topped 14 °C. The warmth lasted to the Turonian–Coniacian boundary, broken only by brief cool spells. Claims of Antarctic ice during the Turonian remain disputed.

  <!-- cret-099 -->

  *Figure: Cretaceous carbon dioxide far above the pre-industrial level.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Ichthyosaurs, the fish-lizards, die out** — c. 93 million years ago (93 Ma)

  Ichthyosaurs had ruled the seas since about 250 million years ago, and they did not fade slowly. Their Cretaceous variety was greater than once thought, perhaps because breaking continents lengthened the coastlines. Then the blows came. A first pulse at the start of the Cenomanian killed two of their three remaining feeding guilds, leaving only unspecialized top predators. After the anoxic event of OAE2: the last time the whole ocean suffocated, only Platypterygius hercynicus survived, and it vanished about 93 million years ago. The end was a pair of abrupt events, probably tied to the upheaval and climate change of the Cenomanian and Turonian. Pliosaurs reportedly vanished in the same anoxic event, and The first mosasaurs slip into the sea took over the oceans.

  <!-- cret-100 -->

  *Figure: The two blows that ended the ichthyosaurs.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Three feeding guilds] -->|early Cenomanian pulse| B[Only apex predators left]
  B -->|anoxic event| C[Only Platypterygius hercynicus]
  C --> D[Extinct]
  D --> E[Mosasaurs take over]
  ```

- **Lava floods across Madagascar** — c. 92–85 million years ago (92–85 Ma)

  Madagascar's rocks keep a timeline of fire that runs from north to south. Flood basalts, vast sheets of runny lava, erupted across the island between about 92 and 85 million years ago, by argon–argon dating. The ages are 88–92 million years in the north and 85–88 million years in the south. The pattern suggests the eruptions swept down the island over several million years.

  <!-- cret-101 -->

- **The Andes switch from stretching to squeezing** — c. 90 million years ago (90 Ma)

  Around 90 million years ago, western South America stopped pulling apart and began to be crushed. Faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned the margin from extension to compression, and the Andean orogeny changed character. At about the same time, the sinking ocean floor switched from south-east to north-east motion. Back-arc basins in central Chile and Mendoza were squeezed and inverted. Uplift turned western Peru's marine basins into dry land, and erosion took hold from the Late Cretaceous onward.

  <!-- cret-102 -->

- **The earliest ticks** — c. 90 million years ago (90 Ma)

  Ticks are older than most of the animals they feed on today. The earliest examples of these small blood-sucking relatives of spiders appear around 90 million years ago. Their first hosts would have been the reptiles, birds and mammals of the Late Cretaceous world.

  <!-- cret-103 -->

- **The last carnosaurs fall** — c. 90 million years ago (90 Ma)

  One of the longest-running lines of giant predators came to an end. Carcharodontosaurids, the last definitive family of carnosaurs, became extinct in the Turonian, around 90 million years ago. Carnosaurs, a group of large meat-eating dinosaurs, had first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago. Their exit left the top-predator role to other theropods.

  <!-- cret-104 -->

- **A disputed anoxic event in the Coniacian–Santonian** — during the Coniacian–Santonian, 90–84 million years ago (89.8–83.6 Ma)

  Not every black shale tells a global story. A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded by organic-rich black shales, has been proposed for the Coniacian–Santonian stages, about 89.8–83.6 million years ago. Its shales are more local than those of the major Cretaceous events, found mainly in the Atlantic and nearby areas. That patchiness fuels a real disagreement: some researchers tie the shales to local conditions rather than to any global change.

  <!-- cret-105 -->

- **The Coniacian Thermal Maximum: a second peak of heat** — c. 87 million years ago (87 Ma)

  The Cretaceous hothouse had more than one summit. After The Cretaceous Thermal Maximum: a hothouse planet and a spell of slight cooling, temperatures climbed again. This second peak, the Coniacian Thermal Maximum, topped out around 87 million years ago, keeping the world in a long run of extreme warmth.

  <!-- cret-106 -->

- **The Niobrara Chalk and its flying reptiles** — c. 87–82 million years ago (87–82 Ma)

  Much of the Great Plains rests on the remains of microscopic sea life. Between 87 and 82 million years ago, the coccoliths, tiny chalky plates of microorganisms, piled up on the floor of The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two as the Niobrara Chalk. Its Smoky Hill Chalk is famous for marine fossils: plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, pterosaurs and primitive aquatic birds. The pterosaur Pteranodon, with wingspans over 6 m, turns up in most of its layers. About 1,200 Pteranodon specimens are known.

  <!-- cret-107 -->

- **Maiasaura, the good mother lizard** — c. 86–71 million years ago (86.3–70.6 Ma)

  The first proof that dinosaurs cared for their young came from a nesting ground in Montana. Maiasaura, a duck-billed dinosaur, lived in Montana and Alberta about 86.3 to 70.6 million years ago. It nested in colonies of closely packed earthen mounds, about 7 m apart, each holding 30 to 40 eggs. Hatchlings had weak legs but worn teeth. They could not have walked off to feed, so adults must have brought food to the nest.

  <!-- cret-108 -->

- **The first duck-billed hadrosaurids** — c. 86 million years ago (86 Ma)

  The duck-billed dinosaurs would become some of the most common plant-eaters of the latest Cretaceous. Their family, the hadrosaurids, first appears around 86 million years ago. Its members included nest-builders like Maiasaura, the good mother lizard.

  <!-- cret-109 -->

- **The Praia Grande crater, hidden off Brazil** — c. 86–84 million years ago (85.8–83.5 Ma)

  Off the coast of Brazil, a scar from space lies under 4 km of rock. An impact in the Santonian made the Praia Grande crater, about 20 km across, in the Santos Basin. Buried deep beneath younger sediment, the crater is well preserved, shielded from the erosion that wipes out most impact scars.

  <!-- cret-111 -->

- **The long Late Cretaceous cooling begins** — during the Santonian–Campanian, 86–72 million years ago (85.7–72.2 Ma)

  From the Santonian on, the great Cretaceous hothouse began to lose its heat. Global climate started to cool near the end of the mid-Cretaceous warmth, a trend that ran on through the Campanian. Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells record peak warmth in the Turonian, then gradual surface cooling to the end of the Maastrichtian. Tropical sea surfaces fell from about 35 °C in the early Campanian to about 28 °C in the Maastrichtian. Turtles declined during one Campanian cool spell. The Late Cretaceous stayed warmer than today, but its cooling trend carried on into the Cenozoic. Whether continental ice sheets formed is unclear, because ocean-temperature estimates conflict.

  <!-- cret-112 -->

  *Figure: Tropical sea surfaces cooled through the late Cretaceous.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Zealandia drifts off and the Tasman Sea opens** — c. 85 million years ago (85 Ma)

  The sea between Australia and New Zealand was born when a continent broke away. Zealandia, stretching from New Caledonia to New Zealand's subantarctic islands, separated from Australia about 85 million years ago. About 83 million years ago, a rift entering eastern Tasmania split the Lord Howe Rise from the South Tasman Rise. The Lord Howe Rise, a ribbon of continental crust 3,000 km long, drifted away. Rifting opened the Tasman Sea, and new ocean crust formed in the deep Tasman Basin. Together with Zealandia tears away from West Antarctica, this left Zealandia an isolated, mostly drowned continent.

  <!-- cret-114 -->

- **The High Arctic volcanoes flare again** — c. 85–60 million years ago (85–60 Ma)

  Some volcanic provinces erupt for tens of millions of years. The High Arctic Large Igneous Province was active from about 130 to 60 million years ago. About 85 million years ago it entered a second phase. From then until about 60 million years ago, it poured out mildly alkaline flood basalts, a chemically distinct lava from its earlier eruptions.

  <!-- cret-113 -->

- **The magnetic field's long calm ends** — c. 84 million years ago (83.65 Ma)

  For 37 million years, Earth's compass never flipped. That long stretch without polarity reversals is called the Cretaceous Normal Superchron, or C34n. A polarity reversal is the moment when magnetic north and south swap places. Calibrated ages place the superchron from 120.964 million years ago to the start of chron C33r at 83.650 million years ago. When it ended, the field began reversing again. Since then, reversals have generally become slowly more frequent.

  <!-- cret-115 -->

  *Figure: The Cretaceous Normal Superchron, a long span with no reversals.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **India breaks free and races north** — c. 83 million years ago (83 Ma)

  India began the fastest continental journey in this course about 83 million years ago. It rifted from Madagascar and drifted rapidly north toward Eurasia. The Indian plate's run, covering about 6,000 km, began around 84 million years ago. By the Paleocene it was moving about 18 cm a year. By about 83.5 million years ago, new seafloor was spreading between India and Antarctica, unevenly near the Kerguelen Plateau. Madagascar was left behind, flooded with Late Cretaceous basalts up to 200 m thick. India's long trip would end in a collision that raised the Himalayas.

  <!-- cret-117 -->

  *Figure: India's break from Madagascar and the start of its drift north.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The North Atlantic begins to open** — c. 83 million years ago (83 Ma)

  The Atlantic opened from south to north, and by the Late Cretaceous the crack was reaching the far north. The ocean began opening between Ireland and Greenland after 85 million years ago. By about 83 million years ago, seafloor spreading had begun between the Rockall Basin and North America. Seafloor spreading is the creation of new ocean crust as two plates move apart. Rifting among the Eurasian, Greenland and North American plates may have started around 81 million years ago, the first steps in splitting the northern continents.

  <!-- cret-118 -->

- **Iberia turns and pushes into Europe** — c. 83–68 million years ago (83–67.7 Ma)

  The Pyrenees owe their existence to Spain's slow shove against France. The Bay of Biscay finished opening into ocean by about 84 million years ago. From about 83 million years ago, Iberia converged with Europe, until it stopped moving relative to Europe 67.7 million years ago. In the Pyrenees, squeezing had already replaced stretching by the early Turonian, about 90 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-116 -->

- **The Ninety East Ridge, a 5,000 km volcanic trail** — c. 82–38 million years ago (82–38 Ma)

  A single straight ridge runs 5,000 km across the floor of the Indian Ocean. The Kerguelen hotspot built this Ninety East Ridge between 82 and 38 million years ago. A hotspot is a fixed plume of hot mantle that punches volcanoes through the plate above it. This one sat at or near a spreading ridge, and as India breaks free and races north carried India north, it left a long line of volcanic rock behind.

  <!-- cret-119 -->

- **The oldest Hawaiian–Emperor volcanoes** — c. 81 million years ago (81 Ma)

  The Hawaiian Islands are only the youngest end of a chain of volcanoes. Its oldest dated volcano, at the far northern end, is 81 million years old. The Emperor seamounts, the oldest and most eroded part of the chain, are 39 to 85 million years old. Each formed over the same hotspot and was then carried away by the moving Pacific plate.

  <!-- cret-120 -->

- **The first palm trees** — c. 80 million years ago (80 Ma)

  Palms, the emblem of tropical beaches, have roots deep in the age of dinosaurs. The first palm trees appear around 80 million years ago. They joined a world already being transformed by flowering plants, and their later spread became a useful sign of warm climates.

  <!-- cret-121 -->

- **Zeleny Gai, a small Ukrainian crater** — c. 80 million years ago (80 ± 20 Ma)

  Not every impact can be pinned down precisely. A small one made the Zeleny Gai crater in Ukraine, 3.5 km across. Its age is known only loosely: 80 ± 20 million years ago, a window wide enough to straddle much of the Late Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-123 -->

- **The Laramide orogeny raises the Rockies** — c. 80–70 million years ago (80–70 Ma)

  The Rocky Mountains began rising far inland, a long way from any plate edge. Mountain building began in western North America in the Late Cretaceous, 80 to 70 million years ago. It unfolded as buoyant terranes, slabs of crust too light to sink, were scraped onto the continent during subduction of the Farallon plate. This Laramide orogeny raised the Rockies. It also started uplifting the Grand Canyon region around 75 million years ago.

  <!-- cret-122 -->

- **Lappajärvi, a Finnish lake in an impact crater** — 78 million years ago (77.85 ± 0.78 Ma)

  One of Finland's largest lakes fills a hole punched by an asteroid. A rock about 1.6 km across struck about 77.85 million years ago, in the Campanian. It left a crater about 22–23 km wide and 750 m deep. Today that crater holds Lake Lappajärvi.

  <!-- cret-124 -->

- **Dinosaur Park, Alberta's riverside graveyard** — c. 76–75 million years ago (76.5–74.8 Ma)

  Few places on Earth hold as many dinosaurs as a stretch of Alberta badlands. Rivers draining to The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two laid down the Dinosaur Park Formation about 76.5–74.8 million years ago, burying many skeletons with their bones still joined. Dinosaur Provincial Park is one of the world's richest dinosaur sites, with 58 dinosaur species among nearly 500 species of fossil life. Such coastal plains, and their diverse communities, were later lost as the seas retreated.

  <!-- cret-125 -->

- **The first Velociraptor** — c. 75 million years ago (75 Ma)

  The real Velociraptor was a feathered hunter of the Late Cretaceous. It first appears around 75 million years ago. It became one of the most famous of the small predatory dinosaurs, and one was later found locked in combat in The Fighting Dinosaurs of the Gobi.

  <!-- cret-128 -->

- **The Fighting Dinosaurs of the Gobi** — c. 75–71 million years ago (75–71 Ma)

  Two dinosaurs died mid-fight and stayed that way for millions of years. In Mongolia's Djadokhta Formation, a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops were buried locked in combat 75–71 million years ago. The pair gives direct evidence of predatory or aggressive behavior among non-avian dinosaurs. How they were buried so suddenly is debated. Suggestions include drowning, a collapsing dune and a sandstorm.

  <!-- cret-127 -->

- **The Manson impact in Iowa** — c. 74 million years ago (73.8 ± 0.3 Ma)

  Beneath the cornfields of Iowa lies a buried scar from space. An asteroid or comet nucleus struck near present-day Manson about 74 million years ago. It left an impact structure about 35 km across, now hidden under younger sediment.

  <!-- cret-129 -->

- **The Atlantic floods Patagonia** — during the Maastrichtian, 72–66 million years ago (72.2–66 Ma)

  At the end of the Cretaceous, the Atlantic reached all the way to the foot of the young Andes. Foreland basins east of the mountains were sinking, and in the Maastrichtian, Atlantic waters flooded in to reach the mountain front. This transgression, an advance of the sea over land, laid down the marine Jagüel and Roca formations in Patagonia. The flooding lasted from the Maastrichtian into the Danian.

  <!-- cret-130 -->

- **The last Bennettitales** — during the Maastrichtian, 72–66 million years ago (72.2–66 Ma)

  Bennettitales looked a little like cycads, and for a long time they were everywhere. These seed plants, also called cycadeoids, had been around since the Permian and were widespread in the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous. Then flowering plants rose, and Bennettitales declined severely through the Late Cretaceous. They died out in most areas toward the end of the period. Their last northern records come from polar latitudes.

  <!-- cret-131 -->

- **The Maastrichtian sea-level fall** — during the Maastrichtian, 72–66 million years ago (72.2–66 Ma)

  In the final stage of the Cretaceous, the seas drained off the continents faster than at any other time in the Mesozoic. Sea level fell further during this Maastrichtian regression than in any other Mesozoic interval. A regression is a retreat of the sea from the land, exposing old seafloor and shrinking shallow coastal habitats. The drop came just before the end of the dinosaurs, and it is one of the proposed contributors to The Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction.

  <!-- cret-133 -->

- **The Maastrichtian chill** — c. 70–68 million years ago (70.5–67.5 Ma)

  The last few million years of the Cretaceous were a time of surprising cold. About 70.5 million years ago, surface and bottom waters cooled sharply, and marine species richness rose by 43%. Cooling peaked about 67.5 million years ago, with surface waters at 13 °C, and richness and productivity began to fall. The Western Interior Seaway was coldest early in the Maastrichtian, about 16 °C, before warming to about 22 °C. From the mid-Maastrichtian, more carbon was stored in the deep sea, possibly through cooling and stronger deep circulation. Near the very end, ice sheets and sea ice appear to have briefly returned to Antarctica.

  <!-- cret-136 -->

  *Figure: The Maastrichtian chill from sharp cooling to its peak.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Mosasaurus, the last giant sea lizard** — c. 70 million years ago (70 Ma)

  The mosasaur that gave the whole group its name arrived late. Mosasaurus evolved around 70 million years ago. By the Maastrichtian, several large mosasaurs shared the Tethys Sea and competed for its prey. They were the ruling marine predators right up to the end of the Cretaceous.

  <!-- cret-138 -->

- **Multituberculates, rodents before rodents** — c. 70 million years ago (70 Ma)

  Long before mice and squirrels existed, another group of mammals filled their roles. Multituberculates increased in diversity around 70 million years ago. In the Late Cretaceous they radiated as plant-eaters and into forms like squirrel-like tree dwellers, reaching a peak of diversity. They were among the most successful mammals of the age of dinosaurs.

  <!-- cret-139 -->

- **The Labrador Sea begins to open** — c. 69 million years ago (69 Ma)

  Greenland began drifting away from North America near the end of the Cretaceous. The Labrador Sea started opening 69 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian. Seafloor spreading in its southern part pushed Greenland north relative to North America. The date is not settled: a 1989 paper dates the sea's first opening to 92 million years ago, not 69.

  <!-- cret-140 -->

- **Modern birds before the asteroid** — c. 69–66 million years ago (69–66 Ma)

  Ducks and their relatives were already flying when the dinosaurs died. Vegavis, from the Maastrichtian, shows that modern birds had begun diversifying before the Cenozoic. Asteriornis, also Maastrichtian, appears close to Galloanserae, the fowl group that was the earliest branch of the neognaths. A Vegavis specimen dated 69–66 million years ago holds the oldest known syrinx, the voice organ of birds.

  <!-- cret-141 -->

- **Quetzalcoatlus, a giant of the skies** — c. 68 million years ago (68 Ma)

  One of the largest animals ever to fly appeared just before the end of the Cretaceous. Quetzalcoatlus, a giant pterosaur, first appears around 68 million years ago. It was among the very last flying reptiles, and its line would end with The last pterosaurs.

  <!-- cret-143 -->

- **Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops arrive** — c. 68–66 million years ago (68–66 Ma)

  The most famous dinosaur matchup in history happened only at the very end. Tyrannosaurus, the largest land predator of western North America, appears in the fossil record 68–66 million years ago. The first species of Triceratops shows up at the same time. Armored Ankylosaurus lived then too and was among the last non-avian dinosaurs. These giants are latecomers: they had only about two million years before the asteroid of The Chicxulub asteroid strikes ended their world.

  <!-- cret-144 -->

- **Hell Creek, the last dinosaur world** — c. 68–66 million years ago (68–65.5 Ma)

  Montana's Hell Creek Formation is where the dinosaurs' final chapter is written. Its rocks record rivers, deltas and swamps on the low eastern coast facing The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two. It yields Tyrannosaurus and Ankylosaurus, and it is a key record of dinosaurs right up to the K–Pg boundary. This Lancian fauna is closer to East Asian and Canadian–Alaskan faunas than most earlier North American ones.

  <!-- cret-142 -->

- **The Deccan Traps flood India with lava** — c. 66–65 million years ago (66.25–65 Ma)

  India holds about 1.5 million cubic kilometers of lava from a single episode of eruptions. The Deccan Traps began erupting in western India 66.25 million years ago, fed largely by the Réunion hotspot. Most of the lava poured out between 66 and 65 million years ago. It came in three phases, two before the K–Pg boundary and one after. The eruptions warmed climate about 3 °C over the last 100,000 years of the Cretaceous, with a brief 5 °C cold snap 30,000 years before the boundary. Plant fossils record a 250 ppm rise in carbon dioxide across the boundary, likely from Deccan activity. Once proposed as a major extinction cause, the Traps are now generally held to have played a minor role at most. That view is contested, though, and some sources still favor a joint cause.

  <!-- cret-145 -->

  *Figure: The Deccan Traps by the numbers.*

  | Measure | Value |
  |---|---|
  | Eruptions begin | 66.25 million years ago |
  | Bulk of lava | 66–65 million years ago |
  | Lava volume | about 1.5 million km³ |
  | Warming | about 3 °C |
  | CO2 rise | 250 ppm |

- **The Chicxulub asteroid strikes** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  In a single moment, a rock about 10 km wide ended the age of dinosaurs. The asteroid struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula and left the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across. Megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. Debris fell across the whole planet as a clay rich in iridium, a metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The clay also holds shocked quartz, grains crushed by enormous pressure, and tektites, droplets of melted glass. Then came an impact winter. Dust and soot lingered, sunlight faded, photosynthesis halted, and the oceans rapidly acidified. Argon dating in 2013 gave an age of 66.043 ± 0.043 million years, matching the K–Pg boundary, and impact glass matches the boundary ash. Chicxulub is widely accepted as the primary cause of The Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction. It is the only mass extinction definitively tied to an impact.

  <!-- cret-147 -->

  *Figure: The Chicxulub impact's effects that led to the K–Pg extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Asteroid strikes Yucatan] --> B[Iridium clay worldwide]
  A --> C[Megatsunamis]
  A --> D[Impact winter]
  D --> E[Photosynthesis halts]
  A --> F[Oceans acidify]
  E --> G[K-Pg extinction]
  F --> G
  ```

- **The Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  About three-quarters of all species on Earth disappeared in what may have been a geological instant. The K–Pg extinction wiped out about 76% of species and 47% of genera, including all non-avian dinosaurs. It was the fifth and latest of the great mass extinctions. On land, every animal heavier than 25 kg died, along with all pterosaurs and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants. At sea it killed plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudist clams. Over 90% of coccolithophore species, the chalk-making plankton, vanished, and about 60% of reef-coral genera. The killing was fast, perhaps under 10,000 years. Ocean productivity and circulation then collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years. Yet some survived. All major mammal lineages and most turtles came through. Mammals then spread into the large-animal niches that the dinosaurs left empty, a story picked up in Mammals inherit the Earth.

  <!-- cret-148 -->

  *Figure: Share lost in the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The last ammonites** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Ammonoids, the coiled-shell cousins of squid, had survived for about 410 million years. They vanished during or soon after the K–Pg extinction. Their tiny drifting eggs and larvae were devastated in the upheaval. Of all the cephalopods, only nautiloids and coleoids, the line of squid and octopus, made it through. A few ammonite genera, such as Baculites and Hoploscaphites, may have lingered briefly into the earliest Danian.

  <!-- cret-149 -->

- **The last belemnites** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Belemnites, squid-like animals with bullet-shaped internal shells, were already in trouble before the asteroid hit. By then they had shrunk to a few high-latitude regions. The K–Pg extinction finished them. As with ammonites, their embryos probably could not survive the acidifying ocean. Sea butterflies, small swimming snails, took the place of their larvae in the food chain.

  <!-- cret-150 -->

- **The last pterosaurs** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  The first vertebrates to fly under their own power did not survive the asteroid. Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs were still present in the Maastrichtian, and likely died out at the K–Pg boundary. In the end every pterosaur perished in that extinction. The skies passed entirely to the birds.

  <!-- cret-152 -->

- **A New Jersey bone bed from the day of disaster** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Very few fossil sites capture the K–Pg mass death itself. One is a bone bed in New Jersey's Hornerstown Formation, called the Main Fossiliferous Layer. The 66-million-year-old layer is packed with marine life from the shallow sea that once covered southern New Jersey. Iridium and shocked quartz in the layer suggest it formed as ecosystems collapsed during the extinction.

  <!-- cret-153 -->

- **The end of the non-avian dinosaurs** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Look in Maastrichtian rocks on any continent and dinosaurs are there; look in the rocks just above and they are gone. Scientists agree that all non-avian dinosaurs, then an estimated 628 to 1,078 species, died out at the K–Pg boundary. Birds are the only dinosaur lineage left. Their large size may have left them exposed, along with few small species and no known ability to burrow, swim or dive. Whether they were already declining is uncertain. Dates published in 2025 on New Mexico beds show diverse faunas into the latest Maastrichtian. Titanosaurs, the last long-necked sauropods, were still thriving when the extinction struck.

  <!-- cret-154 -->

  *Figure: Traits that may have left the non-avian dinosaurs exposed.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Large body size] --> D[Exposed to the K-Pg crisis]
  B[Few small species] --> D
  C[No burrowing, swimming or diving] --> D
  D --> E[All non-avian dinosaurs die out]
  ```

- **Shiva, a disputed second crater** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Some researchers think Chicxulub may not have struck alone. Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues proposed that a structure off India, the potential Shiva crater, formed at the K–Pg boundary and helped cause the extinction. At 450–600 km across, it would far exceed Chicxulub, and it has been dated to about 66 million years ago. But Shiva is only a proposed impact structure, and it has not been confirmed.

  <!-- cret-155 -->

- **Rudist reefs and giant inoceramids vanish** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Some Cretaceous reefs were built not by corals but by clams. These reef-building rudists died out at the K–Pg boundary, along with the giant inoceramid bivalves. Rudists were once thought to have vanished half a million years early, but they apparently fell to the K–Pg event itself. Inoceramids, known from the Permian to the latest Cretaceous, included true giants. Inoceramus shells exceeded 1 m, and one Greenland specimen reached 1.87 m. Most inoceramids, though, had been declining long before the end.

  <!-- cret-156 -->

- **Tanis, a snapshot of the impact's first hour** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Within minutes of the impact, 3,000 km away, the ground in North Dakota began to shake. At Tanis, seismic waves raised seiche waves, sloshing surges in an enclosed sea, 10–100 m high in The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two. The waves flung marine, freshwater and land animals and plants inland. At the same time, microtektites, tiny glass beads blasted from Yucatán, rained down from the sky. Fossil fish from the site even suggest the impact struck in the Northern Hemisphere spring.

  <!-- cret-157 -->

### Cenozoic Era

The Cenozoic opened on a world swept clean. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, mammals rapidly grew in size and diversity, filling the emptied niches. Four bird lineages had survived, among them Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds. Meanwhile the Earth itself kept moving: Apulia began colliding with Europe, and the Laramide orogeny kept raising the Rocky Mountains. This is the era of mammals, and of the mountains and climates that shaped them.

#### Paleogene Period

The Paleogene began in the wreckage of the K–Pg extinction and became the age when mammals took over. Pantodonts were among the first large mammals, and the oldest undisputed placental fossils come from its first years. Multituberculates, the most successful Mesozoic mammals, enjoyed one last peak. Even the rocks recorded the turmoil: early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon in the deep sea.

##### Paleocene Epoch

The Paleocene is the story of recovery. Colorado's Denver Formation records mammals diversifying right after the K–Pg extinction, and the first large mammals soon appeared. Great swamps laid down coal that still powers America, with the Fort Union Formation alone yielding 43% of its coal. Asteroids kept falling too: one struck off Guinea-Bissau near the boundary, another left the 24 km Boltysh crater in Ukraine. By the end of the epoch, a world of small survivors had given way to a warming planet full of new kinds of life.

- **Mammals inherit the Earth** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  When the dust settled after the asteroid, the world was suddenly empty of big animals. The K–Pg extinction had killed every land animal heavier than about 25 kg, leaving many niches open at the start of the Paleocene. Mammals moved in. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, they rapidly increased in size and diversity and filled the vacant roles. Many crown placental groups arose, the branches that lead to living mammals. They included the earliest afrotherians, the African group that now includes elephants, and xenarthrans, the line of sloths and armadillos. Rodents and carnivorans appeared, along with plesiadapiforms, the forerunners of primates. Growth in size took time, though. Most Paleocene mammals stayed small, under about 20 kg, until near the end of the epoch. Still, the shift was permanent. Mammals have been the dominant land animals ever since, and that dominance eventually led to humans.

  <!-- pale-007 -->

- **Modern birds explode into new forms** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Only a handful of bird lineages survived the asteroid, and from them came nearly every bird alive today. Four lineages made it through the K–Pg extinction: the ostrich group, waterfowl, ground fowl and Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds. At the start of the Paleogene they diversified rapidly, filling niches left by extinct Mesozoic bird groups. It was one of the fastest diversifications of any group, with modern bird groups likely split within about four million years. DNA studies trace nearly every modern lineage except fowl and palaeognaths to the Paleocene. Fossils from that time are scarce and mostly waterbirds. The earliest known tree-dwelling crown bird, the mousebird Tsidiiyazhi, dates to about 62 million years ago.

  <!-- pale-009 -->

  *Figure: The four bird lineages that survived the K–Pg extinction.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Nadir, a second impact off West Africa** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  Chicxulub may have had company. An asteroid at least 400 m wide struck the seafloor on the Guinea Plateau, off Guinea-Bissau, leaving a crater about 9.2 km across. It formed at or near the K–Pg boundary, around the same time as Chicxulub, though its age is uncertain by about a million years. The impact would have raised tsunami waves up to 1 km high. It would also have released greenhouse gases from buried black shales.

  <!-- pale-012 -->

- **Pantodonts, the first big plant-eating mammals** — c. 66 million years ago (66 Ma)

  The first mammals to grow large after the extinction were plant-eaters called pantodonts. The earliest, such as the dog-sized Bemalambda, appear in the early Paleocene Shanghuan Formation of China. In North America they show up in the middle Paleocene and grew larger as the epoch went on. Barylambda was the largest Paleocene form, a sign of how quickly mammals were filling the spaces dinosaurs had left.

  <!-- pale-013 -->

- **Corral Bluffs, a window on the recovery** — during the Early Paleocene, 66–62 million years ago (66–61.66 Ma)

  Few places show the world just before and just after the asteroid in one stack of rock. Colorado's Denver Formation does. Its layers span the latest Cretaceous to the early Paleocene, through the boundary event itself. It holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Paleocene mammal faunas, recording mammals diversifying right after the extinction. Its Danian Corral Bluffs locality also yields new species, such as the alligator relative Mandrasuchus.

  <!-- pale-002 -->

- **The oldest undisputed placental mammals** — during the Early Paleocene, 66–62 million years ago (66–61.66 Ma)

  Placental mammals, the group that includes whales, bats and people, had roots in the Cretaceous but became visible only after the dinosaurs died. Placentals, marsupials and monotremes all originated in the Cretaceous, before their fossils become common. The oldest undisputed placental fossils come from the early Paleocene. The first Paleocene land mammal age, the Puercan, brought taeniodonts, early hoofed 'condylarths' and possible primate relatives such as Purgatorius. Most Paleocene mammals, though, have uncertain relationships to living groups.

  <!-- pale-003 -->

- **Multituberculates peak, then fade** — during the Early Paleocene, 66–62 million years ago (66–61.66 Ma)

  The most successful mammals of the dinosaur age had one last golden moment. Multituberculates, rodent-like mammals, reached their peak diversity in the early Paleocene. European and North American forms bounced back quickly after the K–Pg event, but Asian ones were devastated. From the middle Paleocene they declined. They were probably outcompeted by placental mammals such as rodents and hoofed ungulates.

  <!-- pale-011 -->

- **The Alpine collision begins** — during the Paleocene, 66–56 million years ago (66–56 Ma)

  The Alps began to rise when an entire ocean disappeared. By the Paleocene the Piemont-Liguria Ocean had fully subducted, sinking beneath the Apulian plate, and Apulia began colliding with Europe. This collision would go on to raise the Alps and the Apennines. The small Briançonnais microcontinent then arrived at the subduction zone. Africa, Arabia and India had long been converging on Eurasia, but the major phases of Alpine mountain building began in the Paleocene to Eocene. Alpine stresses reached far, uplifting the Sudetes and perhaps faulting rocks as far away as Öland in Sweden.

  <!-- pale-001 -->

- **The great Paleocene coal swamps** — during the Paleocene, 66–56 million years ago (66–56 Ma)

  Much of America's electricity has come from Paleocene swamps. Several major coal deposits formed in the Paleocene. They include the Fort Union Formation, which yields 43% of American coal, Texas's Wilcox Group and Colombia's Cerrejón. Powder River Basin coal began forming about 60 million years ago as the land rose out of a shallow sea. In Wyoming, eroding highlands buried plant matter, building thick coal beds.

  <!-- pale-005 -->

- **The Laramide uplift keeps raising the Rockies** — during the Paleocene, 66–56 million years ago (66–56 Ma)

  The mountain building that began under the dinosaurs kept going long after them. The Laramide orogeny raises the Rockies continued raising the Rocky Mountains through the Paleocene. It deformed the crust deeply, from Canada to northern Mexico, in pulses separated by quiet phases. The Denver Basin sank between 66 and 45 million years ago as the uplift built the Colorado Rockies. Together with the collapse of the continental borderland, the orogeny reversed the course of the California River. When it ended is disputed: one account says the end of the Paleocene, others place it between 55 and 35 million years ago.

  <!-- pale-006 -->

- **Boltysh, an aftershock from space** — 65 million years ago (65.39 ± 0.16 Ma)

  Life had barely begun recovering from Chicxulub when another rock arrived. An impact in what is now Ukraine left the Boltysh crater, 24 km across. Argon–argon dating in 2021 places it in the Danian, about 650,000 years after Chicxulub. That study suggested the impact may have disrupted recovery from the extinction. It might also explain a fern spike, a burst of ferns in the fossil record.

  <!-- pale-016 -->

- **Dan-C2, the first hyperthermal** — c. 65 million years ago (65.2 Ma)

  Not long after the extinction, the oceans felt a fever. Early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon, especially in the deep sea. It was the first of the early Paleogene hyperthermals, brief episodes of rapid warming, at the very base of the Cenozoic. It may have released carbon stored in the deep sea since the mid-Maastrichtian, once deep water warmed past a threshold. Or it may have followed a pulse of Deccan volcanism.

  <!-- pale-017 -->

- **South America's own hoofed mammals** — c. 65–63 million years ago (65–63 Ma)

  South America grew a whole set of hoofed mammals found nowhere else. Its native ungulates, such as notoungulates and litopterns, appeared in the early Paleocene, around 65–63 million years ago. They probably descended from North American 'condylarth' ancestors. Litopterns, for example, appear around 62.5 million years ago. These lineages lasted until the end of the Pleistocene, about 12,000 years ago. Ancient proteins show that litopterns were true ungulates, related to today's horses, rhinos and tapirs.

  <!-- pale-019 -->

- **Plesiadapiforms, forerunners of the primates** — c. 65–55 million years ago (65–55 Ma)

  Fingernails may have first appeared on a small Paleocene mammal. Plesiadapiforms, early relatives or forerunners of primates, first appear in the fossil record between 65 and 55 million years ago. They diversified in North America from about 65.1 million years ago and may be the earliest mammals with nails instead of claws. Purgatorius, a possible primate relative, is among the new mammals of the first Paleocene mammal age, though it may sit outside primates. Timelines place the first true primates around 60 million years ago. Many plesiadapiforms were gone by the Eocene.

  <!-- pale-018 -->

- **Faxe's cold-water coral mounds** — c. 64–63 million years ago (64–63 Ma)

  Corals do not need warm, sunny water. In Denmark, the Baunekule facies of the Faxe Formation preserves an exceptionally intact cold-water coral mound ecosystem from 64–63 million years ago. Dendrophyllia corals dominated the mounds. Gastropods, tubeworms, bivalves and bryozoans lived among them, a whole community frozen in limestone.

  <!-- pale-021 -->

- **Creodonts, the first big mammal meat-eaters** — c. 63 million years ago (63 Ma)

  Before cats and dogs took over, other mammals held the role of carnivore. Creodonts, an important group of meat-eating mammals, evolved about 63 million years ago. The earliest oxyaenids appear in North America's Tiffanian age, from about 62.3 million years ago. Hyainailouroid hyaenodonts, another branch, probably evolved in Afro-Arabia during the late Paleocene.

  <!-- pale-023 -->

- **The Deccan fires die down** — c. 63 million years ago (63 Ma)

  The vast eruptions of The Deccan Traps flood India with lava came in a rush, then faded. The bulk of the lava poured from fissures in the Western Ghats between 66 and 65 million years ago. Two-thirds of it may have formed within a million years around 65.5 million years ago. India's plate motion slowed around 63 million years ago. By then the main phase of Deccan volcanism had ended.

  <!-- pale-024 -->

- **The Latest Danian Event** — c. 62 million years ago (62.2 Ma)

  About 62.2 million years ago, the whole ocean, from surface to floor, warmed by 1.6–2.8 °C. This Latest Danian Event, also called the Top Chron C27n Event, lasted about 200,000 years. It came with rising carbon and ocean acidification, during major Atlantic seafloor spreading and volcanism off southeast Greenland. Egypt's Qreiya 3 site, laid down in oxygen-poor seas after the event, holds over 500 articulated fish fossils.

  <!-- pale-025 -->

- **The first penguins** — c. 62 million years ago (62 Ma)

  Penguins were among the first birds to give up the air for the sea. The earliest, Crossvallia and Kupoupou, appear around 62 million years ago in Antarctica and New Zealand. They are the earliest known birds built for life in water. The early penguin Waimanu is one of the few Paleocene bird fossils of any kind. Later came giants: penguins about 2 m tall lived from about 60 to 30 million years ago.

  <!-- pale-026 -->

- **North America's inland sea drains away** — c. 62 million years ago (62 Ma)

  The sea that once split North America in two did not vanish with the dinosaurs. The seaway had joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic since about 100 million years ago. It lasted into the earliest Paleocene, as told in The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two. In the early Paleocene a remnant still flooded the Mississippi Embayment, over the site of Memphis. Around 62 million years ago, falling sea level and retreating inland seas completed the emergence of North America.

  <!-- pale-027 -->

- **The Labrador Sea opens and Greenland breaks free** — c. 62 million years ago (62 Ma)

  Greenland became its own plate when the ocean floor unzipped around it. Seafloor spreading pushed north from the Central Atlantic, between North America and Greenland. It opened the Labrador Sea around 62 million years ago and Baffin Bay around 57 million years ago. The opening split the North Atlantic Craton, a block of ancient crust shared by Labrador and Greenland. Spreading reached the northern Labrador Sea as Greenland slid past Ellesmere Island. By 56 million years ago, Greenland was a separate plate. By about 54 million years ago, spreading had moved into the northeast Atlantic, between Greenland and Eurasia.

  <!-- pale-028 -->

  *Figure: How seafloor spreading opened the seas around Greenland.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Danian–Selandian event** — c. 60 million years ago (60.5 Ma)

  Around 60.5 million years ago, the coastal seas lost their oxygen. Near the Danian–Selandian boundary, oxygen-poor water spread into shallow seas. Sea level dropped too, most likely through warming and evaporation, since no polar ice existed to lock up water. The event is counted among the early Paleogene hyperthermals, the brief warm spikes that began with Dan-C2, the first hyperthermal.

  <!-- pale-029 -->

- **The North Atlantic Igneous Province erupts** — c. 60–54 million years ago (60.5–54.5 Ma)

  The fire that now feeds Iceland's volcanoes was lit beneath Greenland about 65 million years ago. A mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth, rose there. It was the ancestor of today's Iceland hotspot. Its most active magmatism ran from about 60.5 to 54.5 million years ago. It came in two pulses: a pre-break-up phase from 62 to 58 million years ago and a break-up phase from 56 to 54 million years ago. The result was the third-largest magmatic event of the last 150 million years. It produced roughly 5 million cubic kilometers of rock, spread from Canada and Greenland to Britain. It built flood basalts on Baffin Island. It also made the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles, formed between 63 and 52 million years ago. Volcanism on Greenland's southeast margin coincided with The Latest Danian Event around 62.2 million years ago, and the province's break-up phase helped split Greenland from Europe.

  <!-- pale-030 -->

  *Figure: Phases of the North Atlantic Igneous Province.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The first carnivoramorphans** — c. 60 million years ago (60 Ma)

  The ancestors of cats, dogs, bears and seals arrived about 6 million years after the asteroid. Carnivoramorphs, the group that includes today's carnivorans, first appeared in North America about 60 million years ago. The earliest carnivorans, such as Ravenictis and Pristinictis, are Paleocene. The miacids, ancestors of later carnivores, evolved around the same time.

  <!-- pale-032 -->

- **Eritherium, an elephant ancestor the size of a cat** — c. 60 million years ago (60 Ma)

  The first member of the elephant order weighed no more than a house cat. Proboscideans first evolved in Africa around 60 million years ago, during the Selandian. The earliest known, Eritherium, weighed only about 3–8 kg. From such small beginnings would come mammoths and today's elephants.

  <!-- pale-033 -->

- **The High Arctic volcanoes fall silent** — c. 60 million years ago (60 Ma)

  One of Earth's longest-lived volcanic provinces finally went quiet. The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, active since 130 million years ago, ended around 60 million years ago. Its second phase, from about 85 to 60 million years ago, had brought mildly alkaline magmatism and flood basalts. It covers over 1,000,000 km², one of the largest magmatic complexes on Earth.

  <!-- pale-034 -->

- **India meets Asia** — c. 60 million years ago (60 Ma)

  India's long sprint north ended in a slow-motion crash that still continues. Racing north since the Late Cretaceous, India had begun its collision with Asia by the Paleocene. One account dates the collision to the middle Paleocene, about 60 million years ago, starting the Himalayan orogeny. Southern Tibet's Gangdese batholith, a huge body of once-molten rock, reawakened around 65 million years ago as India approached. It stayed active for 20 million years. Between about 60 and 50 million years ago, the leading edge of Greater India struck the West Burma block. But the timing is genuinely debated. Models range from late Paleocene contact to collision in the middle Eocene, as India hits Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise explains.

  <!-- pale-035 -->

- **Titanoboa and the first rainforest** — c. 60–58 million years ago (60–58 Ma)

  The longest snake ever recorded hunted in a steaming Colombian forest about 60 million years ago. Titanoboa grew over 13 m long. Its world was the Cerrejón Formation, 60–58 million years ago, which holds the earliest record of Neotropical rainforest, on a wet coastal plain near 5°N. Alongside lived Carbonemys, a turtle with a 1.7 m shell. A snake that size implies mean annual temperatures of 30–34 °C, though estimates from leaves run 6–8 °C cooler. The forest's plants already belonged to modern rainforest families such as palms, legumes and aroids. Yet low plant diversity and unspecialized insect damage show it was still recovering from the K–Pg extinction 7 million years later.

  <!-- pale-037 -->

  *Figure: The mean annual temperature range implied by Titanoboa’s size.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Izanagi ridge sinks beneath East Asia** — c. 60–50 million years ago (60–50 Ma)

  An entire spreading ridge vanished under Asia, and with it much of its history. At the start of the Paleogene, the Pacific Ocean floor was made of four plates: the Pacific, Farallon, Kula and Izanagi. Between 60 and 50 million years ago, the Izanagi–Pacific spreading ridge began to be subducted beneath East Asia. Little Izanagi sea floor survives, so the history of that margin is poorly known.

  <!-- pale-036 -->

- **Late Paleocene cooling and brief ice** — c. 60–58 million years ago (59.7–58.1 Ma)

  Even in the warm Paleocene, there may have been moments of ice. From 59.7 to 58.1 million years ago, the burial of organic carbon cooled the climate, lowered sea level and allowed brief ice growth. Some evidence suggests Antarctica began to ice over as early as the late Paleocene, sometime between 60 and 45.5 million years ago. Other evidence disagrees, finding no significant ice sheets or sea ice from the late Paleocene into the early Eocene.

  <!-- pale-038 -->

- **Dinoceratans, horned giants of the late Paleocene** — during the Late Paleocene, 59–56 million years ago (59.24–56 Ma)

  Some of the strangest mammals ever were the dinoceratans, big plant-eaters with horns and tusk-like canine teeth. They appear in the late Paleocene. Early forms such as Prodinoceras show up almost at once in North America and Asia. That timing implies a land link between the continents, probably Beringia. Near the end of the Tiffanian age, the uintatheres among them migrated to North America from Asia.

  <!-- pale-040 -->

- **Rodents and rabbits appear** — during the Late Paleocene, 59–56 million years ago (59.24–56 Ma)

  Rabbits may have begun on an island the size of a continent. Lagomorphs, the rabbit order, appear in the late Paleocene and may have evolved in India while it was isolated at sea. The earliest rodents, such as Tribosphenomys and Paramys, are also Paleocene. Rodents immigrated from Asia to North America in the Clarkforkian age, from about 57.5 million years ago.

  <!-- pale-041 -->

- **The Thulean land bridge** — during the Late Paleocene, 59–56 million years ago (59.24–56 Ma)

  For a time, animals could walk from Britain to Greenland. A land bridge, now sunk beneath the Atlantic, appeared in the late Paleocene and linked the British Isles to Greenland, and so Europe to North America. This Thulean route was open around 57 and 55.8 million years ago. On the other side of the world, Beringia linked North America and Asia at 65.5 and 58 million years ago. The Thulean bridge disappeared in the early Eocene.

  <!-- pale-042 -->

- **The Mid-Paleocene Biotic Event** — c. 59 million years ago (59 Ma)

  Around 59 million years ago, methane from the seafloor sent temperatures spiking. The warming came just before the Selandian–Thanetian boundary, probably from a mass release of deep-sea methane hydrate, methane frozen into ice. A second pulse, MPBE-2, followed 300,000 years later. Together they released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming. At Itzurun, Spain, the event shows as a dark 1 m layer poor in calcium carbonate.

  <!-- pale-044 -->

  *Figure: Carbon released by the two pulses of the Mid-Paleocene Biotic Event.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The long slide into the Eocene hothouse** — c. 58–50 million years ago (58–50 Ma)

  Over eight million years, the world warmed by about 6 °C. From the late Paleocene through the early Eocene, about 58 to 50 million years ago, Earth warmed over the long term, interrupted by sharp hyperthermals. Global mean surface temperature in the latest Paleocene, about 57 million years ago, is estimated at 22.3–28.3 °C. The relatively cool late Paleocene ended with the Thanetian Thermal Event and then The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. As the world warmed, plant diversity at both poles rose through the Paleocene, especially at its end.

  <!-- pale-046 -->

- **The Hiawatha impact under Greenland's ice** — 58 million years ago (57.99 ± 0.54 Ma)

  Under a Greenland glacier lies the crater of an iron asteroid. A metallic asteroid about 1.5 km wide left a 31 km crater, now buried under the Hiawatha Glacier. Argon–argon and uranium–lead dating of zircons in its melt rock give 57.99 ± 0.54 million years, in the late Paleocene. That age rules out a link to the Younger Dryas, a much later cold spell, and the impact has no clear climatic effects.

  <!-- pale-047 -->

- **The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum** — c. 56 million years ago (56 Ma)

  At the end of the Paleocene, Earth released carbon at a pace that rivals the burning of fossil fuels. About 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans. Temperatures spiked and the sea turned more acidic. Global average temperature rose about 5–8 °C during an event that lasted about 200,000 years. Mid-latitude and polar regions may have been warmer than today's tropics. The source of the carbon is still debated. Candidates include magma sills baking organic-rich sediments in The North Atlantic Igneous Province erupts, methane clathrates on the seafloor and kimberlite eruptions at Lac de Gras, Canada. How fast it began is uncertain too: anywhere from a few decades to several thousand years. Deep-sea life took the hit. The event wiped out 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera, bottom-dwelling shelled microbes that had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed. The PETM is linked to one of the smaller mass extinctions, and it marks the start of the Eocene.

  <!-- pale-048 -->

  *Figure: Proposed carbon sources and the effects of the PETM.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Magma sills bake sediments] -.-> D[Carbon release]
  B[Methane clathrates] -.-> D
  C[Kimberlite eruptions] -.-> D
  D --> E[Temperatures spike]
  D --> F[Sea acidifies]
  E --> G[Benthic foraminifera lost]
  F --> G
  ```

##### Eocene Epoch

The Eocene opened in heat. Around its start, oxygen in the atmosphere more or less doubled, and the warmth of the PETM brought modern mammal groups into North America. Primates, songbirds, parrots and loons all appear early in the epoch. India crashed into Eurasia, and Greenland split from Europe. Soon came the EECO, the warmest sustained interval of the whole Cenozoic.

- **Oxygen in the air roughly doubles** — c. 56 million years ago (56 Ma)

  At about the start of the Eocene, roughly 56 million years ago, the air itself changed. The amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled. Every breath taken by an early Eocene animal held far more oxygen than the air of only a short while before. The shift came just as the new, hot epoch began.

  <!-- eoce-003 -->

- **Modern mammal orders burst onto the scene** — c. 56 million years ago (56 Ma)

  Most of the major branches of today's mammals show up in the rocks almost at once. The warming of The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum brought more modern mammal groups into North America while many Paleocene forms declined. The oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear within a brief early Eocene window. Among them are artiodactyls, the even-toed hoofed mammals, and perissodactyls, the odd-toed ones. Hyaenodontids, meat-eaters, arrived too. The odd-toed ungulates seem to have arisen in Asia: Cambaytherium, from western India, dates to roughly 54.5 million years ago. The newcomers shared a new body plan. They had long thin legs, grasping hands and feet, and teeth shaped for chewing. All were small, under 10 kg. In fact, Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

  <!-- eoce-011 -->

  *Figure: How PETM warming reshaped North America's mammals.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[PETM warming] --> B[Modern mammal groups arrive]
  A --> C[Paleocene forms decline]
  B --> D[Artiodactyls]
  B --> E[Perissodactyls]
  B --> F[Hyaenodontids]
  ```

- **The Fur Formation, a Danish fossil treasure** — c. 56–54 million years ago (56–54.5 Ma)

  Northern Denmark keeps a layered diary of the earliest Eocene. About 60 m of diatom-rich clay, with up to 180 ash layers, settled on the earliest Eocene seafloor there. Diatoms are single-celled algae with glassy shells. Laid down just after the PETM, the deposit holds a tropical to subtropical flora that points to a climate about 4–8 °C warmer than today. It preserves abundant fish, insects, reptiles, birds and plants, including one of the richest Eocene fossil insect faunas.

  <!-- eoce-009 -->

- **Champsosaurs, the last crocodile look-alikes, die out** — during the Early Eocene, 56–48 million years ago (56–48.07 Ma)

  Champsosaurus survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, but not the heat that followed. It and its crocodile-like relatives, the neochoristoderes, died out in the early Eocene. Their loss coincides with the turnover of mammals linked to the warmth of the PETM. Only the small lizard-like Lazarussuchus carried the wider choristodere line on, in Europe, until the Miocene.

  <!-- eoce-004 -->

- **Gastornis, the giant flightless bird** — c. 56–40 million years ago (56–40 Ma)

  In the forests of the early Eocene stalked a bird too big to fly. Gastornis, a large flightless bird, appears in the fossil record about 56 million years ago. It lasted a long time, going extinct only about 40 million years ago. Birds, not just mammals, produced giants after the dinosaurs.

  <!-- eoce-010 -->

- **The first true primates** — c. 55 million years ago (55 Ma)

  The oldest ancestor of every monkey, ape and human known so far was a tiny animal called Archicebus achilles. It lived about 55 million years ago, and it is the earliest known ancestor of primates. At the start of the Eocene, true primates spread fast. In North America, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms of Plesiadapiforms, forerunners of the primates. Primates moved between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago, across the land links of the time. Then the family tree branched. Primates split into strepsirrhines, the lemurs and lorises, and haplorhines, the tarsiers and anthropoids. The anthropoids are the branch that would one day include monkeys, apes and people. By about 50 million years ago, both branches had diversified.

  <!-- eoce-014 -->

  *Figure: The two primate branches.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Songbirds, parrots and loons appear** — c. 55 million years ago (55 Ma)

  Many of the birds at a backyard feeder belong to orders born in the Eocene. Songbirds, parrots, loons, swifts and woodpeckers all first appeared then. The oldest known stem loon, Nasidytes, comes from England's London Clay, about 55 million years old. The first perching birds, the passerines, appear around 52.5 million years ago. The woodpecker order dates from the early Eocene, and the kingfisher order from the middle Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-017 -->

- **India hits Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise** — c. 55–50 million years ago (55–50 Ma)

  The world's highest mountains are the crumple zone of a continental crash. India's collision with the Eurasian plate is most often dated to about 55–50 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated. India's northwestern corner touched Eurasia first, about 55 million years ago. Contact along the Yarlung–Zangbo suture, the seam where the two plates join, began around 50 million years ago. The impact shows in India's speed. Around 55 million years ago its plate slowed from about 18–19.5 cm a year to about 4.5 cm a year, circumstantial evidence of the collision. The crash closed the Tethys Ocean there and began thrusting up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. Not everyone accepts this picture. Rival models have a microcontinent colliding first, with India itself arriving only around 40 million years ago, or even at the end of the Oligocene. The timing and nature of the collision remain genuinely contested.

  <!-- eoce-015 -->

  *Figure: India's plate slowed sharply around 55 Ma.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Pyrenees take shape** — c. 55–47 million years ago (55–47 Ma)

  The mountains between Spain and France were built by a long, hard squeeze. Iberia and Europe, converging since about 100 million years ago, collided in the Eocene and Oligocene. From about 55 million years ago the Pyrenees underwent very strong crustal compression, which set up the range's present structure. This main phase lasted until about 47 million years ago. It shortened the crust by about 4 mm a year and stacked sheets of rock one on top of another.

  <!-- eoce-016 -->

- **The North Atlantic splits Greenland from Europe** — c. 54 million years ago (54 Ma)

  The old northern supercontinent Laurasia finally broke in two when the North Atlantic opened. By 56 million years ago Greenland was already its own plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift. Seafloor spreading then crept north from the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay. By about 54 million years ago, it had split Greenland from Eurasia. The break-up volcanism of The North Atlantic Igneous Province erupts ran from about 56 to 54 million years ago, forming the Iceland Plateau and Greenland's Skaergaard intrusion. Extension between North America and Eurasia also opened the Eurasian Basin across the Arctic.

  <!-- eoce-021 -->

- **The London Clay's tropical flora** — c. 54–50 million years ago (54–50 Ma)

  Under the streets of London lie the fruits of a tropical forest. Shallow seas over southeast England laid down the London Clay, rich in fossil seeds and fruits of some 350 plant species. Its flora includes tropical plants that now grow in Asia. They are a sign of how much warmer the early Eocene climate was.

  <!-- eoce-020 -->

- **The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum** — c. 54–49 million years ago (54–49 Ma)

  Alligators once lived north of the Arctic Circle, and palms grew in Alaska. That was the world of the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, the EECO. It was a long spell of extreme greenhouse warmth, the warmest sustained interval of the whole Cenozoic. A series of intense early Eocene hyperthermals set it off, including Eocene Thermal Maximum 2, nicknamed Elmo and Eocene Thermal Maximum 3. Global mean surface temperature is estimated at about 23–30 °C. The hothouse from 56 to 47 million years ago ran about 14 °C warmer than today. Antarctic summers reached about 25 °C. Amphibians, too, lived in the Arctic. The warmth puzzles scientists. Climate models struggle to reproduce such warm poles and mild polar winters, a puzzle called the equable climate problem.

  <!-- eoce-018 -->

  *Figure: Hyperthermals that set off the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[ETM-2] --> C[EECO]
  B[ETM-3] --> C
  C --> D[Warmest Cenozoic interval]
  ```

- **Eocene Thermal Maximum 2, nicknamed Elmo** — c. 54 million years ago (53.7 Ma)

  After the PETM, the Earth ran a second, smaller fever. ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 and was less severe. Its timing is strikingly regular: it came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM. Eccentricity is how stretched Earth's orbit is, and it changes on a slow rhythm. That pattern suggests orbital forcing may have triggered it. Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they led into the warmest part of the Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-022 -->

- **The Green River lakes** — c. 54–48 million years ago (53.5–48.5 Ma)

  Some of the world's most beautiful fossil fish come from lakes in the Rockies. Mountain building there created basins where Lakes Gosiute, Uinta and Fossil Lake laid down the oil shales of the Green River Formation. Their bottom muds held little oxygen. That slowed decay and kept scavengers away, preserving fish, leaves and even soft parts of insects. The formation is perhaps the best record of Cenozoic freshwater life, with fish, crocodilians, birds and mammals. The climate was frost-free, so crocodiles lived among sycamore forests, even as the moist early Eocene turned slightly drier.

  <!-- eoce-023 -->

- **Pakicetids, the first whales, walked on land** — c. 53 million years ago (53 Ma)

  The first whales had hooves. The pakicetids, a family of hoofed land mammals that lived about 53 million years ago, are the earliest whales. Their closest known relative was Indohyus, of the family Raoellidae. Even on land, pakicetids already had a whale's ear: they could hear under water through bone conduction rather than eardrums. Bone conduction carries sound through the skull bones themselves. It was the first step on a remarkable journey. During the Eocene, whales became very diverse and made the full transition from land to sea. That path runs through Ambulocetus, the walking whale to the giant, fully marine Basilosaurus, the giant fully marine whale.

  <!-- eoce-024 -->

- **Eocene Thermal Maximum 3** — c. 53 million years ago (52.8 Ma)

  Hothouse worlds tend to come in a sequence of spikes. ETM-3, informally the K or X event, was another early Eocene hyperthermal, about 52.8 million years ago. It is marked by a pulse of isotopically light carbon, the kind released from organic matter. Its carbon-isotope excursion marks the onset of The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

  <!-- eoce-025 -->

- **Eohippus and the first horses** — c. 52 million years ago (52 Ma)

  The ancestors of horses were small forest animals. The first equids lived in North America by the earliest Eocene, with early relatives of unclear affinity in Europe. Eohippus appeared about 52 million years ago. One of its species branched into various new types of horse. Thousands of complete skeletons come from Eocene layers, mainly in Wyoming's Wind River basin. About 50 million years ago Eohippus graded into Orohippus. That gave rise to Epihippus, with better grinding teeth, about 47 million years ago. Their European cousins, the palaeotheres, arose later in the early Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-027 -->

  *Figure: The early horse line from Eohippus to Miohippus.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Eohippus] -->|c. 50 Ma| B[Orohippus]
  B -->|c. 47 Ma| C[Epihippus]
  ```

- **The first bats take to the air** — c. 52 million years ago (52 Ma)

  Only about 16 million years after the dinosaurs died out, mammals learned to fly. The earliest known bats, such as Onychonycteris, appear about 52 million years ago. With bats, mammals had colonized the air by the Eocene. Bats also travelled far: lineages crossed from Africa to South America during the Eocene, possibly by way of Antarctica.

  <!-- eoce-028 -->

- **Cambay amber, an Indian insect trap** — c. 52–50 million years ago (52–50 Ma)

  Tree resin is a perfect trap for small creatures, and it can hold them for tens of millions of years. Amber from Gujarat, India, preserves an important early Eocene assemblage of arthropods, mostly insects. It dates to about 52–50 million years ago, around the time India was meeting Asia.

  <!-- eoce-026 -->

- **The Okanagan Highlands lakes** — c. 52–48 million years ago (52–48 Ma)

  Even the mountains of the Pacific Northwest grew palms in the Eocene. Lakes in the uplands of British Columbia and Washington preserved detailed plants, insects and fish through The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. Fossil palm beetles at McAbee, dated to about 52.9 million years, show that palms grew there. The 48.7-million-year-old Princeton Chert preserves plants in anatomical detail. It also holds the oldest known ectomycorrhizal fungi, which wrap around tree roots and trade nutrients with them.

  <!-- eoce-029 -->

- **Cats and dogs part ways** — c. 50 million years ago (50 Ma)

  The split between cat people and dog people goes back about 50 million years. The ancestors of cats and of dogs diverged then, among the first true carnivorans. Arctoids, the branch of bears, weasels and raccoons, are known on all continents from 46 million years ago. Early carnivorans stayed small, while oxyaenids and mesonychians held the top-predator roles. Crown-group carnivorans, the branch that includes all living members, first appeared around 42 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-032 -->

- **The Sevier orogeny ends** — c. 50 million years ago (50 Ma)

  A belt of thrust faults in western North America had been folding and stacking rock for a very long time. Deformation in the Sevier fold-and-thrust belt, under way since about 160 million years ago, ended around 50 million years ago. In southwestern Utah, some Sevier thrusts may have stayed active until later in the Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-035 -->

- **Monte Bolca, the fishbowl of Verona** — c. 50–49 million years ago (50–49 Ma)

  Some fossil fish from Italy still show their colors. Near Verona, low-oxygen mud preserved fish so well that their organs are often intact, and skin color can sometimes be read. The site's Pesciara, meaning 'fishbowl', is famous for these extraordinarily well-preserved Eocene fish, from about 50–49 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-034 -->

- **Ambulocetus, the walking whale** — c. 49 million years ago (49 Ma)

  About 49 million years ago, whales were part crocodile in style. Ambulocetus was a probably amphibious early whale that lived, crocodile-like, in the bays and estuaries of the Tethys Ocean, in what is now northern Pakistan. By then, whales had returned to the water. Ambulocetus marks the halfway point between Pakicetids, the first whales, walked on land and fully marine whales.

  <!-- eoce-036 -->

- **The great Eocene cooling begins** — c. 49–34 million years ago (49–34 Ma)

  About 49 million years ago, the planet's thermostat turned, and a long cooling began. The warming climate gave way to cooling, a slow trend that lasted until about 34 million years ago. Changing geography drove the first drop. As Australia and South America drew away from Antarctica, ocean circulation shifted. Falling carbon dioxide kept the cooling going. It was drawn down by organic productivity and by the weathering of new mountains. Models suggest the carbon dioxide mattered more than the isolation of Antarctica's ocean. Signs of cold appeared. Cold-water diatoms suggest winter sea ice formed in the Arctic, and Antarctica shows glaciation by about 37 million years ago. The cooling that began in the middle Eocene ultimately led to the ice ages of the Quaternary.

  <!-- eoce-037 -->

  *Figure: Causes of the Middle–Late Eocene cooling and where it led.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Continents draw away from Antarctica] --> B[Ocean circulation changes]
  B --> D[Cooling]
  C[CO2 falls] --> D
  D --> E[Quaternary ice ages]
  ```

- **The Azolla event: a fern that cooled the world** — c. 48 million years ago (48.5 Ma)

  A tiny floating fern may have helped pull Earth out of its hothouse. In the middle Eocene the Arctic Ocean was almost cut off from the wider seas. Its warm surface and high carbon dioxide let the fern Azolla grow rapidly across it. With modest warmth and 20 hours of polar summer daylight, Azolla can double its mass in two to three days. When the ferns died, they sank to the stagnant seafloor. Over about 800,000 years, they were buried in sediment, building large deposits that locked away carbon. Carbon dioxide fell catastrophically, from about 3,500 ppm in the early Eocene to 650 ppm during the event. The drawdown is believed to have ended the early Eocene warmth about 48.5 million years ago. Temperatures fell rapidly from 49 to 47 million years ago. Soon glacial dropstones, rocks carried out by floating ice, became common in Arctic sediments.

  <!-- eoce-038 -->

  *Figure: How a floating fern drew down carbon and ended early Eocene warmth.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Isolated warm Arctic, high CO2] --> B[Azolla spreads]
  B --> C[Dead ferns sink, buried]
  C --> D[Carbon locked away]
  D --> E[CO2 falls]
  E --> F[Early Eocene warmth ends]
  ```

  *Figure: Carbon dioxide fell catastrophically during the Azolla event.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Lutetian limestone, the stone of Paris** — during the Lutetian, 48–41 million years ago (48.07–41.03 Ma)

  The Louvre is built from the floor of an Eocene sea. In the middle Lutetian, a sea over the Paris Basin laid down marine limestone, later topped by freshwater limestone and marl once the sea withdrew. The Lutetian age, 48.07–41.03 million years ago, is named after this stone, from Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris. Used since Roman times, this 'Paris stone' built many of the city's grandest buildings, including parts of the Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe.

  <!-- eoce-041 -->

- **Rifts open across western Europe** — during the Middle Eocene, 48–38 million years ago (48.07–37.71 Ma)

  The same collision that raised the Alps also tore western Europe open. From the Eocene onward, the ongoing Alpine collision opened a north–south system of rifts, long valleys where the crust pulls apart. The Limagne Graben formed in the middle Eocene and held a lake. Rifting also began in the Bresse Graben.

  <!-- eoce-039 -->

- **Grasses spread and the first savannas appear** — during the Middle Eocene, 48–38 million years ago (48.07–37.71 Ma)

  Grasslands began as a thin fringe along rivers. As the climate cooled and dried after the EECO, grasses began to spread. During the Eocene they moved out from riverbanks into open tracts. Subhumid savannas, open grassy country with scattered trees, are known in South America from the middle Eocene. The change opened new country for grazing animals.

  <!-- eoce-040 -->

- **The Kula plate disappears beneath Alaska** — c. 48 million years ago (48 Ma)

  An entire tectonic plate can be swallowed whole. The Kula plate had been subducting under Alaska and the Yukon since the early Eocene. Around 48 million years ago it was entirely consumed. Only a slab of it remains, deep in the mantle under the Bering Sea.

  <!-- eoce-044 -->

- **Geiseltal, a German lignite treasure** — c. 48–41 million years ago (48–41 Ma)

  A coal mine in central Germany turned out to be a vault of Eocene life. A coastal moorland of lakes and tidal bays there preserved over 50,000 fossil vertebrates, along with insects and plants. Its soft tissues were among the very first found from the Eocene. Its mammals are so characteristic that they define a European land-mammal stage.

  <!-- eoce-043 -->

- **Forests near the poles** — c. 48–41 million years ago (47.5–41.3 Ma)

  Some of the strangest Eocene forests grew where today there is only ice and tundra. High-Arctic river deposits in Nunavut preserve old-growth conifer forests where they stood, with leaf litter preserved down to the molecular level. Swamp cypress and dawn redwood grew on Ellesmere Island, and subtropical plants in Greenland and Alaska. In the far south, pollen from Prydz Bay shows taiga forest grew in Antarctica too.

  <!-- eoce-045 -->

- **The Messel Pit** — c. 47 million years ago (47 Ma)

  In a German pit, fossils still show fur, feathers and the outlines of skin. About 47 million years ago a lake at Messel, in Hesse, Germany, preserved over 1,400 kinds of plants and animals, the best record of its time. It was a maar lake, a deep crater lake left by a volcanic blast, ringed by lush subtropical forest. The climate was close to The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, with a mean yearly temperature of 22 °C, and the site lay 10° farther south. Animals sank into deep, oxygen-poor water where no scavengers reached them, so whole skeletons survive. How they died is debated. Bursts of toxic volcanic gas, like Lake Nyos in 1986, may have killed them; others blame toxic cyanobacterial blooms. Its fossils, from pygmy horses and early primates to bats, keep yielding major discoveries about early mammals and birds.

  <!-- eoce-047 -->

- **The Hawaiian–Emperor bend: the Pacific plate turns** — c. 47 million years ago (47 Ma)

  A sharp elbow in a line of undersea volcanoes records the moment a whole plate changed direction. The kink in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain marks the Pacific plate's sudden swing from northward to northwestward motion about 47 million years ago. The change followed the onset of subduction along the plate's western edge. A wider reorganization of Pacific plate motions started the Izu-Bonin-Mariana and Tonga-Kermadec subduction zones.
