Several causes may have combined to make the bend. A northward pull ended around 47 million years ago, and the hotspot itself had drifted south from about 50 million years ago. The new western subduction zones added their own tug.

  <!-- eoce-048 -->

- **Baltic amber, the great insect vault** — c. 47–35 million years ago (47–35 Ma)

  The biggest single store of fossil insects on Earth is made of tree resin. Baltic amber, the largest amber deposit anywhere, preserves invertebrates, plants and small vertebrates of a subtropical eastern European forest. Its exact age is controversial. Estimates include 47–40 and 43–35 million years ago. Two other major European ambers, from Bitterfeld in Germany and Rovno in Ukraine, date to 38–34 million years ago and share much of its fauna.

  <!-- eoce-046 -->

- **Kishenehn's blood-filled mosquito** — c. 46 million years ago (46.2 Ma)

  A mosquito from Montana died with its last meal still inside it. Oil shale there, about 46.2 million years old, preserves exquisitely detailed insects. Among them is a blood-filled mosquito with traces of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying molecule in blood, still detectable after tens of millions of years.

  <!-- eoce-050 -->

- **Silverpit, a disputed crater under the North Sea** — c. 46–43 million years ago (46–43 Ma)

  Under the North Sea, about 130 km off the Humber estuary, lies a buried structure that looks like a crater. Whether it is one is still argued. A 2025 study says yes: an impact crater about 3.2 km wide, ringed by an 18 km disturbed zone, formed 46–43 million years ago. Others attribute it to moving underground salt, an explanation favored in a 2009 debate. Its impact origin remains disputed.

  <!-- eoce-052 -->

- **The Andes rise and the Altiplano forms** — c. 45 million years ago (45 Ma)

  One of the highest plateaus on Earth began forming in the Eocene. Subduction beneath South America compressed the plate's edge, and the Altiplano started to rise. The high Central Andes and the Bolivian orocline, the great bend in the mountain chain, formed from about 45 million years ago. Major uplift in southern Peru began then too. In northern Peru, the Incaic phase of mountain building struck in the middle and late Eocene. Peru's Western Cordillera had begun rising about 50 million years ago, then paused until the Oligocene. Ever since, the region around the Altiplano and Puna plateaus has been shortened horizontally.

  <!-- eoce-054 -->

- **The Tasmanian Passage opens** — c. 45 million years ago (45 Ma)

  When Australia pulled away from Antarctica, the southern oceans changed course. In one account, the two split around 45 million years ago. Warm equatorial currents were diverted, and a cold-water channel opened between them. The South Tasman Rise had already sunk beneath the sea, forming the Tasmanian Passage. As oceanic crust began separating the continents about 35.5 million years ago, global ocean temperatures dropped significantly. The dates are contested. The general consensus is that the continents had fully separated by 60 million years ago, and 45 million is a minority estimate. A 2013 paper dates the first flow through the gateway, and the cooling, to about 49–50 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-057 -->

- **The Quercy 'natural mummies'** — c. 45–25 million years ago (45–25 Ma)

  In southern France, cracks in limestone became time capsules. Karst fissures, cavities dissolved in the rock, filled with sediment holding mammals, birds, turtles, crocodiles, plants and insects from about 45–25 million years ago. Some amphibians and lizards survive as articulated 'natural mummies', with their soft tissue preserved.

  <!-- eoce-056 -->

- **India and Australia fuse into one plate** — c. 43 million years ago (43 Ma)

  Two of the plates that had drifted apart from Gondwana ended up joined again. The Indo-Australian plate formed when the Indian and Australian plates fused, approximately 43 million years ago. From then on they moved as a single slab of crust.

  <!-- eoce-058 -->

- **The Logoisk crater in Belarus** — c. 42 million years ago (42.3 ± 1.1 Ma)

  Belarus hides a buried crater 15 km wide. A meteorite struck near the town of Lahoysk about 42.3 million years ago and left it. Today it lies beneath younger sediment, invisible at the surface.

  <!-- eoce-059 -->

- **A burst of magnetic reversals** — c. 42 million years ago (42 Ma)

  Around 42 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field could not settle down. It flipped 17 times in 3 million years, swapping north and south again and again. That was a fast pace. Earlier, in a 4-million-year window centered on 54 million years ago, there were 10 reversals, a contrast with the long calm of The magnetic field's long calm ends.

  <!-- eoce-060 -->

  *Figure: Magnetic reversals counted in two windows of the Eocene.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Basilosaurus, the giant fully marine whale** — c. 41–34 million years ago (41.3–33.9 Ma)

  Basilosaurus was a whale, and a huge one. This large predatory archaeocete, an early whale, lived from about 41.3 to 33.9 million years ago. At 17–20 m and up to 15 tonnes, it was one of the largest animals of the Paleogene. It was a top predator of shallow seas, eating sharks, large fish and other marine mammals, especially the smaller whale Dorudon. By the end of the Eocene, whales such as Basilosaurus had become fully aquatic. Its extinction coincides with The Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which ended almost all other archaeocetes.

  <!-- eoce-061 -->

- **The Drake Passage begins to open** — c. 41 million years ago (41 Ma)

  South America and Antarctica were once joined by land. In the early Eocene the Drake Passage, the gap between them, was only a small opening with limited circulation. When it widened is uncertain, with estimates running from 49 to 17 million years ago. Sediments suggest it began opening about 41 million years ago, while tectonic evidence points to about 32 million. The Scotia plate began forming about 40 million years ago, breaking the continuous land from Patagonia to the Antarctic Peninsula. Cooling during the first opening, about 38.5 million years ago, was not global, since the North Atlantic did not cool. Together the Drake and Tasmanian passages ended the Antarctic land bridge in the late Eocene or early Oligocene.

  <!-- eoce-062 -->

- **The Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum** — c. 40 million years ago (40.5–40 Ma)

  For half a million years, the long Eocene cooling went into reverse. From about 40.5 to 40.0 million years ago, a spell of very warm climate interrupted the slide. The warming happened everywhere at once. Mean surface temperature reached about 23 °C, and the Tethys Sea's surface reached 32–36 °C. Carbon dioxide drove it, not methane. One estimate puts CO2 at 4,000 ppm, though other studies find a smaller rise. A minimum in two orbital eccentricity cycles, around 40.2 million years ago, likely helped sustain the warmth. Planktonic foraminifera turned over: acarinids dwindled and morozovellids went extinct.

  <!-- eoce-063 -->

  *Figure: What drove and sustained the Middle Eocene warm spell.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Rising carbon dioxide] --> C[Warming, 40.5-40.0 Ma]
  B[Eccentricity minimum] -.-> C
  C --> D[Foraminifera turnover]
  D --> E[Morozovellids extinct]
  ```

- **Balkanatolia, a lost continent, joins Asia** — c. 40 million years ago (40 Ma)

  About 50 million years ago, Eurasia was not one landmass but three: Western Europe, Balkanatolia and Asia. Balkanatolia, the land that became the Balkans and Anatolia, joined Asia about 40 million years ago. Europe connected only about 34 million years ago. Asian mammals poured in, and they may have driven Balkanatolia's island-like native fauna extinct.

  <!-- eoce-064 -->

  *Figure: When the three pieces of Eurasia joined up.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Eridanos, a lost Baltic river** — c. 40 million years ago (40 Ma)

  Where the Baltic Sea now lies, a great river once flowed. The Eridanos, an ancient river through what is now the Baltic region, began to form about 40 million years ago. Today the Baltic Sea covers the land it once drained.

  <!-- eoce-065 -->

- **Mesohippus, a horse for open country** — c. 40 million years ago (40 Ma)

  As forests thinned, horses had to run. About 40 million years ago Mesohippus appeared suddenly, under strong new selective pressures. Late Eocene horses grew tougher teeth and became larger and leggier, able to outrun predators in open country. Miohippus followed around 36 million years ago, continuing the line from Eohippus and the first horses.

  <!-- eoce-067 -->

- **Rodents and monkeys raft across the Atlantic** — c. 40–36 million years ago (40–36 Ma)

  Some of South America's most famous animals arrived as castaways. About 40 million years ago, caviomorph rodents reached South America, most likely from Africa. Primates followed by 36 million years ago, crossing the same way. The ocean gap was narrower then. Animals floated over on rafts of driftwood or mangrove, perhaps hopping between islands. The rodents gave rise to capybaras, chinchillas and New World porcupines, displacing some small marsupials. Today the descendants of these rafters make up more than twice as many South American species as those of older native mammals.

  <!-- eoce-071 -->

- **Rifting begins in northern Kenya** — c. 40–35 million years ago (40–35 Ma)

  East Africa began to crack open in the Eocene. Volcanism and rifting began around Turkana, in northern Kenya, 40–35 million years ago. The rifting then spread north and south along the Gregory Rift.

  <!-- eoce-070 -->

- **The mid-Tertiary ignimbrite flare-up** — c. 40–25 million years ago (40–25 Ma)

  From about 40 to 25 million years ago, the western United States went through one of Earth's great volcanic outbursts. The eruptions, of andesite to rhyolite lava, produced about 500,000 km³ of explosive and 5 million km³ of effusive rock. Explosive eruptions blast out ash; effusive ones pour out lava. The flare-up followed the end of Laramide compression, as the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion changed. Colorado's San Juan volcanoes became active 40–35 million years ago. New Mexico's Mogollon-Datil field began erupting about 36.2 million years ago. In Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental, Oligocene ash flows stacked ignimbrite sheets, layers of welded volcanic ash, over the largest area of any known series, with ten calderas.

  <!-- eoce-068 -->

- **The last multituberculates** — during the Late Eocene, 38–34 million years ago (37.71–33.9 Ma)

  The longest-reigning mammals of all finally bowed out in the late Eocene. Multituberculates had dominated most mammal assemblages for at least 88 million years, in a lineage that went back to the Jurassic. They had declined since the mid-Paleocene, as Multituberculates peak, then fade describes. The last species, Ectypodus childei, died out in North America near the end of the Eocene, possibly outcompeted by rodents. Only the gondwanatheres outlived them. One account has them lasting into the early Oligocene. Around 35 million years ago, extinctions also struck gastropods, reptiles and amphibians.

  <!-- eoce-076 -->

- **Lake Wanapitei impact** — c. 37 million years ago (37.2 ± 1.2 Ma)

  A round lake in Canada fills the scar of an impact. About 37.2 million years ago, a body from space struck and made a crater 8.4 km across. Today that crater holds Lake Wanapitei.

  <!-- eoce-078 -->

- **The Cascade volcanoes awaken** — c. 37 million years ago (37 Ma)

  The volcanic arc that includes today's Cascade peaks began to burn about 37 million years ago. Volcanism in the Cascade arc of the Pacific Northwest began then. The West Cascades period that followed, from 37 to 17 million years ago, was a time of exceptionally active volcanoes.

  <!-- eoce-079 -->

- **Ice sheets begin to grow on Antarctica** — c. 37–35 million years ago (37–35 Ma)

  By the late Eocene, about 37 million years ago, Antarctica had grown cold enough to hold ice sheets. Oxygen isotopes show ice building up from about 36 million years ago, and permanent ice from about 35 million years ago. Around 35 million years ago, glaciers merged into the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It buried the Gamburtsev Mountains, which remain hidden under the ice. A brief glaciation, the Late Eocene Event, followed about 34.4 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-080 -->

  *Figure: Steps of Antarctica's first ice sheets.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The White River fauna** — c. 37–34 million years ago (37–33.9 Ma)

  Beavers, squirrels and gophers took over North America as the tropics retreated. In North America's Chadronian age, from 37 million years ago, the White River fauna was in full swing. Modern rodent families replaced older tropical ones, alongside early relatives of bears, peccaries and rabbits. The rabbit relatives had come from East Asia, reaching North America in the late Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-082 -->

- **The Mistastin impact in Labrador** — c. 37 million years ago (36.6 Ma)

  In the wilds of Labrador, Canada, lies a crater that was once about 28 km across. An impact made it about 36.6 million years ago, one of several large strikes of the late Eocene.

  <!-- eoce-083 -->

- **Popigai, a giant crater in Siberia** — c. 36 million years ago (35.7 ± 0.2 Ma)

  In northern Siberia lies one of the largest scars ever left by a rock from space. In the late Eocene, a large bolide, an exploding meteor, blasted a 100 km crater there. It is tied as the fourth-largest verified impact structure on Earth. It may be linked to The Eocene–Oligocene extinction. It may also have struck at the same time as the Chesapeake Bay and Toms Canyon impacts.

  <!-- eoce-084 -->

- **The Chesapeake Bay impact** — c. 36 million years ago (35.5 ± 0.3 Ma)

  The shape of Chesapeake Bay owes something to a rock from space. A bolide about 3 km wide struck the eastern shore of North America, then lined with rainforest and shallow limy seas. It left a crater about 85 km wide, now buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. It is one of the best-preserved craters made in the sea. Sediment slumping over its rubble helped shape the bay. The nearby Toms Canyon crater, and possibly Siberia's Popigai, a giant crater in Siberia, may have formed in the same event.

  <!-- eoce-085 -->

- **The Laramide orogeny ends** — c. 35 million years ago (35 Ma)

  The mountain building that raised the Rockies finally wound down, though no one agrees exactly when. The Laramide orogeny, active since the Late Cretaceous, ended sometime between 55 and 35 million years ago. In New Mexico, deformation lasted until about 40 million years ago. As convergence slowed, the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion turned oblique. Volcanism flared across the Basin and Range. Compression gave way to crustal stretching, which in time formed the Basin and Range Province. The orogeny's exact start and end dates remain in dispute.

  <!-- eoce-087 -->

- **Mountain belts rise around the Mediterranean** — c. 35 million years ago (35 Ma)

  Many of the Mediterranean's mountain ranges were born in a single burst of collisions. About 35 million years ago, Adria's Anatolide–Tauride platform entered the subduction trench, beginning the Dinarides, Hellenides and Taurides. Between about 40 and 30 million years ago, subduction began along the western Mediterranean arc of the Tell, Rif, Betic and Apennine chains. The Central and Western Alps formed in a second phase of mountain building, starting at the end of the Eocene, 35 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-088 -->

- **The Ring of Fire takes its modern shape** — c. 35 million years ago (35 Ma)

  The Pacific's ring of volcanoes is surprisingly young in its present form. By about 35 million years ago, the Kula and Farallon plates had been subducted. The Pacific plate was then ringed by subduction much like today's Ring of Fire. The New Zealand subduction zone, the last of its present segments, formed about 35 million years ago.

  <!-- eoce-089 -->

- **Arabia collides with Eurasia and the Zagros rise** — c. 35–26 million years ago (35–26 Ma)

  The mountains of Iran mark where Arabia rammed into Asia. Continental collision between Arabia and Eurasia began about 35 million years ago and continued into the Oligocene, to about 26 million years ago. It closed the Tethys Ocean there and created the Zagros Mountains. Earlier, during the Eocene, a sinking slab of Neotethys ocean floor had broken off near the Arabian margin.

  <!-- eoce-086 -->

- **EOT-1: the first step into the ice age** — c. 34 million years ago (34.1–33.9 Ma)

  Around 34 million years ago, the long cooling crossed a threshold. As carbon dioxide fell, a large ice sheet formed in East Antarctica. Antarctica glaciated in two steps. The first and smaller, EOT-1, came about 34.1–33.9 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary itself. Glaciers sliding off the Gamburtsev Mountains are thought to have seeded the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. By the boundary, an ice sheet in western Antarctica reached the ocean, and glaciers had appeared in Greenland. The oceans changed too. As the Arctic–Atlantic gateway closed, deep overturning circulation shifted from the Pacific to the Atlantic.

  <!-- eoce-090 -->

- **Florissant, a lake of fossils** — c. 34 million years ago (34 Ma)

  In Colorado, a lake dammed by volcanic mudflows became a perfect fossil trap. Diatom blooms in its water finely preserved late Eocene plants and insects, about 34 million years ago. The site is also famous for petrified stumps of giant sequoia relatives.

  <!-- eoce-092 -->

- **Toothed and baleen whales go separate ways** — c. 34 million years ago (34 Ma)

  The great filter-feeding whales began as hunters with teeth. The ancestors of toothed and baleen whales split around 34 million years ago, as the southern oceans' climate changed with the opening of the Drake Passage. The earliest known baleen whale, Mystacodon, 37 to 33 million years old, still had teeth and fed by suction. Later forms carried both baleen and teeth. Then they lost their teeth and became full filter feeders, as all living baleen whales are. Toothed whales are defined by features for echolocation, the use of echoes to sense surroundings, such as a fatty forehead organ called the melon. Oligocene Squalodon skulls give the first hypothesized evidence of it.

  <!-- eoce-094 -->

  *Figure: The steps from toothed ancestors to filter-feeding baleen whales.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Common ancestor] --> B[Toothed whales]
  A --> C[Mystacodon: teeth, suction]
  C --> D[Baleen and teeth]
  D --> E[Toothless filter feeders]
  ```

- **The Eocene–Oligocene extinction** — c. 34 million years ago (33.9 Ma)

  The Eocene closed with the planet flipping from greenhouse to icehouse, and life paid the price. A major extinction and faunal turnover, called the Grande Coupure, or 'great break', in Europe, spanned about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago. It came with sharp cooling, a big drop in sea level and rapid growth of the Antarctic ice sheet. Carbon dioxide fell to about 750–800 ppm. In the sea, hantkeninid planktonic foraminifera went extinct, and their disappearance marks the boundary. Basilosaurus, the giant fully marine whale and nearly all other archaic whales died out. In central North America, the cooling turned over snails, amphibians and reptiles. Some sites show extinctions drawn out over millions of years, beginning in the early Priabonian. The causes are debated and not fully understood. The large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also have played a part.

  <!-- eoce-095 -->

  *Figure: The greenhouse-to-icehouse shift behind the Eocene–Oligocene extinction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[CO2 falls] --> B[Sharp cooling]
  B --> C[Antarctic ice grows]
  C --> D[Sea level drops]
  B --> E[Extinction and turnover]
  D --> E
  ```

##### Oligocene Epoch

About 33.9 million years ago, ice began to build up on Antarctica, and Earth entered the ice age it is still in. The Oligocene is the story of that cooling and everything it touched. Tropical forests shrank toward the equator and grasslands spread around the world. The sea drained from the Obik Sea, joining Europe to Asia, and Asian mammals poured west in a turnover called the 'great break'. Meanwhile Africa pushed into Eurasia, the Alps rose, and the Andes became a major mountain chain.

- **Antarctica freezes and an ice age begins** — c. 34 million years ago (33.9 Ma)

  The ice age you live in today began about 33.9 million years ago, when ice started to build up on Antarctica. That moment opened the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, and it has never ended. The Eocene–Oligocene boundary marks the switch: Earth left its last greenhouse climate and entered the present icehouse, a world with permanent ice at the poles. The main driver was falling carbon dioxide. Once it dropped past a tipping point of about 600 ppm, the Antarctic ice could grow and persist. The north was not spared. Ice-rafted debris, rock dropped on the seafloor by melting icebergs, shows that glaciers had also appeared on Greenland by the start of the Oligocene. For the first time in the Phanerozoic, both poles fell well below freezing at once. Much of what follows in this chapter, from falling seas to spreading grasslands, traces back to this cold turn.

  <!-- olig-012 -->

  *Figure: Falling CO2 started the ice age that continues today.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[CO2 falls past 600 ppm] --> B[Antarctic glaciation]
  B --> C[Late Cenozoic Ice Age]
  ```

- **Ground sloths appear and reach the Caribbean** — during the Early Oligocene, 34–27 million years ago (33.9–27.3 Ma)

  A single femur from Puerto Rico shows that ground sloths had reached the Caribbean by 31 million years ago. The earliest unambiguous ground-sloth fossils come from the early Oligocene, so the group spread fast. By about 30 million years ago the megatheriids had appeared in South America, the family that would later produce the giant ground sloths.

  <!-- olig-008 -->

- **Africa pushes north and the Alps rise** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  Africa kept shoving north into Eurasia, and the crust between them buckled upward. The Alps rose rapidly, and as they did they cut off the remnants of the old Tethys Sea. Most Alpine mountain building happened in the Oligocene and Miocene. The rising range shed its debris northward. From about 30 to 10 million years ago, shallow-marine and continental sediment filled the Molasse basin, a long trough along the northern foot of the Alps. That basin is a record of the mountains wearing down even as they grew.

  <!-- olig-001 -->

- **The Andes grow into a great mountain chain** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  South America's western edge changed its geometry, and a mountain chain answered. Subduction, the sinking of an ocean plate beneath a continent, turned to run more directly into the coast, and the Andes first became a major mountain chain. About 30 million years ago the Andean orogeny, the long mountain-building episode along the margin, was rearranged on a continental scale. The changed subduction fed more volcanism, and the Western Cordillera of the Central Andes began to grow.

  <!-- olig-002 -->

- **Baikal's rift starts pulling apart again** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  In the heart of Siberia, the crust began to stretch once more. Rifting in the Baikal Rift Zone resumed in the Oligocene. Over time the stretching formed graben basins, sunken troughs dropped between faults.

  <!-- olig-004 -->

- **Carnivorans seize the top predator roles** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  In the Eocene, the top hunters had been oxyaenids and mesonychians. In the Oligocene, carnivorans took their place, led by the cat-like nimravids. Across the Old World, dogs, nimravids, bears, weasels and raccoons began to replace the older creodonts. The predator families that still rule land today were settling into their jobs.

  <!-- olig-005 -->

- **Desmostylians take to Oligocene seas** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  Desmostylians were marine mammals with no living descendants, and they make their first appearance in the Oligocene. Early forms such as Behemotops are known from rocks of this epoch. The group did well. By the Late Oligocene it reached its highest diversity, with about nine species.

  <!-- olig-006 -->

- **Grasses leave the wetlands as forests shrink** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  As the planet cooled, the forests lost ground. Tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt, and grasslands expanded around the world. By the early Oligocene, tropical forests in North America and Eurasia had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands. In South America the cooler climate spread savanna, open country with scattered trees. Grasses themselves changed address. They moved out of their old habitats at the edges of wetlands and into open land. Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, a way of fixing carbon typical of grasses that works well when the gas is scarce. Even so, by the end of the epoch grass was still not common enough to make modern savannas. The open landscapes shaped the animals living in them. Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals, a trend that would run on through the Miocene.

  <!-- olig-010 -->

- **The Obik Sea drains and Europe meets Asia** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  For a long time a shallow sea, the Obik Sea, kept Europe and Asia apart. Early in the Oligocene it retreated, and the two landmasses gained a lasting land connection. The cause was falling sea level, which closed the Turgai Strait that ran across it. With the water gone, Europe lay open to Asian mammals. The consequences arrived quickly, in the faunal upheaval described in The Grande Coupure: Asia's mammals overrun Europe.

  <!-- olig-013 -->

- **Oi-2 glaciation drops the sea to a record low** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  Growing Antarctic ice locked up so much water that the sea fell about 75 metres, the largest drop of the past 100 million years. Several pulses of glaciation struck in the middle Oligocene, around a shift in oxygen isotopes called Oi-2. Rivers cut into the exposed continental shelves, leaving gaps in marine rock records worldwide. Lesser turnovers of animal life came at the same time.

  <!-- olig-014 -->

  *Figure: Follow how growing ice on Antarctica emptied the shelves and left gaps in the rock record.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Oi-2 glaciation pulses] --> B[Antarctic ice grows]
  B --> C[Sea level falls about 75 m]
  C --> D[Continental shelves exposed]
  D --> E[Rivers cut into shelves]
  E --> F[Gaps in marine rock records]
  ```

- **Paratethys turns into a giant airless sea** — during the Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago (33.9–23.04 Ma)

  A northern arm of the Tethys, the Paratethys, covered much of central and eastern Europe in the Oligocene. Then a sea-level drop and the rise of Alpine mountain chains partly cut it off. Poorly connected to the world ocean, it became stratified, with layers of water that did not mix. Its depths turned anoxic, starved of oxygen. Sand from the rising mountains buried organic matter in the Maykop Suite, now a source of hydrocarbons around the Black Sea. The Menilite Formation still preserves its deep-sea fish and microbial mats.

  <!-- olig-015 -->

  *Figure: Read down the chain from isolation to an airless sea and buried organic matter.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sea-level drop] --> C[Paratethys partly cut off]
  B[Alpine uplift] --> C
  C --> D[Water stratifies]
  D --> E[Giant anoxic sea]
  E --> F[Organic matter buried in Maykop Suite]
  ```

- **The Grande Coupure: Asia's mammals overrun Europe** — c. 34 million years ago (33.5 Ma)

  Around 33.5 million years ago, Europe's mammals turned over so sharply that the event got a French name meaning 'great break': the Grande Coupure. Before it, Europe had its own cast. Native artiodactyls, palaeothere perissodactyls, and adapid and omomyid primates dominated the landscape. Then falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait, the seaway described in The Obik Sea drains and Europe meets Asia. Asian rhinos and ruminants walked in, and native species went extinct. Asian animals replaced most European mammals. Only some endemic rodent and marsupial families held on. The break brought widespread extinction, and the timing can be read in the rocks. The first Asian immigrants show up in northwest European records about 350,000 years after the break began. The sources differ slightly on placement: the Oligocene's own account puts it at the very start of the epoch.

  <!-- olig-020 -->

  *Figure: How falling sea level let Asian mammals replace Europe's.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sea level falls] --> B[Turgai Strait closes]
  B --> C[Asian rhinos, ruminants enter]
  C --> D[Native species die out]
  ```

- **The Atacama begins its long drought** — c. 33 million years ago (33 Ma)

  The Atacama may be Earth's oldest desert. Its drying began with a proto-Humboldt Current, a cold coastal flow set up when the passage between Tasmania and Antarctica opened about 33 million years ago. After that, humid air was generally lacking there, apart from brief wetter spells.

  <!-- olig-022 -->

- **Greenland stops drifting and an Arctic orogeny ends** — c. 33 million years ago (33 Ma)

  Greenland once moved as a plate of its own, drifting north and rotating anticlockwise. About 33 million years ago that changed. Seafloor spreading in the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay ceased and shifted to the northeast Atlantic. With the spreading stopped, the Eurekan orogeny, a mountain-building episode in the Arctic, came to a close. By the late Oligocene the boundary between North America and Eurasia ran along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and Greenland had rejoined North America. One account dates the end of Labrador Sea spreading somewhat earlier.

  <!-- olig-025 -->

- **The Tasman Gateway opens a southern seaway** — c. 33 million years ago (33 Ma)

  Australia had been drifting slowly away from Antarctica since the Jurassic. About 33 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, the Tasman Gateway between them opened, and abrupt cooling followed. The opening came in stages. Shallow channels south of Tasmania appeared in the Eocene, and deep-ocean routes followed from the mid Oligocene. One estimate puts a deep channel in place by the end of the early Oligocene. On land, southeastern Australia became a place of high rainfall and swamps.

  <!-- olig-026 -->

  *Figure: The gateway opened in stages, from shallow channels to a deep route.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Australia drifts from Antarctica since Jurassic] --> B[Shallow channels, Eocene]
  B --> C[Gateway opens, about 33 Ma]
  C --> D[Deep-ocean routes, mid Oligocene]
  C --> E[Abrupt cooling]
  ```

- **An asteroid strikes Arctic Devon Island** — c. 32–31 million years ago (32–31 Ma)

  An impactor about 2 km wide struck Devon Island in Arctic Canada, leaving the Haughton crater about 23 km across. The blast exposed rock from as deep as 1,700 m. Its age is unsettled. The crater's own record gives 31–32 million years, but other analyses place it in the Eocene, at 39 million years.

  <!-- olig-028 -->

- **Aegyptopithecus and the primates of the Fayum** — c. 30 million years ago (30.2–29.5 Ma)

  In Egypt's Fayum, about 30.2–29.5 million years ago, lived Aegyptopithecus, a catarrhine the size of a howler monkey. It predates the split between apes and Old World monkeys. Its home, the Jebel Qatrani Formation, records tropical forests, swamps and rivers draining north into the Tethys Sea. The formation holds over a dozen primate genera and early elephants such as Phiomia and Moeritherium.

  <!-- olig-030 -->

- **A current wraps Antarctica in cold water** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  A ring of ocean now spins endlessly around Antarctica, and it may have started spinning about 30 million years ago. A steady circumpolar current probably did not form before then. A shallow flow at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary may have started a proto-current, but it was too shallow to circle the continent in earnest. Deep-sea cores south of New Zealand show cold deep currents by the early Oligocene. Once the gateways around Antarctica opened, the current kept cold water circling the continent. It also strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water, the cold, dense water that sinks to the ocean floor. Fossil evidence places its full establishment later, about 23 million years ago, after the Drake Passage opened fully and the Tasman Gateway deepened. The timing is disputed because it rests on the contested opening of the Drake Passage, described in The Drake Passage parts South America from Antarctica. Researchers also still debate how much the current drove Oligocene cooling.

  <!-- olig-032 -->

- **The brontotheres disappear** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  The brontotheres were large hoofed mammals, and about 30 million years ago they went extinct. The Oligocene's own account places their end in the earliest part of the epoch. Either way, a familiar group of big plant-eaters left the stage as the world cooled.

  <!-- olig-033 -->

- **The Caspian Sea basin takes shape** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  The Caspian Sea has deep roots. It is estimated to be about 30 million years old, which makes its basin a product of the Oligocene. Its later story, as it was cut off from the open sea, comes in The Caspian Sea becomes landlocked.

  <!-- olig-034 -->

- **Ethiopian Traps flood the Horn of Africa with lava** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  About 350,000 cubic kilometres of lava erupted around 30 million years ago across Ethiopia, northeast Sudan and southwest Yemen. The source was the Afar mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock, hitting the base of Africa's lithosphere. The lava came out of fissures, layer upon layer, and built the flood-basalt plateau of the Ethiopian Highlands. From 30 to 10 million years ago, shield volcanoes added another 1,000–2,000 m on top. The eruptions coincided with the start of rifting along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, told in Arabia begins to tear away from Africa.

  <!-- olig-036 -->

  *Figure: The Ethiopian Highlands stack shield volcanoes on top of the flood-basalt plateau.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Arabia begins to tear away from Africa** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  For most of the Phanerozoic, Arabia was simply part of the African plate. In the Oligocene it began to split away. Rifting of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden began around 30 million years ago, alongside the Ethiopian flood basalts. It started in the southern Red Sea in the mid Oligocene. By the late Oligocene it had spread along the whole Red Sea–Gulf of Suez system. The Gulf of Suez Rift stayed active from about 28 million years ago to the end of the Miocene. One account dates the final separation of Africa and Arabia to about 25 million years ago.

  <!-- olig-041 -->

- **The Rio Grande rift begins to stretch** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  In what is now the American Southwest, the crust started pulling apart about 30 million years ago, opening the Rio Grande rift. An intense phase of rifting followed from 30 to 20 million years ago, with the crust sliding apart along low-angle faults.

  <!-- olig-042 -->

- **A spreading ridge meets California and the San Andreas is born** — c. 30 million years ago (30 Ma)

  About 30 million years ago, the spreading ridge between the Pacific and Farallon plates reached North America's subduction zone. The San Andreas Fault began to form. The first ridge segment entered the subduction zone near Baja California about 28 million years ago. As the Murray and Mendocino fracture zones arrived, strike-slip motion began, with plates grinding sideways past each other. Basin and Range extension started too. Volcanism ended south of the Cascades, and many western North American terranes, crustal blocks added to the continent, rotated clockwise.

  <!-- olig-043 -->

- **Dominican amber freezes a lost forest** — c. 30–10 million years ago (30–10 Ma)

  Dominican amber, 30–10 million years old, is nearly always clear and rich in inclusions, the remains of living things trapped in the resin. Those inclusions let scientists reconstruct a vanished tropical forest in detail.

  <!-- olig-035 -->

- **La Garita, one of Earth's greatest eruptions** — 28 million years ago (28.175 Ma)

  The eruption that formed La Garita Caldera in Colorado was among the largest and most powerful known in Earth's history. It blasted out the Fish Canyon Tuff, about 5,000 cubic kilometres of ash-flow deposit. The ground then collapsed into a caldera, a huge crater left by the emptied magma chamber. It was one of many calderas in a huge ignimbrite flare-up across Colorado, Utah and Nevada from 40 to 18 million years ago. Its crystals have a second life. Sanidine from the tuff, astronomically dated to 28.175 million years, is a reference standard for argon–argon dating.

  <!-- olig-046 -->

  *Figure: La Garita erupted near the middle of a flare-up lasting from 40 to 18 million years ago.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Drake Passage parts South America from Antarctica** — c. 28 million years ago (28 Ma)

  South America and Antarctica were once joined at their tips. Seafloor spreading along the Scotia Ridge finally parted them by 28 million years ago, forming the Drake Passage. South America became an island continent and began drifting north toward North America. Together with the Tasmanian Gateway in The Tasman Gateway opens a southern seaway, the new opening reshaped Oligocene ocean currents. It may have helped trigger Antarctic glaciation, though models suggest falling carbon dioxide mattered more. The date is one of the most disputed in this chapter. Published estimates for the opening range from 49 to 17 million years ago. One study finds deep-water flow possible by about 31 million years ago. Sources still disagree whether the passage opened near the start or near the end of the Oligocene.

  <!-- olig-048 -->

  *Figure: Estimates for when the Drake Passage opened.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The first pelicans** — c. 28 million years ago (28 Ma)

  Pelicans have an old pedigree. The first members of the group appear in the fossil record about 28 million years ago. That puts the big-billed fishers in the middle of the Oligocene.

  <!-- olig-049 -->

- **Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever** — c. 28 million years ago (28 Ma)

  Paraceratherium was the largest land mammal that ever lived, and it appears in the fossil record about 28 million years ago. This hornless rhino relative weighed up to 15–20 tonnes. Giant indricotheres like it stood up to 6 metres at the shoulder in Eurasia. They were exceptions. Most Oligocene mammals ran much smaller than their Eocene predecessors, and these giants bucked the trend.

  <!-- olig-050 -->

- **Caviomorph rodents spread through South America** — during the Late Oligocene, 27–23 million years ago (27.3–23.04 Ma)

  Caviomorph rodents, the group of South American rodents, had reached Patagonia by the early Oligocene. By the Late Oligocene they had split into all four main lineages. Some grew large and competed with native hoofed mammals, perhaps helping those animals' slow decline after the early Oligocene.

  <!-- olig-052 -->

- **Embrithopods leave the record** — during the Late Oligocene, 27–23 million years ago (27.3–23.04 Ma)

  Embrithopods were an order of mammals that lived only in Afro-Arabia, a branch of the continent's homegrown fauna. Their last record comes from the latest Oligocene, and after that the order is gone. One timeline sets their extinction earlier, at about 30 million years ago.

  <!-- olig-053 -->

- **Proailurus, the first cat** — during the Late Oligocene, 27–23 million years ago (27.3–23.04 Ma)

  The cat family starts with Proailurus. This first felid arose in Asia in the late Oligocene and spread to Europe, and the earliest felid fossils come from Oligocene Europe. Timelines date the first cats to about 30 or 25 million years ago. The saber-toothed look came later: the first cat with saber-tooth features is Pseudaelurus, from the Miocene.

  <!-- olig-054 -->

- **The first elephantimorphs** — during the Late Oligocene, 27–23 million years ago (27.3–23.04 Ma)

  The lineage that would give rise to mastodons and modern elephants made its first appearance in the Late Oligocene. These were the elephantimorphs, the branch of proboscideans that includes both. One timeline dates the first true elephants to about 26 million years ago, though the elephant family proper is traced in The elephant family arises in Africa.

  <!-- olig-056 -->

- **Notoungulates grow teeth that never stop** — during the Late Oligocene, 27–23 million years ago (27.3–23.04 Ma)

  Several South American notoungulate families separately evolved high-crowned cheek teeth that kept growing throughout life. They arrived at the same solution independently. From the Late Oligocene on, such species made up most notoungulates.

  <!-- olig-058 -->

- **The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first forms** — c. 27 million years ago (27 Ma)

  The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first formed about 27 million years ago, probably fed partly by glaciers from the older East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It is a marine ice sheet. Most of its ice rests on rock and sediment well below sea level, ground that would be ocean floor without the ice.

  <!-- olig-060 -->

- **A late Oligocene warm spell** — c. 26–24 million years ago (26.5–24 Ma)

  Between 26.5 and 24 million years ago, the late Oligocene probably warmed, despite low carbon dioxide. Temperatures rose slightly but stayed well below earlier Paleogene levels, and Antarctica stayed heavily glaciated. Pollen from the Tibetan Plateau records the warming. Lanternfish, once confined to shelf seas, spread into the open ocean.

  <!-- olig-061 -->

- **The Farallon Plate breaks up** — c. 26 million years ago (26 Ma)

  About 26 million years ago, the Farallon Plate broke up into the Cocos and Nazca plates. Subduction sped up. Volcanism revived in the Central Andes, and the volcanic arc broadened to about 250 km. Activity rose sharply along the Andes, and the modern volcanic arc and tectonic regime took shape. At the Paleogene–Neogene boundary, Pacific–Farallon spreading stopped and the plate split again into today's Nazca and Cocos plates.

  <!-- olig-062 -->

  *Figure: Trace the Farallon Plate's breakup to the rise of the modern Andean volcanic arc.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Farallon Plate] --> B[Cocos Plate]
  A --> C[Nazca Plate]
  C --> D[Subduction speeds up]
  D --> E[Arc broadens to about 250 km]
  E --> F[Modern Andean volcanic arc]
  ```

- **Tibet rises and the South Asian monsoon strengthens** — c. 26 million years ago (25.8 Ma)

  The South Asian monsoon intensified sharply around 25.8 million years ago. The trigger was the rising Tibetan Plateau. The monsoon itself was not new. Tibetan pollen shows it had already developed by the late Oligocene, and the plateau's growth turned it up. A higher plateau meant a stronger seasonal swing in the winds, and the same link between Tibet and the monsoons returns throughout the Miocene.

  <!-- olig-063 -->

- **Rukwapithecus and the earliest apes and monkeys** — c. 25 million years ago (25.2 Ma)

  In the Rukwa Rift of Tanzania, the Nsungwe Formation is about 25.2 million years old. It yields Rukwapithecus, interpreted as the earliest known ape, or hominoid. The same beds hold Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey. So by then the two groups had already split. That fits molecular estimates placing the split at about 25–30 million years ago, though early catarrhine relationships remain uncertain. The finds reach into a poorly sampled stretch of time, and tectonic changes in East Africa may have shaped how both groups diversified.

  <!-- olig-064 -->

- **Central America begins to close its seaway** — c. 25 million years ago (25 Ma)

  A long chain of volcanoes started the job of joining two continents. By the Oligocene, the Central American volcanic arc began colliding with northwestern South America. That collision, which would eventually close the Central American Seaway, started about 25 million years ago. The process ran for millions of years, through the closure of the deep seaway in The deep seaway between the Americas closes to the final link in The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas.

  <!-- olig-065 -->

- **Riversleigh starts recording a lost rainforest** — c. 25 million years ago (25 Ma)

  Riversleigh in Queensland is Australia's most famous fossil site, and its story begins in the late Oligocene. Some of its fossils are 25 million years old. Its limestones formed in what was once a very wet rainforest, a far cry from the dry country there now. The site keeps recording life for millions of years, as Riversleigh's rainforest animals shows.

  <!-- olig-068 -->

- **The Sea of Japan begins to open** — c. 25 million years ago (25 Ma)

  Around 25 million years ago the Sea of Japan began to open. As it widened, Japan pulled away from the Asian mainland and took the form of today's island arc. The opening continued into the Miocene, as The Sea of Japan opens at both ends describes.

  <!-- olig-069 -->

- **East Africa starts to split open** — c. 25–22 million years ago (25–22 Ma)

  Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano, and it stands at the start of a great tearing. The East African Rift began to develop around the start of the Miocene, 25–22 million years ago. Its fires began earlier. Volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau around 30 million years ago, long before any rifting there. In northern Kenya, rifting and volcanism began around the same time. Then the crack worked its way south. It reached southern Kenya by 12 million years ago and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago. The rift would go on to reshape the landscape of eastern Africa, the setting for much of the human story later in this course.

  <!-- olig-066 -->

  *Figure: Rifting spread south through East Africa over time.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Seals arrive and nautiloids vanish** — c. 24 million years ago (24 Ma)

  The earliest pinnipeds, the group that includes seals, appeared about 24 million years ago, near the end of the Oligocene. Their spread left a curious pattern in the fossil record. From the Oligocene on, nautiloids vanished from each region as pinnipeds appeared there. Wherever the new marine mammals arrived, the ancient shelled hunters of the sea disappeared.

  <!-- olig-074 -->

- **Creodonts retreat to Africa** — c. 23 million years ago (23.04 Ma)

  At the end of the Oligocene, creodonts died out everywhere except Africa and the Middle East. The old predator order, long pushed aside by carnivorans, hung on only in that corner of the world. Its final end is told in The last creodonts disappear.

  <!-- olig-076 -->

- **A deep freeze closes the Oligocene** — c. 23 million years ago (23.04 Ma)

  A deep glaciation lasting 400,000 years marks the Oligocene–Miocene boundary at McMurdo Sound and King George Island in Antarctica. The boundary rests on regional shifts from the warmer late Oligocene to the cooler Miocene. The Miocene opened with the Mi-1 cool event around 23 million years ago, as Antarctica's ice sheets expanded.

  <!-- olig-077 -->

- **The pyrotheres die out** — c. 23 million years ago (23.04 Ma)

  The pyrotheres were a South American mammal order known since the Early Eocene. They were among the continent's distinctive native mammals, alongside astrapotheres, litopterns and notoungulates. Their last record comes at the end of the Oligocene.

  <!-- olig-078 -->

#### Neogene Period

The Neogene opens in a world that was getting cooler, drier and more seasonal. Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start, and grasses kept spreading until they dominated much of the world while forests dwindled. Mountains rose on two continents: the Andes lifted fastest in this time, and sediment from the rising Himalaya built the vast Bengal Fan. In the sea, whales and dolphins reached their greatest diversity and kelp forests first appeared. On land, apes evolved and spread across the Old World.

##### Miocene Epoch

Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, then diversified and spread across the Old World. Around them the world was turning seasonal. Global cooling gave the East Asian Summer Monsoon its modern form, and grasses came to dominate much of the land. The crust was busy too: the Andes rose fastest in this epoch, and the Tian Shan and Altai mountains formed. The oceans gained new life, from kelp forests to the greatest variety of whales and dolphins Earth has known.

- **Africa's plants lose ground to the seasons** — c. 23 million years ago (23.04 Ma)

  Africa's plant life took a sharp hit as the Miocene began. Plant diversity fell steeply, probably because the seasons became more pronounced, with stronger swings between wet and dry. Species suited to steady conditions lost out. The great equatorial forest belt did not simply shrink. Through the whole Miocene it broke apart and rejoined again and again, splitting forest populations and then reconnecting them.

  <!-- mioc-001 -->

- **Apes spread across the Old World** — during the Early Miocene, 23–16 million years ago (23.04–15.98 Ma)

  Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years old, carries the earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan of any ape. It belongs to a group just finding its feet. Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, in the Aquitanian and Burdigalian ages, and then diversified and spread across the Old World. Geography made the spread possible. Once Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, hominoids, the ape group, and proboscideans, the elephant group, could walk out of Africa. Apes crossed in waves. Griphopithecus lived in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago, and Dryopithecus had reached Europe by 12.5 million years ago. One proposal, the 'Out-of-Europe' idea, holds that several great ape species evolved in Eurasia during the Miocene. The crossing itself is the subject of A land bridge sets animals crossing both ways, and the later story of the apes runs through Great apes and gibbons go separate ways to the split of human and chimpanzee lines.

  <!-- mioc-003 -->

- **Himalayan rubble builds the Bengal Fan** — during the Early Miocene, 23–16 million years ago (23.04–15.98 Ma)

  The largest submarine fan on Earth lies under the Bay of Bengal: about 3,000 km long, 1,430 km wide and up to 16.5 km thick. It is made of mountains. Sediment eroded from the rising Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, carried mostly by the Ganges and Brahmaputra, built the Bengal Fan. The oldest sediments recovered from it so far are Early Miocene, so the fan is at least that old. Their minerals and chemistry point to Himalayan origin. So the Himalaya was already a major mountain range 20 million years ago. The fan keeps a running diary of the uplift, and changes in its layers show that Himalayan uplift slowed in the Late Pliocene.

  <!-- mioc-004 -->

  *Figure: Compare the three dimensions of the largest submarine fan on Earth.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The daisy family takes off** — during the Early Miocene, 23–16 million years ago (23.04–15.98 Ma)

  With over 32,000 species, about 10% of all flowering plants, the daisy family rivals the orchids as the largest plant family. The geologic time scale lists it as appearing and diversifying rapidly in the Early Miocene, triggering radiations of rodents, snakes and songbirds. Its roots are older: its oldest fossil pollen, from Antarctica, is 76-66 million years old.

  <!-- mioc-006 -->

- **The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape** — during the Early Miocene, 23–16 million years ago (23.04–15.98 Ma)

  Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene. The mountains mattered too. Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene changed Asian monsoon patterns. Those patterns were tied in turn to glacial periods in the north, so ice far away and rock nearby both shaped the rain. The link between rising Tibet and stronger monsoons, first seen in Tibet rises and the South Asian monsoon strengthens, keeps returning through the Neogene.

  <!-- mioc-007 -->

- **Tian Shan and Altai rise in Central Asia** — during the Early Miocene, 23–16 million years ago (23.04–15.98 Ma)

  India's collision with Eurasia reached far north. The geologic time scale lists the Tian Shan and Altai Mountains as forming in the Early Miocene, as part of the Himalayan orogeny. The Siberian Altai is the northernmost region the collision affected. The Tian Shan rose sharply again in the Late Miocene, blocking westerly winds from the Tarim Basin and drying it.

  <!-- mioc-018 -->

- **The Andes rise fastest in the Miocene** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  The new Nazca Plate dove head-on under South America, and the Andes rose, most of all in the Miocene. The Altiplano began rising in this epoch. By about 13–11 million years ago it was a high plateau, second in size only to Tibet. From the Late Miocene the Altiplano region climbed from low elevations to over 3,000 m. Peru's Western Cordillera, quiet since the Oligocene, rose sharply after about 10 Ma. The uplift ran the length of the range. The Principal Cordillera east of Santiago rose about 20–8 Ma, and Colombia's Eastern Ranges were lifted and eroded faster 12–3 Ma. Near Misti, the Western Cordillera rose 9–4 Ma amid large ignimbrites. Movement on the Atacama Fault raised the Chilean Coast Range, and the Quechua phases of 9–8 and 7–5 Ma deformed northern Peru.

  <!-- mioc-002 -->

  *Figure: Uplift moved from range to range along the Andes through the Miocene.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Whales and dolphins at their most diverse** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  The Miocene ocean held over 20 genera of baleen whales. Only six survive today. Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in this epoch. The boom in baleen whales brought its own hunters: raptorial sperm whales, toothed whales with large biting teeth, apparently evolved to prey on them. From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes. One of those whale-hunters, Livyatan, appears in Livyatan, the sperm whale with giant teeth.

  <!-- mioc-005 -->

  *Figure: Miocene seas held more than three times as many baleen whale genera as today's.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Fram Strait opens a door to the Arctic** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  The Arctic Ocean got one entrance from the Atlantic, and only one. The Fram Strait opened in the Miocene and became the only route for Atlantic water into the Arctic until the Quaternary. Another path existed on the map, the Barents Seaway, but uplift of the continental shelf kept the water from passing through it.

  <!-- mioc-008 -->

- **Diatoms move into fresh water** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Diatoms, single-celled algae in glassy shells, had radiated in the oceans back in the Cretaceous. Freshwater diatoms did not appear until the Miocene. Their diversity rose through the epoch as carbon dioxide and global temperatures fell.

  <!-- mioc-009 -->

- **Grass takes over the world** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Grass did not just spread in the Miocene. It changed the climate that let it spread. As in the Oligocene, grasses kept advancing and came to dominate much of the world while forests dwindled. Early Miocene forests gave way to mixed forest and grassland in the Middle Miocene. Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma. The new grasses were fibrous and fire-tolerant. They co-evolved with herds of grazers that had high-crowned teeth, and those herds displaced woodland and browsing animals. By the Hemingfordian age, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers. Ants, termites, grassland mammals and snakes diversified. A cooler, drier climate and open landscapes were a major cause of the decline of perissodactyls, the odd-toed hoofed mammals. Then came the feedback. Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and pale grass raised albedo, the share of sunlight reflected. Both helped make the climate cooler and drier still.

  <!-- mioc-010 -->

  *Figure: How spreading grasslands, grazers and climate fed one another.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Grasses spread] --> B[High-crowned grazers]
  B --> C[Browsers displaced]
  A --> D[Soils bury carbon, albedo rises]
  D --> E[Cooler, drier climate]
  E --> F[Perissodactyls decline]
  ```

- **Kelp forests rise in Miocene seas** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Two new biomes carried much of Miocene life. One was the grassland. The other grew underwater. Kelp forests, dense stands of giant brown seaweed, first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems. On land and in the sea, then, the epoch built new kinds of habitat at the same time, each feeding a great range of animals.

  <!-- mioc-011 -->

- **Necrolestes, last of an ancient line** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Meridiolestidans were mammals that dominated Late Cretaceous South America. Their last member turned up in the Miocene of Patagonia: Necrolestes, a mole-like burrowing insect-eater. It appears 50 million years after the previous known member of its group, a very long silence in the record.

  <!-- mioc-012 -->

- **Ducks, owls and crows: modern birds appear** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Many birds that would look familiar today show up in the Miocene. Clearly recognisable dabbling ducks, plovers, typical owls, cockatoos and crows all appear in this epoch. Crows of the genus Corvus are first recorded about 17 million years ago. By the end of the Miocene, all or nearly all modern bird groups are thought to have been present.

  <!-- mioc-013 -->

- **Sloth families multiply** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Sloths diversified in the Miocene, when the major sloth families appeared. Their diversity rose and fell through the epoch and then declined at its end. They had already traveled far: a basal sloth group had colonized the Antilles by the early Miocene.

  <!-- mioc-015 -->

- **Snakes boom in North America** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Snakes had been a minor part of North American wildlife. In the Miocene their numbers and diversity rose sharply. Vipers and elapids, the cobra family, first appeared on the continent, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera. Snakes were among the animals that diversified as grassland spread, as Grass takes over the world describes.

  <!-- mioc-016 -->

- **South America's native hoofed mammals thin out** — during the Miocene, 23.0–5.3 million years ago (23.04–5.333 Ma)

  Notoungulates lost 45% of their families during the Miocene, though their number of species stayed stable. Fewer branches carried as many leaves. By the late Miocene, litopterns and notoungulates were the only South American native ungulate groups still standing.

  <!-- mioc-017 -->

- **The Ogallala spreads its gravels over the Plains** — during the Miocene–Early Pliocene, 23.0–3.6 million years ago (23.04–3.6 Ma)

  As the Rockies rose, rivers carried eroded rock east and dumped sand and gravel across the gentle plains in overlapping alluvial fans, fan-shaped spreads of river sediment. These deposits form the Ogallala Formation. They hold the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the world's largest, under about 450,000 km2 of eight states, supplying about 30% of US irrigation groundwater.

  <!-- mioc-014 -->

- **Riversleigh's rainforest animals** — c. 23–16 million years ago (23.03–15.97 Ma)

  Riversleigh's limestone never compacted, so its bones stay three-dimensional. In the Early Miocene, Faunal Zone B, the area was very wet rainforest. Later Middle Miocene layers hold a 15-million-year-old platypus relative, Obdurodon, and the oldest modern bandicoots and bilbies.

  <!-- mioc-019 -->

- **The Central Andes begin erupting ignimbrites** — c. 23 million years ago (23 Ma)

  Ignimbrite is rock made from a glowing avalanche of volcanic ash that welds as it settles. About 23 million years ago, large-scale ignimbrite volcanism began in the Central Andes, and it continues today. North of 21 degrees S, the Oxaya Formation erupted 23 to 18 million years ago. Calderas of the Altiplano-Puna complex have since produced about 15,000 cubic km of ignimbrite, mostly dacite. One early eruption, the Verde Ignimbrite from Aguas Calientes caldera 17.2 million years ago, released 140–300 cubic km. In southern Peru, the Chuquibamba Ignimbrite came from a VEI 7 super-eruption 14.3 to 13.2 million years ago.

  <!-- mioc-021 -->

  *Figure: Compare the volumes of Central Andean ignimbrites, from one early eruption to the complex's total.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Foulden Maar, a forest in a crater lake** — c. 23 million years ago (23 Ma)

  A small crater lake in New Zealand became a fossil archive. Layers of diatomite, rock built from the shells of countless diatoms, settled on its floor. They preserved fish, plants, spiders, insects and pollen from the subtropical forest around the lake.

  <!-- mioc-025 -->

- **An impact gouges the Karakul crater** — c. 23 million years ago (23 Ma)

  A large impact gouged the 52 km Karakul crater in Tajikistan. Its age is poorly pinned. Estimates put it at less than 23 million years, possibly less than 5 million years, so it formed during either the Miocene or the Pliocene.

  <!-- mioc-026 -->

- **Megalodon, the giant shark, appears** — c. 23 million years ago (23 Ma)

  The giant shark megalodon evolved around 23 million years ago, by the usual reckoning. With the sperm whale Livyatan, it was among the large predators that ruled Neogene oceans. Its first appearance is disputed. Some remains are reported from about 28 million years ago, while other estimates are as young as 16 million years.

  <!-- mioc-027 -->

- **Ebelsberg preserves the Paratethys sea life** — c. 23–22 million years ago (23–22 Ma)

  In Upper Austria, a deposit from the Aquitanian age holds a crowded snapshot of the central Paratethys Sea. It preserves huge numbers of plants, fish, marine mammals and invertebrates, the life of the inland sea described in Paratethys turns into a giant airless sea.

  <!-- mioc-024 -->

- **The Alboran Basin and the Betic Corridor open** — c. 23–20 million years ago (23–20 Ma)

  Between 23 and 20 million years ago, spreading thinned the crust south of Spain to just 12-15 km, forming the Alboran Basin. In the early Miocene Iberia rotated and opened the Betic Corridor, a strait joining the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Its fate matters later, in The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out.

  <!-- mioc-020 -->

- **Chiapas amber traps a Mexican forest** — c. 23–15 million years ago (23–15 Ma)

  Resin from trees in Chiapas, Mexico, hardened into amber with life caught inside. It holds insects, other arthropods, plant fragments and even the fungi that grew on leaf surfaces. Together they make a fine-grained record of a Miocene forest.

  <!-- mioc-022 -->

- **East Antarctic glaciers come and go** — c. 23–15 million years ago (23–15 Ma)

  East Antarctica probably held some glaciers during the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago. They were restless. The Ross Sea margin of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene, ice that had not yet settled into a stable cap.

  <!-- mioc-023 -->

- **Granites melt inside the High Himalaya** — c. 22 million years ago (22 Ma)

  Deep inside the growing Himalaya, rock melted. Granites about 22 million years old intruded the High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence in many places. That metamorphic sequence is 30 km thick and forms the backbone of the range, holding its highest peaks. Many of these were leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in crust thickened by collision.

  <!-- mioc-028 -->

- **New Zealand almost drowns** — c. 22 million years ago (22 Ma)

  About 22 million years ago only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level. The rest lay under the sea, a stretch called the Oligocene Drowning Maximum. Isolation on scattered patches of land mattered for evolution. This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa.

  <!-- mioc-029 -->

- **Tibet sinks, then rises again** — c. 22–20 million years ago (21.6–20.4 Ma)

  The Tibetan Plateau did not climb steadily. Between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago it sank about 900 m. Then, between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago, it rose by 500 to 1,000 m, regaining much of the lost height.

  <!-- mioc-030 -->

  *Figure: The plateau first sank, then rose again within a few million years.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[25.5 Ma] -->|sinks about 900 m| B[21.6 Ma]
  B -->|rises 500 to 1,000 m| C[20.4 Ma]
  ```

- **Death at the Agate watering holes** — c. 21–16 million years ago (21–16 Ma)

  In Nebraska, old watering holes became mass graves. Their deposits hold crowds of small rhinos that died together, along with bear dogs, entelodonts, camels and chalicotheres. The animals had gathered at the water, and many died there.

  <!-- mioc-031 -->

- **Lake Pebas floods western Amazonia** — c. 21–8 million years ago (21–8 Ma)

  For millions of years, western Amazonia held a giant wetland. The Pebas Formation records this Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas, from about 21 to 8 million years ago. The formation covers about 1,000,000 square km. Its animals match those of La Venta in Colombia and Urumaco in Venezuela, tying the wetland into a wider northern South American world. Its end came as the Amazon took a new course, told in The Amazon runs across a continent.

  <!-- mioc-032 -->

- **Conifers and cycads branch out** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  About 20 million years ago, some conifer and cycad groups began to diversify as conditions changed. These old seed-plant lines, far older than the grasses spreading around them, found new room in the shifting Miocene climate.

  <!-- mioc-033 -->

- **Rising rift shoulders split Africa's great rivers** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  Around 20 million years ago the western flank of the East African Rift rose. It cut the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin. The map then looked very different. Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and Ethiopian and Ugandan rivers did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile.

  <!-- mioc-034 -->

- **Giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters appear** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  Around 20 million years ago, three very different animals made their debut. The first giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters all appear in the record at about this time. Bird diversity also increased, part of the Miocene's broad remaking of land life.

  <!-- mioc-035 -->

- **Arabia slams into Eurasia and the Tethys narrows** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  In the Early Miocene the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia, cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean. The first step of the closure, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange by 90%. Two forces worked together. Africa-Arabia moved north, and sea level fell as the Antarctic Ice Sheet grew. By the mid-Burdigalian the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses. The dates are contested. Sources place the Tethys closure anywhere from about 35 to 19-12 million years ago. The two-step story used here, ending in The Tethys seaway closes for good, is one reading.

  <!-- mioc-036 -->

- **A land bridge sets animals crossing both ways** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  Gomphotheres and deinotheres, early relatives of elephants, were first out of Africa. They reached India by about 18.3 million years ago and Iberia by 18 million. Their road was a land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia, formed around 20 million years ago. Until then the open Tethyan seaway had kept most animals from crossing. The bridge set off the Great Old World Biotic Interchange, and traffic ran both ways. At least 37 Eurasian lineages entered Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian. Perissodactyls reached Africa for the first time.

  <!-- mioc-037 -->

  *Figure: Animals crossed the new land bridge in both directions.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A([Land bridge forms, about 20 Ma])
  A --> B[Africa to Eurasia: gomphotheres, deinotheres]
  A --> C[Eurasia to Africa: 37 or more lineages]
  B --> D[India by 18.3 Ma]
  B --> E[Iberia by 18 Ma]
  C --> F[First perissodactyls in Africa]
  ```

- **A gravity hole forms in the Indian Ocean** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  South of India, the sea surface sags. This depression, covering about 3 million square km, is Earth's largest gravity anomaly, and it formed around 20 million years ago. Models link it to plumes rising from a sinking slab of old Tethys seafloor, spreading low-density material beneath the Indian Ocean.

  <!-- mioc-038 -->

- **Southern Africa lifts and wears away** — c. 20 million years ago (20 Ma)

  About 20 million years ago, southern Africa was lifted. That uplift began a long spell of erosion. Over the following millions of years, rivers and weather stripped away kilometres of rock from the raised land.

  <!-- mioc-040 -->

- **Most open-ocean sharks vanish** — c. 19 million years ago (19 Ma)

  About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared. Seven in ten kinds of shark that roamed the high seas were simply gone. The ocean did not stay empty for long. The seas that followed came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon, met in Megalodon, the giant shark, appears, and the giant sperm whale Livyatan. The gap left by the lost sharks was filled by some of the biggest hunters the oceans have known.

  <!-- mioc-042 -->

- **St Bathans, New Zealand's lost subtropical fauna** — c. 19–16 million years ago (19–16 Ma)

  The St Bathans fauna of Central Otago, about 19 to 16 million years old, is New Zealand's only Cenozoic land fossil record. It holds early moa, kiwi and adzebills, tuatara relatives, crocodiles, turtles and many bats. Later cooling and drying wiped out its subtropical members.

  <!-- mioc-043 -->

- **Barstow's bones, teeth and footprints** — c. 19–13 million years ago (19–13.4 Ma)

  In California, Miocene rivers and lakes laid down sediments between layers of rhyolite tuff, hardened volcanic ash. Those beds hold abundant vertebrate bones, teeth and footprints, and the ash layers help date them.

  <!-- mioc-041 -->

- **The Vogelsberg, Central Europe's biggest volcanic field** — c. 18–10 million years ago (18.5–10 Ma)

  Central Europe's largest basalt formation covers about 2,500 km2 in Hesse, Germany. It is not one shield volcano but many overlapping volcanoes, built mainly in the Middle Miocene. Dates span 18.5-10 million years ago, peaking 17-15 million years ago. Its eruptions were tied to fault-block movement in the European Cenozoic Rift System.

  <!-- mioc-044 -->

- **The Ethiopian rift begins to unzip** — c. 18 million years ago (18 Ma)

  The Nubian and Somali plates began to pull apart, and Ethiopia started to split. By one account rifting began about 18 million years ago at the south end, about 11 near the Afar and perhaps 8–6 in the centre. A study of the southern rift puts its start earlier, at 20–21 million years ago. Opening of the Gregory rift caused the Afar triple junction to form.

  <!-- mioc-045 -->

- **The Gulf of Suez rift reaches its peak** — c. 18 million years ago (18 Ma)

  In the early Miocene the sea flooded the young Gulf of Suez rift, which then deepened. Rifting peaked in the Burdigalian, around 18 million years ago. In the Middle Miocene the Red Sea rift broke apart along its length, motion shifted to the Dead Sea Transform, and seafloor spreading followed.

  <!-- mioc-047 -->

- **Shanwang, where insect wings keep their colors** — c. 18–17 million years ago (18–17 Ma)

  Over 600 species have come out of the Shanwang site in Shandong, China. The preservation is remarkable. Insects keep intact wing veins and even their colors, and the site also yields birds and mammals.

  <!-- mioc-050 -->

- **Iceland rises above the waves** — c. 18–16 million years ago (18–16 Ma)

  Iceland sits where the Eurasian and North American plates pull apart, right above a mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock. That plume is thought to have built it. The island first rose above the ocean about 18-16 million years ago, and its oldest rocks formed above sea level date to 16.5 million years ago. The double setting gives it repeated volcanism and geysers.

  <!-- mioc-048 -->

- **Great apes and gibbons go separate ways** — c. 18–12 million years ago (18–12 Ma)

  Somewhere between 18 and 12 million years ago, the line leading to great apes split from the line leading to gibbons. Molecular evidence, from comparing living species' DNA, places the common ancestor of the modern hominid group at 18 to 13 million years ago. The fossils are too scarce to name that ancestor. So this key branching point is known mainly from genes, not bones. The great-ape branch would later split again, as Humans and chimpanzees go separate ways shows.

  <!-- mioc-046 -->

- **The Basin and Range begins to stretch** — c. 17 million years ago (17 Ma)

  By the Early Miocene, most of the Farallon plate had been consumed beneath North America, and the Pacific-Farallon Ridge was nearing the continent. About 17 million years ago the crust in the west began to stretch. Tension thinned the land west of the Grand Canyon region and let it drop in blocks, carving a landscape of parallel ranges and basins. The movement has been large. Since extension began, parts of the province have shifted 60 to 300 km sideways, more in the south than the north.

  <!-- mioc-051 -->

- **Randeck Maar, a crater lake in a warm world** — c. 17–15 million years ago (17–15 Ma)

  During the warm Miocene optimum, a crater lake in southwest Germany sat barely above sea level. Its sediments preserved plants, insects, fish and amphibians, a record of lake life in the warmest stretch of the epoch.

  <!-- mioc-052 -->

- **The Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum** — c. 17–14 million years ago (16.9–13.8 Ma)

  Around 15 million years ago, during the warmest part of the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, global temperature averaged about 18.4 °C, and the Antarctic ice cap shrank. Between roughly 17 and 14 million years ago, the climate was about 3 °C warmer than today. Foraminifera, tiny shelled organisms living on the seafloor, keep the timetable in their shells. They put the onset at 16.9 Ma, the peak at 15.3 Ma and the end at 13.8 Ma. A positive shift in carbon isotopes, the Monterey Carbon Excursion, began just before the warmth and ended just after it. The cause is debated. The Columbia River flood basalts in The Columbia River basalts flood the Northwest, helped by volcanic gas at plate margins, are seen as the main driver. Yet the warming began about 16.9 Ma, and the basalts cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma. Something else must have started it, and researchers still disagree on what.

  <!-- mioc-053 -->

  *Figure: Timeline of the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Steens Mountain catches the magnetic field flipping** — c. 17 million years ago (16.7 Ma)

  Lava flows at Steens Mountain in Oregon froze a record of Earth's magnetic field as it reversed, about 16.7 Ma. They suggest the field can shift up to 6 degrees a day, astonishingly fast. The reversal that ended the magnetic period called Chron C5Cr was not one clean flip but a series of reversals and excursions.

  <!-- mioc-055 -->

- **The Columbia River basalts flood the Northwest** — c. 17–16 million years ago (16.7–15.9 Ma)

  Lava buried a whole region in a geological instant. Between 16.7 and 15.9 Ma, the Columbia River flood basalts poured out 95% of all their lava over the Columbia Plateau and Oregon. This large igneous province, linked to the Yellowstone hotspot, totals about 210,000 cubic km of rock. Its Roza Member alone held at least 1,500 cubic km. A mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock, is the most widely accepted cause, though the question is still debated. The eruptions reshaped the volcanic life of the region. They ended the Western Cascades period, and Cascade volcanism stayed at a low point from 17 to 9 Ma. They are often blamed for the warming in The Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum. That link is disputed, because the warming began earlier, around 16.9 Ma, before the main pulse of lava.

  <!-- mioc-054 -->

- **The Yellowstone hotspot's first calderas** — c. 16 million years ago (16.5–15.5 Ma)

  The Yellowstone hotspot is thought to have arrived under North America in the Miocene, and it is still active. Its first calderas formed 16.5 to 15.5 million years ago, among them McDermitt and Virgin Valley, as the Steens flood basalts waned. McDermitt Caldera formed about 16.4 million years ago when a rhyolite lava dome collapsed. Eruptions such as the Longridge Caldera's, 15.6 million years ago, produced up to 400 cubic km of tuff. The hotspot's later track is told in Supereruptions build the Snake River Plain.

  <!-- mioc-056 -->

- **Clarkia's leaves still blush with autumn color** — c. 16 million years ago (16.1–15.9 Ma)

  Some leaves from Idaho's Clarkia beds still show autumn colors when first exposed, then fade as air oxidizes them. Small amounts of ancient DNA have reportedly been isolated from them. The beds lie within the Wanapum Basalts of the Columbia River lavas, dated 16.1 to 15.9 million years ago.

  <!-- mioc-058 -->

- **The hippopotamus lineage begins** — c. 16 million years ago (16 Ma)

  The hippopotamus evolved around 16 million years ago, in the middle of the Miocene. Its family took shape during the warm stretch of the epoch, alongside the many other mammal groups that appeared or diversified then, from mastodons and bovids to kangaroos.

  <!-- mioc-059 -->

- **McGraths Flat keeps microscopic soft tissue** — c. 16–11 million years ago (16–11 Ma)

  Soft tissue almost never fossilizes, and in Australia it is especially rare. At McGraths Flat in New South Wales, unusual conditions preserved microscopic soft-tissue detail. The site has revealed invertebrate species no one had known before.

  <!-- mioc-060 -->

- **Australia begins to collide with Southeast Asia** — during the Middle Miocene, 16–12 million years ago (15.98–11.63 Ma)

  Australia had been drifting north since it broke from Antarctica. In the Middle Miocene, it began to collide with Southeast Asia. The collision did more than crumple crust. It blocked the equatorial ocean flow between the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean, closing a warm-water passage along the equator.

  <!-- mioc-062 -->
