- **The last creodonts disappear** — during the Middle Miocene, 16–12 million years ago (15.98–11.63 Ma)

  The last creodonts, early predatory mammals, died out in the Middle Miocene. They had already retreated to Africa and the Middle East, as Creodonts retreat to Africa describes. Carnivorans now had the predator roles to themselves.

  <!-- mioc-063 -->

- **Most modern seed plants appear** — during the Middle Miocene, 16–12 million years ago (15.98–11.63 Ma)

  Many new plants evolved in the mid-Miocene, including 95% of modern seed plants. Most of the plant kinds growing today, in other words, trace their origin to this one stretch of time.

  <!-- mioc-064 -->

- **The Badenian Flooding refreshes the Paratethys** — c. 15 million years ago (15 Ma)

  About 15 Ma the sea rose across a wide area, an event called the Badenian Flooding. It reconnected the Paratethys with the global ocean. Fresh ocean water flowed in and ventilated its deep basins, ending the long oxygen starvation described in Paratethys turns into a giant airless sea. The sea came alive. It held a tropical to subtropical ecosystem with coral reefs and high biodiversity, and many of its species lived nowhere else.

  <!-- mioc-065 -->

- **First mastodons, bovids and kangaroos** — c. 15 million years ago (15 Ma)

  Around 15 million years ago, three famous groups made their first appearance: mastodons of the genus Mammut, bovids such as cattle and antelopes, and kangaroos. Australian megafauna, the continent's large animals, diversified at the same time.

  <!-- mioc-066 -->

- **Earth's magnetic field flips again and again** — c. 15 million years ago (15 Ma)

  Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times, but around 15 million years ago it was especially restless. At least 51 reversals occurred in a 12-million-year period centred on that date. Each one is written into rocks that cooled while it lasted.

  <!-- mioc-067 -->

- **Lake Vostok is sealed beneath the ice** — c. 15 million years ago (15 Ma)

  Beneath the East Antarctic ice lies a lake, Lake Vostok. Its water is estimated to have been sealed under the thick ice about 15 million years ago, when the ice sheet formed over it. It has stayed cut off from the open air ever since.

  <!-- mioc-068 -->

- **Steinheim, the Ries crater's small neighbor** — c. 15 million years ago (15 Ma)

  About 40 km southwest of the Ries lies a smaller crater, Steinheim, 3.8 km across and also roughly 15 million years old. The two were long thought to come from one binary asteroid. That is now disputed. A 2020 study suggests Steinheim is about 500,000 years younger.

  <!-- mioc-071 -->

- **The Pisco Formation's marine treasures** — c. 15–2 million years ago (15–2 Ma)

  Peru's Pisco Formation ranks among the most important Lagerstätten, fossil sites of exceptional preservation. Its desert rocks hold megalodon, penguins, whales, marine crocodiles and even aquatic sloths. Together they give a crowded, detailed record of the life along South America's Pacific coast, spanning millions of years.

  <!-- mioc-070 -->

- **An asteroid blasts the Ries crater in Germany** — 15 million years ago (14.808 ± 0.038 Ma)

  The blast that hit southern Germany 14.808 ± 0.038 million years ago released about 2.4×10^21 joules, the power of 40 million Hiroshima bombs. An asteroid had struck, carving the 24 km Nördlinger Ries crater. Melted surface sand flew up to 450 km away. It is thought to be the source of moldavites, green glassy tektites found in the Czech Republic. A smaller crater nearby may or may not be linked, as Steinheim, the Ries crater's small neighbor explains.

  <!-- mioc-072 -->

- **Cooling ends the warm Miocene's tropical Europe** — c. 15–14 million years ago (14.8–14.5 Ma)

  During the warm optimum, central Europe held monitor lizards, chameleons, cordylid lizards, alligators and giant turtles. Then a wave of extinctions on land and at sea, the Middle Miocene disruption, followed about 14.8 to 14.5 Ma. The crocodilians Gavialosuchus and Diplocynodon vanished from northern latitudes between 14 and 13.5 Ma. Cooling wiped out the coral reefs of the Paratethys. Desmostylians began a decline they would not recover from.

  <!-- mioc-074 -->

- **The great Middle Miocene cooling** — c. 15–14 million years ago (14.8–14.1 Ma)

  Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C. Around 13.94 Ma, annual temperatures in the Transantarctic Mountains fell 25–30 °C, and their glaciers froze to their beds. This was the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, a major and permanent cooling step between 14.8 and 14.1 Ma that ended the warm optimum. Cold Antarctic deep water increased. The East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded, reaching roughly its present size by 14 Ma. The rocks carry a signal of the change in Earth's orbit. A flip in the 41,000-year obliquity cycle, the slow nodding of Earth's tilt, around 14.0–13.8 Ma is read as a sign of the ice expansion. The cold reached the deep sea too. The resulting change in ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash in the early Tortonian. From here, the Miocene world turns steadily colder and drier.

  <!-- mioc-073 -->

  *Figure: Trace the Middle Miocene cooling from Antarctica's ice to the deep-sea carbonate crash.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Climate Transition, 14.8 to 14.1 Ma] --> B[More cold Antarctic deep water]
  A --> C[East Antarctic Ice Sheet expands]
  C --> D[Near present size by 14 Ma]
  B --> E[Ocean circulation changes]
  E --> F[Miocene Carbonate Crash]
  ```

- **The Chile Triple Junction forms** — c. 14 million years ago (14 Ma)

  About 14 million years ago, the Antarctic Plate began sliding beneath South America. The Chile Ridge, a spreading ridge, collided with the continent near Tierra del Fuego. Where the three plates meet, the Chile Triple Junction formed.

  <!-- mioc-076 -->

- **Paleolake Boreas, a tundra lake in Antarctica** — c. 14 million years ago (14 Ma)

  Around 14 million years ago, a lake in Antarctica sat in tundra conditions, cold but not yet fully icebound. Its sediments preserved ostracods, tiny shelled crustaceans, right down to their soft anatomy.

  <!-- mioc-077 -->

- **The Sea of Japan opens at both ends** — c. 14 million years ago (14 Ma)

  By 14 million years ago, the Sea of Japan basin was open to the northeast and southwest. Rising seas isolated Japan further from the mainland, continuing the opening that began in The Sea of Japan begins to open.

  <!-- mioc-079 -->

- **The Andes cast a rain shadow over Patagonia** — c. 14–12 million years ago (14–12 Ma)

  Mountains can make deserts. As the southern Andes rose 14 to 12 million years ago, they blocked moist air and cast a rain shadow, a dry zone downwind of a range. East of the mountains, the Patagonian Desert formed.

  <!-- mioc-078 -->

- **Tibet nears its modern height** — c. 14–8 million years ago (14–8 Ma)

  India kept pushing into Asia through the Neogene, building the Himalayas, and the Tibetan Plateau climbed with them. East–west rift valleys in the Lhasa and Himalaya terranes suggest the plateau was close to its modern altitude by about 14 to 8 Ma. Sudden mafic volcanism and faster uplift 14 to 11 Ma point to delamination, the peeling away of the dense lower lithosphere beneath Tibet. Accounts differ, however. The plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene, yet some suture zones stayed tropical lowlands into the early Miocene. Its rise affected the Asian monsoons.

  <!-- mioc-080 -->

- **The Tethys seaway closes for good** — c. 14 million years ago (13.8 Ma)

  The second and final step of the Tethys seaway's closure came around 13.8 Ma, as Antarctic glaciers expanded sharply. A link between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean had briefly reopened in the Langhian, then closed for good. Africa collided with Eurasia in the Turkish–Arabian region, and the old seaway disappeared. The timing is contested. Sources date the closure anywhere from about 50 or 35 Ma to 19-12 Ma, and this two-step account, begun in Arabia slams into Eurasia and the Tethys narrows, follows only some of them.

  <!-- mioc-082 -->

- **The Badenian Salinity Crisis** — c. 14–13 million years ago (13.8–13.4 Ma)

  Midway through the Middle Miocene, rising central European mountains and falling sea level cut the Paratethys off from the ocean. Around 13.8 Ma the Bârlad Strait closed, and the Eastern Paratethys became a saltwater lake. Starved of fresh water, the Central Paratethys laid down evaporites, salt left by evaporating water, until about 13.4 Ma. Growing isolation wiped out most small and mid-sized deepwater and open-ocean sharks there. The crisis was a smaller rehearsal of the Mediterranean's own drying in The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out.

  <!-- mioc-081 -->

  *Figure: Read down from the Paratethys losing its ocean link to the salt and shark losses that followed.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Mountains rise, sea level falls] --> B[Paratethys cut off from ocean]
  B --> C[Bârlad Strait closes, 13.8 Ma]
  C --> D[Eastern Paratethys: saltwater lake]
  B --> E[Central Paratethys lays down evaporites]
  B --> F[Open-ocean sharks wiped out]
  ```

- **La Venta's tropical menagerie** — c. 14–12 million years ago (13.8–11.8 Ma)

  La Venta in Colombia holds a rich tropical fauna, with glyptodonts, notoungulates and ground sloths, that lived about 13.8 to 12 million years ago. The site names the Laventan age, the only South American land-mammal age defined north of the equator.

  <!-- mioc-083 -->

- **Ōkueyama's supereruption in Japan** — c. 14 million years ago (13.7 Ma)

  About 13.7 million years ago, Mount Ōkueyama in Japan erupted massively, possibly at VEI 8. That would make it larger than any eruption in recorded history. It was one of several huge eruptions across southwest Japan between 15 and 13 million years ago.

  <!-- mioc-084 -->

- **Fish suffocate in Ngorora's lakes** — c. 13–9 million years ago (13.3–9 Ma)

  In Kenya's Ngorora beds, alkaline lake sediments hold whole fish skeletons, still joined, that died en masse. They suffocated, either during ash falls or when the lake water turned acidic quickly. Each layer marks a sudden die-off.

  <!-- mioc-086 -->

- **The Paratethys turns brackish and its sea life dies** — c. 13 million years ago (12.65 Ma)

  From 13.36 to 12.65 Ma, the Central Paratethys was open sea again. Then the Bârlad Strait reopened, and the sea turned brackish, between salt and fresh. That change caused the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction event.

  <!-- mioc-089 -->

- **The Qaidam Basin dries out** — c. 13 million years ago (12.6 Ma)

  Rock weathers fastest where water is plentiful. Around 12.6 Ma, the weathering of silicate rock in China's Qaidam Basin fell sharply. The drop marks a major aridification event, the basin turning dry. It was one sign of the growing dryness that would spread across Asia and the world later in the Miocene.

  <!-- mioc-090 -->

- **Sivapithecus, the ape with an orangutan's face** — c. 12.0–8.5 million years ago (12.5–8.5 Ma)

  Sivapithecus, a chimpanzee-sized ape, lived in the Indian subcontinent about 12.5-8.5 million years ago. Its face resembled an orangutan's, with a concave profile, large cheekbones and close-set eyes. A skull from Pakistan strengthened the link. One species may have been the orangutans' ancestor.

  <!-- mioc-091 -->

- **Ashfall: a waterhole buried by a distant eruption** — c. 12 million years ago (12 Ma)

  One rhino at Nebraska's Ashfall Fossil Beds still carries an unborn fetus. Ash from the Bruneau-Jarbidge supereruption in Idaho drifted about 1,600 km east and buried a waterhole. Teleoceras rhinos, horses, camels and birds lie articulated. They died of lung failure from inhaled ash.

  <!-- mioc-092 -->

- **Bullock Creek's skulls and horned tortoise** — c. 12 million years ago (12 Ma)

  Bullock Creek in Australia's Northern Territory preserves complete marsupial skulls, the crocodile Baru, an early kangaroo and the horned tortoise Meiolania. Whole skulls are rare finds, and here they give a clear view of the animals of Miocene northern Australia.

  <!-- mioc-093 -->

- **The Eridanos, a lost river, builds a giant delta** — c. 12 million years ago (12 Ma)

  A great river once flowed from Lapland across the Baltic region. By about 12 Ma at the latest, this Eridanos had reached the North Sea area. Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's.

  <!-- mioc-095 -->

- **The Paratethys becomes a brackish megalake** — c. 12 million years ago (12 Ma)

  Around 12 Ma, the Paratethys became a megalake of over 2.8 million km², reaching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan. It was the size of an inland sea but no longer part of the ocean. Its water was brackish, with salinity mostly 12–14‰, far fresher than seawater. Trapped by tectonics and cut off from the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, it became an isolated inland sea that gradually disappeared. Its final crisis is told in The Khersonian crisis empties the megalake.

  <!-- mioc-097 -->

- **Pliohippus and the rise of the grazing horses** — c. 12 million years ago (12 Ma)

  Around 10 Ma, horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth built for grinding tough grass. The family tree behind them branched from Merychippus, the ancestor of Hipparion, Protohippus and Pliohippus. Pliohippus itself arose from Calippus around 12 Ma. Hipparion and its relatives multiplied in North America. At least one of them migrated to Asia and Europe, carrying the grazing horse lineage across the northern continents.

  <!-- mioc-098 -->

- **Supereruptions build the Snake River Plain** — c. 12–11 million years ago (12–11 Ma)

  Two of the eruptions here rank as VEI 8 supereruptions. McMullen, 8.99 Ma, released at least 1,700 km³ of rock, and Grey's Landing, 8.72 Ma, at least 2,800 km³. They belong to a chain. The western Snake River Plain began forming around 12–11 Ma with rhyolite lava and ignimbrite. The Yellowstone hotspot's Picabo caldera erupted the Arbon Valley Tuff about 10.2 Ma, and the Twin Falls field was active 10–8.6 Ma. From 6.6 Ma the Heise field in eastern Idaho produced four big caldera eruptions, starting with 1,500 km³ of Blacktail Tuff at 6.62 Ma. Volcanism marched both ways. Oregon's High Lava Plains spread west from about 10 Ma while the Snake River Plain advanced east.

  <!-- mioc-096 -->

  *Figure: Compare the volumes of the Snake River Plain's great caldera eruptions.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The deep seaway between the Americas closes** — c. 12.0–9.2 million years ago (12–9.2 Ma)

  By 12–9.2 Ma, the deep-ocean links between the Pacific and the Caribbean through Central America had closed. A shallow link lasted until 2.45 Ma at the latest. The first phase of uplift of the Isthmus of Panama is dated to around 12 Ma. In the Late Miocene islands formed between the continents, and ground sloths such as Thinobadistes island-hopped north. Zircons in northern Colombia suggest a full isthmus, not just islands, may already have formed by 10 Ma. Colombia's La Venta fauna is the last purely South American assemblage before the two continents' animals mixed.

  <!-- mioc-094 -->

  *Figure: The seaway between the Americas closed in steps over millions of years.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Amazon runs across a continent** — c. 12–11 million years ago (11.8–11.3 Ma)

  In the Cretaceous, the proto-Amazon flowed west, part of a river system draining from Africa. The river we know flows the other way. Between 11.8 and 11.3 Ma, the Amazon began flowing as a river across the whole continent. Its new course ran through the region once held by the wetland in Lake Pebas floods western Amazonia.

  <!-- mioc-099 -->

###### Late Miocene

About 11 million years ago the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended, and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. The cold reshaped life on every continent. Europe's large mammal diversity fell, and South America's giant crocodilians and native predators faded as wetlands vanished. Off southwest Africa, the cold Benguela Upwelling began. Meanwhile the land kept changing: the modern Yangtze River took shape, and Andean calderas such as Aguas Calientes poured out vast ignimbrites.

- **The Benguela Upwelling begins** — during the Late Miocene, 12.0–5.3 million years ago (11.63–5.333 Ma)

  Off southwestern Africa, cold, nutrient-rich water began rising from the deep in the late Miocene. This Benguela Upwelling likely fed the phytoplankton behind the rich marine fossils of Hondeklip Bay. On land it had the opposite effect. Today the cold Benguela Current along the coast helps keep the Namib Desert arid.

  <!-- mioc-100 -->

- **Europe's big mammals decline** — during the Late Miocene, 12.0–5.3 million years ago (11.63–5.333 Ma)

  Europe's variety of large mammals fell significantly during the Late Miocene. The drying climate picked winners and losers. In Iberia, grazers diversified while browsers declined, as open grass replaced the leaves that browsing animals depended on.

  <!-- mioc-102 -->

- **South America's giant crocodilians vanish** — during the Late Miocene, 12.0–5.3 million years ago (11.63–5.333 Ma)

  Purussaurus, a caiman, was the largest of the Miocene crocodilians. It and the gharial Gryposuchus died out in the late Miocene. Their end probably came as northern South America's wetlands vanished, the swamps and lakes they had depended on.

  <!-- mioc-103 -->

- **The last sebecosuchians hang on in the Antilles** — during the Late Miocene, 12.0–5.3 million years ago (11.63–5.333 Ma)

  Sebecids were the last of the sebecosuchians, land-dwelling relatives of crocodiles. They apparently survived on the Greater Antilles until the late Miocene or early Pliocene, an island refuge for the final members of a long line.

  <!-- mioc-104 -->

- **South America's marsupial-like predators fade** — during the Late Miocene, 12.0–5.3 million years ago (11.63–5.333 Ma)

  For a long time, South America's top meat-eaters were sparassodonts, relatives of marsupials. From the Late Miocene they declined, possibly because of cooling. The borhyaenids, one of their families, are last known from the latest Miocene.

  <!-- mioc-106 -->

- **Danuvius, an ape that may have walked upright** — c. 12 million years ago (11.62 Ma)

  In a clay pit in southern Germany lay the bones of Danuvius guggenmosi, a great ape dated to 11.62 million years ago. Its discoverer argues it both hung in trees and walked upright along branches. That 'extended limb clambering' may have come before human bipedalism. Other researchers disagree. They say the fragmentary remains differ too little from other fossil apes to show how upright walking began.

  <!-- mioc-108 -->

- **Lazarussuchus, last of the choristoderes** — c. 12 million years ago (11.6 Ma)

  Choristoderes were semiaquatic reptiles dating back to the Middle Jurassic. They survived the extinction that killed the dinosaurs, then died out in the Miocene for unclear reasons. The last was Lazarussuchus, a European genus. Its last definite remains are Early Miocene, from the Czech Republic, with possible remains from about 11.6 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-109 -->

- **The Late Miocene Cool Interval begins** — c. 11 million years ago (11 Ma)

  About 11 Ma, the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. From here on, Earth's climate grew increasingly like today's. The cold hit some animals hard. Desmostylians, cold-adapted marine mammals, declined during the Middle to Late Miocene cooling, which may have been harsher than earlier cold spells. Their end comes in The desmostylians die out.

  <!-- mioc-110 -->

- **The modern Yangtze takes shape** — c. 11 million years ago (11 Ma)

  The modern Yangtze River is estimated to have originated around 11 Ma. The evidence lies in the mud it carried. Sedimentation rates suggest that its present outlet to the sea is no older than the late Miocene, about 11 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-111 -->

- **A brief warm pulse at 10.8 Ma** — c. 11 million years ago (10.8–10.7 Ma)

  The Late Miocene cooling did not run smoothly. Around 10.8–10.7 Ma, early in the Late Miocene, a major but short-lived warming broke the trend. Then the cooling resumed, with the climate drifting toward today's.

  <!-- mioc-112 -->

- **Aguas Calientes erupts the Tajamar ignimbrite** — c. 10 million years ago (10.5–10.1 Ma)

  High in the Andes, the Aguas Calientes caldera erupted the Tajamar ignimbrite between 10.5 and 10.1 Ma. About 350 km³ of rock poured out. It was one of a long run of great eruptions in the Central Andes, the volcanism that had begun in The Central Andes begin erupting ignimbrites.

  <!-- mioc-113 -->

- **Ancient Lake Idaho fills for the first time** — c. 10.0–6.4 million years ago (10.1–6.4 Ma)

  Lake Idaho came and went. It existed in a first phase from about 10.1 to 6.4 Ma. Then it vanished, only to return from 4.3 to 2.5 Ma, filling the same region a second time.

  <!-- mioc-114 -->

- **The elephant family arises in Africa** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  Around 10 Ma, the first members of the elephant family, Elephantidae, arose in Africa from gomphotheres. They were part of a broader change. From the Late Miocene many proboscideans grew ever larger tusks and shorter lower jaws. Climate change drove other groups, such as amebelodontids and choerolophodontids, into decline and extinction. The first members of modern elephant genera appeared around 6–5 Ma, at the Miocene–Pliocene transition.

  <!-- mioc-116 -->

- **Greenland's rising edges make room for ice** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  Greenland's ice needed high ground. Around 10 Ma, Greenland's western margin began to rise, later forming plateaus 2,000–3,000 m high. The eastern uplands followed about 5 Ma. This uplift made a single, connected Greenland ice sheet possible. Greenland may have had large glaciers as early as 8–7 Ma, though forests survived there into the Pliocene.

  <!-- mioc-117 -->

- **Ground sloths island-hop to North America** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  Sloths reached North America before any land bridge. Megalonychid and mylodontid ground sloths had island-hopped north by about 10–9 Ma, using islands forming between the Americas. The earliest North American megalonychid, Pliometanastes, lived in the southern US about 9 Ma. Traffic may have gone both ways. Some large North American herbivores may have reached South America 10–9 Ma over an incomplete land bridge. These crossings were an early phase of the exchange described in The Great American Interchange.

  <!-- mioc-118 -->

- **Ten-million-year-old apes of East Africa** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  Ten-million-year-old hominid apes are known from East Africa: Chororapithecus from Ethiopia's Afar rift, and Nakalipithecus. They date from about the time the gorilla branch split from the branch leading to humans and chimpanzees, around 10 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-120 -->

- **The Pannonian Sea is cut off** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  The Paratethys did not vanish all at once. It broke into pieces. Around 10 Ma the Carpathian mountains rose, and their uplift isolated the Pannonian Sea from the rest of the Paratethys. Each such cut left a smaller, more isolated body of water behind, on its own path.

  <!-- mioc-122 -->

- **The Rivera microplate breaks away** — c. 10 million years ago (10 Ma)

  Plates can split into smaller pieces. Around 10 Ma, off western Mexico, the Rivera plate broke away from the Cocos plate. It became a microplate, a small independent slab of crust with its own motion.

  <!-- mioc-124 -->

- **Baja California tears away from Mexico** — c. 10–6 million years ago (10–6 Ma)

  Rifting began opening the Gulf of California 10–6 Ma, tearing the Baja California peninsula northwest from mainland Mexico. Geologists widely date the gulf itself to around 5.3 million years ago, when the rift tore Baja California off the North American plate. The East Pacific Rise, a mid-ocean spreading ridge, pushed up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone. The new gulf changed the rivers around it. Its opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast. By 5.5–5 Ma, streams there had merged into one major river, the subject of The Colorado River starts cutting the Grand Canyon.

  <!-- mioc-119 -->

- **The Altiplano–Puna ignimbrite flare-up** — c. 10–1 million years ago (10–1 Ma)

  About 10,000 km³ of ignimbrite erupted from the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex between 10 and 1 Ma, over crust 70 km thick. It began from below. Mafic magma, rich in iron and magnesium, was injected into the lower crust, and an overturn before 10.6 Ma melted crust and started the eruptions. From about 10 Ma the calderas erupted in four pulses separated by quieter spells. Volcanism peaked 8–4 Ma with huge eruptions at Cerro Panizos, Coranzulí, Vilama, Cerro Guacha and La Pacana.

  <!-- mioc-115 -->

- **Livyatan, the sperm whale with giant teeth** — c. 9.9–8.9 million years ago (9.9–8.9 Ma)

  Livyatan had the largest biting teeth known. This 13.5–17.5 m sperm whale hunted off Peru 9.9–8.9 Ma. Teeth from Chile to Australia suggest it or a close relative ranged widely and survived to about 5 Ma. End-Miocene cooling probably shrank its food supply and caused its extinction.

  <!-- mioc-125 -->

- **Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids arrive** — c. 9.4 million years ago (9.4 Ma)

  North America's cast of mammals changed in the Hemphillian age, from about 9.4 Ma. Old residents bowed out. The last oreodonts, mylagaulids and dromomerycids died out. Newcomers walked in from Asia: deer, bovids, saber-toothed cats and skunks. At home, rabbits and short-faced bears diversified. Several animals now familiar in North America, from deer to skunks, first arrived on the continent in this turnover.

  <!-- mioc-126 -->

- **Asia's winter monsoons grow stronger** — c. 9.2–8.5 million years ago (9.2–8.5 Ma)

  Monsoons blow both ways, wet in summer and dry and cold in winter. The South Asian winter monsoon strengthened about 9.2–8.5 Ma. From 7.9 to 5.8 Ma, the East Asian winter monsoon also grew stronger, as the subarctic front, the boundary of cold northern air, shifted south. Around 5.5 Ma the East Asian winter monsoon intensified rapidly.

  <!-- mioc-127 -->

- **Cerro Ballena's whale graveyard** — c. 9.0–6.5 million years ago (9.03–6.45 Ma)

  In Chile's Atacama Desert lie over 40 whales, along with seals, sailfish, swordfish, sharks and aquatic sloths. They died in four separate mass deaths. Toxic algal blooms, fed by high iron levels, likely poisoned them before waves washed the carcasses ashore.

  <!-- mioc-129 -->

- **Gargano's fissure traps** — c. 9.0–5.5 million years ago (9–5.5 Ma)

  On Gargano in Italy, cracks opened in old Jurassic rock. Miocene mammals and birds fell into these fissures and were buried. Over time they built up large deposits of well-preserved animals. The cracks worked as natural pitfall traps.

  <!-- mioc-131 -->

- **The Lake Malawi basin begins to form** — c. 8.6 million years ago (8.6 Ma)

  The Lake Malawi basin began forming about 8.6 Ma, far earlier than once thought. Water came much later. Deep water first appeared there only 4.5 Ma, millions of years after the basin itself opened in the rift.

  <!-- mioc-133 -->

- **Vilama's VEI 8 supereruption** — c. 8.5–8.4 million years ago (8.5–8.4 Ma)

  Vilama caldera in the Andes erupted the enormous Vilama ignimbrite about 8.5–8.4 Ma, a VEI 8 eruption at the top of the volcanic scale. The 1,000 km³ Sifon ignimbrite, erupted 8.33 Ma, may also have come from Vilama.

  <!-- mioc-134 -->

- **Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus in Europe** — c. 8 million years ago (8 Ma)

  Apes from Greece and Anatolia, Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus, date to about 8 Ma. Some have taken them as a sign that hominins spread beyond Africa early. They are probably members of Homininae, the African great-ape subfamily, but not of the human tribe, Hominini.

  <!-- mioc-136 -->

- **Humans and chimpanzees go separate ways** — c. 8 million years ago (8 Ma)

  Your closest living relative is the chimpanzee, and the question of when the two lines parted has no settled answer. The order of branching is clear. Gibbons split off first, then orangutans, then gorillas, before the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated. Their last common ancestor was probably a small African ape. The date is the hard part. A 2026 meta-analysis found that genome-based estimates fitting the fossil record put the split at about 8 Ma, almost certainly more than 7 Ma. Other molecular estimates scatter widely: 10–13 Ma in 1998, 9.3–6.5 Ma in 2016, 6.6–4.7 Ma in 2022 and 6.3–5.5 Ma in 2025. Fossils pushed back on the youngest numbers. Hominins such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin did not fit older molecular dates of 6–4 Ma. The parting may not have been clean either. The two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3–5.4 Ma. Researchers still disagree, with estimates running from about 13 to 4.7 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-137 -->

  *Figure: Molecular estimates for the human–chimpanzee split.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

  *Figure: The order in which ape lineages branched off.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Gibbons branch off] --> B[Orangutans]
  B --> C[Gorillas]
  C --> D[Chimpanzees and humans split]
  ```

- **The Leporid Datum: rabbits and hares everywhere** — c. 8 million years ago (8 Ma)

  Around 8 Ma, rabbits and hares abruptly diversified and spread across the Northern Hemisphere. The event is sudden and widespread enough to serve as a marker in the rock record, called the Leporid Datum. The spread kept going. By 7 Ma the group had expanded into South America and Africa.

  <!-- mioc-139 -->

- **The world dries out** — c. 8–7 million years ago (8–7 Ma)

  A colder atmosphere holds less moisture. As the globe cooled, the air dried, driving a worldwide trend toward aridity, especially after 8–7 Ma. The effects showed everywhere. Uplift of East Africa helped shrink its rainforests. Australia dried as it drifted into a low-rainfall zone, though its southwest grew wetter 12–8 Ma. The Tian Shan blocked westerly winds and dried the Tarim Basin. In Kenya's Great Rift Valley aridity rose gradually, with wet spells still returning. One theory links the Sahara's drying to a monsoon weakened when the Tethys Sea dried up around 7 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-138 -->

- **The Banda Arc meets Australia** — during the Messinian, 7.2–5.3 million years ago (7.246–5.333 Ma)

  In the Messinian, the Banda Arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands, began colliding with Australia and Timor. Geologists use it as a standard example of how an island arc crashes into a continent and builds a mountain belt, an orogen, along the seam.

  <!-- mioc-142 -->

- **Sahelanthropus and the skull called Toumaï** — c. 7.2–6.8 million years ago (7.2–6.8 Ma)

  A partial skull found in northern Chad, nicknamed Toumaï, is the main evidence for Sahelanthropus. It lived about 7 Ma, with averaged sample ages giving 7.2–6.8 Ma. It is often listed as the first hominin, and the human line of upright-walking apes has been traced back to it. Its place is disputed. Some of its anatomy has been proposed as matching the last common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans, and other researchers reject that reading.

  <!-- mioc-144 -->

- **The desmostylians die out** — c. 7.2–5.3 million years ago (7.2–5.3 Ma)

  Desmostylians are the only known extinct order of marine mammals. Native to the North Pacific, they declined after the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, perhaps because Late Miocene cooling was unusually severe. They died out for good between 7.2 and 5.3 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-143 -->

- **Thalassocnus, the sloth that swam** — c. 7 million years ago (7 Ma)

  A ground sloth went to sea. The oldest fossils of Thalassocnus, adapted to marine life on South America's Pacific coast, date to roughly 7 Ma in Peru. It is now known from many Miocene–Pliocene rock units along the coast, including Chile's Coquimbo Formation.

  <!-- mioc-148 -->

- **C4 grasses take over the grasslands** — c. 7–6 million years ago (7–6 Ma)

  Grass is tough to eat, and a new kind made it tougher. C4 grasses use carbon dioxide and water more efficiently than C3 grasses, the older type. Between 7 and 6 Ma they became ecologically significant, though not yet in the north. As carbon dioxide kept falling, C4 plants came to dominate grasslands over the last 10 million years. They changed who could eat. Silica-rich C4 grasses wore down teeth, and herbivores without high-crowned teeth went extinct worldwide. The cause of the spread is still argued over. Some point to falling carbon dioxide. Others point to rising seasonality and aridity, with wildfires fed by the monsoons. The shift was large enough to mark the whole planet. It left its imprint on the global carbon cycle, visible in carbon isotope records.

  <!-- mioc-145 -->

  *Figure: Falling CO2 favored C4 grasses, which reshaped herbivores.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[CO2 falls] --> B[C4 grasses dominate]
  B --> C[Herbivores without high crowns die]
  ```

- **The sharp Late Miocene cooling** — c. 7.0–5.3 million years ago (7–5.3 Ma)

  Between 7 and 5.3 Ma temperatures fell sharply, most likely from declining carbon dioxide and a smaller swing in Earth's axial tilt. Ocean temperatures dropped to near-modern values, with sea surfaces outside the tropics cooling by about 7–9 °C. Antarctic ice neared its present size. Significant glaciation from 6.26 to 5.50 Ma kept time with the 41,000-year tilt cycle, dominant since 7.7 Ma. A cold spell around 6 Ma advanced glaciers and lowered sea level, helping start the crisis in The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out. Around then the carbon cycle reorganized too: carbon stores on land stopped growing during cold spells.

  <!-- mioc-147 -->

  *Figure: See how the late Miocene cooling led on to the Messinian crisis.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Falling CO2] --> C[Sharp cooling, 7 to 5.3 Ma]
  B[Smaller tilt swing] --> C
  C --> D[Antarctic ice near present size]
  C --> E[Cold spell near 6 Ma]
  E --> F[Glaciers advance, sea level falls]
  F --> G[Messinian salinity crisis begins]
  ```

- **The first mammoth lives in Africa** — c. 6.2–5.3 million years ago (6.2–5.3 Ma)

  Mammoths began not in the frozen north but in Africa. The oldest, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared in southern and eastern Africa around 6.2-5.3 million years ago. Mammoths went on to live in Africa, Asia, Europe and North America until about 4,000 years ago. A 2010 study suggests mammoths and Asian elephants split 7.8-5.8 million years ago, after the African elephant line had branched off 8.8-6.6 million years ago.

  <!-- mioc-149 -->

  *Figure: The molecular split dates come before the oldest mammoth fossil.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Orrorin, an early hominin that walked upright** — c. 6.1–5.7 million years ago (6.1–5.7 Ma)

  In Kenya's Lukeino Formation, fossils of Orrorin tugenensis date from 6.1 to 5.7 Ma. Orrorin appears to have walked upright on two legs about 6 Ma. Its fossils share no derived features, the new traits that mark a lineage, with the great apes. It belongs instead with the early hominins. The rise of two-legged apes at the end of the Miocene sped up the turnover of Africa's animals.

  <!-- mioc-150 -->

- **Trachilos footprints: a puzzle on Crete** — c. 6 million years ago (6.05 Ma)

  On western Crete, possible footprints with hominin-like features have been dated to about 6.05 Ma, older than an earlier 5.7 Ma estimate. If a hominin made them, they would predate other hominin footprints by about two million years. They may instead record an ape that evolved similar feet independently. Critics doubt they are footprints at all, and the claim clashes with the accepted African origin of hominins.

  <!-- mioc-151 -->

- **Argentavis, a giant of the South American skies** — c. 6 million years ago (6 Ma)

  Argentavis had a wingspan of 6 m or more, making it one of the largest flying birds known. This teratorn soared over South America about 6 Ma. It may have fed partly on leftovers from the kills of Thylacosmilus, a saber-toothed predator.

  <!-- mioc-152 -->

- **The Nile carves the deep Eonile gorge** — c. 6.0–5.4 million years ago (6–5.4 Ma)

  At Cairo, the ancestral Nile cut its bed 2,400 m below sea level. As the Mediterranean emptied, the river chased the falling shoreline and carved a deep gorge, the Eonile, through Egypt. At Aswan it reached several hundred metres below sea level. When the sea refilled, the gorge became a gulf that slowly filled with sediment.

  <!-- mioc-153 -->

- **The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out** — c. 6.0–5.3 million years ago (5.96–5.33 Ma)

  Around 5.6 Ma, the Mediterranean Sea dried almost completely within a thousand years. It was the climax of the Messinian salinity crisis. From 5.96 to 5.33 Ma the sea dried out in cycles, sometimes partly and sometimes almost entirely, and evaporites piled up across its floor. The crisis began basin-wide at 5.96 ± 0.02 Ma. The Betic corridor and the precursor of the Strait of Gibraltar closed, sealing the sea off from the Atlantic. Several causes worked together: plate motion at the Gibraltar Arc, mountain uplift in the western Mediterranean, and glacial sea-level falls of about 10 m from about 6.14 Ma. With the sea gone, rivers cut canyons on the scale of the Grand Canyon, as The Nile carves the deep Eonile gorge shows. Native marine animals suffered major extinctions. From 5.5 Ma river water diluted the brines into brackish 'Lago Mare' lakes. Then, at 5.33 Ma, the Strait of Gibraltar reopened, in the flood told in The Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean.

  <!-- mioc-154 -->

  *Figure: The stages of the Messinian salinity crisis.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Atlantic gateways close] --> B[Mediterranean sealed]
  B --> C[Sea dries, evaporites pile up]
  C --> D[River water forms Lago Mare]
  D --> E[Strait of Gibraltar reopens]
  ```

- **Cerro Guacha's supereruption** — c. 5.7 million years ago (5.65 ± 0.01 Ma)

  High in the Andes, about 5.65 Ma, Cerro Guacha erupted the Guacha ignimbrite, roughly 1,200–1,300 km³ of rock. It was one of the giant eruptions at the peak of the Altiplano–Puna flare-up described in The Altiplano–Puna ignimbrite flare-up, when the region's calderas were at their most violent.

  <!-- mioc-155 -->

- **Ardipithecus appears in East Africa** — c. 5.5 million years ago (5.5 Ma)

  The genus Ardipithecus appeared around 5.5 Ma, probably after the human–chimpanzee split, though the two lines may still have been swapping genes. An early form, A. kadabba, joined Sahelanthropus and Orrorin among the first hominins in Africa at the very end of the Miocene. Its fossils from the Middle Awash date 6.5–5.5 Ma.

  <!-- mioc-156 -->

- **The Caspian Sea becomes landlocked** — c. 5.5 million years ago (5.5 Ma)

  The Caspian Sea, some 30 million years old, lost its link to the open ocean about 5.5 Ma. Two forces closed the door. Tectonic uplift raised the land around it, and sea level fell. From then on the Caspian was landlocked, the state in which it survives today.

  <!-- mioc-157 -->

- **Pastos Grandes erupts the Chuhuilla ignimbrite** — 5.5 million years ago (5.45 ± 0.02 Ma)

  At 5.45 ± 0.02 Ma, Pastos Grandes caldera in the Andes erupted the Chuhuilla ignimbrite, about 1,200 km³ of rock. It was the caldera's first great collapse cycle. Pastos Grandes joined a crowd of Andean calderas then erupting on this scale in The Altiplano–Puna ignimbrite flare-up.

  <!-- mioc-158 -->

- **The Dead Sea Transform forms** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  Toward the end of the Miocene, the Arabian plate began colliding with Eurasia. A new boundary developed: the Dead Sea Transform, where the Arabian and African plates now slide past each other. Rifting in the Gulf of Suez, active since Arabia begins to tear away from Africa, ceased.

  <!-- mioc-159 -->

- **Europe's apes disappear** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  About 100 ape species lived across Africa, Asia and Europe during the Miocene. It was the great age of apes. In Europe, that age ended with the epoch. Europe's apes died out at the end of the Miocene as habitats became more uniform. Apes such as Danuvius and Graecopithecus, met earlier in this chapter, belonged to that vanished European ape world.

  <!-- mioc-160 -->

- **The Khersonian crisis empties the megalake** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  Near the end of the Miocene, the Paratethys megalake went through the Khersonian crisis. Conditions and lake levels swung rapidly. The swings wiped out much of the lake's unique fish fauna, species found nowhere else.

  <!-- mioc-161 -->

- **The Miocene ends in warmth** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  The cold of the Messinian did not last. At the end of the Miocene, global temperatures rose again as the swing in Earth's axial tilt grew. Central Asia grew more arid. The Pliocene began warmer than the cool Messinian that came before it.

  <!-- mioc-162 -->

##### Pliocene Epoch

The Pliocene opened with a flood. Atlantic water broke through at the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean. Soon the sea first flooded the land bridge between Alaska and Siberia too. From about 5.3 to 2.7 million years ago, a warm interval interrupted the long-term cooling trend. Old groups such as the oreodonts and the cat-like nimravids died out, the great white shark evolved, and a marine extinction wiped out 36% of large marine species.

- **The sea first floods the Bering land bridge** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  Alaska and Siberia were joined by land for a long time. Near the start of the Pliocene, the sea first flooded that land bridge, and marine life could spread between the Arctic and the Pacific. The Bering Strait is thought to have first opened between 7.4 and 4.8 million years ago. The opening did not last unbroken. Afterward the bridge was flooded and restored again and again, as sea level rose and fell, alternately linking the two oceans and the two continents.

  <!-- plio-001 -->

- **The first tree sloths** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  Today's sloths hang from branches, and the first tree sloths appeared around the start of the Pliocene. Their megalonychid cousins show how sizes shifted. Early megalonychids were small and perhaps partly tree-dwelling. By the Pliocene they had grown to about half the size of the later Megalonyx.

  <!-- plio-003 -->

- **The nimravids die out** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  Nimravids, the cat-like carnivores that had led the Oligocene's predators in Carnivorans seize the top predator roles, were still diverse in the Early Miocene. Around the start of the Pliocene they died out, ending a long run as some of the land's top hunters.

  <!-- plio-005 -->

- **The Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.333 Ma)

  At its peak, the water pouring through the Strait of Gibraltar may have reached about 100 million cubic metres per second, roughly a thousand times today's Amazon. Atlantic water had broken through and was refilling the dried-out Mediterranean, ending the crisis described in The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out. About ninety percent of the basin may have filled within months to two years. At times, sea level inside rose over 10 metres a day. The sea flooded the deep canyon cut by the ancestral Nile, reaching at least as far as Aswan. The modern Nile then began filling that canyon with sediment. The reconnection marks the start of the Zanclean, the first age of the Pliocene. Not everyone accepts the drama. Sources disagree on whether the Mediterranean refilled in one catastrophic flood or more gradually, and the exact timing remains uncertain.

  <!-- plio-009 -->

  *Figure: Follow the refilling from the breach at Gibraltar to the start of the Pliocene.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Atlantic breaks through at Gibraltar] --> B[Basin refills in months to two years]
  B --> C[Sea floods the Nile canyon]
  C --> D[Nile fills canyon with sediment]
  B --> E[Messinian crisis ends]
  E --> F([Zanclean age begins])
  ```

- **The oreodonts vanish** — during the Early Pliocene, 5.3–3.6 million years ago (5.333–3.6 Ma)

  Oreodonts were plant-eating hoofed mammals, and they had stayed diverse ever since the Oligocene, through millions of years of cooling and spreading grass. They had seen the age of the giant Paraceratherium and the rise of the grazing horses. In the earliest Pliocene they disappeared, the end of the decline that began with the turnover described in Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids arrive.

  <!-- plio-006 -->

- **The Pliocene extinction of big sea animals** — during the Pliocene, 5.3–2.6 million years ago (5.333–2.58 Ma)

  In the Pliocene, 36% of large marine species disappeared. The toll ran unevenly: 55% of marine mammals, 43% of sea turtles, 35% of seabirds and 9% of sharks. Warm-blooded and partly warm-blooded animals were hit harder than cold-blooded ones, which points to a shrinking food supply. Sea level also swung more in the Plio-Pleistocene than at any other time in the Cenozoic, driven by growing polar ice. Those swings damaged coastal habitats and may have helped cause several extinctions. After the Central American Seaway closed, tropical whales declined too.

  <!-- plio-007 -->

  *Figure: Marine mammals and sea turtles lost far larger shares than sharks.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Sierra Nevada lifts and tilts** — during the Pliocene, 5.3–2.6 million years ago (5.333–2.58 Ma)

  Between two and three million years ago, the Sierra Nevada was uplifted and tilted westward. Faulting still lifts it, building steep escarpments on its eastern edge. How old its height is remains disputed. Some read recent river cutting as a sign of young uplift. Others find the northern range little changed since 30-40 million years ago.

  <!-- plio-008 -->

- **Mount Kenya, a volcano once taller than Kilimanjaro** — during the Plio-Pleistocene, 5.300–0.012 million years ago (5.333–0.0117 Ma)

  Mount Kenya's original summit was probably over 6,000 m high, perhaps 7,000 m, taller than Kilimanjaro is today. This large stratovolcano, a cone built of layered lava and ash, rose on the shoulder of the East African Rift and was active in the Plio-Pleistocene. Since it went extinct, glaciers have worn it down. Its remains are still Africa's second-highest mountain, topped by Batian at 5,199 m.

  <!-- plio-004 -->

- **The Colorado River starts cutting the Grand Canyon** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.3 Ma)

  The Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago and lowered the Colorado River's base level, the low point it drains toward. Erosion sped up, and most of the canyon's depth was cut by 1.2 Ma. Several studies hold that the river set its course 5-6 million years ago. The canyon's age is debated, though: other studies put parts at 17 to 70 million years old, and segments probably formed at different times.

  <!-- plio-010 -->

- **The great white shark appears** — c. 5.3 million years ago (5.3 Ma)

  The great white shark evolved about 5.3 million years ago. Its young had safe places to grow. Abundant juvenile teeth along Chile's Coquimbo Region show that Pliocene coasts there served as great white shark nurseries. Its rise later gained from the decline of a bigger rival, told in Megalodon disappears.

  <!-- plio-011 -->

- **The Pliocene Warm Interval** — c. 5.3–2.7 million years ago (5.3–2.7 Ma)

  Carbon dioxide levels in the Pliocene were similar to today's. That makes this time a favorite natural experiment: the interval is often treated as a preview of near-future warming. From about 5.3 to 2.7 Ma, the Pliocene Warm Interval interrupted the long-term cooling trend. The epoch opened warmer than the cool Messinian before it. Ice sheets were unstable. Their collapses were much more common in the early to mid Pliocene, between 5 and 3 Ma. The oceans stayed relatively warm, though they kept slowly cooling. The warmest stretch is told in The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period.

  <!-- plio-012 -->

- **Bluff Downs, a Pliocene Queensland riverland** — c. 5.2–3.6 million years ago (5.2–3.6 Ma)

  Between about 5.2 and 3.6 million years ago, animals died and were buried beside large water bodies fringed by riverside forest at Bluff Downs, northern Queensland. It is one of Australia's most significant Pliocene sites, with marsupials from both living and extinct families. A basalt flow dated 3.62 Ma caps the fossil beds, which are at least 4 million years old.

  <!-- plio-013 -->

- **Kauaʻi rises over the Hawaiian hotspot** — c. 5.1 million years ago (5.1 ± 0.2 Ma)

  Kauaʻi, the oldest of the main Hawaiian islands, is 5.1 ± 0.2 million years old. It formed as the Pacific Plate passed over the Hawaiʻi hotspot, a fixed source of rising magma. The plate keeps moving west-northwest, carrying each volcano away, so the chain gets younger toward the southeast.

  <!-- plio-014 -->

- **The Colorado Plateau and River take their modern shape** — c. 5 million years ago (5 Ma)

  About 5 million years ago the Colorado Plateau reached its present height, and the Colorado River settled into a course close to today's. Plateau uplift and the opening of the Gulf of California rearranged the river and its tributaries. About 4 million years ago, the Colorado began reaching the Salton Trough, then still connected to the Gulf.

  <!-- plio-015 -->

- **The last giant-toothed sperm whales** — c. 5 million years ago (5 Ma)

  Teeth from Australia and South Africa show that Livyatan or a close relative still hunted around 5 million years ago, possibly worldwide. By the early Pliocene these giant-toothed sperm whales were gone. Cooling probably made baleen whales larger and fewer, and the predators that fed on them declined with them.

  <!-- plio-016 -->

- **Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion** — c. 5 million years ago (5 Ma)

  Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, first appeared in the Pliocene. Its early species, T. crassidentatus, about 5 million years ago, was the size of a large dog. Later species grew to the weight of a lioness. The genus became Australia's apex predator, the only one of its family until the end of the Pleistocene.

  <!-- plio-017 -->

- **The Paratethys breaks into inland seas** — c. 5 million years ago (5 Ma)

  The Black, Caspian and Aral seas are the remnants of the Paratethys. From about 5 million years ago the old sea grew steadily shallower and largely dried out. During the Pliocene it split into a few inland seas, at times fully cut off from each other. The Pliocene Caspian was a small lake with no outlet.

  <!-- plio-018 -->

- **A Pliocene burst of ignimbrites in the Puna** — c. 5.0–3.8 million years ago (5–3.8 Ma)

  Between 5 and 3.8 Ma, huge ignimbrite eruptions struck the front of the volcanic arc in the northern Puna, part of a magma pulse around 4 Ma. The Puripicar ignimbrite, about 4.2 Ma, alone held some 1,500 cubic kilometres. Later giants followed: the Tara ignimbrite at 3.49 Ma (800 km3) and Pastos Grandes at 2.89 Ma (1,500 km3).

  <!-- plio-019 -->

  *Figure: Compare the volumes of three Puna ignimbrites.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Gray Fossil Site, a Tennessee sinkhole** — c. 4.9–4.5 million years ago (4.9–4.5 Ma)

  Between 4.9 and 4.5 million years ago, a sinkhole pond in a warm, wet Tennessee forest trapped plants and animals. It is the first site of its age known from Appalachia, with new species of red panda, rhinoceros, pond turtle and hickory. Its fossils show eastern North America still shared a living link with Eurasia then.

  <!-- plio-020 -->

- **The Kilgore Tuff supereruption** — c. 4.5 million years ago (4.45 ± 0.05 Ma)

  The Kilgore Tuff eruption in eastern Idaho, rated VEI 8, blasted out about 1,800 cubic kilometres of ash and left a caldera 80 by 60 km. It was the last caldera-forming eruption of the Heise field, active for over 2 million years above the Yellowstone hotspot. As the hotspot track moved northeast, the Picabo and Heise centres subsided.

  <!-- plio-022 -->

- **Ardi, a skeleton caught between trees and ground** — c. 4.4 million years ago (4.4 Ma)

  Ardi is a 4.4-million-year-old female skeleton, the most complete specimen of the early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus. Her species lived in the Afar region of Ethiopia about 4.4 million years ago. Her body shows two worlds at once. Ardi's pelvis shows that walking on two legs was well under way, yet her hands and limbs could still climb trees. Fossils of at least nine more individuals from As Duma in the Afar date to 4.51-4.32 million years ago. The older A. kadabba, met in Ardipithecus appears in East Africa, is considered its direct ancestor.

  <!-- plio-023 -->

- **Australopithecus anamensis, the first australopith** — c. 4.3–3.8 million years ago (4.3–3.8 Ma)

  The oldest known species of Australopithecus, A. anamensis, lived roughly 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago. Its first fossils came from Kanapoi and Allia Bay in northern Kenya, and the Allia Bay finds give the earliest evidence of a two-legged gait. The genus probably arose in eastern Africa around 4 Ma. It later spread across the continent and died out somewhat after 2 Ma. A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Ethiopia shows that A. anamensis overlapped in time with its successor, A. afarensis, in Australopithecus afarensis walks East Africa.

  <!-- plio-024 -->

- **La Pacana's Atana supereruption** — c. 4.2–3.8 million years ago (4.2–3.8 Ma)

  At 2,500-3,500 cubic kilometres, the Atana ignimbrite is the fifth-largest explosive eruption known. It came from La Pacana caldera in the Chilean Andes between about 4.2 and 3.8 million years ago. A much smaller sister eruption, the Toconao ignimbrite, came out at almost the same time. The rocks show no sign of a pause between the two, as if one long event had produced both.

  <!-- plio-025 -->

- **The Hagerman Fossil Beds and their horse** — c. 4.0–3.1 million years ago (4–3.07 Ma)

  The Hagerman fossil beds in Idaho span at least 4 million to 3.07 million years ago and hold at least 200 species. They are among the richest deposits of North America's Blancan age. They also hold the largest known concentration of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens.

  <!-- plio-026 -->

- **Glyptodon, the armored giant** — c. 3.9 million years ago (3.9 Ma)

  Glyptodon was an armadillo relative with a shell of hundreds of bony plates, 2 m long and 400 kg. It and its cousin Glyptotherium evolved in South America from about 3.9 million years ago. This plant-eater lasted from about 3.2 million years ago until about 11,000 years ago, into the early Holocene.

  <!-- plio-028 -->

- **Australopithecus afarensis walks East Africa** — c. 3.9–2.9 million years ago (3.9–2.9 Ma)

  Selam was a three-year-old girl who died at Dikika, Ethiopia, 3.3 million years ago, about 100,000 years before Lucy. She belonged to Australopithecus afarensis, which lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. The 3.58-million-year-old Kadanuumuu skeleton suggests the species already walked fully upright by 3.6 Ma, though not all researchers agree. Tooth chemistry shows a flexible diet, from forest plants to savanna plants. Life was dangerous. Africa then held more large carnivores than today, including hyenas and saber-toothed cats, which likely preyed on australopithecines.

  <!-- plio-027 -->

  *Figure: Key afarensis fossils fall within the species' time span.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **A green North Africa** — c. 3.8–3.3 million years ago (3.8–3.3 Ma)

  North Africa was once green. From about 3.8 to 3.3 million years ago, it went through an extended humid period. Tropical forests in the northwest reached as far as Cape Blanc until around 3.5 Ma. A significant river flowed across the Sahara until 3.35 Ma. Then the trade winds began to dominate, and the region started down the road to desert.

  <!-- plio-029 -->

- **The woolly rhino's ancestor lives in Tibet** — c. 3.7 million years ago (3.7 Ma)

  The woolly rhinoceros's lineage began high on the Tibetan Plateau. Coelodonta thibetana, the oldest known species of its genus, lived there about 3.7 million years ago. The genus later spread to Siberia, Mongolia and China. The woolly rhinoceros itself appeared later, in the Middle Pleistocene.

  <!-- plio-030 -->

- **Footprints in the ash at Laetoli** — c. 3.7 million years ago (3.7 Ma)

  About 3.7 million years ago, three hominins walked across fresh volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania, one stepping in the prints of another. Soft rain then cemented the powdery ash into tuff, rock made of compacted volcanic ash, sealing the tracks. Their makers were probably Australopithecus. The prints closely resemble modern human footprints. They were then the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism. Together with leg bones, the trackways suggest A. afarensis walked well on two legs, though less efficiently than humans.

  <!-- plio-031 -->

- **Little Foot, the most complete early hominin** — c. 3.7 million years ago (3.67 Ma)

  Little Foot is about 90% complete, the most complete early hominin skeleton known. It comes from the Sterkfontein caves of South Africa. A 2015 date of 3.67 million years would make it the earliest known South African australopith. That date is controversial, with estimates from 2.2 to 3.67 million years, and its species is also disputed.

  <!-- plio-032 -->

- **Megatherium, the elephant-sized sloth** — c. 3.6 million years ago (3.6 Ma)

  Megatherium was a giant ground sloth of South America, and its best-known species, M. americanum, reached 3.5-4 tonnes, the size of an elephant. Its oldest remains come from Bolivia and the Pampas and are at least 3.6 million years old. The genus lasted to the end of the Late Pleistocene.

  <!-- plio-034 -->

- **El'gygytgyn, an impact lake that records Arctic climate** — c. 3.6 million years ago (3.6 Ma)

  About 3.6 million years ago, an impact on Siberia's Chukchi Peninsula blasted out a crater 18 km across. The crater now holds a lake about 12 km wide. Its sediments are a climate archive, showing mid-Pliocene Arctic summers 8 °C warmer than today.

  <!-- plio-035 -->

- **Megalodon disappears** — c. 3.6 million years ago (3.6 Ma)

  Megalodon, a shark estimated at 14-24 m long, was among the most powerful predators ever. It hunted worldwide from about 23 million years ago, as Megalodon, the giant shark, appears describes. A 2019 statistical reanalysis of its fossils moved its extinction back to about 3.6 million years ago, earlier than the long-assumed 2.6 million years. Several pressures probably combined. The seas cooled, and falling sea levels shrank its warm nursery waters. Small baleen whales, its prey, declined. Early killer whales were once blamed, but that now looks unlikely; rivalry with white sharks may have played a part. Its loss let great white sharks spread into its waters, and baleen whales grew markedly larger afterward.

  <!-- plio-037 -->

  *Figure: Several pressures combined to end megalodon, and its loss reshaped the sea.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Cooling seas] --> D([Megalodon extinct, about 3.6 Ma])
  B[Falling sea level shrinks nurseries] --> D
  C[Small baleen whales decline] --> D
  D --> E[Great whites spread]
  D --> F[Baleen whales grow larger]
  ```

- **Mammoths and Asian elephants leave Africa** — c. 3.6–3.2 million years ago (3.6–3.2 Ma)

  Around 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago, the elephant genera Elephas and Mammuthus, the mammoths, migrated out of Africa. Mammoths took the route through the Sinai Peninsula. By 3.2 million years ago they had spread into Eurasia, reaching Europe around 3 million years ago. In Asia, elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived, though proboscidean diversity fell sharply during the Late Pliocene. Back in Africa, mammoths became confined to the north of the continent.

  <!-- plio-036 -->

- **Australopiths reach Central Africa** — c. 3.5 million years ago (3.5 Ma)

  Jaw fossils from Koro Toro in Chad, about 3.5 million years old, are the first and only australopiths known from Central Africa. They show australopiths ranged widely, not just in the east and south. These hominins lived in lakeside grassland by an expanded 'Lake Mega-Chad', eating mostly savanna foods. Many researchers assign them to A. afarensis.

  <!-- plio-038 -->

- **Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced rival** — c. 3.5–3.2 million years ago (3.5–3.2 Ma)

  Kenyanthropus was a flat-faced, small-toothed hominin from Lake Turkana in Kenya. Its type skull is about 3.5 million years old, and its fossils span about 3.5 to 3.2 Ma. It shows that more than one hominin lineage lived alongside A. afarensis. It lived among forest and grassland, and may have made the Lomekwian stone tools found nearby.

  <!-- plio-039 -->

- **Camels in the High Arctic** — c. 3.4 million years ago (3.4 Ma)

  Camels once lived inside the Arctic Circle. Fragmentary remains referred to Paracamelus, about 3.4 million years old, come from Ellesmere Island. The world was then 2-3 °C warmer than today, and the island was covered in boreal forest. Collagen sequences confirm these Arctic camels were close relatives of modern Camelus.

  <!-- plio-040 -->

- **Dikika's disputed cut marks** — c. 3.4 million years ago (3.4 Ma)

  At Dikika in Ethiopia, a rib and a thigh bone from hoofed animals bear cut marks, the rib also some crushing. If stone tools made them, they would be the oldest evidence of butchering with sharp-edged tools, at 3.4 million years. The claim is disputed. The bones lay in sandstone, where abrasive sand and gravel also scratched them.

  <!-- plio-041 -->

- **Lomekwi: the oldest stone tools** — c. 3.3 million years ago (3.3 Ma)

  In West Turkana, Kenya, 3.3 million years ago, someone struck one stone against another. The flakes they left at Lomekwi 3 are the oldest known stone tools. The method was simple. The toolmaker pounded a core on an anvil or hit it with a hammerstone, using volcanic rock gathered within 100 m. Who made them is unknown. Kenyanthropus platyops, a 3.5-3.2-million-year-old hominin from Lake Turkana met in Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced rival, may have been the earliest tool user. There are hints of something older. Cut-marked bones about 3.4 million years old from Ethiopia's Lower Awash Valley may be indirect evidence of tool use, though that claim is weaker. These tools open a long chapter. The Paleolithic, which covers almost all of humanity's prehistoric technology, begins with the first stone tools about 3.3 million years ago.

  <!-- plio-044 -->

- **The Phoenix plate stops sinking** — c. 3.3 million years ago (3.3 Ma)

  For over 100 million years, the Phoenix plate had been sinking beneath its neighbors. About 3.3 million years ago, spreading on the Antarctic-Phoenix Ridge stopped, and its subduction slowed or ceased. The plate's remnant was absorbed into the Antarctic plate.

  <!-- plio-046 -->

- **A possible impact in Argentina** — c. 3.3 million years ago (3.3 Ma)

  Around 3.3 million years ago, at the start of the Marplatan land-mammal age, a cosmic impact may have struck Argentina. It has been suggested as a cause of a turnover in South American animals. Both the impact and that link remain uncertain, and the sources call the idea controversial.

  <!-- plio-047 -->

- **The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period** — c. 3.3–3.0 million years ago (3.3–3 Ma)

  Between 3.3 and 3.0 million years ago, carbon dioxide stood near 400 ppm, the level of the year 2000. Global temperatures ran 2-3 °C above today's. This peak of Pliocene warmth is also called the Pliocene Thermal Maximum. The poles warmed most. Arctic summers were about 8 °C warmer than now, and models suggest the Arctic above 70°N was 10-20 °C warmer, with little change in the tropics. Greenland's ice shrank to its highest eastern and southern peaks. Global sea level stood about 25 m higher than today. In southeastern European lakes, viviparid snails diversified rapidly as temperatures rose by as much as 10 °C between 3.3 and 2.9 Ma.

  <!-- plio-045 -->

  *Figure: Warming was strongest in the Arctic and smallest worldwide on average.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Australopithecus africanus and the Taung Child** — c. 3.3–2.1 million years ago (3.3–2.1 Ma)

  The Taung Child, a juvenile skull about 2.8 million years old, was the first early hominin ever found. It belongs to Australopithecus africanus, which lived in South Africa from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago. Its fossils come from Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat and Gladysvale. It walked well on two legs, though less efficiently than humans, and kept a more apelike upper body than East Africa's A. afarensis. It lived in gallery forest bordered by grassland and ate a highly varied diet, including grasses and seeds. Strong swings in climate probably ended it, perhaps along with competition from Homo and Paranthropus robustus.

  <!-- plio-042 -->

- **Lucy, the skeleton that walked before it thought big** — c. 3.2 million years ago (3.2 Ma)

  Lucy's skeleton is about 40% complete, and it settled an old question. She was a female Australopithecus afarensis who lived at Hadar in Ethiopia's Afar region around 3.2 million years ago. Her skull was small and ape-like, but she walked upright on two legs. So walking upright came before larger brains. Her age is well pinned. Ash layers beneath the fossil were argon-dated to 3.22 and 3.18 Ma, the younger only one metre below her. Nearby, the 'First Family' site AL 333, about 3.2 million years old, holds at least thirteen individuals of different ages.

  <!-- plio-048 -->

- **The eastern Pacific's permanent El Niño ends** — c. 3 million years ago (3 Ma)

  In the early to mid Pliocene, the eastern equatorial Pacific stayed warm all the time, in a permanent El Niño-like state. The warm water absorbed sunlight and lowered Earth's reflectivity. Around 3 million years ago, cold surface water appeared there. That change may have helped cool the globe. It may also have changed how Earth's climate responded to the slow cycles of its orbit.

  <!-- plio-049 -->

- **Savannas spread across East Africa** — c. 3 million years ago (3 Ma)

  Around 3 million years ago, as the climate turned cooler and drier, savanna expanded in East Africa. Pliocene cooling may have hastened the loss of forests and the spread of grasslands. Some researchers think the change shaped human evolution. One hypothesis holds that walking upright and other hominin traits evolved as forests opened into savanna. Another links the savanna to fire. Wildfires there were common but easier to survive, and moving into that setting may have been the first step toward early humans' control of fire.

  <!-- plio-050 -->

- **South America's native predators collapse** — c. 3 million years ago (3 Ma)

  Roughly 3 million years ago, South America's native meat-eaters collapsed, including the last sparassodonts, the continent's meat-eating metatherians, relatives of marsupials. Thylacosmilids last occur about 3 Ma, already rare before the continents met. Terror birds also declined after that. The timing does not fit simple replacement by northern invaders. Dogs and weasels reached South America about 2.9 Ma but stayed rare until the Pleistocene. By the Pliocene only two sparassodont families were left, and hathliacynids are last known from the early Pliocene. Their long decline, from the Late Miocene on, may be linked to cooling and the onset of Quaternary glaciation.

  <!-- plio-051 -->

- **The South Asian summer monsoon strengthens** — c. 3 million years ago (2.95 Ma)

  After 2.95 Ma, the South Asian Summer Monsoon grew stronger. The likely cause lay at sea, in the Indonesian Throughflow, the current that carries water from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean between the islands of Indonesia. That flow was reorganized, and the monsoon responded, another sign of how ocean gateways shaped Asia's rains.

  <!-- plio-053 -->

- **Oldowan tools: the first widespread toolkit** — c. 2.9 million years ago (2.9 Ma)

  At Nyayanga on Kenya's Homa Peninsula, the oldest known Oldowan tools date to about 2.9 million years ago. The Oldowan, also called Mode I, was the first widespread stone-tool industry. Hominins across much of Africa used it from about 2.9 Ma until at least 1.7 Ma. Thousands of artifacts at Gona, Ethiopia, are firmly dated to 2.6 Ma. Who made them is uncertain. Tools of about 2.6 Ma at Ledi-Geraru may be the work of early Homo, and Australopithecus garhi is another candidate. The tools served mainly for butchering: 2.5-million-year-old tools lay beside cut-marked bones. Homo habilis made Oldowan tools from about 2.3 Ma.

  <!-- plio-054 -->

  *Figure: Oldowan sites line up across the first million years of the industry.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas** — c. 2.8 million years ago (2.8 Ma)

  Around 2.8 million years ago, a thin strip of land rose between the Americas and changed the oceans of the world. South America became attached to North America through the newly formed Isthmus of Panama. It rose at a convergent plate margin, partly built by volcanoes. The closure was gradual. Surface-water exchange through the seaway may already have been fading by 4.6-4.2 Ma. The closing cut the Caribbean off from Pacific nutrients 4.5-3 Ma. The isthmus closed the last strait outside the polar regions linking the Pacific and Atlantic. It ended the last remnant of a current that had flowed around the equator since the Cretaceous. More heat and salt were pushed toward the North Atlantic. Strengthened Gulf Stream and Humboldt currents cooled the Arctic, eventually leading to the glaciations in Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere. On land, it opened the road for the exchange in The Great American Interchange.

  <!-- plio-056 -->

  *Figure: How the Isthmus of Panama helped cool the Arctic.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Isthmus forms] --> B[Equatorial current ends]
  B --> C[More heat, salt to North Atlantic]
  A --> D[Gulf Stream, Humboldt strengthen]
  D --> E[Arctic cools]
  E --> F[Quaternary glaciations]
  ```

- **The Ledi-Geraru jaw, the first Homo** — c. 2.8 million years ago (2.8–2.75 Ma)

  A jawbone from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia's Afar region, LD 350-1, is the oldest known fossil of the genus Homo. It dates to 2.8-2.75 million years ago. Its age suggests Homo may have evolved from Australopithecus afarensis around then. Homo is assumed to have emerged by about 2.8 Ma, most likely in East Africa's Rift Valley. Teeth from Koobi Fora, Kenya, dated 3-2.7 Ma, may belong to the same species. The origin of Homo coincided with climate changes, but too few fossils are known to say whether climate was the cause.

  <!-- plio-055 -->

- **The Great American Interchange** — c. 2.7 million years ago (2.7 Ma)

  Cats, condors, raccoons and camelids walked south. Armadillos, hummingbirds and opossums headed north. From around 2.7 million years ago, the new land bridge in The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas set off the last and largest wave of migration between the Americas. Ground sloths and glyptodonts reached North America. Xenarthrans, the group of sloths, armadillos and anteaters, were among South America's most successful emigrants. Horses and tapirs entered South America. There, competition from northern hoofed mammals helped push the native ungulates toward extinction. The exchange was lopsided. Extinction rates were much higher in South America, and North American groups diversified greatly in their new home. Crossings had begun earlier, as Ground sloths island-hop to North America shows, but the land bridge turned a trickle into a flood.

  <!-- plio-057 -->

  *Figure: Animals that crossed the new land bridge in each direction.*

  | Moved south | Moved north |
  |---|---|
  | Cats | Armadillos |
  | Condors | Hummingbirds |
  | Raccoons | Opossums |
  | Camelids | Ground sloths |
  | Horses, tapirs | Glyptodonts |

- **Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere** — c. 2.7 million years ago (2.7 Ma)

  Around 2.7 million years ago temperatures dropped, and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere. The evidence lies on the seafloor. Ice-rafted cobbles, dropped by melting icebergs on North Atlantic and North Pacific seabeds, and an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes mark the new Arctic ice. Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one ice sheet covering most of the island, once carbon dioxide fell to 280-320 ppm, 2.7-2.6 Ma. Several causes are suggested. One is falling carbon dioxide. Another is a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north to feed the ice. A weakening Indonesian Throughflow also cut the heat carried toward Antarctica. As sea levels fell, that cooling fed on itself in a self-reinforcing loop.

  <!-- plio-058 -->

  *Figure: A self-reinforcing cooling loop at the onset of northern glaciation.* (cycle; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Paranthropus, the robust hominins, appear** — c. 2.7 million years ago (2.7 Ma)

  The robust hominin genus Paranthropus evolved around 2.7 million years ago. Its earliest species, P. aethiopicus, lived in East Africa about 2.7-2.3 Ma and is known from Lake Turkana. The oldest remains, from Ethiopia's Omo Kibish Formation, date to 2.6 Ma. The genus was still present at the start of the Pleistocene.

  <!-- plio-059 -->

- **Supernovae leave iron-60 on the seafloor** — c. 2.6 million years ago (2.6 Ma)

  Only supernovae, exploding stars, can make radioactive iron-60. Ancient seabed deposits record a large influx of it about 2.6 million years ago. A scattered excess over 10 million years suggests several fairly close supernovae, perhaps from the passing Scorpius-Centaurus group of young stars. So close an explosion could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.

  <!-- plio-060 -->

#### Quaternary Period

Around 2.58 million years ago, ice sheets began to spread across the Northern Hemisphere, and the Quaternary glaciation began. It is still going on. The start is marked by a flip in Earth's magnetic field, from normal to reversed polarity. In North America, glacials and interglacials began to alternate again and again. In Africa, the hominin family branched out, and early Homo appeared beside robust australopithecines.

##### Pleistocene Epoch

The Pleistocene is the age of ice, and it began about 2.58 million years ago as ice sheets spread across the Northern Hemisphere. Ice at both poles dried the globe. Old groups lost ground: outside the Americas, every trunked mammal except the elephants and Stegodon died out. New hunters arrived, among them the saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus. In East Africa, hominin fossils became extraordinarily diverse.

###### Gelasian Age

The Gelasian, the first age of the Pleistocene, opens with Earth's magnetic field flipping about 2.58 million years ago. Ice sheets spread across the north, and the last shallow sea link across Panama closed no later than 2.45 million years ago. An asteroid hit the deep ocean southwest of Chile. Rivers and lakes rearranged too: Ethiopian waters joined the Nile, and earth movements dammed the Murray River into vast Lake Bungunnia. In East Africa, robust australopithecines such as Paranthropus boisei lived beside early Homo.

- **The magnetic flip that starts the Quaternary** — 2.6 million years ago (2.58 ± 0.005 Ma)

  About 2.58 Ma, Earth's magnetic field flipped. It went from normal polarity, the Gauss Chron, to reversed polarity, the Matuyama Chron. Geologists use the flip as a marker. It defines the base of the Gelasian, and so the start of both the Pleistocene and the Quaternary, with the reference section at Monte San Nicola in Sicily. In 2009 the boundary was moved down to 2.58 Ma to match key changes in climate, oceans and life at that time. The flip coincides with a minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, tiny chalky plankton, among them Discoaster pentaradiatus and Discoaster surculus. The weakened field may have left Earth's surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of a supernova.

  <!-- gela-002 -->

- **The Quaternary ice age begins** — c. 2.6 million years ago (2.58 Ma)

  At the height of the glacials, ice at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia. That world began around 2.58 Ma, when ice sheets started to spread across the Northern Hemisphere. This was the start of the Quaternary glaciation, and it is still going on. The start of the Quaternary is tied to the formation of the Arctic ice cap. Greenland had been icing over since the late Pliocene, as Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere describes. From then on, glacials and interglacials, cold spells and warmer breaks, alternated. Through the Pleistocene, mean temperatures fell and the swings between the two grew larger. The south felt it too. In the first Pleistocene glacial, Patagonian ice reached the present Argentine coast.

  <!-- gela-004 -->

- **Mastodons and gomphotheres vanish outside the Americas** — during the Early Pleistocene, 2.60–0.77 million years ago (2.58–0.774 Ma)

  The elephant's relatives had once roamed widely across the Old World. During the Early Pleistocene, every proboscidean outside the Americas that was not a true elephant died out. Mammutids, gomphotheres and deinotheres all disappeared. Only Stegodon survived. Outside the Americas, the trunked mammals were reduced to the elephant family and that one holdout. It was a sharp narrowing for a group that had spread out of Africa in A land bridge sets animals crossing both ways.

  <!-- gela-003 -->

- **The Eltanin asteroid strikes the deep ocean** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.51 ± 0.07 Ma)

  An asteroid about 1–4 km wide plunged into the deep ocean at the edge of the Bellingshausen Sea, about 1,500 km southwest of Chile. It hit sea floor 4–5 km deep and left no known crater. Scientists found the site from an iridium anomaly, an excess of a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids, in sediment cores. The impact probably vaporized about 150 km³ of water. It raised tsunami waves hundreds of metres high.

  <!-- gela-005 -->

- **Ice at both poles dries the planet** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.5 Ma)

  With ice now at both poles, the globe dried out. That drying sped up a long decline in the functional diversity of hoofed mammals around 2.5 Ma, the range of different ways they made a living. Africa cooled and dried about 2.5 Ma, at the same time as the rise of thick-molared Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus. In Australia an aridification event at 2.56 Ma may be linked to the start of Arctic glaciation. Around 2.5 Ma, the Omo–Turkana Basin held a mix of forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, and its grasslands kept spreading through the Early Pleistocene.

  <!-- gela-006 -->

- **Early Homo and robust australopithecines branch out** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.5 Ma)

  About 2.5 Ma, the hominin fossil record of East Africa suddenly fills with variety. Robust australopithecines and early Homo appear first in the Turkana Basin. This looks like an adaptive radiation, a burst of new species filling different ways of life, and it straddles the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary. The first Homo species appeared about 2.5 Ma. Until then, hominins had kept their tree-climbing habits. Brain size rose quickly, and by 2 Ma the first animals classed in the genus Homo had appeared. For a time, several kinds shared the land.
