Paranthropus and early Homo coexisted at the start of the Pleistocene. But only Homo erectus remained for much of it, as Homo erectus appears in Africa tells.

  <!-- gela-007 -->

- **Ethiopian waters join the Nile** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.5 Ma)

  About 2.5 Ma, waters from Ethiopia flowed north for the first time and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile. Farther south, the Rwenzori Mountains rose. Their uplift turned the drainage of paleolake Obweruka east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.

  <!-- gela-009 -->

- **Smilodon and the short-faced bear appear** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.5 Ma)

  About 2.5 Ma, the earliest species of the saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus evolved. That first Smilodon, S. gracilis, probably descended from Megantereon. It lived until 500,000 years ago and reached northern South America in the Great American Interchange. Smilodon lasted in the Americas until at latest 8,200 years ago, perhaps the last saber-toothed cat.

  <!-- gela-013 -->

- **Paranthropus boisei shares Africa with early Homo** — c. 2.5–1.1 million years ago (2.5–1.15 Ma)

  Paranthropus boisei, a robust australopithecine, lived in East Africa about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago. Its oldest remains, from Malema, are about 2.3 million years old. It turns up at Koobi Fora and Olduvai Gorge and outlasted H. habilis. The 1.7-million-year-old skull KNM-ER 406, with a 510 cc brain, shows several hominin species shared Africa at once.

  <!-- gela-011 -->

- **Lake Bungunnia dams the Murray** — c. 2.5–0.5 million years ago (2.5–0.5 Ma)

  About 2.5 Ma, the Grampians of Victoria rose more than 250 m. Earth movements then blocked the Murray River near Swan Reach. Behind the blockage grew Lake Bungunnia, a vast freshwater lake that lasted from 2.5 to 0.5 Ma.

  <!-- gela-010 -->

- **Pre-Illinoian ice reaches Kansas and Missouri** — c. 2.5–0.2 million years ago (2.5–0.2 Ma)

  Researchers once counted two great glaciations in North America's early ice age. They now count 11. From about 2.5 to 0.2 million years ago, the continent went through repeated Pre-Illinoian glacial and interglacial periods. The old named stages, the Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian, were discarded. The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached as far south as the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, and to Douglas County, Kansas. Later Illinoian ice sheets pushed farther still, to near Carbondale, Illinois. Patchy glacial drift, debris dumped by the ice, more than 500,000 years old survives in parts of the Driftless Area of the upper Mississippi.

  <!-- gela-012 -->

  *Figure: Ice sheets reached farther south in later glaciations.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD

  A --> C[Douglas County, Kansas]
  D[Later Illinoian ice] --> E[Near Carbondale, Illinois]
  ```

- **The last seaway across Panama closes** — c. 2.5 million years ago (2.45 Ma)

  The seaway between the Americas closed in stages. A collision began about 25 Ma, and deep-ocean connections closed between 12 and 9.2 Ma. Surface water that kept Atlantic and Pacific salinities alike stopped flowing about 4.6 Ma. A last shallow, temporary breach came as recently as 2.45 Ma, and after that the two oceans were sealed apart.

  <!-- gela-014 -->

- **The Amazon settles into its present course** — c. 2.4 million years ago (2.4 Ma)

  The Amazon had already been a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, as The Amazon runs across a continent describes. It took its present shape later, about 2.4 million years ago. So the river that crosses the continent is old, but its present layout is young. Its shape settled in the same cold, dry stretch that saw ice spread across the north.

  <!-- gela-015 -->

- **Wind-blown dust builds the Loess Plateau** — c. 2.4 million years ago (2.4 Ma)

  About 2.4 Ma, crustal movement and a cold climate started laying down loess on China's Loess Plateau. Loess is fine, wind-blown silt that piles up in thick blankets. Several causes lined up. Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, as The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape describes. Then the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt. The winds carried it away and dropped it, layer upon layer, over the plateau.

  <!-- gela-017 -->

- **Sundaland emerges and mammals reach Java** — c. 2.4 million years ago (2.4 Ma)

  Before about 2.4 Ma, Java had no mammals. Then Sundaland, the shallow shelf of Southeast Asia, emerged as sea level fell. Animals walked across from mainland Asia, among them Sinomastodon bumiajuensis, a dwarf elephant relative, and colonized the newly exposed land.

  <!-- gela-019 -->

- **Oldowan tools spread across and out of Africa** — c. 2.4–1.7 million years ago (2.4–1.7 Ma)

  Between 2.4 and 1.7 million years ago, Oldowan stone tools flourished in eastern Africa and spread to southern Africa. Securely dated Oldowan artifacts 2.4–1.9 million years old at Ain Boucherit, Algeria, carry the industry into North Africa. At Swartkrans, South Africa, Oldowan tools of 2.2–1.8 Ma lie with Paranthropus robustus fossils, and a polished bone point there dates to 1.8–1.5 Ma. The toolmakers also left Africa. By 1.8 Ma early Homo with Oldowan tools lived at Dmanisi, Georgia. The old toolkit proved hard to retire. Even after Acheulean tools appeared about 1.7 Ma, Oldowan tools went on being made, and other traditions replaced them only by about 0.25 Ma.

  <!-- gela-018 -->

  *Figure: The Oldowan spread across Africa and beyond while the Acheulean began beside it.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Homo habilis, the 'handy man'** — c. 2.4–1.6 million years ago (2.4–1.65 Ma)

  Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago. Its brain ranged from about 500 to 900 cm³, and it may still have climbed trees like the australopithecines. It made Oldowan stone tools. Unlike australopithecines, it ate much meat, probably scavenged. Around 2 Ma it may have built the first structures, stones propping up branches. A 1.75 Ma stone circle at Olduvai is the oldest claimed architecture. Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

  <!-- gela-016 -->

- **Giant ground sloths walk into North America** — c. 2.2 million years ago (2.2 Ma)

  Eremotherium eomigrans, the first megatheriid ground sloth in North America, arrived 2.2 Ma across the new Panamanian land bridge. Traffic ran the other way too. Horses that had entered South America in the Great American Interchange evolved into Hippidion around 2.5 Ma.

  <!-- gela-020 -->

- **Shangchen: stone tools in China before Dmanisi?** — c. 2.1 million years ago (2.12 Ma)

  Possible stone tools at Shangchen in central China are dated to 2.12 Ma, about 300,000 years before Dmanisi. If confirmed, they are the oldest known stone tools outside Africa. They are not alone. Pebble tools are reported from Yiron, Israel, at 2.4 Ma, Riwat, Pakistan, at 2.0 Ma and Renzidong, China, at over 2 Ma. Tools perhaps 2.48 million years old come from the Zarqa Valley in Jordan. Together they suggest that Homo habilis or an even earlier species may have spread across Asia before H. erectus. None of these claims is yet settled.

  <!-- gela-021 -->

- **The Waiteariki supereruption** — c. 2.1 million years ago (2.1 Ma)

  A single huge eruption in New Zealand's Tauranga Volcanic Centre produced the Waiteariki ignimbrite, about 870 ± 87 km³ of dense rock. It probably came from the Omanawa Caldera, known only from a gravity anomaly. At least eight other large eruptions struck the area between 2.4 and 1.9 million years ago.

  <!-- gela-022 -->

- **Huckleberry Ridge, Yellowstone's greatest eruption** — c. 2.1 million years ago (2.08 Ma)

  The Huckleberry Ridge eruption made about 2,500 times as much ash as Mount St. Helens in 1980. Its ash is found from southern California to St. Louis. Yellowstone volcanism began 2.15 Ma, and its first and largest cycle climaxed in this VEI 8 eruption. It produced about 2,450–2,500 km³ of material and left the Island Park Caldera, roughly 80 by 65 km. Part of the tuff records a brief wobble of Earth's magnetic field, the Huckleberry Ridge excursion, and is dated very precisely to 2.0773 ± 0.0034 Ma.

  <!-- gela-023 -->

- **Homo erectus appears in Africa** — c. 2 million years ago (2.04 Ma)

  A 2.04-million-year-old skull from Drimolen in South Africa, DNH 134, is the oldest identified Homo erectus. Its owner lived alongside Paranthropus robustus. Other early fossils include the roughly 1.9-million-year-old KNM-ER 2598 and the cranium KNM-ER 3733 from Koobi Fora, Kenya. H. ergaster, often treated as African H. erectus, was the first human with a slender, modern body plan. Its populations spread through grassland and woodland savannas. Those were expanding as the globe dried at the onset of the Quaternary glaciation. The species proved durable. Most H. erectus fossils date from 1.8 to 1 Ma, and it lasted until about 0.6 Ma. For a long time it was the only hominin, the survivor of the crowded field in Early Homo and robust australopithecines branch out, and the first to spread out of Africa, as Homo spreads out of Africa tells.

  <!-- gela-024 -->

  *Figure: The fossil record of Homo erectus.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Altiplano–Puna eruptions die down** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  The giant Andean eruptions did not stop at once. Large ignimbrites kept coming in the central Andes, including the 550 km³ Galán ignimbrite about 2.1 Ma. After 2 Ma, activity in the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex waned. After 1 Ma it was mostly andesitic, a less explosive kind of lava, with no large ignimbrites.

  <!-- gela-025 -->

- **Homo spreads out of Africa** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  The earliest hominins outside Africa date to close to 2 million years ago. They mark the start of expansions led by Homo erectus. In the Early Pleistocene, archaic Homo arose in Africa and spread through Africa and Eurasia, in waves known together as Out of Africa I. The key early sites trace the route. Riwat in Pakistan dates to about 2 Ma, Dmanisi in the Caucasus to 1.81 Ma, and Ubeidiya in the Levant to 1.5 Ma. Climate opened the door. Favorable swings probably opened the Levantine corridor to the adaptable Homo erectus, perhaps only at times. The dispersal has been linked to the Saharan pump around 1.9 Ma, the idea that wet spells greened the Sahara and let animals cross it. By 2.0–1.5 Ma hominins were settling southern Europe and Asia.

  <!-- gela-028 -->

  *Figure: Early hominin sites outside Africa.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

  *Figure: Early sites outside Africa get younger from Pakistan to the Levant.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Homo rudolfensis in East Africa** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  Homo rudolfensis lived in East Africa about 2 million years ago. Most of its fossils come from Koobi Fora and date to 1.9–1.85 Ma. Its molar enamel was almost as thick as that of Paranthropus. Fossils from Ethiopia and Malawi dated 2.5–2.4 Ma could make it the earliest known Homo, but which specimens belong to it is disputed.

  <!-- gela-029 -->

- **Kap København: a lost Greenland world in DNA** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  Mastodons once lived in northern Greenland. Environmental DNA, genetic traces left in sediment, from the Kap København Formation is at least two million years old. It records mastodons, Arctic hares, geese, poplar, birch and willow, horseshoe crabs and corals. Average minimum temperatures there were more than 10 °C warmer than today.

  <!-- gela-030 -->

- **South America's native predators fade further** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  The saber-toothed thylacosmilids were among South America's only large mammal predators in the Pliocene, and they died out about 2 Ma. Their placental counterparts, dogs, weasels and saber-toothed cats, entered South America only in the early Pleistocene. Bears, cats and skunks arrived by about 1 Ma, when the short-faced bear Arctotherium first appears there. The traffic ran north as well. The terror bird Titanis had crossed into North America, but it died out there about 1.8 Ma, perhaps outcompeted by carnivorans. The collapse that began in South America's native predators collapse was now complete.

  <!-- gela-034 -->

- **The Taupō Rift opens in New Zealand** — c. 2 million years ago (2 Ma)

  About 2 Ma, the Taupō Rift and the old Taupō Volcanic Zone formed in New Zealand. Their birth ended major activity in the Coromandel Volcanic Zone. The postulated Omanawa Caldera sat where the old and new rifts met.

  <!-- gela-035 -->

- **The Congo basin takes its present shape** — c. 2.0–1.5 million years ago (2–1.5 Ma)

  The Congo River had a long history of rearrangement, as the rising rift flanks in Rising rift shoulders split Africa's great rivers show. Between about 2.0 and 1.5 Ma, its basin finally acquired its present shape. The great drainage of central Africa took the outline it still has.

  <!-- gela-027 -->

- **Ice-age floods deepen the Grand Canyon** — c. 2.0–1.2 million years ago (2–1.2 Ma)

  From about 2 Ma, wetter ice-age climates swelled the Colorado River, and it cut the Grand Canyon faster than ever before. By 1.2 million years ago the canyon had almost reached its modern depth. Nearby, the upper half of Zion Canyon was carved between about 2 and 1 million years ago.

  <!-- gela-026 -->

- **Australopithecus sediba at Malapa** — c. 2 million years ago (1.98 Ma)

  In Malapa Cave, South Africa, lay two partial skeletons, a juvenile and an adult female, about 1.98 million years old. They belong to Australopithecus sediba, which lived alongside Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus. Malapa may have been a natural death trap. Once proposed as an ancestor of Homo, it may instead be a late relative of A. africanus; the question is contested.

  <!-- gela-036 -->

- **The Acheulean: a toolkit for a million years** — c. 1.9 million years ago (1.95 Ma)

  Acheulean technology first developed about 2 million years ago, growing out of the Oldowan. Finds from Ethiopia date to 1.95 Ma, and Homo erectus is credited with inventing it, refining the older toolkit it had inherited. Early Acheulean tools from West Turkana, Kenya, date to about 1.76 Ma, and those at Kokiselei to 1.7–1.6 Ma. It traveled. Between 1.5 Ma and about 800,000 years ago, it spread from Africa to Asia, the Middle East and Europe, reaching southern India by 1.51 Ma. Its end is poorly defined. Counting the Sangoan, it lasted until as late as 130,000 years ago.

  <!-- gela-037 -->

  *Figure: The Acheulean began in Ethiopia and later reached India.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

###### Calabrian Age

Around 1.8 million years ago, people were already living in the hills of Georgia, far outside Africa, and their bones are the oldest human remains known beyond that continent. Within a few hundred thousand years, Homo erectus stood at Yuanmou in southern China, on Java and beside the Sea of Galilee. At home in Africa, the australopithecines that had walked there since about 4 million years ago died out, and charred bones deep in a South African cave hint that someone was handling fire. Wolves of the genus Canis spread across Eurasia, mammoths crossed into North America, and colossal floods tore across the Channeled Scablands. This chapter follows that restless stretch of the Calabrian Age, when both the planet and the human family were on the move.

- **Dmanisi: the oldest human bones outside Africa** — c. 1.8 million years ago (1.8 Ma)

  Five skulls from a Georgian hillside changed the map of human origins. Hominins lived at Dmanisi from about 1.8 million years ago, and their fossils are the oldest human skeletal remains known outside Africa. Fossils and tools there span 1.85 to 1.77 million years, and argon dating gives 1.81 ± 0.03 million years. Skull 5 is the first complete adult hominin skull from the Early Pleistocene. The people, classed as Homo erectus georgicus, look so much like early African Homo that all early Homo may be one species. One skull belonged to a toothless old individual. Some read it as early evidence that the group cared for its old or disabled.

  <!-- gela-038 -->

- **A magnetic flip marks the start of the Calabrian** — 1.8 million years ago (1.8 Ma)

  Compasses would have pointed the other way for most of the early Pleistocene. Earth's magnetic field sat in a reversed state called the Matuyama chron, broken by short spells of normal polarity. One of these, the Olduvai subchron, lasted from about 1.95 to 1.77 million years ago. The Calabrian Age begins at 1.8 million years ago, just above the top of the Olduvai layers. The same level records the extinction of Discoaster brouweri, a tiny floating alga. Geologists fixed the boundary in rock at Vrica, near Crotone in southern Italy. Before 2009 this level, then dated to 1.806 million years ago, marked the very base of the Pleistocene.

  <!-- gela-039 -->

- **The wolf event spreads Canis across Eurasia** — c. 1.8 million years ago (1.8 Ma)

  Dogs' wild ancestors had a sudden boom. Around 1.8 million years ago Canis evolution exploded across Eurasia, in what is called the wolf event. The large wolf C. falconeri appeared abruptly in Europe, and C. borjgali lived alongside the people at Dmanisi between 1.8 and 1.75 million years ago. Coyote and wolf lineages later split, about 1.5 million years ago. The first coyotes appear about 1.0 million years ago, and the first wolves about 810,000 years ago.

  <!-- gela-040 -->

- **Charred bones hint at the first use of fire** — c. 1.8 million years ago (1.79 Ma)

  Deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, lie charred bones. They have been read as human use of fire about 1.79 million years ago. Yet the cited Wonderwerk study itself dates the burning to about 1.0 million years ago, so the early date is shaky. Other claims include blackened bones at Yuanmou, China, about 1.7 million years ago, and heated red sediment at Koobi Fora, Kenya, about 1.5 million years ago. Some studies read the smaller molars of Homo erectus as a sign of cooking.

  <!-- gela-041 -->

- **Diprotodon, the largest marsupial ever** — c. 1.80–0.78 million years ago (1.77–0.779924 Ma)

  Australia's biggest plant-eater carried its young in a pouch. Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived and the largest herbivore on the continent. Its earliest fossils come from the Nelson Bay Formation in New South Wales and are dated indirectly to between 1.77 million and 780,000 years old. Most specimens are far younger, under 110,000 years. The oldest fossils dated directly, from Floraville, are about 340,000 years old.

  <!-- gela-042 -->

- **Homo erectus reaches China and Java** — c. 1.7 million years ago (1.7 Ma)

  Within a geological eyeblink of leaving Africa, Homo erectus stood at the far edge of Asia. It was at Yuanmou in southern China by 1.7 million years ago and at Sangiran on Java by 1.66 million years ago. A cranium from Lantian dates to 1.63 million years ago, and stone tools in northern China's Nihewan basin to 1.7 to 1.6 million years ago. Yunxian Man in China is dated to 1.77 million years ago. Java's Mojokerto child was once put at 1.81 million years, but is now dated to at most 1.49 million. By 1.3 million years ago, Oldowan tools had reached the 40th parallel at Xiaochangliang. By 1 million years ago the species had spread across Eurasia, mostly south of the 50th parallel.

  <!-- gela-044 -->

  *Figure: Dated Homo erectus sites in China and Java fall within a few hundred thousand years of each other.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The last australopithecines die out** — c. 1.7 million years ago (1.7 Ma)

  A family of upright apes that had lasted more than two million years came to an end. The australopithecines arose in East Africa around 4 million years ago and died out about 1.7 million years ago. South Africa may have been their last refuge until about 2 million years ago. Climate there was growing more volatile, and they faced competition from Homo and Paranthropus. Around 2.07 million years ago, just before Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus arrived, Australopithecus africanus vanished from South Africa's Cradle of Humankind.

  <!-- gela-045 -->

- **Two blasts build the Valles Caldera** — c. 1.6–1.2 million years ago (1.61–1.25 Ma)

  New Mexico's Jemez Mountains hide the scar of two enormous eruptions. The first, the Toledo eruption 1.61 million years ago, laid down the Otowi member of the Bandelier Tuff, a rock made of welded volcanic ash. It produced 216 to 550 km³ of dense rock, and the larger estimate makes it a small supereruption, VEI 8. A second great eruption about 1.25 million years ago laid down the Tshirege member and formed the Valles Caldera. It is one of the best-studied resurgent calderas, craters whose floors later bulged back up.

  <!-- gela-046 -->

- **Turkana Boy, the most complete Homo erectus** — c. 1.6–1.5 million years ago (1.6–1.5 Ma)

  No Homo erectus skeleton is more complete than that of a youth who died near Lake Turkana, Kenya. Known as Turkana Boy, or KNM-WT 15000, he lived between 1.6 and 1.5 million years ago. Some authorities assign him to Homo ergaster instead. His spine holds a clue about language. It could not have supported the well-developed breathing muscles that speech needs.

  <!-- gela-047 -->

- **The first Missoula floods scour the Scablands** — c. 1.5 million years ago (1.5 Ma)

  Floods of staggering size tore across the American Northwest. The oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods swept through the Channeled Scablands sometime before 1.5 million years ago. Their age comes from calcretes, hard limy soil crusts that formed in warm interglacials between flood deposits. Magnetic dating of the layers and luminescence dating, which measures when grains last saw light, back it up.

  <!-- gela-048 -->

- **Mammoths cross into North America** — c. 1.5 million years ago (1.5 Ma)

  Mammoths had been travelers for a long time. They left Africa in the late Pliocene, about 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago. The steppe mammoth arose in East Asia around 1.7 million years ago. It crossed the Bering Land Bridge between 1.5 and 1.3 million years ago and gave rise to the Columbian mammoth. DNA from a Siberian tooth 1.1 to 1.65 million years old reveals the Krestovka lineage, probably the first mammoths to colonize the Americas. Their spread south of Alaska, about 1.4 million years ago, is often used to end the Blancan and start the Irvingtonian land-mammal age. Meanwhile gomphotheres, elephant relatives, moved into South America in the Great American Interchange.

  <!-- gela-049 -->

  *Figure: Follow the mammoths from Africa through East Asia and across the Bering Land Bridge.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Mammoths leave Africa] --> B[Steppe mammoth in East Asia]
  B -->|Bering Land Bridge| C[North America]
  C --> D[Columbian mammoth]
  ```

- **Ubeidiya: Homo erectus in the Levant** — c. 1.5 million years ago (1.5 Ma)

  Just south of the Sea of Galilee, in the Jordan Rift Valley, lies one of the earliest stops on the way out of Africa. Ubeidiya records Homo erectus about 1.5 million years ago. Its layers hold simple Oldowan tools and early Acheulean ones, the shaped hand axes, about 1.4 million years old. A hominin vertebra from the site seems to belong to a different species from the Dmanisi people.

  <!-- gela-050 -->

- **The Mesa Falls eruption at Yellowstone** — c. 1.3 million years ago (1.3 Ma)

  Yellowstone's second great cycle peaked about 1.3 million years ago. The Mesa Falls Tuff eruption threw out more than 280 km³ of material. It formed Henry's Fork Caldera inside the older Island Park Caldera. High-precision argon dating pins the eruption to 1.3001 ± 0.0006 million years ago, an unusually exact date for something so old.

  <!-- gela-054 -->

- **Hominins cross the sea to Flores** — c. 1.3–1.0 million years ago (1.27–1 Ma)

  Reaching the island of Flores meant crossing open sea. The ancestors of Homo floresiensis probably arrived between about 1.27 and 1 million years ago. No stone tools there are older than 1.27 million years, and the oldest found are about 1 million years old. How they crossed is unknown, but Homo erectus may have built rafts by about 840,000 to 800,000 years ago.

  <!-- gela-056 -->

- **The Mid-Pleistocene Transition stretches the ice ages** — c. 1.2–0.7 million years ago (1.25–0.7 Ma)

  The rhythm of the ice ages changed, and the swings grew wilder. Between about 1.25 and 0.7 million years ago, glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 years to lopsided cycles of about 100,000 years. This shift is the Mid-Pleistocene Transition. Afterwards, long cold spells built ice sheets that were thicker, higher and less slippery. Each cycle then ended in a rapid jump to a warm interglacial. Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, the stretch of Earth's orbit, its eccentricity, replaced the tilt of its axis as the main pacemaker of the ice ages. What caused the change is still worked out with models. They reproduce it with two slow trends: falling carbon dioxide in the air, and glaciers gradually scraping loose rock and soil off the northern continents. The new climate reached people too. A severe glacial stage, MIS 22, brought widespread drought to Africa. It may have squeezed human ancestors into a population bottleneck about 1 million years ago.

  <!-- gela-057 -->

  *Figure: Glacial cycles lengthened in the Mid-Pleistocene Transition.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Gregory Rift begins to pull apart** — c. 1.2 million years ago (1.2 Ma)

  East Africa is slowly tearing open. The Gregory Rift, the eastern branch of the East African Rift, began spreading about 1.2 million years ago and still widens about 3 mm a year. Its faulting followed a long burst of large shield volcanoes near the edge of the old continental core, between 5 and 1 million years ago.

  <!-- gela-058 -->

- **Paranthropus, the robust hominins, dies out** — c. 1.2 million years ago (1.2 Ma)

  Big jaws and huge molars were not enough to save them. Paranthropus, the robust hominins, died out about 1.2 million years ago. The youngest Paranthropus boisei fossil, OH 80 from Olduvai Gorge, is about 1.34 million years old, though the species may have lasted to 1 million years ago. One chronology has Australopithecus and Paranthropus making stone tools right up to their extinction, no later than 1.1 million years ago.

  <!-- gela-060 -->

- **Toba's first known caldera forms** — c. 1.2 million years ago (1.2 Ma)

  About 1.2 million years ago, a volcano on Sumatra collapsed into its own emptied magma chamber. It was the earliest known of at least four caldera-forming eruptions at Toba. The same volcano would later produce Toba, the great supereruption, one of the largest eruptions of the last few million years.

  <!-- gela-061 -->

- **Homo antecessor, the pioneer of Western Europe** — c. 1.2–0.8 million years ago (1.2–0.8 Ma)

  Butchered horse bones in southern Spain show people in Western Europe about 1.2 million years ago. Cut marks at Fuente Nueva-3 record archaic humans, probably Homo antecessor, carving up the horse Equus altidens. The name means 'pioneer man', and the species is recorded at Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago. It was once proposed as the last common ancestor of modern humans and Neanderthals. It is now seen as a side branch that split off just before them.

  <!-- gela-059 -->

- **An asteroid strikes Ghana's rainforest** — c. 1.1 million years ago (1.07 Ma)

  About 1.07 million years ago, an asteroid fell into a lush rainforest in Ghana and blasted a crater 10.5 km wide. Lake Bosumtwi, about 8 km across, now fills it. Tektites, glassy beads of melted rock thrown out by the impact, lie in neighboring Ivory Coast. Smaller microtektites turn up in deep-sea sediments west of Africa.

  <!-- gela-064 -->

- **The Kidnappers supereruption buries the North Island** — c. 1 million years ago (1 Ma)

  About 1 million years ago, New Zealand's Mangakino caldera produced one of the largest eruptions in its history. The VEI 8 Kidnappers eruption released about 2,760 km³ of material in total, including about 1,200 km³ of ignimbrite. Ignimbrite is rock laid down by a scalding avalanche of ash and gas. This sheet covers more than 45,000 km², the most widespread ignimbrite on Earth. Eruptions about 1.25 and 1.0 million years ago spread such sheets across the North Island from Auckland to Napier.

  <!-- gela-066 -->

  *Figure: Ignimbrite made up less than half of everything the Kidnappers eruption released.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Kilimanjaro's Kibo and Mawenzi cones awaken** — c. 1 million years ago (1 Ma)

  Africa's highest mountain is a volcano built in stages. Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m tall, has three cones. The oldest, Shira, had been active since 2.4 million years ago. Kibo and Mawenzi began erupting about 1 million years ago. Kibo, the largest, grew in lava phases dated from about 482,000 to 170,000 years ago. Its last activity, 200,000 to 150,000 years ago, formed the summit crater. Kilimanjaro is now a dormant stratovolcano, but fumaroles in Kibo's crater still vent gas.

  <!-- gela-067 -->

- **The Pannonian Sea finally disappears** — c. 1 million years ago (1 Ma)

  A sea in the middle of Europe slowly filled with mud and sand until it was gone. The Pannonian Sea, shallow and landlocked, had existed since about 10 million years ago. It lasted until about 1 million years ago. By then 3 to 4 km of sediment had filled the Pannonian Basin.

  <!-- gela-068 -->

- **The Jaramillo flip of Earth's magnetic field** — c. 990,000–950,000 years ago (990–950 ka)

  For a short spell, Earth's magnetic field swung back to normal in the middle of the reversed Matuyama chron. This Jaramillo subchron is usually dated from 990,000 to 950,000 years ago, though some studies start it at 1.07 million years ago. The causes of such brief reversals are still disputed. A proposed link to the Bosumtwi impact in Ghana has been called highly speculative and refuted.

  <!-- gela-069 -->

- **Footprints on the Norfolk shore** — c. 950,000–850,000 years ago (950–850 ka)

  Footprints pressed into soft sediment at Happisburgh, Norfolk, are the oldest hominin tracks known outside Africa. They were made between about 950,000 and 850,000 years ago, and flint tools lie in the same deposits. Together they are the first evidence of early humans this far north. The makers may have been Homo antecessor. The beds lie between two flips of Earth's magnetic field, the Jaramillo and the The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, Earth's last magnetic flip.

  <!-- gela-070 -->

- **Straight-tusked Palaeoloxodon leaves Africa** — c. 800,000 years ago (800 ka)

  Elephants joined the stream of animals moving out of Africa. At the end of the Early Pleistocene, about 800,000 years ago, the elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread out of Africa and across Eurasia.

  <!-- gela-072 -->

- **A hidden impact scatters glass across Australasia** — c. 790,000 years ago (790 ka)

  About 790,000 years ago, something large hit Earth and sprayed glass over a vast area. The tektites, beads of melted rock, lie across the enormous Australasian strewnfield. Strangely, the crater has never been found. One about 100 km wide in Indochina, perhaps under Tonlé Sap in Cambodia, has been suggested. Artifacts found with the tektites tie a Homo erectus population to the impact and its aftermath. A link to the magnetic reversal of the same era is highly speculative. The two probably just happened around the same time.

  <!-- gela-073 -->

- **Cooking fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov** — c. 780,000 years ago (779.924 ka)

  Heated fish teeth in northern Israel are the oldest likely evidence of cooking. Hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov left them, with traces of fire, around 780,000 years ago. It is the oldest established site outside Africa with continuous fire. Homo erectus or Homo ergaster is claimed to have controlled fire there between 790,000 and 690,000 years ago. The people also gathered and ate 55 kinds of fruits, vegetables, seeds, nuts and tubers.

  <!-- gela-074 -->

###### Chibanian Age

The age we still live in, magnetically speaking, began when Earth's field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron and opening the Brunhes. By then the ice ages had settled into a new rhythm, and the Mid-Pleistocene Transition was complete by about 700,000 years ago. Giants were changing too: gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, and the last clawed chalicotheres lived on only into this stretch of time. In California a VEI 7 eruption poured out about 600 km³ of rock, while lava flows dammed the Colorado River again and again. On the human side, hand axes reached Europe, small hominins lived on Flores, and the lines leading to Neanderthals and Denisovans parted about 640,000 years ago.

- **The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, Earth's last magnetic flip** — 774,000 years ago (774 ± 5 ka)

  About 774,000 years ago, a compass needle would have swung around to point the way it points today. Earth's magnetic field last reversed then, ending the Matuyama chron, known as C1r, and opening the present Brunhes chron, C1n. Nobody knows quite how long the flip took. Estimates range from within a single human lifetime to several thousand years, or about 22,000 years. Part of the confusion is local. The apparent length of the flip at any one site can vary tenfold with geomagnetic latitude and local quirks of the field. Because it shows up worldwide in rock, the reversal is a precious marker. It is a standard tie-point for dating ocean sediment cores and volcanic rocks. In 2020 it was ratified as the golden spike, the GSSP, for the base of the Chibanian Stage, at the Chiba section in Japan.

  <!-- chib-001 -->

- **A turnover of mammals at the Middle Pleistocene** — c. 774,000 years ago (774 ka)

  As the Early Pleistocene gave way to the Middle, the cast of big mammals reshuffled. Sinomastodon died out in East Asia, and with it gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene. Many European carnivores died out, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta. True horses migrated from North America into Eurasia. In Europe the mammoth Mammuthus meridionalis gave way to the Asian steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii. Out of Africa came Palaeoloxodon, including the first straight-tusked elephants, Palaeoloxodon antiquus.

  <!-- chib-003 -->

- **The last chalicotheres, horses with claws** — during the Middle Pleistocene, 774,000–129,000 years ago (774–129 ka)

  Imagine a relative of horses that walked on claws. The chalicotheres, or Ancylopoda, were clawed perissodactyls, the group of hoofed mammals that includes horses and rhinos. Their lineage lasted from the Eocene into the Middle Pleistocene. Sometime in that later stretch, between 774,000 and 129,000 years ago, the last of them disappeared.

  <!-- chib-002 -->

- **The Bishop Tuff eruption opens Long Valley Caldera** — c. 760,000 years ago (760 ka)

  About 760,000 years ago, eastern California exploded. A VEI 7 eruption released about 600 km³ of material, which cooled into a rock called the Bishop Tuff. Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of scorching gas and ash, burned and buried thousands of square miles. Ash blanketed much of the western United States. With its magma chamber drained, the ground above collapsed. The hole left behind, Long Valley Caldera, measures about 32 by 18 km and is one of the largest calderas on Earth.

  <!-- chib-004 -->

- **Lava dams choke the Colorado in the Grand Canyon** — c. 725,000–100,000 years ago (725–100 ka)

  Lava poured into the Grand Canyon more than 150 times. Between 725,000 and 100,000 years ago these basalt flows dammed the Colorado River at least 13 times. Each dam formed in a matter of weeks. Some stood up to 610 m high and 138 km long. How long they held back lakes behind them is still debated.

  <!-- chib-005 -->

- **The 100,000-year ice-age rhythm takes hold** — c. 700,000 years ago (700 ka)

  By about 700,000 years ago, Earth's climate had settled into the beat it still keeps. The Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete. Before it, ice ages came and went in cycles of about 41,000 years. Afterwards they followed lopsided, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years. Ice built up slowly over long cold spells, then melted fast, so the climate swings became more extreme. The warm spells changed too. Interglacials after the transition had more carbon dioxide in the air than those before it. The ice sheets of the new cycles locked up enormous amounts of water. Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m. Each time, the shallow edges of the continents were laid bare as dry land.

  <!-- chib-007 -->

  *Figure: Compare the ice-age rhythm before and after the Mid-Pleistocene Transition.*

  |  | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | Cycle length | about 41,000 years | about 100,000 years |
  | Shape | regular | asymmetric, high-amplitude |
  | Interglacial CO2 | lower | higher |

- **Acheulean hand axes arrive in Europe** — c. 700,000 years ago (700 ka)

  About 700,000 years ago, typical Acheulean bifaces appeared in Europe. These are hand axes, stones flaked on both faces into a teardrop shape. Their sudden arrival has been argued to reflect influence from Africa rather than purely local invention. Late Acheulean culture, usually linked to the spread of Homo heidelbergensis, the muddle in the middle, reached across Europe and Africa by the beginning of the Middle Pleistocene.

  <!-- chib-008 -->

- **Tiny ancestors of the Flores 'hobbit'** — c. 700,000 years ago (700 ka)

  Small people were already small 700,000 years ago. Teeth and a partial jaw found at Mata Menge on Flores come from hominins thought to be ancestors of Homo floresiensis. They were as small as, or smaller than, the much later remains from Liang Bua. The species' small size therefore stayed stable for hundreds of thousands of years.

  <!-- chib-009 -->

- **A 'ghost' lineage splits from modern humans** — c. 700,000 years ago (700 ka)

  Some living Africans carry DNA from a people no one has ever found. An archaic hominin population broke away from the modern human lineage around 700,000 years ago. No fossils of it are known, which is why it is called a ghost lineage. About 35,000 years ago its DNA entered some sub-Saharan hunter-gatherer groups, such as the Biaka and the San.

  <!-- chib-010 -->

- **The Eridanos, a lost river of Europe, dies** — c. 700,000 years ago (700 ka)

  At its height about 2 million years ago, a great river ran some 2,700 km from Lapland across the Baltic region to a vast delta in western Europe. This was the Eridanos. Repeated Scandinavian ice caps destroyed its source area and gouged out the basin where the Baltic Sea later formed. During the first glacial stage of the Cromerian Complex, around 700,000 years ago, its deposits in the Netherlands stopped building up, and the Eridanos was gone.

  <!-- chib-011 -->

- **MIS 16, the Don Glaciation** — c. 676,000–621,000 years ago (676–621 ka)

They pushed north beyond the 50th parallel, to Boxgrove and Eartham Pit in England. Boxgrove in Sussex, about 500,000 years old, is the earliest site in Britain with fossils of Homo. It grew with every later glacial cycle and shrank in each warm spell, again and again.

It was the first of two megafloods that cut through this Weald–Artois Anticline. The flood diverted the Rhine into the English Channel. The north felt it most. South Greenland nearly lost its ice entirely around 410,000 to 400,000 years ago, adding 4.5 to 6 m to sea level. High-latitude seas were warm and the thermohaline circulation, the deep ocean conveyor driven by heat and salt, ran strong. Sea level stood higher than today, and coral reefs expanded. The oldest definite fire-making comes from a Neanderthal site in eastern England, about 400,000 years old. It left burnt soil, handaxes cracked by heat and pyrite, a mineral struck to make sparks.
