The earlier Aso-1, about 266,000 years ago, and Aso-2, about 141,000 years ago, each erupted about 32 km³.

  <!-- chib-070 -->

- **Burials at Krapina** — c. 130,000 years ago (130 ka)

  At Krapina in Croatia, the dead were buried about 130,000 years ago. Some anthropologists see in such burials a growing concern for the dead and a developing belief in an afterlife.

  <!-- chib-071 -->

###### Late Pleistocene Age

The Late Pleistocene opened in warmth. The Last Interglacial followed the Penultimate Glacial Period, and an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Hippos waded as far north as northern England, and sea level probably stood 6 to 9 m above today's. Modern humans were on the move, leaving stone tools in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago and fossils in Israel's caves, while in Java the last Homo erectus lived beside the Solo River. This chapter follows that warm start into the long Last Glacial Period, and the people and animals that lived through it.

- **A green Sahara opens a road out of Africa** — c. 129,000–115,000 years ago (129–115 ka)

  The Sahara was not always a barrier. During the Last Interglacial, an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Lakes and grasslands opened pathways for early humans across northern Africa and Arabia. Modern humans dispersed through North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula at least between 130,000 and 115,000 years ago. Timing mattered. The Red Sea coastal route was extremely dry before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago. Such humid phases come with interglacials and with precession minima, points in the slow wobble of Earth's axis, while glacial stages bring dry spells.

  <!-- late-001 -->

- **The Eemian, the Last Interglacial** — c. 129,000–115,000 years ago (129–115 ka)

  Around 125,000 years ago, forests grew at North Cape, Norway, where today there is only tundra. This was the Last Interglacial, also called the Eemian, or Marine Isotope Stage 5e. It followed the Penultimate Glacial Period and lasted until about 115,000 years ago. It was one of the warmest spells of the last 800,000 years, up to about 2 °C warmer than the Holocene, with carbon dioxide near 280 ppm. Warmth peaked about 128,000 to 123,000 years ago. Arctic summers ran about 2 to 4 °C warmer than in 2011. The warmth was not steady. Abrupt cold spells around 120,000 years ago followed shifts in the North Atlantic Current, the ocean stream that carries tropical heat north. The start of this interglacial, at the end of the Riss glaciation, is the proposed beginning of the Late Pleistocene.

  <!-- late-002 -->

- **Hippos wallow in northern England** — c. 128,000–123,000 years ago (128–123 ka)

  Hippos once wallowed near Stockton-on-Tees in northern England. Interglacial warmth let them range that far north, though outside southern Europe they rarely went east of the Rhine. Europe's temperate landscapes also held straight-tusked elephants, Merck's and narrow-nosed rhinos, Irish elk, aurochs, cave lions and cave hyenas. Warmer seas let tropical 'Senegalese' marine snails, such as cone shells, colonize the Mediterranean.

  <!-- late-003 -->

- **Seas rise as West Antarctic ice collapses** — c. 125,000 years ago (125 ka)

  The last time Earth was about as warm as the early 21st century, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed. That was around 125,000 years ago. At its peak, sea level stood probably 6 to 9 m above today's. Greenland's melting, the expansion of warming seawater and Antarctica all contributed. East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin alone lost ice worth about 0.5 m. Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century. The high water made islands of Fennoscandia and Jutland and flooded much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain. Fossil coral reefs from that highstand are now stranded above the sea, common in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

  <!-- late-004 -->

  *Figure: Warmth, melting ice and high seas link the Eemian highstand together.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Eemian warmth] --> B[West Antarctic Ice Sheet collapses]
  A --> C[Greenland melts and seas expand]
  B --> D[Sea level 6–9 m above today]
  C --> D
  D --> E[Fennoscandia and Jutland become islands]
  ```

- **Klasies River: life on the South African coast** — c. 125,000 years ago (125 ka)

  Caves on South Africa's coast held early people with a varied menu. Excavations at Klasies River found Middle Stone Age homes beginning about 125,000 years ago. Close to both shore and grassland, the people exploited marine life and land animals alike. Their remains include jaws about 119,000 years old and finger bones 90,000 to 100,000 years old.

  <!-- late-005 -->

- **Modern humans reach Arabia** — c. 125,000 years ago (125 ka)

  Stone tools at Jebel Faya, in the United Arab Emirates, show modern humans in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago. Groups may have left Africa by two routes. One ran along the Nile, through Sinai and into the Levant. The other crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait when seas were low. On a raised reef 125,000 years old at Abdur, Eritrea, tools suggest coastal foragers ate shellfish over 100,000 years ago. These early ventures do not seem to have led to lasting settlement. They had faded by about 80,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-006 -->

- **Lake Ouki floods the Altiplano** — c. 120,000–98,000 years ago (120–98 ka)

  High in the Andes, a great lake once filled the Bolivian Altiplano. Lake Ouki spread there about 120,000 to 98,000 years ago, before the later Lake Tauca. Between 115,000 and 100,000 years ago its surface stood above 3,720 m. Over the same span, Lake Ballivián filled the Titicaca basin.

  <!-- late-007 -->

- **Skhul and Qafzeh: modern humans in the Levant** — c. 120,000–80,000 years ago (120–80 ka)

  Two caves in Israel hold some of the earliest Homo sapiens outside Africa. Fossils from Qafzeh and Es-Skhul date to about 120,000 to 80,000 years ago. They mark an early dispersal near the start of the Late Pleistocene, when Neanderthals also lived in the Levant. Then the trail goes cold. No later Homo sapiens fossils are known there until Manot 1, about 54,700 years ago.

  <!-- late-008 -->

- **Giant long-horned bison evolve** — c. 120,000 years ago (119.924 ka)

  As the Laurentide ice melted about 130,000 years ago, steppe bison spread from Alaska into central North America. There they gave rise to the giant long-horned bison, Bison latifrons. It is first known from Colorado's Snowmass site about 120,000 years ago. By 60,000 years ago it had given rise to Bison antiquus, widely considered the ancestor of the modern American bison.

  <!-- late-009 -->

- **Neanderthals hunt elephants at Neumark-Nord** — c. 120,000 years ago (119.924 ka)

  At Neumark-Nord in Germany lie the remains of at least 57 straight-tusked elephants, about 120,000 years old. Neanderthals hunted them there regularly, perhaps every 5 to 6 years, and may have rendered fat from their bones. Systematic butchery at Lehringen, Taubach and Gröbern shows the same. Hunting these giants was widespread in Eemian Germany.

  <!-- late-010 -->

- **Denny, child of a Neanderthal and a Denisovan** — c. 118,000–79,300 years ago (118.1–79.3 ka)

  A tiny bone from Denisova Cave in Russia belonged to a 13-year-old girl with mixed parents. Her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan, making her a first-generation hybrid. The fragment dates to between 118,100 and 79,300 years ago. She was no one-off. About 17% of the Denisova Cave Denisovan genome comes from interbreeding with Altai Neanderthals.

  <!-- late-011 -->

- **Solo Man, the last Homo erectus** — c. 117,000–108,000 years ago (117–108 ka)

  The last known Homo erectus lived beside the Solo River in Java, about 117,000 to 108,000 years ago. These people, called Solo Man, closed a presence on Java that had begun 1.51 to 0.93 million years ago at Sangiran. Their world was changing. By 125,000 years ago a much wetter climate had made Java an island and let tropical rainforest spread. The species probably died out as rainforest replaced the savannas it depended on. It vanished long before modern humans reached the region, roughly 55,000 to 50,000 years ago, and left no living descendants.

  <!-- late-012 -->

- **The Last Glacial Period begins** — c. 115,000 years ago (115 ka)

  About 115,000 years ago the warmth ended. The Last Interglacial gave way to the Last Glacial Period, which lasted until 11,700 years ago. Average temperatures dropped markedly, and warmth-loving woodland species were pushed out of northern Europe. The cold did not arrive all at once. Temperatures fell gradually through the glacial, reaching their lowest at the The last deglaciation begins. Each region has its own name for this ice age. It is the Würm in the Alps, the Devensian in Britain and the Weichselian in northern Europe, broadly matched by the Wisconsin in North America. With so much water locked in ice, the seas fell. Much of Sundaland, the shelf linking Southeast Asia's islands, became dry land. So did most of the Persian Gulf, for most of the glacial.

  <!-- late-014 -->

  *Figure: One ice age, four regional names.*

  | Region | Name of the Last Glacial |
  |---|---|
  | Alps | Würm |
  | Britain | Devensian |
  | Northern Europe | Weichselian |
  | North America | Wisconsin (broadly) |

- **Dansgaard–Oeschger events: sudden glacial warmings** — c. 115,000–11,700 years ago (115–11.7 ka)

  Greenland could warm about 8 °C within 40 years, in the middle of an ice age. Such Dansgaard–Oeschger events, rapid climate swings, happened 25 times during the Last Glacial Period. A rise of 5 °C over 30 to 40 years was more typical. They are best recorded in Greenland ice cores, which reach back to the end of the Eemian about 115,000 years ago. They arose when ice volume and carbon dioxide were middling, a window in which the Atlantic's overturning circulation could flip between two states. Each nudged carbon dioxide up about 5 ppm and weakened the Indonesian–Australian monsoon. A 1,470-year rhythm has been proposed, but it is debated.

  <!-- late-013 -->

- **The hand axe finally disappears** — c. 100,000 years ago (100 ka)

  The hand axe, a design that had spread across continents, finally went out of use. Acheulean tools vanish from the record about then. More complex Middle Paleolithic kits, such as the Mousterian and Aterian industries, replaced them. The Mousterian had already displaced the Acheulean in Europe and the Middle East by around 125,000 years ago. In East Asia it may have lasted until about 50,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-016 -->

- **The Ata supereruption in southern Japan** — c. 100,000 years ago (100 ka)

  About 100,000 years ago, a caldera eruption spread the Ata tephra over southern Japan. Most estimates date it between 100,000 and 109,000 years ago. Rated VEI 7.5, it produced over 300 km³ of tephra.

  <!-- late-017 -->

- **Blombos Cave and the earliest drawing** — c. 100,000–70,000 years ago (100–70 ka)

  A cross-hatched line on a piece of ochre may be the earliest known drawing. It comes from Blombos Cave, on South Africa's southern Cape coast. People used the cave on and off in the Middle Stone Age, about 100,000 to 70,000 years ago. They left engraved ochre, beads of marine shell and finely made bone tools. Then wind-blown sand sealed the cave about 70,000 to 68,000 years ago. People did not return until about 2,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-018 -->

- **Woolly mammoths cross into North America** — c. 100,000 years ago (99.924 ka)

  Woolly mammoths entered North America about 100,000 years ago by crossing the Bering Strait. Where their range met that of Columbian mammoths, the two interbred. Two Late Pleistocene molars from British Columbia carry 21.6% and 34.6% Columbian ancestry. Isotopes in their remains show that Siberia stayed more uniformly cold and dry than the American side of the Bering land bridge.

  <!-- late-019 -->

- **Los Chocoyos, Central America's greatest eruption** — c. 98,000–75,000 years ago (98–75 ka)

  Lake Atitlán in Guatemala fills the crater of the largest known eruption in Central America. The Atitlán caldera blew out about 1,220 km³ of rhyolitic ash, or 730 km³ as dense rock. Pyroclastic currents left deposits 6 to 10 m thick in Chiapas, over 130 km from the vent. The date is uncertain, between 98,000 and 75,000 years ago. The younger estimate puts it close to the Toba supereruption. Whether it disrupted the climate is disputed.

  <!-- late-020 -->

- **The last terror birds die out** — c. 96,000 years ago (96 ka)

  Terror birds, flightless predators of South America, made their last stand with a small species. Psilopterus appears to have survived there until about 96,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-021 -->

- **Kikai's eruption spreads ash across Japan** — c. 94,000 years ago (94.5 ± 4.8 ka)

  About 94,500 years ago, the Kikai caldera in Japan erupted at VEI 7. It spread a layer of rhyolitic ash, the K-Tz tephra, from southern Kyushu to eastern Honshu and out over the Pacific, possibly as far as the Shandong Peninsula. Layered sediments in Lake Suigetsu date it to 94,500 ± 4,800 years ago.

  <!-- late-022 -->

- **Aso-4, the largest of Aso's eruptions** — c. 90,000 years ago (90 ka)

  About 90,000 years ago, Aso caldera on Kyushu erupted 384 km³ of magma, measured as solid rock. That makes it at least VEI 7. Another account rates it VEI 8, spewing about a trillion cubic meters of ash.

  <!-- late-023 -->

- **Bone harpoons at Katanda** — c. 90,000 years ago (90 ka)

  About 90,000 years ago, people in the Semliki River valley of Central Africa carved harpoons from bone. The Katanda harpoons date to the Middle Stone Age. Harpoons were first invented about then, in the late Middle Paleolithic. They brought fish into human diets, a hedge against starvation.

  <!-- late-025 -->

- **A glacial lake floods western Siberia** — c. 90,000–80,000 years ago (90–80 ka)

  When ice blocked the Arctic mouths of the Ob and Yenisei, their water had nowhere to go. A vast lake pooled at the edge of the Barents-Kara Ice Sheet. Its phase 90,000 to 80,000 years ago covered about 610,000 km² and held about 15,000 km³ of water. A second phase, 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, was larger still: about 881,000 km² and 32,000 km³.

  <!-- late-026 -->

  *Figure: The second phase of the lake was larger than the first.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Barents–Kara Ice Sheet dams Arctic rivers** — c. 90,000–50,000 years ago (90–50 ka)

  During the Weichselian glaciation, an ice sheet buried the Barents and Kara seas and the islands of Novaya Zemlya. The Barents–Kara Ice Sheet probably reached Svalbard and Franz Josef Land as well. On land it stretched from the North Russian Plain to the North Siberian Lowland. Its ice dammed great lakes 90,000 to 80,000 and 60,000 to 50,000 years ago. These rerouted rivers that now flow north, such as the Yenisei, Ob, Pechora and Mezen.

  <!-- late-024 -->

- **Shell necklaces at Taforalt** — c. 85,000–82,000 years ago (85–82 ka)

  Someone strung pierced sea shells into a necklace in a cave 40 km from the sea. The shells, from an 85,000 to 82,000-year-old layer at Taforalt in Morocco, are early North African evidence of modern behavior. They probably arrived through an exchange network. Working them into ornaments suggests the shells carried meaning. Marine shells served as beads in North Africa, the Near East and sub-Saharan Africa at least 30,000 years before Europe.

  <!-- late-027 -->

- **Early modern humans in southern China** — c. 80,000 years ago (80 ka)

  Modern human teeth found in China are claimed to be at least 80,000 years old. Liujiang man, among the earliest modern humans in East Asia, is most often dated to at least 67,000 years ago. Finds at Zhirendong cave, possibly over 100,000 years old, may belong to the same early wave.

  <!-- late-028 -->

- **West Antarctic ice grows to the shelf edge** — c. 79,900–29,900 years ago (79.924–29.924 ka)

  In the Eemian, about 130,000 years ago, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet had shrunk to a few small, isolated ice caps. By about 80,000 years ago it was roughly its present size. Then it grew much larger. During the Last Glacial Maximum, which this source puts about 30,000 years ago, it reached the edges of Antarctica's continental shelves.

  <!-- late-029 -->

- **Heinrich events: armadas of icebergs** — c. 75,000–11,000 years ago (75–11 ka)

  Every so often, great fleets of icebergs broke from the Laurentide ice sheet and drifted through Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic. These are Heinrich events, best documented for the Wisconsin glaciation, about 75,000 to 11,000 years ago. As the icebergs melted they dropped rock debris onto the seafloor, leaving layers named after them. They also poured fresh water into the ocean, likely altering its circulation. The effects reached far away. Discharges between 21,000 and 11,500 years ago coincided with droughts in the subtropics. Why the ice sheet became unstable is still debated.

  <!-- late-030 -->

  *Figure: Trace a Heinrich event from the ice sheet to the ocean floor and currents.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Laurentide ice sheet] -->|iceberg fleets| B[Hudson Strait]
  B --> C[North Atlantic]
  C --> D[Rock debris: Heinrich layers]
  C --> E[Fresh water added]
  E --> F[Ocean circulation altered]
  ```

- **Mastodons and giant beavers retreat from the north** — c. 75,000 years ago (74.924 ka)

  In the warm forests of the Last Interglacial, American mastodons lived in North America's far north. About 75,000 years ago, as the Wisconsin glaciation set in, they were wiped out there. That was long before people arrived. From then on mastodons lived only south of the ice sheets. Giant beavers likewise vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago as conditions grew more hostile.

  <!-- late-031 -->

- **Toba, the great supereruption** — 74,000 years ago (73.7 ± 0.3 ka)

  About 74,000 years ago, Toba on Sumatra produced one of the largest eruptions of the Cenozoic. The VEI 8 supereruption released about 2,800 km³ of magma. It left a caldera now filled by Lake Toba and dropped about 5 cm of ash over India. The eruption itself is well dated. Its effects are not. It struck during the rapid cooling into MIS 4. Whether it sped that cooling is debated, and records from the Arabian Sea suggest it did not. The Toba catastrophe theory links the eruption to a sharp fall in human numbers, a population bottleneck. That causal link remains highly controversial. Toba was enormous but not unique. Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

  <!-- late-032 -->

- **MIS 4: the ice sheets advance** — c. 71,000–57,000 years ago (71–57 ka)

  Between about 71,000 and 57,000 years ago, the world plunged into a cold stage known as MIS 4. North America's Wisconsin glaciation had begun about 75,000 years ago. In northwest Europe a very cold phase peaked around 70,000 years ago, and the Sierra Nevada's Tahoe glaciation reached its maximum perhaps about then. Glaciation became continuous on Siberia's Azas Plateau. Southern Hemisphere glaciers reached their greatest extent, as Australasia, Africa and Europe grew colder and drier.

  <!-- late-033 -->

- **The Bering land bridge rises again** — c. 70,000 years ago (70 ka)

  Falling seas turned the strait between Asia and North America into dry land. Glacial sea levels last exposed the Bering land bridge about 70,000 years ago. Through the Late Pleistocene, this region, Beringia, was a mosaic of living communities joining the two continents.

  <!-- late-034 -->

- **Yellowstone's most recent lava flow** — c. 70,000 years ago (70 ka)

  Yellowstone has been quieter than its reputation. After its last great caldera eruption, activity there consisted of basalt flows, rhyolite domes and minor explosive deposits. Its last known magmatic eruption, a lava flow, came about 70,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-037 -->

- **Out of Africa along the Southern Route** — c. 70,000–50,000 years ago (70–50 ka)

  Almost everyone whose family roots lie outside Africa descends from one small band of travelers. People outside Africa today come mainly from a single expansion of Homo sapiens, about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. A small group carrying the maternal lineage called mitochondrial haplogroup L3, perhaps fewer than 1,000 people, crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia. From there they followed the coasts. They worked their way around Arabia and Persia and reached South Asia before 55,000 years ago. Their descendants pressed on toward Southeast Asia and Oceania. Not everyone kept to the shore. Around 50,000 years ago, others entered Eurasia through the Zagros Mountains, and some headed for the steppes of Central Asia. The expansion had a shadow. Extinctions driven by humans began as people spread out of Africa over 60,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-036 -->

  *Figure: The Southern Route out of Africa.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Africa] --> B[Bab-el-Mandeb strait]
  B --> C[Arabian and Persian coasts]
  C --> D[South Asia]
  D --> E[Southeast Asia, Oceania]
  C --> F[Zagros into Eurasia]
  ```

- **Lake Lisan fills the Jordan Rift** — c. 70,000–12,000 years ago (70–12 ka)

  A great lake once filled a deep valley in the Near East. Lake Lisan filled the Jordan Rift Valley in West Asia from about 70,000 to 12,000 years ago, through most of the Last Glacial Period.

  <!-- late-035 -->

- **The first people reach Australia** — c. 65,000 years ago (65 ± 6 ka)

  Reaching Australia meant crossing open sea. People moved from Sunda, the Asian shelf, through the islands of Wallacea to Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea. They had followed the southern coast of Asia to get there. Madjedbebe in northern Australia was possibly occupied by 65,000 ± 6,000 years ago, and at least by 50,000. The older date is disputed. A 2020 study suggested termites had disturbed the layers, and 50,000 years has long been the accepted figure. Settlement of southern Australia came during a wet period between 60,000 and 40,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-038 -->

- **Modern humans mix with Neanderthals and Denisovans** — c. 65,000–47,000 years ago (65–47 ka)

  Leaving Africa did not mean leaving other humans behind. Migrants interbred with archaic people already living outside it, adding their DNA to the modern gene pool. An earlier modern wave had exchanged genes with Neanderthals around 100,000 years ago. Linkage studies date the last Neanderthal gene flow into the ancestors of Europeans to 47,000 to 65,000 years ago. Denisovan genes entered the ancestors of Oceanians after they split from Eurasians, about 50,000 years ago, and before 37,000 years ago. Tianyuan man, who lived in China about 40,000 years ago, carried substantial Neanderthal ancestry.

  <!-- late-039 -->

- **A brief modern human visit to Mandrin Cave** — c. 56,800–51,700 years ago (56.8–51.7 ka)

  In layer E of Mandrin Cave, in France's Rhône valley, lie modern human teeth, including a baby's molar, and stone tools of a style called Neronian. They date to 56,800 to 51,700 years ago. The layers just below and above hold Neanderthal remains and Mousterian tools. The two peoples' stays may have been only years apart. The tools resemble finds at Ksar Akil in Lebanon, suggesting a brief incursion from the Levant. Jean-Jacques Hublin says that idea remains to be confirmed.

  <!-- late-040 -->

- **The last Denisovans** — c. 55,000 years ago (55 ka)

  The Denisovans fade from view slowly. In their namesake cave in the Altai, the Denisova 3 finger bone dates to 76,200 to 51,600 years ago. They are confirmed there only until about 55,000 years ago. Elsewhere, Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in the sediments of the cave that held the Xiahe jaw spans 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, perhaps later. A Denisovan rib fragment from Baishiya Cave, China, is younger still, at 48,000 to 32,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-041 -->

- **The Flores hobbit vanishes** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  The small human of Flores lasted until the newcomers came. Homo floresiensis, nicknamed the 'Hobbit', lived on the island until modern humans arrived about 50,000 years ago. Its bones at Liang Bua date from 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and its youngest stone tools are about 50,000 years old. Its world was already under strain. A drying trend intensified around 61,000 years ago, shrinking fresh water and the dwarf elephant relative it may have hunted. Bones of that animal, Stegodon florensis, lie at Liang Bua with Hobbit tools, a few bearing cut marks. The dwarf Stegodon's last records also date to about 50,000 years ago, around the time modern humans reached Flores.

  <!-- late-043 -->

- **Homo luzonensis, a small human of the Philippines** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  A few teeth and finger bones in Callao Cave revealed a new kind of human on Luzon. Homo luzonensis was small, possibly a pygmy form. Described in 2019, the fossils indicate it lived on the island between 50,000 and 67,000 years ago. Hominins had been active on Luzon far earlier, as early as 771,000 to 631,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-044 -->

- **The last giant python-like snakes** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  Australia was the last home of an ancient line of snakes. Madtsoiids, giant primitive python-like snakes such as Wonambi, survived there until about 50,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-045 -->

- **The great megafauna die-off begins** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  From around 50,000 years ago, most of the large land animals outside Africa died out. The extinction was unprecedented for one reason: it struck the biggest species hardest. About 65% of megafaunal species vanished worldwide. The toll was 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia. The timing tracked people. Losses began in Sahul about 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, each as modern humans arrived. Africa was hit less than other continents. Hunting, climate change or both are blamed. Scientists still argue over the balance, though most accept that humans played at least some part. The damage lasts. Mammal diversity lost since then could take 5 to 7 million years to recover.

  <!-- late-046 -->

  *Figure: Share of megafaunal species lost by region.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Meteor Crater blasted into Arizona** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  About 50,000 years ago, a nickel-iron meteorite about 50 m across slammed into the Colorado Plateau and blasted out Meteor Crater. The land was cooler and damper then: open grassland and woods where mammoths and giant ground sloths roamed. It is called the best-preserved meteorite crater on Earth.

  <!-- late-047 -->

- **The Rotoiti eruption in New Zealand** — c. 50,000 years ago (50 ka)

  About 50,000 years ago, New Zealand's Ōkataina caldera erupted at Rotoiti. It left ignimbrite and tephra spread over a wide area. Paired eruptions at Rotoiti and Earthquake Flat produced about 120 km³ and 10 km³ of material.

  <!-- late-048 -->

- **Procoptodon, the giant short-faced kangaroo** — c. 50,000–45,000 years ago (50–45 ka)

  The largest kangaroo known stood about 2 m tall and weighed up to 240 kg. Procoptodon goliah may have been the largest hopping mammal ever. It died out about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, though some evidence suggests it lasted until 18,000 years ago. Its loss came with the arrival of people, in a fairly stable climate. Hunting, burning of vegetation by people and drought have all been proposed. Which mattered most is debated.

  <!-- late-042 -->

- **The Upper Paleolithic: a burst of new tools and art** — c. 50,000–40,000 years ago (50–40 ka)

  Before 50,000 years ago, stone tools looked much the same everywhere. Then artifacts became markedly more diverse. Africa's Middle Stone Age ended about then, and the Upper Paleolithic began between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago. Signs of modern behavior are unambiguous from 40,000 to 50,000 years ago. Whether this was a sudden 'Great Leap Forward' is debated. Art followed. Spanish cave paintings and the Lion-man figurine date to around 40,000 years ago. The Aurignacian culture flourished in Europe and southwest Asia from 43,000 to 26,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-049 -->

- **Topper and the disputed pre-Clovis claims** — c. 50,000 years ago (49.924 ka)

  Charcoal at a chert quarry in South Carolina sparked a long argument. At Topper, charcoal lay below the Clovis layer, beside chipped chert read as tools, and was radiocarbon dated to about 50,000 years ago. Critics say the chert broke naturally and the charcoal came from a wildfire. They also note that 50,000 years is the limit of radiocarbon dating. Others still cite Topper as a pre-Clovis site, but about 16,000 years old.

  <!-- late-051 -->

- **Genyornis, the last of the giant dromornithid birds** — c. 49,900–39,900 years ago (49.924–39.924 ka)

  Genyornis newtoni stood 2 to 2.5 m tall and could not fly. By the Late Pleistocene it was the only surviving dromornithid, a family that had been diverse in the Miocene. It lived until around 50,000 to 40,000 years ago. At Lake Callabonna its population died about 50,000 years ago as the lake dried up. Burned eggshells 53,900 to 43,400 years old suggest people collected and cooked its eggs before it vanished. Drying lakes and human predation are both proposed causes, and the debate is unresolved.

  <!-- late-050 -->

- **Australia loses its giants** — c. 46,000 years ago (46 ka)

  Every mammal over 1,000 kg on the Australian mainland disappeared. All forms of megafauna there died out in the same rapid window, about 46,000 years ago, considerably earlier than on other continents. The victims included Diprotodon, the largest marsupial known, and the giant monitor lizard Megalania. Diprotodon was last recorded at South Walker Creek about 40,100 years ago. A Zygomaturus from New South Wales, 33,000 to 37,000 years old, is the latest known survivor. The losses followed human arrival rather than any known climate shift. Climate then resembled today's, and drying is judged an unlikely cause. Still, how much people contributed remains controversial.

  <!-- late-052 -->

- **Fire-stick farming reshapes Australia** — c. 46,000 years ago (45.924 ka)

  Australians were shaping their land with fire 46,000 years ago. Ash in the Coral Sea shows fire was already significant there over 100,000 years ago. About 45,000 years ago fire becomes abruptly more common. One geologist attributed the rise to Aboriginal fire-stick farming, the deliberate burning of forests and grasslands. One account holds that dense forest turned into open forest and grassland, favoring eucalyptus, acacia and grasses. How far burning changed the vegetation, and whether it helped drive the megafauna extinctions, is debated.

  <!-- late-053 -->

- **Modern humans reach Flores** — c. 46,000 years ago (45.924 ka)

  Teeth from Liang Bua cave, about 46,000 years old, probably belonged to Homo sapiens. They are the earliest evidence of modern humans on Flores. Stone tools from then on use different raw materials, so modern humans, not Homo floresiensis, likely made them. The newcomers arrived soon after the last records of the Hobbit and the dwarf Stegodon, around 50,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-054 -->

- **Modern humans reach Europe** — c. 45,000 years ago (45 ka)

  Europe was settled by people who already knew how to hunt the big game of the cold steppe. Modern humans came from Central Asia and the Middle East. They had reached northwestern Europe by 45,000 years ago; remains in Germany date to 45,000 to 47,000 years ago. Finds in Italy and Britain date to 43,000 to 45,000 years ago, and by 45,000 years ago people lived as far north as 61° N. Even so, the continent stayed nearly empty. Settling it may have taken 15,000 to 20,000 years, and from 40,000 to 16,000 years ago it held only some 4,000 to 6,000 people. Most of their mixing with Neanderthals had ended before they arrived, by 47,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-055 -->

- **Modern humans push into Siberia and the Arctic** — c. 45,000 years ago (45 ka)

  The remains of Ust'-Ishim man show modern humans in Siberia at 58° N by about 45,000 years ago. People entered the mammoth steppe and reached the Siberian Arctic around then. They reached Japan by about 30,000 years ago, and Siberia above the Arctic Circle by about 27,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-056 -->

- **The Châtelperronian, a Neanderthal toolkit** — c. 44,500–33,000 years ago (44.5–33 ka)

  Curved-backed flint knives from France and Spain raise a question: did Neanderthals pick up new ideas? The Châtelperronian, about 44,500 to 33,000 years ago, was the earliest Upper Paleolithic industry in central and southwestern France and northern Spain. It is the only Upper Paleolithic industry credited to Neanderthals, perhaps copying modern human techniques. Both its reality and its makers are debated. Critics see it as a mix of Mousterian and Aurignacian layers.

  <!-- late-057 -->

- **The straight-tusked elephant's last stand** — c. 44,000 years ago (43.924 ka)

  Its bulls averaged 4 m tall and 13 tonnes, among the largest land mammals ever. Palaeoloxodon antiquus, the straight-tusked elephant, retreated from northern Europe after the Last Interglacial ended about 115,000 years ago. It may have lingered in Britain until 87,000 years ago. Its youngest confirmed remains, from Iberia, are about 44,000 to 43,000 years old. Footprints may stretch its record to 28,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-058 -->

- **Ngwenya, the oldest known mine** — c. 43,000 years ago (43 ka)

  About 43,000 years ago, people at Ngwenya in Eswatini dug hematite out of the ground to make red ochre, a pigment. It is the oldest mining known anywhere.

  <!-- late-059 -->

- **The Laschamp excursion: a brief magnetic flip** — c. 42,200–41,500 years ago (42.2–41.5 ka)

  Between 42,200 and 41,500 years ago, Earth's magnetic field briefly reversed. The flip took about 250 years, and the field stayed reversed for about 440. In transition it fell to 5% of today's strength. With the shield weakened, more cosmic rays reached Earth. They raised the production of beryllium-10 and carbon-14, thinned the ozone layer and altered the circulation of the air. A fossil kauri tree from New Zealand, alive 42,500 to 41,000 years ago, recorded the event in its rings. Claimed links to the megafauna and Neanderthal extinctions, and to cave art, lack supporting evidence.

  <!-- late-060 -->

- **The Lake Mungo burials** — c. 42,000 years ago (42 ka)

  Lake Mungo 1 was burned twice and then covered with ochre carried from hundreds of kilometers away. It is among the oldest known cremations. Human remains from Lake Mungo in southeastern Australia date to about 42,000 years ago. The Willandra Lakes then held deep fresh water, and people lived on their shores 40,000 to 35,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-061 -->

- **The Neanderthals disappear** — c. 40,000 years ago (40 ka)

  About 40,000 years ago they disappeared from the fossil record, and their distinctive tools vanished with them. A 2021 recalibration dates their extinction to 40,700 ± 200 years ago. They had already vanished from northwestern Europe by 44,200 to 40,600 years ago. Modern humans spreading from Africa replaced them across Eurasia. Iberia was one of their last strongholds, with possible holdouts there 37,000 years ago. Another possible refuge was Byzovaya in the Urals, near the Arctic, about 33,000 to 32,000 years ago. They did not vanish entirely. A small amount of Neanderthal DNA survives in people today, a legacy of the interbreeding described in Modern humans mix with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

  <!-- late-062 -->

  *Figure: The Neanderthals' last records step from northwestern Europe to Iberia and the Urals.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Walking to Tasmania** — c. 40,000 years ago (40 ka)

  About 43,000 years ago, low glacial seas exposed the Bassian Plain, a land bridge from mainland Australia to Tasmania. People walked across about 40,000 years ago and became the Aboriginal Tasmanians. Tasmania's megafauna disappeared about 41,000 years ago, apparently through hunting.

  <!-- late-063 -->

- **The last marsupial lions** — c. 40,000 years ago (39.924 ka)

  Australia's top predator was a marsupial. Thylacoleo, the 'pouch lion', lived from the late Pliocene until around 40,000 years ago. Since the Pliocene it had been the only surviving genus of its family, the Thylacoleonidae. It vanished at about the same time as most Australian megafauna. How much climate change or newly arrived people were to blame is debated.

  <!-- late-064 -->

- **The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption near Naples** — 40,000 years ago (39.85 ± 0.14 ka)

  The largest eruption in the history of the Campi Flegrei, near Naples, came from the Archiflegreo volcano. Argon–argon dating puts it at 39,850 ± 140 years ago. It erupted about 200 km³ of magma, or 500 km³ of loose material, and left a rock called the Campanian Ignimbrite. Its ash, the Y-5 layer, spread over about 3,000,000 km². It coincided with a suite of biological and cultural changes in and beyond the Mediterranean. One theory blamed it for the Neanderthals' extinction. A 2021 recalibration, however, puts their disappearance at 40,700 ± 200 years ago, before the eruption.

  <!-- late-065 -->

- **The paintings of Chauvet Cave** — c. 36,900–33,400 years ago (36.924–33.424 ka)

  Chauvet Cave in southeastern France holds some of the world's best-preserved figurative cave paintings. Its floors also keep remains and prints of animals, some now extinct. Radiocarbon dates show two occupations, 37,000 to 33,500 and 31,000 to 28,000 years ago. Most black drawings belong to the first, and the oldest was painted about 36,500 years ago. About 29,000 years ago a cliff collapsed and sealed the entrance.

  <!-- late-066 -->

- **Stegodon fades from mainland Asia** — c. 34,900–19,900 years ago (34.924–19.924 ka)

  Stegodon, an elephant relative, lasted in Asia long after it died out in Africa. It lived across South, Southeast and East Asia. Its last mainland records date to perhaps 35,000 to 30,000 years ago in India and at least 30,000 to 20,000 in China; later claims are unsubstantiated. The harsh Last Glacial Maximum may have contributed. Asian elephants, with more flexible diets, survived. Whether climate, hunting or both caused such losses is debated.

  <!-- late-067 -->

- **The Gravettian spreads across Europe** — c. 33,000–22,000 years ago (33–22 ka)

  Clay fragments at Pavlov I in Moravia bear the impressions of woven textiles, about 26,980 to 24,870 years old. They belong to the Gravettian culture, which succeeded the Aurignacian about 33,000 years ago. It reached as far as Estremadura in Portugal, and Venus figurines are among its hallmarks. It had mostly disappeared by about 22,000 years ago, near the Last Glacial Maximum, though some elements lasted until about 17,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-068 -->

- **Disputed early sites in the Americas** — c. 32,900–24,000 years ago (32.924–24 ka)

  Did people reach the Americas before the last great ice? Stones from Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, thought to be tools, are dated to 26,000 years ago and possibly 33,000. Bluefish Caves in the Yukon may record people 24,000 years ago, though the dates are contested. Mammoth bones at Old Crow Flats, apparently butchered, date to 25,000 to 40,000 years ago. Skeptics note that the oldest sites with many artifacts in undisturbed layers, in eastern Beringia, date to 14,200 to 13,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-069 -->

- **Dogs part ways with wolves** — c. 32,100–18,800 years ago (32.1–18.8 ka)

  The oldest known dog skeletons, from Siberia's Altai Mountains and a cave in Belgium, date to about 33,000 years ago. Mitochondrial DNA puts the split of dogs from wolves 32,100 to 18,800 years ago, pointing to a European origin among hunter-gatherers. A 2021 review instead places the start of domestication in Siberia, 26,000 to 19,700 years ago, among Ancient North Eurasians. From there dogs spread east and west.

  <!-- late-070 -->

- **The ancestors of Native Americans reach Beringia** — c. 32,000 years ago (32 ka)

  About 36,000 years ago, the ancestors of the first Americans split from Ancient East Asians and moved north into Siberia. They lived as far east as Beringia before 32,000 years ago. Lake sediments in northern Alaska suggest they burned landscapes there as early as 34,000 years ago. Through the Last Glacial Maximum, a population of at most a few thousand lived in Beringia. There, 25,000 to 20,000 years ago, the Ancestral Native American lineage formed.

  <!-- late-071 -->

- **Ice bulldozes the Dogger Bank** — c. 31,600–23,100 years ago (31.6–23.1 ka)

  Dogger Bank began as mud on the bed of a glacial lake. Then the ice advanced and shoved those sediments into a ridge, a thrust moraine. This happened about 31,600 to 23,100 years ago.

  <!-- late-072 -->

- **Cave hyenas die out across Eurasia** — c. 30,900–19,900 years ago (30.924–19.924 ka)

  Cave hyenas were apex predators that hunted horses, bison and aurochs. They ranged from Western Europe to Southeast Asia, and their bones are common in Last Glacial cave deposits. Their youngest well-dated European remains are about 31,000 years old, perhaps 24,000. In northeast Asia they lasted until about 20,000 years ago. Why they vanished is not fully understood. Climate alone seems insufficient, and human activity and dwindling prey probably contributed.

  <!-- late-073 -->

- **The Ito eruption forms the Aira Caldera** — c. 30,000 years ago (30 ka)

  About 30,000 years ago, the colossal Ito eruption tore open Aira Caldera on Kyushu, spreading tephra and ignimbrite over the land. Seawater later flooded the caldera, helping form Kagoshima Bay, 200 m deep. Sakurajima volcano now rises inside it.

  <!-- late-075 -->

- **The Sahara dries as the Mousterian Pluvial ends** — c. 30,000 years ago (30 ka)

  Until about 30,000 years ago, a long wet spell called the Mousterian Pluvial kept northern Africa well watered and cooler than today. When the pluvial ended, the Sahara turned arid. In the north of the Chad Basin, eolianite, sand dunes later hardened into rock, began to form 40,000 to 20,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-077 -->

- **Lake Bonneville begins to rise** — c. 30,000–13,000 years ago (30–13 ka)

  About 30,000 years ago, a lake in Utah no bigger than today's Great Salt Lake began to grow. The name Lake Bonneville covers it from 30,000 to 13,000 years ago, while glaciers worldwide were expanded. It was not itself fed by an ice sheet's edge. After about 24,000 years ago it rose rapidly. It reached its highest level, the Bonneville shoreline, about 17,500 years ago.

  <!-- late-076 -->

- **Europe's ice-age megafauna at their peak** — c. 27,000–21,000 years ago (27–21 ka)

  The cold was good for big animals, up to a point. Megafauna were most abundant in Europe around 27,000 to 21,000 years ago, thanks to the cold stadial climate. A mammoth steppe stretched from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon. But as cold peaked in the Last Glacial Maximum, around 23,000 years ago, Europe's top predators began to die out.

  <!-- late-079 -->

- **The Last Glacial Maximum** — c. 26,000–20,000 years ago (26–20 ka)

  Around 21,000 years ago, the world was about 6 °C colder on average than today. That may sound modest, but it buried continents. Ice sheets began advancing about 33,000 years ago in both hemispheres. Between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago they reached their greatest extent of the Last Glacial Period. This peak is the Last Glacial Maximum. Ice up to 3 km thick covered much of northern Europe, Asia and North America, as well as Greenland and Antarctica. In the Northern Hemisphere, people and animals retreated to refugia. These were sheltered areas where they could survive until the ice withdrew. The maximum also marks a turning point. From here the ice would begin to retreat, as told in The last deglaciation begins.

  <!-- late-080 -->

  *Figure: The ice built up, peaked, and drove life into refugia.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Ice sheets advance, from 33,000 years ago] --> B[Greatest extent, 26,000–20,000 years ago]
  B --> C[Ice up to 3 km thick]
  B --> D[People and animals retreat to refugia]
  ```

- **Oruanui, the world's most recent supereruption** — 26,000 years ago (25.675 ± 0.09 ka)

  About 25,700 years ago, Taupō Volcano in New Zealand produced the most recent supereruption on Earth, rated VEI 8. It burst up through a system of lakes. Water and magma met, making it the largest phreatomagmatic eruption known, a blast driven by flashing steam. It produced about 530 km³ of magma as ash fall, ignimbrite and fill inside the caldera. Lake Huka was destroyed, and the caldera left behind now holds Lake Taupō. The eruption may have deepened the glacial cold in New Zealand and the nearby Pacific. Afterward the new lake filled to about 75 m above today's level, then cut through its ignimbrite dam less than 22,500 years ago.

  <!-- late-081 -->

- **Andean and Patagonian glaciers reach their peak** — c. 25,200–23,100 years ago (25.2–23.1 ka)

  In the far south, the ice peaked a little earlier than in the north. Southern Hemisphere ice sheets grew from about 33,000 years ago. Northern Andean glaciers peaked around 27,000 years ago, and those of Chiloé 26,000 years ago, building a long moraine system. Around the Strait of Magellan, glaciers peaked 25,200 to 23,100 years ago. The Patagonian Ice Sheet covered all of Chile south of Puerto Montt and spilled into Argentina, where the dry climate stopped it.

  <!-- late-082 -->

- **The Laurentide ice sheet at its maximum** — c. 25,000–21,000 years ago (25–21 ka)

  Ice once stood over Manhattan. After retreating between 52,000 and 40,000 years ago, the Laurentide Ice Sheet grew fast again. By the Late Wisconsin, about 25,000 to 21,000 years ago, North America's ice reached its maximum. It covered Canada east of the Rockies and pushed south to the Missouri and Ohio rivers. Ice sheets reached to about the 45th parallel north. In the Rockies, the Pinedale glaciation peaked 23,500 to 21,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-083 -->

- **Lake Sajsi on the Altiplano** — c. 25,000–19,000 years ago (25–19 ka)

  During the Last Glacial Maximum, a lake called Sajsi filled the Uyuni basin on the Bolivian Altiplano. It lasted from 25,000 to 19,000 years ago and was deepest 23,000 years ago. It was a forerunner of the larger Lake Tauca that would follow.

  <!-- late-084 -->

- **The Mal'ta boy and the Ancient North Eurasians** — c. 24,000 years ago (24 ka)

  About 24,000 years ago, a boy was buried at Mal'ta, near Lake Baikal in Siberia, with artifacts and a Venus figurine. Mal'ta is the oldest known site in eastern Siberia. It had houses walled with bone and about thirty female figurines, a type previously found only in Europe. The boy's people, the Ancient North Eurasians, passed their genes to Native Americans, Siberians and Europeans alike.

  <!-- late-085 -->

- **The cave bear dies out** — c. 24,000 years ago (23.924 ka)

  The cave bear of Europe and Asia died out about 24,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum. Its decline began long before. Ancient DNA shows its numbers falling steeply from about 40,000 years ago, as the Aurignacian began and modern humans arrived. By around 35,000 years ago it was no longer abundant in Central Europe.

  <!-- late-086 -->

- **Wild cereals harvested at Ohalo II** — c. 23,000 years ago (23 ka)

  Long before farming, people were gathering grain. About 23,000 years ago, people near the Sea of Galilee were cultivating emmer, barley and oats. At Ohalo II, a lakeshore camp of that age, flint blades carry a gloss from cutting stems. They are the earliest known composite harvesting tools, blades set into handles. Humans were processing and eating wild cereal grains by then.

  <!-- late-088 -->

- **The White Sands footprints** — c. 23,000–21,000 years ago (23–21 ka)

  In New Mexico's White Sands, people once walked across wet mud among ice-age animals. The site holds perhaps hundreds of thousands of human and animal tracks. Seeds in the layers date the human footprints to 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum. If correct, they are possibly the oldest evidence of people in the Americas. Skeptics say the seeds took up old carbon from groundwater. That would put the maximum age at only 15,500 to 13,500 years. Pollen and quartz-grain dating in 2023, and mud dating in 2025, supported the older ages. The debate continues.

  <!-- late-087 -->

- **The Fennoscandian ice sheet at its maximum** — c. 22,000 years ago (22 ka)

  The ice of Scandinavia swallowed the mountains whole. The Fennoscandian Ice Sheet buried the entire Scandinavian Mountains. It reached the edge of the mid-Norwegian shelf by about 26,000 years ago, then merged with Barents Sea and British ice. It spread into Denmark, Germany, Poland and the former USSR. Its maximum came at different times in different places. It reached Denmark, Germany and western Poland about 22,000 years ago, and Lithuania and Belarus about 19,000. Its margin began to retreat 22,000 to 17,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-089 -->

- **The paintings of Lascaux** — c. 22,000–17,000 years ago (22–17 ka)

  Lascaux Cave in France's Vézère valley holds some of the most celebrated paintings of the Upper Paleolithic. They show mainly large animals, matching the local wildlife known from fossils of the time. Many generations worked on them. Their age is still debated. The usual estimate, 17,000 to 22,000 years ago, places them in the early Magdalenian.

  <!-- late-090 -->

- **The Solutrean toolmakers of glacial Europe** — c. 22,000–17,000 years ago (22–17 ka)

  During the Last Glacial Maximum, about 22,000 to 17,000 years ago, the Solutrean flint industry flourished in France, Spain and Portugal. It followed the Gravettian. Its people lived west of the Alps in a glacial refuge, between forest steppe and steppe tundra. They used toolmaking techniques not seen before and not rediscovered for millennia. Blended with earlier traditions, the Solutrean gave rise to the Magdalenian.

  <!-- late-091 -->

- **Sea level bottoms out at 125 m below today** — c. 21,000 years ago (21 ka)

  Around 21,000 years ago, so much water was locked in ice, mostly in the Laurentide sheet, that the oceans stood about 125 m lower than today. Land bridges opened. The Bering land bridge joined Siberia and Alaska, and the Bassian Plain linked Tasmania to Australia. On the Great Barrier Reef, coral growth moved seaward with the falling water. It reached farthest from today's coast around 20,700 to 20,500 years ago.

  <!-- late-092 -->

- **Xianren Cave: the oldest pottery** — c. 20,000–19,000 years ago (20–19 ka)

  Pottery was invented by hunters, not farmers. Sherds from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, radiocarbon-dated to 20,000 to 19,000 years ago, are the earliest pottery known anywhere. Mobile foragers made the pots during the Last Glacial Maximum. Scorch marks suggest they cooked with them. Pottery had been thought to begin with the Neolithic, around 10,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-093 -->

- **The last deglaciation begins** — c. 19,000 years ago (19 ka)

  Antarctica felt the thaw first. Around 22,000 years ago it warmed abruptly, by about 6 °C. The ice sheets had been largest between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Northern warming began near 20,000 years ago, and northern ice began to retreat around 19,000 years ago. The start may have been sudden. A brief event, lasting at most 500 years, may have raised sea level by as much as 10 m, a surge called meltwater pulse 19ka. Northern warming stayed limited until about 14,600 years ago, and the retreat sped up around 15,000 years ago. The melting was neither steady nor simultaneous. Ice still covered most of Great Britain until about 16,000 years ago. The totals were vast. Over the whole deglaciation, global mean temperature rose about 5 °C and high latitudes over 10 °C. Sea level climbed more than 120 m.

  <!-- late-096 -->

  *Figure: Steps of the last deglaciation.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Southern Ocean breathes out carbon dioxide** — c. 19,000–11,500 years ago (19–11.5 ka)

  Where did the carbon go during the ice age, and how did it come back? Ice cores show carbon dioxide at 180 to 210 ppm during ice ages, rising to 280 to 300 ppm in warm interglacials. During the Last Glacial Maximum, the extra carbon was stored in the deep ocean, held down by layering in the Southern Ocean. Over the deglaciation, about 19,000 to 11,000 years ago, stronger winds and retreating sea ice may have stirred the deep Southern Ocean and released it. The rise came in three abrupt pulses. It paused during the Antarctic Cold Reversal, 14,700 to 13,000 years ago. Rising carbon dioxide warmed the globe out of the glacial maximum. Its rapid increase eased about 11,500 years ago, as the deglaciation ended.

  <!-- late-095 -->

  *Figure: Follow the carbon from the deep Southern Ocean back into the air.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Carbon stored in deep ocean] --> B[Stronger winds, retreating sea ice]
  B --> C[Deep Southern Ocean overturns]
  C --> D[CO2 released in pulses]
  D --> E[Globe warms out of glacial]
  ```

- **The Basal Pumice eruption and Vesuvius's Somma caldera** — c. 18,000 years ago (18.224 ka)

  Vesuvius began forming about 25,000 years ago in the Codola eruption. From about 19,000 years ago it switched to large explosive, caldera-forming Plinian eruptions. About 18,300 years ago, the VEI 6 Basal Pumice eruption first formed the Somma caldera. Quieter lava eruptions followed. The most recent of its great Plinian blasts came in AD 79.

  <!-- late-097 -->

- **Rising seas begin to drown Sundaland** — c. 18,000 years ago (18 ka)

  At the Last Glacial Maximum, with sea level about 120 m lower, Borneo, Java and Sumatra were joined to Asia. The whole Sunda Shelf lay exposed as dry land, called Sundaland. Around 18,000 years ago rising seas began to swallow part of it. The flooding went on until about 5000 BC.

  <!-- late-099 -->

- **The Oldest Dryas and Heinrich event 1** — c. 18,000–14,700 years ago (18–14.7 ka)

  Just as the ice began to melt, the north plunged back into cold. The Oldest Dryas, a cold stadial, interrupted the retreat from about 18,000 to 14,700 years ago. Heinrich event 1 cooled the North Atlantic and weakened the ocean's overturning circulation. Rain belts shifted south, drying northern Africa. Europe was dry, treeless, grassy tundra. Iberian mountain glaciers that had nearly vanished surged back into the valleys 16,800 to 16,500 years ago. Yet species were already returning from refuges in the Carpathians, Italy, Spain and Greece, brown bears among them. Globally, rising carbon dioxide still warmed the planet about 2 °C, nearly half of it in the stadial's last centuries.

  <!-- late-098 -->

  *Figure: Heinrich event 1 set off a chain from the North Atlantic to Africa.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Heinrich event 1] --> B[North Atlantic cools]
  A --> C[Overturning circulation weakens]
  C --> D[Rain belts shift south]
  D --> E[Northern Africa dries]
  ```

- **The Southern Hemisphere thaws fast** — c. 18,000 years ago (17.8 ka)

  In southern Chile, rapid warming from 17,800 years ago brought interglacial temperatures within about 1,000 years. Glaciers retreated and Valdivian rainforest spread. A 2017 study linked a thinning of stratospheric ozone about 17,700 years ago to this sudden speed-up. The Patagonian Ice Sheet had peaked about 18,000 to 17,500 years ago, covering about 480,000 km² with over 500,000 km³ of ice. Its northern edge then melted rapidly. The meltwater freshened the nearby ocean and altered its circulation, with effects near and far. Around 18,000 years ago, glaciers also began to retreat on Antarctica's Alexander Island and melted from New Zealand's Tongariro.

  <!-- late-100 -->

- **Lake Tauca and the Central Andean Pluvial** — c. 17,500–15,900 years ago (17.5–15.9 ka)

  On the Bolivian Altiplano, Lake Tauca rose from about 18,000 years ago. It peaked 16,500 years ago and stayed high until 15,500 years ago. The wetter first stage of the Central Andean Pluvial Event lasted from 17,500 to 15,900 years ago. Many explanations link the wet phase to circulation changes during Heinrich event 1, which carried more moisture onto the Altiplano.

  <!-- late-101 -->

- **The earliest true domestic dogs** — c. 17,400–17,100 years ago (17.41–17.096 ka)

  The dog was the only animal people domesticated in the Pleistocene. The most widely accepted earliest dog is the Erralla dog from the Basque Country, Spain, dated 17,410 to 17,096 years ago. Disputed remains go back 36,000 years. The Bonn–Oberkassel dog, about 14,500 years old, is the oldest known dog buried together with people. People also brought dogs with them into North America.

  <!-- late-102 -->

- **The Bonneville flood** — c. 17,000 years ago (17.4 ka)

  Lake Bonneville once covered about 83,000 km² of northern Utah. About 17,400 years ago it reached its highest level. Then it broke through a natural dam of alluvial fans at Red Rock Pass. A flood crest 120 m high raced toward the Snake River. At its peak, about 930,000 m³ of water passed every second. The torrent scoured the Snake River Canyon and created Shoshone Falls. It drained about 5,000 km³ of water and lowered the lake 107 m, to the Provo shoreline. Unlike the repeated Missoula floods, the Bonneville flood happened only once.

  <!-- late-103 -->

  *Figure: One breach, one flood, and a lake dropped to a new shoreline.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Lake Bonneville at highest level] --> B[Dam breaks at Red Rock Pass]
  B --> C[Flood toward Snake River]
  C --> D[Canyon scoured, Shoshone Falls formed]
  B --> E[Lake drops 107 m to Provo shoreline]
  ```

- **The Pacific coast opens a path south** — c. 17,000–15,000 years ago (17–15 ka)

  Retreating glaciers on the Alaska Peninsula opened a way from Beringia to the Pacific coast by around 17,000 years ago. After that, the coastal corridor became livable. The ice barrier between interior Alaska and the coast broke up from about 16,200 years ago. The coast range was fully free of ice by 16,000 to 15,000 years ago. Kelp forests, estuaries and other shoreline habitats could have formed an open migration route.

  <!-- late-104 -->

- **A proposed Caspian flood into the Black Sea** — c. 17,000–14,000 years ago (17–14 ka)

  Andrei Chepalyga proposed a flood from the Caspian into the Black Sea about 17,000 to 14,000 years ago. In his scenario, melting Scandinavian ice raised the Caspian up to 50 m above today's level from about 16,000 years ago. The water spilled west through the Manych–Kerch spillway. It would have raised the Black Sea by 60 to 70 m, flooding land once used for settlement or hunting. This 'Late Pleistocene Great Flood' is one researcher's hypothesis, not an established event.

  <!-- late-105 -->

- **The Vashon ice reaches Puget Sound** — c. 17,000 years ago (16.95 ka)

  Ice once rolled over the site of Seattle. The Puget Lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet passed there about 17,950 years ago and reached its maximum near Tenino about 16,950 years ago. From about 16,850 years ago it retreated about 340 m a year. A breached ice dam released a major outburst flood. By about 16,000 years ago, the ice had pulled back far enough for seawater to refill Puget Sound.

  <!-- late-106 -->

- **Woolly mammoths and rhinos retreat to the far north** — c. 16,900–11,700 years ago (16.924–11.7 ka)

  As the ice age waned, the giants of the cold lost their ground. Woolly rhinos vanished from Europe 17,000 to 15,000 years ago. Their youngest reliable bones, from the Urals and northeast Siberia, are about 14,200 to 14,000 years old. Bølling–Allerød warmth likely brought more rain and snow, turning their low grass and herb habitat into shrubs and woods. Woolly mammoths disappeared from most of Europe by 14,000 years ago. They left Alaska and the Yukon about 13,300 years ago, roughly 1,000 years after people arrived. From about 15,000 years ago, wet tundra and forest replaced most of Siberia's mammoth steppe. By the Younger Dryas, mammoths survived only in its far north. DNA shows a final crash about 12,000 years ago, from which they never recovered. Whether habitat loss or hunting mattered more is still debated.

  <!-- late-107 -->

  *Figure: The cold-adapted giants retreat region by region toward the end of the ice age.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **People spread through the Americas** — c. 16,000–13,000 years ago (16–13 ka)

  Scholars agree on the basic story: the first Americans came from Siberia. They spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum, around 16,000 to 13,000 years ago. Ice sheets blocked the inland routes until about 16,000 years ago. A route along the Pacific coast may have opened by 17,000 years ago. Around 16,000 years ago, the northern and southern Native American genetic branches split. Sites older than the Clovis culture, now widely accepted, trace the spread. Cooper's Ferry in Idaho dates to about 15,800 years ago. Page-Ladson in Florida dates to about 14,550, and Paisley Caves in Oregon to about 14,200. People reached South America around 15,000 years ago, before its megafauna died out.

  <!-- late-109 -->

  *Figure: Widely accepted pre-Clovis sites in the Americas.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Baltic Ice Lake** — c. 16,000–11,700 years ago (16–11.7 ka)

  Before the Baltic was a sea, it was a lake of meltwater. About 16,000 years ago, the retreating Weichselian ice reached the southern Baltic shore, and meltwater pooled along it. A well-defined Baltic Ice Lake existed by 14,600 years ago. By 13,000 BC it stretched from southern Sweden to Estonia. It lasted until about 11,700 years ago, close to the start of the Holocene.

  <!-- late-108 -->

- **Meadowcroft Rockshelter and the pre-Clovis debate** — c. 16,000 years ago (15.924 ka)

  Radiocarbon dates suggest people used Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Pennsylvania from 16,000 years ago, possibly 19,000. That would put them there before the Clovis era. Critics suspect contamination by ancient carbon from local coal-bearing rock, though later tests support the early dates. Opinion stays split. A 2013 survey found that 38% of archaeologists accepted the dates and 20% rejected them.

  <!-- late-110 -->

- **Rising seas flood the Persian Gulf** — c. 15,000 years ago (15 ka)

  For most of the ice age, the Persian Gulf was a dry basin. About 15,000 years ago, seas swollen by melting ice sheets began to flood it. The filling was slow. Much of the Gulf floor was still dry 12,000 to 9,000 years ago. The modern marine Gulf took shape in the early Holocene, by about 6,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-113 -->

- **The Missoula floods scour the Scablands** — c. 15,000–13,000 years ago (15–13 ka)

  An ice dam on the Clark Fork River held back Glacial Lake Missoula, up to about 2,500 km³ of water. The dam kept failing and re-forming. Between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago it unleashed dozens of floods, about one every 55 years. The largest discharged about 10 km³ an hour. It swept across eastern Washington and into Oregon's Willamette Valley. Together the floods stripped about 210 km³ of loess, sediment and basalt from the land, carving the Channeled Scablands.

  <!-- late-112 -->

  *Figure: The ice dam failed and re-formed again and again, releasing dozens of floods.* (cycle; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Altai megaflood** — c. 15,000–12,000 years ago (15–12 ka)

  Near the end of the last glaciation, glaciers in the Altai Mountains dammed the Chuya River. A large lake, holding up to 600 km³, filled the Chuya and Kurai basins. According to some geomorphologists, it burst in cataclysmic floods down the Katun River. The floods left giant ripples in the ground, up to 18 m high.

  <!-- late-111 -->

- **Magdalenian hunters return to the north** — c. 15,000 years ago (14.924 ka)

  The Magdalenian reindeer hunters, 21,000 to 13,000 years ago, descended mainly from Gravettian groups who had sheltered in southwestern Europe during the Last Glacial Maximum. Around 15,000 years ago, after the harsh Oldest Dryas, they moved north again. They reached Britain and, eastward, Poland. From about 14,000 years ago, Western Hunter-Gatherers linked to the Epigravettian spread north across the Alps and largely replaced them.

  <!-- late-115 -->

- **The cave lion dies out** — c. 14,900–12,900 years ago (14.924–12.924 ka)

  Cave lions vanished almost at once across their whole range, about 15,000 to 14,000 years ago. In North America they hung on roughly 1,000 years longer. They were already weakened. A population bottleneck between 47,000 and 18,000 years ago, probably driven partly by unstable climate, had cut their genetic diversity. The final cause is unknown. Climate change, shrinking prey and competition with other carnivores and humans have all been suggested.

  <!-- late-114 -->

- **The Antarctic Cold Reversal** — c. 14,700–13,000 years ago (14.7–13 ka)

  While the north warmed, the far south turned cold. Between 14,700 and 13,000 years ago, the Southern Hemisphere south of 40° S saw intense cooling of air and ocean. Temperatures fell, carbon dioxide stopped rising and glaciers advanced again, as in New Zealand's Southern Alps. Tasmania records a matching cold spell. A meltwater pulse, probably from the Antarctic or Laurentide ice sheet, is thought to have caused it. It may have pushed the southern polar front north and brought more rain and snow to the Andes. After about 13,000 years ago warming resumed, and glaciers pulled back abruptly from the moraines they had built.

  <!-- late-116 -->

- **The Bølling–Allerød warming** — c. 14,700–12,900 years ago (14.69–12.89 ka)

  About 14,690 years ago, the Northern Hemisphere warmed abruptly. This was the start of the Bølling–Allerød interstadial, a warm interval that lasted until about 12,890 years ago. Greenland's NorthGRIP ice core records the onset at 14,600 years ago, and methane in the air rose about 14,700 years ago. The engine was the ocean. A stronger Atlantic overturning circulation carried heat north. Meanwhile the Southern Hemisphere cooled, as told in The Antarctic Cold Reversal. This tug-of-war, with one hemisphere warming as the other cools, is called the 'polar seesaw'. By the Allerød phase, temperatures in the northern Atlantic had climbed almost to present-day levels. The warmth reopened the north. People spread back across Eurasia from the refuges where they had sheltered during the glacial peak. In Beringia, shrub tundra replaced dry steppe after 14,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-117 -->

  *Figure: The polar seesaw at the Bølling–Allerød.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Stronger Atlantic overturning] --> B[Heat carried north]
  B --> C[North warms]
  A --> D[South cools]
  ```

- **Meltwater pulse 1A: the fastest sea-level rise** — c. 14,600–14,300 years ago (14.65–14.3 ka)

  In about 400 to 500 years, global sea level rose 16 to 25 m. That is roughly 40 to 60 mm a year, the fastest known rate of rise since the ice age. This surge, meltwater pulse 1A, is blamed on the rapid collapse of continental ice sheets. It began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice. The West Antarctic ice sheet shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt rise around 14,500 years ago. Of all the named meltwater pulses, it is the most widely recognized and least disputed.

  <!-- late-118 -->

- **The African humid period begins** — c. 14,600–14,500 years ago (14.6–14.5 ka)

  Lake Victoria was dry around 15,000 years ago. Then North Africa turned wetter, about 14,600 to 14,500 years ago, as Heinrich event 1 ended and the Bølling–Allerød warming began. Summer sunshine at least 4% stronger than today's, aided by changes in plants, dust and greenhouse gases, strengthened the African monsoon. Lake Victoria refilled and overflowed. Lakes Albert and Tana spilled into the White and Blue Nile, and the Nile took its current form about 15,000 years ago. Lakes such as Lake Chad formed or grew, glaciers grew on Kilimanjaro, and the Sahara shrank.

  <!-- late-119 -->

- **Monte Verde, a camp at the end of the Americas** — c. 14,000 years ago (14.5 ka)

  In southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago, people built a tent-like structure about 20 feet long from wood and animal hides. This settlement, Monte Verde II, is one of the widely accepted sites older than Clovis. Its people were probably territorial, living in their river basin most of the year alongside late Pleistocene megafauna.

  <!-- late-120 -->

- **The Natufians settle down before farming** — c. 14,400–11,400 years ago (14.45–11.45 ka)

  People in the Levant settled into villages before they farmed. The Natufian culture, radiocarbon-dated to 12,500 to 9,500 BC, supported sedentary or semi-sedentary communities. Its settlements were larger and more permanent than earlier ones. Some had round stone buildings, as at Ain Mallaha, and they hold the first evidence of food storage. Natufians harvested wild cereals and hunted gazelles. Then the cold, dry Younger Dryas pushed early settled groups back toward a more mobile life.

  <!-- late-121 -->

- **Paisley Caves and the oldest DNA in North America** — c. 14,000 years ago (14.3 ka)

  Fossilized human dung from Oregon's Paisley Caves, radiocarbon dated to about 14,300 to 14,400 years ago, holds the oldest human DNA found in North America. The DNA ties these pre-Clovis people to Siberia or Asia. They ate plants, seeds, rodents, fish and insects. Critics question whether the coprolites are human and whether their dates hold. They suspect that human DNA leached into them later.

  <!-- late-122 -->

- **The Great Lakes basins begin to fill** — c. 14,000 years ago (14 ka)

  The Great Lakes sit in holes the ice dug. Around 14,000 years ago, retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved, and meltwater filled them. In Wisconsin, too, the ice began to retreat about then as the climate warmed.

  <!-- late-123 -->

- **The Older Dryas cold snap** — c. 14,000 years ago (14 ka)

  Between the warm Bølling and Allerød phases, about 14,000 years ago, came a brief cold stadial, the Older Dryas. Its dates vary by about 400 years between methods, but it lasted only a century or two. Ice advanced again in places, as in the Littleton–Bethlehem readvance and Canada's Shulie Lake phase.

  <!-- late-124 -->

- **The Americas lose their megafauna** — c. 13,800–11,400 years ago (13.8–11.4 ka)

  Every mammal over 1,000 kg in the Americas disappeared. About 72% of North American and 83% of South American megafaunal species died out. In North America the losses clustered around 13,800 to 11,400 years ago, with the onset of the Younger Dryas and the Clovis culture. Across the Americas they spanned 3,000 years at most. Ground sloths, litopterns and the last notoungulates vanished from the mainland around 12,000 years ago, along with most other large mammals. People did hunt them. Butchered bones, such as an Ohio ground sloth dated 13,738 to 13,435 years ago, prove it. Whether hunting, climate change or both caused the extinctions is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least some human role. The loss even touched the air. Without the American megafauna, methane production is estimated to have fallen by about 9.6 million tons a year.

  <!-- late-127 -->

  *Figure: South America lost an even larger share of its megafaunal species than North America.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **An ice-free corridor opens east of the Rockies** — c. 14,000 years ago (13.724 ± 0.5 ka)

  By 21,000 years ago, the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets had merged east of the Rocky Mountains, closing the way into North America's interior. A gap between them opened about 13,800 ± 500 years ago, by 2022 estimates. Older studies put it at 13,000 to 12,000 years ago. Either way, that is later than the earliest widely accepted archaeological sites. The corridor could not have carried the first people south.

  <!-- late-128 -->

- **The Clovis culture spreads across North America** — c. 13,000–12,800 years ago (13.05–12.75 ka)

  At Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, stone tools lay among the bones of Columbian mammoths. This is the type site of the Clovis culture, which spanned about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago. Its hallmark was the fluted Clovis point, a large leaf-shaped spear point also used for cutting. Clovis people were mobile hunter-gatherers who relied on big game, especially mammoths. They may have contributed to the megafauna extinctions, a controversial idea. They were not the first Americans. A 2022 study found the ice-free corridor impassable until about 13,800 years ago, long after people had reached lands south of the ice. From about 12,750 to 12,600 years ago, Clovis gave way to regional cultures such as Folsom.

  <!-- late-129 -->

- **The Laacher See eruption** — 13,000 years ago (13.006 ± 0.009 ka)

  About 13,006 years ago, a VEI 6 eruption in western Germany, comparable to Pinatubo in 1991, expelled about 6 km³ of magma. It left the crater lake of Laacher See. Its ash dammed the Rhine into a lake of 140 km². When that dam broke, the outburst flood left deposits as far as Bonn. Research in the 1990s proposed it as the trigger of the Younger Dryas. But it came more than a century before that cold spell began.

  <!-- late-130 -->

- **Lake Agassiz, the giant meltwater lake** — c. 13,000 years ago (13 ka)

  At its greatest extent, Lake Agassiz may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today and about the area of the Black Sea. Fed by meltwater from the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet, it spread over parts of Manitoba, Ontario, Minnesota, North Dakota and Saskatchewan around 13,000 years ago. From about 13,500 years ago it overflowed south through Glacial River Warren toward the Mississippi. At times it drained east to Lake Superior or northwest to the Arctic. Its huge freshwater releases are thought to have disrupted ocean circulation and affected climate and sea level. One drainage, about 13,000 years ago, has long been the most supported explanation for the The Younger Dryas: one last cold snap.

- **The Champlain Sea floods the St. Lawrence** — c. 13,000–10,000 years ago (13–10 ka)

  The ice was gone, but the land it had pressed down was still low. About 13,000 years ago rising seas flooded the St. Lawrence and Ottawa valleys, forming the Champlain Sea. About 12,000 years ago, the ice dam holding Lake Vermont failed. The lake dropped 91 m within hours or days before salt water swept in. As the land slowly rebounded, the sea shrank, lasting until about 10,000 years ago.

  <!-- late-131 -->

- **Hunter-gatherers reach Cyprus** — c. 13,000–12,000 years ago (12.95–11.95 ka)

  Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 11,000 to 10,000 BC. The Aetokremnos site may record their hunting of the island's dwarf hippos and dwarf elephants. They also brought wild boar to the island, around 12,000 years ago. Cyprus's dwarf elephant and pygmy hippopotamus later vanished. The genet Genetta plesictoides died out after humans and invasive species arrived.

  <!-- late-133 -->

- **The Irish elk's brief return** — c. 13,000 years ago (12.924 ka)

  The Irish elk, a giant deer, almost vanished during the Last Glacial Maximum. Few remains date between 27,500 and 14,600 years ago, and none between 23,300 and 17,500. In the warm Bølling–Allerød it recolonized northern Europe. Most Irish remains date to the Allerød, around 13,000 years ago. Then the Younger Dryas cold shrank its range again. By the end of that period, it had vanished from northern Europe.

  <!-- late-134 -->

- **Pygmy mammoths of the Channel Islands** — c. 13,000 years ago (12.924 ka)

  Columbian mammoths that reached California's Channel Islands shrank into pygmy mammoths, under half the mainland size. They lived there from 80,000 to 13,000 years ago. Their youngest records, about 13,000 years old, coincide with three changes: rising seas shrinking the islands, declining conifer forests and the first people. The people of Arlington Springs Man, on Santa Rosa Island, are thought to have hunted them. Whether climate or hunting mattered more is debated.

  <!-- late-135 -->

- **The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis** — c. 13,000 years ago (12.9 ka)

  In 2007 Richard Firestone and colleagues proposed a dramatic cause for the The Younger Dryas: one last cold snap. A comet or meteor impact or airburst about 12,900 years ago, they argued, disrupted Atlantic circulation and also killed off the megafauna. It remains a fringe hypothesis. Most relevant experts reject it for lack of clear evidence. The Hiawatha crater, once linked to it, proved to be 58 million years old.

  <!-- late-137 -->

- **The Younger Dryas: one last cold snap** — c. 12,900–11,700 years ago (12.9–11.7 ka)

  In Greenland, the temperature fell by up to 10 °C, and the cooling took three years or less. The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, was the last cold phase of the Last Glacial Period, a return to glacial conditions. Annual temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America and 2 to 6 °C in Europe. Scientists agree on the mechanism: a severe weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, the current that carries heat north. What triggered that weakening is less certain. A meltwater flood from Lake Agassiz and a volcanic trigger are both proposed. The effects rippled worldwide. The Southern Hemisphere warmed, drought hit the region of the African humid period, and lakes on the Altiplano reached a peak. Then it ended as rapidly as it began. Dramatic warming over about 50 years closed the cold spell, and with it the Pleistocene.

  <!-- late-136 -->
