- **Arctodus, the short-faced bear, dies out** — c. 13,000 years ago (12.724 ka)

  Arctodus simus averaged about 625 kg and could reach 957 kg, making it one of the largest land carnivorans ever. It ranged across North America. It vanished from Beringia about 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum, possibly from sharp cooling tied to Heinrich event 2. Elsewhere it lasted until about 12,800 years ago. Plant changes that cut its food supply and competition with brown bears are suggested causes, though the debate continues.

  <!-- late-138 -->

- **The last scimitar-toothed cats** — c. 12,700 years ago (12.715–12.655 ka)

  Homotherium, a lion-sized cat with long, flat, blade-like fangs, weighed up to about 250 kg. For some 4 million years it had lived across North America, Eurasia and Africa. Its youngest well-dated remains, from southern Alberta, are about 12,715 to 12,655 years old. With Smilodon, it was among the last of the saber-toothed machairodonts. Its extinction, like Smilodon's, has been linked to the loss of the big prey it relied on, such as mammoths, bison and horses. Whether climate or hunting drove those losses is debated.

  <!-- late-139 -->

- **The last Columbian mammoths** — c. 12,700–12,100 years ago (12.705–12.124 ka)

  Bigger than the woolly mammoth, the Columbian mammoth stood up to 4.2 m tall and weighed up to 12.5 tonnes. It ranged from southern Canada to Costa Rica. Its latest calibrated date, from Colorado's Dent site, is 12,705 to 12,124 years ago, as the Younger Dryas began. No survivors into the Holocene are recorded. Clovis people hunted or scavenged it. Its extinction is blamed on habitat loss from climate change, on human hunting, or on both.

  <!-- late-140 -->

- **Lake Lahontan at its highest** — c. 13,000 years ago (12.7 ka)

  About 12,700 years ago, Lake Lahontan covered over 22,000 km² of the Great Basin, centered on today's Carson Sink. At this Sehoo highstand it was about 270 m deep near Pyramid Lake. It was one of North America's largest lakes of the last glacial period. Then the changing climate at the end of the Pleistocene began to dry it out.

  <!-- late-141 -->

- **Castoroides, the giant beaver, dies out** — c. 12,000–11,500 years ago (12.05–11.501 ka)

  A beaver the size of a bear, weighing about 90 to 125 kg, once lived in North America. Castoroides was the largest known beaver and the continent's largest Pleistocene rodent. It vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago. Its last populations lived in the lowlands south of the Great Lakes. The youngest specimens, from New York, date to about 12,050 to 11,501 years ago, overlapping Paleo-Indian artifacts by up to a thousand years.

  <!-- late-142 -->

- **Pica glass in the Atacama** — c. 12,000 years ago (12 ka)

  Patches of natural glass lie in the Atacama Desert, dated to about 12,000 years ago. Where Pica glass came from is unsettled. One account blames a surge in wildfires. A list of possible impact structures counts it as an inferred impact whose crater has not been found.

  <!-- late-144 -->

- **Macrauchenia, among the last litopterns** — c. 12,000 years ago (11.924 ka)

  Macrauchenia was a long-necked hoofed mammal and one of the last of the Litopterna, an order native to South America for over 60 million years. It died out around 12,000 years ago with most large mammals of the Americas. People had reached South America at least 14,500 years ago. At Paso Otero 5 in the Argentine Pampas, its burned bones lie with Fishtail spear points among other extinct megafauna. Whether hunting or climate change caused its end is debated.

  <!-- late-145 -->

##### Holocene Epoch

About 11,700 years ago, the cold of the Younger Dryas broke, and with it the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene ended. The abrupt warming set the remaining ice sheets of North America and Europe melting fast, and the sea jumped about 60 m in the early Holocene. Mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands took over the vast mammoth steppe, and many of its giant animals died out. In the Fertile Crescent, people began growing crops and herding animals. This last stretch of the course is the world people built their history in.

###### Greenlandian Age

The Greenlandian is the opening age of the Holocene, a time of melting ice and rising water. It began when the Younger Dryas cold spell ended about 11,700 years ago, and the warming set the last northern ice sheets collapsing. Sea level jumped about 60 m between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, while a stronger African monsoon pushed rain far north into the Sahara. Megafauna kept dying out, and in the Fertile Crescent people began to farm and herd. At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised stone pillars near the time of the first permanent settlements.

- **Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent** — c. 12,000 years ago (11.7 ka)

  Barley was among the first crops: it was domesticated in the Near East around 11,000 years ago. The warming from 11.7 ka coincides with the earliest farming in the Fertile Crescent. In that arc of land, crop growing and herding opened the Neolithic, the farming phase of the Stone Age. Its first farmers tamed sheep, goats, cattle and later pigs, along with cereals such as wheat and barley, and legumes. Domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP. Between 8500 and 7000 BC people across the region took up the systematic husbandry of plants and animals. The new way of life also travelled by sea: Neolithic settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BC. A milder climate after The Younger Dryas ends and the Holocene begins made the change possible, and from here it spread, as Farming rises far beyond the Fertile Crescent shows.

  <!-- gree-004 -->

- **The Younger Dryas ends and the Holocene begins** — 12,000 years ago (11.7 ka)

  Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years. The jump came in three steps of five years each. It ended the Younger Dryas, a cold spell that began about 12,800 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. Its close also closed the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene, and opened the Holocene, the epoch people still live in. Geologists mark that boundary with a GSSP, a reference point fixed in rock or ice. Here it is a sample in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, matched to the end of the Younger Dryas and ratified in 2008. After the sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian. Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since. In the American Southwest, the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

  <!-- gree-005 -->

  *Figure: Follow the chain from the end of the Younger Dryas to the start of the Holocene.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Younger Dryas cold spell] -->|ends| B[Greenland warms about 8 °C]
  B --> C[Last Glacial Period and Pleistocene close]
  C --> D[Holocene interglacial begins]
  D --> E[Gentler warming through the Greenlandian]
  ```

- **Forest and wetland swallow the mammoth steppe** — c. 12,000 years ago (11.7 ka)

  Forests replaced much of the open habitat of the large grazers as the climate turned warmer and wetter. At the start of the Holocene, mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands displaced the vast mammoth steppe, the cold grassland that had fed mammoths and their neighbors. Higher temperatures and rainfall shrank that habitat, fragmenting animal populations and then driving them extinct. By about 10,000 years ago, patches of closed larch and pine forest had developed in northern Siberia. Only then did forbs, the flowering herbs that grazers ate, decline, as woody plants and grasses came to dominate.

  <!-- gree-006 -->

- **Ice Age wolf lineages collapse** — c. 12,000 years ago (11.7 ka)

  The wolves that howl today are not the wolves of the Ice Age. At the start of the Holocene, ancient wolves in Alaska, Siberia and Europe lost most of their genetic diversity, and they overlap little with modern wolves. In North America a population bottleneck almost erased ancient wolf diversity. One line held on far to the east: the Japanese wolf turned out to be the last of the Siberian Pleistocene wolves.

  <!-- gree-008 -->

- **The Baltic Ice Lake gives way to the Yoldia Sea** — c. 11,700–10,700 years ago (11.7–10.7 ka)

  The Baltic Ice Lake ended close to the start of the Holocene. Its level fell to sea level, letting salt water flow into the basin and opening the Yoldia Sea stage, about 11,700–10,700 years BP. Pine and birch pollen rose sharply around the basin from 11,500 BP, a sign of trees moving in. People followed: they lived on its Estonian shores by 11,200–10,200 BP. Next came The Ancylus Lake fills the Baltic basin.

  <!-- gree-001 -->

- **The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene** — during the Greenlandian, 11,700–8,200 years ago (11.7–8.2 ka)

  From the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene, most animals over 45 kg vanished, including 80% of those over a tonne. Faunal density and diversity collapsed. Many megafauna species died out during the Greenlandian itself, keeping up the extinction rate of the end of the Late Pleistocene. In the Colombian Andes, spores of dung fungi, which thrive on the droppings of big grazers, record a second wave of extinction around 10,990 BP. Climate change is one main explanation, and human activity is the other. The balance between them is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least some human role. Human activity is also blamed for the ongoing Holocene extinction, which began roughly 10,000 years ago.

  <!-- gree-007 -->

  *Figure: Two proposed causes feed the extinctions; how much each mattered is still argued.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Climate change] --> C[Megafauna extinctions]
  B[Human activity] -.->|debated share| C
  C --> D[Faunal density and diversity collapse]
  ```

- **The early Holocene sea rises 60 meters** — c. 11,700–4,200 years ago (11.7–4.2 ka)

  Between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, sea level jumped about 60 m. The water came from the continental ice sheets as they melted away, as Northern ice sheets melt fast describes, and the rise ran fastest while they melted. Background rates of about 6–10 mm a year were broken by brief bursts of 30–60 mm a year. Then the pace slackened, from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm a year by 4,200 years ago. The rising water drowned vast lowlands and turned parts of continents into islands. It cut off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania from the lands they had joined, a story told in Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea and Rising seas cut off Tasmania and New Guinea. Along Brazil's Bahia coast, mangroves followed the shoreline and spread inland as the sea rose. The modern map of coasts and straits is largely the work of these few thousand years.

  <!-- gree-003 -->

  *Figure: Rates of early Holocene sea-level rise, from the fastest bursts to the slow pace reached by 4,200 years ago.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Northern ice sheets melt fast** — 11,700 years ago (c. 9700 BCE)

  Most of the ice-sheet melting and sea-level rise of the last deglaciation came after about 11,000 years ago. The trigger was the abrupt warming that opened the Holocene, around 9700 BC, which set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets in North America and Europe. An ice sheet's surface mass balance is its yearly gain of snow minus its loss to melting. For the Laurentide ice sheet it turned negative only in the early Holocene, once radiative forcing and summer temperatures rose. In northern British Columbia, the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away by about 11,000 years ago. Later, from 8,500 BP, ice pouring from the collapsing Laurentide ice sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic.

  <!-- gree-009 -->

- **Meltwater pulse 1B: a burst that may not have been** — c. 11,500–11,200 years ago (9550 BCE–9250 BCE)

  Barbados coral cores were once read as a 28 m rise in sea level in about 500 years around 11,300 years ago. That reading made Meltwater pulse 1B, a proposed burst of rapid post-glacial sea-level rise between 11,500 and 11,200 years ago, look dramatic. One study put it at 13 m in 300 years, about 40 mm a year; others cut it to 7.5 m or less than 6 m. A peak in Antarctic iceberg discharge about 11,300 years ago suggests Antarctica contributed significantly. Yet some researchers found at best a modest speed-up. Its size, and even its existence, are still debated.

  <!-- gree-010 -->

  *Figure: Published estimates of the pulse's size differ several-fold.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Hunter-gatherers raise the pillars of Göbekli Tepe** — c. 11,500–9,950 years ago (9500 BCE–8000 BCE)

  Göbekli Tepe, in Upper Mesopotamia in today's Turkey, was built around 9500 BCE and used until about 8000 BCE. Its circular enclosures hold large stone pillars, among the oldest known megaliths, many carved with reliefs of wild animals. The early circles date to c. 9000 BCE. Its builders were not farmers but hunter-gatherers, who hunted gazelle and ground much cereal. Sources differ on whether any of that cereal was domesticated.

  <!-- gree-011 -->

- **The Sahara turns green** — 11,000 years ago (c. 9050 BCE)

  From 11,000 years ago, a giant Lake Mega-Chad covered more than 350,000 km² of the Chad Basin. The cause lay in Earth's orbit. Between 11,000 and 10,000 BP, perihelion, the point where Earth passes closest to the Sun, fell at the June solstice. That raised summer sunlight by about 8% and pushed a stronger African monsoon farther north. Grasses, trees and lakes covered much of the Sahara, in a humid period that had begun about 14,600 years ago. Lake Kivu began overflowing into Lake Tanganyika by about 10,500 BP, and lakes formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago. People moved into the greening desert: Takarkori was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

  <!-- gree-015 -->

  *Figure: How a shift in Earth's orbit turned the Sahara green.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Perihelion at June solstice] --> B[Summer sunlight up about 8%]
  B --> C[Stronger African monsoon pushes north]
  C --> D[Grasses, trees and lakes in the Sahara]
  C --> E[Lake Mega-Chad]
  ```

- **Lake Algonquin floods the upper Great Lakes** — 11,000 years ago (c. 9050 BCE)

  Glacial Lake Algonquin first flooded about 11,000 years before present, filling the basin of the upper Great Lakes with meltwater. By then the Laurentide ice front had pulled back to the northern edges of Lakes Superior and Huron. The lake was a passing stage in the long retreat of that ice, described in Northern ice sheets melt fast.

  <!-- gree-016 -->

- **South America's last notoungulates die out** — 11,000 years ago (c. 9050 BCE)

  An order of hoofed mammals found only in South America lasted some 61 million years and then was gone. Notoungulata lived from about 61 million to 11,000 years ago. The order included Toxodon, a rhinoceros-sized grazer, which belongs among the late victims of the extinctions described in The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene.

  <!-- gree-017 -->

- **North America loses its sloths, horses and short-faced bears** — 11,000 years ago (c. 9050 BCE)

  In Arizona's Rampart Cave, dung of the Shasta ground sloth built up from 13,000 BP and then stopped suddenly at 11,000 BP. Around that time the last giant ground sloths died out in North America, short-faced bears vanished, and all native horses disappeared. Horses had evolved largely in North America; they died out there and were reintroduced only in the 15th century. Of the continent's odd-toed hoofed mammals, only Baird's tapir, reaching into southern Mexico, survived. Ground sloths did not vanish everywhere. On Caribbean islands they lingered until about 4,000 years ago, as The Caribbean's last ground sloths tells.

  <!-- gree-018 -->

- **Wakamiko Caldera erupts in southern Japan** — c. 11,000–9,000 years ago (9050 BCE–7050 BCE)

  Some time between 9050 and 7050 BCE, Wakamiko Caldera, nested inside Kyushu's Aira Caldera, produced an eruption of about 12 km³. It rates VEI 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the scale that ranks eruptions by the volume they throw out. The date range is wide, but the blast was among the large ones of the early Holocene.

  <!-- gree-019 -->

- **Glyptodon and its armored kin die out** — 10,900 years ago (c. 8970 BCE)

  Glyptodon, a giant plant-eating relative of the armadillo, had lived in South America since about 3.2 million years ago, and died out around 11,000 years ago. A wetter post-glacial climate replaced C3 grasses with C4 grasses and southern beech, killing off grazing specialists such as glyptodonts and toxodonts. Human hunting may also have contributed. Its relatives Doedicurus and Panochthus held on, on the Argentine Pampas into the early Holocene, living alongside people for at least 4,000 years.

  <!-- gree-021 -->

- **The first livestock: goats, sheep, pigs and cattle** — c. 10,900–9,920 years ago (8974 BCE–7974 BCE)

  By 10,000 years ago, hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed. That simple choice marks the slide from hunting to herding. Zooarchaeology is the study of animal remains from human sites. It shows that goats, pigs, sheep and taurine cattle were the first livestock, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago. The earliest dates in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs and c. 8000 BCE for cattle. The milder climate after the Younger Dryas made it possible. Domestication began a rapid shift in the evolution, ecology and demography of people and of many animal and plant species. It brought a cost too: in Eurasia, domestic animals overtook other primates as the main source of new human infections.

  <!-- gree-020 -->

  *Figure: The earliest dates for each kind of livestock in northern Mesopotamia.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Ancylus Lake fills the Baltic basin** — c. 10,700–9,800 years ago (8750 BCE–7850 BCE)

  After The Baltic Ice Lake gives way to the Yoldia Sea, the land itself rose. Post-glacial uplift cut off the Baltic basin and turned it into the freshwater Ancylus Lake, from about 10,700 to 9,800 years BP. The growing lake forced people on the former Yoldia shore near Pärnu to retreat inland. It drained to the sea through the Dana River between 10,200 and 9,800 BP, and salt water began entering at 9,800 BP.

  <!-- gree-023 -->

  *Figure: The Baltic basin switched between fresh and salt water as ice melted and land rose.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Yoldia Sea] -->|post-glacial uplift| B[Ancylus Lake, fresh water]
  B -->|drains via Dana River| C[Salt water enters, 9,800 BP]
  ```

- **The last mainland woolly mammoths** — 10,000 years ago (c. 8050 BCE)

  Trackways at St. Mary Reservoir in Canada show a mammoth herd of adults, subadults and young still roaming there 11,300–11,000 years ago. Within a few thousand years the mainland herds were gone. In Eurasia, cold-adapted giants such as the woolly mammoth and woolly rhinoceros were generally the last of the megafauna to go, around 10,000 BP. The youngest European remains come from the Southern Urals, 9650 BCE, and Cherepovets in Russia, 9290–9180 BCE. The youngest mainland fossils of all, from Siberia's Kyttyk Peninsula, are 9,650 years old. A small population lived on much longer on Wrangel Island, as The last mammoths die on Wrangel Island tells.

  <!-- gree-031 -->

- **The modern coyote appears** — 10,000 years ago (c. 8050 BCE)

  Not every Ice Age lineage ended in extinction. The modern coyote appeared around 10,000 years ago, most likely descended from the Pleistocene coyote. It came through the great die-off described in The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene as a smaller, newer form of an old line.

  <!-- gree-033 -->

- **The last woolly rhinoceroses** — c. 10,000–9,600 years ago (8050 BCE–7650 BCE)

  The youngest woolly rhinoceros bones, from the Southern Urals, date to 9450 BCE. Its DNA lingered later in the ground: it was last detected in permafrost near Russia's Kolyma River, dated to 8050–7650 BCE. Its range had shrunk toward Siberia from 17,000 years ago. Its loss was part of the end-Pleistocene event that wiped out most large land animals.

  <!-- gree-032 -->

- **Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea** — c. 10,000–7,000 years ago (8050 BCE–5050 BCE)

  Britain was once not an island. In the early Holocene, a lowland called Doggerland linked eastern Britain to northern France, the Low Countries, north-west Germany and Jutland. Most evidence of people living there dates to the Mesolithic, the hunter-gatherer age before farming. By 9000 BCE a large tidal bay had formed between eastern England and Dogger Bank, and rapid sea-level rise followed. Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago the rising sea broke Doggerland into low islands and then submerged it completely. Dogger Bank became an island, and Britain was finally cut off from the European mainland around 6500 BCE.

  <!-- gree-028 -->

- **Farming rises far beyond the Fertile Crescent** — c. 10,000–7,000 years ago (8050 BCE–5050 BCE)

  Drainage ditches at Kuk Swamp in highland New Guinea show taro and other crops cultivated by about 11,000 BP, perhaps by 8000 BCE. The Near East was not the only cradle of farming. Between 10,000 and 7,000 BP, plants and animals were rapidly domesticated in tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa and Central America. Maize was domesticated in Mesoamerica from about 7000 BCE, and rice in the Far East. Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's earliest Neolithic site with wheat, barley and herding, is dated variously from 8500 to 6500 BCE. Cereal farming and herding reached the eastern Sahara by about 7000 BC.

  <!-- gree-029 -->

- **The Bering land bridge floods** — 10,000 years ago (c. 8000 BCE)

  Around 8000 BCE, rising seas flooded the Beringian land bridge and closed the main migration route from Siberia. The drowning formed the Bering Strait and separated Asia from the Americas. The date is not settled. Estimates from Bering Strait depths and the global sea-level curve alone put the final drowning earlier, around 11,000 years BP. Either way, the flood was part of the rise described in The early Holocene sea rises 60 meters.

  <!-- gree-035 -->

- **The Scandinavian ice sheet melts away** — 9,700 years ago (c. 7750 BCE)

  The Scandinavian ice sheet withdrew into the mountains as it shrank, leaving Russia by 10.6 ka and Finland by 10.1 ka. Its centre over southern Norway vanished about a thousand years after that. By 9.7 ka, the last remnant of the Fennoscandian ice sheet lay in the eastern Sarek Mountains. Freed of its weight, the land began to rise, as Scandinavia and Canada spring back describes.

  <!-- gree-038 -->

  *Figure: The ice sheet's retreat, from Russia to its last remnant in the Sarek Mountains.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Holocene Climatic Optimum begins** — c. 9,500–5,500 years ago (7550 BCE–3550 BCE)

  Northern Hemisphere heating peaked about 9,000 years ago, when Earth's axial tilt was 24° and perihelion fell in northern summer. That timing opened the Holocene Climatic Optimum, a warm period lasting roughly from 9,500 to 5,500 years BP. The warmth did not arrive everywhere at once. In New Zealand and Antarctica the warmest stretch, often called the Early Holocene Climatic Optimum, came earlier, roughly 10,500 to 8,000 years ago. The Amery Ice Shelf in Antarctica retreated about 80 km landward during that southern warm spell. North-western North America peaked 11,000–9,000 years ago, while the Laurentide ice sheet still chilled eastern Canada. The peak itself comes in The Holocene's warmest centuries.

  <!-- gree-039 -->

- **Sapropel S1 darkens the eastern Mediterranean floor** — c. 9,500–5,500 years ago (7550 BCE–3550 BCE)

  Between 9,500 and 5,500 years ago, the eastern Mediterranean laid down its latest sapropel, a dark, organic-rich mud that forms when bottom waters lose oxygen. This S1 layer is tied to the African humid period. Greater Nile and other river discharge freshened the sea, stratifying it and making it eutrophic. Sapropels recur about every 21,000 years, following Earth's orbital cycles. When Nile discharge fell, deposition off its delta stopped.

  <!-- gree-041 -->

- **Scandinavia and Canada spring back** — c. 9,500–5,000 years ago (7550 BCE–3050 BCE)

  Freed of ice, Scandinavia rose 9–13 mm a year between 9,500 and 5,000 years ago. Geologists call this post-glacial rebound, the slow rise of crust once a heavy ice sheet is gone. The movements triggered large earthquakes in Scandinavia about 9,000 years ago, forming postglacial faults. In Canada, the rising land drained the Champlain Sea by about 10,000 years ago. Hudson Bay, the Great Lakes and Fennoscandia are still rebounding.

  <!-- gree-040 -->

- **The last sabre-toothed Smilodon** — c. 9,080–8,190 years ago (7129 BCE–6239 BCE)

  The North American Smilodon fatalis ranged from Alberta to north-western South America, and its youngest remains date to 7615–7305 BCE. Its southern cousin held out a little longer. The youngest remains of Smilodon populator, at Itapipoca in Brazil, date to 7129–6239 BCE. With them, the last Smilodon species died out.

  <!-- gree-042 -->

- **The last American mastodons** — c. 9,060–8,760 years ago (7110 BCE–6810 BCE)

  Mastodons, mammoths and horses roamed North America as recently as 10,000 years ago. In Minnesota the giant animals were gone by about 9,000 years ago. The youngest remains of the American mastodon date to 7110–6810 BCE, among the last of the continent's Ice Age giants described in The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene.

  <!-- gree-043 -->

- **Today's Great Barrier Reef starts to grow** — 9,000 years ago (c. 7050 BCE)

  The living Great Barrier Reef is younger than it looks. It is believed to have begun growing on an older platform about 9,000 years ago, as the seas of The early Holocene sea rises 60 meters rose over the land.

  <!-- gree-044 -->

- **Pluvial Lake Lahontan dries up** — 9,000 years ago (c. 7050 BCE)

  By about 9,000 years ago, Lake Lahontan in the Great Basin had largely disappeared in its extended form. It was a pluvial lake, one fed by the wetter climate of the glacial age. Further south, tufa, a limestone crust laid down in lake water, at Lake Cahuilla records a wet period that ended 9,000 years before present.

  <!-- gree-045 -->

- **Did the Mediterranean pour into the Black Sea?** — 8,800 years ago (c. 6850 BCE)

  A catastrophic inflow of Mediterranean seawater is proposed to have flooded the Black Sea, which was then a freshwater lake. The idea is controversial. The flood was first dated to about 7,600 years ago, then redated in 2003 to 8,800 years ago, c. 6800 BCE. Other authors argue instead for a gradual inundation of the basin. Opponents point to water flowing out of the basin as late as 15,000 years ago, and to sill sediments building up from before 10,000 years ago. The question remains open.

  <!-- gree-046 -->

- **Kurile Lake caldera blasts Kamchatka** — c. 8,410–8,360 years ago (6460 BCE–6414 BCE)

  Ash from one eruption in Kamchatka fell up to 1,700 km away. In 6460–6414 BCE a very large eruption formed the present Kurile Lake caldera and its ignimbrite, a rock welded from hot volcanic ash flows. Rated VEI 7, it produced about 155 km³ of material. Two sulfate spikes in Greenland's GISP2 ice core, around 6470 and 6476 BC, may record it. It ranks with Fisher, Kikai and Mazama among the largest eruptions around the Pacific Ring of Fire, during an especially active spell in 6600–6400 BCE.

  <!-- gree-049 -->

###### Northgrippian Age

The Northgrippian opens with a shock: global temperatures dropped abruptly around 8,200 years ago, as Lake Agassiz drained almost completely. Off Norway, three submarine landslides moved about 3,500 km³ of debris, among the largest known. Then the warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, as the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split and rising seas made Tasmania an island. William Ruddiman argues that early farmers clearing forest began raising greenhouse gases about this time. The age closes with eruptions such as Mount Mazama's, whose collapse left the caldera of Crater Lake.

- **The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap** — 8,200 years ago (c. 6250 BCE)

  In Greenland, the temperature fell 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years. Around 8,200 years ago global temperatures dropped abruptly, and the cool spell lasted two to four centuries; its coldest phase lasted about 60 years. The likely cause was a flood of fresh water. A meltwater pulse, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway draining into the North Atlantic, may have weakened Atlantic overturning by 55–62%. That overturning is the ocean circulation that carries warm surface water north, so slowing it chilled the lands around the Atlantic. The event shows up far beyond the North Atlantic. Cave records from Eurasia to South America and southern Africa show it. Methane fell 15%, and North and East Africa turned drier. Its signal in the NGRIP1 Greenland ice core is the GSSP for the base of the Northgrippian, set at 8,236 years before 2000. The drainage itself is told in Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway drain into the sea.

  <!-- nort-001 -->

  *Figure: The likely chain behind the 8.2-kiloyear cooling.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Agassiz and Ojibway drain] --> B[Meltwater into North Atlantic]
  B -.-> C[Overturning weakens]
  C --> D[Abrupt cooling]
  ```

- **Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway drain into the sea** — 8,200 years ago (c. 6250 BCE)

  The final drainage of one giant North American lake raised global sea level by an estimated 0.8 to 2.8 m. As the last ice over Hudson Bay melted, Lake Agassiz drained almost completely in its final major drainage shift. Neighbouring Lake Ojibway, comparable in size, likely drained at the same time, perhaps in two floods through a broken ice dam and beneath the ice. This freshwater flood is the leading suspected trigger of The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap. The lake had a long history before its end. It refilled as the ice withdrew north of today's Canada–US border around 10,000 years ago, and abandoned its southern outlet by about 9400 BP.

  <!-- nort-002 -->

  *Figure: Melting ice let the lakes drain, and the flood is the leading suspect for the 8.2 ka cooling.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Last Hudson Bay ice melts] --> B[Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway drain]
  B --> C[Sea level up 0.8 to 2.8 m]
  B -.->|leading suspect| D[8.2-kiloyear cooling]
  ```

- **The Storegga Slides send a tsunami across the North Atlantic** — c. 8,180–8,120 years ago (6225 BCE–6170 BCE)

  Tsunami sand in Scotland lies up to 29 km inland and 4 m above today's normal tide level. It came from Norway. There, three submarine landslides at the edge of the continental shelf moved about 3,500 km³ of debris along 290 km of shelf, among the largest known. An earthquake that destabilised methane clathrate, an icy solid that traps methane in seabed mud, is thought to have triggered the collapse. The slides set off large tsunamis, and waves up to 20 m high hit Scotland and the Faroe Islands. The tsunami may also have flooded Doggerland's last low-lying land, though its impact there is debated.

  <!-- nort-004 -->

- **Did early farmers warm the planet?** — 8,000 years ago (c. 6050 BCE)

  Carbon dioxide rose markedly from about 8,000 years ago, and methane some 3,000 years later. William Ruddiman argues that forest clearing by early farmers caused that rise in greenhouse gases. If he is right, human influence on climate began long before industry. Other researchers challenge the idea. Critics counter with data from an earlier interglacial, and say all interglacials differ.

  <!-- nort-005 -->

- **The Holocene's warmest centuries** — 8,000 years ago (c. 6050 BCE)

  The warmest 200 years of the Holocene, around 6,500 years ago, were about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century. The climate had recovered from the cold snap of The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap and climbed to the highest temperatures of the epoch. The warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, and polar ice caps shrank to their Holocene minimum. Rain belts moved with the heat. Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo valley got up to twice today's rainfall, and a stable climate fostered farming in China. The peak did not last. The warmth was followed by a slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium until about two centuries ago, a long cooling traced in Neoglacial cooling sets in. Only the warming described in Rapid global warming since the mid-20th century broke that trend.

  <!-- nort-008 -->

- **The last steppe bison** — 8,000 years ago (c. 6050 BCE)

  The steppe bison, a grazer of the mammoth steppe, survived in north-central eastern Siberia until about 8,000 years ago. Traces may stretch later. Bison DNA in northeastern Siberian permafrost may extend its survival to 5050–3800 BCE. The youngest North American remains, from Yukon, date to 3628–3377 BCE.

  <!-- nort-009 -->

- **Menengai collapses in Kenya's Rift Valley** — 8,000 years ago (c. 6050 BCE)

  Menengai is a shield volcano, a broad, gently sloping cone, on the floor of Kenya's Rift Valley. About 8,000 years ago it collapsed to form its 12 × 8 km caldera, the bowl left when a volcano's summit falls in. The eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 70 km³ of material.

  <!-- nort-010 -->

- **Rising seas cut off Tasmania and New Guinea** — 8,000 years ago (c. 6050 BCE)

  Aboriginal Tasmanians had walked to their land across a land bridge about 40,000 years ago. Post-glacial sea-level rise then flooded the Bassian Plain, forming Bass Strait, making Tasmania an island and cutting its people off from the mainland. To the north, New Guinea separated from mainland Australia about 8,000 years ago, ending Sahul, the single landmass they had formed. The New Guinea land bridge was fully flooded by then. Over the next 2,000 years, thousands of Torres Strait and coastal islands formed.

  <!-- nort-011 -->

- **The Laurentide Ice Sheet's final collapse** — c. 8,000–6,500 years ago (6050 BCE–4550 BCE)

  Central Asia stayed at near-glacial temperatures until a North American ice sheet collapsed around 8,000 BP. About 8,000 years ago the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split into two lobes, over Quebec–Labrador and Keewatin. Its final melting came between 8 and 7 ka. After it, global sea level rose at a much slower rate. Ice discharge from the collapsing sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic until 6,700 BP. Ice finally left Nunavik about 6,500 years ago, ending the long retreat that began in Northern ice sheets melt fast.

  <!-- nort-006 -->

- **The Mississippi and Rhine deltas take shape** — 7,900 years ago (c. 5970 BCE)

  Deltas need a steady sea to grow. As sea-level rise slowed, the modern Mississippi River delta plain began to build around 8,000–7,500 years ago. In the Netherlands, the Holocene Rhine–Meuse delta began forming about 8,000 years ago, shaped by sea-level rise and tectonic subsidence. By switching course every 1,000–1,500 years, the Mississippi built six delta complexes. Such deltas became major farming and population centres.

  <!-- nort-012 -->

- **The last Irish elk** — 7,700 years ago (c. 5750 BCE)

  The Irish elk, or giant deer, survived in western Russia until around 7,700 years ago, as Ice Age megafauna losses continued. By the early Holocene its range had shrunk dramatically. Its youngest eastern records, near Lake Baikal, date to 10,700–10,400 BP. Its latest dated remains include finds at Kamyshlov and Maloarkhangelsk, Russia, from the 6th millennium BCE, and it likely died out soon after.

  <!-- nort-013 -->

- **Mount Mazama blows apart and leaves Crater Lake** — 7,700 years ago (c. 5750 BCE)

  A 48 km ash column reached the stratosphere when Oregon's Mount Mazama, active again after 20,000 quiet years, ended in a VEI 7 eruption. Its collapse left the caldera that now holds Crater Lake. The USGS has called it the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past million years. Ash fell across eight western US states and three Canadian provinces. The orange Mazama Ash covers at least 900,000 km² of the northern Great Plains and reaches Greenland's ice sheet, making it a standard dating marker. Its aerosols may have cooled mid- to high northern latitudes by 0.6–0.7 °C for one to three years. Ashfall drove people out, leaving one Alberta site empty for about 200 years.

  <!-- nort-014 -->

- **Farming spreads into Europe** — 7,500 years ago (c. 5550 BCE)

  Farming took about 2,500 years, 8500–6000 BP, to travel from the Aegean to Britain. It appears in the Aegean by c. 6500 BCE, and the Baltic followed around 5500 BP. Fast sea-level rise, the 8.2 ka cooling and loss of coastal land may have helped push this Neolithic Revolution into Europe. In Central Europe, human impact first shows in pollen records from 7,500 BP and becomes substantial after 6,300 BP. An Early Neolithic lakeshore village at La Marmotta, Italy, dates to about 5700 BC. From about 7,500 years ago, European Neolithic farmers also crossed from Iberia into Northwest Africa.

  <!-- nort-015 -->

- **Sundaland's last lowlands go under** — c. 7,500–6,200 years ago (5550 BCE–4250 BCE)

  The Gulf of Thailand was dry, arid land before 7,500 BP. A marine transgression, the sea advancing over land, drowned it from 7,500 to 6,200 BP. It was part of Sundaland, the exposed Sunda Shelf of Southeast Asia, flooded as rising seas followed the 8.2 ka cool period. Its partial submergence, under way since 18,000 years ago, continued until about 5000 BC.

  <!-- nort-016 -->

- **Megatherium, the giant ground sloth, dies out** — 7,300 years ago (c. 5370 BCE)

  Megatherium americanum was a ground sloth of up to 4 tonnes and 6 m long. It died out in Argentina around 5370 BC. Its latest remains, at Campo Laborde, show signs of human hunting and butchery. Habitat modelling suggests its suitable range had already shrunk and broken up by the mid-Holocene, so both people and a changing land may have played a part.

  <!-- nort-017 -->

- **Kikai-Akahoya: the Holocene's biggest eruption** — 7,300 years ago (c. 5350 BCE)

  Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of hot gas and ash, crossed the sea to reach southern Kyushu, up to 100 km away. They came from Japan's submarine Kikai Caldera, in the Akahoya eruption. It was a VEI 7 event, one of only six confirmed eruptions of its size in the Holocene. A 2024 study put the ejecta at 332–457 km³, the largest eruption of the past 11,700 years. Ash fell as far as Hokkaido. Two large earthquakes shook the region during the eruption, and a megatsunami left deposits along western Japan's coast up to 300 km away. It transformed southern Kyushu's vegetation and hit the early Jōmon culture there hard. Recovery took nearly 1,000 years, though local pottery traditions survived.

  <!-- nort-018 -->

- **The Ilumetsa craters in Estonia** — c. 7,170–7,000 years ago (5220 BCE–5050 BCE)

  Two probable meteorite craters, about 80 m and 50 m wide, formed together in southeastern Estonia. The word probable matters. No meteorite fragments or shock features have been found, so their impact origin is likely but not proven.

  <!-- nort-019 -->

- **Lake Mashū's caldera forms on Hokkaido** — 7,000 years ago (c. 5050 BCE)

  An eruption on Hokkaido created the caldera that now holds Lake Mashū. It is listed at VEI 6, with about 18.6 km³ of material. The sources round its date to around 7,000 years ago. The Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program gives a calibrated radiocarbon date of 5550 ± 100 BCE, about 500 years older.

  <!-- nort-020 -->

- **Neoglacial cooling sets in** — 6,000 years ago (c. 4050 BCE)

  About 6,000 years ago, the post-glacial warming trend ended and a long cooling trend began. This is Neoglaciation, the spell after The Holocene's warmest centuries when glaciers advanced or re-formed, though it has no single clear start. In East Asia its start coincided with a major weakening of the summer monsoon. In western North America, mountain glaciers that had melted away entirely re-formed shortly before 5000 BP. Orbital models suggest this cooling trend would continue for another 23,000 years.

  <!-- nort-022 -->

- **The sea stops rising** — 6,000 years ago (c. 4050 BCE)

  Global sea level had been rising steadily since 20,000 years ago. About 6,000 years ago it levelled off, and it has been fairly stable since. The rate of rise fell from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm, beginning some 4,000 years of near-stable sea level. In places the sea overshot today's level: off Santa Catarina, Brazil, it peaked about 2.1 m above present 5,800–5,000 BP. The last rising water drowned the last land bridges, such as the southern Kuril link to Hokkaido around 6,000 BP.

  <!-- nort-024 -->

- **The green Sahara dries into desert** — c. 6,000–5,000 years ago (4050 BCE–3050 BCE)

  Dust off Mauritania rose sharply within a few centuries. It was a sign that the African humid period, which had kept the Sahara green, was ending. The end came about 6,000–5,000 years ago, often put at 5,500 BP, and the green Sahara began turning into desert. North of the monsoon belt, drying came in one step within 500 years. Orbital shifts cut rainfall and raised temperatures, undoing the changes that had greened the desert in The Sahara turns green. Overgrazing has also been proposed as a trigger. Lakes dried and vegetation vanished. Dust from basins such as Bodélé, now Earth's largest dust source, grew. Shrinking wetlands lowered atmospheric methane. People suffered too. North Africa's population fell within a millennium, and many inner-Arabian settlements were abandoned about 5,300 years ago.

  <!-- nort-021 -->

  *Figure: How the green Sahara turned into desert.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Orbital shifts] --> B[Less rainfall]
  B --> C[Lakes dry, plants vanish]
  C --> D[More dust]
  C --> E[Less methane]
  ```

- **Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptions** — c. 5,950–4,950 years ago (4000 BCE–3000 BCE)

  Mount Pinatubo's famous 1991 eruption was not its largest. During its earlier Crow Valley eruptive period, it produced pyroclastic flows two to three times larger than those of 1991. That eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 12 km³ of material.

  <!-- nort-025 -->

- **The 5.9-kiloyear drought drives herders to the Nile** — 5,900 years ago (c. 3900 BCE)

  Around 3900 BCE, an aridification event, a sharp turn toward drier climate, struck the Sahara. Pastoral herders were forced to migrate into the Nile valley to survive. Farther east, in Hoti Cave in Arabia, the record shows the Indian monsoon retreating southward about 5,900 years ago. The event corresponds to Bond event 4, about 3900 BC, one of eight North Atlantic ice-rafting events. The Sahara's drying may have driven the spread of farming in the Sahel. The desert had re-formed by 3500–3000 BC.

  <!-- nort-026 -->

- **Mammoths outlast the mainland on St. Paul Island** — 5,700 years ago (c. 3750 BCE)

  A small woolly mammoth population survived on St. Paul Island, Alaska, until about 3750 BC, long after mainland mammoths vanished. People were not to blame: there is no evidence of prehistoric people on the island. Bone dates and environmental records tightly fix their end to around 5,600 years ago. The most likely cause is that fresh water ran short.

  <!-- nort-027 -->

- **The Piora Oscillation chills the Alps** — c. 5,600–5,000 years ago (3650 BCE–3050 BCE)

  Around 5,375 BP a sudden rise of Lake Constance, a sign of cooling, forced people to abandon the Arbon-Bleiche 3 lakeshore village. The Piora Oscillations were two cold periods in Alpine climate history, named after Switzerland's Val Piora. They coincided with the end of the African humid period. From 5,600 to 5,000 years ago, cooling and erratic rainfall were widespread. The Arctic cooled, sea ice spread and Atlantic overturning weakened.

  <!-- nort-028 -->

- **Ötzi the Iceman dies in the Alps** — 5,300 years ago (c. 3350 BCE)

  About 5,300 years ago a man was killed on the Tisenjoch pass, on today's Austrian–Italian border. Glacier ice at about 3,210 m preserved him as a natural mummy, now known as Ötzi, the oldest known human mummy. He carried both a copper axe and a flint knife. Einkorn and barley grains found beside him reflect the Neolithic farming that had spread into Europe.

  <!-- nort-029 -->

- **The Morasko craters near Poznań** — 5,000 years ago (c. 3050 BCE)

  Near today's Poznań, Poland, a meteorite fall made a field of seven craters about 5,000 years ago. The largest is about 100 m wide. It is one of several small Holocene crater fields in this course, alongside The Ilumetsa craters in Estonia and The Kaali craters form on Saaremaa.

  <!-- nort-031 -->

- **Mount Rainier collapses into the Osceola Mudflow** — 5,000 years ago (c. 3050 BCE)

  About 5,000 years ago, a huge part of Mount Rainier slid away, taking about 490 m off its summit. The debris avalanche fed the Osceola Mudflow, a torrent of mud and rock. It reached the sites of today's Tacoma and south Seattle.

  <!-- nort-032 -->

- **Burckle crater: a disputed impact** — 5,000 years ago (c. 3050 BCE)

  Beneath the southwest Indian Ocean lies a 29 km undersea feature. The Holocene Impact Working Group proposes that it is an impact crater about 5,000 years old. Its backers link it to floods that affected Sumerian civilization. Other geologists dispute that the Burckle feature is an impact crater at all.

  <!-- nort-033 -->

- **Iron falls on Campo del Cielo** — c. 5,000–4,000 years ago (3050 BCE–2050 BCE)

  Sometime between about 5,000 and 4,000 years ago, a shower of iron meteorites fell on the plains bordering Argentina's Chaco Province. That strewn field is called Campo del Cielo. It is one of several Holocene meteorite falls in this course, from The Morasko craters near Poznań to Iron rains on Sikhote-Alin.

  <!-- nort-030 -->

- **The Henbury crater field in central Australia** — 4,700 years ago (c. 2750 BCE)

  A fragmented meteorite blasted over a dozen craters in central Australia. The field is no older than about 4,700 years. It is one of the few impacts in a populated area and among the best-preserved small crater fields on Earth.

  <!-- nort-034 -->

- **Cerro Blanco: the Central Andes' largest eruption** — 4,300 years ago (c. 2300 BCE)

  Cerro Blanco in Argentina produced the largest known eruption of the Central Andes. The VEI 7 event formed its youngest caldera and thick ignimbrites. It released about 110 km³ of tephra, the fragments thrown out by an eruption, comparable to the largest Holocene eruptions. That tephra is now a regional time marker. Ground beneath the volcano is still subsiding, which may be a lasting effect of the eruption.

  <!-- nort-035 -->

###### Meghalayan Age

The youngest age of the Holocene begins with a drought: a severe one that began about 4,200 years ago and probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC. Around 4,000 years ago a major pan-tropical change dried East Africa, and the last dwarf woolly mammoths died on Wrangel Island. Great eruptions punctuate the age, from Vesuvius in the Avellino eruption to the catastrophic blast that devastated Thera. Island survivors, such as the Caribbean ground sloths, outlasted their mainland kin, while mainland thylacines vanished. The age runs on to the present day.

- **The 4.2-kiloyear drought topples empires** — 4,200 years ago (c. 2250 BCE)

  Nile floods failed, irrigated fields salted up, and kingdoms fell. A severe drought began about 4,200 years ago and, starting around 2200 BC, probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC. It ranks among the Holocene's harshest climate events. Intense aridity is recorded from North Africa and the Middle East to Arabia, India and midcontinental North America. The East Asian summer monsoon weakened sharply. Models link the drought to a major weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation. The tropical rain belt, the ITCZ, shifted abruptly south. The drought is thought to have helped topple Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and China's Liangzhu culture. A stalagmite in India's Mawmluh Cave marks it as the base of the Meghalayan, 4,250 years before 2000. That choice is debated. Critics argue the drought was neither global nor neatly timed, so it makes an awkward boundary.

  <!-- megh-001 -->

  *Figure: How an ocean change may have toppled ancient states.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Atlantic overturning weakens] --> B[Rain belt shifts south]
  B --> C[Severe drought]
  C --> D[Nile floods fail]
  D -.-> E[Old Kingdom falls]
  ```

- **The last mammoths die on Wrangel Island** — 4,000 years ago (c. 2050 BCE)

  The last mammoths anywhere lived on an Arctic island. A small population of dwarf woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island, in the Siberian Arctic, until about 4,000 years ago. They outlasted mainland mammoths, whose end is told in The last mainland woolly mammoths, by some 6,000 years. The latest Wrangel remains are dated to 1795–1675 BCE. Their extinction did not coincide with human arrival; the island had been a human-free refuge.

  <!-- megh-005 -->

- **The humid period ends across East and equatorial Africa** — c. 4,000–2,500 years ago (2050 BCE–550 BCE)

  In the Sahara, Lake Teli dried out completely about 4,200 years ago. Groundwater-fed Lake Yoa turned hypersaline, far saltier than the sea, by 4,000 years ago. A major pan-tropical environmental change took place around then, and drying in East Africa peaked. Blue Nile discharge fell noticeably. Its sediment load rose as vegetation thinned in the catchment from 4,000–3,600 years ago. The end came later nearer the equator, between 4,000 and 2,500 years ago, and West Africa had a long dry phase 3,500–1,700 years ago. South of the equator, at Lake Malawi, drying began only about 1,000 years ago.

  <!-- megh-004 -->

- **Mount St. Helens lays down its Yn tephra** — 3,800 years ago (c. 1860 BCE)

  Long before the blast described in Mount St. Helens erupts in 1980, Mount St. Helens had a far larger eruption. About 1860 BCE it laid down its Yn, or Smith Creek, tephra in a VEI 6 eruption of roughly 15 km³. That layer of ash is part of the volcano's long record of violent eruptions.

  <!-- megh-007 -->

- **The Avellino eruption buries a Bronze Age village** — 3,800 years ago (c. 1800 BCE)

  Near Nola, a hastily abandoned village and thousands of fleeing footprints lie buried under pumice and ash. Around 1800 BC, Vesuvius erupted in the VEI 6 Avellino eruption, one of at least three prehistoric eruptions much larger than that of AD 79. It destroyed several Bronze Age settlements. Pyroclastic surges travelled 15 km northwest of the vent, leaving deposits up to 3 m deep where Naples now stands.

  <!-- megh-008 -->

- **A weakening monsoon dries the Indus valley** — 3,800 years ago (c. 1800 BCE)

  Most cities of the Indus civilisation were abandoned by about 1700 BCE. Around 4,000 years ago the monsoon-fed Ghaggar-Hakra rivers became seasonal as that civilisation waned. From about 1800 BCE the Indus Valley grew markedly cooler and drier as the monsoon weakened. The Indian summer monsoon stayed weaker from 3,510 to 2,550 BP, apart from a strong interval 3,400–3,200 BP.

  <!-- megh-009 -->

- **Aniakchak and the frost of 1627 BC** — 3,600 years ago (c. 1630 BCE)

  Frost-damaged tree rings record extreme global cooling in 1627 BC. For years it was blamed on Thera. Then ash in the matching Greenland sulfate spike was matched to Alaska's Mount Aniakchak instead. Aniakchak erupted at VEI 6, ejecting about 50 km³ of material. A 2019 revised Greenland ice-core chronology dates it to 1628 BC.

  <!-- megh-010 -->

- **The Minoan eruption of Thera** — 3,600 years ago (c. 1600 BCE)

  Minoan Akrotiri was destroyed, and its ash became a marker layer at nearly every eastern Mediterranean site. A catastrophic Plinian eruption, a tall, sustained explosive column, devastated the Aegean island of Thera, or Santorini, around 1600 BC. It left the caldera that forms the island's central bay. Rated VEI 7, it ejected about 28–41 km³ dense-rock equivalent, one of the largest volcanic events in human history. With earthquakes and tsunamis it struck nearby islands and the coast of Crete. Chinese annals of yellow skies and summer frost may record its volcanic winter. Its exact date has been fiercely debated for decades. Radiocarbon favours the 17th–16th century BC, while archaeology points to about 1550–1480 BC.

  <!-- megh-011 -->

- **The Caribbean's last ground sloths** — 3,500 years ago (c. 1550 BCE)

  Mainland ground sloths had died out about 11,000 years ago, as North America loses its sloths, horses and short-faced bears tells. Their island relatives outlived them. Caribbean ground sloths, the group's last survivors, lived on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico possibly until 1550 BCE, much as Wrangel Island's mammoths outlasted theirs.

  <!-- megh-014 -->

- **Did the last litopterns live into the late Holocene?** — 3,500 years ago (c. 1550 BCE)

  Litopterns were an order of South American native hoofed mammals that arose 62.5 million years ago. They are usually thought to have vanished about 12,000 years ago. A 2025 study challenges that. It radiocarbon-dated a Xenorhinotherium specimen to 3,493–4,217 years ago, suggesting the order survived into the late Holocene. That claim rests on a single date, so it remains unconfirmed.

  <!-- megh-015 -->

- **The Kaali craters form on Saaremaa** — c. 3,480–3,400 years ago (1530 BCE–1450 BCE)

  A meteor of 20–80 tonnes broke up in the air over Saaremaa, Estonia, and blasted nine craters. The largest is 110 m across. The blast incinerated vegetation up to 6 km away, and it is one of the few impacts in a populated area. The latest estimates place it shortly after 1530–1450 BC, though published ages vary by up to 6,000 years.

  <!-- megh-016 -->

- **Thylacine and devil vanish from mainland Australia** — c. 3,230–3,180 years ago (1277 BCE–1229 BCE)

  The consensus is that thylacines died out on mainland Australia around 1277–1229 BCE. The latest mainland Tasmanian devil remains share that date. Competition with human hunters and dingoes is the likely cause, with a warming climate also proposed. Both animals survived only in Tasmania, long before European settlement. The thylacine's final end there is told in The last thylacine dies in Hobart.

  Irish tree rings show a decade of stunted growth after one Icelandic eruption. Hekla's H3 eruption, one of Iceland's largest of the Holocene, threw about 7.3 km³ of rock into the atmosphere, a VEI 5 event. Its traces reach Scottish peat bogs, and Hekla's big prehistoric eruptions left date-marker layers across northern Europe. It probably cooled the northern parts of the globe for a few years. Recalibrated with IntCal20, it dates to 1063 ± 140 BCE.

- **Pinatubo's Maraunot eruption** — 3,000 years ago (c. 1050 BCE)

  Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted at VEI 6 around 1050 BCE, during its Maraunot eruptive period. It ejected about 12.5 km³ of material. The volcano would erupt on that scale again in Pinatubo cools the world in 1991.

  <!-- megh-020 -->

- **The Homeric solar minimum** — c. 2,750–2,550 years ago (800 BCE–600 BCE)

  For about two centuries, the Sun went quiet. A deep, persistent grand solar minimum, the Homeric Minimum, lasted from about 800 to 600 BC. It is linked to the Homeric Climate Oscillation, or 2.8 kyr event, when western North America and Europe grew colder. Whether they also grew wetter or drier is debated. Germany's Meerfelder Maar records a lasting shift to colder, wetter, windier weather. The Göschenen I glacier advance in the Alps relates to it.

  <!-- megh-023 -->

- **The central Sahara becomes a lasting desert** — 2,700 years ago (c. 750 BCE)

  At Libya's Wadi Tanezzuft, rivers kept flowing long after the rains failed. Water stored in dunes and the Tassili mountains fed them until 2,700 years ago, when they finally stopped. By then the central Sahara had become a desert, and it has remained one ever since. Arabia's long drying trend, under way since 7,000–5,000 years ago, continued until 2,700 years ago. Brief humid spells still returned, as in Roman North Africa and around the Dead Sea between 500 BCE and 300 CE. At the Tanezzuft oasis, the drying trend after 1,600 years ago helped end the Garamantian civilisation.

- **Raoul Island blasts open the Denham caldera** — 2,200 years ago (c. 250 BCE)

  At one spot on Raoul Island, 40 m of pumice lies under 80 m of ignimbrite. About 2,200 years ago, a major dacitic explosion on the island, in the Kermadecs, formed the 6.5 by 4 km Denham caldera. Rated VEI 6 and about the size of Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, it left the Fleetwood tephra.

  <!-- megh-025 -->

- **The Roman Warm Period** — c. 2,200–1,550 years ago (250 BCE–400 CE)

  From about 250 BC to AD 400, unusually warm weather prevailed in Europe and the North Atlantic. This was the Roman Warm Period, or Roman Climatic Optimum. Alpine glaciers show AD 100–400 was markedly warmer than the centuries around it, and Iceland had a warm spell from 230 BC to AD 140. Yet a 2019 analysis of a much larger proxy dataset found it was a regional phenomenon, not a globally coherent episode.

  <!-- megh-026 -->

  The largest single source of dust on Earth today is a dried lakebed. Lake Chad shrank to about 5% of its former size. Its deep northern Bodélé basin, cut off from the Chari River, dried out completely about 2,000–1,000 years ago. Its dust is the lasting mark of The green Sahara dries into desert.

  <!-- megh-027 -->

- **Madagascar loses its giants after people arrive** — c. 2,000–900 years ago (50 BCE–1050 CE)

  At least 17 giant lemur species vanished from Madagascar, nearly all after people colonised the island about 2,000 years ago. Cut-marked bones show humans by 350 BCE, and Bornean Austronesians arrived by 500 CE. The largest animals vanished soon after. Others fell to prolonged hunting as settlers spread about 1,000 years ago, when areas now lemurless held 20 or more lemur species. Malagasy hippos and elephant birds are thought to have died out in 750–1050 AD. The youngest Aepyornis maximus remains date to 1040–1380 CE. Giant lemurs held on into modern times: Megaladapis to 630 ± 50 BP, Palaeopropithecus to 510 ± 80 BP. That makes this one of history's most recent megafaunal extinctions. The land changed too. Aridification began nearly 3,000 years ago, and human-set fires deforested the island.

- **Okmok and the cold of 43 BCE** — 2,000 years ago (c. 43 BCE)

  In 43 BCE, Alaska's Okmok volcano had its second Holocene caldera-forming eruption, rated VEI 6. It sent about 15–16 teragrams of sulfur into the stratosphere, cooling the Northern Hemisphere by 0.7–7.4 °C. With another eruption a year or two earlier, it made 43 BCE and the next two years among the coldest of the last 2,500 years. Cold, famine and failed Nile floods followed. This may have helped end Ptolemaic Egypt amid Rome's crisis, though a direct link is unproven.

  Every Plinian eruption is measured against one: the eruption that destroyed Pompeii. Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, a VEI 5 event of about 3.2 km³ that killed more than 2,000 people. Collapsing eruption columns sent pyroclastic currents over Herculaneum and Pompeii, and Oplontis and Stabiae were also destroyed. No later Vesuvius eruption was as large.

  Its pyroclastic flow was hot enough to burn forest 160 km from Lake Taupō. The Hatepe, Taupō Volcano's most recent major eruption, is dated to 232 CE ± 10, partly by wiggle-matching the rings of a tree it killed. It ejected roughly 100–120 km³ of material, 30 km³ of it within a few minutes, making it one of the largest eruptions of the last 5,000 years. No one saw it: it struck before people settled New Zealand. Afterwards Lake Taupō refilled and expanded, and temporary lakes formed in the Reporoa basin.

It ranks among the most intense eruptions of the Holocene, alongside Thera, Cerro Blanco and Tambora. Some evidence once made Ilopango the source of the 539/540 eruption of the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A newer study dates it to 431 instead.

- **The volcanic winter of 536** — c. 536 CE

  European summers fell up to 2.5 °C below normal. Tree rings show the sharpest cold in mid-July to early August 536 across North America and Eurasia. The extreme weather of 535–536 CE ranks among the notable climate events in Earth history. It is attributed to a large eruption of unknown source around 536, rated VEI 6–7. Its climate impact is compared with Tambora in 1815, Samalas in 1257 and the 1452/1453 mystery eruption. A violent eruption of Krakatoa in 535 was once proposed as the cause. Drilling in the Sunda Strait ruled out an eruption there that year.

- **The Late Antique Little Ice Age** — 536–660 CE

  Scandinavia may have lost up to half its population in a century of cold. That cooling of the Northern Hemisphere lasted from AD 536 to about 660, beginning with The volcanic winter of 536. It coincided with three large eruptions, in 535/536, 539/540 and 547, and one study suggests a global cooling of 2 °C. The second eruption cut European summer temperatures by up to 2.7 °C in 539–540. Sea-ice feedback and a deep solar minimum in the 600s prolonged the cold. It coincided with the Plague of Justinian, which began in 541. It strained the Eastern Roman and Sassanid empires and contributed to the migrations of the Lombards and early Slavs.

  Ash from one Alaskan volcano blankets north-western Canada. Mount Churchill erupted at VEI 6 around 847 CE, ejecting about 50 km³ and laying the eastern lobe of the White River Ash. An earlier VEI 6 eruption, about 145–345 CE, had laid the northern lobe.

- **The Millennium eruption of Paektu Mountain** — c. 946 CE

  Ashfall records from Nara suggest the eruption began about 2 November 946. Paektu, or Baekdu, Mountain on the China–North Korea border produced its VEI 6 Millennium eruption that year. It ranks with Thera, Hatepe, Samalas and Tambora among the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years. Its date is unusually exact. Tree rings counted from the 774–775 Miyake carbon spike, together with Greenland ice-core tephra, fix it to late 946.

  <!-- megh-039 -->

- **The Medieval Warm Period** — 950–1250 CE

  The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool stayed warm and saline from 1000 to 1400, with temperatures close to today's, then cooled. A warm spell, the Medieval Warm Period or Medieval Climate Anomaly, lasted from about 950 to 1250, just before the Little Ice Age. Reconstructions show warmth in the eleventh and early fifteenth centuries, though the twentieth century was warmer still. Evidence does not show globally synchronous warmth, so the term has limited use for hemispheric or global trends. The warmth may have sent extra fresh water into the North Atlantic, possibly disrupting ocean circulation ahead of The Little Ice Age.

  <!-- megh-040 -->

- **Samalas erupts and buries a city on Lombok** — 1257 CE

  Eruption columns rose 38–43 km over the Indonesian island of Lombok in 1257. Samalas erupted catastrophically, with a VEI of 7, one of the Holocene's largest eruptions. Pyroclastic flows buried much of Lombok, destroyed the city of Pamatan and left the 6–7 km Segara Anak caldera. Ice cores worldwide record a large sulfate spike. The aerosols caused a volcanic winter, cooling by about 0.7 °C in 1258 and 1.2 °C in 1259. Cold, wet weather brought floods, crop failures and famine in Europe and Japan in 1258–1259, though the scale of the anomalies is still debated. The eruption may have helped trigger the Little Ice Age.

  <!-- megh-042 -->

- **Quilotoa wakes after 14,000 years** — c. 1280 CE

  After 14,000 years of dormancy, Quilotoa in Ecuador produced its 1280 Plinian eruption, rated VEI 6. Its collapse left a 3 km caldera. Pyroclastic flows and lahars, volcanic mudflows, reached the Pacific, and ash spread across the northern Andes. With Samalas, it is linked to a cold, dry interval on the South American Altiplano between 1200 and 1450.

  <!-- megh-045 -->

- **The Little Ice Age** — 1300–1850 CE

  Mountain glaciers advanced in Europe, Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia, and Atlantic pack ice grew from about 1250. The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic, from about 1300 to about 1850. Despite its name, it was not a true global ice age. Across the Northern Hemisphere it was a modest cooling of under 1 °C relative to late twentieth-century levels. Its regional maxima came at different times. Onset was between 1200 and 1400 in the north and about two centuries later in the south. It ended in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Proposed causes include volcanism, low solar activity, ocean circulation changes and human depopulation. Climate models point to volcanism as the main driver, which ties it to eruptions such as Samalas erupts and buries a city on Lombok, The 1452/1453 mystery eruption and Huaynaputina, South America's largest witnessed eruption.

  ```mermaid
  B[Low solar activity] -.-> E
  C[Ocean circulation changes] -.-> E

  ```

  Chelonoidis alburyorum was the last West Indian giant tortoise. It vanished island by island. It lasted on the Abacos to 1170 CE, on Grand Turk to 1200 and on Middle Caicos to about 1400.

- **Moa hunted to extinction** — c. 1445 CE

  Ovens near the Waitaki River mouth alone held an estimated 29,000–90,000 moa. Moa were nine species of wingless birds up to about 3.6 m tall, New Zealand's largest land animals and dominant herbivores until the Māori arrived. Hunting, and to a lesser degree forest clearance, wiped them out, probably within 100 years of human settlement. Middens, ancient rubbish heaps, hold huge numbers of their bones. By 1445 all moa were gone. Haast's eagle, the giant raptor that had preyed on them, disappeared with them.

  <!-- megh-051 -->

- **The 1452/1453 mystery eruption** — c. 1452 CE

  Central Europe had seven cold summers in the 1450s. The cause was an undocumented eruption in 1452/1453, known mainly from its climate signal; it may have been at Kuwae in Vanuatu. One table rates it VEI 7. It triggered a second pulse of Little Ice Age cooling. With Samalas and Tambora, it was among the strongest cooling events of the last millennium.

  <!-- megh-052 -->

- **The Grindelwald Fluctuation** — 1560–1630 CE

  From the 1560s to the 1630s, glaciers at Grindelwald, Switzerland, expanded markedly, part of a worldwide glacial expansion. Temperatures ran 1–2 °C below twentieth-century averages, among the lowest of the Holocene. Eruptions of Colima (1585), Nevado del Ruiz (1595) and Huaynaputina (1600) likely contributed. Yet the cooling began about 15 years before the first of them.

  <!-- megh-056 -->

- **Huaynaputina, South America's largest witnessed eruption** — 1600 CE

  On 19 February 1600, Huaynaputina in southern Peru began the largest eruption ever witnessed in South America, rated VEI 6. It killed perhaps 1,000–1,500 people, buried the surrounding land under 2 m of volcanic rock and coated nearby El Misti in ash. Its sulfur cut sunlight by about 1.9 W/m². The summer of 1601 was among the Northern Hemisphere's coldest of the last six centuries. Frosts and harvest failures followed from Sweden to China and Japan, probably including Russia's famine of 1601–1603. With Samalas and the 1452/1453 eruption, it may have helped bring on the Little Ice Age's coldest phase.

  <!-- megh-057 -->

- **A carbon dioxide dip around 1610** — c. 1610 CE

  Conquest and disease killed as many as 90% of Indigenous Americans. Around 50 million hectares of their farmland may have returned to forest. Regrowth of tropical American forests from 1500 to 1650 may have stored 2–5 Pg of carbon. Atmospheric carbon dioxide fell around 1610, a drop that shows in ice at Law Dome, Antarctica. Those mass deaths may explain it, though Huaynaputina's eruption may have contributed. The link is debated: critics argue pre-Columbian farming did not clear forest on a modern scale, so regrowth should have had little effect. A 2015 report suggested 1610 as one possible start of the Anthropocene.

  <!-- megh-058 -->

- **The last wild aurochs dies in Poland** — 1627 CE

  The aurochs, the wild ancestor of most modern cattle, once ranged across Eurasia, North Africa and India. Only the European form survived into historical times. Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left one herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest. The last of them died there in 1627.

  <!-- megh-059 -->

- **The Maunder Minimum** — 1645–1715 CE

  From 1645 to 1715 the Sun was unusually quiet. Sunspots were minimal, and deposition of carbon-14 and beryllium-10 rose. This Maunder Minimum fell in the coldest part of the Little Ice Age; one of three especially cold intervals began about 1650. Yet the Sun was not the main cause. Northern Hemisphere cooling began before the minimum, and climate models make volcanism the larger driver.

  <!-- megh-060 -->

- **The dodo vanishes from Mauritius** — c. 1662 CE

  The dodo was a large, flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius. It was last seen in 1662 and may have vanished from the main island by the 1640s. Sailors ate many, but introduced pigs and other species likely did more harm. The dodo became an early poster species for human-caused extinction. Other Mascarene birds followed, including the Réunion rail, last recorded in 1674, the Rodrigues rail in 1726 and the Réunion ibis in 1763.

  <!-- megh-062 -->

- **The 1700 Cascadia earthquake and its orphan tsunami** — 1700 CE

  Around 9 pm on 26 January 1700, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake ruptured the 1,000 km Cascadia subduction zone off North America's Pacific coast. A subduction zone is where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. Coasts from British Columbia to Oregon dropped up to 2 m and were buried by tsunami sand, leaving drowned ghost forests. Drowned red cedars in Oregon and Washington have outermost rings from 1699, the last growing season before the earthquake. The tsunami crossed the Pacific and struck Honshu, Japan, about ten hours later. There it was recorded as an orphan tsunami, a wave with no felt earthquake. Oral traditions of several coastal peoples recall earthquakes and saltwater floods. It remains the zone's last megathrust earthquake.

  <!-- megh-063 -->

- **Methane climbs 2.6-fold** — 1750–2025 CE

  Methane makes up just 3% of greenhouse emissions by mass, but about 23% of climate forcing. Since about 1750, atmospheric methane rose from 722 ppb to 1,936 ppb by 2025. That 2.6-fold increase is the highest level in at least 800,000 years, and human activities caused almost all of it. After a decade of near-zero growth, methane began climbing again in 2007, with sharp rises in 2015–2019 and a record annual jump in 2021. Isotopes suggest recent growth comes mainly from microbial sources such as wetlands and agriculture rather than fossil fuels. From 2010 to 2019, methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

  <!-- megh-065 -->

  *Figure: Atmospheric methane before industry and in 2025.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The Great Lisbon earthquake** — 1755 CE

  On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, killing around 100,000 people. It was one of the most destructive earthquakes in history. It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s.

  <!-- megh-066 -->

- **Steller's sea cow: gone in 27 years** — c. 1768 CE

  Steller's sea cow was the largest known sirenian, a plant-eating sea mammal, at up to 10 m and 5–10 tonnes. It survived as a relict in the Bering Sea's Commander Islands. Discovered in 1741, it was hunted for meat and hides until it was gone by 1768, just 27 years later.

  <!-- megh-067 -->

- **The Industrial Revolution starts the greenhouse rise** — c. 1780 CE

  For 10,000 years before the mid-18th century, carbon dioxide stayed near 280 ppm. It has since risen 54%. The turn came with the Industrial Revolution, around 1780 and the steam engine, when large-scale greenhouse gas emissions began to warm Earth. Antarctic ice cores record the highest greenhouse gas levels from the Industrial Revolution on. The IPCC takes 1750 as its pre-industrial baseline. Warm decades became more common. Recorded extinctions mounted too: over 322 species are often cited as lost to humans since then, a toll followed in Extinctions soar above the background rate. The Industrial Revolution is one proposed start of the Anthropocene, though humans had already reshaped much of Earth's landscape. Its gases set up the changes of Rapid global warming since the mid-20th century and The Keeling Curve climbs at Mauna Loa.

  <!-- megh-068 -->

- **The Laki fissure poisons Iceland** — 1783–1784 CE

  About a fifth of Iceland's people died after the Laki eruption. From June 1783 to February 1784, the 40 km Laki fissure poured out about 15 km³ of lava. It was one of history's largest effusive eruptions, those that pour out lava rather than explode. Its lava fields cover 565 km² of southeast Iceland. Fluorine and chlorine poisoning devastated farming. The eruption released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide. In Northern Hemisphere ice cores its sulfate signal exceeds even that of Samalas, and the sulfur caused substantial cooling. Famine cost Egypt a sixth of its people in 1784, and hardship in Europe may have fed the French Revolution.

  <!-- megh-069 -->

- **Tambora, the most powerful eruption on record** — 1815 CE

  On 10 April 1815, an eruption column rose 45 km over the Indonesian island of Sumbawa. Tambora was at its climax. Its eruption that April was the most powerful in recorded history, a VEI 7 that ejected 37–45 km³ of material. It is also the most recent confirmed VEI-7 eruption. About 10,000–11,000 people died directly. Another 49,000–90,000 died from famine and disease on Sumbawa, Lombok and Bali. The eruption's reach went far beyond the islands. Its sulfur dioxide formed a stratospheric sulfate veil, a haze of fine droplets high above the weather. In 1815 people saw it as a persistent dry fog that dimmed the Sun. That veil brought the global chill described in 1816, the Year Without a Summer.

  <!-- megh-071 -->

- **1816, the Year Without a Summer** — 1816 CE

  Frost and snow struck New England and Quebec in June 1816, ruining most North American crops. Tambora's aerosols had lowered global temperatures by about 0.4–0.7 °C, and 1816 became the Year Without a Summer across the Northern Hemisphere. Harvests failed across Europe in the worst famine of the nineteenth century. India's monsoon failed, and a new cholera strain spread from Bengal. 1816 was the Northern Hemisphere's second-coldest year since about 1400. The 1810s were the coldest decade on record, aided by an eruption around 1809. The cold also fell during the Dalton Minimum, a period of unusually low solar radiation.

  <!-- megh-072 -->
